PREFACE
序言

There is not much to say about these stories. The first four are the last ones I have written. The others follow in the order in which they were originally published.
这些短篇没什么好说的。前四篇是我写的最新的。其余的按最初发表的顺序排列。
The first one I wrote was ‘Up in Michigan’, written in Paris in 1921. The last was ‘Old Man at the Bridge’, cabled from Barcelona in April of 1938.
我写的第一篇是《密歇根上岸》，1921 年在巴黎写成。最后一篇是《桥上的老人》，1938 年 4 月从巴塞罗那发电报时写成。
I wrote ‘The Killers’, ‘To-day Is Friday’, ‘Ten Indians’, part of ‘Fiesta’, and the first third of ‘To Have and Have Not’ in Madrid. It was always a good place for working. So was Paris, and so were Key West, Florida, in the cool months; the ranch, near Cooke City, Montana; Kansas City; Chicago; Toronto, and Havana, Cuba.
我在马德里写了《杀手们》、《今天是星期五》、《十个印第安人》、《节日》的部分内容，以及《有与无》的前三分之一。那里一直是个适合工作的地方。巴黎也是，佛罗里达州基韦斯特在凉爽的月份也是；还有牧场，靠近蒙大拿州库克市；堪萨斯城；芝加哥；多伦多；以及古巴哈瓦那。
Some other places were not so good, but maybe we were not so good when we were in them.
有些地方并不那么好，但也许是我们在那些地方时自身并不那么好。
There are many kinds of stories in this book. I hope that you will find some that you like. Reading them over, the ones I liked the best, outside of those that have achieved some notoriety so that school teachers include them in story collections that their pupils have to buy in story courses, and you are always faintly embarrassed to read them and wonder whether you really wrote them or did you maybe hear them, somewhere, are ‘The Short Happy Life of Francis Macomber’, ‘In Another Country’, ‘Hills Like White Elephants’, ‘A Way You’ll Never Be’, ‘The Snows of Kilimanjaro,’ ‘A Clean, Well-Lighted Place’, and a story called ‘The Light of the World’, which nobody else ever liked. There are some others too. Because if you did not like them you would not publish them.
这本书里有许多不同类型的故事。希望你能找到一些你喜欢的。重读这些故事时，我最喜欢的那些，除去那些因为臭名远扬而被学校教师收入故事选集、他们的小学生在叙事课程中不得不购买的那些——读起来你总会有点尴尬，怀疑这些究竟是你写的还是你可能在某处听来的——包括《弗朗西斯·麦科姆的短暂快乐人生》（The Short Happy Life of Francis Macomber）、《在另一个国家》（In Another Country）、《像白象的山》（Hills Like White Elephants）、《你将永远不会成为的样子》（A Way You’ll Never Be）、《乞力马扎罗的雪》（The Snows of Kilimanjaro）、《一个明净良好的地方》（A Clean, Well-Lighted Place），以及一篇名为《世界之光》（The Light of the World）的故事，别的人从来没有喜欢过。还有其他一些。因为如果你不喜欢它们，你就不会把它们出版。
In going where you have to go, and doing what you have to do, and seeing what you have to see, you dull and blunt the instrument you write with. But I would rather have it bent and dulled and know I had to put it on the grindstone again and hammer it into shape and put a whetstone to it, and know that I had something to write about, than to have it bright and shining and nothing to say, or smooth and well oiled in the closet, but unused.
去你必须去的地方，做你必须做的事，去看你必须看的东西时，你用来写作的工具会被磨钝削钝。但我宁可它被弯折、被磨钝，并且知道我得再把它放到磨石上，用锤子把它敲成形，再拿油石磨一磨，知道我有东西可写，也不愿它光亮闪闪却无话可说，或者抛光上油后躺在橱柜里不用。
Now it is necessary to get to the grindstone again. I would like to live long enough to write three more novels and twenty-five more stories. I know some pretty good ones.
现在又必须回到磨石前。我希望能活得足够长，再写三部长篇小说和二十五个短篇故事。我心里已有一些相当不错的故事。

Ernest Hemingway
欧内斯特·海明威

THE FIRST FORTY-NINE STORIES
《前四十九篇短篇小说》

THE SHORT HAPPY LIFE OF FRANCIS MACOMBER
弗朗西斯·麦科姆伯的短暂而幸福的一生

It was now lunch time and they were all sitting under the double green fly of the dining tent pretending that nothing had happened.
现在是午饭时间，他们都坐在餐帐篷的双层绿色防雨布下，假装什么也没发生。
‘Will you have lime juice or lemon squash?’ Macomber asked.
“你要青柠汁还是柠檬爽饮？”麦科姆伯问道。
‘I’ll have a gimlet,’ Robert Wilson told him.
“我要一杯吉姆莱特，”罗伯特·威尔逊告诉他。
‘I’ll have a gimlet too. I need something,’ Macomber’s wife said.
“我也要一杯金格利。我需要点什么，”马康伯的妻子说道。
‘I suppose it’s the thing to do,’ Macomber agreed. ‘Tell him to make three gimlets.’
“我想这就是该做的，”马康伯同意道。“叫他做三杯金格利。”
The mess boy had started them already, lifting the bottles out of the canvas cooling bags that sweated wet in the wind that blew through the trees that shaded the tents.
伙食男孩已经开始动手了，把瓶子从帆布冷却袋里拿出来，那些袋子在吹过帐篷树荫的风里淌着汗珠。
‘What had I ought to give them?’ Macomber asked.
“我应该给他们多少？”马康伯问道。
‘A quid would be plenty,’ Wilson told him. ‘You don’t want to spoil them.’
“一个英镑就够了，”威尔逊对他说。“你可别把他们宠坏了。”
‘Will the headman distribute it?’
“头目会分发吗？”
‘Absolutely.’
“绝对会的。”
Francis Macomber had, half an hour before, been carried to his tent from the edge of the camp in triumph on the arms and shoulders of the cook, the personal boys, the skinner and the porters. The gun-bearers had taken no part in the demonstration. When the native boys put him down at the door of his tent, he had shaken all their hands, received their congratulations, and then gone into the tent and sat on the bed until his wife came in. She did not speak to him when she came in and he left the tent at once to wash his face and hands in the portable wash basin outside and go over to the dining tent to sit in a comfortable canvas chair in the breeze and the shade.
半小时前，弗朗西斯·麦康伯被厨师、贴身伙计、剥皮工和搬运工们架在胳膊和肩膀上，从营地边缘凯旋般抬回他的帐篷。抬枪的并未参与这一庆祝。当本地伙计们把他放到帐篷门口时，他挨个握了他们的手，接受了祝贺，然后走进帐篷，坐在床上等他妻子进来。她进来时没有和他说话，他便立刻出去在外面的便携洗脸盆洗了脸和手，然后走到饭帐里，坐在一把舒适的帆布椅上，享受微风和荫凉。
Mrs. Macomber looked at Wilson quickly. She was an extremely handsome and well-kept woman of the beauty and social position which had, five years before, commanded five thousand dollars as the price of endorsing, with photographs, a beauty product which she had never used. She had been married to Francis Macomber for eleven years.
麦康伯太太迅速看了威尔逊一眼。她是一个极为漂亮、打理得很好的妇人，五年前凭着容貌和社会地位，用带有照片的代言为一种她从未使用过的美容产品背书，索价五千美元。她和弗朗西斯·麦康伯结婚已有十一年。
‘He is a good lion, isn’t he?’ Macomber said. His wife looked at him now. She looked at both these men as though she had never seen them before.
“他是一头好狮子，不是吗？”麦康伯说。他的妻子现在看着他。她看着这两个人，仿佛从未见过他们。
One, Wilson, the white hunter, she knew she had never truly seen before. He was about middle height with sandy hair, a stubby moustache, a very red face and extremely cold blue eyes with faint white wrinkles at the corners that grooved merrily when he smiled. He smiled at her now and she looked away from his face at the way his shoulders sloped in the loose tunic he wore with the four big cartridges held in loops where the left breast pocket should have been, at his big brown hands, his old slacks, his very dirty boots, and back to his red face again. She noticed where the baked red of his face stopped in a white line that marked the circle left by his Stetson hat that hung now from one of the pegs of the tent pole.
一、威尔逊，那个白猎人，她知道自己从未真正见过。他个子中等，砂色头发，短短的八字胡，脸非常红，眼睛极冷的蓝色，眼角有细细的白色皱纹，笑起来时那皱纹欢快地绉起。他现在对她笑，她把视线从他的脸移开，看他穿着宽松短上衣时肩膀的下垂，左胸口本应有的口袋处挂着四颗大弹药筒环扣，他那双又大又棕的手，旧长裤，极脏的靴子，又回到他那张红脸上。她注意到他脸上烤得红的部分在一条白线处停止，那白线标出他那顶 Stetson 帽子曾留下的圆圈，帽子现在挂在帐篷杆的一个钉子上。
‘Well, here’s to the lion,’ Robert Wilson said. He smiled at her again and, not smiling, she looked curiously at her husband.
“好吧，为狮子干杯，”Robert Wilson 说。他又冲她笑，她没有笑，满怀好奇地看着丈夫。
Francis Macomber was very tall, very well built if you did not mind that length of bone, dark, his hair cropped like an oarsman, rather thin-lipped, and was considered handsome. He was dressed in the same sort of safari clothes that Wilson wore except that his were new, he was thirty-five years old, kept himself very fit, was good at court games, had a number of big-game fishing records, and had just shown himself, very publicly, to be a coward.
弗朗西斯·麦康伯个子很高，身材健硕，若不介意骨架偏长，肤色偏黑，头发剪得像赛艇手那样短，嘴唇较薄，被认为长得英俊。他穿着与 Wilson 相同款式的狩猎服，只是他的衣服是新的，年三十五，自我保养得很好，擅长球类运动，有几项大鱼捕获记录，而且刚刚当众证明了自己是个懦夫。
‘Here’s to the lion,’ he said. ‘I can’t ever thank you for what you did.’
“为那头狮子干杯，”他说。“我永远也无法感谢你所做的一切。”
Margaret, his wife, looked away from him and back to Wilson.
他的妻子玛格丽特把视线从他身上移开，回望向 Wilson。
‘Let’s not talk about the lion,’ she said.
“别再谈那头狮子了，”她说。
Wilson looked over at her without smiling and now she smiled at him.
威尔逊看着她，面无表情，她这才朝他笑了笑。
‘It’s been a very strange day,’ she said. ‘Hadn’t you ought to put your hat on even under the canvas at noon? You told me that, you know.’
“今天真是很奇怪的一天，”她说。“你中午在帐篷下面也应该戴上帽子，不是吗？你可是告诉过我这点的。”
‘Might put it on,’ said Wilson.
“可以戴上，”威尔逊说。
‘You know you have a very red face, Mr. Wilson,’ she told him and smiled again.
“威尔逊先生，你的脸很红，”她对他说，又笑了起来。
‘Drink,’ said Wilson.
“喝点吧，”Wilson 说。
‘I don’t think so,’ she said. ‘Francis drinks a great deal, but his face is never red.’
“我可不认为，”她说。“Francis 喝很多酒，但他的脸从不红。”
‘It’s red to-day,’ Macomber tried a joke.
“今天倒红了，”Macomber 试着开玩笑。
‘No,’ said Margaret. ‘It’s mine that’s red to-day. But Mr. Wilson’s is always red.’
“不，”Margaret 说。“今天红的是我的。但 Mr. Wilson 的脸总是红的。”
‘Must be racial,’ said Wilson. ‘I say, you wouldn’t like to drop my beauty as a topic, would you?’
“肯定是种族问题，”威尔逊说。“我说，你不会想把我的美貌当作话题吧，对吧？”
‘I’ve just started on it.’
“我才刚开始说呢。”
‘Let’s chuck it,’ said Wilson.
“别聊了，”威尔逊说。
‘Conversation is going to be so difficult,’ Margaret said.
“交谈会变得很困难的，”玛格丽特说。
‘Don’t be silly, Margot,’ her husband said.
“别傻了，玛戈特，”她丈夫说。
‘No difficulty,’ Wilson said. ‘Got a damn fine lion.’
“没什么难的，”威尔逊说。“那狮子真他妈的好。”
Margot looked at them both and they both saw that she was going to cry. Wilson had seen it coming for a long time and he dreaded it. Macomber was past dreading it.
玛戈特看着他们两人，他们都看出她要哭了。威尔逊早已预感到这一幕，他很害怕。麦科姆已经不再害怕了。
‘I wish it hadn’t happened. Oh, I wish it hadn’t happened,’ she said and started for her tent. She made no noise of crying but they could see that her shoulders were shaking under the rose-coloured, sun-proofed shirt she wore.
“我真希望没发生。哦，我真希望没发生，”她说着朝帐篷走去。她没有出声哭，但他们可以看出她那件玫瑰色防晒衬衫下的肩膀在颤抖。
‘Women upset,’ said Wilson to the tall man. ‘Amounts to nothing. Strain on the nerves and one thing’n another.’
“女人心烦，”威尔逊对那位高个子说。“无足轻重。神经紧张，或这或那的事儿。”
‘No,’ said Macomber. ‘I suppose that I rate that for the rest of my life now.’
“不，”麦康伯说。“我想从今以后这一点会一直印在我心上了。”
‘Nonsense. Let’s have a spot of the giant killer,’ said Wilson. ‘Forget the whole thing. Nothing to it anyway.’
“胡说。来点猛兽活儿吧，”威尔逊说。“忘掉这一切。根本没什么大不了的。”
‘We might try,’ said Macomber. ‘I won’t forget what you did for me though.’
“我们可以试试，”麦康伯说。“不过我不会忘记你为我所做的。”
‘Nothing,’ said Wilson. ‘All nonsense.’
“没什么，”威尔逊说。“都是胡扯。”
So they sat there in the shade where the camp was pitched under some wide-topped acacia trees with a boulder-strewn cliff behind them, and a stretch of grass that ran to the bank of a boulder-filled stream in front with forest beyond it, and drank their just-cool lime drinks and avoided one another’s eyes while the boys set the table for lunch. Wilson could tell that the boys all knew about it now and when he saw Macomber’s personal boy looking curiously at his master while he was putting dishes on the table he snapped at him in Swahili. The boy turned away with his face blank.
于是他们就坐在营地下的树荫里，营地搭在几棵冠幅宽大的金合欢树下，身后是布满巨石的峭壁，前面是一片草地，延伸到布满巨石的小溪岸边，外面是森林。他们喝着刚刚放凉的青柠饮料，互不相视，仆人们则摆桌准备午餐。威尔逊能够看出这些仆人现在都知道了这件事；当他看到麦康伯的贴身仆人在把碟子放到桌上时好奇地看着主人，威尔逊就用斯瓦西里语冲他厉声喝斥。那仆人脸上没有表情地转过头去。
‘What were you telling him?’ Macomber asked.
“你跟他说什么了？”麦康伯问。
‘Nothing. Told him to look alive or I’d see he got about fifteen of the best.’
“没说什么。叫他快点，不然我会让他挨上十来下好的。”
‘What’s that? Lashes?’
“那是什么？鞭打吗？”
‘It’s quite legal,’ Wilson said. ‘You’re supposed to fine them.’
“这是合法的，”Wilson 说。“你应该罚款他们。”
‘Do you still have them whipped?’
“你们还会把他们鞭打吗？”
‘Oh, yes. They could raise a row if they chose to complain. But they don’t. They prefer it to the fines.’
“哦，会的。如果他们选择抱怨，可能会闹事。但他们不会。他们更喜欢鞭打而不是罚款。”
‘How strange!’ said Macomber.
“多奇怪！”麦康伯说道。
‘Not strange, really,’ Wilson said. ‘Which would you rather do? Take a good birching or lose your pay?’
“不算奇怪，”威尔逊说。“你宁愿挨一顿好揍，还是丢了工资？”
Then he felt embarrassed at asking it and before Macomber could answer he went on, ‘We all take a beating every day, you know, one way or another.’
然后他为自己问这个问题感到尴尬，麦康伯还没回答，他又接着说：“你知道，我们每天都要挨打，不管用什么方式。”
This was no better. ‘Good God,’ he thought. ‘I am a diplomat, aren’t I?’
这并不好。他想：“我的天哪，我不是个外交官吗？”
‘Yes, we take a beating,’ said Macomber, still not looking at him. ‘I’m awfully sorry about that lion business. It doesn’t have to go any further, does it? I mean no one will hear about it, will they?’
“是的，我们挨了打，”麦康伯说，仍然没有看他。“关于那件狮子事我真很抱歉。这事不必再闹下去，对吧？我的意思是不会有人听说的，是吗？”
‘You mean will I tell it at the Mathaiga Club?’ Wilson looked at him now coldly. He had not expected this. So he’s a bloody fourletter man as well as a bloody coward, he thought. I rather liked him too until to-day. But how is one to know about an American?
“你的意思是我会在 Mathaiga 俱乐部把这事告诉人？”威尔逊现在冷冷地看着他。他没预料到这一点。原来他既是个可恶的伪君子，又是个可恶的懦夫，他想。我以前还挺喜欢他的，直到今天。但怎么能摸透一个美国人呢？
‘No,’ said Wilson. ‘I’m a professional hunter. We never talk about our clients. You can be quite easy on that. It’s supposed to be bad form to ask us not to talk though.’
“不，”威尔逊说。“我是个职业猎人。我们从不谈论客户。你可以放心。这倒是礼数上不该强求我们别说。”
He had decided now that to break would be much easier. He would eat, then, by himself and could read a book with his meals. They would eat by themselves. He would see them through the safari on a very formal basis - what was it the French called it? Distinguished consideration - and it would be a damn sight easier than having to go through this emotional trash. He’d insult him and make a good clean break. Then he could read a book with his meals and he’d still be drinking their whisky. That was the phrase for it when a safari went bad. You ran into another white hunter and you asked, ‘How is everything going?’ and he answered, ‘Oh, I’m still drinking their whisky,’ and you knew everything had gone to pot.
他现在决定分手会容易得多。他会自己吃饭，然后可以一边吃一边看书。他们会各自用餐。他会以一种非常正式的方式陪他们完成狩猎旅行——法国人怎么称的来着？高雅的体面——这总比要经历这些情绪垃圾容易多了。他会侮辱他，然后干净利落地断绝关系。那样他就可以一边吃饭一边看书，而且仍然会喝他们的威士忌。这就是狩猎队走散时的说法。你碰到另一个白猎人，问：“一切进展如何？”他回答：“哦，我还在喝他们的威士忌，”你就知道一切都完了。
‘I’m sorry,’ Macomber said and looked at him with his American face that would stay adolescent until it became middle-aged, and Wilson noted his crew-cropped hair, fine eyes only faintly shifty, good nose, thin lips and handsome jaw. ‘I’m sorry I didn’t realize that. There are lots of things I don’t know.’
“对不起，”麦康伯说着，用那张带着美国气息的脸看着他，那张脸会一直保持着少年感直到变成中年，威尔逊注意到他那剪得很短的头发，漂亮的眼睛只是略显飘忽，端正的鼻子，薄唇和英俊的下颌。“对不起，我没意识到这一点。我有很多事情不懂。”
So what could he do, Wilson thought. He was all ready to break
那么他能做什么呢，威尔逊想。他已经准备好要断绝关系了
it off quickly and neatly and here the beggar was apologizing after he had just insulted him. He made one more attempt. ‘Don’t worry about me talking,’ he said. ‘I have a living to make. You know in Africa no woman ever misses her lion and no white man ever bolts.’
他干脆利落地做完了，那个乞丐在刚刚侮辱了他之后还在道歉。他又试了一次。“别担心我会说太多，”他说。“我得谋生。你知道在非洲，没有女人会错过她的狮子，也没有白人会逃跑。”
‘I bolted like a rabbit,’ Macomber said.
“我像兔子一样逃跑了，”麦康伯说。
Now what in hell were you going to do about a man who talked like that, Wilson wondered.
现在该对一个那样说话的人怎么办，威尔逊心想。
Wilson looked at Macomber with his flat, blue, machine-gunner’s eyes and the other smiled back at him. He had a pleasant smile if you did not notice how his eyes showed when he was hurt.
威尔逊用他那扁平的、蓝色的、机枪手般的眼睛看着麦康伯，而另一个人对他回以微笑。他的笑容令人愉快，除非你注意到他受伤时眼中的神色。
‘Maybe I can fix it up on buffalo,’ he said. ‘We’re after them next, aren’t we?’
“也许我能在水牛身上弥补，”他说。“我们接下来不是要打它们吗？”
‘In the morning if you like,’ Wilson told him. Perhaps he had been wrong. This was certainly the way to take it. You most certainly could not tell a damned thing about an American. He was all for Macomber again. If you could forget the morning. But, of course, you couldn’t. The morning had been about as bad as they come.
“早上可以，如果你愿意，”威尔逊对他说。也许他之前判断错了。这无疑是该有的态度。你根本无法看出一个美国人的真面目。他又完全站在马康伯那边了。如果你能忘掉早上的事。但当然，你忘不了。那早晨糟透了。
‘Here comes the Memsahib,’ he said. She was walking over from her tent looking refreshed and cheerful and quite lovely. She had a very perfect oval face, so perfect that you expected her to be stupid. But she wasn’t stupid, Wilson thought, no, not stupid.
“夫人来了，”他说。她正从帐篷那边走来，看上去神采奕奕、心情愉快，而且相当美丽。她有一张极为完美的椭圆脸，完美到让人以为她会愚蠢。但威尔逊想，她并不愚蠢，不，绝不愚蠢。
‘How is the beautiful red-faced Mr. Wilson? Are you feeling better, Francis, my pearl?’
“红脸帅气的威尔逊先生怎么样？感觉好些了吗，弗朗西斯，我的珍珠？”
‘Oh, much,’ said Macomber.
“哦，很多，”马康伯说。
‘I’ve dropped the whole thing,’ she said, sitting down at the table. ‘What importance is there to whether Francis is any good at killing lions? That’s not his trade. That’s Mr. Wilson’s trade. Mr. Wilson is really very impressive killing anything. You do kill anything, don’t you?’
“我已经把整件事抛到一边了，”她一边坐到桌旁一边说。“弗朗西斯会不会杀狮子有什么重要性？那不是他的行当。那是威尔逊先生的行当。威尔逊先生杀起东西来真让人印象深刻。你什么都能杀，是吧？”
‘Oh, anything,’ said Wilson. ‘Simply anything.’ They are, he thought, the hardest in the world; the hardest, the cruellest, the most predatory and the most attractive and their men have softened or gone to pieces nervously as they have hardened. Or is it that they pick men they can handle? They can’t know that much at the age they marry, he thought. He was grateful that he had gone through his education on American women before now because this was a very attractive one.
“哦，什么都行，”威尔逊说。“简直什么都行。”他们是，他想，他们是世上最顽固的；最残忍的、最掠夺性的、也是最有魅力的，而她们的男人在她们变得强硬的同时变得柔弱或精神崩溃。还是说她们挑选的是能被她们控制的男人？他想，他们在结婚时不可能知道那么多。他庆幸自己在此之前已经经历过对美国女性的“教育”，因为她真是个很有魅力的女人。
‘We’re going after buff in the morning,’ he told her.
“明早我们去打水牛，”他告诉她。
‘I’m coming,’ she said.
“我来了，”她说。
‘No you’re not.’
“不，你不来。”
‘Oh, yes, I am. Mayn’t I, Francis?’
“哦，我要去。我不能去吗，弗朗西斯？”
‘Why not stay in camp?’
“为什么不呆在营地？”
‘Not for anything,’ she said. ‘I wouldn’t miss something like to-day for anything.’
“绝不是因为什么，”她说。“我才不会为了像今天这样的事错过呢。”
When she left, Wilson was thinking, when she went off to cry she seemed a hell of a fine woman. She seemed to understand, to realize, to be hurt for him and for herself and to know how things really stood. She is away for twenty minutes and now she is back, simply enamelled in that American female cruelty. They are the damnedest women. Really the damnedest.
她走后，威尔逊在想，当她去哭的时候，她看起来真像个了不起的女人。她似乎明白，似乎觉察到，既为他又为自己感到受伤，也知道事情的真实状况。她走了二十分钟，现在又回来了，完全显露出那种美国女人的残酷。她们真是该死的女人。真是该死的。
‘We’ll put on another show for you to-morrow,’ Francis Macomber said.
“我们明天再给你表演一次，”弗朗西斯·麦康伯说。
‘You’re not coming,’ Wilson said.
“你不来，”威尔逊说。
‘You’re very mistaken,’ she told him. ‘And I want so to see you perform again. You were lovely this morning. That is if blowing things’ heads off is lovely.’
“你大错特错了，”她对他说。“而且我多想再看看你表演。你今天早上真迷人。要是把人脑袋炸飞也能算迷人的话。”
‘Here’s the lunch,’ said Wilson. ‘You’re very merry, aren’t you?’
“午饭来了，”威尔逊说。“你很高兴，是不是？”
‘Why not? I didn’t come out here to be dull.’
“为什么不？我可不是来这儿无聊的。”
‘Well, it hasn’t been dull,’ Wilson said. He could see the boulders in the river and the high bank beyond with the trees and he remembered the morning.
“嗯，确实不无聊，”威尔逊说。他看见河里的巨石和对岸高高的河堤以及那边的树木，想起了早上的情景。
‘Oh, no,’ she said. ‘It’s been charming. And to-morrow. You don’t know how I look forward to to-morrow.’
“噢，不，”她说。“这一直很愉快。还有明天。我有多么盼望明天，你是不会知道的。”
‘That’s eland he’s offering you,’ Wilson said.
“他给你的是大羚羊（eland），”威尔逊说。
‘They’re the big cowy things that jump like hares, aren’t they?’
“它们是那种像野兔一样跳的又大又像牛的动物，对吧？”
‘I suppose that describes them,’ Wilson said.
“我想这样描述也行，”威尔逊说。
‘It’s very good meat,’ Macomber said.
“这是很好的肉，”麦康伯说。
‘Did you shoot it, Francis?’ she asked.
“这是你射的吗，弗朗西斯？”她问道。
‘Yes.’
“是的。”
‘They’re not dangerous, are they?’
“它们不危险，对吗？”
‘Only if they fall on you,’ Wilson told her.
“只要它们朝你倒下就行，”威尔逊对她说。
‘I’m so glad.’
“我太高兴了。”
‘Why not let up on the bitchery just a little, Margot,’ Macomber said, cutting the eland steak and putting some mashed potato, gravy and carrot on the down-turned fork that tined through the piece of meat.
“玛戈，别那么刻薄了，好好收敛一点行不行，”麦考伯一边切着角鹿肉，一边把一些土豆泥、肉汁和胡萝卜放在向下的叉子上，叉齿叉在那块肉上。
‘I suppose I could,’ she said, ‘since you put it so prettily.’
“我想我可以的，”她说，“既然你这么好听地说出来了。”
‘To-night we’ll have champagne for the lion,’ Wilson said. ‘It’s a bit too hot at noon.’
“今晚我们要为那只狮子喝香槟，”Wilson 说。“中午太热了，不合适。”
‘Oh, the lion,’ Margot said. ‘I’d forgotten the lion!’
“哦，狮子，”Margot 说。“我都忘了狮子了！”
So, Robert Wilson thought to himself, she is giving him a ride, isn’t she? Or do you suppose that’s her idea of putting up a good show? How should a woman act when she discovers her husband is a bloody coward? She’s damn cruel, but they’re all cruel. They govern, of course, and to govern one has to be cruel sometimes. Still, I’ve seen enough of their damn terrorism.
于是，Robert Wilson 心想，她是在给他撑场面，是不是？还是你以为那是她认为的体面表演？当一个女人发现她的丈夫是个彻头彻尾的懦夫时，她该怎么做？她确实狠毒，但她们都是狠毒的。她们要统治，当然，要统治有时就得残忍。不过，我已经见识够了她们该死的恐怖统治。
‘Have some more eland,’ he said to her politely.
“再吃点大羚羊肉吧，”他礼貌地对她说。
That afternoon, late, Wilson and Macomber went out in the motor car with the native driver and the two gun-bearers. Mrs. Macomber stayed in the camp. It was too hot to go out, she said, and she was going with them in the early morning. As they drove off Wilson saw her standing under the big tree looking pretty rather than beautiful in her faintly rosy khaki, her dark hair drawn back off her forehead and gathered in a knot low on her neck, her face as fresh, he thought, as though she were in England. She waved to them as the car went off through the swale of high grass and curved around through the trees into the small hills of orchard bush.
那天下午，天色已晚，Wilson 和 Macomber 与当地司机和两个持枪人一起开着汽车出发。Mrs. Macomber 留在营地。她说外面太热，早晨再跟他们去。车子开走时，Wilson 看到她站在大树下，身着略带淡粉色的卡其布衣服，看上去更像“漂亮”而非“美丽”，深色头发向后梳起，在脖颈后方扎成一团，他觉得她的脸颊看起来像是在英格兰一样清新。车子穿过高草的洼地，绕过树林，驶进果园灌木的矮丘时，她向他们挥手。
In the orchard bush they found a herd of impala, and leaving the car they stalked one old ram with long, widespread horns and Macomber killed it with a very creditable shot that knocked the buck down at a good two hundred yards and sent the herd off bounding wildly and leaping over one another’s backs in long, leg-drawn-up leaps as unbelievable and as floating as those one makes sometimes in dreams.
在果园灌木丛中他们发现了一群黑斑羚，便离开汽车，潜行靠近一只长而展开角的老公羊，Macomber 用一记相当精彩的射击把公羊在两百码左右的距离打倒了，羚群惊跳而起，疯狂奔逃，互相跃过对方的背，做出那种在梦里有时会出现的长而收腿的不可思议、仿佛飘浮的跳跃。
‘That was a good shot,’ Wilson said. ‘They’re a small target.’
“那一枪不错，”Wilson 说。“它们是个小目标。”
‘Is it a worth-while head?’ Macomber asked.
“那头值钱吗？”Macomber 问。
‘It’s excellent,’ Wilson told him. ‘You shoot like that and you’ll have no trouble.’
“太棒了，”威尔逊对他说，“你这样射击，没什么好担心的。”
‘Do you think we’ll find buffalo to-morrow?’
“你觉得我们明天能找到水牛吗？”
‘There’s a good chance of it. They feed out carly in the morning and with luck we may catch them in the open.’
“很有可能。清晨它们出来觅食，运气好的话我们可能会在开阔地碰上它们。”
‘I’d like to clear away that lion business,’ Macomber said. ‘It’s not very pleasant to have your wife see you do something like that.’
“我想把那头狮子的事了结了，”麦康伯说，“让你妻子看到你做那种事总是不太舒服。”
I should think it would be even more unpleasant to do it, Wilson thought, wife or no wife, or to talk about it having done it. But he
我想做了这事会更令人不快，威尔逊想，不管有没有妻子，或者事后谈论这件事也一样难受。但他
said, ‘I wouldn’t think about that any more. Anyone could be upset by his first lion. That’s all over.’ .
说：“我不会再想这事了。任何人第一次对付狮子都会心里不安。那都过去了。”
But that night after dinner and a whisky and soda by the fire before going to bed, as Francis Macomber lay on his cot with the mosquito bar over him and listened to the night noises it was not all over. It was neither all over nor was it beginning. It was there exactly as it happened with some parts of it indelibly emphasized and he was miserably ashamed of it. But more than shame he felt cold, hollow fear in him. The fear was still there like a cold slimy hollow in all the emptiness where once his confidence had been and it made him feel sick. It was still there with him now.
但那晚吃过晚饭，在睡前在火旁喝了杯威士忌苏打之后，弗朗西斯·麦康伯躺在有蚊帐的行军床上，听着夜里的声音，事情并没有全部结束。既不算全然结束，也不算刚刚开始。它恰恰如实地存在着，其中有些部分被永久性地强调了，他为此感到极度羞愧。但比羞愧更多的是，他感到一种冰冷、空洞的恐惧。那种恐惧仍然像一处寒冷黏滑的空洞存在于曾经充满自信的空虚之中，令他感到恶心。它依然与他同在。
It had started the night before when he had awakened and heard the lion roaring somewhere up along the river. It was a deep sound and at the end there were sort of coughing grunts that made him seem just outside the tent, and when Francis Macomber woke in the night to hear it he was afraid. He could hear his wife breathing quietly, asleep. There was no one to tell he was afraid, nor to be afraid with him, and, lying alone, he did not know the Somali proverb that says a brave man is always frightened three times by a lion; when he first sees his track, when he first hears him roar and when he first confronts him. Then while they were eating breakfast by lantern light out in the dining tent, before the sun was up, the lion roared again and Francis thought he was just at the edge of camp.
前一晚就开始了，他醒来时听到河那边某处狮子在吼。声音低沉，尾音有几声像咳嗽似的哼，使人觉得它就在帐篷外面；弗朗西斯·麦康伯半夜醒来听见那声时感到害怕。他能听到妻子睡着后轻轻的呼吸声。没有人知道他害怕，也没有人可以与他同感害怕，孤身躺着，他不知道索马里有句谚语说勇敢的人会被狮子吓三次：第一次看到它留下的足迹，第二次第一次听到它的吼声，第三次第一次面对它。然后在他们在餐帐里用灯笼光吃早饭、太阳还没升起的时候，狮子又吼了一声，弗朗西斯以为它就在营地边缘。
‘Sounds like an old-timer,’ Robert Wilson said, looking up from his kippers and coffee. ‘Listen to him cough.’
“听起来像个老家伙，”罗伯特·威尔逊一边放下熏鱼和咖啡一边说。“听它咳。”
‘Is he very close?’
“它很近吗？”
‘A mile or so up the stream.’
“顺着河流上游大约一英里左右。”
‘Will we see him?’
“我们能看到他吗？”
‘We’ll have a look.’
“我们去看看。”
‘Does his roaring carry that far? It sounds as though he were right in camp.’
“他的吼声能传那么远吗？听起来好像就在营地里似的。”
‘Carries a hell of a long way,’ said Robert Wilson. ‘It’s strange the way it carries. Hope he’s a shootable cat. The boys said there was a very big one about here.’
“传得很远，”罗伯特·威尔逊说。“它的声音传得怪远的。希望那是一只能射的猫。伙计们说这附近有一只非常大的。”
‘If I get a shot, where should I hit him,’ Macomber asked, ‘to stop him?’
“如果我要开枪，应该打哪里，”马科姆问，“才能把他打住？”
‘In the shoulders,’ Wilson said. ‘In the neck if you can make it. Shoot for bone. Break him down.’
“打肩膀，”威尔逊说。“能打到脖子就打脖子。打准骨头。把他打倒。”
‘I hope I can place it properly,’ Macomber said.
“希望我能打准，”马科姆说。
‘You shoot very well,’ Wilson told him. ‘Take your time. Make sure of him. The first one in is the one that counts.’
“你开枪很棒，”威尔逊告诉他。“慢点来。确保命中。第一个打中的那一枪最重要。”
‘What range will it be?’
“会有多远？”
‘Can’t tell. Lion has something to say about that. Don’t shoot unless it’s close enough so you can make sure.’
“说不准。狮子说了算。别开枪，除非足够近，能把握准。”
‘At under a hundred yards?’ Macomber asked.
“四十多码以内？”麦康伯问。
Wilson looked at him quickly.
威尔逊迅速看了他一眼。
‘Hundred’s about right. Might have to take him a bit under. Shouldn’t chance a shot at much over that. A hundred’s a decent range. You can hit him wherever you want at that. Here comes the Memsahib.’
‘百码差不多。可能要往近了点。别冒险打超过那个距离的。百码是个合适的射程。你想打哪里都能打到。夫人来了。’
‘Good morning,’ she said. ‘Are we going after that lion?’
‘早上好，’她说。‘我们要去追那只狮子吗？’
‘As soon as you deal with your breakfast,’ Wilson said. ‘How are you feeling?’
‘等你把早餐处理完就走，’Wilson 说。‘你感觉怎么样？’
‘Marvellous,’ she said. ‘I’m very excited.’
‘太好了，’她说。‘我非常兴奋。’
‘I’ll just go and see that everything is ready.’ Wilson went off. As he left the lion roared again.
“我去看看一切都准备好了。”威尔森走开了。就在他离开时，狮子又吼了一声。
‘Noisy beggar,’ Wilson said. ‘We’ll put a stop to that.’
“讨厌的家伙，”威尔森说。“我们要把它治一治。”
‘What’s the matter, Francis?’ his wife asked him.
“怎么了，弗朗西斯？”他的妻子问他。
‘Nothing,’ Macomber said.
“没事，”麦考伯说。
‘Yes, there is,’ she said. ‘What are you upset about?’
“有，是的，”她说。“你在生什么气？”
‘Nothing,’ he said.
“没事，”他说。
‘Tell me,’ she looked at him. ‘Don’t you feel well?’
“跟我说，”她看着他。“你身体不舒服吗？”
‘It’s that damned roaring,’ he said. ‘It’s been going on all night, you know.’
“是那该死的轰鸣声，”他说。“你知道的，整夜都在响。”
‘Why didn’t you wake me,’ she said. ‘I’d love to have heard it.’
“你为什么不叫醒我，”她说，“我真想听听。”
‘I’ve got to kill the damned thing,’ Macomber said, miserably.
“我得把那混蛋干掉，”麦考默痛苦地说。
‘Well, that’s what you’re out here for, isn’t it?’
“那不就是你出来的目的吗？”
‘Yes. But I’m nervous. Hearing the thing roar gets on my nerves.’
“是的。但我很紧张。听那东西咆哮让我心烦意乱。”
‘Well, then, as Wilson said, kill him and stop his roaring.’
“好吧，那就像 Wilson 说的，杀了他，别让他再吼了。”
‘Yes, darling,’ said Francis Macomber. ‘It sounds easy, doesn’t it ?’
“是的，亲爱的，”Francis Macomber 说。“听起来很容易，不是吗？”
‘You’re not afraid, are you?’
“你不害怕吧？”
‘Of course not. But I’m nervous from hearing him roar all night.’
“当然不害怕。但整夜听他吼让我很紧张。”
‘You’ll kill him marvellously,’ she said. ‘I know you will. I’m awfully anxious to see it.’
“你会把他杀得漂亮极了，”她说。“我知道你会的。我非常想看一看。”
‘Finish your breakfast and we’ll be starting.’
“吃完你的早餐，我们就出发。”
‘It’s not light yet,’ she said. ‘This is a ridiculous hour.’
“还没亮呢，”她说。“这点钟真荒唐。”
Just then the lion roared in a deep-chested moaning, suddenly
就在这时，狮子发出一声深沉而低沉的咆哮，忽然间
guttural, ascending vibration that seemed to shake the air and ended in a sigh and a heavy, deep-chested grunt.
发出一种喉音般上升的震动，似乎震颤着空气，最后以一声叹息和沉重、深沉的鼻息结束。
‘He sounds almost here,’ Macomber’s wife said.
“他听起来几乎就在这里，”麦康伯的妻子说。
‘My God,’ said Macomber. ‘I hate that damned noise.’
“天哪，”麦康伯说，“我讨厌那该死的声音。”
‘It’s very impressive.’
“那很惊人。”
‘Impressive. It’s frightful.’
“真了不起。太可怕了。”
Robert Wilson came up then carrying his short, ugly, shockingly big-bored 505 Gibbs and grinning.
罗伯特·威尔逊这时走了过来，肩扛着那支短粗难看、膛口惊人粗大的 505 Gibbs，咧嘴笑着。
‘Come on,’ he said. ‘Your gun-bearer has your Springfield and the big gun. Everything’s in the car. Have you solids?’
“走吧，”他说。“你的枪童把你的 Springfield 和大口径枪都带来了。车里一应俱全。你带实弹了吗？”
‘Yes.’
“带了。”
‘I’m ready,’ Mrs. Macomber said.
“我准备好了，”麦康伯太太说。
‘Must make him stop that racket,’ Wilson said. ‘You get in front. The Memsahib can sit back here with me.’
“得让他把那声音停下，”威尔逊说。“你到前面去。夫人可以和我一起坐在后面。”
They climbed into the motor car and, in the grey first daylight, moved off up the river through the trees. Macomber opened the breach of his rifle and saw he had metal-cased bullets, shut the bolt and put the rifle on safety. He saw his hand was trembling. He felt in his pocket for more cartridges and moved his fingers over the cartridges in the loops of his tunic front. He turned back to where Wilson sat in the rear seat of the doorless, box-bodied motor car beside his wife, them both grinning with excitement, and Wilson leaned forward and whispered.
他们爬上汽车，在灰蒙蒙的晨光里，沿着河穿过树林驶去。麦康伯掰开步枪的枪膛，看到他装的是金属弹头，扣上复进栓并把保险挂上。他看到自己的手在颤抖。他在口袋里摸寻更多子弹，又用手指触摸军装前面弹环里的子弹。他回头看见威尔逊坐在无门、箱式车的后座上，靠在他妻子旁边，两人都兴奋地咧着嘴笑，威尔逊向前倾身低声说。
‘See the birds dropping. Means the old boy has left his kill.’
“看那些鸟落下。说明那老家伙已经离开了他的猎物。”
On the far bank of the stream Macomber could see, above the trees, vultures circling and plummeting down.
在溪流的对岸，麦康伯看见树顶上有秃鹫盘旋，然后俯冲下来。
‘Chances are he’ll come to drink along here,’ Wilson whispered. ‘Before he goes to lay up. Keep an eye out.’
“很可能他会沿着这儿来喝水，”威尔逊低声说。“在他去找地方休息之前。盯着点儿。”
They were driving slowly along the high bank of the stream which here cut deeply to its boulder-filled bed, and they wound in and out through big trees as they drove. Macomber was watching the opposite bank when he felt Wilson take hold of his arm. The car stopped.
他们沿着溪流的高岸慢慢行驶，这里溪水切割得很深，露出满是巨石的河床，他们开车时在大树间穿来穿去。麦康伯正盯着对岸看，这时感觉到威尔逊抓住了他的胳膊。汽车停了。
‘There he is,’ he heard the whisper. ‘Ahead and to the right. Get out and take him. He’s a marvellous lion.’
“他在那儿，”他听见低声说。“前面偏右。下车去射他。他是一头了不起的狮子。”
Macomber saw the lion now. He was standing almost broadside, his great head up and turned toward them. The early morning breeze that blew toward them was just stirring his dark mane, and the lion looked huge, silhouetted on the rise of bank in the grey
马科姆这才看清那头狮子。它几乎是侧身站着，巨大的头抬起，转向他们。拂面而来的清晨微风刚好吹动它浓密的鬃毛，狮子看起来巨大，在灰色的晨光里轮廓分明地映在土堤的隆起上，肩膀厚实，浑圆的躯体结实地挺着。
morning light, his shoulders heavy, his barrel of a body bulking smoothly.
清晨的光线中，它的肩膀沉重，圆桶般的身体平滑地隆起。
‘How far is he?’ asked Macomber, raising his rifle.
“多远？”马科姆抬起步枪问。
‘About seventy-five. Get out and take him.’
“大约七十五码。下车，去打它。”
‘Why not shoot from where I am?’
“为什么不从我现在的位置开枪？”
‘You don’t shoot them from cars,’ he heard Wilson saying in his ear. ‘Get out. He’s not going to stay there all day.’
“不能从车里对着它们开枪，”他听到威尔逊在他耳边说。“下车。他不会一直待在那儿的。”
Macomber stepped out of the curved opening at the side of the front seat, on to the step and down on to the ground. The lion still stood looking majestically and coolly toward this object that his eyes only showed in silhouette, bulking like some super-rhino. There was no man smell carried toward him and he watched the object, moving his great head a little from side to side. Then watching the object, not afraid, but hesitating before going down the bank to drink with such a thing opposite him, he saw a man figure detach itself from it and he turned his heavy head and swung away toward the cover of the trees as he heard a cracking crash and felt the slam of a 30 − 06220 30 − 06220 30-0622030-06220-grain solid bullet that bit his flank and ripped in sudden hot scalding nausea through his stomach. He trotted, heavy, big-footed, swinging wounded full-bellied, through the trees toward the tall grass and cover, and the crash came again to go past him ripping the air apart. Then it crashed again and he felt the blow as it hit his lower ribs and ripped on through, blood sudden hot and frothy in his mouth, and he galloped toward the high grass where he could crouch and not be seen and make them bring the crashing thing close enough so he could make a rush and get the man that held it.
马科姆从前座侧面的弧形开口跨出，踏上踏板，落到地面上。那只狮子仍然威严而冷静地盯着这个它眼中只显为轮廓的东西，体积庞大，像只超级犀牛。没有人的气味传向它，它注视着那东西，略微左右摇动着它那巨大的头。然后在注视着那东西时，并不害怕，只是在犹豫是否要下到河岸去饮水，面对着那样的东西，它看到有个人影从那东西上分离出来，它转动沉重的头，随着一声爆裂般的巨响朝树丛的掩护处甩开，同时感觉到一颗 30 − 06220 30 − 06220 30-0622030-06220 号全金属被甲实心子弹猛击它的侧 flank 并在胃里撕裂出突如其来的灼热恶心感。它沉重地小跑着，大脚步，伤着、满腹，穿过树丛奔向高草和掩护，再次传来那一声巨响，从它旁边掠过，撕裂着空气。 然后又撞了一下，他感到那一击打在下肋并穿透过去，血一下变得又热又泡沫般在嘴里，他飞奔向高草丛，想要蹲下不被看见，让他们把那撞击的东西带得足够近，以便他可以猛扑过去抓住那个拿着它的人。
Macomber had not thought how the lion felt as he got out of the car. He only knew his hands were shaking and as he walked away from the car it was almost impossible for him to make his legs move. They were stiff in the thighs, but he could feel the muscles fluttering. He raised the rifle, sighted on the junction of the lion’s head and shoulders and pulled the trigger. Nothing happened though he pulled until he thought his finger would break. Then he knew he had the safety on and as he lowered the rifle to move the safety over he moved another frozen pace forward, and the lion seeing his silhouette now clear of the silhouette of the car, turned and started off at a trot, and, as Macomber fired, he heard a whunk that meant that the bullet was home; but the lion kept on going. Macomber shot
Macomber 并没有想过狮子下车时的感受。他只知道自己的手在发抖，离开车走开时几乎无法使腿动起来。大腿僵硬，但他能感觉到肌肉在颤动。他举起来复枪，对准狮子头与肩膀的交接处瞄准并扣动扳机。尽管他扣到觉得手指要断了，什么也没发生。然后他才知道保险开着，他把枪口向下放以便把保险拨开，又僵硬地向前迈了一步，狮子看到它的轮廓现在已从车的轮廓中显露出来，转身开始小跑，当 Macomber 开枪时，他听到一声沉闷的击中声，意味着子弹命中；但狮子继续向前。Macomber 又开了枪
again and everyone saw the bullet throw a spout of dirt beyond the trotting lion. He shot again, remembering to lower his aim, and they all heard the bullet hit, and the lion went into a gallop and was in the tall grass before he had the bolt pushed forward.
又一次，所有人都看到子弹在小跑的狮子身后掀起一股土柱。他又开了一枪，记得把瞄准降低些，大家都听到子弹命中声，狮子冲起快跑，等他把栓推上去时已钻进了高草。
Macomber stood there feeling sick at his stomach, his hands that held the Springfield still cocked, shaking, and his wife and Robert Wilson were standing by him. Beside him too were the two gunbearers chattering in Wakamba.
麦科伯站着觉得胃里翻腾，握着 Springfield 的手还扣着扳机，颤抖着，他的妻子和罗伯特·威尔逊站在他身旁。两名说瓦坎巴语的枪手也在他身边喋喋不休。
‘I hit him,’ Macomber said. ‘I hit him twice.’
“我打中了，”麦科伯说。“我打中了两次。”
‘You gut-shot him and you hit him somewhere forward,’ Wilson said without enthusiasm. The gun-bearers looked very grave. They were silent now.
“你打的是腹部，另有一发打在较前的位置，”威尔逊没什么热情地说。枪手们都显得很严肃。他们这会儿沉默了。
‘You may have killed him,’ Wilson went on. ‘We’ll have to wait a while before we go in to find out.’
“也许你已经把他打死了，”威尔逊继续说。“我们得等一会儿再进去确认。”
‘What do you mean?’
“你什么意思？”
‘Let him get sick before we follow him up.’
“等他病倒了我们再跟上去。”
‘Oh,’ said Macomber.
“哦，”麦康伯说。
‘He’s a hell of a fine lion,’ Wilson said cheerfully. ‘He’s gotten into a bad place though.’
“那是一头了不起的狮子，”威尔逊高兴地说。“不过他已经进入了一个危险的地段。”
‘Why is it bad?’
“为什么危险？”
‘Can’t see him until you’re on him.’
“在那里你看不到他，直到他就在你面前。”
‘Oh,’ said Macomber.
“哦，”麦考伯说。
‘Come on,’ said Wilson. ‘The Memsahib can stay here in the car. We’ll go to have a look at the blood spoor.’
“过来，”Wilson 说。“Memsahib 可以留在车里。我们去看看血迹。”
‘Stay here, Margot,’ Macomber said to his wife. His mouth was very dry and it was hard for him to talk.
“别走，Margot，”Macomber 对妻子说。他嘴很干，说话很吃力。
‘Why?’ she asked.
“为什么？”她问。
‘Wilson says to.’
“Wilson 说要这样。”
‘We’re going to have a look,’ Wilson said. ‘You stay here. You can see even better from here.’
“我们去看看，”Wilson 说。“你留在这里。从这里看得更清楚。”
‘All right.’
“好吧。”
Wilson spoke in Swahili to the driver. He nodded and said, ‘Yes, Bwana.’
Wilson 用斯瓦西里语对司机说了几句。司机点点头，说：“是的，Bwana。”
Then they went down the steep bank and across the stream, climbing over and around the boulders and up the other bank, pulling up by some projecting roots, and along it until they found where the lion had been trotting when Macomber first shot. There was dark blood on the short grass that the gun-bearers pointed out with grass stems, and that ran away behind the river bank trees.
然后他们顺着陡峭的河岸下去，过了溪流，绕过和爬过大卵石，上到对岸，靠着一些突出的树根拉着往上，沿着河岸走，直到找到那只狮子在 Macomber 第一次开枪时小跑过的地方。枪手们用草茎指出短草上的深色血迹，血迹在河岸后的树丛后面延去。
‘What do we do?’ asked Macomber.
“我们怎么办？”麦康伯问。
‘Not much choice,’ said Wilson. ‘We can’t bring the car over. Bank’s too steep. We’ll let him stiffen up a bit and then you and I’ll go in and have a look for him.’
“没多少选择，”威尔森说。“我们开不了车过去。坡太陡了。等他僵硬了点儿，你和我再进去找他。”
‘Can’t we set the grass on fire?’ Macomber asked.
“我们不能把草点着吗？”麦康伯问。
‘Too green.’
“太绿了。”
‘Can’t we send beaters ?’
“我们不能派打猎的人去吗？”
Wilson looked at him appraisingly. ‘Of course we can,’ he said. ‘But it’s just a touch murderous. You see we know the lion’s wounded. You can drive an unwounded lion - he’ll move on ahead of a noise - but a wounded lion’s going to charge. You can’t see him until you’re right on him. He’ll make himself perfectly flat in cover you wouldn’t think would hide a hare. You can’t very well send boys in there to that sort of a show. Somebody bound to get mauled.’
威尔逊审视着他。“当然可以，”他说，“但那样有点像自寻死路。你看，我们知道狮子受了伤。你可以赶一只没受伤的狮子——它会在听到动静时往前走开——但受伤的狮子会冲上来。你在离它很近之前看不见它。它会把自己完全贴在你认为连兔子都藏不住的掩蔽物里。你可不能把孩子们派到那种场面去。总有人会被撕伤的。”
‘What about the gun-bearers?’
“那拿枪的呢？”
‘Oh, they’ll go with us. It’s their shauri. You see, they signed on for it. They don’t look too happy though, do they?’
“哦，他们会和我们一块去。那是他们的 shauri。你看，他们是签了字的。不过他们看起来不太高兴，是吧？”
‘I don’t want to go in there,’ said Macomber. It was out before he knew he’d said it.
“我不想进去，”马科姆说。这话脱口而出，连他自己都没意识到。
‘Neither do I,’ said Wilson very cheerily. ‘Really no choice though.’ Then, as an afterthought, he glanced at Macomber and saw suddenly how he was trembling and the pitiful look on his face.
“我也不想，”威尔逊很高兴地说，“不过真没得选择。”接着，他忽然瞥了马科姆一眼，看到他在发抖，脸上是可怜的神情。
‘You don’t have to go in, of course,’ he said. ‘That’s what I’m hired for, you know. That’s why I’m so expensive.’
“当然，你不必进去，”他说。“你知道的，我就是受雇来做这事的。这也是我这么贵的原因。”
‘You mean you’d go in by yourself? Why not leave him there?’
“你的意思是你会一个人进去？为什么不把他留在那里？”
Robert Wilson, whose entire occupation had been with the lion and the problem he presented, and who had not been thinking about Macomber except to note that he was rather windy, suddenly felt as though he had opened the wrong door in an hotel and seen something shameful.
罗伯特·威尔逊，他整个职业生涯都在与狮子及其带来的问题打交道，平日里并不怎么考虑麦康伯，除了觉得他有点夸夸其谈；此刻却突然感觉仿佛在旅馆里推错了门，看见了可耻的东西。
‘What do you mean?’
“你是什么意思？”
‘Why not just leave him?’
“为什么不就把他丢下不管呢？”
‘You mean pretend to ourselves he hasn’t been hit?’
“你的意思是要对自己假装他没中弹？”
‘No. Just drop it.’
“不。就放下它。”
‘It isn’t done.’
“还没死。”
‘Why not?’
“为什么不？”
‘For one thing, he’s certain to be suffering. For another, someone else might run on to him.’
“首先，他肯定很痛苦。其次，可能会有人跑到他那里去。”
‘I see.’
“我明白了。”
‘But you don’t have to have anything to do with it.’
“但你完全不必插手。”
‘I’d like to,’ Macomber said. ‘I’m just scared, you know.’
“我愿意的，”麦康伯说，“我只是害怕，你知道的。”
‘I’ll go ahead when we go in,’ Wilson said, 'with Kongoni tracking. You keep behind me and a little to one side. Chances are we’ll hear him growl. If we see him we’ll both shoot. Don’t worry about anything. I’ll keep you backed up. As a matter of fact, vou know, perhaps you’d better not go. It might be much better. Why don’t you go over and join the Memsahib while I just get it over with?"
“我们进去的时候我先走，”威尔逊说，“用孔戈尼追踪。你跟在我后面，稍微偏一边。大概我们会听到它咆哮。如果看到它我们俩都开枪。别担心任何事。我会掩护你。事实上，你知道，也许你最好别去。可能会好得多。你为什么不去找夫人，等我把这事处理掉？”
‘No, I want to go.’
“不要，我要去。”
‘All right,’ said Wilson. ‘But don’t go in if you don’t want to. This is my shauri now, you know.’
“好吧，”Wilson 说。“但你不想进去就别进去。你知道的，这是我的事了。”
‘I want to go,’ said Macomber.
“我要去，”Macomber 说。
They sat under a tree and smoked.
他们坐在树下抽烟。
‘Want to go back and speak to the Memsahib while we’re waiting?’ Wilson asked.
“要不要我们回去跟夫人说说，同时等着？”威尔逊问。
‘No.’
“不。”
‘I’ll just step back and tell her to be patient.’
“我就回去跟她说要有耐心。”
‘Good,’ said Macomber. He sat there, sweating under his arms, his mouth dry, his stomach hollow feeling, wanting to find courage to tell Wilson to go on and finish off the lion without him. He could not know that Wilson was furious because he had not noticed the state he was in earlier and sent him back to his wife. While he sat there Wilson came up. ‘I have your big gun,’ he said. ‘Take it. We’ve given him time, I think. Come on.’
“好，”马康伯说。他坐在那里，腋下汗湿，口干，胃里一阵空虚，想鼓起勇气告诉威尔逊继续去把狮子解决掉，不需要他。但他不知道威尔逊恼火的是，自己早先没有注意到他的状态就把他遣回去陪妻子。正当他坐着时，威尔逊走了过来。“我把你的大枪拿来了，”他说。“拿着吧。我看我们已经给了它时间，走吧。”
Macomber took the big gun and Wilson said:
马科姆拿起那把大枪，威尔逊说：
‘Keep behind me and about five vards to the right and do exactly as I tell you.’ Then he spoke in Swahili to the two gun-bearers who looked the picture of gloom.
“跟在我后面，右侧约五码，照我说的去做。”然后他用斯瓦西里语对两个抬枪的仆人说道，那两人面露愁色。
‘Let’s go,’ he said.
“我们走吧，”他说。
‘Could I have a drink of water?’ Macomber asked. Wilson spoke to the older gun-bearer, who wore a canteen on his belt and the man unbuckled it, unscrewed the top and handed it to Macomber, who took it noticing how heavy it seemed and how hairy and shoddy the felt covering was in his hand. He raised it to drink and looked ahead at the high grass with the flat-topped trees behind it. A breeze was blowing toward them and the grass rippled gently in the wind. He looked at the gun-bearer and he could see the gun-bearer was suffering too with fear.
“我能喝点水吗？”马科姆问。威尔逊对年长的抬枪人说话，那个抬枪人腰间别着水壶，他解开带子，拧开盖子，把水壶递给马科姆。马科姆接过它，注意到它看上去很重，覆着的毡布又毛糙又低劣。他抬起水壶想喝，目光望向前方高高的草丛，背后是平顶的树木。一阵微风朝他们吹来，草随风轻轻起伏。他看着那抬枪人，发现那人也因恐惧而痛苦。
Thirty-five yards into the grass the big lion lay flattened out along the ground. His ears were back and his only movement was a slight twitching up and down of his long, black-tufted tail. He had turned at bay as soon as he had reached this cover and he was sick with the wound through his full belly, and weakening with the wound through his lungs that brought a thin foamy red to his mouth each time he breathed. His flanks were wet and hot and flies were on the little opening the solid bullets had made in his tawny hide, and his big yellow eyes, narrowed with hate, looked straight ahead, only blinking when the pain came as he breathed, and his claws dug in the soft baked earth. All of him, pain, sickness, hatred and all of his remaining strength, was tightening into an absolute concentration for a rush. He could hear the men talking and he waited, gathering all of himself into this preparation for a charge as soon as the men would come into the grass. As he heard their voices his tail stiffened to twitch up and down, and, as they came into the edge of the grass, he made a coughing grunt and charged.
三十五码外的草丛里，巨大的狮子贴着地面趴着。它的耳朵向后靠，唯一的动作是那条带黑色簇毛的长尾巴微微上下抽动。它一到这片掩蔽就转身断后，腹部贯穿的伤口让它病入膏肓，贯穿肺部的伤口使它每次呼吸时嘴里都涌出稀薄的红色泡沫，体力渐衰。它的两侧湿热，苍白的皮毛上那颗实心子弹打出的细小伤口上有苍蝇盘踞，狭长的黄色大眼睛充满仇恨直视前方，只有在呼吸时疼痛来袭才眨眼，爪子紧抓着干硬的土壤。所有的一切——疼痛、病痛、仇恨以及所剩无几的力量——都凝聚成一种绝对的集中，准备一次冲锋。它能听见人们的谈话声，等待着，把自己全部聚拢，准备在那些人一进草丛便发起猛扑。听到他们的声音时，它的尾巴僵直起来随即上下抽动，当他们走到草丛边缘时，它发出一声咳嗽般的粗重叫声，猛然冲了出去。
Kongoni, the old gun-bearer, in the lead watching the blood spoor, Wilson watching the grass for any movement, his big gun ready, the second gun-bearer looking ahead and listening, Macomber close to Wilson, his rifle cocked, they had just moved into the grass when Macomber heard the blood-choked coughing grunt, and saw the swishing rush in the grass. The next thing he knew he was running; running wildly, in panic in the open, running toward the stream.
孔戈尼，那个年老的枪伕，走在最前边盯着血迹，威尔逊注视着草丛里有没有动静，大枪准备着，第二个枪伕向前看并倾听，麦考伯靠近威尔逊，步枪上膛，他们刚走进草丛，麦考伯就听到那被血堵住的咳嗽似的哼声，看见草丛里有掠动的擦响。接着他发现自己在奔跑；在空旷处惊慌失措地狂奔，朝小溪方向跑去。
He heard the ca-ra-wong! of Wilson’s big rifle, and again in a second crashing carawong! and turning saw the lion, horriblelooking now, with half his head seeming to be gone, crawling toward Wilson in the edge of the tall grass while the red-faced man worked the bolt on the short ugly rifle and aimed carefully as another blasting carawong! came from the muzzle, and the crawling, heavy, yellow bulk of the lion stiffened and the huge, mutilated head slid forward and Macomber, standing by himself in the clearing where he had run, holding a loaded rifle, while two black men and a white man looked back at him in contempt, knew the lion was dead. He came toward Wilson, his tallness all seeming a naked reproach, and Wilson looked at him and said:
他听见威尔逊那支大步枪发出的“咔——拉——翁！”声，又在第二声“砰”的巨响中转身，看见那狮子此刻可怖极了，半个头仿佛被掏去了，正沿着高草边爬向威尔逊，红脸男人正操着短而丑陋的步枪的枪栓，小心瞄准，随着枪口又传来一声震耳的“砰”，那头沉重、发黄、匍匐的狮躯僵住了，巨大的、残缺的头滑向前去，麦康伯站在他先前跑到的空地上，独自一人手里拿着缴满子的步枪，两个黑人和一个白人带着轻蔑的目光回望着他，他知道那狮子死了。他走近威尔逊，他的高大在一切看来都像赤裸的责难，威尔逊看着他说：
‘Want to take pictures?’
“要拍照吗？”
‘No,’ he said.
“不要，”他说。
That was all anyone had said until they reached the motor car. Then Wilson had said:
直到他们走到汽车边之前，这是一句话也没人再说的。然后威尔逊说：
‘Hell of a fine lion. Boys will skin him out. We might as well stay here in the shade.’
“真是头好狮子。伙计们会把它剥了皮。我们不如就待在这儿乘着阴凉。”
Macomber’s wife had not looked at him nor he at her and he had sat by her in the back seat with Wilson sitting in the front seat. Once he had reached over and taken his wife’s hand without looking at her and she had removed her hand from his. Looking across the stream to where the gun-bearers were skinning out the lion he could see that she had been able to see the whole thing. While they sat there his wife had reached forward and put her hand on Wilson’s shoulder. He turned and she had leaned forward over the low seat and kissed him on the mouth.
麦康伯的妻子既不看他，他也不看她，他靠在后座坐在她身边，威尔逊坐在前座。曾有一回他伸手去牵妻子的手却没看她，她也把手从他手里抽了回去。望着对岸那些抬枪的人在剥狮子皮，他看出她能把整件事都看得清清楚楚。就在他们坐着的时候，他妻子向前伸手把手搭在威尔逊的肩上。他转过头来，她便从低矮的座位上前倾，亲了他一下嘴。
‘Oh, I say,’ said Wilson, going redder than his natural baked colour.
“哦，我说，”威尔逊脸比他那自然晒得红的肤色更红了。
‘Mr. Robert Wilson,’ she said. ‘The beautifully red-faced Mr. Robert Wilson.’
“罗伯特·威尔逊先生，”她说。“那位脸颊红得真漂亮的罗伯特·威尔逊先生。”
Then she sat down beside Macomber again and looked away across the stream to where the lion lay, with uplifted, white-muscled tendon-marked naked forearms, and white bloating belly, as the black men fleshed away the skin. Finally the gun-bearers brought the skin over, wet and heavy, and climbed in behind with it, rolling it up before they got in, and the motor car started. No one had said anything more until they were back in camp.
然后她又坐到马康伯身旁，望向小溪对岸狮子躺着的地方，那儿狮子的前臂裸露，白色肌腱分明、抬起着，腹部胀白，黑人们正在剥掉皮。最后抬枪的把那张湿重的皮毛抬了过来，背在后面，进车前把它卷好，汽车发动了。直到回到营地，没人再说话。
That was the story of the lion. Macomber did not know how the lion had felt before he started his rush, nor during it when the unbelievable smash of the 505 with a muzzle velocity of two tons had hit him in the mouth, nor what kept him coming after that, when the second ripping crash had smashed his hind quarters and he had come crawling on toward the crashing, blasting thing that had destroyed him. Wilson knew something about it and only expressed it by saying, ‘Damned fine lion’, but Macomber did not know how Wilson felt about things either. He did not know how his wife felt except that she was through with him.
那就是关于那头狮子的经过。马康伯不知道狮子在开始冲锋前是什么感觉，也不知道在那不可思议的一击——口径为 505、初速如两吨重击般的打击——击中它口部时它是如何感受的，也不知道在随后第二次撕裂般的撞击摧毁了它的后躯后，是什么支撑它继续爬行，朝着那摧毁它的爆裂轰鸣之物爬来。威尔逊对此略知一二，只说了句“该死的好狮子”。但马康伯也不知道威尔逊对这些事情的感受。他唯一知道的是，他的妻子对他不再抱有感情。
His wife had been through with him before but it never lasted. He was very wealthy, and would be much wealthier, and he knew she would not leave him ever now. That was one of the few things he really knew. He knew about that, about motor cycles - that was earliest-about motor cars, about duck-shooting, about fishing,
他妻子以前跟他闹过别扭，但从来没有持久。他非常富有，将来会更富有，他知道现在她永远不会离开他了。这是他真正知道的为数不多的事情之一。他知道那件事，知道摩托车——那是最早知道的——知道汽车，知道打鸭子，知道钓鱼，
trout, salmon and big-sea, about sex in books, many books, too many books, about all court games, about dogs, not much about horses, about hanging on to his money, about most of the other things his world dealt in, and about his wife not leaving him. His wife had been a great beauty and she was still a great beauty in Africa, but she was not a great enough beauty any more at home to be able to leave him and better herself and she knew it and he knew it. She had missed the chance to leave him and he knew it. If he had been better with women she would probably have started to worry about him getting another new, beautiful wife; but she knew too much about him to worry about him either. Also, he had always had a great tolerance which seemed the nicest thing about him if it were not the most sinister.
知道鳟鱼、鲑鱼和大海鱼，知道书中的性，许多书，太多书了，知道所有的球类游戏，知道狗，马知道得不多，知道守住他的财产，知道他世界里大多数其他事物，也知道妻子不会离开他。他妻子曾经是大美人，在非洲她仍然是大美人，但在家里她已不再是那种足以离开他、使自己更好的大美人了，她知道这一点，他也知道。他错过了离开他的机会，他知道这一点。如果他在对待女人方面表现得更好些，她也许会开始担心他会娶另一个新的、美丽的妻子；但她对他了解得太多，也不会为他担心。此外，他一直容忍力极强，这似乎是他最讨人喜欢的特质——如果它不是最险恶的那一项的话。
All in all they were known as a comparatively happily married couple, one of those whose disruption is often rumoured but never occurs, and as the society columnist put it, they were adding more than a spice of adventure to their much envied and ever-enduring Romance by a Safari in what was known as Darkest Africa until the Martin Johnsons lighted it on so many silver screens where they were pursuing Old Simba the lion, the buffalo, Tembo the elephant and as well collecting specimens for the Museum of Natural History. This same columnist had reported them on the verge at least three times in the past and they had been. But they always made it up. They had a sound basis of union. Margot was too beautiful for Macomber to divorce her and Macomber had too much money for Margot ever to leave him.
总的说来，他们被认为是婚姻相对幸福的一对，那种常常被传要分裂却从未真的分开的夫妻，正如社会专栏作家所说，他们通过一次被称为“最为幽暗的非洲”的狩猎旅行，为那令人羡慕、持久不衰的浪漫增添了不止一点冒险的味道，直到 Martin Johnson 夫妇把它们拍上了那么多银幕，他们在片中追捕老狮子辛巴、野牛、象王坦博，同时也为自然历史博物馆采集标本。这个专栏作家曾在过去至少三次报道他们濒临分手，而他们确实曾濒临。但他们总会和好。他们的结合有着牢固的基础。Margot 对 Macomber 来说太美，以致于他不会与她离婚；而 Macomber 又太有钱，Margot 不可能离开他。
It was now about three o’clock in the morning and Francis Macomber, who had been asleep a little while after he had stopped thinking about the lion, wakened and then slept again, woke suddenly, frightened in a dream of the bloody-headed lion standing over him, and listening while his heart pounded, he realized that his wife was not in the other cot in the tent. He lay awake with that knowledge for two hours.
现在大约是凌晨三点，Francis Macomber 在停止想那只狮子后睡了一会儿，又醒来又睡去，突然从梦中惊醒，梦见那只血淋淋的狮子站在他面前，他在心脏扑通乱跳中听着，意识到妻子不在帐篷里另一架床上。他带着这个念头清醒地躺了两个小时。
At the end of that time his wife came into the tent, lifted her mosquito bar and crawled cozily into bed.
两个小时后，他的妻子走进帐篷，掀起蚊帐，舒舒服服地钻进床里。
‘Where have you been?’ Macomber asked in the darkness.
“你去哪儿了？”黑暗中 Macomber 问道。
‘Hello,’ she said. ‘Are you awake?’
“你好，”她说。“你醒着吗？”
‘Where have you been?’
“你去哪儿了？”
‘I just went out to get a breath of air.’
“我只是出去透透气。”
‘You did, like hell.’
“你才透气呢，鬼才信。”
‘What do you want me to say, darling?’
“亲爱的，你要我说什么？”
‘Where have you been?’
“你去哪儿了？”
‘Out to get a breath of air.’
“出去透透气。”
‘That’s a new name for it. You are a bitch.’
“这可真是个新说法。你就是个婊子。”
‘Well, you’re a coward.’
“好吧，你是个懦夫。”
‘All right,’ he said. ‘What of it?’
“好吧，”他说。“那又怎样？”
‘Nothing as far as I’m concerned. But please let’s not talk darling, because I’m very sleepy.’
“就我而言没什么。但请别谈了，亲爱的，因为我很困。”
‘You think that I’ll take anything.’
“你以为我会容忍任何事。”
‘I know you will, sweet.’
“我知道你会的，亲爱的。”
‘Well, I won’t.’
“好吧，我不会的。”
‘Please, darling, let’s not talk. I’m so very sleepy.’
“拜托，亲爱的，我们别说了。我好困。”
‘There wasn’t going to be any of that. You promised there wouldn’t be.’
“那可不行。你答应过不会那样的。”
‘Well, there is now,’ she said sweetly.
“好吧，那现在就会这样，”她甜甜地说。
‘You said if we made this trip that there would be none of that. You promised.’
“你说过我们要是来了这趟就不会有那些事。你答应过的。”
‘Yes, darling. That’s the way I meant it to be. But the trip was spoiled yesterday. We don’t have to talk about it, do we?’
“是的，亲爱的。我本来就是那样打算的。但这趟行程昨天就被毁了。我们不用再谈了，好吗？”
‘You don’t wait long when you have an advantage, do you?’
“你有了优势就不肯多等，是不是？”
‘Please let’s not talk. I’m so sleepy, darling.’
“请别谈了。我好困，亲爱的。”
‘I’m going to talk.’
“我要说话。”
‘Don’t mind me then, because I’m going to sleep.’ And she did.
“那就别理我吧，因为我要睡觉了。”她说着便睡着了。
At breakfast they were all three at the table before daylight and Francis Macomber found that, of all the many men that he had hated, he hated Robert Wilson the most.
早餐时他们仨天未亮就坐到桌旁，弗朗西斯·马科姆发现，在他所憎恨的众多人中，他最恨的是罗伯特·威尔逊。
‘Sleep well?’ Wilson asked in his throaty voice, filling a pipe.
“睡得好吗？”威尔逊用那低沉的声音问，一边填烟斗。
‘Did you?’
“你做了吗？”
‘Topping,’ the white hunter told him.
“在顶上，”白猎人告诉他。
You bastard, thought Macomber, you insolent bastard.
可恶的家伙，麦康伯想，你这傲慢的混蛋。
So she woke him when she came in, Wilson thought, looking at them both with his flat, cold eyes. Well, why doesn’t he keep his wife where she belongs? What does he think I am, a bloody plaster saint? Let him keep her where she belongs. It’s his own fault.
所以她进来时把他叫醒了，威尔逊想着，用他那平静冷漠的目光看着他们两人。好吧，他怎么不把他妻子放在她该呆的地方？他以为我是什么，个该死的创可贴圣人吗？就让他把她放在该呆的地方。这都是他自找的。
‘Do you think we’ll find buffalo?’ Margot asked, pushing away a dish of apricots.
“你觉得我们会找到水牛吗？”玛戈推开一盘杏子问道。
‘Chance of it,’ Wilson said and smiled at her. ‘Why don’t you stay in camp?’
“有可能，”威尔逊说着朝她微笑。“你为什么不待在营地呢？”
‘Not for anything,’ she told him.
“无论如何都不去，”她告诉他。
‘Why not order her to stay in camp?’ Wilson said to Macomber.
“你为什么不命令她待在营地呢？”威尔逊对麦考伯说。
‘You order her,’ said Macomber coldly.
“你命令她吧，”麦康伯冷冷地说。
‘Let’s not have any ordering, nor,’ turning to Macomber, ‘any silliness, Francis,’ Margot said quite pleasantly.
“别再发号施令了，”玛格特相当愉快地说，转向麦康伯，“也别再装腔作势了，弗朗西斯。”
‘Are you ready to start?’ Macomber asked.
“你准备好出发了吗？”麦康伯问道。
‘Any time,’ Wilson told him. 'Do you want the Memsahib to go?’
“随时可以，”威尔逊告诉他。“你要夫人一同去吗？”
‘Does it make any difference whether I do or not?’
“我做或不做，有什么关系吗？”
The hell with it, thought Robert Wilson. The utter complete hell with it. So this is what it’s going to be like. Well, this is what it’s going to be like, then.
见鬼去吧，罗伯特·威尔逊想。彻底的见鬼。这事就会这样。好吧，那就照这样吧。
‘Makes no difference,’ he said.
“没关系，”他说。
‘You’re sure you wouldn’t like to stay in camp with her yourself and let me go out and hunt the buffalo?’ Macomber asked.
“你确定你不愿意和她一起留在营地，让我出去打野牛吗？”马科伯问。
‘Can’t do that,’ said Wilson. ‘Wouldn’t talk rot if I were you.’
“那可不行，”威尔逊说。“我劝你别瞎扯。”
‘I’m not talking rot. I’m disgusted.’
“我没在胡说。我是厌恶了。”
‘Bad word, disgusted.’
“别用那种词，‘厌恶’不该说。”
‘Francis, will you please try to speak sensibly?’ his wife said.
“弗朗西斯，你能不能尽量讲得有理一点？”他的妻子说。
‘I speak too damned sensibly,’ Macomber said. ‘Did you ever eat such filthy food?’
“我说得太他妈像个理智的人了，”麦康伯说。“你吃过这么肮脏的食物吗？”
‘Something wrong with the food?’ asked Wilson quietly.
“食物有什么问题吗？”威尔逊平静地问。
‘No more than with everything else.’
“和其他一切没什么不同。”
‘I’d pull yourself together, laddybuck,’ Wilson said very quietly. ‘There’s a boy waits at table that understands a little English.’
“振作起来，laddybuck，”威尔逊非常平静地说。“有个侍者会一点英语。”
‘The hell with him.’
“去他的。”
Wilson stood up and puffing on his pipe strolled away, speaking a few words in Swahili to one of the gun-bearers who was standing waiting for him. Macomber and his wife sat on at the table. He was staring at his coffee cup.
威尔逊站起身，叼着烟斗漫步离开，边走边用斯瓦西里语对站着等候的一个持枪人说了几句话。麦康伯和他的妻子坐在桌旁。他直愣愣地盯着咖啡杯。
‘If you make a scene I’ll leave you, darling,’ Margot said quietly.
“如果你闹事我就离开你，亲爱的，”玛戈特平静地说。
‘No, you won’t.’
“不，你不会。”
‘You can try it and see.’
“你可以试试看。”
‘You won’t leave me.’
“你不会离开我。”
‘No,’ she said. ‘I won’t leave you and you’ll behave yourself.’
“不，”她说。“我不会离开你，你要规规矩矩的。”
‘Behave myself? That’s a way to talk. Behave myself.’
“规规矩矩？这话怎么说的。规规矩矩。”
‘Yes. Behave yourself.’
“好吧。规矩点。”
‘Why don’t you try behaving?’
“你怎么不试着规矩点呢？”
‘I’ve tried it so long. So very long.’
“我已经试了那么久。太久了。”
‘I hate that red-faced swine,’ Macomber said. ‘I loathe the sight of him.’
“我恨那个满脸通红的混蛋，”Macomber 说，“看到他我就厌恶。”
‘He’s really very nice.’
“他人真的很好。”
‘Oh, shut up,’ Macomber almost shouted. Just then the car came up and stopped in front of the dining tent and the driver and the two gun-bearers got out. Wilson walked over and looked at the husband and wife sitting there at the table.
“哦，闭嘴，”麦康伯几乎喊道。就在这时，汽车开来停在餐帐篷前，司机和两个抬枪者下了车。威尔逊走过去看着坐在那张桌旁的夫妻。
‘Going shooting?’ he asked.
“去打猎吗？”他问。
‘Yes,’ said Macomber, standing up. ‘Yes.’
“是的，”麦康伯站起来说。“是的。”
‘Better bring a woolly. It will be cool in the car,’ Wilson said.
“最好带件羊毛衣。车里会凉。”威尔逊说。
‘I’ll get my leather jacket,’ Margot said.
“我去拿我的皮夹克，”玛格特说。
‘The boy has it,’ Wilson told her. He climbed into the front with the driver and Francis Macomber and his wife sat, not speaking, in the back seat.
“那小子拿着呢，”威尔逊告诉她。他和司机坐到前排，弗朗西斯·麦康伯和他的妻子沉默不语地坐在后座。
Hope the silly beggar doesn’t take a notion to blow the back of my head off, Wilson thought to himself. Women are a nuisance on safari.
希望这个愚蠢的混蛋别突然想把我后脑勺炸了，威尔逊心里想。女人在狩猎旅行上真是个麻烦。
The car was grinding down to cross the river at a pebbly ford in the grey daylight and then climbed, angling up the steep bank, where Wilson had ordered a way shovelled out the day before so they could reach the parklike wooded rolling country on the far side.
汽车在灰色的晨光中嘎吱作响，驶过一处铺着卵石的涉水浅滩，随后沿着陡峭的河岸爬升，朝上倾斜。威尔逊前一天已命人把路铲出来，好让他们能到达对岸那片如公园般、树木成荫的起伏地带。
It was a good morning, Wilson thought. There was a heavy dew and as the wheels went through the grass and low bushes he could smell the odour of the crushed fronds. It was an odour like verbena and he liked this early morning smell of the dew, the crushed bracken and the look of the tree trunks showing black through the early morning mist, as the car made its way through the untracked, parklike country. He had put the two in the back seat out of his mind now and was thinking about buffalo. The buffalo that he was after stayed in the daytime in a thick swamp where it was impossible to get a shot, but in the night they fed out into an open stretch of country and if he could come between them and their swamp with the car, Macomber would have a good chance at them in the open. He did not want to hunt buff with Macomber in thick cover. He did not want to hunt buff or anything else with Macomber at all, but he was a professional hunter and he had hunted with some rare ones in his time. If they got buff to-day there would only be rhino to come and the poor man would have gone through his dangerous game and things might pick up. He’d have nothing more
这是个好早晨，威尔逊想。露水很重，车轮碾过草丛和矮灌木时，他能闻到被碾碎的叶片的气味。那气味像香茅草，他喜欢这种清晨露水的味道，喜欢被压碎的蕨类的气息，也喜欢树干在晨雾中显出黑色的景象，车子穿过这片无人践踏、如公园般的地带。他现在已把坐在后座的那两个人抛诸脑后，正在想水牛。他要追的水牛白天呆在一片浓密的沼泽里，那里根本无法射击，但夜里它们会到开阔地带觅食，如果他能开车把自己置于它们和沼泽之间，麦康伯就在开阔地有很好的机会。他不想在浓密的掩蔽处和麦康伯一起打水牛。他根本不想和麦康伯一同打水牛或做任何事，但他是个职业猎人，生平也和一些奇怪的人打过交道。如果今天他们能弄到水牛，接下来只剩犀牛了，可怜的那人就把危险猎物都经历过了，事情或许会好转。他就再也不会有了
to do with the woman and Macomber would get over that too. He must have gone through plenty of that before by the look of things. Poor beggar. He must have a way of getting over it. Well, it was the poor sod’s own bloody fault.
与那个女人有关的事，麦康伯也会渡过的。就凭外表看，他以前肯定也经历过不少这类事。可怜的家伙。他肯定有办法挺过去。唉，这该死的家伙活该。
He, Robert Wilson, carried a double size cot on safari to accommodate any windfalls he might receive. He had hupted for a certain clientele, the international, fast, sporting set, where the women did not feel they were getting their money’s worth unless they had shared that cot with the white hunter. He despised them when he was away from them although he liked some of them well enough at the time, but he made his living by them; and their standards were his standards as long as they were hiring him.
他，罗伯特·威尔逊，外出打猎时带着一张加大号的折叠床，以应付可能的意外之财。他为某类客人当过向导，那些国际化、奢侈而爱好运动的圈子，那里若女人们没和白猎人同睡一张床就觉得没值回票价。离开那些人时他鄙视他们，尽管当时他对其中的一些人也颇为喜欢，但他靠他们谋生；只要他们雇他，他们的标准就是他的标准。
They were his standards in all except the shooting. He had his own standards about the killing and they could live up to them or get someone else to hunt them. He knew, too, that they all respected him for this. This Macomber was an odd one though. Damned if he wasn’t. Now the wife. Well, the wife. Yes, the wife, Mm, the wife. Well, he’d dropped all that. He looked around at them. Macomber sat grim and furious. Margot smiled at him. She looked younger to-day, more innocent and fresher and not so professionally beautiful. What’s in her heart God knows, Wilson thought. She hadn’t talked much last night. At that it was a pleasure to see her.
他们在除射击以外的所有方面都按他的标准来行事。他在杀猎方面有自己的标准，猎物要么达到这些标准，要么就让别人去打。他也知道，他们都因此尊重他。这个麦康伯倒是个古怪的人。见鬼，他真是。现在说说那位妻子。唉，那位妻子。是的，妻子，嗯，妻子。好吧，他把那些都抛在一边了。他环顾四周。麦康伯面色阴沉，愤怒不已。玛歌对他微笑。她今天看起来更年轻了，更纯真、更有生气，也不像以前那样职业化的美丽。上帝知道她心里装的是什么，威尔逊想着。她昨晚话不多。就这一点来说，看见她令人愉快。
The motor car climbed up a slight rise and went on through the trees and then out into a grassy prairie-like opening and kept in the shelter of the trees along the edge, the driver going slowly and Wilson looking carefully out across the prairie and all along its far side. He stopped the car and studied the opening with his field glasses. Then he motioned the driver to go on and the car moved slowly along, the driver avoiding wart-hog holes and driving around the mud castles ants had built. Then, looking across the opening, Wilson suddenly turned and said:
汽车爬上一处缓坡，穿过树丛，随后驶入一片像草原一样的空地，沿着边缘在树荫下行进，司机开得很慢，Wilson 小心地向草原及其远侧张望。他停车，用望远镜端详那片空地。然后他示意司机继续前行，汽车慢慢移动，司机绕开疣猪的洞，绕过蚂蚁堆起的泥土小塔。接着，Wilson 望向空地，忽然转身说道：
‘By God, there they are!’
“该死，就在那里！”
And looking where he pointed, while the car jumped forward and Wilson spoke in rapid Swahili to the driver, Macomber saw three huge, black animals looking almost cylindrical in their long heaviness, like big black tank cars, moving at a gallop across the far edge of the open prairie. They moved at a stiff-necked, stiff-bodied gallop and he could see the upswept wide black horns on their heads as they galloped heads out; the heads not moving.
当他指着的方向时，汽车向前一跃，Wilson 用快速的斯瓦西里语对司机说话，Macomber 看见三只巨大的黑色动物，以其长而沉重近乎圆柱形的体态，在远处草原边缘飞奔着，像大型黑色坦克车。它们以僵直的颈项和僵硬的身体疾奔，他能看见它们扬起的宽阔黑角在奔跑中高高翘起；头部向外伸出，但不动。
‘They’re three old bulls,’ Wilson said. ‘We’ll cut them off before they get to the swamp.’
“是三头老公牛，”Wilson 说。“我们得在它们到达沼泽之前把它们截住。”
The car was going a wild forty-five miles an hour across the open, and as Macomber watched, the buffalo got bigger and bigger until he could see the grey, hairless, scabby look of one huge bull and how his neck was a part of his shoulders and the shiny black of his horns as he galloped a little behind the others that were strung out in that steady plunging gait; and then, the car swaving as though it had just jumped a road, they drew up close and he could see the plunging hugeness of the bull, and the dust in his sparsely haired hide, the wide boss of horn and his outstretched, wide-nostrilled muzzle, and he was raising his rifle when Wilson shouted, Not from the car, you fool!’ and he had no fear, only hatred of Wilson, while the brakes clamped on and the car skidded, ploughing sideways to an almost stop and Wilson was out on one side and he on the other, stumbling as his feet hit the still speeding-by of the earth, and then he was shooting at the bull as he moved away, hearing the bullets whunk into him, emptying his rifle at him as he moved steadily away, finally remembering to get his shots forward into the shoulder, and as he fumbled to re-load, he saw the bull was down. Down on his knees, his big head tossing, and seeing the other two still galloping he shot at the leader and hit him. He shot again and missed and he heard the carawonging roar as Wilson shot and saw the leading bull slide forward on to his nose.
汽车以狂野的四十五英里每小时在旷野上疾驰，麦康伯看着，那群水牛越来越大，直到他能看清一头巨大公牛灰色、无毛、布满痂的模样，能看清它的脖子与肩融为一体，以及它在稍稍落后于那些以那种稳定有力的步伐串成一列的同伴时，角上闪着的黑光；然后，车子像刚刚越过一条路般猛地摆动，他们靠得很近，他能看清那公牛扑击般的庞大，和它稀疏毛皮上的尘土，角的大块基座以及它伸展开、鼻孔宽阔的口鼻部，他正举枪时，威尔森喊道：“别在车里开，蠢货！”他心中没有恐惧，只有对威尔森的憎恨，刹车夹上，车子打滑，侧着犁到几乎停下，威尔森从一侧跳下，他也从另一侧跌下，脚踏在仍在疾驶的地面上踉跄，然后他朝那头公牛开枪，听见子弹“砰砰”打进它体内，在它稳步离去时把枪打空，终于记起来把枪口对准肩膀射击，当他忙着重新装弹时，他看见那公牛倒下了。 他跪着，大头摇摆着，看到另外两个人还在疾驰，他朝领头的那头射去，射中了。他又开了一枪，打偏了，他听到卡拉窝般的怒吼声，见到 Wilson 开了一枪，看见领头的公牛前滑倒，趴在鼻子上。
‘Get that other,’ Wilson said. ‘Now you’re shooting!’
“去打那头，”Wilson 说。“现在你会打了！”
But the other bull was moving steadily at the same gallop and he missed, throwing a spout of dirt, and Wilson missed and the dust rose in a cloud and Wilson shouted, ‘Come on. He’s too far!’ and grabbed his arm and they were in the car again, Macomber and Wilson hanging on to the sides and rocketing swayingly over the uneven ground, drawing up on the steady, plunging, heavy-necked, straight-moving gallop of the bull.
但另一头公牛仍以同样的疾驰稳步前进，他射偏了，扬起一股土花，Wilson 也射偏了，尘土卷成一团，Wilson 喊道：“快点。他太远了！”拉着他的手臂，他们又回到车上，Macomber 和 Wilson 抓着车侧，摇晃着像火箭一样在崎岖不平的地面上飞驰，靠近那头稳重、猛冲、脖子粗壮、直线前进的公牛的奔跑。
They were behind him and Macomber was filling his rifle, dropping shells onto the ground, jamming it, clearing the jam, then they were almost up with the bull when Wilson yelled ‘Stop!’ and the car skidded so that it almost swung over and Macomber fell forward on to his feet, slammed his bolt forward and fired as far forward as he could aim into the galloping, rounded black back, aimed and shot again, then again, and the bullets, all of them
他们在牛的后面，Macomber 正在给步枪装弹，弹壳掉到地上，卡壳了，又把卡壳弄开，然后他们几乎追上了公牛，Wilson 大喊“停！”汽车打滑，几乎翻过来，Macomber 向前扑到两脚上，把枪栓猛地往前推，尽可能向前瞄准那圆弧状、奔跑着的黑色背部开火，又瞄准再开了一枪，然后又一次，子弹，全部都
hitting, had no effect on the buffalo that he could see. Then Wilson shot, the roar deafening him, and he could see the bull stagger. Macomber shot again, aiming carefully, and down he came, onto his knees.
打击，对他看得见的水牛毫无作用。然后威尔逊开枪了，轰鸣声震聋了他的耳朵，他看到公牛踉跄。麦康伯又开了一枪，瞄得很准，公牛倒下了，跪在地上。
‘All right,’ Wilson said. ‘Nice work. That’s the three.’
“好样的，”威尔逊说。“干得漂亮。三头都解决了。”
Macomber felt a drunken elation.
麦康伯感到一阵醉一般的狂喜。
‘How many times did you shoot?’ he asked.
“你打了多少枪？”他问。
‘Just three,’ Wilson said. ‘You killed the first bull. The biggest one. I helped you finish the other two. Afraid they might have got into cover. You had them killed. I was just mopping up a little. You shot damn well.’
“就三头，”Wilson 说。“你打死了第一头。最大那头。我帮你收掉另外两头。怕它们会钻进灌木。你已经把它们打死了。我只是去收尾。你枪法真他妈好。”
‘Let’s go to the car,’ said Macomber. ‘I want a drink.’
“我们回车上去吧，”Macomber 说。“我想喝一杯。”
‘Got to finish off that buff first,’ Wilson told him. The buffalo was on his knees and he jerked his head furiously and bellowed in pig-eyed, roaring rage as they came toward him.
“得先把那头水牛收了，”Wilson 对他说。那头水牛跪在地上，猛地扭动脑袋，朝他们走来时发出猪眼般的咆哮与怒吼。
‘Watch he doesn’t get up,’ Wilson said. Then, ‘Get a little broadside and take him in the neck just behind the ear.’
“小心别让它站起来，”Wilson 说。然后，“上前一点，横着站，打它耳后脖子那儿。”
Macomber aimed carefully at the centre of the huge, jerking, rage-driven neck and shot. At the shot the head dropped forward.
马康伯小心地瞄准那粗大、抽搐着、被愤怒驱使的脖子中央并开了枪。枪响时，头颅向前掉了下去。
‘That does it,’ said Wilson. ‘Got the spine. They’re a hell of a looking thing, aren’t they?’
“就是这样，”威尔逊说。“打中了脊柱。它们看起来真他妈的吓人，不是吗？”
‘Let’s get the drink,’ said Macomber. In his life he had never felt so good.
“去喝一杯吧，”马康伯说。他这辈子从未有过如此畅快的感觉。
In the car Macomber’s wife sat very white faced. ‘You were marvellous, darling,’ she said to Macomber. ‘What a ride.’
在车里，马康伯的妻子脸色苍白地坐着。“你太了不起了，亲爱的，”她对马康伯说。“真是一段精彩的旅程。”
‘Was it rough?’ Wilson asked.
“凶险吗？”威尔逊问。
‘It was frightful. I’ve never been more frightened in my life.’
“太可怕了。我这一生从未如此惊恐过。”
‘Let’s all have a drink,’ Macomber said.
“我们都来喝一杯吧，”麦康伯说。
‘By all means,’ said Wilson. ‘Give it to the Memsahib.’ She drank the neat whisky from the flask and shuddered a little when she swallowed. She handed the flask to Macomber who handed it to Wilson.
“当然了，”威尔逊说。“把它给太太吧。”她从酒壶里直接喝下纯威士忌，吞下时微微颤了一下。她把酒壶递给麦康伯，麦康伯又递给了威尔逊。
‘It was frightfully exciting,’ she said. ‘It’s given me a dreadful headache. I didn’t know you were allowed to shoot them from cars though.’
“太刺激了，”她说。“我头疼得厉害。我还不知道可以在车里开枪打它们呢。”
‘No one shot from cars,’ said Wilson coldly.
“没有人在车里开枪。”威尔逊冷冷地说。
‘I mean chase them from cars.’
“我是说从车里追它们。”
‘Wouldn’t ordinarily,’ Wilson said. ‘Seemed sporting enough to
“通常不会这样，”威尔逊说。“不过看起来倒是挺有运动精神的”
me though while we were doing it. Taking more chance driving that way across the plain full of holes and one thing and another than hunting on foot. Buffalo could have charged us each time we shot if he liked. Gave him every chance. Wouldn’t mention it to anyone though. It’s illegal if that’s what you mean.’
“我倒是觉得我们那样开车穿过满是坑洞的平原去猎，比步行狩猎更冒险。水牛每次我们开枪都可以冲过来。给了它们每次的机会。不过我不会跟任何人提起的。你如果是说那是非法的话，那就是非法。”
‘It seemed very unfair to me,’ Margot said, ‘chasing those big helpless things in a motor car.’
“在我看来那很不公平，”玛戈说，“在汽车里追那些又大又无助的东西。”
‘Did it?’ said Wilson.
“是吗？”威尔逊说。
‘What would happen if they heard about it in Nairobi?’
“如果纳罗比那边知道了会怎么样？”
‘I’d lose my licence for one thing. Other unpleasantnesses,’ Wilson said, taking a drink from the flask. ‘I’d be out of business.’
“我会丢掉执照，还有别的麻烦，”威尔逊说着，从水壶里喝了一口。“我会失去生意。”
‘Really?’
“真的？”
‘Yes, really.’
“是的，真的。”
‘Well,’ said Macomber, and he smiled for the first time all day. ‘Now she has something on you.’
“嗯，”马克伯默说着，今天这是他第一次微笑。“现在她有了把柄。”
‘You have such a pretty way of putting things, Francis,’ Margot Macomber said. Wilson looked at them both. If a four-letter man marries a five-letter woman, he was thinking, what number of letters would their children be? What he said was 'We lost a gunbearer. Did you notice it?’
“你说话真会拐弯，弗朗西斯，”玛格·麦康伯说。威尔逊看着他们俩。他心想：如果一个四个字母的男人娶了一个五个字母的女人，他们的孩子会有多少个字母？他说的是：“我们丢了一个枪仆。你们注意到了吗？”
‘My God, no,’ Macomber said.
“我的天，不，”麦康伯说。
‘Here he comes,’ Wilson said. ‘He’s all right. He must have fallen off when we left the first bull.’
“他来了，”威尔逊说。“他没事。我们离开第一头公牛的时候他一定摔下去了。”
Approaching them was the middle-aged gun-bearer, limping along in his knitted cap, khaki tunic, shorts and rubber sandals, gloomyfaced and disgusted looking. As he came up he called out to Wilson in Swahili and they all saw the change in the white hunter’s face.
向他们走来的是那个中年枪仆，戴着针织帽，穿着卡其色长衫、短裤和橡胶凉鞋，一瘸一拐的，脸色阴郁、显得厌烦。他走近时用斯瓦希里语向威尔逊喊了几句，他们都看到了白人猎人脸上的变化。
‘What does he say?’ asked Margot.
“他说什么？”玛格说。
‘He says the first bull got up and went into the bush,’ Wilson said with no expression in his voice.
“他说第一头公牛起来跑进灌木丛了，”威尔逊说，声音平淡无表情。
‘Oh,’ said Macomber blankly.
“哦，”麦康伯茫然地说。
‘Then it’s going to be just like the lion,’ said Margot, full of anticipation.
“那就会和狮子一样了，”玛格充满期待地说。
‘It’s not going to be a damned bit like the lion,’ Wilson told her. ‘Did you want another drink, Macomber?’
“这根本不会像那只狮子，”威尔逊对她说。“麦考伯，你还想再来一杯吗？”
‘Thanks, yes,’ Macomber said. He expected the feeling he had had about the lion to come back but it did not. For the first time in his life he really felt wholly without fear. Instead of fear he had a feeling of definite elation.
“谢谢，好。”麦考伯说。他以为关于那只狮子的感觉会再次袭来，但并没有。人生中第一次，他真的完全没有了恐惧。取而代之的是一种确切的兴高采烈的感觉。
‘We’ll go and have a look at the second bull,’ Wilson said. ‘I’ll tell the driver to put the car in the shade.’
“我们去看看第二头公牛，”威尔逊说。“我会告诉司机把车停到阴凉处。”
‘What are you going to do?’ asked Margot Macomber.
“你打算做什么？”玛戈·麦考伯问。
‘Take a look at the buff,’ Wilson said.
“看看那头水牛，”Wilson 说。
‘I’ll come.’
“我去。”
‘Come along.’
“跟上来。”
The three of them walked over to where the second buffalo bulked blackly in the open, head forward on the grass, the massive horns swung wide.
三人走到那头在空地上黑沉沉的大水牛跟前，头伏在草地上，硕大的角向外张开。
‘He’s a very good head,’ Wilson said. ‘That’s close to a fifty-inch spread.’
“他的脑袋很好，”威尔逊说。“这接近五十英寸的角距。”
Macomber was looking at him with delight.
麦考伯高兴地看着他。
‘He’s hateful looking,’ said Margot. ‘Can’t we go into the shade?’
“他长得讨厌，”玛格说。“我们不能到树荫下去吗？”
‘Of course,’ Wilson said. ‘Look,’ he said to Macomber, and pointed. ‘See that patch of bush?’
“当然可以，”威尔逊说。“看，”他说着对麦考伯指了指。“看到那片灌木丛了吗？”
‘Yes.’
“是的。”
‘That’s where the first bull went in. The gun-bearer said when he fell off the bull was down. He was watching us helling along and the other two buff galloping. When he looked up there was the bull up and looking at him. Gun-bearer ran like hell and the bull went off slowly into that bush.’
“那头公牛就是从那里扎进去的。抬枪手说当它从公牛身上摔下来时公牛是趴下的。他看着我们沿着山坳跑，另外两头水牛在疾驰。等他抬头时，那头公牛站起来朝他看。抬枪手像疯了一样跑开了，而那头公牛慢慢地钻进那片灌木丛里。”
‘Can we go in after him now?’ asked Macomber eagerly.
“我们现在可以进去追它吗？”马康伯渴望地问。
Wilson looked at him appraisingly. Damned if this isn’t a strange one, he thought. Yesterday he’s scared sick and to-day he’s a ruddy fire-eater.
威尔逊打量着他。真该死，这人还真奇怪，他心想。昨天他吓得要命，今天却成了个该死的逞能者。
‘No, we’ll give him a while.’
“不会，我们再给他一点时间。”
‘Let’s please go into the shade,’ Margot said. Her face was white and she looked ill.
“请到树荫下去吧，”Margot 说。她脸色发白，显得很不舒服。
They made their way to the car where it stood under a single wide-spreading tree and all climbed in.
他们走到停在一棵大树下的车旁，一起爬了上去。
‘Chances are he’s dead in there,’ Wilson remarked. ‘After a little we’ll have a look.’
“很可能他已经死在里面了，”Wilson 说。“过一会儿我们去看看。”
Macomber felt a wild unreasonable happiness that he had never known before.
马科姆感到一种从未有过的疯狂而无理的幸福。
‘By God, that was a chase,’ he said. ‘I’ve never felt any such feeling. Wasn’t it marvellous, Margot?’
“天哪，那真是一场追逐，”他说。“我从未有过这种感觉。太神奇了，不是吗，玛戈？”
‘I hated it.’
“我恨它。”
‘Why?’
“为什么？”
‘I hated it,’ she said bitterly. ‘I loathed it.’
“我恨它，”她苦涩地说。“我厌恶它。”
‘You know, I don’t think I’d ever be afraid of anything again,’ Macomber said to Wilson. ‘Something happened in me after we first saw the buff and started after him. Like a dam bursting. It was pure excitement.’
“你知道，我想我以后再也不会害怕任何事了，”麦考伯对威尔逊说。“在我们第一次看到那头犀牛并开始追它之后，我内心发生了变化。就像大坝决堤。那是纯粹的兴奋。”
‘Cleans out your liver,’ said Wilson. Damn funny things happen to people.’
“把你肝脏都清清爽爽，”威尔逊说。“该死的，有趣的事会发生在别人身上。”
Macomber’s face was shining. ‘You know, something did happen to me,’ he said. ‘I feel absolutely different.’
麦考伯的脸在发光。“你知道，确实发生了些事，”他说。“我感觉完全不一样了。”
His wife said nothing and eyed him strangely. She was sitting far back in the seat and Macomber was sitting forward talking to Wilson who turned sideways talking over the back of the front seat.
他妻子什么也没说，奇怪地看着他。她坐在座位的后面很远处，马科姆伯坐到前面，和威尔逊说话，威尔逊转过身越过前座的靠背对着他说话。
‘You know, I’d like to try another lion,’ Macomber said. ‘I’m really not afraid of them now. After all, what can they do to you?’
“你知道，我想再试一次狮子，”马科姆伯说。“我现在真的不怕它们了。毕竟，它们能对你做什么呢？”
‘That’s it,’ said Wilson. ‘Worst one can do is kill you. How does it go? Shakespeare. Damned good. See if I can remember. Oh, damned good. Used to quote it to myself at one time. Let’s see. “By my troth, I care not; a man can die but once; we owe God a death, and let it go which way it will he that dies this year is quit for the next.” Damned fine, eh?’
“就是这样，”威尔逊说。“它们最多也就把你杀了。怎么说来着？莎士比亚。太妙了。看我还能不能记得。哦，太妙了。以前我常常对自己引用这句。让我想想。‘照我说，我不在乎；人只会死一次；我们欠上帝一死，任它往哪个方向去吧，那今年死去的人明年就免了。’真不错，不是吗？”
He was very embarrassed, having brought out this thing he had lived by, but he had seen men come of age before and it always moved him. It was not a matter of their twenty-first birthday.
他说出这句他以此为生的话时非常尴尬，但他曾见过男人在这句话下成长，这总是让他感动。这并不是他们二十一岁生日的问题。
It had taken a strange chance of hunting, a sudden precipitation into action without opportunity for worrying beforehand, to bring this about with Macomber, but regardless of how it had happened it had most certainly happened. Look at the beggar now, Wilson thought. Sometimes all their lives. Their figures stay boyish when they’re fifty. The great American boy-men. Damned strange people. But he liked this Macomber now. Damned strange fellow. Probably meant the end of cuckoldry too. Well, that would be a damned good thing. Damned good thing. Beggar had probably been afraid all his life. Don’t know what started it. But over now. Hadn’t had time to be afraid with the buff. That and being angry too. Motor car too. Motor cars made it familiar. Be a damn fire-eater now. He’d seen it in the war work the same way. More of a change than any loss of virginity. Fear gone like an operation. Something else grew in its place. Main thing a man had. Made him into a man. Women knew it too. No bloody fear.
把麦康伯变成这样，是一次奇怪的狩猎偶然——突然投入行动，来不及事先担心——不管怎么发生的，确实发生了。看看这个懦夫吧，威尔逊想。有时终其一生也是如此。他们的身材到五十岁仍显孩童般。伟大的美式少年男人。该死的奇怪人。但他现在喜欢这个麦康伯。该死的奇怪家伙。可能也意味着戴绿帽子的日子结束了。嗯，那会是件该死的好事。该死的好事。这个懦夫大概一辈子都在怕。不知道是什么触发的。但现在结束了。打羚羊的时候没来得及害怕。那还有愤怒。还有汽车。汽车让这种事变得熟悉。现在会变成个该死的勇夫。他在战争中也见过同样的变化。比任何失去童贞的变化都大。恐惧像手术一样消失了。取而代之的是别的东西。男人最重要的东西。把他变成了男人。女人们也知道这一点。毫无他妈的恐惧。
From the far corner of the seat Margaret Macomber looked at the
从座位远角，玛格丽特·麦康伯望着
two of them. There was no change in Wilson. She saw Wilson as she had seen him the day before when she had first realized what his great talent was. But she saw the change in Francis Macomber now.
两个里头的一个。威尔逊没有任何变化。她看到威尔逊，像前一天第一次意识到他那伟大才能时所看到的一样。但她现在看到了弗朗西斯·麦康伯的变化。
‘Do you have that feeling of happiness about what’s going to happen?’ Macomber asked, still exploring his new wealth.
“你对将要发生的事有没有那种幸福的感觉？”麦康伯问，仍在探索他的新财富。
‘You’re not supposed to mention it,’ Wilson said, looking in the other’s face. ‘Much more fashionable to say you’re scared. Mind you, you’ll be scared too, plenty of times.’
“你别提那东西，”威尔逊说着，看着对方的脸。“说你害怕更加流行。别忘了，你也会害怕的，很多次。”
‘But you have a feeling of happiness about action to come?’
“可是你对即将到来的行动有幸福的感觉吗？”
‘Yes,’ said Wilson. ‘There’s that. Doesn’t do to talk too much about all this. Talk the whole thing away. No pleasure in anything if you mouth it up too much.’
“是的，”威尔逊说。“确实如此。不要把这些事说得太多。话一多就把一切都说没了。要是把嘴一开，什么都没了乐趣。”
‘You’re both talking rot,’ said Margot. ‘Just because you’ve chased some helpless animals in a motor car you talk like heroes.’
“你们两个胡说八道，”玛格特说。“仅仅因为你们坐着车追过一些无助的动物，就装得像英雄似的。”
‘Sorry,’ said Wilson. ‘I have been gassing too much.’ She’s worried about it already, he thought.
“抱歉，”威尔逊说。“我确实废话太多了。”他心想，她已经在为此担心了。
‘If you don’t know what we’re talking about, why not keep out of it?’ Macomber asked his wife.
“既然你不知道我们在说什么，何不闭嘴别参合进来？”麦考伯问他的妻子。
‘You’ve gotten awfully brave, awfully suddenly,’ his wife said contemptuously, but her contempt was not secure. She was very afraid of something.
“你突然变得勇敢得可怕了，”他的妻子轻蔑地说，但她的轻蔑并不牢靠。她很害怕某些东西。
Macomber laughed, a very natural laugh. ‘You know I have,’ he said. ‘I really have.’
麦康伯笑了，笑得很自然。“你知道的，我确实变了，”他说。“我真的变了。”
‘Isn’t it sort of late?’ Margot said bitterly. Because she had done the best she could for many years back and the way they were together now was no one person’s fault.
“这是不是有点晚了？”玛戈特苦涩地说。因为多年来她已经尽了最大努力，而他们现在的相处方式并不是某个人的错。
‘Not for me,’ said Macomber.
“对我来说不晚，”麦康伯说。
Margot said nothing but sat back in the corner of the seat.
玛戈什么也没说，只是靠在座位的角落里。
‘Do you think we’ve given him time enough?’ Macomber asked Wilson cheerfully.
“你觉得我们给他足够的时间了吗？”麦攻伯高高兴兴地问威尔逊。
‘We might have a look,’ Wilson said. ‘Have you any solids left?’
“我们可以去看看，”威尔逊说，“你们还有固体食物吗？”
"The gun-bearer has some.’
“枪夫有一些。”
Wilson called in Swahili and the older gun-bearer, who was skinning out one of the heads, straightened up, pulled a box of solids out of his pocket and brought them over to Macomber, who filled his magazine and put the remaining shells in his pocket.
威尔逊用斯瓦西里语叫了几声，正在剥一颗头皮的那个年长的携枪手站直身子，从口袋里掏出一盒子弹递给马康伯，马康伯把弹匣装满，把剩下的弹壳放进了口袋。
‘You might as well shoot the Springfield,’ Wilson said. ‘You’re
“不如把斯普林菲尔德枪也一起打了，”威尔逊说。“你还
used to it. We’ll leave the Mannlicher in the car with the Memsahib. Your gun-bearer can carry your heavy gun. I’ve this damned cannon. Now let me tell you about them.’ He had saved this until the last because he did not want to worry Macomber. ‘When a buff comes he comes with his head high and thrust straight out. The boss of the horns covers any sort of brain shot. The only shot is straight into the nose. The only other shot is into his chest, or, if you’re to one side, into the neck or the shoulders. After they’ve been hit once they take a hell of a lot of killing. Don’t try anything fancy. Take the easiest shot there is. They’ve finished skinning out that head now. Should we get started?’
已经习惯了。曼利彻步枪就留在车里跟那位孟萨伊布女士一起。你的枪夫可以替你扛那支重枪。我带着这该死的大口径枪。现在让我告诉你它们的情况。’ 他把这话留到最后说，因为不想让马考伯担心。‘当水牛冲过来时，它是昂着头把脑袋直伸出来的。那对角的顶端挡住了任何对脑袋的射击。唯一的射击方位是直射鼻子。另一个可行的是射胸口，或者如果你在一侧，就射颈部或肩膀。他们第一次被击中以后，要把它们杀死可要费一番功夫。别玩花活儿。就打最容易的一枪。他们现在已经把那头的皮剥干净了。我们开始吧？’
He called to the gun-bearers, who came up wiping their hands, and the older one got into the back.
他喊着给持枪手们，那些人擦着手上来，年纪较大的一个上了后座。
‘I’ll only take Kongoni,’ Wilson said. ‘The other can watch to keep the birds away.’
“我只打康戈尼，”威尔逊说。“另一个留着监视，别让鸟儿来捣乱。”
As the car moved slowly across the open space toward the island of brushy trees that ran in a tongue of foliage along a dry watercourse that cut the open swale, Macomber felt his heart pounding and his mouth was dry again, but it was excitement, not fear.
汽车慢慢驶过空地，朝着沿着干涸水道伸出的、成片灌木丛的小岛走去，那水道切穿了开阔的洼地。马科姆感到心脏怦怦直跳，口又干了，但那是兴奋，不是恐惧。
‘Here’s where he went in,’ Wilson said. Then to the gun-bearer in Swahili, ‘Take the blood spoor.’
“他就是从这儿进去的，”威尔逊说。随后用斯瓦西里语对抬枪手说：“取血迹追踪。”
The car was parallel to the patch of brush. Macomber, Wilson and the gun-bearer got down. Macomber, looking back, saw his wife, with the rifle by her side, looking at him. He waved to her and she did not wave back.
