汽车与那片灌木并行停下。马科姆、威尔逊和抬枪手下了车。马科姆回头看到妻子把步枪放在身旁望着他。他朝她挥手，她却没有回挥。
The brush was very thick ahead and the ground was dry. The middle-aged gun-bearer was sweating heavily and Wilson had his hat down over his eyes and his red neck showed just ahead of Macomber. Suddenly the gun-bearer said something in Swahili to Wilson and ran forward.
灌木在前面很浓，地面很干。那中年扛枪的汗流浃背，威尔逊把帽檐压到眼睛下面，红脖子从麦考姆伯前面露出来。忽然扛枪的用斯瓦西里语对威尔逊说了些什么，然后向前跑去。
‘He’s dead in there,’ Wilson said. ‘Good work,’ and he turned to grip Macomber’s hand and as they shook hands, grinning at each other, the gun-bearer shouted wildly and they saw him coming out of the bush sideways, fast as a crab, and the bull coming, nose out, mouth tight closed, blood dripping, massive head straight out, coming in a charge, his little pig eyes bloodshot as he looked at them. Wilson, who was ahead, was kneeling shooting, and Macomber, as he fired, unhearing his shot in the roaring of Wilson’s gun, saw fragments like slate burst from the huge boss of the horns, and the
“他在里面死了，”威尔逊说。“干得好。”他转过身去握住麦考姆伯的手，当他们相互握手、相视咧嘴笑时，扛枪的狂喊起来，他们看到他像螃蟹一样横着跑出灌木丛，牛也冲了出来，鼻子伸出，嘴紧闭，血在滴，粗大的头直直伸出，正朝着他们冲来，那小小的猪眼血丝暴露，盯着他们。走在前面的威尔逊跪着开枪，麦考姆伯也开了枪，在听不见自己枪声的同时被威尔逊枪声的轰鸣淹没，他看到像板岩一样的碎片从巨大的牛角突起处炸开，且
head jerked; he shot again at the wide nostrils and saw the horns jolt again and fragments fly, and he did not see Wilson now and, aiming carefully, shot again with the buffalo’s huge bulk almost on him and his rifle almost level with the coming head, nose out, and he could see the little wicked eyes and the head started to lower, and he felt a sudden white-hot, blinding flash explode inside his head and that was all he ever felt.
头猛地一抖；他又朝那宽大的鼻孔开了一枪，看到角又一震，碎片飞溅，他此刻没有看到 Wilson，瞄准稳当又开了一枪，水牛那巨大的身躯几乎压到他身上，他的步枪几乎与迎面而来的头齐平，鼻子伸出，他能看到那邪恶的小眼睛，头开始低下，他感到一阵白热、致盲的闪光在脑内爆炸，那就是他所感受到的一切。
Wilson had ducked to one side to get in a shoulder shot. Macomber had stood solid and shot for the nose, shooting a touch high each time and hitting the heavy horns, splintering and chipping them like hitting a slate roof, and Mrs. Macomber in the car, had shot at the buffalo with the 6.5 Mannlicher as it seemed about to gore Macomber and had hit her husband about two inches up and a little to one side of the base of his skull.
Wilson 侧身躲开以便打肩部一枪。Macomber 站得稳固，瞄准鼻子，每次都打得稍高，击中了厚重的角，使之像砸到石板屋顶一样裂开、崩碎；而坐在车里的 Mrs. Macomber 在水牛似乎要用角刺戳 Macomber 时，用 6.5 Mannlicher 向水牛开了枪，子弹打在她丈夫颅底基部上方约两英寸并稍偏一侧的地方。
Francis Macomber lay now, face down, not two yards from where the buffalo lay on his side and his wife knelt over him with Wilson beside her.
Francis Macomber 此刻俯卧着，脸朝下，离那头侧躺着的水牛不到两码，他的妻子跪在他身旁，Wilson 站在她旁边。
‘I wouldn’t turn him over,’ Wilson said.
“我不会把他翻过来，”Wilson 说。
The woman was crying hysterically.
那个女人歇斯底里地哭着。
‘I’d get back in the car,’ Wilson said. ‘Where’s the rifle?’
“我还是回车里去，”威尔逊说。“步枪在哪儿？”
She shook her head, her face contorted. The gun-bearer picked up the rifle.
她摇着头，脸扭曲着。持枪的人捡起了步枪。
‘Leave it as it is,’ said Wilson. Then, ‘Go get Abdulla so that he may witness the manner of the accident.’
“就那样放着，”威尔逊说。然后，“去把阿卜杜拉叫来，让他作证这起事故的经过。”
He knelt down, took a handkerchief from his pocket, and spread it over Francis Macomber’s crew-cropped head where it lay. The blood sank into the dry, loose earth.
他跪下，从口袋里掏出一块手帕，盖在弗朗西斯·麦康伯那剃成寸头的头上，头颅就那样躺着。血渗进了干燥松散的土壤。
Wilson stood up and saw the buffalo on his side, his legs out, his thinly-haired belly crawling with ticks. ‘Hell of a good bull,’ his brain registered automatically. ‘A good fifty inches, or better. Better.’ He called to the driver and told him to spread a blanket over the body and stay by it. Then he walked over to the motor car where the woman sat crying in the corner.
威尔逊站起身，看见水牛倒在他这边，腿伸开，稀疏毛发的腹部爬满了蜱虫。“真是头好公牛，”他的大脑自动记录道。“有五十英寸，或更大。更大。”他喊司机过来，告诉他在尸体上盖一条毯子并守着。然后他走向停着的汽车，女人蜷在角落里哭泣。
‘That was a pretty thing to do,’ he said in a toneless voice. ‘He would have left you too.’
“那可真漂亮的事干得，”他用平淡的声音说。“他也会离开你的。”
‘Stop it,’ she said.
“别说了，”她说。
‘Of course it’s an accident,’ he said. ‘I know that.’
“当然是意外，”他说。“我知道。”
‘Stop it,’ she said.
“别这样，”她说。
‘Don’t worry,’ he said. ‘There will be a certain amount of
“别担心，”他说，“会有一定程度的”
unpleasantness but I will have some photographs taken that will be very useful at the inquest. There’s the testimony of the gun-bearers and the driver too. You’re perfectly all right.’
不愉快的事，但我会让人照些照片，在验尸时会很有用。还有枪手和司机的证词。你完全没事。
‘Stop it,’ she said.
“别闹了，”她说。
‘There’s a hell of a lot to be done,’ he said. ‘And I’ll have to send a truck off to the lake to wireless for a plane to take the three of us into Nairobi. Why didn’t you poison him? That’s what they do in England.’
“有一大堆事要做，”他说。“我还得派辆卡车到湖边去无线电呼叫飞机，把我们三个人送到内罗毕。你为什么不毒死他？英国人都这么干的。”
‘Stop it. Stop it. Stop it,’ the woman cried.
“别这样。别这样。别这样，”那个女人喊道。
Wilson looked at her with his flat blue eyes.
威尔逊用他那双冰冷的蓝眼睛看着她。
‘I’m through now,’ he said. ‘I was a little angry. I’d begun to like your husband.’
“我现在完了，”他说。“我有点生气。我开始喜欢你丈夫了。”
‘Oh, please stop it,’ she said. ‘Please, please stop it.’
“哦，求你别这样，”她说。“求你，求你别这样。”
‘That’s better,’ Wilson said. ‘Please is much better. Now I’ll stop.’
“这好多了，”威尔逊说。“请要好得多。现在我会住嘴了。”

THE CAPITAL OF THE WORLD
世界之都

Madrid is full of boys named Paco, which is the diminutive of the name Francisco, and there is a Madrid joke about a father who came to Madrid and inserted an advertisement in the personal columns of El Liberal which said: Paco meet me at Hotel Montana noon Tuesday all is forgiven papa, and how a squadron of Guardia Civil had to be called out to disperse the eight hundred young men who answered the advertisement. But this Paco, who waited on table at the Pension Luarca, had no father to forgive him, nor anything for the father to forgive. He had two older sisters who were chambermaids at the Luarca, who had gotten their place through coming from the same village as a former Luarca chambermaid who had proven hardworking and honest and hence given her village and its products a good name; and these sisters had paid his way on the autobus to Madrid and gotten him his job as an apprentice waiter. He came from a village in a part of Extremadura where conditions were incredibly primitive, food scarce, and comforts unknown, and he had worked hard ever since he could remember.
马德里到处都是叫 Paco 的男孩，Paco 是 Francisco 这个名字的昵称。马德里有个笑话，说有个父亲到马德里来，在《El Liberal》的征婚栏里登了条广告：Paco 周二中午在 Montana 旅馆见我，一切已被原谅——爸爸。结果不得不出动一中队的 Guardia Civil 去驱散回答广告的八百名青年。但这位在 Luarca 旅馆当侍者的 Paco，并没有一个需要被原谅的父亲，也没有什么需要父亲去原谅的事。他有两个在 Luarca 当女佣的姐姐，她们是通过与一位来自同一村庄、在 Luarca 被证明勤劳诚实的前任女佣的推荐得到这份工作的；因此她们为自己的村庄和出产赢得了好名声。这两个姐姐出钱让他乘公交到马德里，并帮他在那儿找到了学徒侍应的工作。他来自西班牙 Extremadura 一处条件极其原始、食物匮乏、从未有过舒适生活的村庄，从他记事起就一直很努力地干活。
He was a well built boy with very black, rather curly hair, good teeth and a skin that his sisters envied, and he had a ready and unpuzzled smile. He was fast on his feet and did his work well and he loved his sisters, who seemed beautiful and unsophisticated; he loved Madrid, which was still an unbelievable place, and he loved his work which, done under bright lights, with clean linen, the wearing of evening clothes, and abundant food in the kitchen, seemed romantically beautiful.
他是个身材匀称的男孩，头发很黑，有点卷，牙齿很好，皮肤让他的姐妹们嫉妒，他总是带着随和而不困惑的微笑。脚步敏捷，工作做得很好，他爱他的姐妹们，认为她们既美丽又不世故；他爱马德里，那仍像个难以置信的地方；他也爱他的工作——在明亮的灯光下，干净的亚麻布，穿着晚礼服，厨房里有丰盛的食物，工作显得浪漫而美好。
There were from eight to a dozen other people who lived at the Luarca and ate in the dining-room, but for Paco, the youngest of the three waiters who served at table, the only ones who really existed were the bull-fighters.
住在卢阿尔卡旅馆并在餐厅吃饭的人有八到十二个不等，但对帕科来说——三个餐厅服务员中最年轻的——真正存在的只有斗牛士们。
Second-rate matadors lived at that pension because the address in the Calle San Jeronimo was good, the food was excellent and the room and board was cheap. It is necessary for a bull-fighter to give the appearance, if not of prosperity, at least of respectability, since
那些二流的斗牛士住在那家寄宿旅馆，因为位于圣赫罗尼莫街的地址好，食物极佳，食宿便宜。对斗牛士来说，看起来至少要有体面，虽然不必富有，这是必要的，因为...
decorum and dignity rank above courage as the virtues most highly prized in Spain, and bull-fighters stayed at the Luarca until their last pesetas were gone. There is no record of any bull-fighter having left the Luarca for a better or more expensive hotel; second-rate bullfighters never became first rate; but the descent from the Luarca was swift since anyone could stay there who was making anything at all and a bill was never presented to a guest unasked until the woman who ran the place knew that the case was hopeless.
在西班牙，礼仪与尊严被视为比勇气更重要的美德，斗牛士们会在卢阿尔卡住到最后一枚佩塞塔花光为止。没有任何记录显示有斗牛士为了更好或更昂贵的旅馆而离开卢阿尔卡；二流的斗牛士从未成为一流；但从卢阿尔卡走下坡路是迅速的，因为任何有一点收入的人都能在那里住，而且在经营那家旅馆的女人确信无可挽回之前，从未主动向客人出示账单。
At this time there were three full matadors living at the Luarca as well as two very good picadors, and one excellent banderillero. The Luarca was luxury for the picadors and the banderilleros who, with their families in Seville, required lodging in Madrid during the spring season; but they were well paid and in the fixed employ of fighters who were heavily contracted during the coming season and the three of these subalterns would probably make much more apiece than any of the three matadors. Of the three matadors one was ill and trying to conceal it; one had passed his short vogue as a novelty; and the third was a coward.
那时卢阿尔卡住着三位正式的斗牛士，另外还有两名很好的骑矛手和一名出色的舞镖手。对于那些春季赛季需要在马德里住宿而家人住在塞维利亚的骑矛手和舞镖手来说，卢阿尔卡算是奢侈之所；但他们报酬丰厚，并受雇于在即将到来的赛季中签有重合同的斗牛士，这三名下属每人可能赚得比三位斗牛士中任何一人都多。三位斗牛士中有一位生病并试图隐瞒；一位已过其作为新奇人物的短暂风头；第三位是个懦夫。
The coward had at one time, until he had received a peculiar atrocious horn wound in the lower abdomen at the start of his first season as a full matador, been exceptionally brave and remarkably skilful and he still had many of the hearty mannerisms of his days of success. He was jovial to excess and laughed constantly with and without provocation. He had, when successful, been very addicted to practical jokes, but he had given them up now. They took an assurance that he did not feel. This matador had an intelligent, very open face and he carried himself with much style.
这个懦夫曾在一度——直到他在作为正式斗牛士的第一个赛季开始时在下腹部受到一种特殊而残酷的角伤——一直非常勇敢且技艺非凡，而且他仍保留着许多昔日成功时那种健壮的举止。他过于快活，常常无端或有因地大笑。当他得意时，极喜欢恶作剧，但现在已经不再做了。那些玩笑需要他不具备的自信。这位斗牛士面容聪慧而十分开阔，举止颇有风度。
The matador who was ill was careful never to show it and was meticulous about eating a little of all the dishes that were presented at the table. He had a great many handkerchiefs which he laundered himself in his room and, lately, he had been selling his fighting suits. He had sold one, cheaply, before Christmas and another in the first week of April. They had been very expensive suits, had always been well kept and he had one more. Before he had become ill he had been a very promising, even a sensational, fighter and, while he himself could not read, he had clippings which said that in his debut in Madrid he had been better than Belmonte. He ate alone at a small table and looked up very little.
那位生病的斗牛士小心翼翼地从不显露病态，并且对桌上呈上的每一道菜都认真地只吃一点。他有很多手帕，都自己在房间里洗，而且最近开始卖他的斗牛服。他在圣诞节前以低价卖过一套，又在四月的第一周卖过一套。那些都是非常昂贵的服装，一直保养得很好，他还有一套。在生病之前，他是个很有前途，甚至是轰动一时的斗牛士，虽然他自己不会读书，但他保存着剪报，上面说他在马德里的初次登场比 Belmonte 更出色。他独自坐在一张小桌旁，很少抬头。
The matador who had once been a novelty was very short and
曾经被视为新奇事物的那位斗牛士个子很矮，
brown and very dignified. He also ate alone at a separate table and he smiled very rarely and never laughed. He came from Valladolid, where the people are extremely serious, and he was a capable matador; but his style had become old-fashioned before he had ever succeeded in endearing himself to the public through his virtues, which were courage and a calm capability, and his name on a poster would draw no one to a bull ring. His novelty had been that he was so short that he could barely see over the bull’s withers, but there were other short fighters, and he had never succeeded in imposing himself on the public’s fancy.
棕色的，十分庄重。他也单独在一张桌子上吃饭，很少微笑，绝不大笑。他来自巴利亚多利德，那里的人民极为严肃，他曾是个有能力的斗牛士；但在他的美德——勇气和冷静的能力——还未能使他为公众所喜爱之前，他的风格就已显得过时，海报上的他的名字不会吸引任何人到斗牛场去看。他的独特之处在于个子很矮，几乎看不见公牛的肩背，但也有其他矮个的斗牛士，而且他从未能让公众对他产生好感。
Of the picadors one was a thin, hawk-faced, grey-haired man, lightly built but with legs and arms like iron, who always wore cattlemen’s boots under his trousers, drank too much every evening and gazed amorously at any woman in the pension. The other was huge, dark, brown-faced, good-looking, with black hair like an Indian and enormous hands. Both were great picadors although the first was reputed to have lost much of his ability through drink and dissipation, and the second was said to be too headstrong and quarrelsome to stay with any matador more than a single season.
其中一个骑马持矛刺手瘦削，鹰勾脸，灰发，身材轻巧但手脚如铁，裤子外总是穿着牛仔靴，每晚饮酒过度，并且对旅馆里任何女人都含情脉脉地凝视。另一个则巨大，肤色黝黑，面容英俊，黑发像印第安人，双手粗大。两人都是出色的骑马持矛刺手，尽管第一个人据说因酗酒和放荡而丧失了许多本领，第二个人则被传为性情太刚烈、好争吵，无法在任何一位斗牛士身边待超过一个赛季。
The banderillero was middle-aged, grey, cat-quick in spite of his years and, sitting at the table, he looked a moderately prosperous business man. His legs were still good for this season, and when they should go he was intelligent and experienced enough to keep regularly employed for a long time. The difference would be that when his speed of foot would be gone he would always be frightened where now he was assured and calm in the ring and out of it.
那名插彩箭手年届中年，尽管年岁已高却灰发敏捷，坐在桌旁显得像个小有成就的商人。他的腿在这个赛季里依然灵便，而当腿脚不行时，他足够聪明且经验丰富，能够长期保持规律的工作。不同之处在于，当他的脚步速度消失时，他将总是变得胆怯，而现在他在斗牛场内外却是自信而沉着的。
On this evening every one had left the dining-room except the hawk-faced picador who drank too much, the birthmarked-faced auctioneer of watches at the fairs and festivals of Spain, who also drank too much, and two priests from Galicia who were sitting at a corner table and drinking if not too much certainly enough. At that time wine was included in the price of the room and board at the Luarca, and the waiters had just brought fresh bottles of Valdepeñas to the tables of the auctioneer, then to the picador and, finally, to the two priests.
那天晚上除了面容像鹰的斗马者（他喝得太多）、在西班牙各地集市和节日拍卖手表的那位有胎记的拍卖师（他也喝得太多），以及坐在角落桌旁、喝得如果说不上太多至少也够劲的两位来自加利西亚的神父外，饭厅里的人都走光了。那时在 Luarca 旅馆的房价和膳食里已包含葡萄酒，侍者们刚把新开的一瓶瓶 Valdepeñas 端到拍卖师的桌上，然后是斗马者的桌，最后才到那两位神父的桌前。
The three waiters stood at the end of the room. It was the rule of the house that they should remain on duty until the diners whose tables they were responsible for should all have left, but the one who served the table of the two priests had an appointment to go to an
三个侍者站在房间的一端。旅馆的规矩是，侍者必须值班直到他负责的客人桌上的所有人都离开，但负责那两位神父桌的那位约好要去参加一个
Anarcho-Syndicalist meeting and Paco had agreed to take over his table for him.
无政府工团主义者的集会，Paco 已同意帮他顶替照看那张桌子。
Upstairs the matador who was ill was lying face down on his bed alone. The matador who was no longer a novelty was sitting looking out of his window preparatory to walking out to the café. The matador who was a coward had the older sister of Paco in his room with him and was trying to get her to do something which she was laughingly refusing to do. This matador was saying ‘Come on, little savage.’
楼上那个生病的斗牛士俯卧在床上，独自一人。那个已不再新鲜的斗牛士坐着望着窗外，准备到咖啡馆去。那个懦弱的斗牛士房里有帕科的姐姐在，他正试图让她做一件她笑着拒绝做的事。这个斗牛士说：“来吧，小野孩子。”
‘No,’ said the sister. ‘Why should I?’
“不要，”姐姐说。“我为什么要呢？”
‘For a favour.’
“帮个忙。”
‘You’ve eaten and now you want me for dessert.’
“你吃饱了，现在想拿我当甜点。”
‘Just once. What harm can it do?’
“就一次。能有什么坏处？”
‘Leave me alone. Leave me alone, I tell you.’
“别烦我。别烦我，我告诉你。”
‘It is a very little thing to do.’
“这只是件很小的事。”
‘Leave me alone, I tell you.’
“别烦我，我告诉你。”
Down in the dining-room the tallest of the waiters, who was overdue at the meeting, said, ‘Look at those black pigs drink.’
餐厅里最瘦高的侍者——他开会迟到——说：“看那些黑猪喝酒。”
"That’s no way to speak,’ said the second waiter. ‘They are decent clients. They do not drink too much.’
“别那样说，”第二个侍者说。“他们是体面的客人。喝得不多。”
‘For me it is a good way to speak,’ said the tall one. ‘There are the two curses of Spain, the bulls and the priests.’
“对我来说那样说很对，”高个儿说。“西班牙有两大祸害，公牛和神父。”
‘Certainly not the individual bull and the individual priest,’ said the second waiter.
“当然不是指单个的公牛和单个的神父，”第二个侍者说。
‘Yes,’ said the tall waiter. ‘Only through the individual can you attack the class. It is necessary to kill the individual bull and the individual priest. All of them. Then there are no more.’
“是的，”高个儿的侍者说。“只有通过个人你才能攻击阶级。必须杀死那头单独的公牛和那位单独的牧师。全部都要。那样就没了。”
‘Save it for the meeting,’ said the other waiter.
“留到会议上说吧，”另一个侍者说。
‘Look at the barbarity of Madrid,’ said the tall waiter. ‘It is now half-past eleven o’clock and these are still guzzling.’
“看看马德里的野蛮行为，”高个儿的侍者说。“现在已经十一点半了，他们还在大吃大喝。”
"They only started to eat at ten,’ said the other waiter. ‘As you know there are many dishes. That wine is cheap and these have paid for it. It is not a strong wine.’
“他们十点才开始吃的，”另一个侍者说。“你知道菜很多。那酒便宜，他们也付了钱。酒不烈。”
‘How can there be solidarity of workers with fools like you?’ asked the tall waiter.
“工人怎么可能和像你这样的傻瓜团结？”高个侍者问道。
‘Look,’ said the second waiter who was a man of fifty. ‘I have worked all my life. In all that remains of my life I must work. I have no complaints against work. To work is normal.’
“听着，”第二个侍者说，他五十岁左右。“我一辈子都在工作。在我余下的日子里我也必须工作。我对工作没有怨言。工作是正常的。”
‘Yes, but the lack of work kills.’
“是啊，但没有工作会要人命。”
‘I have always worked,’ said the older waiter. ‘Go on to the meeting. There is no necessity to stay.’
“我一直在工作，”年长的侍者说。“去开会吧。没必要留下来。”
‘You are a good comrade,’ said the tall waiter. ‘But you lack all ideology.’
“你是个好同志，”高个侍者说。“但你缺乏所有的意识形态。”
‘Mejor si me falta eso que el otro,’ said the older waiter (meaning it is better to lack that than work). ‘Go on to the mitin.’
“若是我缺了那个总比缺工作强，”年长的侍者说（意思是缺那个比缺工作好）。“去参加 mitin 吧。”
Paco had said nothing. He did not yet understand politics but it always gave him a thrill to hear the tall waiter speak of the necessity for killing the priests and the Guardia Civil. The tall waiter represented to him revolution and revolution also was romantic. He himself would like to be a good catholic, a revolutionary, and have a steady job like this, while, at the same time, being a bull-fighter.
帕科什么也没说。他还不懂政治，但每当听到高个侍者谈论必须杀掉神父和国家宪兵时，他总是激动不已。对他来说，高个侍者象征着革命，而革命本身也很浪漫。他自己既想成为一个虔诚的天主教徒、一个革命者，又想有像这样的稳定工作，同时还能成为一名斗牛士。
‘Go on to the meeting, Ignacio,’ he said. ‘I will respond for your work.’
“去开会吧，Ignacio，”他说。“你的工作我来担着。”
‘The two of us,’ said the older waiter.
“我们两个，”年长的侍者说。
‘There isn’t enough for one,’ said Paco. ‘Go on to the meeting.’
“一个人都不够，”帕科说。“去开会吧。”
‘Pues, me voy,’ said the tall waiter. ‘And thanks.’
“Pues, me voy，”高个儿的侍者说。“谢谢。”
In the meantime, upstairs, the sister of Paco had gotten out of the embrace of the matador as skilfully as a wrestler breaking a hold and said, now angry, ‘These are the hungry people. A failed bullfighter. With your ton-load of fear. If you have so much of that, use it in the ring.’
与此同时，楼上，帕科的妹妹像摔跤手挣脱锁技一样熟练地从斗牛士的怀里挣脱出来，现在愤怒地说：“这些人才是饿肚子的。个失败的斗牛士。带着你那吨重的恐惧。如果你有那么多，就拿去擂台上用吧。”
‘That is the way a whore talks.’
“妓女就是那样说话的。”
‘A whore is also a woman, but I am not a whore.’
“妓女也是女人，但我不是妓女。”
‘You’ll be one.’
“你会成为的。”
‘Not through you.’
“不会因为你。”
‘Leave me,’ said the matador who, now, repulsed and refused, felt the nakedness of his cowardice returning.
“离开我，”那位被拒绝后感到怯懦赤裸重返的斗牛士说。
‘Leave you? What hasn’t left you?’ said the sister. ‘Don’t you want me to make up the bed? I’m paid to do that.’
“要我离开你？还有什么没离开你？”姐姐说。“你不想让我铺床吗？这是我的工作。”
‘Leave me,’ said the matador, his broad good-looking face wrinkled into a contortion that was like crying. ‘You whore. You dirty little whore.’
“离开我，”斗牛士说，他那张英俊宽阔的脸因抽搐而皱成一副像要哭的模样。“你这个婊子。你这个肮脏的小婊子。”
‘Matador,’ she said, shutting the door. ‘My matador.’
“Matador，”她说着关上门。“我的 matador。”
Inside the room the matador sat on the bed. His face still had the contortion which, in the ring, he made into a constant smile which frightened those people in the first row of seats who knew what they were watching. ‘And this,’ he was saying aloud. ‘And this. And this.’
屋里，斗牛士坐在床上。他的脸上还带着那种扭曲的表情，在擂台上他把那表情变成了一个持续的微笑，吓到了那些坐在前排、知道自己所见之人的观众。“还有这个，”他喃喃道。“还有这个。还有这个。”
He could remember when he had been good and it had only been three years before. He could remember the weight of the heavy goldbrocaded fighting jacket on his shoulders on that hot afternoon in May when his voice had still been the same in the ring as in the café, and how he sighted along the point-dipping blade at the place in the top of the shoulders where it was dusty in the short-haired black hump of muscle above the wide, wood-knocking, splinteredtipped horns that lowered as he went in to kill, and how the sword pushed in as easy as into a mound of stiff butter with the palm of his hand pushing the pommel, his left arm crossed low, his left shoulder forward, his weight on his left leg, and then his weight wasn’t on his leg. His weight was on his lower belly and as the bull raised his head the horn was out of sight in him and he swung over on it twice before they pulled him off it. So now when he went in to kill, and it was seldom, he could not look at the horns and what did any whore know about what he went through before he fought? And what had they been through that laughed at him? They were all whores and they knew what they could do with it.
他记得自己曾经优秀，那只是三年前的事。他记得在那个五月炙热的下午披着沉重的金缎格斗外衣时的感受，那时他在擂台里的声音和在咖啡馆里一样，他记得当他瞄准那柄点着尖端的刀刃，对准肩顶处——在那短毛、黑色的肌肉驼峰上有一处积了灰的地方，正好在那对宽大、会敲打木头、尖端开裂的角上方——当公牛低头准备被他杀死时，他记得刀如何刺入，就像用手掌顶着剑柄把刀推进一堆硬黄油一样容易，他的左臂低搭交叉，左肩向前，重心压在左腿上，然后他的重心不在腿上了。他的重心落在下腹部，随着牛抬头，角已经藏进了它体内，他在角上翻了两圈，直到人们把他从牛身上拉下来。所以现在当他再次出手杀戮时——这种事很少发生——他无法直视那对角，而哪个妓女又知道他在搏斗前经历了什么？而她们又曾经历过什么，竟敢嘲笑他？她们全是妓女，她们知道能用它做些什么。
Down in the dining-room the picador sat looking at the priests. If there were women in the room he stared at them. If there were no women he would stare with enjoyment at a foreigner, un inglés, but lacking women or strangers, he now stared with enjoyment and insolence at the two priests. While he stared the birth-marked auctioneer rose and folding his napkin went out, leaving over half the wine in the last bottle he had ordered. If his accounts had been paid up at Luarca he would have finished the bottle.
餐厅里坐着的骑枪手盯着那两个神父看。若房间里有女人，他就盯着女人看。若没有女人，他便津津有味地盯着一个外国人看，un inglés，但既无女人也无陌生人，他现在便带着得意和傲慢盯着这两个神父看。当他盯着看的时候，那位有胎记的拍卖师起身，折好餐巾走了出去，留下了他点的最后一瓶酒里一半多的酒。如果他在卢阿尔卡的账已经结清，他就会把那瓶酒喝完。
The two priests did not stare back at the picador. One of them was saying, ‘It is ten days since I have been here waiting to see him and all day I sit in the ante-chamber and he will not receive me.’
那两个神父并没有回盯骑枪手看。其中一个说：“我来等他已经十天了，整天我都在前厅坐着，他就是不接见我。”
‘What is there to do?’
“那能怎样？”
‘Nothing. What can one do? One cannot go against authority.’
“没什么。能做什么呢？人不能违抗权威。”
‘I have been here for two weeks for nothing. I wait and they will not see me.’
“我在这里两周都是白等。他们不见我。”
‘We are from the abandoned country. When the money runs out we can return.’
“我们来自被弃之地。钱一用完我们就回去。”
"To the abandoned country. What does Madrid care about Galicia? We are a poor province.’
“被弃之地。马德里怎么会关心加利西亚？我们是个穷省。”
‘One understands the action of our brother Basilio.’
“人们能理解我们兄弟巴西里奥的行为。”
‘Still I have no real confidence in the integrity of Basilio Alvarez.’
“不过我仍然对巴西里奥·阿尔瓦雷斯的人品没有真正的信心。”
‘Madrid is where one learns to understand. Madrid kills Spain.’
“马德里是学会理解的地方。马德里扼杀西班牙。”
‘If they would simply see one and refuse.’
“要是他们能直接见面然后拒绝就好了。”
‘No. You must be broken and worn out by waiting.’
“不。你必须被等待折磨得粉碎和筋疲力尽。”
‘Well, we shall see. I can wait as well as another.’
“好吧，我们拭目以待。我也能像别人一样等。”
At this moment the picador got to his feet, walked over to the priests’ table and stood, grey-headed and hawk-faced, staring at them and smiling.
就在这时，那位骑矛手站起身，走到神父们的桌旁，站着，灰发、鹰脸，盯着他们笑。
‘A torero,’ said one priest to the other.
“一位斗牛士，”一位神父对另一位说。
‘And a good one,’ said the picador and walked out of the diningroom, grey-jacketed, trim-waisted, bow-legged, in tight breeches over his high-heeled cattleman’s boots that clicked on the floor as he swaggered quite steadily, smiling to himself. He lived in a small, tight, professional world of personal efficiency, nightly alcoholic triumph, and insolence. Now he lit a cigar and tilting his hat at an angle in the hallway went out to the café.
“而且是个好斗牛士，”骑矛手说着，走出餐厅，穿着灰色夹克、收腰、弯腿，紧身裤套在高跟牧牛靴外，靴子在地板上咔嗒作响，他大步摇摆却颇为稳重，嘴角带着自得的微笑。他生活在一个小而紧凑的职业世界里——个人效率、夜间的酒精胜利和傲慢。现在他点上一支雪茄，斜着戴帽子走过走廊，出了咖啡馆。
The priests left immediately after the picador, hurriedly conscious of being the last people in the dining-room, and there was no one in the room now but Paco and the middle-aged waiter. They cleared the tables and carried the bottles into the kitchen.
神父们在骑马镞手离开后立即离开了，匆忙地意识到自己是餐厅里最后几个人，房间里现在只剩下帕科和那个中年侍者。他们收拾了桌子，把瓶子端进了厨房。
In the kitchen was the boy who washed the dishes. He was three years older than Paco and was very cynical and bitter.
厨房里有个洗碗的小伙子。他比帕科大三岁，非常愤世嫉俗，满腹苦涩。
‘Take this,’ the middle-aged waiter said, and poured out a glass of the Valdepeñas and handed it to him.
“拿着，”中年侍者说着，倒了一杯 Valdepeñas 递给他。
‘Why not?’ the boy took the glass.
“为什么不？”那个小伙子接过了杯子。
‘Tu, Paco?’ the older waiter asked.
“是你，帕科？”年长的侍者问。
‘Thank you,’ said Paco. The three of them drank.
“谢谢，”帕科说。他们三人喝了口。
‘I will be going,’ said the middle-aged waiter.
“我要走了，”那位中年侍者说。
‘Good night,’ they told him.
“晚安，”他们对他说。
He went out and they were alone. Paco took a napkin one of the priests had used and standing straight, his heels planted, lowered the napkin and with head following the movement, swung his arms in the motion of a slow sweeping veronica. He turned and advancing his right foot slightly, made the second pass, gained a little terrain on the imaginary bull and made a third pass, slow, perfectly timed and suave, then gathered the napkin to his waist and swung his hips away from the bull in a media-veronica.
他走了出去，他们只剩下他们两个人。帕科取过一张神父用过的餐巾，站直，脚跟着地，放低餐巾，随着头的转动摆动手臂，做出缓慢的横扫式“veronica”。他转身，右脚向前迈了一点，做了第二道，向这头想象中的公牛推进了一些地形，又做第三道，缓慢、节奏完美、优雅，然后把餐巾收向腰间，胯部向外一摆，做出一次“media-veronica”。
The dishwasher, whose name was Enrique, watched him critically and sneeringly.
洗碗工名叫恩里克，看着他，带着挑剔和嘲讽的神情。
‘How is the bull?’ he said.
“公牛怎样？”他说。
‘Very brave,’ said Paco. ‘Look:’
“很勇猛，”帕科说。“看：”
Standing slim and straight he made four more perfect passes, smooth, elegant and graceful.
他站得笔直纤长，又做了四次完美的传球，动作流畅、优雅而有韵律。
‘And the bull?’ asked Enrique standing against the sink, holding his wine glass and wearing his apron.
“那头公牛呢？”恩里克靠在水槽边问，手里端着酒杯，身上还系着围裙。
‘Still has lots of gas,’ said Paco.
“还有很多劲儿，”帕科说。
‘You make me sick,’ said Enrique.
“你让我恶心，”恩里克说。
‘Why?’
“为什么？”
‘Look.’
“看。”
Enrique removed his apron and citing the imaginary bull he sculptured four perfect, languid gypsy veronicas and ended up with a rebolera that made the apron swing in a stiff arc past the bull’s nose as he walked away from him.
恩里克脱下围裙，面对想象中的公牛，他雕出四个完美、慵懒的吉普赛式维罗尼卡舞步，最后以一个雷波莱拉收尾，围裙随着他走开时在牛鼻子前划出一道生硬的弧线。
‘Look at that,’ he said. ‘And I wash dishes.’
“看看那个，”他说。“而且我还洗碗。”
‘Why?’
“为什么？”
‘Fear,’ said Enrique. ‘Miedo. The same fear you would have in a ring with a bull.’
“恐惧，”恩里克说。“Miedo。就是那种在斗牛场里面对公牛时会有的恐惧。”
‘No,’ said Paco. ‘I wouldn’t be afraid.’
“不，”帕科说。“我不会害怕。”
‘Leche!’ said Enrique. ‘Everyone is afraid. But a torero can control his fear so that he can work the bull. I went in an amateur fight and I was so afraid I couldn’t keep from running. Every one thought it was very funny. So would you be afraid. If it wasn’t for fear every bootblack in Spain would be a bull-fighter. You, a country boy, would be frightened worse than I was.’
“Leche！”恩里克说。“人人都会害怕。但斗牛士可以控制他的恐惧，才能应付那头牛。我去参加过一场业余的斗牛比赛，当时害怕得跑都跑不掉。大家都觉得很好笑。你也会害怕的。要不是因为怕，西班牙每个擦皮鞋的小伙子都能成斗牛士。你，乡下来的孩子，会比我还要害怕的。”
‘No,’ said Paco.
“不会，”帕科说。
He had done it too many times in his imagination. Too many times he had seen the horns, seen the bull’s wet muzzle, the ear twitching, then the head go down and the charge, the hoofs thudding and the hot bull pass him as he swung the cape, to re-charge as he swung the cape again, then again, and again, and again, to end winding the bull around him in his great media-veronica, and walk swingingly away, with bull hairs caught in the gold ornaments of his jacket from the close passes; the bull standing hypnotized and the crowd applauding. No, he would not be afraid. Others, yes. Not he. He knew he would not be afraid. Even if he ever was afraid he knew that he could do it anyway. He had confidence. ‘I wouldn’t be afraid,’ he said.
他在想象中演练过太多次了。太多次他看见了牛角，看见牛湿漉漉的口鼻，耳朵抽动，然后低下头冲来，蹄子震地，热牛擦过他，他挥着斗篷，牛再次冲来，他再挥斗篷，然后又一次，又一次，直到把牛绕成他那套大回旋式的媒体—维罗尼卡，潇洒地走开，牛毛粘在他衣服的金饰上，那是近距离擦过留下的；牛呆立着像被催眠，观众鼓掌。不会，他不会害怕。别人也许会。他不会。他知道自己不会害怕。即便他曾经害怕，他也知道自己无论如何都能做到。他有自信。“我不会害怕，”他说。
Enrique said, ‘Leche,’ again.
恩里克再说了一句，“Leche。”
Then he said, ‘If we should try it?’
然后他说，“那我们要不要试试？”
‘How?’
“怎么做？”
‘Look,’ said Enrique. ‘You think of the bull but you do not think of the horns. The bull has such force that the horns rip like a knife, they stab like a bayonet, and they kill like a club. Look,’ he opened a table drawer and took out two meat knives. ‘I will bind these to the legs of a chair. Then I will play bull for you with the chair held before my head. The knives are the horns. If you make those passes then they mean something.’
“看，”恩里克说。“你想到的是公牛，但你没有想到牛角。公牛的力气大得像刀子一样撕裂，像刺刀一样刺入，像棍棒一样致命。看，”他打开桌子的抽屉，拿出两把肉刀。“我要把这些绑在椅子的腿上。然后我会拿着椅子挡在头前，替你扮公牛。刀就是牛角。如果你做那些动作，那就有意义了。”
‘Lend me your apron,’ said Paco. ‘We’ll do it in the diningroom.’
“把你的围裙借我，”帕科说。“我们在餐厅里练。”
‘No,’ said Enrique, suddenly not bitter. ‘Don’t do it, Paco.’
“不，”恩里克说，突然不再苦涩。“别做，帕科。”
‘Yes,’ said Paco. ‘I’m not afraid.’
“是的，”帕科说。“我不害怕。”
‘You will be when you see the knives come.’
“等你看到刀子来了你就会怕了。”
‘We’ll see,’ said Paco. ‘Give me the apron.’
“咱们走着瞧，”帕科说。“把围裙给我。”
At this time, while Enrique was binding the two heavy-bladed razor-sharp meat knives fast to the legs of the chair with two soiled napkins holding the half of each knife, wrapping them tight and then knotting them, the two chambermaids, Paco’s sisters, were on their way to the cinema to see Greta Garbo in ‘Anna Christie’. Of the two priests, one was sitting in his underwear reading his breviary and the other was wearing a nightshirt and saying the rosary. All the bull-fighters except the one who was ill had made their evening appearance at the Café Fornos, where the big, dark-haired picador was playing billiards, the short, serious matador was sitting at a crowded table before a coffee and milk, along with the middle-aged banderillero and other serious workmen.
这时，恩里克将两把刃厚且锋利如剃刀的肉刀，用两条脏餐巾把每把刀的一半固定在椅腿上，缠得紧紧的然后打结。与此同时，两位女佣——帕科的姐妹——正去电影院看格丽塔·嘉宝主演的《安娜·克里斯蒂》。两位神父中有一位穿着内衣坐着念他的晨祷经，另一位穿着睡衣念着玫瑰经。除了那个生病的斗牛士外，所有斗牛士都到 Café Fornos 出场了：那位个子高、黑发的骑矛手在打台球，矮个儿、神情严肃的斗牛士坐在一张挤满人的桌前喝着咖啡加奶，旁边还有那位中年的 banderillero 和其他一些认真工作的同伴。
The drinking, grey-headed picador was sitting with a glass of cazalas brandy before him staring with pleasure at a table where the matador whose courage was gone sat with another matador who had renounced the sword to become a banderillero again, and two very houseworn-looking prostitutes.
那个喝酒、灰发的骑马刺客坐着，面前放着一杯 cazalas 白兰地，愉快地盯着一张桌子看，桌旁坐着那个已失去勇气的斗牛士和另一个放下长剑又恢复当旗手的斗牛士，以及两个看起来非常憔悴的妓女。
The auctioneer stood on the street corner talking with friends. The tall waiter was at the Anarcho-Syndicalist meeting waiting for an opportunity to speak. The middle-aged waiter was seated on the terrace of the Café Alvarez drinking a small beer. The woman who owned the Luarca was already asleep in her bed, where she lay on her back with the bolster between her legs; big, fat, honest, clean, easy-going, very religious and never having ceased to miss or pray
拍卖师站在街角与朋友们交谈。高个儿的侍者在无政府工团会议上等待发言的机会。中年侍者坐在阿尔瓦雷斯咖啡馆的露台上喝着一小杯啤酒。拥有 Luarca 的女人已经在床上睡着，她仰卧，将抱枕夹在两腿之间；又大又肥、诚实、干净、性情温和、非常虔诚，从未停止过为她的丈夫祈祷或想念——他现在已经死了，二十年了。她每天如此。
daily for her husband, dead, now, twenty years. In his room, alone, the matador who was ill lay fate down on his bed with his mouth against a handkerchief.
在他的房间里，独自一人，那位生病的斗牛士躺在床上，用口对着一块手帕，命运仿佛已放下在他身上。
Now, in the deserted dining-room, Enrique tied the last knot in the napkins that bound the knives to the chair legs and lifted the chair. He pointed the legs with the knives on them forward and held the chair over his head with the two knives pointing straight ahead, one on each side of his head.
现在，在空荡荡的餐厅里，Enrique 把绑着刀子的餐巾最后一个结系好，提起了椅子。他把带刀的椅腿朝前，举起椅子到头顶，两个刀尖笔直朝前，各在他头的两侧。
‘It’s heavy,’ he said. ‘Look, Paco. It is very dangerous. Don’t do it.’ He was sweating.
“很重，”他说。“看，Paco。非常危险。别这样做。”他在出汗。
Paco stood facing him, holding the apron spread, holding a fold of it bunched in each hand, thumbs up, first finger down, spread to catch the eye of the bull.
Paco 面对着他站着，撑着围裙，双手各捏着一折围裙，拇指朝上，食指朝下，摊开以吸引公牛的目光。
‘Charge straight,’ he said. ‘Turn like a bull. Charge as many times as you want.’
“直冲，”他说。“像公牛一样转。想冲几次就冲几次。”
‘How will you know when to cut the pass?’ asked Enrique. ‘It’s better to do three and then a media.’
“你怎么知道什么时候停刀？”恩里克问道。“最好做三次然后再做一次半刺。”
‘All right,’ said Paco. ‘But come straight. Huh, torito! Come on, little bull!’
“好吧，”帕科说。“但要直来。哎，小公牛！来吧，小牛！”
Running with head down Enrique came toward him and Paco swung the apron just ahead of the knife blade as it passed close in front of his belly and as it went by it was, to him, the real horn, white-tipped, black, smooth, and as Enrique passed him and turned to rush again it was the hot, blood-flanked mass of the bull that thudded by, then turned like a cat and came again as he swung the cape slowly. Then the bull turned and came again and, as he watched the onrushing point, he stepped his left foot two inches too far forward and the knife did not pass, but had slipped in as easily as into a wineskin and there was a hot scalding rush above and around the sudden inner rigidity of steel and Enrique shouting, ‘Ay! Ay! Let me get it out! Let me get it out!’ and Paco slipped forward on the chair the apron cape still held, Enrique pulling on the chair as the knife turned in him, in him, Paco.
恩里克低着头朝他跑来，帕科把披布在刀刃前方刚好挥过，在那贴近他腹部掠过的一刻，对他来说那就是真正的牛角，白尖、黑亮、光滑；当恩里克从他身边掠过又转身准备再冲时，紧接着撞击他的是那团带血滚烫的牛体，砰地掠过，然后像猫一样转身又冲来，他慢慢挥动披布。牛又转身冲来，当他盯着前冲的尖角时，他左脚向前迈了两英寸太多，刀没有穿过，而是像割开皮囊般顺利滑入，刹那之间一股灼热的喷涌在钢铁突然的内在僵硬处上方和周围爆发，恩里克喊道：“哎！哎！让我拔出来！让我拔出来！”帕科仍抓着披布从椅子上向前滑去，恩里克一边把椅子拉回那把刀在他体内转动，转在他体内，帕科。
The knife was out now and he sat on the floor in the widening warm pool.
刀现在拔出来了，他坐在地板上，围着愈发扩大的温热血泊。
‘Put the napkin over it. Hold it!’ said Enrique. ‘Hold it tight. I will run for the doctor. You must hold in the haemorrhage.’
“把餐巾盖上。按住！”恩里克叫道。“按紧点。我去找医生。你得止住出血。”
‘There should be a rubber cup,’ said Paco. He had seen that used in the ring.
“应该有个橡皮杯子，”帕科说。他在拳赛里见过有人用。
‘I came straight,’ said Enrique, crying. ‘All I wanted was to show the danger.’
“我马上就来，”恩里克哭着说。“我只是想指示危险。”
‘Don’t worry,’ said Paco, his voice sounding far away. ‘But bring the doctor.’
“别担心，”帕科说，声音听起来很遥远。“但要把医生叫来。”
In the ring they lifted you and carried you, running with you, to the operating room. If the femoral artery emptied itself before you reached there they called the priest.
在擂台上他们把你抬起来、背起来，跑着把你送到手术室。如果股动脉在到达之前就放尽了血，他们就叫神父。
‘Advise one of the priests,’ said Paco, holding the napkin tight against his lower abdomen. He could not believe that this had happened to him.
“通知一个神父，”帕科说着，把餐巾紧按在下腹部。他不敢相信这种事会发生在自己身上。
But Enrique was running down the Carrera San Jeronimo to the all-night first-aid station and Paco was alone, first sitting up, then huddled over, then slumped on the floor, until it was over, feeling his life go out of him as dirty water empties from a bathtub when the plug is drawn. He was frightened and he felt faint and he tried to say an act of contrition and he remembered how it started but before he had said, as fast as he could, ‘Oh, my God, I am heartily sorry for having offended Thee who are worthy of all my love and I firmly resolve …’ he felt too faint and he was lying face down on the floor and it was over very quickly. A severed femoral artery empties itself faster than you can believe.
但恩里克正沿着卡雷拉圣赫罗尼莫跑向通宵急救站，帕科独自一人，先是坐起来，然后蜷着身子，再然后瘫倒在地，直到一切结束，感觉自己的生命像浴缸拔了塞子那样脏水般流尽。他很害怕，感到晕眩，试图念一篇悔罪经文，他记得事情是如何开始的，但在他尽可能快地说出“噢，我的上帝，我由衷为得罪你——配得我一切爱慕者——而感到懊悔，并且我坚决决定……”之前，他感到太虚弱，脸朝下躺在地上，一切很快就结束了。被切断的股动脉放血比你能相信的还要快。
As the doctor from the first-aid station came up the stairs accompanied by a policeman who held on to Enrique by the arm, the two sisters of Paco were still in the moving-picture palace of the Gran Via, where they were intensely disappointed in the Garbo film, which showed the great star in miserable low surroundings when they had been accustomed to see her surrounded by great luxury and brilliance. The audience disliked the film thoroughly and were protesting by whistling and stamping their feet. All the other people from the hotel were doing almost what they had been doing when the accident happened, except that the two priests had finished their devotions and were preparing for sleep, and the grey-haired picador had moved his drink over to the table with the two houseworn prostitutes. A little later he went out of the café with one of them. It was the one for whom the matador who had lost his nerve had been buying drinks.
当来自急救站的医生在一名警察的陪同下上了楼，那位警察挽着恩里克的手臂时，帕科的两个姐妹仍在格兰维亚的大电影宫里，她们对嘉宝的那部片子极为失望——这部片子把这位大明星置于可怜的卑微环境中，而她们习惯于看到她被奢华与光辉环绕。观众彻底不喜欢这部片子，正通过吹口哨和跺脚来表示抗议。旅馆里其他人几乎还在做着事故发生时正在做的事，只是两位神父已做完祷告，正准备睡觉，那个灰发的卡皮拉多把酒杯挪到了那两位年久失修的妓女的桌旁。稍后他和其中一位走出了咖啡馆。那正是那位在丧失勇气的斗牛士一直给买酒的那位妓女。
The boy Paco had never known about any of this nor about what all these people would be doing on the next day and on other days to come. He had no idea how they really lived nor how they ended.
男孩帕科从来不知道这些事，也不知道这些人第二天乃至将来会做些什么。他根本不知道他们真实的生活，也不知道他们的结局。
He did not even realize they ended. He died, as the Spanish phrase has it, full of illusions. He had not had time in his life to lose any of them, nor even, at the end, to complete an act of contrition.
他甚至没有意识到这些幻想已经结束。用西班牙语的话说，他死时充满了幻想。他一生中来不及失去任何一个幻想，甚至在临终也来不及完成一次懺悔的行为。
He had not even had time to be disappointed in the Garbo picture which disappointed all Madrid for a week.
他甚至来不及对那部让整个马德里失望一周的歌堡（Garbo）电影感到失望。
Kilimanjaro is a snow covered mountain 19,710 feet high, and is said to be the highest mountain in Africa. Its western summit is called the Masai ‘Ngàje Ngài’, the House of God. Close to the western summit there is the dried and frozen carcass of a leopard. No one has explained what the leopard was seeking at that altitude.
乞力马扎罗是一座海拔 19,710 英尺的积雪覆盖的山，据说是非洲最高的山。它的西峰被马赛人称为“Ngàje Ngài”，即上帝之屋。在西峰附近有一具干瘪并已冰封的豹子尸体。没有人能解释那只豹子在那样的高度究竟在寻找什么。

THE SNOWS OF KILIMANJARO
乞力马扎罗的雪

‘The marvellous thing is that it’s painless,’ he said. ‘That’s how you know when it starts.’
“奇妙的是这毫无痛感，”他说。“你就是这样知道它开始了。”
‘Is it really?’
“真的吗？”
‘Absolutely. I’m awfully sorry about the odour, though. That must bother you.’
“绝对是真的。可我很抱歉那气味，肯定会让你不舒服。”
‘Don’t! Please don’t.’
“别说！求你别说。”
‘Look at them,’ he said. 'Now is it sight or is it scent that brings them like that?’
“看着它们，”他说。“现在，是视力把它们吸引过来，还是嗅觉？”
The cot the man lay on was in the wide shade of a mimosa tree and as he looked out past the shade on to the glare of the plain there were three of the big birds squatted obscenely, while in the sky a dozen more sailed, making quick-moving shadows as they passed.
那人躺的营床在一棵含羞草树浓密的树荫里，他望过树荫，看到平原刺眼的光里，三只大鸟下趴着，姿态猥琐，而天空中还有十几只盘旋，掠过时投下快速移动的影子。
‘They’ve been there since the day the truck broke down,’ he said. ‘To-day’s the first time any have lit on the ground. I watched the way they sailed very carefully at first in case I ever wanted to use them in a story. That’s funny now.’
“卡车抛锚那天起它们就一直在那里，”他说。“今天是第一次有鸟落到地上。我起初很仔细地观察它们盘旋的方式，以防哪天想在故事里用到它们。现在想起来真有趣。”
‘I wish you wouldn’t,’ she said.
“我希望你别那样，”她说。
‘I’m only talking,’ he said. ‘It’s much easier if I talk. But I don’t want to bother you.’
“我只是说说而已，”他说。“我说话比较容易。但我不想打扰你。”
‘You know it doesn’t bother me,’ she said. ‘It’s that I’ve gotten so very nervous not being able to do anything. I think we might make it as easy as we can until the plane comes.’
“你知道这不打扰我，”她说。“只是我因为什么都做不了而变得非常紧张。我想我们可以在飞机来之前尽可能让事情简单一些。”
‘Or until the plane doesn’t come.’
“或者直到飞机不来。”
‘Please tell me what I can do. There must be something I can do.’
“请告诉我我能做什么。一定有事我能做的。”
‘You can take the leg off and that might stop it, though I doubt it. Or you can shoot me. You’re a good shot now. I taught you to shoot, didn’t I?’
“你可以把腿切掉，也许那会止住血，尽管我怀疑。或者你可以射杀我。你现在是个好枪手。我不是教你打枪了吗？”
‘Please don’t talk that way. Couldn’t I read to you?’
“请别那样说。我能给你读点东西吗？”
‘Read what?’
“读什么？”
‘Anything in the book bag that we haven’t read.’
“书包里我们还没读过的任何东西。”
‘I can’t listen to it,’ he said. ‘Talking is the easiest. We quarrel and that makes the time pass.’
“我听不下去，”他说。“说话是最容易的。我们吵架，这样时间就过去了。”
‘I don’t quarrel. I never want to quarrel. Let’s not quarrel any more. No matter how nervous we get. Maybe they will be back with another truck to-day. Maybe the plane will come.’
“我不吵架。我从不想吵架。别再吵了。不管我们多紧张。也许他们今天会开另一辆卡车回来。也许飞机会来。”
‘I don’t want to move,’ the man said. ‘There is no sense in moving now except to make it easier for you.’
“我不想动，”那个男人说。“现在动没有意义，除非是为了让你更容易一些。”
‘That’s cowardly.’
“那是懦弱。”
‘Can’t you let a man die as comfortably as he can without calling him names? What’s the use of slanging me?’
“你就不能让人舒服点儿地去死吗，别给他贴标签？骂我有什么用？”
‘You’re not going to die.’
“你不会死的。”
‘Don’t be silly. I’m dying now. Ask those bastards.’ He looked over to where the huge, filthy birds sat, their naked heads sunk in the hunched feathers. A fourth planed down to run quick-legged and then waddle slowly toward the others.
“别傻了。我现在就要死了。问问那些混蛋们吧。”他望向那些巨大的、肮脏的鸟儿栖息的地方，它们赤裸的头埋在弯曲的羽毛里。另一只掠空而下，跑着靠近然后慢慢一瘸一蹬地挪向其他鸟。
‘They are around every camp. You never notice them. You can’t die if you don’t give up.’
“它们出现在每个营地周围。你从没注意到它们。如果你不放弃，你就不会死。”
‘Where did you read that? You’re such a bloody fool.’
“你从哪里读到的？你真是个该死的傻瓜。”
‘You might think about someone else.’
“你可以考虑别人。”
‘For Christ’s sake,’ he said. ‘That’s been my trade.’
“看在上帝的份上，”他说。“那一直是我的职业。”
He lay then and was quiet for a while and looked across the heat shimmer of the plain to the edge of the bush. There were a few Tommies that showed minute and white against the yellow and, far off, he saw a herd of zebra, white against the green of the bush. This was a pleasant camp under big trees against a hill, with good water, and close by, a nearly dry water hole where sand grouse flighted in the mornings.
然后他躺着，安静了一会儿，望着平原上热浪的闪烁直到灌木丛的边缘。有几只小小的英军士兵在黄色背景上显得微白，远处，他看到一群斑马，在灌木的绿色中显得白皙。这是一个宜人的营地，树木茂盛，倚着一座小山，有良好的水源，附近有一个几乎干涸的水坑，清晨时沙鸻在那里飞来。
‘Wouldn’t you like me to read?’ she asked. She was sitting on a canvas chair beside his cot. ‘There’s a breeze coming up.’
“你难道不想让我读吗？”她问道。她坐在他铁床旁的一把帆布椅子上。“有风吹过来了。”
‘No thanks.’
“不用了，谢谢。”
‘Maybe the truck will come.’
“也许卡车会来。”
‘I don’t give a damn about the truck.’
“我才不在乎那辆卡车呢。”
‘I do.’
“我愿意。”
‘You give a damn about so many things that I don’t.’
“你在乎的东西比我在乎的多多了。”
‘Not so many, Harry.’
“没那么多，哈里。”
‘What about a drink?’
“要不要喝一杯？”
‘It’s supposed to be bad for you. It said in Black’s to avoid all alcohol. You shouldn’t drink.’
“这对你不好。Black’s 上说要避免一切酒精。你不应该喝。”
‘Molo!’ he shouted.
“莫洛！”他喊道。
‘Yes, Bwana.’
“是，布瓦纳。”
‘Bring whisky-soda.’
“拿来威士忌苏打水。”
‘Yes, Bwana.’
“是的，布瓦纳。”
‘You shouldn’t,’ she said. ‘That’s what I mean by giving up. It says it’s bad for you. I know it’s bad for you.’
“你不应该的，”她说。“那就是我所说的放弃。上面写着对你不好。我知道这对你不好。”
‘No,’ he said. ‘It’s good for me.’
“不，”他说。“这对我有好处。”
So now it was all over, he thought. So now he would never have a chance to finish it. So this was the way it ended in a bickering over a drink. Since the gangrene started in his right leg he had no pain and with the pain the horror had gone and all he felt now was a great tiredness and anger that this was the end of it. For this, that now was coming, he had very little curiosity. For years it had obsessed him; but now it meant nothing in itself. It was strange how easy being tired enough made it.
所以现在都结束了，他想。这样他就再也没有机会完成它了。原来就是在为了一杯酒而争吵中结束的。既然坏疽从他的右腿开始，他没有疼痛，连同疼痛一起恐惧也消失了，他现在只感到极度的疲倦和对这件事就此结束的愤怒。对这一切，即将到来的事情，他几乎没有好奇心。多年来它一直困扰着他；但现在它本身不再意味着什么。令人惊奇的是，疲倦到足够的程度竟然使一切变得如此容易。
Now he would never write the things that he had saved to write until he knew enough to write them well. Well, he would not have to fail at trying to write them either. Maybe you could never write them, and that was why you put them off and delayed the starting. Well, he would never know, now.
现在他永远也写不出那些他原本要等到足够懂得如何好好写出来才会动笔的东西了。好吧，他也不用再经历为写这些东西而失败的尝试了。也许这些东西你根本就写不了，这就是你一直拖延、迟迟不肯动手的原因。嗯，现在他永远也不会知道了。
‘I wish we’d never come,’ the woman said. She was looking at him holding the glass and biting her lip. ‘You never would have gotten anything like this in Paris. You always said you loved Paris. We could have stayed in Paris or gone anywhere. I’d have gone anywhere. I said I’d go anywhere you wanted. If you wanted to shoot we could have gone shooting in Hungary and been comfortable.’
“我真希望我们从来没来过，”那个女人说。她看着他，手里拿着酒杯，咬着嘴唇。“你在巴黎根本不会遇到这种事。你总说你爱巴黎。我们本可以留在巴黎，或者去任何地方。我愿意去任何地方。我说过只要你想去哪儿我就去。如果你想打猎，我们本可以去匈牙利打猎，住得很舒适。”
‘Your bloody money,’ he said.
“你那该死的钱，”他说。
‘That’s not fair,’ she said. ‘It was always yours as much as mine. I left everything and I went wherever you wanted to go and I’ve done what you wanted to do. But I wish we’d never come here.’
“那不公平，”她说。“那些钱一直和你的一样是我们的。我放弃了一切，去你想去的任何地方，做了你想做的事。但我真希望我们从来没来过这里。”
‘You said you loved it.’
“你说过你爱它。”
‘I did when you were all right. But now I hate it. I don’t see why that had to happen to your leg. What have we done to have that happen to us?’
“你刚才没事的时候我喜欢。可现在我讨厌它了。我不明白为什么你的腿非得这样受伤。我们做了什么会招来这种事？”
‘I suppose what I did was to forget to put iodine on it when I
“我想我可能是忘了在上面抹碘酒。”
first scratched it. Then I didn’t pay any attention to it because I never infect. Then, later, when it got bad, it was probably using that weak carbolic solution when the other antiseptics ran out that paralysed the minute blood vessels and started the gangrene.’ He looked at her, ‘What else?’
先是划破了。后来我没当回事，因为我从不感染。可是后来情况严重了，大概是用那种稀薄的酚溶液——当其他防腐剂用尽时才用的——那东西让微小血管瘫痪，导致了坏疽。’他看着她，‘还有别的事吗？’
‘I don’t mean that.’
“我不是那个意思。”
"If we could have hired a good mechanic instead of a half-baked kikuyu driver, he would have checked the oil and never burned out that bearing in the truck.’
“要是我们能雇个好点的机械师，而不是一个半吊子的基库尤司机，他本来会检查机油，根本不会把卡车的那个轴承烧坏。”
‘I don’t mean that.’
“我不是那个意思。”
‘If you hadn’t left your own people, your goddamned Old Westbury, Saratoga, Palm Beach people to take me on -’
“要不是你把你自己那帮人——你那该死的奥德威斯特布里、萨拉托加、棕榈滩那些人——都甩了去带我——”
‘Why, I loved you. That’s not fair. I love you now. I’ll always love you. Don’t you love me?’
“为什么，我爱过你。那不公平。我现在也爱你。我会永远爱你。你难道不爱我吗？”
‘No,’ said the man. ‘I don’t think so. I never have.’
“没有，”那人说。“我想不…不是的。我从来没有爱过。”
‘Harry, what are you saying? You’re out of your head.’
“哈里，你在说什么？你疯了吗。”
‘No. I haven’t any head to go out of.’
“没有。我根本没脑子可以疯。”
‘Don’t drink that,’ she said. ‘Darling, please don’t drink that. We have to do everything we can.’
“别喝那个，”她说。“亲爱的，别喝那个。我们得尽一切可能。”
‘You do it,’ he said. ‘I’m tired.’
“你去做吧，”他说。“我累了。”
Now in his mind he saw a railway station at Karagatch and he was standing with his pack and that was the headlight of the Simplon-Orient cutting the dark now and he was leaving Thrace then after the retreat. That was one of the things he had saved to write, with, in the morning at breakfast, looking out the window and seeing snow on the mountains in Bulgaria and Nansen’s Secretary asking the old man if it were snow and the old man looking at it and saying, No, that’s not snow. It’s too early for snow. And the Secretary repeating to the other girls, No, you see. It’s not snow and them all saying, It’s not snow, we were mistaken. But it was the snow all right and he sent them on into it when he evolved the exchange of populations. And it was snow they tramped along in until they died that winter.
现在在他脑海中，他看见卡拉加奇的一个火车站，他背着包站着，那是 Simplon-Orient 的车头灯切开黑暗，他当时正要离开色雷斯，那是撤退之后。他曾把那件事保留着要写下来——早晨吃早餐时，看着窗外保加利亚山上的雪，Nansen 的秘书问那位老人那是不是雪，老人看了看说，不，那不是雪。下雪还太早。秘书又对其他姑娘们重复说，不，你看，这不是雪，她们都说，不是雪，我们弄错了。可那确实是雪，当他实施人口交换时，他把她们送进了那雪中。他们就在那雪地里跋涉，直到那个冬天死去。
It was snow too that fell all Christmas week that year up in the Gauertal, that year they lived in the woodcutter’s house with the big square porcelain stove that filled half the room, and they slept on mattresses filled with beech leaves, the time the deserter came with his feet bloody in the snow. He said the police were right behind
那年在高尔塔尔整个圣诞周也下雪，他们住在伐木工的房子里，屋里有那口把半间屋子都占了的大方形瓷炉，睡在装着山毛榉叶的床垫上，那次逃兵赤着脚踏着雪来找他们。他说警察就在后面跟着
him and they gave him woollen socks and held the gendarmes talking until the tracks had drifted over.
他，他们给他毛袜子，和宪兵们聊着天，直到足迹被雪掩没为止。
In Schrunz, on Christmas day, the snow was so bright it hurt your eyes when you looked out from the weinstube and saw everyone coming home from church. That was where they walked up the sleigh-smoothed urine-yellowed road along the river with the steep pine hills, skis heavy on the shoulder, and where they ran that great run down the glacier above the Madlener-haus, the snow as smooth to see as cake frosting and as light as powder and he remembered the noiseless rush the speed made as you dropped down like a bird.
在施伦茨，圣诞节那天，雪亮得刺眼，从葡萄酒小馆里向外看去，看到大家从教堂回来时会觉得眼睛疼。就是在那条被雪橇压平、尿黄的路上沿着河走，河边是陡峭的松林，他们把滑雪板扛在肩上沉甸甸地走着；也是他们从马德勒纳屋上方的冰川上那次飞驰而下的地方，雪面看起来像蛋糕糖霜一样光滑，轻得像粉末，他记得像鸟儿般俯冲下去时那无声的速度呼啸。
They were snow-bound a week in the Madlener-haus that time in the blizzard playing cards in the smoke by the lantern light and the stakes were higher all the time as Herr Lent lost more. Finally he lost it all. Everything, the skischule money and all the season’s profit and then his capital. He could see him with his long nose, picking up the cards and then opening, ‘Sans Voir’. There was always gambling then. When there was no snow you gambled and when there was too much you gambled. He thought of all the time in his life he had spent gambling.
那次暴风雪把他们困在 Madlener-haus 里整整一周，灯笼的光下烟雾弥漫着，他们玩牌，赌注越来越高，因为 Lent 先生输了更多。最后他把一切都输光了。所有的滑雪学校的钱、整个季节的利润，随后连他的本钱也没了。他能想象到他那长长的鼻子，捡起牌，然后摊开，说道，“Sans Voir”。那时总是在赌博。没有雪的时候就赌，有雪太多的时候也赌。他想起自己一生中为赌博耗费的所有时光。
But he had never written a line of that, nor of that cold, bright Christmas day with the mountains showing across the plain that Johnson had flown across the lines to bomb the Austrian officers’ leave train, machine-gunning them as they scattered and ran. He remembered Johnson afterwards coming into the mess and starting to tell about it. And how quiet it got and then somebody saying, ‘You bloody murderous bastard!’
但他从来没有写下过那一切，也没有写下那个寒冷而明亮的圣诞节，山脉横亘在平原那边，Johnson 飞越战线去轰炸奥地利军官的休假列车，列车解散奔逃时对着他们机枪扫射。他记得 Johnson 之后走进军粮帐开始讲那事。然后屋里变得多么安静，接着有人说，‘你这个该死的杀人狂！’
Those were the same Austrians they killed then that he skied with later. No, not the same. Hans, that he skied with all that year, had been in the Kaiser-Jägers and when they went hunting hares together up the little valley above the saw-mill they had talked of the fighting on Pasubio and of the attack on Pertica and Asalone and he had never written a word of that. Nor of Monte Corno, nor the Siete Commum, nor of Arsiedo.
那些人就是他们后来一起滑雪时曾杀死的那些奥地利人。不，不是同一个人。汉斯——那年他整年一起滑雪的那位——曾在凯泽猎兵队服役，当他们一起到锯木厂上方的小山谷里打野兔时，他们曾谈起帕苏比奥的战斗以及对佩尔蒂卡和阿萨隆的进攻，而他对此从未写下一字。蒙特科尔诺、塞特·科穆姆、阿尔谢多也是如此。
How many winters had he lived in the Voralberg and the Arlberg? It was four and then he remembered the man who had the fox to sell when they had walked into Bludenz, that time to buy presents, and the cherry pip taste of good kirsch, the fast-slipping rush of running powder-snow on crust, singing 'Hil Hol said
他在福拉尔贝格和阿尔贝格过了多少个冬天？是四个，然后他想起那次他们走进布卢登茨要买礼物时，有个要卖狐狸皮的人，还有好基尔什那樱桃核的味道，粉雪在硬壳上快速滑落的急速感，唱着“希尔霍尔说
Rolly!’ as you ran down the last stretch to the steel drop, taking it straight, then running the orchard in three turns and out across the ditch and on to the icy road behind the inn. Knocking your bindings loose, kicking the skis free and leaning them up against the wooden wall of the inn, the lamplight coming from the window, where inside, in the smoky, new-wine smelling warmth, they were playing the accordion.

He had loved too much, demanded too much, and he wore it all out.
所以，他心想，我们停止争吵是对的。他和这个女人从不怎么争吵，而与那些他深爱的女人们，他却常常争吵，争吵得最后，总是随着争吵的腐蚀，毁掉了他们之间的一切。他曾爱得太深，要得太多，最终把一切耗尽了。
He thought about alone in Constantinople that time, having quarrelled in Paris before he had gone out. He had whored the whole time and then, when that was over, he had failed to kill his loneliness, but only made it worse, he had written her, the first one, the one who left him, a letter telling her how he had never been able to kill it… How when he thought he saw her outside the Regence one time it made him go all faint and sick inside, and that he would follow a woman who looked like her in some way, along the Boulevard, afraid to see it was not she, afraid to lose the feeling it gave him. How everyone he had slept with had only made him miss her more. How what she had done could never matter since he knew he could not cure himself of loving her. He wrote this letter at the Club, cold sober, and mailed it to New York asking her to write him at the office in Paris. That seemed safe. And that night missing her so much it made him feel hollow sick inside, he wandered up past Taxim’s, picked a girl up and took her out to supper. He had gone to a place to dance with her afterwards, she danced badly, and left her for a hot Armenian slut, that swung her belly against him so it almost scalded. He took her away from a British gunner subaltern after a row. The gunner asked him outside and they fought in the street on the cobbles in the dark. He’d hit him twice, hard, on the side of the jaw and when he didn’t go down he knew he was in for a fight. The gunner hit him in the body, then beside his eye. He swung with his left again and landed and the gunner fell on him and grabbed his coat and tore the sleeve off and he clubbed him twice behind the ear and then smashed him with his right as he pushed him away. When the gunner went down his head hit first and he ran with the girl because they heard the M.P.s coming. 他想起在君士坦丁堡那次独自一人，那次是他在去之前在巴黎吵过架。他整段时间都在嫖，然后，当那结束后，他没有杀死他的孤独，只是让它更糟，他给她写信，给那个第一个离开他的女人，写了一封信告诉她他从未能摆脱那种孤独……当他记得有一次在勒让斯外面以为看见她时，那使他全身一阵发晕作呕，他说他会跟着一个在某种程度上看起来像她的女人，沿着大街走，害怕发现那并非她，害怕失去那种感觉。他睡过的每一个女人只让他更想念她。她所做的根本无关紧要，因为他知道自己无法治愈对她的爱。他在俱乐部里冷静清醒地写了这封信，寄到纽约，叫她给巴黎的他办公室回信。那样似乎安全。那夜他想她想得难受得在心里空洞作呕，他在塔克西姆附近闲逛，拣了个女孩，带她出去吃了顿晚饭。 后来他带她去一个地方跳舞，她舞得很糟，然后他把她丢给了一个火辣的亚美尼亚荡妇，她把肚子贴着他摆动，几乎烫到他。他在一次争吵后从一个英国炮兵少尉手里把她带走。炮兵到外面找他，他们在黑暗中在鹅卵石街道上打了起来。他狠狠地打了他两下，下颌旁边，当他没有倒下时，他就知道要硬碰硬了。炮兵打他的身体，又打到他眼睛旁。他又用左手挥过去命中，炮兵倒在他身上，抓住他的外套撕掉了袖子，他在后脑勺连砸了他两下，然后把他推开时用右手狠狠击打。当炮兵倒下时是头先着地，他们听见宪兵来了就和那个女孩跑了。 他们上了出租车，绕博斯普鲁斯去了 Rimmily Hissa，绕了一圈，在凉爽的夜色里又回到床上，她感觉到
as over-ripe as she looked but smooth, rose-petal, syrupy, smoothbellied, big-breasted and needed no pillow under her buttocks, and he left her before she was awake looking blousy enough in the first daylight and turned up at the Pera Palace with a black eye, carrying his coat because one sleeve was missing.

That was the day he’d first seen dead men wearing white ballet skirts and upturned shoes with pompoms on them. The Turks had come steadily and lumpily and he had seen the skirted men running and the officers shooting into them and running then themselves and he and the British observer had run too until his lungs ached and his mouth was full of the taste of pennies and they stopped behind some rocks and there were the Turks coming as lumpily as ever. Later he had seen the things that he could never think of and later still he had seen, much worse. So when he got back to Paris that time he could not talk about it or stand to have it mentioned. And there in the café as he passed was that American poet with a pile of saucers in front of him and a stupid look on his potato face talking about the Dada movement with a Roumanian who said his name was Tristan Tzara, who always wore a monocle and had a headache, and, back at the apartment with his wife that now he loved again, the quarrel all over, the madness all over, glad to be home, the office sent his mail up to the flat. So then the letter in answer to the one he’d written came in on a platter one morning and when he saw the hand-writing he went cold all over and tried to slip the letter underneath another. But his wife said, ‘Who is that letter from, dear?’ and that was the end of the beginning of that.
那是他第一次看到穿着白色芭蕾舞裙、脚上穿着向上弯的带着绒球的舞鞋的死人。土耳其人步履沉重地不断逼近，他看见穿裙子的士兵奔跑，军官向他们开枪，随后军官们也开始跑，他和那位英国观察员也跟着跑，直到肺部剧痛，嘴里满是铜钱的味道，他们在几块岩石后停住，土耳其人还像往常一样沉重地走来。后来他见过一些他永远无法想起的事，再往后还见过更糟的事。所以那次回到巴黎时，他无法谈论那件事，也无法忍受有人提起。在他路过的那家咖啡馆里，正有个美国诗人坐着，面前堆着一摞茶托，土豆似的脸上带着愚蠢的表情，正和一个自称叫 Tristan Tzara 的罗马尼亚人在谈论达达主义，那人总是戴着单片眼镜并且头疼。回到与现在又重新相爱的妻子的公寓里，争吵已经结束，疯狂已经结束，庆幸回到家，办公室把他的邮件送到了公寓。 于是有一天早晨，他回信的那封信被人端了上来，他一看到笔迹就浑身发冷，想把信悄悄塞到另一封信下面。但他妻子问道：“亲爱的，那封信是谁寄来的？”于是这就是一切开端的终结。

There was a log house, chinked white with mortar, on a hill above the lake. There was a bell on a pole by the door to call the people in to meals. Behind the house were fields and behind the fields was the timber. A line of lombardy poplars ran from the house to the dock. Other poplars ran along the point. A road went up to the hills along the edge of the timber and along that road he picked blackberries. Then that log house was burned down and all the guns that had been on deer foot racks above the open fireplace were burned and afterwards their barrels, with the lead melted in the magazines, and the stocks burned away, lay out on the heap of ashes that were used to make lye for the big iron soap kettles, and you asked Grandfather if you could have them to play with, and he said, no. You see they were his guns still and he never bought any others. Nor did he hunt any more. The house was rebuilt in the same place out of lumber now and painted white and from its porch you saw the poplars and the lake beyond; but there were never any more guns. The barrels of the guns that had hung on the deer feet on the wall of the log house lay out there on the heap of ashes and no one ever touched them.
山坡上有一座原木屋，墙缝用白色灰浆填了缝，坐落在湖上方。门旁的柱子上挂着一口铃，用来召人吃饭。房子后面是田地，田地后面是林地。一排柳叶白杨从房子一直延到码头。其他的白杨沿着岬角伸展。一条路沿着林地边缘上山，沿着那条路他采过黑莓。后来那座原木屋被烧毁了，原本挂在敞开壁炉上方鹿足枪架上的所有枪都被烧毁，随后它们的枪管（枪膛里的铅在弹仓里熔化了）和枪托被烧尽，散落在用来为大铁制肥皂锅制造碱液的灰堆上，你去问祖父能否把它们拿去玩，他说不行。你明白，那些枪仍然是他的，他从未买过别的枪。他也不再打猎了。后来在同一地点用木材重建了房子，并刷成了白色，从门廊你能看到白杨和远处的湖；但再也没有枪了。挂在圆木屋墙上鹿蹄上的那几管枪口就躺在外面的那堆灰里，没人再去碰它们。
In the Black Forest, after the war, we rented a trout stream and there were two ways to walk to it. One was down the valley from Triberg and around the valley road in the shade of the trees that bordered the white road, and then up a side road that went up through the hills, past many small farms, with the big Schwarzwald houses, until that road crossed the stream. 在黑森林，战后我们租了一条鳟鱼溪，有两条路可以走到那里。一路是从特里贝格顺谷而下，沿着被树荫掩映、紧挨着白色公路的山谷路绕行，然后走上一条小路，这条路沿着山丘往上，经过许多小农庄和大型的 Schwarzwald 房屋，直到那条路横过小溪。那就是我们钓鱼的起点。
The other way was to climb steeply up to the edge of the woods and then go across the top of the hills through the pine woods, and then out to the edge of a meadow and down across this meadow to the bridge. There were birches along the stream and it was not big, but narrow, clear and fast, with pools where it had cut under the roots of the birches. 另一条路则是陡峭地爬上林缘，然后沿着山顶穿过松树林，再到达一片草地边缘，沿着这片草地向下穿过去到桥边。溪流两岸有桦树，溪不宽，但清澈而湍急，在桦树根部冲出了一些深潭。特里贝格那家旅馆的业主那季生意兴隆。非常愉快，我们都成了好朋友。

The Concierge who entertained the trooper of the Garde Republicaine in her loge, his horse-hair-plumed helmet on a chair. The locataire across the hall whose husband was a bicycle racer and her joy that morning at the Cremerie when she had opened L’Auto and seen where he placed third in Paris-Tours, his first big race. She had blushed and laughed and then gone upstairs crying with the yellow sporting paper in her hand. The husband of the woman who ran the Bal Musette drove a taxi and when he, Harry, had to take an early plane the husband knocked upon the door to wake him and they each drank a glass of white wine at the zinc of the bar before they started. He knew his neighbours in that quarter then because they all were poor.
你可以那样说，但你无法指挥康特雷斯卡普广场——花贩们在街上给花染色，染料顺着铺路流下，流到公共汽车开始停靠的地方；那儿有总是醉于酒和劣质白兰地的老人和妇女；有在寒冷中流鼻涕的孩子们；还有爱好者咖啡馆里肮脏汗臭、贫穷和酗酒的气味，以及他们上方居住的那些在巴尔·缪塞特跳舞的妓女。门房在她的门房里招待共和国卫队的士兵，他的马鬃羽饰头盔放在一把椅子上。对面走廊的住户，她丈夫是个自行车赛选手，今晨她在奶油店打开《L’Auto》看到他在巴黎—图尔赛中得到第三名，这是他的第一个大赛，她为此欣喜。她脸红、笑着，然后手里拿着那张黄色体育报纸上楼哭去。经营巴尔·缪塞特的女人的丈夫开出租车，哈里要赶早班飞机时，那丈夫敲门把他唤醒，他们在出发前在吧台的锌面板上各喝了一杯白葡萄酒。那时他认识那一带的邻居，因为他们都很穷。
Around that Place there were two kinds: the drunkards and the sportifs. The drunkards killed their poverty that way; the sportifs took it out in exercise. They were the descendants of the Communards and it was no struggle for them to know their politics. They knew who had shot their fathers, their relatives, their brothers, and their friends when the Versailles troops came in and took the town after the Commune and executed anyone they could catch with calloused hands, or who wore a cap, or carried any other sign he was a working man. And in that poverty, and in that quarter across the street from a Boucherie Chevaline and a wine-co-operative he had uritten the start of all he was to do. There never was another part of Paris that he loved like that, the sprawling trees, the old white plastered houses painted brown below, the long green of the autobus in that round square, the purple flower dye upon the paving, the sudden drop down the hill of the rue Cardinal Lemoine to the River, and the other way the narrow crowded world of the rue Mouffetard. The street that ran up toward the Pantheon and the other that he always took with the bicycle, the only asphalted street in all that
在那一带有两类人：醉汉和好动的人。醉汉们用酗酒来掩盖他们的贫困；好动的人则通过锻炼来发泄。他们是巴黎公社成员的后裔，所以明白自己的政治立场对他们来说毫不费力。他们知道在凡尔赛军队进城、镇压公社并处决所有能抓到的人时，谁开枪打死了他们的父亲、亲人、兄弟和朋友——那些有茧的手、戴着便帽或带有任何其他表明他是工人的标志的人都会被抓。就在那贫穷中，在马路对面靠近一家 Boucherie Chevaline 和一家葡萄酒合作社的那个街区，他开始了他将要做的一切。巴黎没有其他任何地方能像那里那样被他热爱：那伸展开的树木、下面涂成褐色的旧白色灰泥房屋、那圆形广场里长长的绿色公共汽车、铺路上的紫色花染、Cardinal Lemoine 街向下俯冲到河边的骤降，以及另一头通向狭窄而拥挤的 Mouffetard 街的世界。他向万神殿方向延伸的那条街和他总是骑自行车走的那条街——在那一带唯一铺了沥青的街道。
quarter, smooth under the tyres, with the high narrow houses and the cheap tall hotel where Paul Verlaine had died. There were only two rooms in the apartments where they lived and he had a room on the top floor of that hotel that cost him sixty francs a month where he did his writing, and from it he could see the roofs and chimney pots and all the hills of Paris.
一刻钟的路程，轮胎下平滑，伴着高而窄的房屋和那家廉价高大的宾馆——保罗·韦尔莱讷去世的地方。他们居住的公寓里只有两个房间，而他在那家宾馆的顶楼有一间房，月租六十法郎，在那里他写作，从窗里可以看到屋顶、烟囱以及巴黎的所有小山。
From the apartment you could only see the wood and coal man’s place. He sold wine, too, bad wine. The golden horse’s head outside the Boucherie Chevaline where the carcasses hung yellow gold and red in the open window, and the green painted co-operative where they bought their wine; good wine and cheap. The rest was plaster walls and the windows of the neighbours. The neighbours who, at night, when someone lay drunk in the street, moaning and groaning in that typical French ivresse that you were propaganded to believe did not exist, would open their windows and then the murmur of talk.
从公寓里只能看到卖木材和煤的店铺。他也卖酒，劣酒。马肉店门外的金色马头标志，那里屠宰的肉在开着的窗里挂着，黄得像金子也有红色，还有他们买酒的绿色涂漆合作社；好酒而且便宜。其余是抹灰的墙壁和邻居的窗户。夜里，当有人醉倒在街上，发出那种典型的法国醉态的呻吟和呜咽——你被宣传告知那种醉态并不存在时——邻居们会打开窗户，随之传来低声的谈话。
‘Where is the policeman? When you don’t want him the bugger is always there. He’s sleeping with some concierge. Get the Agent.’ Till someone threw a bucket of water from a window and the moaning stopped. ‘What’s that? Water. Ah, that’s intelligent.’ And the windows shutting. Marie, his femme de ménage, protesting against the eight-hour day saying, ‘If a husband works until six he gets only a little drunk on the way home and does not waste too much. If he works only until five he is drunk every night and one has no money. It is the wife of the working man who suffers from this shortening of hours.’
“警察在哪里？当你不需要他时，那家伙总在。肯定又和哪个门房睡觉去了。叫来军需官。”直到有人从窗户扔下一桶水，呻吟才停了。“那是什么？水。啊，这就聪明了。”然后窗户关上。Marie，他的女仆，反对八小时工作制，说：“如果丈夫工作到六点，回家路上只会稍微醉一点，不会浪费太多钱。如果只工作到五点，他每晚都醉，家里就没钱。正是工作的男人的妻子要为这种缩短工作时间受苦。”
‘Wouldn’t you like some more broth?’ the woman asked now.
“还要一些清汤吗？”女人现在问。
‘No, thank you very much. It is awfully good.’
“不，谢谢你。味道非常好。”
‘Try just a little.’
“尝一点点吧。”
‘I would like a whisky-soda.’
“我要一杯威士忌苏打水。”
‘It’s not good for you.’
“那对你不好。”
‘No. It’s bad for me. Cole Porter wrote the words and the music. This knowledge that you’re going mad for me.’
“不。它对我有害。科尔·波特既写了词又作了曲。这句‘你知道我为你疯狂’。”
‘You know I like you to drink.’
“你知道我喜欢你喝酒。”
‘Oh yes. Only it’s bad for me.’
“哦，是的。只是对我不好。”
When she goes, he thought. I’ll have all I want. Not all I want but all there is. Ayee, he was tired. Too tired. He was going to sleep a little while. He lay still and death was not there. It must
她走的时候，他想。我就会得到我想要的一切。不是我想要的一切，而是所有存在的。啊，他累了。太累了。他要小睡一会儿。他躺着一动不动，死没有来。它一定
have gone around another street. It went in pairs, on bicycles, and moved absolutely silently on the pavements.
绕了另一条街。它成双出现，骑着自行车，在人行道上绝对无声地移动。
No, he had never written about Paris. Not the Paris that he cared about. But what about the rest that he had never written?
不，他从未写过巴黎。不是他在乎的那个巴黎。但那些他从未写过的其他地方又如何？
What about the ranch and the silvered grey of the sage brush, the quick, clear water in the irrigation ditches, and the heavy green of the alfalfa? The trail went up into the hills and the cattle in the summer were as shy as deer. The bawling and the steady noise and slow moving mass raising a dust as you brought them down in the fall. And behind the mountains, the clear sharpness of the peak in the evening light and, riding down along the train in the moonlight, bright across the valley. Now he remembered coming down through the timber in the dark holding the horse’s tail when you could not see and all the stories that he meant to write.
那牧场呢？鼠尾草的银灰色，灌溉沟里清澈快捷的水，苜蓿的浓绿？小径爬上山岗，夏天的牛像鹿一样胆小。秋天赶下山时那撕心的哀叫、持续不断的喧闹和缓慢挪动的庞大群体扬起的尘土。还有山那边，傍晚光线里山峰清晰的峭拔，在月光下沿着山脊向下延伸，明亮地横贯山谷。现在他记起在黑暗中穿过林地时拉着马尾下山——看不见路时那样——以及他打算写下的所有故事。
About the half-wit chore boy who was left at the ranch that time and told not to let anyone get any hay, and that old bastard from the Forks who had beaten the boy when he had worked for him stopping to get some feed. The boy refusing and the old man saying he would beat him again. The boy got the rifle from the kitchen and shot him when he tried to come into the barn and when they came back to the ranch he’d been dead a week, frozen in the corral, and the dogs had eaten part of him. But what was left you packed on a sled wrapped in a blanket and roped on and you got the boy to help you haul it, and the two of you took it out over the road on skis, and sixty miles down to town to turn the boy over. He having no idea that he would be arrested. Thinking he had done his duty and that you were his friend and he would be rewarded. He’d helped to haul the old man in so everybody could know how bad the old man had been, and how he’d tried to steal some feed that didn’t belong to him, and when the sheriff put the handcuffs on the boy he couldn’t believe it. Then he’d started to cry. That was one story he had saved to write. He knew at least twenty good stories from out there and he had never written one. Why?
关于那次留在牧场的半傻差事小子，你吩咐他别让任何人拿干草；还有那个从 Forks 来的老混蛋，他曾在小子给他干活时打过人，停下来要些饲料。小子拒绝了，老人说要再打他一次。老人想进谷仓时小子从厨房拿了步枪把他打死了；他们回到牧场时老人已经在围栏里冻死了一个星期，狗把他吃掉了一部分。剩下的你用毯子包好捆在雪橇上，让小子帮你拉，你们俩穿着滑雪板把他运过公路，顺着路走了六十英里到城里把小子交出去。小子完全不知道自己会被逮捕，以为自己是尽了义务，你是他的朋友，会有报酬。他帮忙把老人运来，好让大家知道老人有多坏，和他试图偷别人不属于他的饲料的事；警长给小子铐上手铐时他简直不敢相信，随后他开始哭起来。那是他存着准备写下来的一个故事。 他知道那里至少有二十个好故事，但从未写过一个。为什么？
‘You tell them why,’ he said.
“你告诉他们为什么，”他说。
‘Why what, dear?’
“什么为什么，亲爱的？”
‘Why nothing.’
“没有为什么。”
She didn’t drink so much, now, since she had him. But if he
她现在没那么常喝了，自从有了他之后。但如果他
lived he would never write about her, he knew that now. Nor about any of them. The rich were dull and they drank too much, or they played too much backgammon. They were dull and they were repetitious. He remembered poor Julian and his romantic awe of them and how he had started a story once that began, "The very rich are different from you and me.’ And how someone had said to Julian, Yes, they have more money. But that was not humorous to Julian. He thought they were a special glamorous race and when he found they weren’t it wrecked him just as much as any other thing that wrecked him.
他活着时他永远不会写她的事，他现在知道了。也不会写他们任何人的事。富人乏味，他们喝得太多，或是玩西洋双陆棋玩得太多。他们乏味而且单调重复。他想起可怜的朱利安和他对富人的浪漫敬畏，想起他曾写过一个开头是“非常富有的人和你我不一样”的故事。有人对朱利安说，是的，他们更有钱。但对朱利安来说那并不可笑。他认为他们是一个特殊而有魅力的种族，当他发现事实并非如此时，这毁了他，就像毁掉他的其他任何事一样。
He had been contemptuous of those who wrecked. You did not have to like it because you understood it. He could beat anything, he thought, because nothing could hurt him if he did not care.
他轻视那些崩溃的人。你不必喜欢那点东西，因为你能理解它。他以为自己可以打败任何东西，因为只要他不在乎，就没有什么能伤到他。
All right. Now he would not care for death. One thing he had always dreaded was the pain. He could stand pain as well as any man, until it went on too long, and wore him out, but here he had something that had hurt frightfully and just when he had felt it breaking him, the pain had stopped.
好吧。他现在不再畏惧死亡了。有一件事他一直害怕，那就是痛苦。他能像任何人一样忍受痛苦，直到它持续得太久，把他折磨垮，但在这里他经历了极其剧烈的疼痛，就在他感觉要被它击垮的时候，疼痛却停止了。
He remembered long ago when Williamson, the bombing officer, had been hit by a stick bomb someone in a German patrol had thrown as he was coming in through the wire that night and, screaming, had begged everyone to kill him. He was a fat man, very brave, and a good officer, although addicted to fantastic shows. But that night he was caught in the wire, with a flare lighting him up and his bowels spilled out into the wire, so when they brought him in, alive, they had to cut him loose. Shoot me, Harry. For Christ sake shoot me. They had had an argument one time about our Lord never sending you anything you could not bear and someone’s theory had been that meant that a certain time the pain passed you out automatically. But he had always remembered Williamson, that night. Nothing passed out Williamson until he gave him all his morphine tablets that he had always saved to use himself and then they did not work right away.
他记得很久以前，当威廉姆森——负责轰炸的军官——那晚穿过铁丝网回来时，被德国巡逻队扔来的手榴弹击中，尖叫着求所有人杀了他。那人很胖，很勇敢，也是个好军官，虽然沉迷于奇特的表演。但那晚他被困在铁丝网里，照明弹把他照得一清二楚，他的肠子散落在铁丝网中，所以当他们把他接进来、还活着时，不得不把他割下来。“射杀我，哈利。为了上帝开枪杀了我。”他们曾经因为我们主从不让你承受你不能承受的东西而争论过，有人理论说那意味着在某个时刻疼痛会自动把你弄昏。但他一直记得威廉姆森，那一晚。没有什么能把威廉姆森弄昏，直到他们把他一直为自己保留的所有吗啡片都给了他，但那也没有立刻起作用。
Still this now, that he had, was very easy; and if it was no worse as it went on there was nothing to worry about. Except that he would rather be in better company.
尽管如此，他现在的这状态，很轻松；如果情况在继续下去也不会更糟，那就无须担心。只不过他宁愿有更好的陪伴。
He thought a little about the company that he would like to have.
他稍微想了想自己想要的那种陪伴。
No, he thought, when everything you do, you do too long, and do too late, you can’t expect to find the people still there. The people are all gone. The party’s over and you are with your hostess now.
不，他想道，当你做的每一件事都做得太久、做得太晚时，就别指望还能找到那些人。人都走光了。聚会结束了，你现在只剩下你的女主人。
I’m getting as bored with dying as with everything else, he thought.
他想，我对死亡也像对其他一切一样感到厌倦。
‘It’s a bore,’ he said out loud.
“真无聊，”他出声说。
‘What is, my dear?’
“什么无聊，亲爱的？”
‘Anything you do too bloody long.’
“凡事做得太久都会腻的。”
He looked at her face between him and the fire. She was leaning back in the chair and the firelight shone on her pleasantly lined face and he could see that she was sleepy. He heard the hyena make a noise just outside the range of the fire.
他看着她在他和火堆之间的脸。她向后倚在椅子上，火光照在她那带着愉悦皱纹的脸上，他看得出她困了。他听见鬣狗在火光范围外发出声响。
‘I’ve been writing,’ he said. ‘But I got tired.’
“我一直在写，”他说。“但我累了。”
‘Do you think you will be able to go to sleep?’
“你觉得你能睡得着吗？”
‘Pretty sure. Why don’t you turn in?’
“我挺确定的。你为什么不去睡觉？”
‘I like to sit here with you.’
“我喜欢和你一起坐在这里。”
‘Do you feel anything strange?’ he asked her.
“你有没有感觉到什么奇怪的？”他问她。
‘No. Just a little sleepy.’
“没有。只是有点想睡。”
‘I do,’ he said.
“是的，”他说。
He had just felt death come by again.
他刚又感到死亡走近了。
‘You know the only thing I’ve never lost is curiosity,’ he said to her.
“你知道我唯一从未失去的就是好奇心，”他对她说。
‘You’ve never lost anything. You’re the most complete man I’ve ever known.’
“你从未失去过什么。你是我所认识的最完整的人。”
‘Christ,’ he said. ‘How little a woman knows. What is that? Your intuition?’
“天哪，”他说。“女人真是知道得太少了。那是什么？你的直觉？”
Because, just then, death had come and rested its head on the foot of the cot and he could smell its breath.
因为，就在那时，死亡来到了，头靠在小床的脚边，他能闻到它的气息。
‘Never believe any of that about a scythe and a skull,’ he told her. ‘It can be two bicycle policemen as easily or be a bird. Or it can have a wide snout like a hyena.’
“别相信那些关于镰刀和骷髅的说法，”他对她说。“它也可能是两个骑自行车的警察，或者是一只鸟。或者也可能有像鬣狗那样宽阔的口鼻。”
It had moved up on him now, but it had no shape any more. It simply occupied space.
它现在已经靠近他了，但已不再有任何形状。它只是占据着空间。
‘Tell it to go away.’

It did not go away but moved a little closer.
它没有走开，反而向前挪近了一点。

“你这口气真够呛，”他对它说。“你这个臭混蛋。”
It moved up closer to him still and now he could not speak to it, and when it saw he could not speak it came a little closer, and now
它又靠近了些，他现在不能对它说话，当它看到他不能说话时便又向前挪了一点，现在
he tried to send it away without speaking, but it moved in on him so its weight was all upon his chest, and while it crouched there and he could not move, or speak, he heard the woman say, ‘Bwana is asleep now. Take the cot up very gently and carry it into the tent.’
他试着不出声把它推开，可它挪到他身上，整个重量都压在他的胸口；当它蹲在那里，他动弹不得、说不出话时，他听见女人说：“Bwana 现在睡着了。要轻轻地把担架抬起来，抬进帐篷去。”
He could not speak to tell her to make it go away and it crouched now, heavier so he could not breathe. And then, while they lifted the cot, suddenly it was all right and the weight went from his chest.
他说不出话来叫她把它赶走，它现在蹲得更重，他无法呼吸。然后，当他们抬起担架时，突然间一切都好了，重量从他胸口消失了。
It was morning and had been morning for some time and he heard the plane. It showed very tiny and then made a wide circle and the boys ran out and lit the fires, using kerosene, and piled on grass so there were two big smudges at each end of the level place and the morning breeze blew them toward the camp and the plane circled twice more, low this time, and then glided down and levelled off and landed smoothly and, coming walking toward him, was old Compton in slacks, a tweed jacket and a brown felt hat.
天已是早晨，而且早晨已经有一阵子了，他听见飞机的声音。飞机先显得很小，然后划出一个大圈，男仆们跑出去点起火，用煤油，堆上草，所以在平坦地的两端各有两堆大烟柱，晨风把烟吹向营地，飞机又绕了两圈，这次低飞，然后滑降、平飞并平稳着陆，走过来的是老 Compton，穿着便裤、花呢夹克和一顶棕色毡帽。
‘What’s the matter, old cock?’ Compton said.
“怎么回事，老兄？”Compton 说道。
‘Bad leg,’ he told him. ‘Will you have some breakfast?’
“腿有毛病，”他告诉他。“要吃点早饭吗？”
‘Thanks. I’ll just have some tea. It’s the Puss Moth, you know. I won’t be able to take the Memsahib. There’s only room for one. Your lorry is on the way.’
“谢谢。我就喝点茶。你知道那是 Puss Moth。我可带不了太太。只能坐一个人。你的卡车在路上了。”
Helen had taken Compton aside and was speaking to him. Compton came back more cheery than ever.
海伦把 Compton 拉到一边和他说话。Compton 回来时比以往更高兴。
‘We’ll get you right in,’ he said. ‘I’ll be back for the Mem. Now I’m afraid I’ll have to stop at Arusha to refuel. We’d better get going.’
“我们会把你安顿好，”他说。“我会回来接太太。现在恐怕得在阿鲁沙停一下加油。我们最好赶紧动身。”
‘What about the tea?’
“那茶怎样了？”
‘I don’t really care about it, you know.’
“我其实不太在意，你知道的。”
The boys had picked up the cot and carried it around the green tents and down along the rock and out on to the plain and along past the smudges that were burning brightly now, the grass all consumed, and the wind fanning the fire, to the little plane. It was difficult getting him in, but once in he lay back in the leather seat, and the leg was stuck straight out to one side of the seat where Compton sat. Compton started the motor and got in. He waved to Helen and to the boys and, as the clatter moved into the old familiar roar, they swung around with Compie watching for wart-hog holes and roared, bumping, along the stretch between the fires and with the last bump rose and he saw them all standing below, waving, and
那些男孩抬起担架，把他抬过绿色的帐篷，沿着岩石走下，走到平原上，经过现在烧得正旺、草都被烧光、被风扇动着火苗的烟斑，来到那架小飞机旁。把他放进去很费劲，但一旦放进去他就靠在皮座椅上，腿被楔在座位的一侧，靠着坐着的 Compton。Compton 发动了引擎，钻了进去。他向 Helen 和那些男孩招手，随着机器的喀嚓声变成熟悉的轰鸣，他们绕着转，Compie 留心着疣猪洞，沿着火堆间的路颠簸着咆哮前行，最后一次颠簸时起飞了，他看到他们都站在下面挥手，和
the camp beside the hill, flattening now, and the plain spreading, clumps of trees, and the bush flattening, while the game trails ran now smoothly to the dry waterholes, and there was a new water that he had never known of. The zebra small rounded backs now, and the wildebeeste, big-headed dots seeming to climb as they moved in long fingers across the plain, now scattering as the shadow came toward them, they were tiny now, and the movement had no gallop, and the plain as far as you could see, grey-yellow now and ahead old Compie’s tweed back and the brown felt hat. Then they were over the first hills and the wildebeeste were trailing up them, and then they were over mountains with sudden depths of green-rising forest and the solid bamboo slopes, and then the heavy forest again, sculptured into peaks and hollows until they crossed, and hills sloped down and then another plain, hot now, and purple brown, bumpy with heat and Compie looking back to see how he was riding. Then there were other mountains dark ahead.
营地在小山旁，地势正变平，平原展开，成簇的树丛，灌木也变矮，野兽的小路如今顺畅地通向干涸的水坑，而且有一处他从未知道过的新水源。斑马那小小的圆背现在可见，角马那大头的点状群像在穿过平原时像手指般伸展，随着它们移动显得在攀升，阴影向它们逼近时又四散，现在都变得很小，动作不再有奔腾的节奏，放眼望去的平原如今呈灰黄色，前面是老康比那件粗花呢外套的背影和褐色毡帽。然后他们越过了第一道山丘，角马沿山丘缓缓爬升，接着越过群山，山里突显出绿意浓密的森林和结实的竹坡，又进入浓密的林区，被雕塑般的峰峦与凹谷切割，直到穿过去，山坡下沉，然后又是一片平原，此刻炙热，呈紫褐色，因热气起伏不平，康比回头看他骑得如何。然后前方又出现了些黑暗的山峦。
And then instead of going on to Arusha they turned left, he evidently figured that they had the gas, and looking down he saw a pink sifting cloud, moving over the ground, and in the air, like the first snow in a blizzard, that comes from nowhere, and he knew the locusts were coming up from the South. Then they began to climb and they were going to the East it seemed, and then it darkened and they were in a storm, the rain so thick it seemed like flying through a waterfall, and then they were out and Compie turned his head and grinned and pointed and there, ahead, all he could see, as wide as all the world, great, high, and unbelievably white in the sun, was the square top of Kilimanjaro. And then he knew that there was where he was going.
然后他们没有继续去阿鲁沙，而是向左拐，他显然估计他们带够了燃料费，低头看见一片粉红色的筛状云在地面上移动，在空中像暴风雪中的第一场雪那样从无处而来，他知道蝗虫正从南方爬上来。然后他们开始爬升，似乎要往东方向去，天色变暗，暴风雨降临，雨下得如此密集，仿佛在穿越一座瀑布一样，随后又雨过天晴，Compie 转过头咧嘴笑着指着前方，那里——他所能看到的，像整个世界一样宽广，高大，在阳光下难以置信地白——就是乞力马扎罗的方形山顶。然后他知道，那就是他的目的地。
Just then the hyena stopped whimpering in the night and started to make a strange, human, almost crying sound. The woman heard it and stirred uneasily. She did not wake. In her dream she was at the house on Long Island and it was the night before her daughter’s debut. Somehow her father was there and he had been very rude. Then the noise the hyena made was so loud she woke and for a moment she did not know where she was and she was very afraid. Then she took the flashlight and shone it on the other cot that they had carried in after Harry had gone to sleep. She could see his bulk under the mosquito bar but somehow he had gotten his leg
就在这时，鬣狗在夜里停止了呜咽，发出一种奇怪的、几乎像人哭泣的声音。那个女人听到后不安地动了动。她没有醒来。在梦里她在长岛的房子里，前一晚是她女儿的初次亮相。不知怎的她的父亲也在那儿，而且他很粗鲁。然后鬣狗发出的声音变得很大，她醒来，有一会儿不知道自己身处何处，感到非常害怕。随后她拿起手电筒，照向哈里睡着后他们搬进来的另一张简易床。她能看见蚊帐下他那魁梧的身躯，但不知怎的，他的腿竟然得了缠住...
out and it hung down alongside the cot. The dressings had all come down and she could not look at it.
露出来，垂在小床旁边。敷料都已脱落，她无法直视它。
‘Molo,’ she called. ‘Molo! Molo!’
“莫洛，”她喊道。“莫洛！莫洛！”
Then she said, ‘Harry, Harry!’ Then her voice rising, 'Harry! Please, Oh Harry ! ’
然后她喊道：“哈里，哈里！”随后声音提高，“哈里！求你，哦哈里！”
There was no answer and she could not hear him breathing.
没有回应，她也听不到他的呼吸声。
Outside the tent the hyena made the same strange noise that had awakened her. But she did not hear him for the beating of her heart.
帐篷外，鬣狗发出那种曾把她惊醒的奇怪声音。但她因心跳声而听不见它。

OLD MAN AT THE BRIDGE
桥上的老人与桥

An old man with steel rimmed spectacles and very dusty clothes sat by the side of the road. There was a pontoon bridge across the river and carts, trucks, and men, women and children were crossing it. The mule-drawn carts staggered up the steep bank from the bridge with soldiers helping push against the spokes of the wheels. The trucks ground up and away heading out of it all and the peasants plodded along in the ankle deep dust. But the old man sat there without moving. He was too tired to go any farther.
一个戴着钢边眼镜、衣服满是灰尘的老人坐在路边。河上有一座浮桥，马车、卡车以及男人、女人和孩子们都在通过。骡子拉的马车摇摇晃晃从桥上爬上陡峭的河岸，士兵们用力推着车轮的辐条帮忙。卡车隆隆驶上驶去，离开这一切，农民们在及踝的尘土中蹒跚前行。但老人就那样坐着一动不动。他太累了，走不动了。
It was my business to cross the bridge, explore the bridgehead beyond and find out to what point the enemy had advanced. I did this and returned over the bridge. There were not so many carts now and very few people on foot, but the old man was still there.
我的任务是过桥、侦察桥头阵地并查明敌人推进到了什么程度。我做完这些事又从桥上返回。现在马车不多了，徒步的人也很少，但那个老人仍然在那里。
‘Where do you come from?’ I asked him.
“你从哪儿来？”我问他。
‘From San Carlos,’ he said, and smiled.
“从圣卡洛斯来，”他说着，微笑了。
That was his native town and so it gave him pleasure to mention it and he smiled.
那是他的故乡，所以提起它令他高兴，他便笑了。
‘I was taking care of animals,’ he explained.
“我是在照看动物，”他解释道。
‘Oh,’ I said, not quite understanding.
“哦，”我说，有些不明白。
