‘Yes,’ he said, ‘I stayed, you see, taking care of animals. I was the last one to leave the town of San Carlos.’
“是的，”他说，“你看，我留下来照看动物。我是最后一个离开圣卡洛斯镇的人。”
He did not look like a shepherd nor a herdsman and I looked at his black dusty clothes and his grey dusty face and his steel rimmed spectacles and said, ‘What animals were they?’
他看起来既不像牧羊人也不像牧牛人，我看着他那黑乎乎沾满灰尘的衣服、灰尘覆盖的灰色面庞和钢边眼镜，说道， “都是什么动物？”
‘Various animals,’ he said, and shook his head. ‘I had to leave them.’
“各种动物，”他说，摇着头。“我不得不离开它们。”
I was watching the bridge and the African looking country of the Ebro Delta and wondering how long now it would be before we would see the enemy, and listening all the while for the first noises that would signal that ever mysterious event called contact, and the old man still sat there.
我在看着桥和有着非洲风貌的埃布罗三角洲乡野，想着还要过多久我们才会看到敌人，并且一直侧耳倾听那将预示着那个神秘事件——接触——的第一声响，老人仍旧坐在那里。
‘What animals were they?’ I asked.
“都是什么动物？”我问。
‘There were three animals altogether,’ he explained. ‘There were two goats and a cat and then there were four pairs of pigeons.’
“总共有三种动物，”他解释道。“有两只山羊、一只猫，然后还有四对鸽子。”
‘And you had to leave them?’ I asked.
“你不得不留下他们吗？”我问。
‘Yes. Because of the artillery. The captain told me to go because of the artillery.’
“是的。因为炮火。上尉叫我离开，是因为炮火。”
‘And you have no family?’ I asked, watching the far end of the bridge where a few last carts were hurrying down the slope of the bank.
“你没有家人吗？”我问着，看着桥的远端，几辆最后的马车正匆匆沿着河岸的斜坡向下行去。
‘No,’ he said, ‘only the animals I stated. The cat, of course, will be all right. A cat can look out for itself, but I cannot think what will become of the others.’
“没有，”他说，“只有我提到的那些动物。猫当然没事。猫能照顾自己，但我想不出其他动物会怎么办。”
‘What politics have you?’ I asked.
“你有什么政治主张吗？”我问。
‘I am without politics,’ he said. ‘I am seventy-six years old. I have come twelve kilometres now and I think now I can go no farther.’
“我没有政治主张，”他说。“我七十六岁了。我已经走了十二公里，现在觉得自己再也走不动了。”
‘This is not a good place to stop,’ I said. ‘If you can make it, there are trucks up the road where it forks for Tortosa.’
“这里不是停车的好地方，”我说。“如果你能坚持到那儿，道路分岔往托尔托萨方向有卡车。”
‘I will wait a while,’ he said, 'and then I will go. Where do the trucks go?’
“我会等一会儿，”他说，“然后我会走。那些卡车去哪儿？”
‘Towards Barcelona,’ I told him.
“去巴塞罗那，”我对他说。
‘I know of no one in that direction,’ he said, ‘but thank you very much. Thank you again very much.’
“我在那个方向上不认识任何人，”他说，“但非常感谢你。再次非常感谢。”
He looked at me very blankly and tiredly, then said, having to share his worry with someone, "The cat will be all right, I am sure. There is no need to be unquiet about the cat. But the others. Now what do you think about the others?’
他显得很茫然又疲惫，然后说，必须与人分担他的忧虑，“那只猫会没事的，我肯定。没必要为那只猫不安。但其他的呢。现在你认为其他的会怎么样？”
‘Why, they’ll probably come through it all right.’
“哦，他们大概都能挺过去的。”
‘You think so?’
“你这样认为？”
‘Why not?’ I said, watching the far bank where now there were no carts.
“为什么不呢？”我说，看着远岸，现在那里已经没有马车了。
‘But what will they do under the artillery when I was told to leave because of the artillery?’
“可是在炮火下他们会怎么办？当我因为炮火被叫走时他们怎么办？”
‘Did you leave the dove cage unlocked?’ I asked.
“你把鸽子笼没锁吗？”我问。
‘Yes.’
“是的。”
‘Then they’ll fly.’
“那他们就会飞走。”
‘Yes, certainly they’ll fly. But the others. It’s better not to think about the others,’ he said.
“是的，当然他们会飞走。但其他的呢。最好别去想其他的，”他说。
‘If you are rested I would go,’ I urged. ‘Get up and try to walk now.’
“如果你休息够了我还是会走，”我劝道。“起来，现在试着走走。”
‘Thank you,’ he said and got to his feet, swayed from side to side and then sat down backwards in the dust.
“谢谢你，”他说着站起身，左右摇晃着，然后朝后坐在尘土里。
‘I was only taking care of animals,’ he said dully, but no longer to me. ‘I was only taking care of animals.’
“我只是照顾动物，”他木然地说，但不再对我说。“我只是照顾动物。”
There was nothing to do about him. It was Easter Sunday and the Fascists were advancing toward the Ebro. It was a grey overcast day with a low ceiling so their planes were not up. That and the fact that cats know how to look after themselves was all the good luck that old man would ever have.
他无可救药了。那是复活节星期天，法西斯正在向埃布罗推进。天空阴沉低垂，云层很低，所以他们的飞机没有出动。老头唯一的好运也不过如此：再加上猫会照顾自己，这就是他所能拥有的全部好事。

UP IN MICHIGAN
在密歇根上方

Jim Gilmore came to Hortons Bay from Canada. He bought the blacksmith shop from old man Horton. Jim was short and dark with big moustaches and big hands. He was a good horseshoer and did not look much like a blacksmith even with his leather apron on. He lived upstairs above the blacksmith shop and took his meals at D. J. Smith’s.
吉姆·吉尔莫从加拿大来到霍顿湾。他从老霍顿手里买下了铁匠铺。吉姆个子矮，肤色偏黑，留着大胡子，手也很大。他是个不错的马掌匠，即便戴着皮围裙也看不太像铁匠。他住在铁匠铺上面的楼上，在 D. J. Smith’s 用餐。
Liz Coates worked for Smith’s. Mrs. Smith, who was a very large clean woman, said Liz Coates was the neatest girl she’d ever seen. Liz had good legs and always wore clean gingham aprons and Jim noticed that her hair was always neat behind. He liked her face because it was so jolly but he never thought about her.
丽兹·科茨在 Smith’s 工作。史密斯太太是个非常干净且体型硕大的女人，她说丽兹·科茨是她见过的最整洁的女孩。丽兹有一双好腿，总是穿着干净的方格布围裙，吉姆注意到她的头发总是梳得很整齐。他喜欢她的脸，因为看起来很快乐，但他从没想过要追求她。
Liz liked Jim very much. She liked it the way he walked over from the shop and often went to the kitchen door to watch for him to start down the road. She liked it about his moustache. She liked it about how white his teeth were when he smiled. She liked it very much that he didn’t look like a blacksmith. She liked it how much D. J. Smith and Mrs. Smith liked Jim. One day she found that she liked it the way the hair was black on his arms and how white they were above the tanned line when he washed up in the washbasin outside the house. Liking that made her feel funny.
莉兹非常喜欢吉姆。她喜欢他从商店走过来的样子，经常走到厨房门口等着看他沿着路走来。她喜欢他的小胡子。她喜欢他微笑时牙齿有多白。她非常喜欢他看起来不像个铁匠。她喜欢 D. J. Smith 和 Smith 太太有多喜欢吉姆。一天她发现她喜欢他手臂上黑黑的毛，以及他在屋外的洗脸盆洗脸时，晒黑线以上的皮肤有多么白。喜欢这些让她感觉很奇怪。
Hortons Bay, the town, was only five houses on the main road between Boyne City and Charlevoix. There was the general store and post-office with a high false front and maybe a wagon hitched out in front, Smith’s house, Stroud’s house, Dillworth’s house, Horton’s house, and Van Hoosen’s house. The houses were in a big grove of elm trees and the road was very sandy. Up the road a ways was the Methodist church and down the road the other direction was the township school. The blacksmith shop was painted red and faced the school.
霍顿湾镇只有五幢房子，位于博因城和查利沃伊之间的主路上。那里有带高假面墙的杂货店兼邮局，门前也许还拴着一辆马车，史密斯家，斯特劳德家，迪尔沃斯家，霍顿家，以及范胡森家。房子们坐落在一大片榆树林中，路是非常沙质的。往路上远处有一座卫理公会教堂，往相反方向下去是乡镇学校。铁匠铺漆成红色，正对着学校。
A steep sandy road ran down the hill to the bay through the timber. From Smith’s back door you could look out across the woods that ran down to the lake and across the bay. It was very beautiful in the spring and summer, the bay blue and bright and usually
一条陡峭的沙路从山上穿过林地向海湾延伸。站在史密斯家的后门可以看到向下延伸到湖边并横跨海湾的树林。春夏季节景色非常美，海湾湛蓝明亮，通常
whitecaps on the lake out beyond the point from the breeze blowing from Charlevoix and Lake Michigan. From Smith’s back door Liz could see ore barges way out in the lake going toward Boyne City. When she looked at them they didn’t seem to be moving at all but if she went in and dried some more dishes and then came out again they would be out of sight beyond the point.
湖面在岬角以外因查尔沃瓦和密歇根湖吹来的微风而泛起白沫波。站在史密斯家的后门，丽兹可以看到很远处湖上驶向博因城的矿砂驳船。她看着它们时，它们似乎根本没有动，可是如果她进屋去把更多的碟子擦干再出来时，它们就已在岬角那边看不见了。
All the time now Liz was thinking about Jim Gilmore. He didn’t seem to notice her much. He talked about the shop to D. J. Smith and about the Republican Party and James G. Blaine. In the evenings he read The Toledo Blade and the Grand Rapids paper by the lamp in the front room or went out spearing fish in the bay with a jacklight with D. J. Smith. In the fall he and Smith and Charley Wyman took a wagon and tent, grub, axes, their rifles and two dogs and went on a trip to the pine plains beyond Vanderbilt deer hunting. Liz and Mrs. Smith were cooking for four days for them before they started. Liz wanted to make something special for Jim to take but she didn’t finally because she was afraid to ask Mrs. Smith for the eggs and flour and afraid if she bought them Mrs. Smith would catch her cooking. It would have been all right with Mrs. Smith but Liz was afraid.
现在李兹整天都在想着吉姆·吉尔摩。他似乎并不怎么注意她。他和 D. J. Smith 谈店里的事，也谈共和党和詹姆斯·G·布莱恩。傍晚时分，他在前屋的灯下读《托莱多之刃》或《大急流城报》，有时便和 D. J. Smith 拿着荧光灯出海刺鱼。秋天，他、史密斯和查理·怀曼拉了一辆马车，带上帐篷、干粮、斧头、步枪和两只狗，去范德比尔特以外的松林平原打鹿。出发前，李兹和史密斯太太为他们做了四天的饭。李兹本想给吉姆做点特别的吃的带着，但最后没做，因为她怕去向史密斯太太要鸡蛋和面粉，又怕如果自己买了史密斯太太会发现她在做饭。其实史密斯太太不会介意，但李兹就是害怕。
All the time Jim was gone on the deer hunting trip Liz thought about him. It was awful while he was gone. She couldn’t sleep well from thinking about him but she discovered it was fun to think about him too. If she let herself go it was better. The night before they were to come back she didn’t sleep at all, that is she didn’t think she slept because it was all mixed up in a dream about not sleeping and really not sleeping. When she saw the wagon coming down the road she felt weak and sick sort of inside. She couldn’t wait till she saw Jim and it seemed as though everything would be all right when he came. The wagon stopped outside under the big elm and Mrs. Smith and Liz went out. All the men had beards and there were three deer in the back of the wagon, their thin legs sticking stiff over the edge of the wagon box. Mrs. Smith kissed D. J. and he hugged her. Jim said ‘Hello, Liz,’ and grinned. Liz hadn’t known just what would happen when Jim got back but she was sure it would be something. Nothing had happened. The men were just home, that was all. Jim pulled the burlap sacks off the deer and Liz looked at them. One was a big buck. It was stiff and hard to lift out of the wagon.
吉姆去打鹿那几天，莉兹一直想着他。他不在的时候真难熬。她因想他而睡不好觉，但她也发现想他很有意思。如果她任由自己放开去想会更好。应该他们回来前一晚她根本没睡，那就是她觉得自己没睡，因为一切都混在一个关于没睡的梦里，梦里她确实没睡。她看到马车沿路驶来时，心里感到一阵虚弱和恶心。她迫不及待想见到吉姆，似乎只要他一来一切就会好起来。马车在大榆树下停了下来，史密斯太太和莉兹走了出去。所有男人都留着胡子，马车后厢里有三只鹿，瘦长的腿僵硬地搭在车厢边上。史密斯太太亲了 D. J.，他抱了抱她。吉姆说：“你好，莉兹，”并咧嘴笑了。莉兹并不确切知道吉姆回来会发生什么，但她确信会有点什么。什么也没发生。那些男人只是回来了，仅此而已。吉姆把麻袋从鹿身上拽下来，莉兹看着它们。其中有一只是大公鹿。它僵硬，很难从车厢里抬出来。
‘Did you shoot it, Jim?’ Liz asked.
“是你打的吗，吉姆？”丽兹问。
‘Yeah. Ain’t it a beauty?’ Jim got it on to his back to carry to the smokehouse.
“是啊。漂亮吧？”吉姆把它背到背上，准备扛到烟熏屋去。
That night Charley Wyman stayed to supper at Smith’s. It was too late to get back to Charlevoix. The men washed up and waited in the front room for supper.
那天晚上，查理·怀曼在史密斯家留下来吃晚饭。回查尔沃瓦已太晚了。男人们洗了手，坐在前厅等着吃饭。
‘Ain’t there something left in that crock, Jimmy?’ D. J. Smith asked, and Jim went out to the wagon in the barn and fetched in the jug of whisky the men had taken hunting with them. It was a four-gallon jug and there was quite a little slopped back and forth in the bottom. Jim took a long pull on his way back to the house. It was hard to lift such a big jug up to drink out of it. Some of the whisky ran down on his shirt front. The two men smiled when Jim came in with the jug. D. J. Smith sent for glasses and Liz brought them. D. J. poured out three big shots.
“坛子里难道还有剩的吗，吉米？”D. J.·史密斯问，吉姆便去了谷仓里的马车，拿来了男人们打猎时带去的那壶威士忌。那是个四加仑的大壶，壶底还晃着不少酒。吉姆回房路上长长地喝了一口。把这么大的壶抬起来喝很费劲。有些威士忌顺着他的衬衫前襟流下来。吉姆端着壶进来时，两人都笑了。D. J.·史密斯让人拿来杯子，丽兹端来了。D. J.倒了三大杯。
'Well, here’s looking at you, D. J., said Charley Wyman.
“好吧，敬你，D. J.，”查理·怀曼说。
‘That damn big buck, Jimmy,’ said D. J.
“该死的大公鹿，吉米，”D. J. 说。
‘Here’s all the ones we missed, D. J.,’ said Jim, and downed his liquor.
“这些就是我们漏掉的，D. J.，”吉姆说着把酒一饮而尽。
‘Tastes good to a man.’
“男人喝着就是好受。”
‘Nothing like it this time of year for what ails you.’
“这个季节对你的病没什么比这更好的了。”
‘How about another, boys?’
“再来一杯，伙计们？”
‘Here’s how, D. J.’
“照这样来，D. J。”
‘Down the creek, boys.’
“顺着小溪走，孩子们。”
‘Here’s to next year.’
“为明年干杯。”
Jim began to feel great. He loved the taste and the feel of whisky. He was glad to be back to a comfortable bed and warm food and the shop. He had another drink. The men came in to supper feeling hilarious but acting very respectable. Liz sat at the table after she put on the food and ate with the family. It was a good dinner. The men ate seriously. After supper they went into the front room again and Liz cleaned off with Mrs. Smith. Then Mrs. Smith went upstairs and pretty soon Smith came out and went upstairs too. Jim and Charley were still in the front room. Liz was sitting in the kitchen next to the stove pretending to read a book and thinking about Jim. She didn’t want to go to bed yet because she knew Jim would be coming out and she wanted to see him as he went out so she could take the way he looked up to bed with her.
吉姆开始感到心情极好。他喜欢威士忌的味道和感觉。他很庆幸能回到舒适的床、热腾腾的食物和那家商店。他又喝了一杯。那些男人们进来吃晚饭时觉得非常兴奋，但举止却很体面。莉兹在摆好饭菜后坐到桌旁，与家人一起吃饭。那是一顿不错的晚餐。男人们严肃地吃着。晚饭后他们又回到前屋，莉兹和史密斯太太一起收拾清洁。然后史密斯太太上了楼，不久史密斯也走出来然后上了楼。吉姆和查理还在前屋。莉兹坐在厨房炉子旁假装看书，心里想着吉姆。她还不想上床，因为她知道吉姆会出来，她想在他出去的时候看到他，好把他上楼时的模样带回自己的脑海。
She was thinking about him hard and then Jim came out. His eyes
她正专心想着他，这时吉姆走了出来。他的眼睛
were shining and his hair was a little rumpled. Liz looked down at her book. Jim came over back of her chair and stood there and she could feel him breathing and then he put his arms around her. Her breasts felt plump and firm and the nipples were erect under his hands. Liz was terribly frightened, no one had ever touched her, but she thought, ‘He’s come to me finally. He’s really come.’
阳光在他眼里闪烁，他的头发有点乱。莉兹低头看着书。吉姆从她椅背那边走过来站着，她能感觉到他的呼吸，然后他搂住了她。她的胸部感觉饱满而坚挺，乳头在他的手下挺立。莉兹极度害怕，从来没人碰过她，但她想，“他终于来找我了。他真的来了。”
She held herself stiff because she was so frightened and did not know anything else to do and then Jim held her tight against the chair and kissed her. It was such a sharp, aching, hurting feeling that she thought she couldn’t stand it. She felt Jim right through the back of the chair and she couldn’t stand it and then something clicked inside of her and the feeling was warmer and softer. Jim held her tight hard against the chair and she wanted it now and Jim whispered, ‘Come on for a walk.’
她因为害怕而僵住，不知道该怎么办，然后吉姆把她紧紧按在椅子上并亲了她。那是一种尖锐、刺痛、疼痛的感觉，她觉得自己快受不了。她透过椅背感受到吉姆的存在，她受不了，然后她内心有什么东西咔嚓一响，那感觉变得更温暖、更柔和。吉姆把她紧紧按在椅子上，她现在渴望这事，吉姆低声说，“出去散散步吧。”
Liz took her coat off the peg on the kitchen wall and they went out the door. Jim had his arm around her and every little way they stopped and pressed against each other and Jim kissed her. There was no moon and they walked ankle-deep in the sandy road through the trees down to the dock and the warehouse on the bay. The water was lapping in the piles and the point was dark across the bay. It was cold but Liz was hot all over from being with Jim. They sat down in the shelter of the warehouse and Jim pulled Liz close to him. She was frightened. One of Jim’s hands went inside her dress and stroked over her breast and the other hand was in her lap. She was very frightened and didn’t know how he was going to go about things but she snuggled close to him. Then the hand that felt so big in her lap went away and was on her leg and started to move up it.
莉兹从厨房墙上的衣架上取下外套，他们走出门去。吉姆挽着她的胳膊，走着走着每一会儿就停下来相互贴近，吉姆亲她。没有月亮，他们走在树丛间那条沙土路上，脚踝浸在沙里，往码头和海湾边的仓库方向走去。水拍打着木桩，海湾对岸的岬角一片黑暗。很冷，但和吉姆在一起让莉兹浑身发热。他们在仓库的遮蔽处坐下，吉姆把莉兹拉到身边。她很害怕。吉姆的一只手探进她的裙子，抚过她的胸部，另一只手放在她的腿上。她非常害怕，不知道他要怎么做，但她还是依偎在他怀里。然后那只在她腿上感觉很大的手移开了，放到她的大腿上并开始向上移动。
‘Don’t, Jim,’ Liz said. Jim slid the hand farther up.
“不要，吉姆，”莉兹说。吉姆把手滑得更往上去了。
‘You mustn’t, Jim. You mustn’t.’ Neither Jim nor Jim’s big hand paid any attention to her.
“你别这样，吉姆。你别这样。”吉姆和吉姆那只大手都没理会她。
The boards were hard. Jim had her dress up and was trying to do something to her. She was frightened but she wanted it. She had to have it but it frightened her.
木板很硬。吉姆掀起了她的裙子，正试图对她做些什么。她很害怕，但她想要。她必须得到它，但这让她害怕。
‘You mustn’t do it, Jim. You mustn’t.’
“你不能这样，吉姆。你不能。”
‘I got to. I’m going to. You know we got to.’
“我得这么做。我会这么做。你知道我们非得这么做不可。”
‘No we haven’t, Jim. We ain’t got to. Oh, it isn’t right. Oh, it’s so big and it hurts so. You can’t. Oh, Jim. Jim. Oh.’
“不，我们不必，吉姆。我们并不非得。哦，这不对。哦，这太巨大了，太痛了。你不能。哦，吉姆。吉姆。哦。”
The hemlock planks of the docks were hard and splintery and cold and Jim was heavy on her and he had hurt her. Liz pushed
码头上的铁杉木板又硬又易碎又冰冷，吉姆压得她沉重，他伤害了她。莉兹挣开（推开）
him, she was so uncomfortable and cramped. Jim was asleep. He wouldn’t move. She worked out from under him and sat up and straightened her skirt and coat and tried to do something with her hair. Jim was sleeping with his mouth a little open. Liz leaned over and kissed him on the cheek. He was still asleep. She lifted his head a little and shook it. He rolled his head over and swallowed. Liz started to cry. She walked over to the edge of the dock and looked down to the water. There was a mist coming up from the bay. She was cold and miserable and everything felt gone. She walked back to where Jim was lying and shook him once to make sure. She was crying.
她在他身上睡得很不舒服，浑身拘束。吉姆睡着了，动也不动。她从他下面钻出来，坐起身，理了理裙子和外套，试着整理头发。吉姆睡得嘴微微张着。莉兹俯身在他脸颊上吻了一下。他仍然睡着。她把他的头抬起一点，摇了摇。他转了下头，咽了口唾沫。莉兹开始哭了。她走到码头边往水面看去。海湾上升起一层薄雾。她觉得冷，痛苦，所有东西都像消失了一样。她走回吉姆躺着的地方，轻轻摇了摇他以确定。他在哭。
‘Jim,’ she said. ‘Jim. Please, Jim.’
“吉姆，”她说。“吉姆。拜托，吉姆。”
Jim stirred and curled a little tighter. Liz took off her coat and leaned over and covered him with it. She tucked it around him neatly and carefully. Then she walked across the dock and up the steep sandy road to go to bed. A cold mist was coming up through the woods from the bay.
吉姆动了动，缩得更紧了。莉兹脱下外套，俯身把外套盖在他身上。她把外套整整齐齐、小心地裹好。然后她走过码头，沿着陡峭的沙路上床去。冷雾正从海湾穿过树林升起。

ON THE QUAI AT SMYRNA
在斯穆尔纳的码头上

The strange thing was, he said, how they screamed every night at midnight. I do not know why they screamed at that time. We were in the harbour and they were all on the pier and at midnight they started screaming. We used to turn the searchlight on them to quiet them. That always did the trick. We’d run the searchlight up and down over them two or three times and they stopped it. One time I was senior officer on the pier and a Turkish officer came up to me in a frightful rage because one of our sailors had been most insulting to him. So I told him the fellow would be sent on ship and be most severely punished. I asked him to point him out. So he pointed out a gunner’s mate, most inoffensive chap. Said he’d been most frightfully and repeatedly insulting; talking to me through an interpreter. I couldn’t imagine how the gunner’s mate knew enough Turkish to be insulting. I called him over and said, ‘And just in case you should have spoken to any Turkish officers.’
他奇怪的是，他们每晚午夜都会尖叫。我不知道他们为什么在那个时候尖叫。我们在港口，他们都在码头上，到了午夜他们就开始尖叫。我们常常把探照灯照在他们身上以让他们安静下来。那招总是管用。我们会把探照灯在他们身上上下扫两三次，他们就停了。一次我在码头当高级军官，有个土耳其军官怒气冲冲地跑来找我，说我们一个水兵对他极为无礼。因此我告诉他，那人会被送上船并受到严厉惩罚。我请他指认。所以他指了一个炮手学徒，是个非常无害的小伙子。他说那人反复极其无礼；通过翻译跟我说的。我实在想不通那个炮手学徒怎么会懂得足够的土耳其语去侮辱人。我把他叫过来，说，‘以防万一你确实和哪些土耳其军官说过话，’
‘I haven’t spoken to any of them, sir.’
‘我没有和他们任何人说过话，长官。’
‘I’m quite sure of it,’ I said, ‘but you’d best go on board ship and not come ashore again for the rest of the day.’
‘我很肯定，’我说，‘但你最好上船去，今天剩下的时间别再上岸了。’
Then I told the Turk the man was being sent on board ship and would be most severely dealt with. Oh, most rigorously. He felt topping about it. Great friends we were.
然后我告诉土耳其人那人要被押上船，并且会受到最严厉的惩处。哦，极其严厉。他为此显得很得意。我们是多么要好的朋友啊。
The worst, he said, were the women with dead babies. You couldn’t get the women to give up their dead babies. They’d have babies dead for six days. Wouldn’t give them up. Nothing you could do about it. Had to take them away finally. Then there was an old lady, most extraordinary case. I told it to a doctor and he said I was lying. We were clearing them off the pier, had to clear off the dead ones, and this old woman was lying on a sort of litter. They said, ‘Will you have a look at her, sir?’ So I had a look at her and just then she died and went absolutely stiff. Her legs drew up and she drew up from the waist and went quite rigid. Exactly as though she had been dead over night. She was quite dead and absolutely rigid. I told a medical chap about it and he told me it was impossible.
他说最糟的是那些抱着死婴的妇女。你无法让这些妇女放弃她们的死婴。她们的婴儿死了六天都不肯放手。什么也拿她们没办法。最后只好把她们带走。还有一个老妇人，情况非常离奇。我把这事告诉一个医生，他说我在撒谎。我们在把他们从码头清理走，得把死去的那些清走，这个老妇人躺在一种担架似的东西上。他们说，“先生，你能看看她吗？”于是我去看了看她，正好那时她就死了，而且完全僵直。她的腿蜷起了，从腰部也缩起来，变得很僵硬。就好像她已经死了一夜似的。她确实已死，完全僵硬。我把这事告诉一个医学界的人，他却说那不可能。
They were all out there on the pier and it wasn’t at all like an earthquake or that sort of thing because they never knew about the Turk. They never knew what the old Turk would do. You remember when they ordered us not to come in to take off any more? I had the wind up when we came in that morning. He had any amount of batteries and could have blown us clean out of the water. We were going to come in, run close along the pier, let go the front and rear anchors and then shell the Turkish quarter of the town. They would have blown us out of water but we would have blown the town simply to hell. They just fired a few blank charges at us as we came in. Kemal came down and sacked the Turkish commander. For exceeding his authority or some such thing. He got a bit above himself. It would have been the hell of a mess.
他们都在码头外面，完全不像地震之类的事，因为他们从来不知道那个土耳其人会做什么。他们从不了解那老土耳其人会怎么行动。你还记得他们命令我们不要再进来卸货吗？我们那天早上进港的时候我心里紧张。他有大量炮弹，完全可以把我们炸得粉身碎骨。我们本打算进港，沿着码头靠近行驶，放下前后锚，然后轰击城里的土耳其区。他们本可以把我们炸沉，但我们也会把那个镇子彻底炸成烂摊子。他们只是向我们靠近时打了几声空包弹。Kemal 下来撤了那名土耳其指挥官的职。说是越权什么的。他有点自作主张。那本会是一场大混乱。
You remember the harbour. There were plenty of nice things floating around in it. That was the only time in my life I got so I dreamed about things. You didn’t mind the women who were having babies as you did those with the dead ones. They had them all right. Surprising how few of them died. You just covered them over with something and let them go to it. They’d always pick out the darkest place in the hold to have them. None of them minded anything once they got off the pier.
你还记得那个港口。里面漂着许多好东西。那是我一生中唯一一次会梦见事物。那些生孩子的女人并不像那些死去的女人那样让你介意。她们都生下来了。令人惊讶的是死得那么少。你只要给她们盖上点东西，然后让它们去吧。她们总是在船舱里挑最暗的地方生孩子。一旦离开码头，她们就什么都不在乎了。
The Greeks were nice chaps too. When they evacuated they had all their baggage animals they couldn’t take off with them so they just broke their forelegs and dumped them into the shallow water. All those mules with their forelegs broken pushed over into the shallow water. It was all a pleasant business. My word, yes, a most pleasant business.
希腊人也不错。当他们撤离时，那些不能带走的负重动物也带不走了，于是他们就把前腿折断，把它们丢进浅水里。所有那些前腿折断的骡子被推倒进浅水。这是一桩愉快的事情。我的老天，是的，极其愉快的一桩事。

IN OUR TIME
在我们这个时代

Everybody was drunk. The whole battery was drunk going along the road in the dark. We were going to the Champagne. The lieutenant kept riding his horse out into the fields and saying to him, ‘I’m drunk, I tell you, mon vieux. Oh, I am so soused.’ We went along the road all night in the dark and the adjutant kept riding up alongside my kitchen and saying, ‘You must put it out. It is dangerous. It will be observed.’ We were fifty kilometres from the front but the adjutant worried about the fire in my kitchen. It was funny going along that road. That was when I was a kitchen corporal.
大家都喝醉了。整支电池沿着夜路行进时都醉了。我们要去香槟区。中尉不断骑着马往田里去，对他说：“我醉了，我跟你说，mon vieux。哦，我喝得烂醉。”我们整夜在黑暗中沿着路走，副官不停地骑到我厨房旁边来说：“你得把它熄了。很危险。会被发现的。”我们离前线五十公里，可副官却担心我厨房的火。沿着那条路走真有趣。那会儿我还是个厨房下士。

*/ INDIAN CAMP
*/ 印第安人营

At the lake shore there was another rowboat drawn up. The two Indians stood waiting.
湖边靠岸着另一只小船。两个印第安人站着等候。
Nick and his father got in the stern of the boat and the Indians shoved it off and one of them got in to row. Uncle George sat in the stern of the camp rowboat. The young Indian shoved the camp boat off and got in to row Uncle George.
尼克和他父亲坐在船尾，印第安人把船推开，其中一个上船划桨。乔治叔叔坐在营地小船的尾部。年轻的印第安人把营船推开，上船为乔治叔叔划桨。
The two boats started off in the dark. Nick heard the oarlocks of the other boat quite a way ahead of them in the mist. The Indians rowed with quick choppy strokes. Nick lay back with his father’s arm around him. It was cold on the water. The Indian who was rowing them was working very hard, but the other boat moved farther ahead in the mist all the time.
两只小船在黑暗中出发。尼克听见另一只船的橹枢在雾中远远地领先他们的声音。印第安人用短促而急的划桨动作划着。尼克靠着，父亲的胳膊搭在他身上。水面上很冷。划船的印第安人很卖力，但那只船在雾中一直越划越远。
‘Where are we going, Dad?’ Nick asked.
“我们要去哪里，爸爸？”尼克问。
‘Over to the Indian camp. There is an Indian lady very sick.’
“去印第安营地。那儿有个印第安妇人病得很重。”
‘Oh,’ said Nick.
“哦，”尼克说。
Across the bay they found the other boat beached. Uncle George was smoking a cigar in the dark. The young Indian pulled the boat way up on the beach. Uncle George gave both the Indians cigars.
他们在海湾对面发现另一只船搁浅着。乔治叔叔在黑暗中抽着雪茄。年轻的印第安人把船拉上了很远的海滩。乔治叔叔给了两个印第安人雪茄。
They walked up from the beach through a meadow that was soaking wet with dew, following the young Indian who carried a
他们沿着被露水浸透的草地从海滩往上走，跟在拿着灯笼的年轻印第安人后面。
lantern. Then they went into the woods and followed a trail that led to the logging road that ran back into the hills. It was much lighter on the logging road as the timber was cut away on both sides. The young Indian stopped and blew out his lantern and they all walked on along the road.
然后他们进了林子，沿着一条通往山里采伐路的小径走去。因为两边的林木都被砍掉了，采伐路上亮得多。年轻的印第安人停下，吹灭了灯笼，他们便沿着路继续走。
They came around a bend and a dog came out barking. Ahead were the lights of the shanties where the Indian bark-peelers lived. More dogs rushed out at them. The two Indians sent them back to the shanties. In the shanty nearest the road there was a light in the window. An old woman stood in the doorway holding a lamp.
他们绕过一个弯，一只狗跑出来大声吠叫。前面是印第安人剥树皮工人住的简陋小屋的灯光。更多的狗冲出来向他们扑去。两个印第安人把狗赶回了小屋。靠近路边的一间小屋窗户里有灯光。一个老妇人站在门口，手里拿着一盏灯。
Inside on a wooden bunk lay a young Indian woman. She had been trying to have her baby for two days. All the old women in the camp had been helping her. The men had moved off up the road to sit in the dark and smoke out of range of the noise she made. She screamed just as Nick and the two Indians followed his father and Uncle George into the shanty. She lay in the lower bunk, very big under a quilt. Her head was turned to one side. In the upper bunk was her husband. He had cut his foot very badly with an axe three days before. He was smoking a pipe. The room smelled very bad.
在一张木铺上躺着一个年轻的印度妇女。她已经试图生孩子两天了。营地里所有年长的妇女都在帮她。男人们都搬到路那边去，坐在黑暗中抽烟，避开她发出的噪声。就在尼克和两个印度人跟着他的父亲和乔治叔叔走进小屋时，她尖叫起来。她躺在下铺，裹在被子下显得很大。她的头偏向一侧。上铺是她的丈夫。三天前他用斧头把脚砍得很重。他在抽烟斗。房间里味道很难闻。
Nick’s father ordered some water to be put on the stove, and while it was heating he spoke to Nick.
尼克的父亲让人在炉子上烧些水，水热的时候他对尼克说话。
‘This lady is going to have a baby, Nick,’ he said.
“这位女士要生孩子了，尼克，”他说。
‘I know,’ said Nick.
“我知道，”尼克说。
‘You don’t know,’ said his father. ‘Listen to me. What she is going through is called being in labour. The baby wants to be born and she wants it to be born. All her muscles are trying to get the baby born. That is what is happening when she screams.’
“你不知道，”他父亲说。“听我说。她现在经历的叫做分娩。孩子想要出生，她也想让孩子出生。她全身的肌肉都在努力把孩子生出来。她一喊就是这个原因。”
‘I see,’ Nick said.
“我明白了，”尼克说。
Just then the woman cried out.
就在这时，女人喊了一声。
‘Oh, Daddy, can’t you give her something to make her stop screaming?’ asked Nick.
“哦，爸爸，你不能给她点什么让她别喊吗？”尼克问。
‘No. I haven’t any anaesthetic,’ his father said. ‘But her screams are not important. I don’t hear them because they are not important.’
“没有。我没有任何麻醉剂，”他父亲说。“但她的尖叫声不重要。我听不见，因为它们不重要。”
The husband in the upper bunk rolled over against the wall.
上铺的丈夫翻身靠向墙壁。
The woman in the kitchen motioned to the doctor that the water was hot. Nick’s father went into the kitchen and poured about half of the water out of the big kettle into a basin. Into the water left in the kettle he put several things he unwrapped from a handkerchief.
厨房里的女人示意医生水是热的。尼克的父亲进了厨房，把大水壶里大约一半的水倒进了一只盆子。壶里剩下的水里，他从手帕里拿出几样东西放了进去。
‘Those must boil,’ he said, and began to scrub his hands in the basin of hot water with a cake of soap he had brought from the camp. Nick watched his father’s hands scrubbing each other with the soap. While his father washed his hands very carefully and thoroughly, he talked.
“那些必须煮沸，”他说着，开始用他从营地带来的香皂在热水盆里搓洗双手。尼克看着父亲用香皂互相搓洗着的手。当父亲非常仔细、彻底地洗手时，他一边说话。
‘You see, Nick, babies are supposed to be born head first, but sometimes they’re not. When they’re not they make a lot of trouble for everybody. Maybe I’ll have to operate on this lady. We’ll know in a little while.’
“你看，尼克，婴儿应该是头先出来的，可有时候不是。不是的话就会给大家带来很多麻烦。也许我得给这位女士动手术。过一会儿就知道了。”
When he was satisfied with his hands he went in and went to work.
当他的手合适了，他就进去开始工作。
‘Pull back that quilt, will you, George?’ he said. ‘I’d rather not touch it.’
“乔治，把那条被子拉回去，好吗？”他说。“我倒不太愿意碰它。”
Later when he started to operate Uncle George and three Indian men held the woman still. She bit Uncle George on the arm and Uncle George said, ‘Damn squaw bitch!’ and the young Indian who had rowed Uncle George over laughed at him. Nick held the basin for his father. It all took a long time.
后来当他开始动手术时，乔治叔和三个印度人按住了那位妇人。她咬了乔治叔的胳膊，乔治叔说：“该死的女巫！”划船把乔治叔划过来的那个年轻印度人朝他笑。尼克给他父亲扶着盆。整个过程花了很长时间。
His father picked the baby up and slapped it to make it breathe and handed it to the old woman.
他的父亲抱起婴儿，打了几下让它喘气，然后把孩子递给了老妇人。
‘See, it’s a boy, Nick,’ he said. ‘How do you like being an interne?’
“看，是个男孩，Nick，”他说。“当寄宿医生成了怎样？”
Nick said, ‘All right.’ He was looking away so as not to see what his father was doing.
Nick 说，“好吧。”他把目光移开，不想看他父亲在做什么。
‘There. That gets it,’ said his father and put something into the basin.
“好了，这就行了，”他父亲说着，向盆里放了些什么。
Nick didn’t look at it.
尼克没看它。
‘Now,’ his father said, ‘there’s some stitches to put in. You can watch this or not, Nick, just as you like. I’m going to sew up the incision I made.’
“现在，”他父亲说，“要缝几针。你可以看，也可以不看，尼克，随你喜欢。我准备把我开的切口缝起来。”
Nick did not watch. His curiosity had been gone for a long time.
尼克没有看。他的好奇心早已消失。
His father finished and stood up. Uncle George and the three Indian men stood up. Nick put the basin out in the kitchen.
他父亲说完站起来了。乔治叔叔和三个印度人也都站了起来。尼克把脸盆端到厨房里。
Uncle George looked at his arm. The young Indian smiled reminiscently.
乔治叔叔看着他的胳膊。那个年轻的印度人带着回忆的微笑。
‘I’ll put some peroxide on that, George,’ the doctor said.
“我给你那儿擦点双氧水，乔治，”医生说。
He bent over the Indian woman. She was quiet now and her eyes were closed. She looked very pale. She did not know what had become of the baby or anything.
他俯身看那名印度妇女。她现在安静了，眼睛闭着。她看起来很苍白。她不知道孩子怎样了，或发生了什么事。
‘I’ll be back in the morning,’ the doctor said, standing up. ‘The nurse should be here from St. Ignace by noon and she’ll bring everything we need.’
“我早上会回来的，”医生站起来说。“护士应该会在中午从圣伊纳斯过来，她会带来我们需要的一切。”
He was feeling exalted and talkative as football players are in the dressing room after a game.
他感到振奋且多话，像赛后更衣室里的橄榄球运动员那样。
‘That’s one for the medical journal, George,’ he said. ‘Doing a Caesarian with a jack-knife and sewing it up with nine-foot, tapered gut leaders.’
“这可得登上医学期刊，乔治，”他说。“用折刀做剖腹产，然后用九英尺长、逐渐变细的肠线把它缝上。”
Uncle George was standing against the wall, looking at his arm.
乔治叔叔靠在墙边，盯着自己的手臂看。
‘Oh, you’re a great man, all right,’ he said.
“哦，你真是个了不起的人，没错，”他说。
‘Ought to have a look at the proud father. They’re usually the worst sufferers in these little affairs,’ the doctor said. ‘I must say he took it all pretty quietly.’
“应该看看那自豪的父亲。他们通常在这些小事情里受得最重，”医生说。“我得说他受得相当平静。”
He pulled back the blanket from the Indian’s head. His hand came away wet. He mounted on the edge of the lower bunk with the lamp in one hand and looked in. The Indian lay with his face toward the wall. His throat had been cut from ear to ear. The blood had flowed down into a pool where his body sagged the bunk. His head rested on his left arm. The open razor lay, edge up, in the blankets.
他把毯子从那个印度人的头上拉开。他的手带着湿气。单手拿着灯，他站到下铺边上往里看。那个印度人面朝墙躺着。喉咙从一耳朵割到另一耳朵。血顺着流到他身体下塌的铺位上形成一滩。他的头靠在左臂上。剃刀敞开着，刀刃朝上，躺在毯子里。
‘Take Nick out of the shanty, George,’ the doctor said.
“把 Nick 从小屋里带出去，George，”医生说。
There was no need of that. Nick, standing in the door of the kitchen, had a good view of the upper bunk when his father, the lamp in one hand, tipped the Indian’s head back.
那没有必要。尼克站在厨房门口，看得清上铺的情况，他父亲一手拿着灯，把那个印第安人的头向后仰。
It was just beginning to be daylight when they walked along the logging road back toward the lake.
天刚破晓时，他们沿着伐木路往回走，朝湖边走去。
‘I’m terribly sorry I brought you along, Nickie,’ said his father, all his post-operative exhilaration gone. ‘It was an awful mess to put you through.’
“尼基，真抱歉把你带来了，”他父亲说，所有术后那种兴奋感全消了。“把你弄得这么狼狈，真是太糟糕了。”
‘Do ladies always have such a hard time having babies?’ Nick asked.
“女人生孩子总是这么难吗？”尼克问。
‘No, that was very, very exceptional.’
“不会，那实在是非常非常罕见的事。”
‘Why did he kill himself, Daddy?’
“他为什么要自杀，爸爸？”
‘I don’t know, Nick. He couldn’t stand things, I guess.’
“我不知道，尼克。我想他是受不了那些事了。”
‘Do many men kill themselves, Daddy?’
“很多男人会自杀吗，爸爸？”
‘Not very many, Nick.’
“没有多少，尼克。”
‘Do many women?’
“很多女人会这么做吗？”
‘Hardly ever.’
“几乎不会。”
‘Don’t they ever?’
“她们从来不这样吗？”
‘Oh, yes. They do sometimes.’
“哦，是的。他们有时会去的。”
‘Daddy?’
“爸爸？”
‘Yes.’
“嗯？”
‘Where did Uncle George go ?’
“乔治叔叔去哪儿了？”
‘He’ll turn up all right.’
“他会回来的。”
‘Is dying hard, Daddy?’
“死去难吗，爸爸？”
‘No, I think it’s pretty easy, Nick. It all depends.’
“不，我想挺容易的，尼克。一切都要看情况。”
They were seated in the boat, Nick in the stern, his father rowing. The sun was coming up over the hills. A bass jumped, making a circle in the water. Nick trailed his hand in the water. It felt warm in the sharp chill of the morning.
他们坐在小船上，尼克在船尾，父亲划着桨。太阳从山岗上升起。一个鲈鱼跃出水面，在水中画了个圈。尼克把手拖在水里。清晨的寒意很刺骨，但水摸起来温暖。
In the early morning on the lake sitting in the stern of the boat with his father rowing, he felt quite sure that he would never die.
清晨，在湖上坐在船尾，父亲划桨时，他非常确定自己永远不会死。
Minarets stuck up in the rain out of Adrianople across the mud flats. The carts were jammed for thirty miles along the Karagatch road. Water buffalo and cattle were hauling carts through the mud. No end and no beginning. Just carts loaded with everything they owned. The old men and women, soaked through, walked along keeping the cattle moving. The Maritza was running yellow almost up to the bridge. Carts were jammed solid on the bridge with camels bobbing along through them. Greek cavalry herded along the procession. Women and kids were in the carts couched with mattresses, mirrors, sewing machines, bundles. There was a woman having a kid with a young girl holding a blanket over her and crying. Scared sick looking at it. It rained all through the evacuation.
雨中，从亚得里亚诺普尔越过泥滩耸立出尖塔。沿着卡拉加奇路，马车塞了三十英里。水牛和牛在泥地里拉着车。没有尽头也没有开始。只是装着他们所有东西的车。老人和女人浑身湿透，边走边赶着牲畜。马里察河的水几乎涨到桥边，发黄地奔流着。桥上车流堵得水泄不通，骆驼在车群中点头穿行。希腊骑兵驱赶着队伍前进。女人和孩子们躺在车里，蜷着身子，带着床垫、镜子、缝纫机、包裹。一个女人正在临产，一个年轻女孩把毯子搭在她身上哭着。看着这一幕令人心惊胆战。撤离期间一直在下雨。

THE DOCTOR AND THE DOCTOR'S WIFE

Dick Boulton came from the Indian camp to cut up logs for Nick’s father. He brought his son Eddy and another Indian named Billy Tabeshaw with him. They came in through the back gate out of the woods, Eddy carrying the long cross-cut saw. It flopped over his shoulder and made a musical sound as he walked. Billy Tabeshaw carried two big cant-hooks. Dick had three axes under his arm.
迪克·鲍尔顿从印第安人营地来为尼克的父亲劈木头。他带来了儿子埃迪和另一个名叫比利·塔贝肖的印第安人。他们从后门从树林里进来，埃迪扛着那把长的两人锯。锯片搭在他肩上，走路时发出有节奏的响声。比利·塔贝肖扛着两把大撬棍。迪克腋下夹着三把斧头。
He turned and shut the gate. The others went on ahead of him down to the lake shore where the logs were buried in the sand.
他转身关上了门。其他人走在他前面，下到湖岸，那里木头埋在沙里。
The logs had been lost from the big log booms that were towed down the lake to the mill by the steamer Magic. They had drifted up on to the beach and if nothing were done about them sooner or later the crew of the Magic would come along the shore in a rowboat, spot the logs, drive an iron spike with a ring on it into the end of each one and then tow them out into the lake to make a new boom. But the lumbermen might never come for them because a few logs were not worth the price of a crew to gather them. If no one came for them they would be left to waterlog and rot on the beach.
这些原木是从被轮船 Magic 拖到锯厂的大浮木排中丢失的。它们被冲到海滩上，如果不尽快处理，迟早 Magic 的船员会划着小船沿着岸边来，发现这些原木，在每根木头的一端钉上一根带环的铁钉，然后把它们拖回湖中组成新的浮木排。但伐木工人也可能根本不会来，因为几根原木的价值不值得派一队人去打捞。如果没人来取，它们就会被留在海滩上浸水腐烂。
Nick’s father always assumed that this was what would happen, and hired the Indians to come down from the camp and cut the
尼克的父亲一直以为事情会是这样的，于是雇了印第安人从营地下来，用双人交叉锯把树干锯开，然后用楔子劈成一捆捆的劈柴和壁炉用的大块木料。
logs up with the cross-cut saw and split them with a wedge to make cord wood and chunks for the open fireplace. Dick Boulton walked around past the cottage down to the lake. There were four big beech logs lying almost buried in the sand. Eddy hung the saw up by one of its handles in the crotch of a tree. Dick put the three axes down on the little dock. Dick was a half-breed and many of the farmers around the lake believed he was really a white man. He was very lazy but a great worker once he was started. He took a plug of tobacco out of his pocket, bit off a chew and spoke in Ojibway to Eddy and Billy Tabeshaw.
木头用锯子锯开后，迪克·鲍尔顿绕过小屋走到湖边。沙里几乎埋着四大段山毛榉原木。埃迪把锯子的一只把手挂在一棵树的叉处。迪克把三把斧头放在小码头上。迪克是个混血儿，湖附近的许多农民都认为他实际上是个白人。他很懒，但一旦开始干活就干得很出力。他从口袋里掏出一块嚼烟，咬了一口，用奥吉布瓦语对埃迪和比利·塔贝肖说话。
They sunk the ends of their cant-hooks into one of the logs and swung against it to loosen it in the sand. They swung their weight against the shafts of the cant-hooks. The log moved in the sand. Dick Boulton turned to Nick’s father.
他们把撬钩的尖端插进其中一段原木，靠着用力摆动把它从沙里松动。他们把身体的分量压在撬钩的柄上。原木在沙里动了。迪克·鲍尔顿转向尼克的父亲。
‘Well, Doc,’ he said, ‘that’s a nice lot of lumber you’ve stolen.’
“好极了，医生，”他说，“这可是一大堆你偷来的好木头。”
‘Don’t talk that way, Dick,’ the doctor said. ‘It’s driftwood.’
“别那样说，迪克，”医生说。“那只是浮木。”
Eddy and Billy Tabeshaw had rocked the log out of the wet sand and rolled it toward the water.
艾迪和比利·塔贝肖把木头从湿沙里掀出来，往水边滚去。
‘Put it right in,’ Dick Boulton shouted.
“把它放进去，”迪克·鲍尔顿喊道。
‘What are you doing that for?’ asked the doctor.
“你们这是干什么？”医生问。
‘Wash it off. Clean off the sand on account of the saw. I want to see who it belongs to,’ Dick said.
“把它洗干净。把锯子弄出的沙子洗掉。我想看看是谁的，”迪克说。
The log was just awash in the lake. Eddy and Billy Tabeshaw leaned on their cant-hooks sweating in the sun. Dick kneeled down in the sand and looked at the mark of the scaler’s hammer in the wood at the end of the log.
那根原木在湖里刚好露出水面。埃迪和比利·塔贝肖撑着木钩在烈日下出汗。迪克跪在沙地上，看着原木尾端刻刀锤留下的印记。
‘It belongs to White and McNally,’ he said, standing up and brushing off his trousers knees.
“这是怀特和麦克纳利的，”他站起身，拍去裤膝上的沙子说。
The doctor was very uncomfortable.
医生非常不自在。
‘You’d better not saw it up then, Dick,’ he said, shortly.
“那你最好别把它锯了，迪克，”他简短地说。
‘Don’t get huffy, Doc,’ said Dick. ‘Don’t get huffy. I don’t care who you steal from. It’s none of my business.’
“别生气，医生，”迪克说。“别生气。我才不管你从谁那儿偷的。这不关我的事。”
‘If you think the logs are stolen, leave them alone and take your tools back to the camp,’ the doctor said. His face was red.
“如果你认为这些原木是偷来的，就别动它们，把你的工具拿回营地去，”医生说。他脸色通红。
‘Don’t go off at half cock, Doc,’ Dick said. He spat tobacco juice on the log. It slid off, thinning in the water. ‘You know they’re stolen as well as I do. It don’t make any difference to me.’
“别冲动行事，医生，”迪克说。他往原木上吐了口烟汁。烟汁滑落，在水里变薄。 “你知道它们是偷来的，就像我知道的一样。对我来说没什么区别。”
‘All right. If you think the logs are stolen, take your stuff and get out.’
“好吧。如果你认为那些木头是偷来的，就把你的东西拿走，滚出去。”
'Now, Doc - ’
“现在，医生——”
‘Take your stuff and get out.’
“把你的东西拿走，滚出去。”
‘Listen, Doc.’
“听着，医生。”
‘If you call me Doc once again, I’ll knock your eye teeth down your throat.’
“你再叫我一次‘医生’，我就把你的犬齿打进你喉咙里去。”
‘Oh, no, you won’t, Doc.’
“哦，不会的，医生。”
Dick Boulton looked at the doctor. Dick was a big man. He knew how big a man he was. He liked to get into fights. He was happy. Eddy and Billy Tabeshaw leaned on their cant-hooks and looked at the doctor. The doctor chewed the beard on his lower lip and looked at Dick Boulton. Then he turned away and walked up the hill to the cottage. They could see from his back how angry he was. They all watched him walk up the hill and go inside the cottage.
迪克·鲍尔顿看着医生。迪克是个大汉。他清楚自己有多大个子。他喜欢打架。他很高兴。埃迪和比利·塔贝肖靠着撬钩看着医生。医生咬着下唇上的胡须，看着迪克·鲍尔顿。然后他转身走上山坡，往小屋走去。他背影就能看出有多生气。他们都看着他走上山坡，进了小屋。
Dick said something in Ojibway. Eddy laughed but Billy Tabeshaw looked very serious. He did not understand English but he had sweat all the time the row was going on. He was fat with only a few hairs of moustache like a Chinaman. He picked up the two cant-hooks. Dick picked up the axes and Eddy took the saw down from the tree. They started off and walked up past the cottage and out the back gate into the woods. Dick left the gate open. Billy Tabeshaw went back and fastened it. They were gone through the woods.
迪克用奥吉布瓦语说了些什么。埃迪笑了，但比利·塔贝肖看上去很严肃。他不懂英语，但那场争执一直让他汗流浃背。他胖乎乎的，只有几根像中国人那样的胡须。他拣起两根撬钩。迪克拿起斧头，埃迪从树上取下锯子。他们出发了，走过小屋，出后门进了树林。迪克没把门关上。比利·塔贝肖回去把门拴上。他们穿过树林走远了。
In the cottage the doctor, sitting on the bed in his room, saw a pile of medical journals on the floor by the bureau. They were still in their wrappers unopened. It irritated him.
在小屋里，坐在自己房间床上的医生看到梳妆柜旁地板上有一摞医学期刊。它们仍包着套，未曾拆封。这让他很恼火。
‘Aren’t you going back to work, dear?’ asked the doctor’s wife from the room where she was lying with the blinds drawn.
“亲爱的，你不回去上班吗？”医生的妻子从拉上百叶窗躺着的房间里问。
‘No!’
“不！”
‘Was anything the matter?’
“有什么不对劲吗？”
‘I had a row with Dick Boulton.’
“我和迪克·博尔顿吵了一架。”
‘Oh,’ said his wife. ‘I hope you didn’t lose your temper, Henry.’
“哦，”他的妻子说。“我希望你没有发脾气，亨利。”
‘No,’ said the doctor.
“没有，”医生说。
‘Remember, that he who ruleth his spirit is greater than he that taketh a city,’ said his wife. She was a Christian Scientist. Her Bible, her copy of Science and Health and her Quarterly were on a table beside her bed in the darkened room.
“记住，能治服自己心灵的，比攻取一座城池的更为伟大，”他的妻子说。她是个基督教科学派信徒。她的《圣经》，她的《Science and Health》以及她的季刊放在昏暗房间床边的桌子上。
Her husband did not answer. He was sitting on his bed now,
她丈夫没有回答。他现在正坐在床上，
cleaning a shotgun. He pushed the magazine full of heavy yellow shells and pumped them out again. They were scattered on the bed.
擦拭一把猎枪。他把装满沉重黄色弹壳的弹匣推进去又拉出来。弹壳散落在床上。
‘Henry,’ his wife called. Then paused a moment. ‘Henry!’
“亨利，”他的妻子叫道。然后停顿了片刻。“亨利！”
‘Yes,’ the doctor said.
“是的，”医生说。
‘You didn’t say anything to Boulton to anger him, did you?’
“你没对保尔顿说什么激怒他吧？”
‘No,’ said the doctor.
“没有，”医生说。
‘What was the trouble about, dear?’
“亲爱的，出什么事了？”
‘Nothing much.’
“没什么大不了的。”
‘Tell me, Henry. Please don’t try and keep anything from me. What was the trouble about?’
“告诉我吧，亨利。请别对我隐瞒。到底发生了什么事？”
‘Well, Dick owes me a lot of money for pulling his squaw through pneumonia and I guess he wanted a row so he wouldn’t have to take it out in work.’
“嗯，迪克欠我很多钱，因为我把他那印第安妻子从肺炎里救了出来，我想他就是想找事儿，这样就不用用劳动去还债了。”
His wife was silent. The doctor wiped his gun carefully with a rag. He pushed the shells back in against the spring of the magazine. He sat with the gun on his knees. He was very fond of it. Then he heard his wife’s voice from the darkened room.
他的妻子沉默了。医生用抹布仔细地擦拭他的枪。他把弹壳往回推，顶在弹匣的弹簧上。他双膝上架着枪坐着。他非常喜欢这把枪。然后他听到妻子的声音从昏暗的房间里传来。
‘Dear, I don’t think, I really don’t think that anyone would really do a thing like that.’
“亲爱的，我不认为，我真的不认为会有人真能做出那种事来。”
‘No?’ the doctor said.
“不会吧？”医生说。
‘No. I can’t really believe that anyone would do a thing of that sort intentionally.’
“不会。我真不敢相信会有人故意做那种事。”
The doctor stood up and put the shotgun in the corner behind the dresser.
医生站起来，把猎枪放在梳妆台后面的角落里。
‘Are you going out, dear?’ his wife said.
“亲爱的，你要出去吗？”他的妻子说。
‘I think I’ll go for a walk,’ the doctor said.
“我想我去散散步，”医生说。
‘If you see Nick, dear, will you tell him his mother wants to see him?’ his wife said.
“亲爱的，如果你见到尼克，能告诉他他妈妈想见他吗？”他的妻子说。
The doctor went out on the porch. The screen door slammed behind him. He heard his wife catch her breath when the door slammed.
医生走到门廊上。纱门在他身后砰地关上了。他听见门关上时妻子倒吸了口气。
‘Sorry,’ he said, outside her window with the blinds drawn.
“抱歉，”他在她拉着百叶窗的窗外说。
‘It’s all right, dear,’ she said.
“没关系，亲爱的，”她说。
He walked in the heat out of the gate and along the path into the hemlock woods. It was cool in the woods even on such a hot day. He found Nick sitting with his back against a tree, reading.
他顶着炎热走出大门，沿着小路进了铁杉林。即使是在这样炎热的日子里，林中也很凉爽。他看到尼克靠着一棵树坐着，正在看书。
‘Your mother wants you to come and see her,’ the doctor said.
“你妈妈要你去看看她，”医生说。
‘I want to go with you,’ Nick said.
“我想和你一块去，”尼克说。
We were in a garden at Mons. Young Buckley came in with his patrol from across the river. The first German I saw climbed up over the garden wall. We waited till he got one leg over and then potted him. He had so much equipment on and looked awfully surprised and fell down into the garden. Then three more came over farther down the wall. We shot them. They all came just like that.
我们在蒙斯的一个花园里。年轻的巴克利带着他的巡逻队从河对岸过来了。我见到的第一个德国人翻过花园墙。我等到他把一条腿搭上去就朝他开了枪。他身上带着那么多装备，看上去非常惊讶，摔进了花园。然后又有三个从墙下更远的地方爬了过来。我们把他们都打死了。他们都是那样过来的。

# THE END OF SOMETHING
# 某事的终结

In the old days Hortons Bay was a lumbering town. No one who lived in it was out of sound of the big saws in the mill by the lake. Then one year there were no more logs to make lumber. The lumber schooners came into the bay and were loaded with the cut of the mill that stood stacked in the yard. All the piles of lumber were carried away. The big mill building had all its machinery that was removable taken out and hoisted on board one of the schooners by the men who had worked in the mill. The schooner moved out of the bay toward the open lake carrying the two great saws, the travelling carriage that hurled the logs against the revolving, circular saws, and all the rollers, wheels, belts and iron piled on a hull-deep load of lumber. Its open hold covered with canvas and lashed tight, the sails of the schooner filled and it moved out into the open lake, carrying with it everything that had made the mill a mill and Hortons Bay a town.
过去霍顿湾是一个伐木镇。住在那里的没有一个人听不到湖边锯木厂里大锯的声音。然后有一年再也没有原木可供制材。伐木的双桅帆船驶入海湾，把堆在厂场里的厂切板装上船。所有的木材堆都被运走。大厂房里可拆卸的机器都被从厂里工作的工人卸下，吊上其中一艘帆船。那艘帆船载着两台大锯、把原木掷向旋转圆锯的行走式推架，以及所有的滚筒、轮子、皮带和铁件，连同吃水深重的木材载荷一起驶出海湾，朝开阔的湖面驶去。它用帆布盖好并牢牢捆扎着敞开的舱口，帆鼓起，向开阔的湖面驶去，带走了所有让那座厂成为厂、让霍顿湾成为镇的东西。
The one-story bunk houses, the eating-house, the company store, the mill offices, and the big mill itself stood deserted in the acres of sawdust that covered the swampy meadow by the shore of the bay.
平房宿舍、食堂、公司商店、厂办办公室以及那座大厂都孤零零地立在覆盖着沿湾岸沼泽草地数英亩锯屑的地方。
Ten years later there was nothing of the mill left except the broken white limestone of its foundations showing through the swampy second growth as Nick and Marjorie rowed along the shore. They were trolling along the edge of the channel bank where the bottom dropped off suddenly from sandy shallows to twelve feet of dark water. They were trolling on their way to the point to set night lines for rainbow trout.
十年过去了，除了基座上破碎的白色石灰岩露出在沼泽地的矮生新林之间，磨坊已不复存在。尼克和玛乔里在岸边划船时，看见那些石头。
‘There’s our old ruin, Nick,’ Marjorie said.
“那是我们的旧废墟，尼克，”玛乔里说。
Nick, rowing, looked at the white stone in the green trees.
正在划桨的尼克望着绿树中的白色石头。
‘There it is,’ he said.
“就是那里，”他说。
‘Can you remember when it was a mill?’ Marjorie asked.
“你还能记得它还是磨坊的时候吗？”玛乔丽问。
‘I can just remember,’ Nick said.
“我记得一点点，”尼克说。
‘It seems more like a castle,’ Marjorie said.
“倒更像是一座城堡，”玛乔丽说。
Nick said nothing. They rowed on out of sight of the mill, following the shore line. Then Nick cut across the bay.
尼克没有说话。他们划着船离开了看不见的磨坊，沿着海岸线前行。然后尼克横穿了海湾。
‘They aren’t striking,’ he said.
“它们没有咬钩，”他说。
‘No,’ Marjorie said. She was intent on the rod all the time they trolled, even when she talked. She loved to fish. She loved to fish with Nick.
“不，”玛乔丽说。他们拖钓时她始终盯着鱼竿，哪怕在说话的时候也是。她喜欢钓鱼。她喜欢和尼克一起钓鱼。
Close beside the boat a big trout broke the surface of the water. Nick pulled hard on one oar so the boat would turn and the bait spinning far behind would pass where the trout was feeding. As the trout’s back came up out of the water the minnows jumped wildly. They sprinkled the surface like a handful of shot thrown into the water. Another trout broke water, feeding on the other side of the boat.
就在船边不远处，一条大鳟鱼跃出水面。尼克猛拉一只桨让船转向，好让远在后面的诱饵转到鳟鱼觅食的地方。当鳟鱼的背部从水面露出时，小鱼惊慌地跳动。它们像一把散弹撒在水面上。另一条鳟鱼在船的另一侧破水觅食。
‘They’re feeding,’ Marjorie said.
“它们在觅食，”玛乔丽说。
‘But they won’t strike,’ Nick said.
“但它们不会上钩的，”尼克说。
He rowed the boat around to troll past both the fceding fish, then headed it for the point. Marjorie did not reel in until the boat touched the shore.
他把船划到两条将要进食的鱼旁边钓过去，然后把船头往那处岬角划去。马乔里直到船靠岸才收线。
They pulled the boat up the beach and Nick lifted out a pail of live perch. The perch swam in the water in the pail. Nick caught three of them with his hands and cut their heads off and skinned them while Marjorie chased with her hands in the bucket, finally caught a perch, cut its head off and skinned it. Nick looked at her fish.
他们把船拖上沙滩，尼克掏出一桶活鲈鱼。鲈鱼在桶里的水中游动。尼克用手抓住三条，把它们的头砍掉并去皮，马乔里则在桶里用手追着，终于抓到一条，砍掉它的头并去皮。尼克看了看她的鱼。
‘You don’t want to take the ventral fin out,’ he said. ‘It’ll be all right for bait but it’s better with the ventral fin in.’
“你别把腹鳍去掉，”他说，“当饵可以，但留着腹鳍更好。”
He hooked each of the skinned perch through the tail. There were two hooks attached to a leader on each rod. Then Marjorie rowed the boat out over the channel-bank, holding the line in her teeth, and looking toward Nick, who stood on the shore holding the rod and letting the line run out from the reel.
他把每条去鳞的鲈鱼从尾巴穿上钩子。每根鱼竿上的主线都有两个鱼钩。然后玛乔丽划船把船撑到河道堤外，嘴里含着线，朝岸上站着拿着鱼竿、让线从卷轴上放出的尼克望去。
‘That’s about right,’ he called.
“差不多了，”他喊道。
‘Should I let it drop?’ Marjorie called back, holding the line in her hand.
“我应该放下去吗？”玛乔丽喊回去，手里握着钓线。
‘Sure. Let it go.’ Marjorie dropped the line overboard and watched the baits go down through the water.
“当然。放开它。”玛乔丽把线放入水中，注视着鱼饵沉入水里。
She came in with the boat and ran the second line out the same way. Each time Nick set a heavy slab of driftwood across the butt of the rod to hold it solid and propped it up at an angle with a small slab. He reeled in the slack line so the line ran taut out to where the bait rested on the sandy floor of the channel and set the click on the reel. When a trout, feeding on the bottom, took the bait it would run with it, taking line out of the reel in a rush and making the reel sing with the click on.
她把船划回来，并用同样的方式放出第二条鱼线。每次都是尼克把一块沉重的浮木横放在鱼竿的杆尾以把它固定住，然后用一小块木板把竿支成一个角度。他收紧多余的线，让鱼线绷直，伸到饵料放在水道沙底的地方，并把卷线器的咔嗒器设好。当一条在底层觅食的鳟鱼吞下饵料时，它会带着饵猛冲，迅速从卷线器上拉出鱼线，使卷线器在咔嗒声中鸣响。
Marjorie rowed up the point a little way so she would not disturb the line. She pulled hard on the oars and the boat went way up the beach. Little waves came in with it. Marjorie stepped out of the boat and Nick pulled the boat high up the beach.
玛乔丽把船向岬角划去一小段距离，以免打扰到鱼线。她用力划桨，船一路被推上了海滩。小浪随着船涌来。玛乔丽从船上走下，尼克把船拉得很高，推到沙滩上。
‘What’s the matter, Nick ?’ Marjorie asked.
“怎么了，尼克？”玛乔丽问道。
‘I don’t know,’ Nick said, getting wood for a fire.
“我不知道，”尼克说着，去取火柴和木材生火。
They made a fire with driftwood. Marjorie went to the boat and brought a blanket. The evening breeze blew the smoke toward the point, so Marjorie spread the blanket out between the fire and the lake.
他们用漂流木生了火。玛乔里走到船边拿来一条毯子。晚风把烟吹向岬角，玛乔里把毯子铺在火堆与湖之间。
Marjorie sat on the blanket with her back to the fire and waited for Nick. He came over and sat down beside her on the blanket. In back of them was the close second-growth timber of the point and in front was the bay with the mouth of Hortons Creek. It was not quite dark. The fire-light went as far as the water. They could both see the two steel rods at an angle over the dark water. The fire glinted on the reels.
玛乔里背对着火坐在毯子上等尼克。他走过来，坐在她旁边的毯子上。他们身后是岬角近处的二次生林，前面是有霍顿溪入海口的海湾。天色还未全黑。火光一直照到水面。他们都能看到那两根斜倚在黑暗水面上的钢杆。火光在渔线轮上闪着光。
Marjorie unpacked the basket of supper.
玛乔里把晚餐篮子打开了。
‘I don’t feel like eating,’ said Nick.
“我不想吃。”尼克说。
‘Come on and eat, Nick.’
“来吧，吃吧，尼克。”
‘All right.’
“好吧。”
They ate without talking, and watched the two rods and the firelight in the water.
他们一边吃一边沉默着，看着两根钓竿和水中的火光。
‘There’s going to be a moon to-night,’ said Nick. He looked across the bay to the hills that were beginning to sharpen against the sky. Beyond the hills he knew the moon was coming up.
“今晚会有月亮的，”尼克说。他望向海湾对面的山峦，那些山峦渐渐在天际显得轮廓分明。他知道月亮正从山后升起。
‘I know it,’ Marjorie said happily.
“我知道的，”玛乔丽高兴地说。
‘You know everything,’ Nick said.
“你什么都知道，”尼克说。
‘Oh, Nick, please cut it out! Please, please don’t be that way!’
“哦，尼克，求你别这样了！拜托，拜托，别那样！”
‘I can’t help it,’ Nick said. ‘You do. You know everything. That’s the trouble. You know you do.’
“我忍不住，”尼克说。“你就是这样。你什么都知道。问题就在这里。你知道你知道。”
Marjorie did not say anything.
玛乔丽没有说话。
'I’ve taught you everything. You know you do. What don’t you know, anyway?’
“我把一切都教给你了。你知道的，你确实知道。究竟有什么是不知道的？”
‘Oh, shut up,’ Marjorie said. ‘There comes the moon.’
“哦，闭嘴，”玛乔丽说。“月亮出来了。”
They sat on the blanket without touching each other and watched the moon rise.
他们坐在毯子上，互不相触，静静看着月亮升起。
‘You don’t have to talk silly,’ Marjorie said. ‘What’s really the matter?’
“你不用胡扯，”Marjorie 说。“到底怎么了？”
‘I don’t know.’
“我不知道。”
‘Of course you know.’
“你当然知道。”
‘No, I don’t.’
“不，我不知道。”
‘Go on and say it.’
“说吧，快说。”
Nick looked on at the moon, coming up over the hills.
尼克望着月亮，从山后升起。
‘It isn’t fun any more.’
“已经不再有趣了。”
He was afraid to look at Marjorie. Then he looked at her. She sat there with her back toward him. He looked at her back. ‘It isn’t fun any more. Not any of it.’
他不敢看玛乔丽。然后他看了看她。她坐着，背对着他。他看着她的背。“已经不再有趣了。所有的一切都不再有趣。”
She didn’t say anything. He went on. ‘I feel as though everything was gone to hell inside of me. I don’t know, Marge. I don’t know what to say.’
她什么也没说。他继续说：“我觉得好像我的内心全他妈地完了。我不知道，玛吉。我不知道该说什么。”
He looked on at her back.
他看着她的背影。
‘Isn’t love any fun?’ Marjorie said.
“爱情难道一点也不有趣吗？”玛乔丽说。
‘No,’ Nick said. Marjorie stood up. Nick sat there, his head in his hands.
“不，”尼克说。玛乔丽站起来。尼克坐着，双手抱头。
‘I’m going to take the boat,’ Marjorie called to him. ‘You can walk back around the point.’
“我要坐船去，”Marjorie 朝他喊道。“你可以绕着岬角走回去。”
‘All right,’ Nick said. ‘I’ll push the boat off for you.’
“好吧，”Nick 说。“我帮你把船推开。”
‘You don’t need to,’ she said. She was afloat in the boat on the water with the moonlight on it. Nick went back and lay down with his face in the blanket by the fire. He could hear Marjorie rowing on the water.
“不用了，”她说。她坐在船上，漂在水面上，月光洒在船上。Nick 回去躺在毯子里，脸埋在毯子里靠着火堆。他能听见 Marjorie 在水上划桨的声音。
He lay there for a long time. He lay there while he heard Bill come into the clearing walking around through the woods. He felt Bill coming up to the fire. Bill didn’t touch him, either.
他就那么躺了很久。他躺着，听见 Bill 穿过树林走进空地的声音。他感觉到 Bill 走到火边。Bill 也没有碰他。
‘Did she go all right?’ Bill said.
“她走得顺利吗？”比尔问。
‘Yes,’ Nick said, lying, his face on the blanket.
“是的，”尼克说，撒了谎，脸贴在毯子上。
‘Have a scene?’
“闹起来了吗？”
‘No, there wasn’t any scene.’
“没有，没闹。”
‘How do you feel?’
“你感觉怎么样？”
‘Oh, go away, Bill! Go away for a while.’
“哦，走开，比尔！走开一会儿。”
Bill selected a sandwich from the lunch basket and walked over to have a look at the rods.
比尔从午餐篮里挑了一个三明治，走过去看看鱼竿。
It was a frightfully hot day. We’d jammed an absolutely perfect barricade across the bridge. It was simply priceless. A big old wrought-iron grating from the front of a house. Too heavy to lift and you could shoot through it and they would have to climb over it. It was absolutely topping. They tried to get over it, and we potted them from forty yards. They rushed it, and officers came out alone and worked on it. It was an absolutely perfect obstacle. Their officers were very fine. We were frightfully put out when we heard the flank had gone, and we had to fall back.
那天热得要命。我们在桥上安放了一道绝对完美的路障。简直无价。一块大大的旧锻铁格栅，原本在一幢房子的正面。太重搬不动，子弹可以穿过格栅打过去，他们就得翻过去。简直棒极了。他们试图翻过来，我们在四十码外把他们打倒。 他们冲上来，军官们独自出来处理它。这是一个绝对完美的障碍。他们的军官很不错。当我们听说侧翼已被突破、不得不撤退时，我们非常沮丧。

THE THREE-DAY BLOW
三日狂风

The rain stopped as Nick turned into the road that went up through the orchard. The fruit had been picked and the fall wind blew through the bare trees. Nick stopped and picked up a Wagner apple from beside the road, shiny in the brown grass from the rain. He put the apple in the pocket of his Mackinaw coat.
雨停了，尼克拐进那条穿过果园往上的路。水果已被采摘，秋风穿过光秃的树梢。尼克停下，从路边的褐色草丛里摘起一个瓦格纳苹果——雨后光亮发亮。他把苹果放进麦金诺大衣的口袋里。
The road came out of the orchard on to the top of the hill. There was the cottage, the porch bare, smoke coming from the chimney. In back was the garage, the chicken coop and the second-growth timber like a hedge against the woods behind. The big trees swayed far over in the wind as he watched. It was the first of the autumn storms.
那条路从果园出来，到了山顶。那儿有座小屋，门廊空荡，烟从烟囱里冒出。后面是车库、鸡窝和像篱笆似的二次生长林木，抵在身后的树林前。大树在风中远远地摇摆着，他看着。那是第一场秋季风暴。
As Nick crossed the open field above the orchard the door of the cottage opened and Bill came out. He stood on the porch looking out.
当尼克越过果园上方的空地时，小屋的门开了，比尔走了出来。他站在门廊上朝外望去。
‘Well, Wemedge?’ he said.
“嗯，Wemedge？”他说。
‘Hey, Bill,’ Nick said, coming up the steps.
“嘿，Bill，”Nick 上了台阶说。
They stood together, looking out across the country, down over the orchard, beyond the road, across the lower fields and the woods of the point to the lake. The wind was blowing straight down the lake. They could see the surf along Ten Mile point.
他们并肩站着，眺望着乡间，越过果园，越过那条路，越过下方的田地和半岛的树林，望向湖面。风正顺湖面直吹。他们能看到 Ten Mile 半岛沿岸的浪花。
‘She’s blowing,’ Nick said.
“刮起风了，”Nick 说。
‘She’ll blow like that for three days,’ Bill said.
“她会这样闹三天的，”比尔说。
‘Is your dad in?’ Nick said.
“你爸在家吗？”尼克说。
‘No. He’s out with the gun. Come on in.’
“不在。他出去拿枪了。进来吧。”
Nick went inside the cottage. There was a big fire in the fireplace. The wind made it roar. Bill shut the door.
尼克走进小屋。壁炉里有一堆大火。风把火吹得呼呼作响。比尔关上了门。
‘Have a drink?’ he said.
“喝一杯吗？”他说。
He went out to the kitchen and came back with two glasses and a pitcher of water. Nick reached the whisky bottle from the shelf above the fireplace.
他走到厨房，端来两只玻璃杯和一壶水。尼克从壁炉上方的架子上拿下威士忌酒瓶。
‘All right?’ he said.
“都好吧？”他说。
‘Good,’ said Bill.
“好，”比尔说。
They sat in front of the fire and drank the Irish whisky and water.
他们坐在火堆前喝着爱尔兰威士忌兑水。
‘It’s got a swell, smoky taste,’ Nick said, and looked at the fire through the glass.
“有一种浓郁的烟熏味，”Nick 说着，透过玻璃看着火堆。
‘That’s the peat,’ Bill said.
“那是泥炭，”Bill 说。
‘You can’t get peat into liquor,’ Nick said.
“你不能把泥炭放进酒里，”Nick 说。
‘That doesn’t make any difference,’ Bill said.
“那没关系，”比尔说。
‘You ever seen any peat?’ Nick asked.
“你见过泥炭吗？”尼克问。
‘No,’ said Bill.
“没见过，”比尔说。
‘Neither have I,’ Nick said.
“我也没见过，”尼克说。
His shoes, stretched out on the hearth, began to steam in front of the fire.
他的鞋子伸在壁炉前，开始冒蒸汽。
‘Better take your shoes off,’ Bill said.
“最好把鞋脱了，”比尔说。
‘I haven’t got any socks on.’
“我没穿袜子。”
‘Take them off and dry them and I’ll get you some,’ Bill said. He went upstairs into the loft and Nick heard him walking about overhead. Upstairs was open under the roof and was where Bill and his father and he, Nick, sometimes slept. In back was a dressing room. They moved the cots back out of the rain and covered them with rubber blankets.
“脱了把它们烤干，我去给你拿双，”比尔说。他上楼去了阁楼，尼克听见他在头顶上来回走。楼上靠屋顶是敞开的，平时比尔和他父亲还有他——尼克——有时候就在那儿睡。后面有个更衣室。他们把行军床挪回到避雨的地方，用橡胶毯盖好。
Bill came down with a pair of heavy wool socks.
比尔拿来一双厚重的羊毛袜。
‘It’s getting too late to go around without socks,’ he said.
“现在不戴袜子出去太晚了，”他说。
‘I hate to start them again,’ Nick said. He pulled the socks on and slumped back in the chair, putting his feet up on the screen in front of the fire.
“我真不想再开始穿它们了，”尼克说。他把袜子穿上，瘫坐回椅子上，把脚搭在火炉前的挡火网上。
‘You’ll dent in the screen,’ Bill said. Nick swung his feet over to the side of the fireplace.
“你会把挡火网压凹的，”比尔说。尼克把脚挪到壁炉的一侧。
‘Got anything to read?’ he asked.
“有什么可读的吗？”他问。
‘Only the paper.’
“只有报纸。”
‘What did the Cards do?’
“红雀队做得怎么样？”
‘Dropped a double header to the Giants.’
“在双重赛中输给了巨人队。”
‘That ought to cinch it for them.’
“那应该能把他们稳住了。”
‘It’s a gift,’ Bill said. ‘As long as McGraw can buy every good ball player in the league there’s nothing to it.’
“这是天赐的，”比尔说。“只要麦格劳能把联赛里所有优秀的球员都买下，那就没得玩了。”
‘He can’t buy them all,’ Nick said.
“他买不过来所有人，”尼克说。
‘He buys all the ones he wants,’ Bill said. ‘Or he makes them discontented so they have to trade them to him.’
“他买他想买的那些，”比尔说。“或者让他们不满，好把人家逼着跟他交易。”
‘Like Heinie Zim,’ Nick agreed.
“像海尼·齐姆那样，”尼克同意道。
‘That bonehead will do him a lot of good.’
“那个笨蛋对他会有很大帮助。”
Bill stood up.
比尔站了起来。
‘He can hit,’ Nick offered. The heat from the fire was baking his legs.
“他会打，”尼克说。火堆的热量在灼烤他的腿。
‘He’s a sweet fielder, too,’ Bill said. ‘But he loses ball games.’
“他也很会守场，”比尔说。“但他会把比赛输掉。”
‘Maybe that’s what McGraw wants him for,’ Nick suggested.
“也许那正是麦格劳要他来的原因，”尼克建议道。
‘Maybe,’ Bill agreed.
“也许吧，”比尔同意道。
‘There’s more always to it than we know about,’ Nick said.
“事情总比我们知道的要复杂得多，”尼克说。
‘Of course. But we’ve got pretty good dope for being so far away.’
“当然。不过我们这么远，消息已经相当灵通了。”
‘Like how much better you can pick them if you don’t see the horses.’
“比如说，如果看不到马，你就能看得更清楚他们多好选。”
‘That’s it.’
“就是这样。”
Bill reached down the whisky bottle. His big hand went all the way around it. He poured the whisky into the glass Nick held out.
比尔把手伸向威士忌瓶。他那只大手完全包住了瓶子。他把威士忌倒进尼克递过来的杯子里。
‘How much water?’
“要多少水？”
‘Just the same.’
“就跟平常一样。”
He sat down on the floor beside Nick’s chair.
他坐在尼克椅子旁边的地板上。
‘It’s good when the fall storms come, isn’t it?’ Nick said.
“秋季风暴一来，感觉真好，是不是？”尼克说。
‘It’s swell.’
“太棒了。”
‘It’s the best time of year,’ Nick said.
“现在是一年中最好的季节，”Nick 说。
‘Wouldn’t it be hell to be in town?’ Bill said.
“待在城里那得多糟糕？”Bill 说。
‘I’d like to see the World Series,’ Nick said.
“我倒想看世界大赛，”Nick 说。
‘Well, they’re always in New York or Philadelphia now,’ Bill said. ‘That doesn’t do us any good.’
“唉，他们现在总是在纽约或费城，”比尔说。“那对我们没什么用。”
‘I wonder if the Cards will ever win a pennant?’
“我不知道红雀队有没有朝一垒旗（pennant）冲过冠军？”
‘Not in our lifetime,’ Bill said.
“我们这辈子不会的，”比尔说。
‘Gee, they’d go crazy,’ Nick said.
“哇，他们会疯了的，”尼克说。
‘Do you remember when they got going that once before they had the train wreck?’
“你还记得他们以前开车出事那次吗？就是那次火车出轨的事？”
‘Boy!’ Nick said, remembering.
“天哪！”尼克说，想起来了。
Bill reached over to the table under the window for the book that
比尔伸手到窗下的桌子上去拿那本书
lay there, face down, where he had put it when he went to the door. He held his glass in one hand-and the book in the other, leaning back against Nick’s chair.
那本书面朝下放在那里，是他去门口时放的。他一手拿着酒杯，另一手拿着那本书，身体向后靠在尼克的椅背上。
‘What are you reading?’
“你在看什么？”
‘Richard Feverel.’
“《理查德·费弗里尔》。”
‘I couldn’t get into it.’
“我没读进去。”
‘It’s all right,’ Bill said. ‘It ain’t a bad book, Wemedge.’
“还行，”比尔说。“不算本烂书，温米奇。”
‘What else have you got I haven’t read?’ Nick asked.
“还有什么我没读过的？”尼克问。
‘Did you read the Forest Lovers?’
“你读过《森林情人》吗？”
‘Yup. That’s the one where they go to bed every night with the naked sword between them.’
“读过。就是那本他们每晚睡觉时把那把赤裸的剑放在两人之间的书。”
‘That’s a good book, Wemedge.’
“那是本好书，温米奇。”
‘It’s a swell book. What I couldn’t ever understand was what good the sword would do. It would have to stay edge up all the time because if it went over flat you could roll right over it and it wouldn’t make any trouble.’
“这是本好书。我从来不明白那把剑有什么用。它得一直竖着放着，否则要是翻倒了你可以直接滚过去，根本起不了作用。”
‘It’s a symbol,’ Bill said.
“那是个象征意义，”比尔说。
‘Sure,’ said Nick, ‘but it isn’t practical.’
“当然，”尼克说，“但它不实用。”
‘Did you ever read Fortitude?’
“你读过《Fortitude》吗？”
‘It’s fine,’ Nick said. ‘That’s a real book. That’s where his old man is after him all the time. Have you got any more by Walpole?’
“没事，”尼克说。“那是真的书。那就是他老爸一直缠着他的原因。你还有沃波尔的别的书吗？”
‘The Dark Forest,’ Bill said. ‘It’s about Russia.’
“《黑暗森林），”比尔说。“是关于俄罗斯的。”
‘What does he know about Russia?’ Nick asked.
“他懂什么俄罗斯？”尼克问。
‘I don’t know. You can’t ever tell about those guys. Maybe he was there when he was a boy. He’s got a lot of dope on it.’
“我不知道。你永远猜不透那些人。也许他小时候去过那里。他对那地方有很多内幕。”
‘I’d like to meet him,’ Nick said.
“我想见见他，”尼克说。
‘I’d like to meet Chesterton,’ Bill said.
“我想见见切斯特顿，”比尔说。
‘I wish he was here now,’ Nick said. 'We’d take him fishing to the ‘Voix to-morrow.’
“真希望他现在在这儿，”尼克说。“我们明天带他去‘Voix’钓鱼。”
‘I wonder if he’d like to go fishing,’ Bill said.
“我想知道他是否愿意去钓鱼，”比尔说。
‘Sure,’ said Nick. ‘He must be about the best guy there is. Do you remember the Flying Inn ?’
“当然，”尼克说。“他一定是最棒的人之一。你还记得《飞行客栈》吗？”
‘If an angel out of heaven
“如果天使从天上
Gives you something else to drink,
给你喝别的东西，
Thank him for his kind intentions;
感谢他那善意的意图；
Go and pour them down the sink!’
“去，把它们倒进洗手池里！”
‘That’s right,’ said Nick. ‘I guess he’s a better guy than Walpole.’
“没错，”尼克说。“我想他比沃尔波尔好。”
‘Oh, he’s a better guy, all right,’ Bill said.
“哦，他确实是个更好的人，”比尔说。
‘But Walpole’s a better writer.’
“不过沃尔波尔写得更好。”
‘I don’t know,’ Nick said. ‘Chesterton’s a classic.’
“我不知道，”尼克说。“切斯特顿是经典。”
‘Walpole’s a classic, too,’ Bill insisted.
“沃波尔也是经典，”比尔坚持说。
‘I wish we had them both here,’ Nick said. 'We’d take them both fishing to the ‘Voix to-morrow.’
“真希望我们两个都带在这儿，”尼克说。“明天我们把他们俩都带去‘Voix’钓鱼。”
‘Let’s get drunk,’ Bill said.
“那就去喝醉吧，”比尔说。
‘All right,’ Nick agreed.
“好吧，”Nick 同意道。
‘My old man won’t care,’ Bill said.
“我老子不会介意的，”Bill 说。
‘Are you sure?’ said Nick.
“你确定吗？”Nick 问。
‘I know it,’ Bill said.
“我知道的，”Bill 说。
‘I’m a little drunk now,’ Nick said.
“我现在有点醉了，”尼克说。
‘You aren’t drunk,’ Bill said.
“你没醉，”比尔说。
He got up from the floor and reached for the whisky bottle. Nick held out his glass. His eyes fixed on it while Bill poured.
他从地板上站起来，伸手去拿威士忌酒瓶。尼克递出他的酒杯。比尔倒酒时，尼克的眼睛盯着杯子。
Bill poured the glass half full of whisky.
比尔把杯子倒到一半满。
‘Put in your own water,’ he said. ‘There’s just one more shot.’
“自己把水倒进来，”他说。“只剩最后一枪了。”
‘Got any more?’ Nick asked.
“还有别的吗？”尼克问。
‘There’s plenty more but dad only likes me to drink what’s open.’
“还有很多，但爸只让我喝开了的。”
‘Sure,’ said Nick.
“好吧，”尼克说。
‘He says opening bottles is what makes drunkards,’ Bill explained.
“他说是开瓶子会把人变成酒鬼，”比尔解释道。
‘That’s right,’ said Nick. He was impressed. He had never thought of that before. He had always thought it was solitary drinking that made drunkards.
“那倒也是，”尼克说。他印象深刻。以前从没这么想过。他一直以为是独自喝酒才会把人变成酒鬼。
‘How is your dad?’ he asked respectfully.
“你爸怎么样？”他恭敬地问。
‘He’s all right,’ Bill said. ‘He gets a little wild sometimes.’
“他没事，”比尔说。“有时候会有点疯狂。”
‘He’s a swell guy,’ Nick said. He poured water into his glass out of the pitcher. It mixed slowly with the whisky. There was more whisky than water.
“他是个好人，”尼克说。他从水壶里往自己的杯子里倒水。水慢慢地和威士忌混在一起。威士忌比水多。
‘You bet your life he is,’ Bill said.
“你打赌你的命他就是，”比尔说。
‘My old man’s all right,’ Nick said.
“我老爸没问题，”尼克说。
‘You’re damn right he is,’ said Bill.
“你说得对极了，”比尔说。
‘He claims he’s never taken a drink in his life,’ Nick said, as though announcing a scientific fact.
“他说他一辈子没喝过酒，”尼克说，仿佛在宣布一个科学事实。
‘Well, he’s a doctor. My old man’s a painter. That’s different.’
“那他是医生。我老爸是画家。那不一样。”
‘He’s missed a lot,’ Nick said sadly.
“他亏大了，”尼克可怜地说。
‘You can’t tell,’ Bill said. ‘Everything’s got its compensations.’
“你说不准，”比尔说。“每样东西都有它的补偿。”
‘He says he’s missed a lot himself,’ Nick confessed.
“他说他自己也错过了很多，”尼克承认道。
‘Well, dad’s had a tough time,’ Bill said.
“嗯，爸爸一直过得很艰难，”比尔说。
‘It all evens up,’ Nick said.
“一切都会扯平的，”尼克说。
They sat looking into the fire and thinking of this profound truth.
他们坐着望着火堆，思索着这个深刻的真理。
‘I’ll get a chunk from the back porch,’ Nick said. He had noticed while looking into the fire that the fire was dving down. Also he wished to show he could hold his liquor and be practical. Even if his father had never touched a drop Bill was not going to get him drunk before he himself was drunk.
“我去后廊搬一块木头，”尼克说。他看着篝火时注意到火快熄了。他也想表现出自己能喝酒又很实在。即使他父亲从不沾酒，比尔也不打算在自己醉之前先把他灌醉。
‘Bring one of the big beech chunks,’ Bill said. He was also being consciously practical.
“拿一块大山毛榉的木头，”比尔说。他也刻意表现得很实在。
Nick came in with the log through the kitchen and in passing knocked a pan off the kitchen table. He laid the log down and picked up the pan. It had contained dried apricots, soaking in water. He carefully picked up all the apricots off the floor, some of them had gone under the stove, and put them back in the pan. He dipped some more water on to them from the pail by the table. He felt quite proud of himself. He had been thoroughly practical.
尼克抱着木柴从厨房里进来，顺手把厨房桌上的一个锅碰翻了。他把木头放下，捡起锅。锅里原本装着泡在水里的干杏。他小心地把地上的杏子全捡起来，有些滚到炉子下面去了，然后放回锅里。他又从桌边的水桶舀了些水浇上去。他为自己感到相当自豪。他确实非常实在。
He came in carrying the log and Bill got up from the chair and helped him put it on the fire.
他抱着木头进来，比尔从椅子上站起来，帮他把木头放到火上。
‘That’s a swell log,’ Nick said.
“那是一根好木柴，”尼克说。
‘I’d been saving it for the bad weather,’ Bill said. ‘A log like that will burn all night.’
“我一直留着它给坏天气用，”比尔说。“像那样的木柴能烧一整夜。”
"There’ll be coals left to start the fire in the morning,’ Nick said.
“早晨还会有余烬用来起火，”尼克说。
‘That’s right,’ Bill agreed. They were conducting the conversation on a high plane.
“没错，”比尔同意道。他们在高层次上进行着这场谈话。
‘Let’s have another drink,’ Nick said.
“再喝一杯吧，”尼克说。
‘I think there’s another bottle open in the locker,’ Bill said.
“我记得储物柜里还有一瓶开着的，”比尔说。
He kneeled down in the corner in front of the locker and brought out a square-faced bottle.
他在储物柜前的角落里跪下，拿出一只方形瓶子的酒。
‘It’s Scotch,’ he said.
“是苏格兰威士忌，”他说。
‘I’ll get some more water,’ Nick said. He went out into the kitchen again. He filled the pitcher with the dipper, dipping cold spring water from the pail. On his way back to the living room he passed a mirror in the dining room and looked in it. His face looked strange. He smiled at the face in the mirror and it grinned back at him. He winked at it and went on. It was not his face but it didn’t make any difference.
“我去再拿点水，”尼克说。他又走进厨房。用舀子从桶里舀冷泉水，把水壶装满。回到客厅的路上，他经过餐厅的一面镜子，看了看。镜子里的脸看起来很奇怪。他对镜中的脸笑了笑，镜中那张脸也对他咧嘴笑。 他对着它眨了眨眼，然后继续走。那并不是他的脸，但这并不重要。
Bill had poured out the drinks.
比尔已经把酒端好了。
‘That’s an awfully big shot,’ Nick said.
“那可真是一大杯，”尼克说。
‘Not for us, Wemedge,’ Bill said.
“对我们可不算，威梅奇，”比尔说。
‘What’ll we drink to?’ Nick asked, holding up the glass.
“为哪一件事干杯？”尼克举起杯子问。
‘Let’s drink to fishing,’ Bill said.
“为钓鱼干杯，”比尔说。
‘All right,’ Nick said. ‘Gentlemen, I give you fishing.’
“好，”尼克说。“诸位，敬你们——钓鱼。”
‘All fishing,’ Bill said. ‘Everywhere.’
“凡是钓鱼，”比尔说。“到处都是。”
‘Fishing,’ Nick said. ‘That’s what we drink to.’
“钓鱼，”尼克说。“这就是我们为之干杯的东西。”
‘It’s better than baseball,’ Bill said.
“这比棒球强，”比尔说。
‘There isn’t any comparison,’ said Nick. ‘How did we ever get talking about baseball?"
“根本没法比，”尼克说。“我们怎么会开始谈棒球的？”
‘It was a mistake,’ Bill said. ‘Baseball is a game for louts.’
“那是个错误，”比尔说。“棒球是蠢汉玩的游戏。”
They drank all that was in their glasses.
他们把杯子里的酒都喝光了。
‘Now let’s drink to Chesterton.’
“现在让我们为切斯特顿干一杯。”
‘And Walpole,’ Nick interposed.
“还有沃波尔，”尼克插话道。
Nick poured out the liquor. Bill poured in the water. They looked at each other. They felt very fine.
尼克倒出酒来。比尔倒进水。他们互相看了一眼。感觉非常畅快。
‘Gentlemen,’ Bill said, ‘I give you Chesterton and Walpole.’
“先生们，”比尔说，“我把 Chesterton 和 Walpole 推荐给你们。”
‘Exactly, gentlemen,’ Nick said.
“正是如此，先生们，”尼克说。
They drank. Bill filled up the glasses. They sat down in the big chairs in front of the fire.
他们喝着。比尔把杯子又添满。他们坐在炉火前的大椅子上。
‘You were very wise, Wemedge,’ Bill said.
“你很聪明，Wemedge，”比尔说。
‘What do you mean?’ asked Nick.
“你什么意思？”尼克问。
‘To bust off that Marge business,’ Bill said.
“把那个玛吉的事了断，”比尔说。
' '  ^("' "){ }^{\text {' }} I guess so,’ said Nick.
“我想也是，”尼克说。
‘It was the only thing to do. If you hadn’t, by now you’d be back home working trying to get enough money to get married.’
“那是唯一可做的事。要是你没那样做，到现在你可能已经回家，拼命工作，想攒够钱结婚了。”
Nick said nothing.
尼克什么也没说。
‘Once a man’s married he’s absolutely bitched,’ Bill went on. ‘He hasn’t got anything more. Nothing. Not a damn thing. He’s done for. You’ve seen the guys that get married.’
“一个人一结了婚就完了，”比尔继续说。“他再也没有什么了。什么都没有。什么狗屁都没有。他完蛋了。你见过那些结婚的人。”
Nick said nothing.
尼克什么也没说。
‘You can tell them,’ Bill said. ‘They get this sort of fat married look. They’re done for.’
“你可以看得出来的，”比尔说。“他们都有那种结了婚的发福模样。他们完蛋了。”
‘Sure,’ said Nick.
“当然，”尼克说。
‘It was probably bad busting it off,’ Bill said. ‘But you always fall for somebody else and then it’s all right. Fall for them but don’t let them ruin you.’
“可能把它弄断确实不太好，”比尔说。“但你总会爱上别人，那样就没事了。爱上他们，但别让他们毁了你。”
‘Yes,’ said Nick.
“是，”尼克说。
‘If you’d have married her you would have had to marry the whole family. Remember her mother and that guy she married.’
“要是你娶了她，就得娶整个家族。记住她的母亲和她嫁的那个家伙。”
Nick nodded.
尼克点了点头。
‘Imagine having them around the house all the time and going to Sunday dinners at their house, and having them over to dinner and her telling Marge all the time what to do and how to act.’
“想想整天把他们关在家里，周日还要去他们家吃饭，邀请他们来吃饭，她老跟玛奇指手画脚，教她该做什么、该怎么表现。”
Nick sat quiet.
尼克沉默了。
‘You came out of it damned well,’ Bill said. ‘Now she can marry somebody of her own sort and settle down and be happy. You can’t mix oil and water and you can’t mix that sort of thing any more than if I’d marry Ida that works for Strattons. She’d probably like it, too.’
“你从里面出来得漂亮，”比尔说。“现在她可以嫁给跟她相配的人，安定下来，过得幸福。油水不能混，人与人也不能混，就像我要是娶了在 Strattons 工作的艾达，那也行不通。她可能还会喜欢那样。”
Nick said nothing. The liquor had all died out of him and left him alone. Bill wasn’t there. He wasn’t sitting in front of the fire or going fishing to-morrow with Bill and his dad or anything. He wasn’t drunk. It was all gone. All he knew was that he had once had Marjorie and that he had lost her. She was gone and he had sent her away. That was all that mattered. He might never see her again. Probably he never would. It was all gone, finished.
尼克什么也没说。酒劲已经完全散了，只剩下他孤零零一个人。比尔不在。他没有坐在火堆前，也没有和比尔与他父亲一起去钓鱼或做别的事。他不再醉了。一切都结束了。他所知道的只是他曾经拥有过马乔里，而他失去了她。她走了，是他把她送走的。那就是全部重要的事情。他可能再也见不到她了。很可能永远不会了。一切都完了，结束了。
‘Let’s have another drink,’ Nick said.
“再喝一杯吧，”尼克说。
Bill poured it out. Nick splashed in a little water.
比尔给他倒了酒。尼克往里泼了一点水。
‘If you’d gone on that way we wouldn’t be here now,’ Bill said.
“如果你一直那样下去，我们现在就不会在这里了，”比尔说。
That was true. His original plan had been to go down home and get a job. Then he had planned to stay in Charlevoix all winter so he could be near Marge. Now he did not know what he was going to do.
那是真的。他原本打算回家去找份工作。然后他又打算整个冬天都呆在沙尔勒瓦，以便能靠近玛姬。现在他不知道自己将要做什么。
‘Probably we wouldn’t even be going fishing to-morrow,’ Bill said. ‘You had the right dope, all right.’
“可能明天我们甚至都不会去钓鱼，”比尔说。“你确实有那个消息。”
‘I couldn’t help it,’ Nick said.
“我也没办法，”尼克说。
‘I know. That’s the way it works out,’ Bill said.
“我知道。事情就是这么发展的，”比尔说。
‘All of a sudden everything was over,’ Nick said. ‘I don’t know why it was. I couldn’t help it. Just like when the three-day blows come now and rip all the leaves off the trees.’
“突然间一切都结束了，”尼克说。“我不知道为什么会这样。我无能为力。就像现在那三天的大风，把树上的叶子都刮光了。”
‘Well, it’s over. That’s the point,’ Bill said.
“嗯，已经结束了。重点就是这个，”比尔说。
‘It was my fault,’ Nick said.
“是我的错，”尼克说。
‘It doesn’t make any difference whose fault it was,’ Bill said.
“是谁的错并不重要，”比尔说。
‘No, I suppose not,’ Nick said.
“不，我想不是，”尼克说。
The big thing was that Marjorie was gone and that probably he would never see her again. He had talked to her about how they would go to Italy together and the fun they would have. Places they would be together. It was all gone now.
最重要的是玛乔丽走了，而且他很可能再也见不到她了。他曾和她谈论过一起去意大利，会有多么快乐。他们会一起去的地方。现在这一切都没了。
‘So long as it’s over that’s all that matters,’ Bill said. ‘I tell you, Wemedge, I was worried while it was going on. You played it right. I understand her mother is sore as hell. She told a lot of people you were engaged.’
“只要结束了，这就是最重要的，”比尔说。“我跟你说，温奇，我那会儿可真担心。你处理得很对。我听说她母亲恼得要命。她告诉了很多人说你们订婚了。”
‘We weren’t engaged,’ Nick said.
“我们没订婚，”尼克说。
‘It was all around that you were.’
“都是围着你转的。”
‘I can’t help it,’ Nick said. ‘We weren’t.’
“我也没办法，”尼克说。“我们并不是那样的。”
‘Weren’t you going to get married?’ Bill asked.
“你们不是要结婚吗？”比尔问。
‘Yes. But we weren’t engaged,’ Nick said.
“是的。但我们并没有订婚，”尼克说。
‘What’s the difference?’ Bill said judicially.
“有什么区别？”比尔带着审判般的语气说。
‘I’ don’t know. There’s a difference.’
“我不知道。确实有区别。”
‘I don’t see it,’ said Bill.
“我看不出来，”比尔说。
‘All right,’ said Nick. ‘Let’s get drunk.’
“好吧，”尼克说。“我们去喝醉吧。”
‘All right,’ Bill said. ‘Let’s get really drunk.’
“好吧，”比尔说。“我们好好喝一顿。”
‘Let’s get drunk and then go swimming,’ Nick said.
“我们先喝醉然后去游泳，”尼克说。
He drank off his glass.
他把杯子里的酒一饮而尽。
‘I’m as sorry as hell about her but what could I do?’ he said. ‘You know what her mother was like!’
“我对她也可恨得很，可我能怎么办？你知道她妈妈是个什么样的人！”他说道。
‘She was terrible,’ Bill said.
“她太可怕了，”比尔说。
‘All of a sudden it was over,’ Nick said. ‘I oughtn’t to talk about it.’
“突然就结束了，”尼克说。“我不该谈论它。”
‘You aren’t,’ Bill said. ‘I talked about it and now I’m through. We won’t ever speak about it again. You don’t want to think about it. You might get back into it again.’
“你没谈，”比尔说。“我已经谈完了。我们再也不提这事。你别去想它。你可能会重新陷进去。”
Nick had not thought about that. It had seemed so absolute. That was a thought. That made him feel better.
尼克以前没想过这点。那看起来是那么绝对。那是一个想法。那让他感觉好些。
‘Sure,’ he said. ‘There’s always that danger.’
“当然，”他说。“总有那种危险。”
He felt happy now. There was not anything that was irrevocable. He might go into town Saturday night. To-morrow was Thursday.
他现在感到快乐。一切都还未成定局。他星期六晚上也许会进城。明天是星期四。
‘There’s always a chance,’ he said.
“总有机会的，”他说。
‘You’ll have to watch yourself,’ Bill said.
“你得小心点，”比尔说。
‘I’ll watch myself,’ he said.
“我会注意的，”他说。
He felt happy. Nothing was finished. Nothing was ever lost. He would go into town on Saturday. He felt lighter, as he had felt before Bill started to talk about it. There was always a way out.
他感到高兴。没什么结束的。没什么永远失去的。他星期六要进城。他感到轻快，就像在比尔开始谈论这件事之前的感觉。总是有出路。
‘Let’s take the guns and go down to the point and look for your dad,’ Nick said.
“我们把枪拿上，下到岬角去找你父亲吧，”尼克说。
‘All right.’
“好。”
Bill took down the two shotguns from the rack on the wall. He
比尔从墙上的枪架上取下两支猎枪。 他
opened a box of shells. Nick put on his Mackinaw coat and his shoes. His shoes were stiff from drying. He was still quite drunk but his head was clear.
打开了一盒弹壳。 尼克穿上了他的麦金诺外套和鞋子。 他的鞋子因为干燥而变硬。 他仍然相当醉，但头脑清醒。
‘How do you feel?’ Nick asked.
“你感觉怎么样？”尼克问。
‘Swell. I’ve just got a good edge on.’ Bill was buttoning up his sweater.
“好极了。 我刚好状态正好。” 比尔正在扣上他的羊毛套衫。
‘There’s no use getting drunk.’
“喝醉也没用。”
‘No. We ought to get outdoors.’
“不是的。我们应该到外面去。”
They stepped out the door. The wind was blowing a gale.
他们走出门去。风在狂吹。
‘The birds will lie right down in the grass with this,’ Nick said.
“这种风里鸟儿会直接躺在草里，”Nick 说。
They struck down toward the orchard.
他们朝果园砍下去。
‘I saw a woodcock this morning,’ Bill said.
“我今天早上看见一只野鹬，”比尔说。
‘Maybe we’ll jump him,’ Nick said.
“也许我们会把它惊出来，”尼克说。
‘You can’t shoot in this wind,’ Bill said.
“这风里你打不着，”比尔说。
Outside now the Marge business was no longer so tragic. It was not even very important. The wind blew everything like that away.
现在外边那桩玛吉的事已不再那么悲惨了。甚至不再那么重要。风把一切都吹散了。
‘It’s coming right off the big lake,’ Nick said.
“风正从大湖那边刮过来，”尼克说。
Against the wind they heard the thud of a shotgun.
顶着风他们听见一声猎枪的闷响。
‘That’s dad,’ Bill said. ‘He’s down in the swamp.’
“那是爸爸，”比尔说。“他在沼泽里倒下了。”
‘Let’s cut down that way,’ Nick said.
“我们往那边下去吧，”Nick 说。
‘Let’s cut across the lower meadow and see if we jump anything,’ Bill said.
“我们穿过下边的草地走走，看看能不能碰上什么，”Bill 说。
‘All right,’ Nick said.
“好吧，”Nick 说。
None of it was important now. The wind blew it out of his head. Still he could always go into town Saturday night. It was a good thing to have in reserve.
这些事现在都不重要了。风把它们从他脑子里吹走了。不过他仍然可以周六晚上进城。这是件可以留作后路的好事。
They shot the six cabinet ministers at half-past six in the morning against the wall of a hospital. There were pools of water in the courtyard. There were wet dead leaves on the paving of the courtyard. It rained hard. All the shutters of the hospital were nailed shut. One of the ministers was sick with typhoid. Two soldiers carried him downstairs and out into the rain. They tried to hold him up against the wall but he sat down in a puddle of water. The other five stood very quietly against the wall. Finally the officer told the soldiers it was no good trying to make him stand up. When they fired the first volley he was sitting down in the water with his head on his knees.
他们在早上六点半把六位内阁大臣押到医院的墙边枪决。院子里有积水。院子铺道上有湿漉漉的枯叶。雨下得很大。医院的所有百叶窗都钉死了。其中一位大臣得了伤寒。两个士兵把他抬下楼，抬到雨中。他们试图把他靠在墙上，但他坐在一个水坑里。其余五人安静地靠在墙边站着。最后军官告诉士兵们，想让他站起来没用了。第一阵齐射时他坐在水里，头枕在膝上。

∗ ∗ ^(**){ }^{*} THE BATTLER
∗ ∗ ^(**){ }^{*} 战斗者

Nick stood up. He was all right. He looked up the track at the lights of the caboose going out of sight around the curve. There was water on both sides of the track, then tamarack swamp.
尼克站了起来。他没事。他朝铁轨上方看去，看到货车车厢的灯光沿曲线逐渐消失。铁轨两侧都有积水，外面是落叶松沼泽。
He felt of his knee. The pants were torn and the skin was barked. His hands were scraped and there were sand and cinders driven up under his nails. He went over to the edge of the track down the little slope to the water and washed his hands. He washed them carefully in the cold water, getting the dirt out from the nails. He squatted down and bathed his knee.
他摸了摸自己的膝盖。裤子被撕破，皮肤擦伤。手被擦破，沙子和炉渣塞进了指甲缝里。他走到跑道边，顺着小坡走到水边，洗了手。他在冷水里仔细洗着，把指甲里的脏东西洗干净。他蹲下洗着膝盖。
That lousy crut of a brakeman. He would get him some day. He would know him again. That was a fine way to act.
那个可恶的刹车工混蛋。总有一天他会找他的。他会再次认出他来。那真是干得好。
‘Come here, kid,’ he said. ‘I got something for you.’
“过来，孩子，”他说。“我有东西给你。”
He had fallen for it. What a lousy kid thing to have done.
他上当了。真是件可耻的孩子气事。
They would never suck him in that way again.
他们再也不会那样把他吸引过去了。
‘Come here, kid, I got something for you.’ Then wham and he lit on his hands and knees beside the track.
“过来，孩子，我有东西给你。”然后猛地一把，他扑到跑道旁边跪在手和膝上。
Nick rubbed his eye. There was a big bump coming up. He would have a black eye, all right. It ached already. That son of a crutting brakeman.
尼克揉了揉眼睛。那里起了一个大包。他肯定会有个黑眼圈。已经开始疼了。那个该死的刹车工的儿子。
He touched the bump over his eye with his fingers. Oh, well, it was only a black eye. That was all he had gotten out of it. Cheap at the price. He wished he could see it. Could not see it looking into
他用手指摸了摸眼睛上的肿包。唉，不过是个黑眼圈。那就是他得到的全部。便宜得很。他希望自己能看到它。看不见，朝里看着
the water, though. It was dark and he was a long way off from anywhere. He wiped his hands on his trousers and stood up, then climbed the embankment to the rails.
水面不见了光。他周围漆黑一片，离任何地方都很远。他把手在裤子上擦了擦，站起身，爬上路堤走到铁轨边。
He started up the track. It was well ballasted and made easy walking. The smooth roadbed like a causeway went on ahead through the swamp. Nick walked along. He must get to somewhere.
他沿着轨道向前走。路基铺得很好，走起来轻松。像路堤似的平整路床穿过沼泽向前延伸。Nick 一边走一边想着，他总得到某个地方去。
