Nick had swung on to the freight train when it slowed down for the yards outside of Walton Junction. The train, with Nick on it, had passed through Kalkaska as it started to get dark. Now he must be nearly to Mancelona. Three or four miles of swamp. He stepped along the track, walking so he kept on the ballast between the ties, the swamp ghostly in the rising mist. His eye ached and he was hungry. He kept on hiking, putting the miles of track back of him. The swamp was all the same on both sides of the track.
Nick 是在货车放慢到 Walton Junction 外的编组场时跳上去的。火车在天开始暗下来时，连带着有 Nick 的车厢驶过了 Kalkaska。现在他差不多该到 Mancelona 了。三四英里的沼泽。他沿着铁轨迈步，走在枕木之间的道碴上，沼泽在升起的雾气里显得幽幽渺渺。他眼睛发酸，肚子饿得咕咕叫。他不停地赶路，把一里又一里的铁轨甩到身后。轨道两边的沼泽全都一样。
Ahead there was a bridge. Nick crossed it, his boots ringing hollow on the iron. Down below the water showed black between the slits of ties. Nick kicked a loose spike and it dropped inte the water. Beyond the bridge were hills. It was high and dark on both sides of the track. Up the track Nick saw a fire.
前面有座桥。Nick 走过桥，靴子在铁上敲出空洞的响声。桥下透过枕木的缝隙看见黑乎乎的水面。Nick 踢掉一根松了的钉子，它掉进了水里。桥的那边是山坡。轨道两侧都高而黑。Nick 抬眼沿着轨道望去，看见了火光。
He came up the track toward the fire carefully. It was off to one side of the track, below the railway embankment. He had only seen the light from it. The track came out through a cut and where the fire was burning the country opened out and fell away into woods. Nick dropped carefully down the embankment and cut into the woods to come up to the fire through the trees. It was a beechwood forest and the fallen beechnut burrs were under his shoes as he walked between the trees. The fire was bright now, just at the edge of the trees. There was a man sitting by it. Nick waited behind the tree and watched. The man looked to be alone. He was sitting there with his head in his hands looking at the fire. Nick stepped out and walked into the firelight.
他沿着小路小心翼翼朝火堆走来。火堆在小路一侧，铁路路堤下面。他只看见了火光。小路通过一道切口伸出来，火烧着的地方地势开阔，向下延伸进树林。尼克小心地顺着路堤下来，钻进树林，从树间走到火堆那儿。那是片山毛榉林，地上踩着掉落的山毛榉壳，他在树间行走时能听到。火堆现在很亮，就在树林边缘。有个男人坐在火旁。尼克在树后等着观察。那男人看起来是独自一人。他坐着把头埋在双手里望着火。尼克走出来，走进了火光里。
The man sat there looking into the fire. When Nick stopped quite close to him he did not move.
那个男人坐着凝视着火。尼克走到他很近时，他也没有动。
‘Hello!’ Nick said.
“你好！”尼克说。
The man looked up.
那男人抬起头。
‘Where did you get the shiner?’ he said.
“你哪儿来的黑眼圈？”他说。
‘A brakeman busted me.’
“是个列车员打的我。”
‘Off the through freight?’
“是那趟直达货列的列车员吗？”
‘Yes.’
“是的。”
‘I saw the bastard,’ the man said. 'He went through here ‘bout an hour and a half ago. He was walking along the top of the cars slapping his arms and singing.’
“我看到那混蛋了，”那人说。“大概一个半小时前从这儿过。他沿着车顶走着，拍着胳膊唱歌。”
‘The bastard!’
“该死的混蛋！”
‘It must have made him feel good to bust you,’ the man said seriously.
“打你肯定让他感觉很好，”那人一本正经地说。
‘I’ll bust him.’
“我会打他的。”
‘Get him with a rock sometime when he’s going through,’ the man advised.
“等他经过的时候用石头打他一次，”那人建议道。
‘I’ll get him.’
“我会打他的。”
‘You’re a tough one, aren’t you?’
“你可真厉害，是吧？”
‘No,’ Nick answered.
“不，”尼克回答。
‘All you kids are tough.’
“你们这些孩子都很厉害。”
‘You got to be tough,’ Nick said.
“你得坚强，”Nick 说。
‘That’s what I said.’
“我就是这么说的。”
The man looked at Nick and smiled. In the firelight Nick saw that his face was misshapen. His nose was sunken, his eyes were slits, he had queer-shaped lips. Nick did not perceive all this at once, he only saw the man’s face was queerly formed and mutilated. It was like putty in colour. Dead looking in the firelight.
那人看着 Nick 笑了。在篝火的光里，Nick 看出他的脸畸形不整。他的鼻子塌陷，眼睛成了缝，嘴唇形状怪异。Nick 并不是一下子全部看清这些，他只是觉得那人的脸轮廓奇怪、残缺。在火光下颜色像软泥，显得死气沉沉。
‘Don’t you like my pan?’ the man asked.
“你不喜欢我的锅吗？”那人问道。
Nick was embarrassed.
尼克感到尴尬。
‘Sure,’ he said.
“当然喜欢，”他说。
‘Look here!’ the man took off his cap.
“看这里！”那人脱下了他的帽子。
He had only one ear. It was thickened and tight against the side of his head. Where the other ear should have been there was a stump.
他只有一只耳朵。那只耳朵变厚，紧贴着他的头侧。另一只耳朵本该在的位置只剩下个残端。
‘Ever see one like that?’
“见过这样的么？”
‘No,’ said Nick. It made him a little sick.
“没有，”尼克说。这让他有些恶心。
‘I could take it,’ the man said. 'Don’t you think I could take it, kid?’
“我能拿下他，”那人说。“你不觉得我能拿下他，孩子？”
‘You bet!’
“你说对了！”
‘They all bust their hands on me,’ the little man said. ‘They couldn’t hurt me.’
“他们都拿我没辙，”那个小个子男人说。“他们伤不了我。”
He looked at Nick. ‘Sit down,’ he said. ‘Want to eat?’
他看着尼克。“坐下，”他说。“要不要吃点？”
‘Don’t bother,’ Nick said. ‘I’m going on to the town.’
“别麻烦了，”尼克说。“我要去镇上。”
‘Listen!’ the man said. ‘Call me Ad.’
“听着！”那人说。“叫我阿德。”
‘Sure!’
“好！”
‘Listen,’ the little man said. ‘I’m not quite right.’
“小声点，”那个矮个子说。“我有点不对劲。”
‘What’s the matter?’
“怎么了？”
‘I’m crazy.’
“我疯了。”
He put on his cap. Nick felt like laughing.
他戴上帽子。尼克想笑。
‘You’re all right,’ he said.
“你没事的，”他说。
‘No, I’m not. I’m crazy. Listen, you ever been crazy?’
“不，我不行。我疯了。听着，你有没有发过疯？”
‘No,’ Nick said. ‘How does it get you?’
“不会，”尼克说。 “它怎么影响你？”
‘I don’t know,’ Ad said. ‘When you got it you don’t know about it. You know me, don’t you?’
“我不知道，”阿德说。 “得了的时候你不知道。你认识我，不是吗？”
‘No.’
“不认识。”
‘I’m Ad Francis.’
“我是阿德·弗朗西斯。”
‘Honest to God?’
“真是跟神一样诚实吗？”
‘Don’t you believe it?’
“你不信吗？”
‘Yes.’
“信。”
Nick knew it must be true.
尼克知道这一定是真的。
‘You know how I beat them?’
“你知道我是怎么把他们打败的吗？”
‘No,’ Nick said.
“不知道，”尼克说。
‘My heart’s slow. It only beats forty a minute. Feel it.’
“我的心跳得很慢。每分钟只有四十下。摸摸看。”
Nick hesitated.
尼克犹豫了。
‘Come on,’ the man took hold of his hand. ‘Take hold of my wrist. Put your fingers there.’
“过来，”那人抓住他的手。“抓住我的手腕。把你的手指放那里。”
The little man’s wrist was thick and the muscles bulged above the bone. Nick felt the slow pumping under his fingers.
小个子男人的手腕很粗，骨头上方肌肉隆起。尼克感觉到手指下缓慢的跳动。
‘Got a watch?’
“有手表吗？”
‘No.’
“没有。”
‘Neither have I,’ Ad said. ‘It ain’t any good if you haven’t got a watch.’
“我也没有，”阿德说。“没手表的话可不行。”
Nick dropped his wrist.
尼克放下了手腕。
‘Listen,’ Ad Francis said. ‘Take ahold again. You count and I’ll count up to sixty.’
“听着，”阿德·弗朗西斯说。“再抓紧点。你数，我来数到六十。”
Feeling the slow hard throb under his fingers Nick started to count. He heard the little man counting slowly, one, two, three, four, five, and on-aloud.
尼克感到指间下方缓慢而有力的脉动，开始数起来。他听见那个小个子慢慢地数着，一、二、三、四、五，接着往下数。
‘Sixty,’ Ad finished. ‘That’s a minute. What did you make it?’
“六十，”阿德说完。“那是一分钟。你测得多少？”
‘Forty,’ Nick said.
“四十，”尼克说。
‘That’s right,’ Ad said happily. ‘She never speeds up.’
“没错，”阿德高兴地说。“她从来不加速。”
A man dropped down the railroad embankment and came across the clearing to the fire.
一个男人从铁路堤坡上跳下，穿过空地来到篝火旁。
‘Hello, Bugs!’ Ad said.
“你好，Bugs！”阿德说。
‘Hello!’ Bugs answered. It was a negro’s voice. Nick knew from
“你好！”Bugs 回答。那是一个黑人男子的声音。尼克从
the way he walked that he was a negro. He stood with his back to them, bending over the fire. He straightened up.
他的走路方式就知道他是个黑人。他背对着他们站着，弯着身子朝火堆。随后他直起身来。
‘This is my pal Bugs,’ Ad said. ‘He’s crazy, too.’
“这是我的朋友 Bugs，”阿德说。“他也疯了。”
‘Glad to meet you,’ Bugs said. ‘Where you say you’re from?’
“很高兴见到你，”巴格斯说。“你说你来自哪儿？”
‘Chicago,’ Nick said.
“芝加哥，”尼克说。
‘That’s a fine town,’ the negro said. ‘I didn’t catch your name.’
“那是个好地方，”那黑人说。“我没听清你的名字。”
‘Adams. Nick Adams.’
“亚当斯。尼克·亚当斯。”
‘He says he’s never been crazy, Bugs,’ Ad said.
“他说他从来没发过疯，巴格斯，”艾德说。
‘He’s got a lot coming to him,’ the negro said. He was unwrapping a package by the fire.
“他活该遭报应，”那个黑人说。他正坐在火边拆开一个包裹。
‘When are we going to eat, Bugs?’ the prizefighter asked.
“我们什么时候吃饭，巴格斯？”那拳击手问。
‘Right away.’
“马上就吃。”
‘Are you hungry, Nick ?’
“你饿了吗，尼克？”
‘Hungry as hell.’
“饿死了。”
‘Hear that, Bugs?’
“听见了吗，巴格斯？”
‘I hear most of what goes on.’
“我大部分都能听见。”
‘That ain’t what I asked you.’
“那不是我问你的。”
‘Yes. I heard what the gentleman said.’
“是的。我听到那位先生说的话了。”
Into a skillet he was laying slices of ham. As the skillet grew hot the grease sputtered and Bugs, crouching on long nigger legs over the fire, turned the ham and broke eggs into the skillet, tipping it from side to side to baste the eggs with the hot fat.
他把火腿片放进煎锅。锅热了，油脂噼啪作响，Bugs 蹲在火边，修长的黑人腿上那姿势弯着身子，把火腿翻过来，然后把鸡蛋打进煎锅，左右倾斜锅子，用热油给鸡蛋浇油。
‘Will you cut some bread out of that bag, Mister Adams?’ Bugs turned from the fire.
“Adams 先生，你能从那个包里切些面包吗？”Bugs 从火边转过身来。
‘Sure.’
“好。”
Nick reached in the bag and brought out a loaf of bread. He cut six slices. Ad watched him and leaned forward.
尼克从袋子里伸手掏出一条面包。他切了六片。阿德斯看着他，身体向前倾。
‘Let me take your knife, Nick,’ he said.
“让我拿你的刀吧，尼克，”他说。
‘No, you don’t,’ the negro said. ‘Hang on to your knife, Mister Adams.’
“不，你别拿，”那个黑人说。“把你的刀抓稳，阿德斯先生。”
The prizefighter sat back.
拳击手向后靠去。
‘Will you bring me the bread, Mister Adams?’ Bugs asked. Nick brought it over.
“亚当斯先生，你能把面包递给我吗？”巴格斯问。尼克把面包端了过来。
‘Do you like to dip your bread in the ham fat?’ the negro asked.
“你喜欢把面包蘸火腿油吗？”那个黑人问。
‘You bet!’
“当然啦！”
‘Perhaps we’d better wait until later. It’s better at the finish of the meal. Here.’
“也许我们还是晚一点再吃吧。吃完饭时再吃更好。来。”
The negro picked up a slice of ham and laid it on one of the pieces of bread, then slid an egg on top of it.
那黑人拿起一片火腿放在其中一片面包上，然后在上面滑了一只鸡蛋。
‘Just close the sandwich, will you, please, and give it to Mister Francis.’
“请把三明治合上，好吗，递给弗朗西斯先生。”
Ad took the sandwich and started eating.
阿德接过三明治开始吃起来。
‘Watch out how that egg runs,’ the negro warned. ‘This is for you, Mister Adams. The remainder for myself.’
“当心那只蛋跑了，”那个黑人警告道。“这是给你的，亚当斯先生。剩下的给我自己。”
Nick bit into the sandwich. The negro was sitting opposite him beside Ad. The hot fried ham and eggs tasted wonderful.
尼克咬了一口三明治。黑人坐在他对面，亚德旁边。热煎火腿和鸡蛋味道极好。
‘Mister Adams is right hungry,’ the negro said. The little man whom Nick knew by name as a former champion fighter was silent. He had said nothing since the negro had spoken about the knife.
“亚当斯先生很饿，”黑人说。尼克认识名字的那位小个子男人——一位前任冠军拳手——沉默着。自从黑人提到那把刀后，他一句话也没说。
‘May I offer you a slice of bread dipped right in the hot ham fat?’ Bugs said.
“要不要我给你一片蘸了热火腿油的面包？”巴格斯说。
‘Thanks a lot.’
“多谢了。”
The little white man looked at Nick.
那个个子矮小的白人看着尼克。
‘Will you have some, Mister Adolph Francis?’ Bugs offered from the skillet.
“阿道夫·弗朗西斯先生，要来点吗？”巴格斯从煎锅里递过来。
Ad did not answer. He was looking at Nick.
阿德没有回答。他在看着尼克。
‘Mister Francis?’ came the nigger’s soft voice.
“弗朗西斯先生？”那个黑人的声音很温和。
Ad did not answer. He was looking at Nick.
阿德没有回答。他在看着尼克。
‘I spoke to you, Mister Francis,’ the nigger said softly.
“我在跟你说话，弗朗西斯先生，”那个黑人轻声说。
Ad kept on looking at Nick. He had his cap down over his eyes. Nick felt nervous.
阿德仍然盯着尼克看。他把帽檐压到眼睛上。尼克感到很紧张。
‘How the hell do you get that way?’ came out from under the cap sharply at Nick. ‘Who the hell do you think you are? You’re a snotty bastard. You come in here where nobody asks you and eat a man’s food and when he asks to borrow a knife you get snotty.’
“你他妈怎么会变成这样？”从帽檐下尖声对尼克叫道。“你他妈以为你是谁？你个自以为是的混蛋。你大摇大摆地进来，没人请你，吃别人的饭，当人家借把刀你还摆臭脸。”
He glared at Nick, his face was white and his eyes almost out of sight under the cap.
他怒视着尼克，脸色发白，眼睛几乎被帽檐遮住。
‘You’re a hot sketch. Who the hell asked you to butt in here?’
“你真是个惹事精。谁他妈让你插嘴了？”
‘Nobody.’
“没人。”
‘You’re damn right nobody did. Nobody asked you to stay either. You come in here and act snotty about my face and smoke my cigars and drink my liquor and then talk snotty. Where the hell do you think you get off?’
“该死的，当然没人要你呆着。也没人叫你留下。你进我这儿对我脸色横，还抽我的雪茄喝我的酒，然后摆出一副傲慢样。你以为你凭什么这么嚣张？”
Nick said nothing. Ad stood up.
尼克一言不发。阿德站了起来。
‘I’ll tell you, you yellow-livered Chicago bastard. You’re going to get your can knocked off. Do you get that?’
“我告诉你，你这只胆小鬼、芝加哥的畜生。我要把你踢得飞起。明白了吗？”
Nick stepped back. The little man came toward him slowly,
尼克后退了几步。那个小个子慢慢向他走来，
stepping flat-footed forward, his left foot stepping forward, his right dragging up to it.
他平着脚向前迈步，左脚先踏出，右脚拖着跟上。
‘Hit me,’ he moved his head. ‘Try and hit me.’
“打我，”他摆动着头。“试着打我。”
‘I don’t want to hit you.’
“我不想打你。”
‘You don’t get out of it that way. You’re going to take a beating, see? Come on and lead at me.’
“你别想就这么躲过去。你得挨打，懂吗？上来，冲我出手。”
‘Cut it out,’ Nick said.
“别闹了，”尼克说。
‘All right, then, you bastard.’
“好吧，你这个混蛋。”
The little man looked down at Nick’s feet. As he looked down the negro, who had followed behind him as he moved away from the fire, set himself and tapped him across the base of the skull. He fell forward and Bugs dropped the cloth-wrapped blackjack on the grass. The little man lay there, his face in the grass. The negro picked him up, his head hanging, and carried him to the fire. His face looked bad, the eyes open. Bugs laid him down gently.
小个子低头看了看尼克的脚。正当他低头的时候，那个跟在他后面从火堆边走过来的黑人稳住了身子，用掌根在他的后脑勺敲了一下。他向前倒下，巴格斯把用布包着的警棍扔在草地上。小个子躺在那儿，脸贴着草。那个黑人把他抱起来，头无力地垂着，带到火边。他的脸色不好，眼睛睁着。巴格斯轻轻把他放下。
‘Will you bring me the water in the bucket, Mister Adams?’ he said. ‘I’m afraid I hit him just a little hard.’
“亚当斯先生，你能把桶里的水拿来给我吗？”他说。“恐怕我打得有点重了。”
The negro splashed water with his hand on the man’s face and pulled his ear gently. The eyes closed.
那个黑人用手把水拍到那人的脸上，又轻轻拉了拉他的耳朵。眼睛闭上了。
Bugs stood up.
巴格斯站了起来。
‘He’s all right,’ he said. ‘There’s nothing to worry about. I’m sorry, Mister Adams.’
“他没事，”他说。“不用担心。抱歉，亚当斯先生。”
‘It’s all right.’ Nick was looking down at the little man. He saw the blackjack on the grass and picked it up. It had a flexible handle and was limber in his hand. It was made of worn black leather with a handkerchief wrapped around the heavy end.
“没关系。”尼克低头看着那个小个子男人。他看到草地上的短棒，把它捡了起来。短棒的把手有些弹性，握在手里很灵活。它是用旧黑皮做的，粗的一端包着一块手帕。
"That’s a whalebone handle,’ the negro smiled. ‘They don’t make them any more. I didn’t know how well you could take care of yourself and, anyway, I didn’t want you to hurt him or mark him up no more than he is.’
“那是鲸须手柄，”黑人笑着说。“他们不再做这种的了。我不知道你能照顾好自己到什么程度，而且反正我也不想让你伤到他或把他弄得比现在更糟。”
The negro smiled again.
黑人又笑了。
‘You hurt him yourself.’
“是你亲手伤的他。”
‘I know how to do it. He won’t remember nothing of it. I have to do it to change him when he gets that way.’
“我知道该怎么做。他不会记得这些的。我要这么做是为了在他变成那样的时候改变他。”
Nick was still looking down at the little man, lying, his eyes closed in the firelight. Bugs put some wood on the fire.
尼克仍然低头看着那个小个子人，躺着，眼睛在火光中闭着。巴格斯往火里添了些木头。
‘Don’t you worry about him none, Mister Adams. I seen him like this plenty of times before.’
“亚当斯先生，你别为他担心。我以前见他这样很多次了。”
‘What made him crazy?’ Nick asked.
“是什么把他弄疯的？”尼克问。
‘Oh, a lot of things,’ the negro answered from the fire. ‘Would you like a cup of this coffee, Mister Adams?’
“哦，很多事，”那个黑人从火边回答。“亚当斯先生，要不要来杯这个咖啡？”
He handed Nick the cup and smoothed the coat he had placed under the unconscious man’s head.
他把杯子递给尼克，把放在昏迷男子头下的外套抚平。
‘He took too many beatings, for one thing,’ the negro sipped the coffee. ‘But that just made him sort of simple. Then his sister was his manager and they was always being written up in the papers all about brothers and sisters and how she loved her brother and how he loved his sister, and then they got married in New York and that made a lot of unpleasantness.’
“有一个原因是他挨了太多打，”那个黑人啜了一口咖啡说，“但那反倒让他有点迟钝。再说他姐姐是他的经纪人，报纸上老是写他们兄妹的事，说她多爱她弟弟，他多爱他姐姐，然后他们在纽约结了婚，这就惹来不少不快。”
‘I remember about it.’
“我记得那事。”
‘Sure. Of course they wasn’t brother and sister no more than a rabbit, but there was a lot of people didn’t like it either way and they commenced to have disagreements, and one day she just went off and never come back.’
“当然。我当然知道他们并不是亲兄妹，就像兔子也不是，但很多人不管怎样都不喜欢，于是就开始争执，有一天她就走了，再也没回来。”
He drank the coffee and wiped his lips with the pink palm of his hand.
他喝了咖啡，用手掌带着些粉色的那一面擦了擦嘴唇。
‘He just went crazy. Will you have some more coffee, Mister Adams?’
“他就疯了。亚当斯先生，要再来点咖啡吗？”
‘Thanks.’
“谢谢。”
‘I seen her a couple of times,’ the negro went on. ‘She was an awful good-looking woman. Looked enough like him to be twins. He wouldn’t be bad-looking without his face all busted.’
“我见过她好几次，”那个黑人接着说。“她可真是漂亮。长得跟他差不多，像双胞胎似的。要不是他那张脸全毁了，他也不会难看。”
He stopped. The story seemed to be over.
他停住了。故事似乎结束了。
‘Where did you meet him?’ asked Nick.
“你在哪儿遇到他的？”尼克问。
‘I met him in jail,’ the negro said. ‘He was busting people all the time after she went away and they put him in jail. I was in for cuttin’ a man.’
“我是在监狱里遇到他的，”那个黑人说。“她走了以后他一直在揪人，结果他们把他关进了监狱。我是因为捅了人进来的。”
He smiled, and went on soft-voiced:
他笑了，声音柔和地接着说：
‘Right away I liked him and when I got out I looked him up. He likes to think I’m crazy and I don’t mind. I like to be with him and I like seeing the country and I don’t have to commit no larceny to do it. I like living like a gentleman.’
“我立刻就喜欢上他了，下车后我去找过他。他喜欢以为我疯了，我不介意。我喜欢和他在一起，也喜欢到处看看风景，而且我不必为此去偷东西。我喜欢像个绅士那样生活。”
‘What do you all do?’ Nick asked.
“你们都做什么？”尼克问。
‘Oh, nothing. Just move around. He’s got money.’
“哦，没什么。就是到处走走。他有钱。”
‘He must have made a lot of money.’
“他肯定是赚了很多钱。”
‘Sure. He spent all his money, though. Or they took it away from him. She sends him money.’
“当然。他把钱都花光了，或者是他们把钱拿走了。她给他寄钱。”
He poked up the fire.
他拨了拨火。
‘She’s a mighty fine woman,’ he said. ‘She looks enough like him to be his own twin.’
“她是个很了不起的女人，”他说。“她长得和他极像，简直像他的孪生兄弟。”
The negro looked over at the little man, lying breathing heavily. His blond hair was down over his forehead. His mutilated face looked childish in repose.
那个黑人望了望躺着、呼吸沉重的小个子男人。金色的头发垂在额前。他那被毁伤的脸在静卧时看起来有些孩子气。
‘I can wake him up any time now, Mister Adams. If you don’t mind I wish you’d sort of pull out. I don’t like to not be hospitable, but it might disturb him back again to see you. I hate to have to thump him and it’s the only thing to do when he gets started. I have to sort of keep him away from people. You don’t mind, do you, Mister Adams? No, don’t thank me, Mister Adams. I’d have warned you about him but he seemed to have taken such a liking to you and I thought things were going to be all right. You’ll hit a town about two miles up the track. Mancelona they call it. Goodbye. I wish we could ask you to stay the night but it’s just out of the question. Would you like to take some of that ham and some bread with you? No? You better take a sandwich,’ all this in a low, smooth, polite nigger voice.
“我现在可以把他叫醒，亚当斯先生。如果你不介意的话，我希望你能有点儿尽快离开。我不喜欢不待客，但见到你可能又会把他刺激回来。我不愿意敲打他，可一旦他开始就只有那样做。我得尽量把他和别人隔开。你不介意吧，亚当斯先生？不，不用谢我，亚当斯先生。我本来想提醒你他这个人的，可他好像很喜欢你，我以为没事的。你过两英里左右就能到镇上。叫 Mancelona。他们那儿就那名字。再见了。真希望能请你住一晚，但实在不行。要带点那火腿和面包吗？不要？你最好还是带个三明治吧。”——这一切都用低沉、平滑、礼貌的黑人的声音说出。
‘Good. Well, good-bye, Mister Adams. Good-bye and good luck!’
“好。嗯，再见了，亚当斯先生。再见，祝你好运！”
Nick walked away from the fire across the clearing to the railway tracks. Out of the range of the fire he listened. The low soft voice of the negro was talking. Nick could not hear the words. Then he heard the little man say, ‘I got an awful headache, Bugs.’
尼克离开篝火，穿过空地走向铁轨。出到篝火声外，他侧耳倾听。那黑人低而柔和的声音在说话，尼克听不清词句。然后他听见那个矮个子说：“巴格斯，我头疼得厉害。”
‘You’ll feel better, Mister Francis,’ the negro’s voice soothed. ‘Just you drink a cup of this hot coffee.’
“你会好些的，弗朗西斯先生，”那黑人声音安慰道。“你就喝一杯这热咖啡。”
Nick climbed the embankment and started up the track. He found he had a ham sandwich in his hand and put it in his pocket. Looking back from the mounting grade before the track curved into the hills he could see the firelight in the clearing.
尼克爬上堤坡，顺着小径往上走。他发现手里有一块火腿三明治，就把它放进了口袋。从小径进入山丘前那段上坡回头看，他能看到空地上的火光。
Nick sat against the wall of the church where they had dragged him to be clear of machine-gun fire in the street. Both legs stuck out awkwardly. He had been hit in the spine. His face was sweaty and dirty. The sun shone on his face. The day was very hot. Rinaldi, big backed, his equipment sprawling, lay face downward against the wall. Nick looked straight ahead brilliantly. The pink wall of the house opposite had fallen out from the roof, and an iron bedstead hung twisted toward the street. Two Austrian dead lay in the rubble in the shade of the house. Up the street were other dead. Things were getting forward in the town. It was going well. Stretcherbearers would be along any time now. Nick turned his head carefully and looked at Rinaldi. ‘Senta Rinaldi. Senta. You and me we’ve made a separate peace.’ Rinaldi lay still in the sun breathing with difficulty. ‘Not patriots.’ Nick turned his head carefully away smiling sweatily. Rinaldi was a disappointing audience.
尼克靠在他们为让他避开街上机关枪火力而把他拖到的教堂墙边坐着。两条腿僵硬地伸出来。他的脊椎受了伤。脸上汗水和灰尘交杂。阳光照在他的脸上。天气很热。里纳尔迪背部宽阔，装备散落，面朝下靠在墙边躺着。尼克目光灿烂地直视前方。对面房子的粉红色墙壁从屋顶处塌了下来，一副铁床架扭曲着向街道悬挂。两名奥地利人死者躺在房屋阴影下的瓦砾中。街上更上方还有其他死者。城里的事情在推进。情况进展得很好。担架手随时会来。尼克小心地转过头看着里纳尔迪。“听着，里纳尔迪。听着。你我之间已达成了单独的和解。”里纳尔迪静静地躺在阳光下，呼吸困难。“不是爱国者。”尼克带着汗意小心地把头转开，笑着。里纳尔迪是个令人失望的听众。

A VERY SHORT STORY
一个很短的故事

One very hot evening in Padua they carried him up on to the roof and he could look out over the top of the town. There were chimney swifts in the sky. After a while it got dark and the searchlights came out. The others went down and took the bottles with them. He and Luz could hear them below on the balcony. Luz sat on the bed. She was cool and fresh in the hot night.
在帕多瓦一个非常炎热的夜晚，他们把他抬到屋顶上，他可以俯视整个镇子。天上有烟囱燕。过了一会儿天黑了，聚光灯亮起来。其他人下去把瓶子一并带走了。他和卢斯能从阳台上听到他们的声音。卢斯坐在床上。她在闷热的夜里显得凉爽而清新。
Luz stayed on night duty for three months. They were glad to let her. When they operated on him she prepared him for the operating table; and they had a joke about friend or enema. He went under the anaesthetic holding tight on to himself so he would not blab about anything during the silly, talky time. After he got on crutches he used to take the temperatures so Luz would not have to get up from the bed. There were only a few patients, and they all knew about it. They all liked Luz. As he walked back along the halls he thought of Luz in his bed.
卢斯在夜班值了三个月。他们很乐意让她值班。给他动手术时她把他准备上手术台；他们还拿“朋友还是灌肠”开了个玩笑。他在麻醉下去时紧紧抓住自己，好让自己在那段傻乎乎、唠叨的时间里不胡说八道。拄着拐杖后，他常常替卢斯量体温，这样她就不用从床上起身了。病人不多，大家都知道这事。大家都喜欢卢斯。他顺着走廊走回去时，想到床上的卢斯。
Before he went back to the front they went into the Duomo and prayed. It was dim and quiet, and there were other people praying. They wanted to get married, but there was not enough time for the
在他返回前线之前，他们进了大教堂祈祷。教堂里昏暗而安静，还有其他人在祈祷。他们想结婚，但时间不够了，
banns, and neither of them had birth certificates. They felt as though they were married, but they wanted everyone to know about it, and to make it so they could not lose it.
结婚公告都没有登，他们也没有出生证明。他们觉得自己已是夫妻，但又想让所有人都知道这件事，并且要让这件事无法被夺走。
Luz wrote him many letters that he never got until after the armistice. Fifteen came in a bunch to the front and he sorted them by dates and read them all straight through. They were all about the hospital, and how much she loved him and how it was impossible to get along without him and how terrible it was missing him at night.
卢斯给他写了许多信，他直到停战后才收到。十五封信一并寄到了前线，他按日期整理并连读了所有信。信里全是关于医院的事情，关于她有多爱他、没有他生活无法继续，以及夜里多么想念他的苦楚。
After the armistice they agreed he should go home to get a job so they might be married. Luz would not come home until he had a good job and could come to New York to meet her. It was understood he would not drink, and he did not want to see his friends or anyone in the States. Only to get a job and be married. On the train from Padua to Milan they quarrelled about her not being willing to come home at once. When they had to say good-bye, in the station at Milan, they kissed good-bye, but were not finished with the quarrel. He felt sick about saying good-bye like that.
停战后他们约定他回国找一份工作，好结婚。卢斯不愿回家，除非他有一份好工作并能到纽约去接她。他们约定他不喝酒，他也不想见朋友或在国内的任何人。只是去找工作然后结婚。从帕多瓦到米兰的火车上，他们因她不愿立即回家而争吵。到了米兰车站要道别时，他们接吻告别，但争吵并未结束。他为那样道别而感到难受。
He went to America on a boat from Genoa. Luz went back to Pordonone to open a hospital. It was lonely and rainy there and there was a battalion of arditi quartered in the town. Living in the muddy, rainy town in the winter, the major of the battalion made love to Luz, and she had never known Italians before, and finally wrote to the States that theirs had been only a boy and girl affair. She was sorry, and she knew he would probably not be able to understand, but might some day forgive her, and be grateful to her, and she expected, absolutely unexpectedly, to be married in the spring. She loved him as always, but she realized now it was only a boy and girl love. She hoped he would have a great career, and believed in him absolutely. She knew it was for the best.
他乘一艘从热那亚开来的船去了美国。卢斯回到波尔多内去开一家医院。那里寂寞多雨，镇上驻扎着一营阿尔迪蒂（arditi）突击队。冬天住在这个泥泞多雨的小镇里，那营的少校和卢斯发生了关系，她以前从未了解过意大利人，最后给美国写信说他们之间不过是小孩子式的男女之事。她很后悔，也知道他大概不会理解，但将来或许会原谅她，会感激她，而且她预计，完全出乎意料地，会在春天结婚。她仍像往常一样爱他，但现在意识到那只是小孩子式的男女之爱。她希望他会有一番伟大的事业，完全相信他。她知道这是最好的结果。
The major did not marry her in the spring, or any other time. Luz never got an answer to the letter to Chicago about it. A short time after he contracted gonorrhoea from a sales girl in a loop department store while riding in a taxicab through Lincoln Park.
那位少校并没有在春天或其他任何时候娶她。卢斯从来没有收到那封寄到芝加哥的信的回信。不久之后，那少校在一次打车穿过林肯公园时，从一家环形百货店（loop department store）的一名售货员那里感染了淋病。
While the bombardment was knocking the trench to pieces at Fossalta, he lay very flat and sweated and prayed oh jesus christ get me out of here. Dear jesus please get me out. Christ please please please christ. If you’ll only keep me from getting killed I’ll do anything you say. I believe in you and I’ll tell everyone in the world that you are the only one that matters. Please please dear jesus. The shelling moved farther up the line. We went to work on the trench and in the morning the sun came up and the day was hot and muggy and cheerful and quiet. The next night back at Mestre he did not tell the girl he went upstairs with at the Villa Rossa about Jesus. And he never told anybody.
当炮火在佛萨尔塔把战壕炸得支离破碎时，他趴得很低，出汗并且祈祷，哦，耶稣基督，求你带我离开这里。亲爱的耶稣，请把我带走。基督，求你，求你，求你。只要你保佑我别被杀，我就会照你说的去做。我信你，我会告诉全世界你是唯一重要的。求求你，亲爱的耶稣。炮火向前线更远处移动了。我们回去修理战壕，早晨太阳升起，天气又热又闷，但愉快而宁静。第二天夜里回到梅斯特雷时，他没有把在 Villa Rossa 和他上楼去的那个姑娘有关耶稣的事告诉她。他也从未告诉过任何人。

#) SOLDIER'S HOME
#) 复员士兵之家

Krebs went to the war from a Methodist college in Kansas. There is a picture which shows him among his fraternity brothers, all of them wearing exactly the same height and style collar. He enlisted in the Marines in 1917 and did not return to the United States until the second division returned from the Rhine in the summer of 1919.
克雷布斯从堪萨斯的一所卫斯理学院去参战。有一张照片显示他与他的兄弟会成员们在一起，他们都戴着完全相同高度和式样的领子。1917 年他参军入海军陆战队，直到第二师在 1919 年夏从莱茵河回国他才回到美国。
There is a picture which shows him on the Rhine with two German girls and another corporal. Krebs and the corporal look too big for their uniforms. The German girls are not beautiful. The Rhine does not show in the picture.
有一张照片，拍的是他在莱茵河畔，跟两个德国女孩和另一个下士在一起。克雷布斯和那名下士穿制服显得太瘦小。那两个德国女孩并不漂亮。照片里看不到莱茵河。
By the time Krebs returned to his home town in Oklahoma the greeting of heroes was over. He came back much too late. The men from the town who had been drafted had all been welcomed elaborately on their return. There had been a great deal of hysteria. Now the reaction had set in. People seemed to think it was rather ridiculous for Krebs to be getting back so late, years after the war was over.
当克雷布斯回到他在俄克拉何马的家乡时，英雄受欢迎的热潮已经结束。他回来得太晚了。小镇上那些被征召走的人回来的时候都受到了隆重的欢迎。曾经有过一阵极度的狂热。现在，反应期已经到来。人们似乎觉得克雷布斯回来得如此之晚——战争结束多年后——有些可笑。
At first Krebs, who had been at Belleau Wood, Soissons, the Champagne, St. Mihiel and in the Argonne, did not want to talk about the war at all. Later he felt the need to talk but no one wanted to hear about it. His town had heard too many atrocity stories to be thrilled by actualities. Krebs found that to be listened to at all he had to lie, and after he had done this twice he, too, had a reaction
起初，克雷布斯——曾在贝洛森林、索伊松、香槟、圣米耶尔和阿尔贡作战——根本不想谈论战争。后来他觉得有必要谈谈，但没人愿意听。他的家乡听腻了太多暴行故事，已经无法被真实经历激动。克雷布斯发现，要有人听他讲，他就得撒谎；在他这样做了两次之后，他自己也产生了反应。
against the war and against talking about it. A distaste for everything that had happened to him in the war set in because of the lies he had told. All of the times that had been able to make him feel cool and clear inside himself when he thought of them; the times so long back when he had done the one thing, the only thing for a man to do, easily and naturally, when he might have done something else, now lost their cool, valuable quality and then were lost themselves.
他反对战争，也反对谈论战争。由于他所说的谎言，他对在战争中经历的一切产生了厌恶。那些曾经在他心里让他感觉冷静清晰的往事；那些很久以前他做了一个人应当做的、唯一该做的事时，轻而易举、自然的行为——而他本可能做别的事——现在失去了那种冷静而宝贵的特质，随后也随之消失了。
His lies were quite unimportant lies and consisted in attributing to himself things other men had seen, done or heard of, and stating as facts certain apocryphal incidents familiar to all soldiers. Even his lies were not sensational at the pool room. His acquaintances, who had heard detailed accounts of German women found chained to machine-guns in the Argonne forest and who could not comprehend, or were barred by their patriotism from interest in, any German machine-gunners who were not chained, were not thrilled by his stories.
他的谎言其实无足轻重，主要是把别的男人见过、做过或听说过的事归到自己身上，或把某些为所有士兵所熟知的传闻性事件当作事实来陈述。即便在台球室，他的这些谎话也不算耸人听闻。他的熟人们曾听说过在阿尔贡森林里被拴在机枪上的德国妇女的详尽描述，那些人无法理解，或者出于爱国心而对任何未被拴住的德国机枪手不感兴趣，因此并不会被他的故事所激动。
Krebs acquired the nausea in regard to experience that is the result of untruth or exaggeration, and when he occasionally met another man who had really been a soldier and they talked a few minutes in the dressing room at a dance he fell into the easy pose of the old soldier among other soldiers: that he had been badly, sickeningly frightened all the time. In this way he lost everything.
克雷布斯对经历产生了那种因虚假或夸张而来的作呕感，当他偶尔遇到另一个确实当过兵的人，两人在舞会的更衣室里聊上几分钟时，他就会摆出老兵在同僚面前的老练姿态：他整个时间都害怕得要命、恶心难受。就这样他失去了一切。
During this time, it was late summer, he was sleeping late in bed, getting up to walk down town to the library to get a book, eating lunch at home, reading on the front porch until he became bored and then walking down through the town to spend the hottest hours of the day in the cool dark of the pool room. He loved to play pool.
那段时间，已是晚夏，他在床上睡得很晚，起床后走到城里去图书馆借书，在家吃午饭，在前廊读书直到厌倦，然后步行穿过小镇，在台球室的阴凉处度过一天中最热的时光。他喜欢打台球。
In the evening he practised on his clarinet, strolled down town, read and went to bed. He was still a hero to his two young sisters. His mother would have given him breakfast in bed if he had wanted it. She often came in when he was in bed and asked him to tell her about the war, but her attention always wandered. His father was non-committal.
晚上他练单簧管，漫步到城里，读书然后上床睡觉。他在两个妹妹眼里仍是个英雄。要是他愿意，他母亲会给他端早餐到床上。她常常在他还在床上时进来，让他给她讲战争的事情，但她的注意力总是游移不定。他父亲则态度不置可否。
Before Krebs went away to the war he had never been allowed to drive the family motor car. His father was in the real estate business and always wanted the car to be at his command when he required it to take clients out into the country to show them a piece of farm property. The car always stood outside the First National Bank
在克雷布斯去参战之前，他从来不被允许开家里的汽车。他父亲从事房地产生意，总想在需要时能随时支配那辆车，带客户到郊外去看一块农场物业。那辆车总是停在第一国民银行外面。
building where his father had an office on the second floor. Now, after the war, it was still the same car.
那栋楼他父亲在二楼有个办公室。现在，战争结束后，车还是同一辆。
Nothing was changed in the town except that the young girls had grown up. But they lived in such a complicated world of already defined alliances and shifting feuds that Krebs did not feel the energy or the courage to break into it. He liked to look at them, though. There were so many good-looking young girls. Most of them had their hair cut short. When he went away only little girls wore their hair like that or girls that were fast. They all wore sweaters and shirt waists with round Dutch collars. It was a pattern. He liked to look at them from the front porch as they walked on the other side of the street. He liked to watch them walking under the shade of the trees. He liked the round Dutch collars above their sweaters. He liked their silk stockings and flat shoes. He liked their bobbed hair and the way they walked.
镇子里没有什么变化，只是那些年轻女孩长大了。但她们生活在一个既有既定联盟又不断变化的纷争构成的复杂世界里，克雷布斯既没有精力也没有勇气闯入其中。不过他喜欢看她们。姑娘们长得都很好看。大多数人把头发剪短了。当他离开的时候，只有小女孩才那样留发，或者是放荡的女孩。她们都穿着毛衣和带圆形荷兰领的衬衫裙。这是一种式样。他喜欢从前廊上看着她们从街对面走过。他喜欢看她们在树荫下行走。他喜欢她们毛衣上方的圆形荷兰领。他喜欢她们的丝质长袜和平底鞋。他喜欢她们的短发和她们的步态。
When he was in town their appeal to him was not very strong. He did not like them when he saw them in the Greek’s ice cream parlour. He did not want them themselves really. They were too complicated. There was something else. Vaguely he wanted a girl but he did not want to have to work to get her. He would have liked to have a girl but he did not want to have to spend a long time getting her. He did not want to get into the intrigue and the politics. He did not want to have to do any courting. He did not want to tell any more lies. It wasn’t worth it.
当他在城里的时候，对他们的吸引力并不强。他在希腊人的冰激凌店里看到他们时并不喜欢他们。他其实并不想要他们自己。他们太复杂了。还有别的东西。他模糊地想要一个女孩，但又不想为得到她而费劲。他愿意有个女孩，但又不想花很长时间去得到她。他不想卷入那些阴谋和权谋。他不想去追求。他不想再撒谎了。不值得。
He did not want any consequences. He did i.ul want any consequences ever again. He wanted to live along without consequences. Besides he did not really need a girl. The army had taught him that. It was all right to pose as though you had to have a girl. Nearly everybody did that. But it wasn’t true. You did not need a girl. That was the funny thing. First a fellow boasted how girls meant nothing to him, that he never thought of them, that they could not touch him. Then a fellow boasted that he could not get along without girls, that he had to have them all the time, that he could not go to sleep without them.
他不想要任何后果。他真的不想再有任何后果了。他想要没有后果地生活。而且他其实并不真需要一个女孩。军队教会了他这一点。装出好像非得要个女孩不可也无妨。几乎所有人都那样做。但那不是真的。你并不需要一个女孩。这就是可笑的地方。起先有人夸口说女孩对他毫无意义，他从不想她们，她们触不到他。然后又有人夸口说离不开女孩，必须时刻有她们，没她们就睡不着。
That was all a lie. It was all a lie both ways. You did not need a girl unless you thought about them. He learned that in the army. Then sooner or later you always got one. When you were really ripe for a girl you always got one. You did not have to think about it. Sooner or later it would come. He had learned that in the army.
那全都是谎言。两方面都是谎言。除非你去想她们，否则你并不需要女孩子。他在军队里学会了这点。然后迟早你总会遇到一个。当你真的到了想要女孩子的年纪，你总会遇到一个。你不必去想它。迟早它会到来。他在军队里学会了这点。
Now he would have liked a girl if she had come to him and not wanted to talk. But here at home it was all too complicated. He knew he could never get through it all again. It was not worth the trouble. That was the thing about French girls and German girls. There was not all this talking. You couldn’t talk much and you did not need to talk. It was simple and you were friends. He thought about France and then he began to think about Germany. On the whole he had liked Germany better. He did not want to leave Germany. He did not want to come home. Still, he had come home. He sat on the front porch.
现在如果有女孩来到他身边而且不想说话，他会喜欢这样的女孩。但在家里这一切就太复杂了。他知道自己再也过不来那些事了。那不值得费那个劲。这就是法国女孩和德国女孩的区别。没有这么多唠叨。你不能多说话，也不需要多说话。简单得很，你们就是朋友。他想起了法国，接着又开始想起德国。总体上他更喜欢德国。他不想离开德国。他不想回家。然而，他还是回来了。他坐在前廊上。
He liked the girls that were walking along the other side of the street. He liked the look of them much better than the French girls or the German girls. But the world they were in was not the world he was in. He would like to have one of them. But it was not worth it. They were such a nice pattern. He liked the pattern. It was exciting. But he would not go through all the talking. He did not want one badly enough. He liked to look at them all, though. It was not worth it. Not now when things were getting good again.
他喜欢走在街对面的那些女孩。他比起法国女孩或德国女孩更喜欢她们的样子。但她们所处的世界不是他所处的世界。他会想要其中一个。但那不值得。她们的花样太好看了。他喜欢那种花样。很刺激。但他不愿意去应付所有的交谈。他并不那么强烈地想要一个。不过他喜欢看她们所有人。那不值得。现在尤其不值得。现在事情又开始好起来了。
He sat there on the porch reading a book on the war. It was a history and he was reading about all the engagements he had been in. It was the most interesting reading he had ever done. He wished there were more maps. He looked forward with a good feeling to reading all the really good histories when they would come out with good detail maps. Now he was really learning about the war. He had been a good soldier. That made a difference.
他坐在门廊上读一本关于战争的书。那是一本历史书，他在读自己参加过的所有战役。那是他读过的最有趣的读物。他希望有更多地图。他怀着美好的期待盼着那些带有详尽地图的优秀史书出版。现在他真正开始了解战争了。他曾是个好士兵。那很重要。
One morning after he had been home about a month his mother came into his bedroom and sat on the bed. She smoothed her apron.
有一天早晨，大约在他回家一个月后，他母亲走进他的卧室，坐到床上。她抚平了围裙。
‘I had a talk with your father last night, Harold,’ she said, ‘and he is willing for you to take the car out in the evenings.’
“我昨晚和你父亲谈过了，哈罗德，”她说，“他愿意让你晚上开车出去。”
‘Yeah?’ said Krebs, who was not fully awake. ‘Take the car out? Yeah?’
“是吗？”克雷布斯半醒着说。“开车出去？是吗？”
‘Yes. Your father has felt for some time that you should be able to take the car out in the evenings whenever you wished, but we only talked it over last night.’
“是的。你父亲早就觉得你应该可以在想要的时候晚上开车出去，但我们是昨晚才把这事儿谈清楚的。”
‘I’ll bet you made him,’ Krebs said.
“我打赌是你说服他的，”克雷布斯说。
‘No. It was your father’s suggestion that we talk the matter over.’
“不是。是你父亲建议我们把这事谈一谈。”
‘Yeah. I’ll bet you made him,’ Krebs sat up in bed.
“是啊。我敢打赌是你逼他的，”克雷布斯坐起身说。
‘Will you come down to breakfast, Harold?’ his mother said.
“哈罗德，你要下来吃早饭吗？”他母亲说。
‘As soon as I get my clothes on,’ Krebs said.
“我一穿好衣服就下来，”克雷布斯说。
His mother went out of the room and he could hear her frying something downstairs while he washed, shaved and dressed to go down into the dining-room for breakfast. While he was eating breakfast his sister brought in the mail.
他母亲走出房间，他一边洗脸、刮胡子、穿衣准备下楼去餐厅吃早饭，一边能听见她在楼下煎着什么。吃早饭时，他妹妹把邮件拿进来了。
‘Well, Hare,’ she said. 'You old sleepy-head. What do you ever get up for?’
“好了，Hare，”她说。“你这大懒虫。你什么时候起得来过？”
Krebs looked at her. He liked her. She was his best sister.
克雷布斯看着她。他喜欢她。她是他最好的妹妹。
‘Have you got the paper?’ he asked.
“你拿到报纸了吗？”他问。
She handed him The Kansas City Star and he shucked off its brown wrapper and opened it to the sporting page. He folded The Star open and propped it against the water pitcher with his cereal dish to steady it, so he could read while he ate.
她递给他《堪萨斯城星报》，他剥开棕色的包纸，翻到体育版。他把《星报》摊开，用盛麦片的碗把它靠在水壶上稳住，这样边吃边看。
‘Harold,’ his mother stood in the kitchen doorway, ‘Harold, please don’t muss up the paper. Your father can’t read his Star if it’s been mussed.’
“哈罗德，”他母亲站在厨房门口，“哈罗德，别把报纸弄皱了。你父亲要是看不清他的《星报》怎么办。”
‘I won’t muss it,’ Krebs said.
“我不会弄皱的，”克雷布斯说。
His sister sat down at the table and watched him while he read.
他妹妹坐到桌旁，看着他读报。
‘We’re playing indoor over at school this afternoon,’ she said. ‘I’m going to pitch.’
“我们今天下午在学校里打室内比赛，”她说。“我将上投。”
‘Good,’ said Krebs. ‘How’s the old wing?’
“好，”克雷布斯说。“旧队怎么样？”
‘I can pitch better than lots of the boys. I tell them all you taught me. The other girls aren’t much good.’
“我投得比很多男孩都好。我都跟他们说是你教我的。其他女孩不太行。”
‘Yeah?’ said Krebs.
“是吗？”克雷布斯说。
‘I tell them all you’re my beau. Aren’t you my beau, Hare?’
“我都告诉他们你是我的情人。你不是我的情人吗，哈里？”
‘You bet.’
“当然是。”
'Couldn’t your brother really be your beau just because he’s your brother?’
“就因为他是你哥哥，他就不能真是你的情人吗？”
‘I don’t know.’
“我不知道。”
‘Sure you know. Couldn’t you be my beau, Hare, if I was old enough and if you wanted to ?’
“你知道的。如果我年纪够大，而且你愿意，你能做我的男朋友吗，哈里？”
‘Sure. You’re my girl now.’
“当然。你现在是我的女孩了。”
‘Am I really your girl?’
“我真的是你的女孩吗？”
‘Sure.’
“当然。”
‘Do you love me?’
“你爱我吗？”
‘Uh, huh.’
“嗯，爱。”
‘Will you love me always?’
“你会永远爱我吗？”
‘Sure.’
“当然。”
‘Will you come and watch me play indoor?’
“你会过来看看我打室内球吗？”
‘Maybe.’
“也许吧。”
‘Aw, Hare, you don’t love me. If you loved me, you’d want to come over and watch me play indoor.’
“唉，哈里，你不爱我。如果你爱我，你会想过来看看我打室内球的。”
Krebs’s mother came into the dining-room from the kitchen. She carried a plate of two fried eggs and some crisp bacon on it and a plate of buckwheat cakes.
克雷布斯的母亲从厨房走进餐厅。她端着一盘两个煎蛋和一些脆培根，还有一盘荞麦煎饼。
‘You run along, Helen,’ she said. ‘I want to talk to Harold.’
“你去吧，海伦，”她说。“我想和哈罗德谈谈。”
She put the eggs and bacon down in front of him and brought in a jug of maple syrup for the buckwheat cakes. Then she sat down across the table from Krebs.
她把鸡蛋和培根放到他面前，又端来一壶枫糖浆配荞麦煎饼。然后她在克雷布斯对面坐下。
‘I wish you’d put down the paper a minute, Harold,’ she said.
“哈罗德，我希望你把报纸放下片刻，”她说。
Krebs took down the paper and folded it.
克雷布斯放下报纸，把它对折。
‘Have you decided what you are going to do yet, Harold?’ his mother said, taking off her glasses.
“哈罗德，你决定要做什么了吗？”他母亲摘下眼镜说。
‘No,’ said Krebs.
“不，”克雷布斯说。
‘Don’t you think it’s about time?’ His mother did not say this in a mean way. She seemed worried.
“你不觉得现在差不多该决定了吗？”他母亲不是刻薄地说这话。她看起来很担心。
‘I hadn’t thought about it,’ Krebs said.
“我没有想过这个问题，”克雷布斯说。
‘God has some work for everyone to do,’ his mother said. ‘There can be no idle hands in His Kingdom.’
“上帝为每个人都安排了工作，”他母亲说。“在祂的国度里不能有闲着的手。”
‘I’m not in His Kingdom,’ Krebs said.
“我不在祂的国度里，”克雷布斯说。
‘We are all of us in His Kingdom.’
“我们所有人都在祂的国度里。”
Krebs felt embarrassed and resentful as always.
克雷布斯像往常一样感到尴尬和愤懑。
‘I’ve worried about you so much, Harold,’ his mother went on. ‘I know the temptations you must have been exposed to. I know how weak men are. I know what your own dear grandfather, my own father, told us about the Civil War, and I have prayed for you. I pray for you all day long, Harold.’
“哈罗德，我一直为你担心，”他母亲继续说。“我知道你可能接触到的诱惑。我知道男人是多么软弱。我知道你亲爱的祖父，我自己的父亲，曾经告诉我们的关于内战的事，我也为你祈祷。我整天都在为你祈祷，哈罗德。”
Krebs looked at the bacon fat hardening on his plate.
克雷布斯看着盘子上凝固的培根油。
‘Your father is worried, too,’ his mother went on. ‘He thinks you have lost your ambition, that you haven’t got a definite aim in life. Charley Simmons, who is just your age, has a good job and is going to be married. The boys are all settling down; they’re all determined to get somewhere; you can see that boys like Charley Simmons are on their way to being really a credit to the community.’
“你父亲也很担心，”他母亲接着说。“他觉得你丧失了雄心，没有一个明确的人生目标。查理·西蒙斯，和你年龄相仿，有一份好工作，而且即将结婚。大家都在安定下来了；他们都决心有所成就；你可以看出像查理·西蒙斯这样的男孩正走在成为社区真正骄傲的路上。”
Krebs said nothing.
克雷布斯一句话也没说。
‘Don’t look that way, Harold,’ his mother said. ‘You know we love you and I want to tell you for your own good how matters stand. Your father does not want to hamper your freedom. He thinks you should be allowed to drive the car. If you want to take
“别往那边看，哈罗德，”他母亲说道。“你知道我们爱你，我是为你好，想把情况告诉你。你父亲不想限制你的自由。他认为你应该被允许开车。如果你想去”
some of the nice girls out riding with you, we are only too pleased. We want you to enjoy yourself. But you are going to have to settle down to work, Harold. Your father doesn’t care what you start in at. All work is honourable as he says. But you’ve got to make a start at something. He asked me to speak to you this morning and then you can stop in and see him at his office.’
“和你一起出来骑马的一些漂亮姑娘，我们很高兴。我们希望你玩得开心。但哈罗德，你得安下心来工作。你父亲不在乎你做什么。他说所有工作都是光荣的。但你得开始做点什么。他今天早上让我来跟你说一声，然后你可以顺便去他办公室见他。”
‘Is that all?’ Krebs said.
“就这些吗？”克雷布斯说。
‘Yes. Don’t you love your mother, dear boy?’
“是的。你不爱你母亲吗，亲爱的孩子？”
‘No,’ Krebs said.
“没有，”克雷布斯说。
His mother looked at him across the table. Her eyes were shiny. She started crying.
他的母亲隔着桌子看着他。她的眼睛湿润。他开始哭起来。
‘I don’t love anybody,’ Krebs said.
“我不爱任何人，”克雷布斯说。
It wasn’t any good. He couldn’t tell her, he couldn’t make her see it. It was silly to have said it. He had only hurt her. He went over and took hold of her arm. She was crying with her head in her hands.
这毫无用处。他不能告诉她，他无法让她明白。说了这话很愚蠢。他只是伤了她。他走过去握住她的手臂。她把头埋在手里哭着。
‘I didn’t mean it,’ he said. ‘I was just angry at something. I didn’t mean I didn’t love you.’
“我不是那个意思，”他说。“我只是因为某事生气。我不是说我不爱你。”
His mother went on crying. Krebs put his arm on her shoulder.
他的母亲继续哭着。克雷布斯把手搭在她的肩上。
‘Can’t you believe me, mother?’
“你就不能相信我吗，妈妈？”
His mother shook her head.
他的母亲摇了摇头。
‘Please, please, mother. Please believe me.’
“求你了，求你了，妈妈。求你相信我。”
‘All right,’ his mother said chokily. She looked up at him. ‘I believe you, Harold.’
“好吧，”他母亲哽咽着说。她抬头看着他。“我相信你，哈罗德。”
Krebs kissed her hair. She put her face up to him.
克雷布斯吻了吻她的头发。她把脸贴向他。
‘I’m your mother,’ she said. ‘I held you next to my heart when you were a tiny baby.’
“我是你妈妈，”她说。“你还是个小婴儿的时候，我把你抱在胸前。”
Krebs felt sick and vaguely nauseated.
克雷布斯感到恶心，隐约有些作呕。
‘I know, Mummy,’ he said. ‘I’ll try to be a good boy for you.’
“我知道，妈妈，”他说。“我会尽量做个好孩子。”
‘Would you kneel and pray with me, Harold?’ his mother asked.
“哈罗德，你愿意跪下来和我一起祈祷吗？”他母亲问。
They knelt down beside the dining-room table and Krebs’s mother prayed.
他们在餐桌旁跪下，克雷布斯的母亲祈祷。
‘Now, you pray, Harold,’ she said.
“现在，你祈祷吧，哈罗德，”她说。
‘I can’t,’ Krebs said.
“我不能，”克雷布斯说。
‘Try, Harold.’
“试着祈祷，哈罗德。”
‘I can’t.’
“我做不到。”
‘Do you want me to pray for you?’
“要我为你祈祷吗？”
‘Yes.’
“是的。”
So his mother prayed for him and then they stood up and Krebs
于是他母亲为他祈祷，然后他们站起来，克雷布斯
kissed his mother and went out of the house. He had tried so to keep his life from being complicated. Still, none of it had touched him. He had felt sorry for his mother and she had made him lie. He would go to Kansas City and get a job and she would feel all right about it. There would be one more scene maybe before he went away. He would not go down to his father’s office. He would miss that one. He wanted his life to go smoothly. It had just gotten going that way. Well, that was all over now, anyway. He would go over to the schoolyard and watch Helen play indoor baseball.
亲了亲母亲就出了门。他一直努力不让自己的生活变得复杂。然而，这一切都没有触及到他。他为母亲感到难过，而母亲要他撒了谎。他会去堪萨斯城找工作，母亲会因此放心。也许在他走之前还会有一场争执。他不会去父亲的办公室。那一场他要错过。他希望自己的生活顺顺当当地进行。事情本来正朝那方向开始。嗯，现在这一切都结束了。他要去操场看看海伦打室内棒球。
At two o’clock in the morning two Hungarians got into a cigar store at Fifteenth Street and Grand Avenue. Drevitts and Boyle drove up from the Fifteenth Street police station in a Ford. The Hungarians were backing their wagon out of an alley. Boyle shot one off the seat of the wagon and one out of the wagon box. Drevitts got frightened when he found they were both dead. Hell Jimmy, he said, you oughtn’t to have done it. There’s liable to be a hell of a lot of trouble.
凌晨两点，两名匈牙利人在第十五街和大大道的一家雪茄店里进了店。Drevitts 和 Boyle 开着一辆福特从第十五街警局赶来。那两名匈牙利人正把他们的货车从巷子里倒出来。Boyle 向车座上的一人开了一枪，又向车厢里的一人开了一枪。Drevitts 发现他们俩都死了就吓坏了。该死的 Jimmy，他说，你本不该这么做。可能会惹来一大堆麻烦。
  • They’re crooks, ain’t they? said Boyle. They’re wops, ain’t they? Who the hell is going to make any trouble?
    他们是歹徒，不是吗？Boyle 说。他们是意大利佬，不是吗？谁他妈会闹事？
  • That’s all right maybe this time, said Drevitts, but how did you know they were wops when you dumped them?
    这次也许没事，Drevitts 说，可你怎么知道他们是意大利佬就朝他们开枪的？
Wops, said Boyle, I can tell wops a mile off.
意大利佬，Boyle 说，我隔一英里就能看出谁是意大利佬。

THE REVOLUTIONIST
革命者

In 1919 he was travelling on the railroads in Italy, carrying a square of oilcloth from the headquarters of the party written in indelible pencil and saying here was a comrade who had suffered very much under the Whites in Budapest and requesting comrades to aid him in any way. He used this instead of a ticket. He was very shy and quite young and the train men passed him on from one crew to another. He had no money, and they fed him behind the counter in railway eating houses.
1919 年他在意大利乘火车旅行，带着一块油布，上面用不褪色的铅笔写着党总部的字样，并说明这里有一位在布达佩斯被白军严重迫害的同志，请求同志们以任何方式帮助他。他用这张写着求援的油布代替车票。他很羞涩，非常年轻，列车员把他从一班交给另一班。他没有钱，车站餐室的伙计们在柜台后面喂他吃饭。
He was delighted with Italy. It was a beautiful country, he said. The people were all kind. He had been in many towns, walked much, and seen many pictures. Giotto, Masaccio, and Piero della Francesca he bought reproductions of and carried them wrapped in a copy of Avanti. Mantegna he did not like.
他对意大利非常欣喜。他说这是个美丽的国家。人们都很友善。他去过许多城镇，走了很多路，看了许多画作。他买了乔托、马萨乔和皮耶罗·德拉·弗朗切斯卡的复制画，用一份《Avanti》包着带着。曼特尼亚他不喜欢。
He reported at Bologna, and I took him with me up into the Romagna where it was necessary I go to see a man. We had a good trip together. It was early September and the country was pleasant. He was a Magyar, a very nice boy and very shy. Horthy’s men had done some bad things to him. He talked about it a little. In spite of Hungary, he believed altogether in the world revolution.
他在博洛尼亚报到，我带他上罗马涅去，因为我必须去见一个人。我们一起旅途愉快。那是九月初，乡间很宜人。他是个马札尔人，一个非常好而且很害羞的年轻人。霍尔蒂的人对他做过一些坏事。他稍微谈了那件事。尽管遭遇了匈牙利的事，他还是完全相信世界革命。
‘But how is the movement going in Italy?’ he asked.
“但意大利的运动进展得怎么样？”他问。
‘Very badly,’ I said.
“很糟，”我说。
‘But it will go better,’ he said. ‘You have everything here. It is the one country that everyone is sure of. It will be the starting point of everything.’
“但会好起来的，”他说。“你们这里一切俱全。这是唯一人人都确信的国家。它将成为一切的出发点。”
I did not say anything.
我没有说话。
At Bologna he said good-bye to us to go on the train to Milano and then to Aosta to walk over the pass into Switzerland. I spoke to him about the Mantegnas in Milano. ‘No,’ he said, very shyly, he did not like Mantegna. I wrote out for him where to eat in Milano and the addresses of comrades. He thanked me very much, but his mind was already looking forward to walking over the pass. He was very eager to walk over the pass while the weather held good. He loved the mountains in the autumn. The last I heard of him the Swiss had him in jail near Sion.
在博洛尼亚他和我们告别，去坐火车去米兰，然后到奥斯塔，准备翻过山口进入瑞士。我和他谈起米兰的曼特尼亚（Mantegna）画作。“不，”他非常害羞地说，他不喜欢 Mantegna。我给他写下了在米兰吃饭的地点和几个同志的地址。他非常感谢我，但他的心已经盼着去翻山口了。他非常渴望在天气好的时候翻越山口。他喜欢秋天的山。最后一次听说他，是瑞士人在锡永附近把他关进了监狱。
The first matador got the horn through his sword hand and the crowd hooted him. The second matador slipped and the bull caught him through the belly and he hung on to the horn with one hand and held the other tight against the place, and the bull rammed him wham against the wall and the horn came out, and he lay in the sand, and then got up like crazy drunk and tried to slug the men carrying him away and yelled for his sword but he fainted. The kid came out and had to kill five bulls because you can’t have more than three matadors, and the last bull he was so tired he couldn’t get the sword in. He couldn’t hardly lift his arm. He tried five times and the crowd was quiet because it was a good bull and it looked like him or the bull and then he finally made it. He sat down in the sand and puked and they held a cape over him while the crowd hollered and threw things down into the bull ring.
第一个斗牛士被牛角穿透了持剑的那只手，观众朝他嘘声。第二个斗牛士滑倒了，公牛把他的腹部顶住，他单手抓住牛角，另一只手紧按着伤口，公牛猛地把他撞到围墙上，牛角拔出来了，他躺在沙地上，然后像个喝醉疯了一样爬起来，试图揍抬走他的那些人，大喊要他的剑，但他昏了过去。小伙子出来了，得杀五头牛，因为斗牛士不能超过三个，最后那头牛他累得拿不动剑了。他几乎抬不起来胳膊。他试了五次，观众都安静了，因为那是头好牛，看起来不是他就是牛会完事，然后他终于做到了。他坐在沙地上吐了，众人把披风盖在他身上，观众大喊并向斗牛场里扔东西。

MR. AND MRS. ELLIOT
埃利奥特先生和夫人

Mr. and Mrs. Elliot tried very hard to have a baby. They tried as often as Mrs. Elliot could stand it. They tried in Boston after they were married and they tried coming over on the boat. They did not try very often on the boat because Mrs. Elliot was quite sick. She was sick and when she was sick she was sick as Southern women are sick. That is women from the southern part of the United States. Like all Southern women Mrs. Elliot disintegrated very quickly under sea sickness, travelling at night, and getting up too early in the morning. Many of the people on the boat took her for Elliot’s mother. Other people who knew they were married believed she was going to have a baby. In reality she was forty years old. Her years had been precipitated suddenly when she started travelling.
艾略特先生和艾略特太太非常努力地想要一个孩子。他们尽可能多地尝试，只要艾略特太太能忍受得了。他们在结婚后的波士顿尝试过，也在乘船时尝试过。他们在船上并不常尝试，因为艾略特太太很容易晕船。她一晕船就是那种南方女人晕得厉害。这里指的是来自美国南部的女人。像所有南方女人一样，艾略特太太在晕船、夜间旅行和早晨起得太早时，会很快变得虚弱不堪。船上的许多人都把她当作艾略特的母亲。其他知道他们已婚的人则相信她会怀孕。实际上她已经四十岁了。自从开始旅行后，她的年华仿佛一下子加速了。
She had seemed much younger, in fact she had seemed not to have any age at all, when Elliot had married her after several weeks of making love to her after knowing her for a long time in her tea shop before he had kissed her one evening.
在艾略特娶她之前的那段时间里，他在她的茶室认识她很久，几周的缠绵之后某个晚上吻了她——那时她看起来要年轻得多，实际上甚至显得没有年龄感。
Hubert Elliot was taking postgraduate work in law at Harvard when he was married. He was a poet with an income of nearly ten thousand dollars a year. He wrote very long poems rapidly. He was
休伯特·艾略特在哈佛攻读法学研究生时结了婚。他是个诗人，年收入近一万美元。他写诗很长，而且写得很快。他
twenty-five years old and had never gone to bed with a woman until he married Mrs. Elliot. He wanted to keep himself pure so that he could bring to his wife the same purity of mind and body that he expected of her. He called it to himself living straight. He had been in love with various girls before he kissed Mrs. Elliot and always told them sooner or later that he had led a clean life. Nearly all the girls lost interest in him. He was shocked and really horrified at the way girls would become engaged to and marry men whom they must know had dragged themselves through the gutter. He once tried to warn a girl he knew against a man of whom he had almost proof that he had been a rotter at college and a very unpleasant incident had resulted.
二十五岁，直到娶了艾略特太太之前从未与女人同床。他想保持清白，以便把他对妻子所期望的那种心灵与身体的纯洁带给她。他把这称作过正直的生活。他在吻别艾略特太太之前爱过几个女孩，并且总会迟早告诉她们他过的是清洁的生活。几乎所有女孩对他都失去了兴趣。他对女孩们会与那些她们明知曾在污水沟里挣扎过的男人订婚并嫁给他们的做法感到震惊，甚至真正害怕。有一次他曾试图警告一个他认识的女孩，告诉她当心一个他几乎有证据证明在大学时就是个流氓的男人，结果引发了一件非常不愉快的事件。
Mrs. Elliot’s name was Cornelia. She had taught him to call her Calutina, which was her family nickname in the South. His mother cried when he brought Cornelia home after their marriage but brightened very much when she learned they were going to live abroad.
艾略特太太名叫科内莉亚。她教他叫她 Calutina，那是她在南方的家人昵称。他把科内莉亚带回家后他母亲哭了，但在得知他们要去国外生活时变得非常高兴。
Cornelia had said, ‘You dear sweet boy,’ and held him closer than ever when he had told her how he had kept himself clean for her. Cornelia was pure too. ‘Kiss me again like that,’ she said.
科妮莉娅说：“你这可爱甜美的孩子，”当他告诉她他为了她一直保持清白时，她比以往任何时候都抱得更紧。科妮莉娅本身也很纯洁。“再那样吻我一次，”她说。
Hubert explained to her that he had learned that way of kissing from hearing a fellow tell a story once. He was delighted with his experiment and they developed it as far as possible. Sometimes when they had been kissing together a long time, Cornelia would ask him to tell her again that he had kept himself really straight for her. The declaration always set her off again.
休伯特向她解释说，他是听一个人讲故事时学到那种吻法的。他对自己的尝试感到高兴，于是尽可能地发展它。有时当他们长时间热吻后，科妮莉娅会要求他再对她说一遍他为了她保持真诚的事。那番宣言总能再次激起她的情绪。
At first Hubert had no idea of marrying Cornelia. He had never thought of her that way. She had been such a good friend of his, and then one day in the little back room of the shop they had been dancing to the gramophone while her girl friend was in the front of the shop and she looked up into his eyes and he had kissed her. He could never remember just when it was decided that they were to be married. But they were married.
起初休伯特并不打算娶科妮莉娅。他从未那样想过她。她一直是他很好的朋友，然后有一天在店铺后面的小屋里，当她的女友在店前时，他们在留声机旁跳舞，她抬头看着他的眼睛，他便吻了她。他始终记不清究竟是什么时候决定要结婚的。但他们确实结婚了。
They spent the night of the day they were married in a Boston hotel. They were both disappointed but finally Cornelia went to sleep. Hubert could not sleep and several times went out and walked up and down the corridor of the hotel in his new Jaegar bathrobe that he had bought for his wedding trip. As he walked he saw all the pairs of shoes, small shoes and big shoes, outside the doors
他们在结婚当天的夜晚住在波士顿的一家旅馆里。他们俩都有些失望，但康妮莉亚最终睡着了。科伯特睡不着，好几次出去穿着他为蜜月买的新 Jaegar 浴袍在旅馆的走廊里来回走着。他走着时看见了所有门外成双的鞋子，小鞋和大鞋。
of the hotel rooms. This set his heart to pounding and he hurried back to his own room but Cornelia was asleep. He did not like to waken her and soon everything was quite all right and he slept peacefully.
这使他的心怦怦直跳，他急忙回到自己的房间，但康妮莉亚已经睡着了。他不愿叫醒她，很快一切都安静下来，他也安然入睡。
The next day they called on his mother and the next day they sailed for Europe. It was possible to try to have a baby but Cornelia could not attempt it very often although they wanted a baby more than anything else in the world. They landed at Cherbourg and came to Paris. They tried to have a baby in Paris. Then they decided to go to Dijon where there was summer school and where a number of people who crossed on the boat with them had gone. They found there was nothing to do in Dijon. Hubert, however, was writing a great number of poems and Cornelia typed them for him. They were all very long poems. He was very severe about mistakes and would make her re-do an entire page if there was one mistake. She cried a good deal and they tried several times to have a baby before they left Dijon.
第二天他们去拜访了他的母亲，接着第二天便启航前往欧洲。他们可以尝试要一个孩子，但康妮莉娅不能经常尝试，尽管他们比世上任何事都更想要一个孩子。他们在瑟堡登陆，来到了巴黎。他们在巴黎尝试要一个孩子。然后他们决定去第戎，那儿有暑期学校，也有一些与他们同船的人去了那里。他们发现第戎无事可做。然而，休伯特写了大量诗歌，康妮莉娅为他打字。那些都是很长的诗。他对错误非常严厉，如果有一个错误就会让她重做整整一页。她常常哭泣，他们在离开第戎前曾多次尝试要孩子。
They came to Paris and most of their friends from the boat came back too. They were tired of Dijon and anyway would now be able to say that after leaving Harvard or Columbia or Wabash they had studied at the University of Dijon down in the Côte d’Or. Many of them would have preferred to go to Languedoc, Montpellier or Perpignan if there are universities there. But all those places are too far away. Dijon is only four and a half hours from Paris and there is a diner on the train.
他们来到巴黎，船上大多数朋友也都回来了。他们厌倦了第戎，而且现在总算可以说在离开哈佛或哥伦比亚或瓦巴什之后，他们曾在科多尔的第戎大学学习过。他们中许多人更愿意去朗格多克、蒙彼利埃或佩皮尼昂，如果那些地方有大学的话。但所有那些地方都太远了。第戎离巴黎只有四个半小时，而且火车上有餐车。
So they all sat around the Café du Dome, avoiding the Rotonde across the street because it is always so full of foreigners for a few days and then the Elliots rented a château in Touraine through an advertisement in the New York Herald. Elliot had a number of friends by now all of whom admired his poetry and Mrs. Elliot had prevailed upon him to send over to Boston for her girl friend who had been in the tea shop. Mrs. Elliot became much brighter after her girl friend came and they had many good cries together. The girl friend was several years older than Cornelia and called her Honey. She too came from a very old Southern family.
于是他们都围坐在 Café du Dome，避开街对面的 La Rotonde，因为那里总是有几天挤满了外国人，随后埃利奥特一家通过《纽约先驱报》上的一则广告在图雷纳租了座城堡。埃利奥特现在有好些朋友，所有人都欣赏他的诗，埃利奥特太太说服他从波士顿把在茶馆里遇见的她的闺蜜接过来。闺蜜来了以后，埃利奥特太太显得精神多了，她们一起痛痛快快地哭了好几场。那位闺蜜比科尼利亚大好几年，称她为“亲爱的”。她也出自一个非常古老的南方家族。
The three of them, with several of Elliot’s friends who called him Hubie, went down to the château in Touraine. They found Touraine to be a very flat hot country very much like Kansas. Elliot had nearly enough poems for a book now. He was going to bring
他们三人和几个叫他 Hubie 的 Elliot 的朋友一起去了图赖讷的那座城堡。他们觉得图赖讷是一个非常平坦、酷热的地方，很像堪萨斯。Elliot 现在已经差不多有足够的诗篇可以出一本书了。他正打算带着
it out in Boston and had already sent his cheque to, and made a contract with, a publisher.
把它放在波士顿，已经把支票寄给并与一家出版社签了合同。
In a short time the friends began to drift back to Paris. Touraine had not turned out the way it looked when it started. Soon all the friends had gone off with a rich young and unmarried poet to a seaside resort near Trouville. There they were all very happy.
不久朋友们开始陆续回到巴黎。图雷讷并没有像起初看起来那样发展。很快所有朋友都跟着一位年轻富有且未婚的诗人去了特鲁维尔附近的一个海滨度假村。在那里他们都非常快乐。
Elliot kept on at the château in Touraine because he had taken it for all summer. He and Mrs. Elliot tried very hard to have a baby in the big hot bedroom on the big, hard bed. Mrs. Elliot was learning the touch system on the typewriter, but she found that while it increased the speed it made more mistakes. The girl friend was now typing practically all of the manuscripts. She was very neat and efficient and seemed to enjoy it.
埃利奥特留在图林地区的城堡里，因为他把那里租下了整个夏天。他和艾略特太太在那间又大又热、床又大又硬的卧室里努力想要一个孩子。艾略特太太在学习打字机的触摸打字法，但她发现虽然速度提高了，错误却更多。女友现在几乎在为所有手稿打字。她非常整洁高效，似乎很享受这件事。
Elliot had taken to drinking white wine and lived apart in his own room. He wrote a great deal of poetry during the night and in the morning looked very exhausted. Mrs. Elliot and the girl friend now slept together in the big medieval bed. They had many a good cry together. In the evening they all sat at dinner together in the garden under a plane tree and the evening wind blew and Elliot drank white wine and Mrs. Elliot and the girl friend made conversation and they were all quite happy.
艾略特开始喝白葡萄酒，住在自己的房间里。他晚上写了很多诗，早上看起来非常疲惫。艾略特太太和那个女友现在一起睡在大号的中世纪床上。她们常常痛痛快快地哭一场。傍晚他们都在一棵悬铃木下的花园里一同吃晚饭，晚风吹拂，艾略特喝着白葡萄酒，艾略特太太和女友交谈着，大家都十分快乐。
They whack - whacked the white horse on the legs and he kneed himself up. The picador twisted the stirrups straight and pulled and hauled up into the saddle. The horse’s entrails hung down in a blue bunch and swung backward and forward as he began to canter, the monos whacking him on the back of his legs with the rods. He cantered jerkily along the barrera. He stopped stiff and one of the monos held his bridle and walked him forward. The picador kicked in his spurs, leaned forward and shook his lance at the bull. Blood pumped regularly from between the horse’s front legs. He was nervously wobbly. The bull could not make up his mind to charge.
他们用棒子——猛击白马上腿部，马用膝盖顶起自己。骑手把马镫拉正，向后拉扯，把马重新固定在鞍上。马的内脏垂成一绺蓝色，随着它开始小跑而前后摆动，助手们用棍子打在它的大腿后侧。他在围栏旁蹒跚地小跑着。它僵住了停下，其中一个助手扶着缰绳把它往前牵。骑手踢动马刺，向前倾身，朝公牛挥动长枪。血从马前腿之间规律地涌出。它神经质地摇摆不定。公牛无法决定是否冲上来。

CATIN THE RAIN
雨中的猫

There were only two Americans stopping at the hotel. They did not know any of the people they passed on the stairs on their way to and from their room. Their room was on the second floor facing the sea. It also faced the public garden and the war monument. There were big palms and green benches in the public garden. In the good weather there was always an artist with his easel. Artists liked the way the palms grew and the bright colours of the hotels facing the gardens and the sea. Italians came from a long way off to look up at the war monument. It was made of bronze and glistened in the rain It was raining. The rain dripped from the palm trees. Water stood in pools on the gravel paths. The sea broke in a long line in the rain and slipped back down the beach to come up and break again in a long line in the rain. The motor cars were gone from the square by the war monument. Across the square in the doorway of the café a waiter stood looking out at the empty square.
旅馆里只有两个美国人。上下房间时经过楼梯上的人，他们都不认识。房间在二楼，朝海。房间也面向公园和战争纪念碑。公园里有高大的棕榈树和绿色的长椅。天气好时，总有一位带画架的画家。画家喜欢棕榈树的生长姿态以及面向公园和大海的旅馆鲜艳的色彩。意大利人从很远的地方来仰望战争纪念碑。纪念碑由青铜制成，在雨中闪闪发光。正在下雨。雨水从棕榈树上滴落。水在砂砾小径上汇成水洼。大海在雨中一长线地拍打海面，然后沿着海滩滑回去，再次涌上来，在雨中又一长线地拍打。战争纪念碑广场上的汽车已不见了。广场对面咖啡馆的门口有一名侍者站着，望着空荡的广场。
The American wife stood at the window looking out. Outside right under their window a cat was crouched under one of the dripping green tables. The cat was trying to make herself so compact that she would not be dripped on.
美国妻子站在窗边往外看。窗外就在他们窗下，有一只猫蜷缩在一张滴着水的绿色桌子下面。那只猫正尽力把自己缩得很紧，好不要被滴到水。
‘I’m going down and get that kitty,’ the American wife said.
“我要下去把那只小猫抱起来，”美国妻子说。
‘I’ll do it,’ her husband offered from the bed.
“我去吧，”她丈夫在床上提议。
‘No, I’ll get it. The poor kitty out trying to keep dry under a table.’
“不，我去。可怜的小猫在桌子下面躲雨。”
The husband went on reading, lying propped up with the two pillows at the foot of the bed.
丈夫继续看书，靠着床尾的两个枕头半躺着。
‘Don’t get wet,’ he said.
“别淋湿了，”他说。
The wife went downstairs and the hotel owner stood up and bowed to her as she passed the office. His desk was at the far end of the office. He was an old man and very tall.
妻子下了楼，旅馆老板起身在她经过办公室时向她鞠躬。他的办公桌在办公室的尽头。他是个又老又高的男人。
‘Il piove,’ the wife said. She liked the hotel-keeper.
“Il piove，”妻子说。她喜欢这位旅馆老板。
‘Si, si, Signora, brutto tempo. It’s very bad weather.’
“Si, si, Signora, brutto tempo。It’s very bad weather。”
He stood behind his desk in the far end of the dim room. The wife liked him. She liked the deadly serious way he received any complaints. She liked his dignity. She liked the way he wanted to serve her. She liked the way he felt about being a hotel-keeper. She liked his old, heavy face and big hands.
他站在昏暗房间远端的办公桌后。妻子喜欢他。她喜欢他处理任何投诉时那种严肃认真的样子。她喜欢他的庄重。她喜欢他想要为她服务的态度。她喜欢他对作为旅馆老板这份职业的感觉。她喜欢他那张古老而厚重的脸和大手。
Liking him she opened the door and looked out. It was raining harder. A man in a rubber cape was crossing the empty square to the café. The cat would be around to the right. Perhaps she could go along under the eaves. As she stood in the doorway an umbrella opened behind her. It was the maid who looked after their room.
她喜欢他，于是打开门朝外看。雨下得更大了。一个穿着橡胶披风的男人正穿过空荡的广场走向咖啡馆。猫会从右边绕过去。也许她可以沿着檐下走。她站在门口时，一把伞在她身后打开。是照顾他们房间的女仆。
‘You must not get wet,’ she smiled, speaking Italian. Of course, the hotel-keeper had sent her.
“你不能淋湿了，”她笑着用意大利语说。当然，是旅馆老板派她来的。
With the maid holding the umbrella over her, she walked along the gravel path until she was under their window. The table was there, washed bright green in the rain, but the cat was gone. She was suddenly disappointed. The maid looked up at her.
女仆为她打着伞，她沿着碎石小路走到他们窗下。桌子在那里，雨水冲洗得亮绿一片，但那只猫不见了。她猛然感到失望。女仆抬头看着她。
‘Ha perduto qualque cosa, Signora?’
“Ha perduto qualque cosa, Signora？”
‘There was a cat,’ said the American girl.
“有一只猫，”美国女孩说。
‘A cat?’
“一只猫？”
‘Si, il gatto.’
“是的，猫。”
‘A cat?’ the maid laughed. ‘A cat in the rain?’
“猫？”女佣笑了。“雨里的一只猫？”
‘Yes,’ she said, ‘under the table.’ Then, ‘Oh, I wanted it so much. I wanted a kitty.’
“是的，”她说，“在桌子底下。”接着，“哦，我太想要了。我想要一只小猫。”
When she talked English the maid’s face tightened.
当她说英语时，女佣的脸变得紧绷。
‘Come, Signora,’ she said. ‘We must get back inside. You will be wet.’
“过来，Signora，”她说。“我们得回屋去。你会被淋湿的。”
‘I suppose so,’ said the American girl.
“我想是吧，”美国姑娘说。
They went back along the gravel path and passed in the door. The maid stayed outside to close the umbrella. As the American girl passed the office, the padrone bowed from his desk. Something felt very small and tight inside the girl. The padrone made her feel very
他们沿着碎石路走回屋里，穿过门。女佣留在外面收伞。当美国姑娘经过办公室时，padrone 从课桌前鞠了个躬。姑娘内心有一种很小很紧的感觉。padrone 让她觉得自己很
small and at the same time really important. She had a momentary feeling of being of supreme importance. She went on up the stairs. She opened the door of the room. George was on the bed, reading.
渺小，同时又真的很重要。她一时感觉自己至关重要。她继续上楼。她打开房门。乔治正躺在床上看书。
‘Did you get the cat?’ he asked, putting the book down.
“你把猫弄到手了吗？”他放下书问。
‘It was gone.’
“它不见了。”
‘Wonder where it went to?’ he said, resting his eyes from reading. She sat down on the bed.
“真想知道它跑哪儿去了？”他说，闭目休息一下。她坐到床上。
‘I wanted it so much,’ she said. ‘I don’t know why I wanted it so much. I wanted that poor kitty. It isn’t any fun to be a poor kitty out in the rain.’
“我多想要它啊，”她说。“我也不知道为什么会那么想要。我就是想要那只可怜的小猫。在雨里当只可怜的小猫可一点也不好受。”
George was reading again.
乔治又在看书。
She went over and sat in front of the mirror of the dressing table looking at herself with the hand glass. She studied her profile, first one side and then the other. Then she studied the back of her head and her neck.
她走过去，坐在梳妆台的镜子前，用手镜看着自己。她打量着自己的侧脸，先是一边，然后是另一边。接着她又端详着后脑和脖颈。
‘Don’t you think it would be a good idea if I let my hair grow out?’ she asked, looking at her profile again.
“你不觉得我把头发留长一点会更好吗？”她又看着自己的侧脸问道。
George looked up and saw the back of her neck, clipped close like a boy’s.
乔治抬头，看见她后颈，像男孩一样被剪得很短。
‘I like it the way it is.’
“我就喜欢现在这样。”
‘I get so tired of it,’ she said. ‘I get so tired of looking like a boy.’
“我真厌倦了，”她说。“我真厌倦了看起来像个男孩。”
George shifted his position in the bed. He hadn’t looked away from her since she started to speak.
乔治在床上挪了挪身子。自从她开始说话，他就一直没有移开视线。
‘You look pretty darn nice,’ he said.
“你看起来挺漂亮的，”他说。
She laid the mirror down on the dresser and went over to the window and looked out. It was getting dark.
她把镜子放在梳妆台上，走到窗前向外看。天色渐暗。
‘I want to pull my hair back tight and smooth and make a big knot at the back that I can feel,’ she said. ‘I want to have a kitty to sit on my lap and purr when I stroke her.’
“我想把头发往后紧紧梳起，弄成一个在后脑勺能摸得到的大发髻，”她说。“我想要一只小猫坐在我膝上，当我抚摸它时它会咕噜叫。”
‘Yeah?’ George said from the bed.
“是吗？”乔治从床上说。
‘And I want to eat at a table with my own silver and I want candles. And I want it to be spring and I want to brush my hair out in front of a mirror and I want a kitty and I want some new clothes.’
“还有，我想在有我自己的银餐具的桌子上吃饭，我想要蜡烛。我想要春天，我想在镜子前梳理我的头发，我想要一只小猫和一些新衣服。”
‘Oh, shut up and get something to read,’ George said. He was reading again.
“哦，闭嘴，去找点儿东西看吧，”乔治说。他又在看书了。
His wife was looking out of the window. It was quite dark now and still raining in the palm trees.
他的妻子望着窗外。现在天已经很黑，棕榈树间仍在下雨。
‘Anyway, I want a cat,’ she said. ‘I want a cat. I want a cat now. If I can’t have long hair or any fun, I can have a cat.’
“反正，我要一只猫，”她说。“我要一只猫。我现在就要一只猫。如果我不能留长发或享受乐趣，那我至少能有只猫。”
George was not listening. He was reading his book. His wife looked out of the window where the light had come on in the square.
乔治没有在听。他在看他的书。他的妻子望着窗外，广场的灯光亮了起来。
Someone knocked at the door.
有人敲门。
‘Avanti,’ George said. He looked up from his book.
“进来吧，”乔治说。他从书中抬起头。
In the doorway stood the maid. She held a big tortoiseshell cat pressed tight against her and swung down against her body.
门口站着女佣。她怀里抱着一只大玳瑁猫，紧贴着她的身体垂着尾巴。
‘Excuse me,’ she said, ‘the padrone asked me to bring this for the Signora.’
“对不起，”她说，“padrone 让我把这个送给 Signora。”
The crowd shouted all the time and threw pieces of bread down into the ring, then cushions and leather wine bottles, keeping up whistling and yelling. Finally the bull was too tired from so much bad sticking and folded his knees and lay down and one of the cuadrilla leaned out over his neck and killed him with the puntilla. The crowd came over the barrera and around the torero and two men grabbed him and held him and someone cut off his pigtail and was waving it and a kid grabbed it and ran away with it. Afterwards I saw him at the café. He was very short with a brown face and quite drunk and he said after all it has happened before like that. I am not really a good bull-fighter.
人群一直在喊叫，往竞技场里扔面包屑，接着扔坐垫和皮酒瓶，持续着口哨声和叫嚷声。最后那头公牛被这么多拙劣的刺杀弄得太累，屈膝躺下，队伍里有个人探过身去在它的颈项上用短匕首刺死了它。人群翻过围栏，围到斗牛士周围，两个人抓住他按住，有人割下了他的辫子挥舞着，一个小孩抢过辫子跑了。后来我在咖啡馆看见了他。他个子很矮，脸色黝黑，喝得相当醉，他说这事以前也有过。他并不是真正的好斗牛士。

OUT OF SEASON
淡季

On the four lire Peduzzi had earned by spading the hotel garden he got quite drunk. He saw the young gentleman coming down the path and spoke to him mysteriously. The young gentleman said he had not eaten but would be ready to go as soon as lunch was finished. Forty minutes or an hour.
佩杜齐靠在旅馆花园里铲土挣的四里拉把自己喝醉了。他看见那位年轻绅士走下小路，神秘地跟他搭话。那位年轻绅士说他还没吃饭，但午饭一结束就可以走。四十分钟或一小时。
At the cantina near the bridge they trusted him for three more grappas because he was so confident and mysterious about his job for the afternoon. It was a windy day with the sun coming out from behind the clouds and then going under in sprinkles of rain. A wonderful day for trout fishing.
在桥附近的酒馆里，他们又让他赊账三杯 grappa，因为他对下午的工作显得那么自信又神秘。那天刮着风，太阳时而从云后露出，时而又在零星细雨中隐去。钓鳟鱼的美好日子。
The young gentleman came out of the hotel and asked him about the rods. Should his wife come behind with the rods? ‘Yes,’ said Peduzzi, ‘let her follow us.’ The young gentleman went back into the hotel and spoke to his wife. He and Peduzzi started down the road. The young gentleman had a musette over his shoulder. Peduzzi saw the wife, who looked as young as the young gentleman, and was wearing mountain boots and a blue beret, start out to follow them down the road, carrying the fishing rods, unjointed, one in each hand. Peduzzi didn’t like her to be way back there. ‘Signorina,’ he called, winking at the young gentleman, ‘come up here and walk with us. Signora, come up here. Let us all walk
那位年轻绅士从旅馆出来，问他关于鱼竿的事。要他妻子拿着鱼竿跟在后面吗？“是的，”佩杜齐说，“让她跟着我们。”年轻绅士回到旅馆去同妻子说话。他和佩杜齐沿路走下去。年轻绅士肩上挎着一个小包。佩杜齐看见那位看起来和年轻绅士一样年轻的夫人，穿着山地靴，戴着蓝色贝雷帽，开始提着未接的鱼竿跟在他们后面走，每只手各拿一根。佩杜齐不喜欢她在那样远的地方。“Signorina，”他喊道，向那位年轻绅士眨眼，“上来这儿，和我们一起走。Signora，上来这儿。让我们都一起走
together.’ Peduzzi wanted them all three to walk down the street of Cortina together.
一起走吧。”佩杜齐想让他们三个人一起沿着科尔蒂纳的大街走下去。
The wife stayed behind, following rather sullenly. ‘Signorina,’ Peduzzi called tenderly, ‘come up here with us.’ The young gentleman looked back and shouted something. The wife stopped lagging behind and walked up.
妻子落在后面，神色有些阴郁地跟着。佩杜齐温柔地喊道：“Signorina，和我们一起来这儿吧。”那位年轻绅士回头大声喊了什么。妻子不再落后，走上前去。
Everyone they met walking through the main street of the town Peduzzi greeted elaborately. Buon’ di, Arturo! Tipping his hat. The bank clerk stared at him from the door of the Fascist café. Groups of three and four people standing in front of the shops stared at the three. The workmen in their stone-powdered jackets working on the foundations of the new hotel looked up as they passed. Nobody spoke or gave any sign to them except the town beggar, lean and old, with a spittle-thickened beard, who lifted his hat as they passed.
他们沿镇上的主街走时，佩杜齐遇到的每一个人都被他隆重地招呼。Buon’ di，Arturo！他掠下一下帽子。银行的书记员从法西斯咖啡馆的门口盯着他看。成群的三五个人站在商店门前也盯着这三人看。正在为新旅馆打地基、衣服上沾满石粉的工人们抬头看了他们一眼。除了镇上的乞丐——瘦削而年老，胡须因唾沫而结厚——在他们经过时抬起帽子外，没有人和他们说话或有任何表示。
Peduzzi stopped in front of a store with the window full of bottles and brought his empty grappa bottle from an inside pocket of his old military coat. ‘A little to drink, some marsala for the Signora, something, something to drink.’ He gestured with the bottle. It was a wonderful day. 'Marsala, you like marsala, Signorina? A little marsala?’
佩杜齐在一家橱窗里摆满瓶子的商店前停下，从他那件旧军大衣的内袋里掏出空的格拉帕酒瓶。“来点儿喝的，给 Signora 来点马萨拉，什么的，来点儿喝的。”他一面用瓶子比划。天气极好。“马萨拉，你喜欢马萨拉吗，Signorina？来点马萨拉吗？”
The wife stood sullenly. ‘You’ll have to play up to this,’ she said. ‘I can’t understand a word he says. He’s drunk, isn’t he?’
妻子闷闷不乐地站着。“你得配合一下，”她说。“我一句也听不懂。他是不是喝醉了？”
The young gentleman appeared not to hear Peduzzi. He was thinking, what in hell makes him say marsala? That’s what Max Beerbohm drinks.
那位年轻绅士似乎没听见佩杜齐。他在想，见鬼的，是什么让他说 marsala？那是 Max Beerbohm 喝的。
‘Geld,’ Peduzzi said finally, taking hold of the young gentleman’s sleeve. ‘Lire.’ He smiled, reluctant to press the subject but needing to bring the young gentleman into action.
“Geld，”佩杜齐终于说，抓住年轻绅士的袖子。“Lire。”他笑了，虽然不愿再追问，但需要把这位年轻绅士催促起来。
The young gentleman took out his pocketbook and gave him a ten-lira note. Peduzzi went up the steps to the door of the Specialty of Domestic and Foreign Wines shop. It was locked.
那位年轻绅士掏出钱包，给了他一张十里拉的票据。佩杜齐上了台阶，来到 Domestic and Foreign Wines Specialty 店的门前。门锁着。
‘It is closed until two,’ someone passing in the street said scornfully. Peduzzi came down the steps. He felt hurt. ‘Never mind,’ he said, ‘we can get it at the Concordia.’
“外面有人嘲讽地说：‘关到两点。’佩杜齐下了台阶，感到受了伤害。‘没关系，’他说，‘我们可以到 Concordia 去。’
They walked down the road to the Concordia three abreast. On the porch of the Concordia, where the rusty bobsleds were stacked, the young gentleman said, ‘Was wollen sie?’ Peduzzi handed him the ten-lira note folded over and over. ‘Nothing,’ he said, ‘anything.’ He was embarrassed. ‘Marsala, maybe. I don’t know. Marsala?’
他们并排三人走到 Concordia。Concordia 门廊上锈迹斑斑的雪橇堆着，年轻绅士说：‘Was wollen sie?’ 佩杜齐把那张折来折去的十里拉纸币递给他。‘无所谓，’他说，‘随便。’他有些窘迫。‘也许来瓶马沙拉酒。我不知道。马沙拉酒？’
The door of the Concordia shut on the young gentleman and the wife. ‘Three marsalas,’ said the young gentleman to the girl behind the pastry counter. ‘Two, you mean?’ she asked. ‘No,’ he said, ‘one for a vecchio.’ ‘Oh,’ she said, ‘a vecchio,’ and laughed, getting down the bottle. She poured out the three muddy looking drinks into three glasses. The wife was sitting at a table under the line of newspapers on sticks. The young gentleman put one of the marsalas in front of her. ‘You might as well drink it,’ he said, ‘maybe it’ll make you feel better.’ She sat and looked at the glass. The young gentleman went outside the door with a glass for Peduzzi but could not see him.
Concordia 的门把年轻绅士和妻子关在了里面。年轻绅士对糕点柜台后面的女孩说：‘三杯马沙拉。’‘你是说两杯吗？’她问。‘不，’他说，‘一杯给个老头。’‘哦，’她说，‘一个老头，’笑着拿下了那瓶酒。她把那三杯浑浊的酒分别倒进三只玻璃杯里。妻子坐在一排插着报纸的杆子下的一张桌旁。年轻绅士把其中一杯马沙拉放到她面前。‘你干脆喝了吧，’他说，‘也许会让你感觉好点。’她坐着看着杯子。年轻绅士端着一杯走到门外给佩杜齐，但看不见他。”
‘I don’t know where he is,’ he said, coming back into the pastry room carrying the glass.
“我不知道他在哪儿，”他说着，端着玻璃回到糕点房。
‘He wanted a quart of it,’ said the wife.
“他要了一夸脱，”妻子说。
‘How much is a quarter litre?’ the young gentleman asked the girl.
“四分之一升是多少？”那位年轻绅士问女孩。
‘Of the bianco? One lira.’
“白酒的吗？一里拉。”
‘No, of the marsala. Put these two in, too,’ he said, giving her his own glass and the one poured for Peduzzi. She filled the quarter litre wine measure with a funnel. ‘A bottle to carry it,’ said the young gentleman.
“不，是马沙拉酒。也把这两杯也放进去，”他说着，把自己的杯子和为 Peduzzi 倒的那杯递给她。她用漏斗把那一刻升的酒量倒满。“带个瓶子装着，”那位年轻绅士说。
She went to hunt for a bottle. It all amused her.
她去找瓶子去了。这一切都让她觉得好笑。
‘I’m sorry you feel so rotten, Tiny,’ he said. ‘I’m sorry I talked the way I did at lunch. We were both getting at the same thing from different angles.’
“可怜你觉得这么糟，Tiny，”他说。“抱歉午饭时我那样说话。我们其实都在从不同的角度谈同一件事。”
‘It doesn’t make any difference,’ she said. ‘None of it makes any difference.’
“没关系的，”她说。“这些都无关紧要。”
‘Are you too cold?’ he asked. ‘I wish you’d worn another sweater.’
“你冷吗？”他问。“我真希望你换件毛衣。”
‘I’ve got on three sweaters.’
“我已经穿了三件毛衣了。”
The girl came in with a very slim brown bottle and poured the marsala into it. The young gentleman paid five lire more. They went out the door. The girl was amused. Peduzzi was walking up and down at the other end out of the wind and holding the rods.
女孩端进来一只很瘦的棕色瓶子，把马萨拉酒倒进去。那位年轻绅士又多付了五里拉。他们走出门去。女孩觉得好笑。佩杜齐在另一端来回走着，躲在无风处，手里拿着鱼竿。
‘Come on,’ he said, ‘I will carry the rods. What difference does it make if anybody sees them? No one will trouble us. No one will make any trouble for me in Cortina. I know them at the municipio. I have been a soldier. Everybody in this town likes me. I sell frogs. What if it is forbidden to fish? Not a thing. Nothing. No trouble. Big trout, I tell you. Lots of them.’
“来吧，”他说，“我来拿鱼竿。有人看见又怎样？不会有人来找麻烦的。科尔蒂纳不会有人对我出手的。我在市政厅的人都认识我。我当过兵。这个镇上的人都喜欢我。我卖青蛙。就算捕鱼被禁止又怎样？一点事都没有。没麻烦。大鳟鱼，我跟你说。很多的。”
They were walking down the hill toward the river. The town
他们正沿着小路往河边走去。镇上
was in back of them. The sun had gone under and it was sprinkling rain. ‘There,’ said Peduzzi, pointing to a girl in the doorway of a house they passed. ‘My daughter.’
在他们身后。太阳已经落下，开始下着小雨。 “在那里，”佩杜齐说着，指向他们经过的一所房子门口的一个女孩。 “我的女儿。”
‘His doctor,’ the wife said, ‘has he got to show us his doctor?’
“他的医生，”妻子说，“他非得让我们看看他的医生吗？”
‘He said his daughter,’ said the young gentleman.
“他说的是他女儿，”年轻绅士说。
The girl went into the house as Peduzzi pointed.
女孩按照佩杜齐指的走进了屋子。
They walked down the hill across the fields and then turned to follow the river bank. Peduzzi talked rapidly with much winking and knowingness. As they walked three abreast the wife caught his breath across the wind. Once he nudged her in the ribs. Part of the time he talked in d’Ampezzo dialect and sometimes in Tyroler German dialect. He could not make out which the young gentleman and his wife understood the best so he was being bilingual. But as the young gentleman said, Ja, Ja, Peduzzi decided to talk altogether in Tyroler. The young gentleman and the wife understood nothing.
他们沿着田地下山，然后转向顺着河岸走。佩杜齐说话很快，频频眨眼，显得很会打探情况。他们并排行走时，妻子迎着风吸入他的气息。有一次他用肘轻推了她的肋骨。有时候他用安佩佐方言说话，有时候用提洛尔德语方言。他搞不清这位年轻绅士和他的妻子更能听懂哪一种，所以便两种语言都说。但当年轻绅士说了 Ja，Ja 以后，佩杜齐决定干脆全用提洛尔语说。年轻绅士和妻子一句也听不懂。
‘Everybody in the town saw us going through with these rods. We’re probably being followed by the game police now. I wish we weren’t in on this damn thing. This damned old fool is so drunk, too.’
“镇上每个人都看到我们拿着这些杆子过去了。现在大概有猎物巡警在跟着我们。我真希望我们没掺和进这该死的事。这该死的老傻瓜还喝得醉醺醺的。”
‘Of course you haven’t got the guts to just go back,’ said the wife. ‘Of course you have to go on.’
“你当然没有胆子就这么回去，”妻子说。“你当然得继续走下去。”
‘Why don’t you go back? Go on back, Tiny.’
“你为什么不回去？回去吧，Tiny。”
‘I’m going to stay with you. If you go to jail we might as well both go.’
“我要和你一起留下。如果你要进监狱，那我们就一起进。”
They turned sharp down the bank and Peduzzi stood, his coat blowing in the wind, gesturing at the river. It was brown and muddy. Off on the right there was a dump heap.
他们猛然向河岸下转，佩杜齐站着，外套在风中飘动，朝河比划。河水又褐又浑。在右边有一处垃圾堆。
‘Say it to me in Italian,’ said the young gentleman.
“用意大利语对我说，”那位年轻绅士说。
‘Un’ mezz’ ora. Piu d’ un’ mezz’ ora.’
“Un’ mezz’ ora. Piu d’ un’ mezz’ ora.”
‘He says it’s at least a half-hour more. Go on back, Tiny. You’re cold in this wind anyway. It’s a rotten day and we aren’t going to have any fun, anyway.’
“他说至少还要半个小时。回去吧，Tiny。你在这风里会冷的。天气糟透了，反正我们也不会有什么乐趣。”
‘All right,’ she said, and climbed up the grassy bank.
“好吧，”她说着，爬上了长满草的河堤。
Peduzzi was down at the river and did not notice her till she was almost out of sight over the crest. ‘Frau!’ he shouted. ‘Frau! Fräulein! You’re not going.’
Peduzzi 在河边，直到她几乎越过堤顶消失才注意到她。“Frau！”他喊道。“Frau！Fräulein！你不能走。”
She went on over the crest of the hill.
她越过山脊走了下去。
‘She’s gone!’ said Peduzzi. It shocked him.
“她走了！”佩杜齐说。他感到很震惊。
He took off the rubber bands that held the rod segments together and commenced to joint up one of the rods.
他解下把杆节连在一起的橡皮圈，开始把其中一根杆子接好。
‘But you said it was half an hour farther.’
“可你说过还要半小时才到啊。”
‘Oh, yes. It is good half an hour down. It is good here, too.’
“哦，是的。往下走半小时多一点很好。这里也很好。”
‘Really?’
“真的吗？”
‘Of course. It is good here and good there, too.’
“当然。这里好，那里也好。”
The young gentleman sat down on the bank and jointed up a rod, put on the reel and threaded the line through the guides. He felt uncomfortable and afraid that any minute a gamekeeper or a posse of citizens would come over the bank from the town. He could see the houses of the town and the campanile over the edge of the hill. He opened his leader box. Peduzzi leaned over and dug his flat, hard thumb and forefinger in and tangled the moistened leaders.
年轻人坐在河岸上，接上鱼竿，装上卷线器，把钓线穿过导环。他感到不自在，害怕随时会有猎场看守或一群市民从镇上翻过河岸过来。他能看到镇上的房屋和山边的钟楼。他打开了领线盒。佩杜齐俯身，用他那扁平而粗糙的拇指和食指掏进去，把湿漉漉的领线弄得缠在一起。
‘Have you some lead?’
“你有铅子吗？”
‘No.’
“没有。”
‘You must have some lead.’ Peduzzi was excited. ‘You must have piombo. Piombo. A little piombo. Just here. Just above the hook or your bait will float on the water. You must have it. Just a little piombo.’
“你一定要有铅子。”佩杜齐激动地说。“你必须有 piombo。Piombo。一点点 piombo。就在这里。就在钩子上面，否则你的饵会漂在水面上。你必须有。就一点点 piombo。”
‘Have you got some?’
“你有吗？”
‘No.’ He looked through his pockets desperately, sifting through the cloth dirt in the lining of his inside military pockets. ‘I haven’t any. We must have piombo.’
“不行。”他在口袋里拼命翻找，掏出内侧军用口袋里衬的布屑。“我没有。我们一定得有 piombo。”
‘We can’t fish then,’ said the young gentleman, and unjointed the rod, reeling the line back through the guides. ‘We’ll get some piombo and fish to-morrow.’
“那我们就不能钓鱼了，”那位年轻绅士说着，把鱼竿拆开，把鱼线从导环里一圈圈卷回去。“我们明天去弄些 piombo 再钓。”
