‘But listen, caro, you must have piombo. The line will lie flat on the water.’ Peduzzi’s day was going to pieces before his eyes. ‘You must have piombo. A little is enough. Your stuff is all clean and new but you have no lead. I would have brought some. You said you had everything.’
“不过听着，caro，你一定得有 piombo。线才会平放在水面上。”佩杜齐的一天在他眼前瓦解。“你一定得有 piombo。少量就够了。你的东西都干净崭新，可就是没有 lead。我本来会带一些。你说你什么都有。”
The young gentleman looked at the stream discoloured by the melting snow. ‘I know,’ he said, ‘we’ll get some piombo and fish to-morrow.’
那位年轻绅士看着被融雪染色的溪流。“我知道，”他说，“我们明天去弄些 piombo 再钓。”
‘At what hour in the morning? Tell me that.’
“早上几点？告诉我。”
‘At seven.’
“七点。”
The sun came out. It was warm and pleasant. The young gentleman felt relieved. He was no longer breaking the law. Sitting on
太阳出来了。天气温暖宜人。年轻绅士松了口气。他不再是在违法。坐在
the bank he took the bottle of marsala out of his pocket and passed it to Peduzzi. Peduzzi passed it back. The young gentleman took a drink of it and passed it to Peduzzi again. Peduzzi passed it back again. ‘Drink,’ he said, ‘drink. It’s your marsala.’ After another short drink the young gentleman handed the bottle over. Peduzzi had been watching it closely. He took the bottle very hurriedly and tipped it up. The grey hairs in the folds of his neck oscillated as he drank, his eyes fixed on the end of the narrow brown bottle. He drank it all. The sun shone while he drank. It was wonderful. This was a great day, after all. A wonderful day.
河岸上，他从口袋里掏出那瓶马萨拉酒递给佩杜齐。佩杜齐又递回来。年轻绅士喝了一口，又把瓶子递给佩杜齐。佩杜齐再次递回。“喝，”他说，“喝。是你的马萨拉酒。”又喝了一小口后，年轻绅士把瓶子递了过去。佩杜齐一直紧盯着它。他匆忙接过瓶子，把瓶口倾了起来。颈项褶皱里的鬓发在他喝酒时颤动着，他的眼睛盯着那细长褐色瓶子的瓶口。他把酒全喝光了。他喝酒的时候太阳照着。这真美好。毕竟这是个伟大的一天。美好的一天。
‘Senta, caro! In the morning at seven.’ He had called the young gentleman caro several times and nothing had happened. It was good marsala. His eyes glistened. Days like this stretched out ahead. It would begin at seven in the morning.
“‘Senta, caro！明天早上七点。’” 他叫了这位年轻先生好几次，可是没什么动静。那是上好的马萨拉酒。他的眼睛闪着光。像这样的日子在前面延展开来。明早七点就要开始。
They started to walk up the hill toward the town. The young gentleman went on ahead. He was quite a way up the hill. Peduzzi called to him.
他们开始朝山上小镇走去。那位年轻先生走在前头。他已经走到山坡相当高的地方。佩杜齐朝他喊了一声。
‘Listen, caro, can you let me take five lire for a favour?’
“‘听着，caro，你能不能让我收你五里拉，帮个忙？’”
‘For to-day?’ asked the young gentleman frowning.
“‘就今天的？’” 那位年轻先生皱着眉问。
‘No, not to-day. Give it to me to-day for to-morrow. I will provide everything for to-morrow. Pane, salami, formaggio, good stuff for all of us. You and I and the Signora. Bait for fishing, minnows, not worms only. Perhaps I can get some marsala. All for five lire. Five lire for a favour.’
“不是今天。今天给我，为明天准备。我会为明天准备一切。Pane，salami，formaggio，对我们大家都好的东西。你和我还有女士。钓饵，小鱼，不只是蚯蚓。也许我能弄到一些 marsala。五里拉就行。为了一件恩惠，五里拉。”
The young gentleman looked through his pocketbook and took out a two-lira note and two ones.
那位年轻绅士翻开钱包，掏出一张两里拉的钞票和两张一里拉的。
‘Thank you, caro. Thank you,’ said Peduzzi, in the tone of one member of the Cariton Club accepting the Morning Post from another. This was living. He was through with the hotel garden, breaking up frozen manure with a dung fork. Life was opening out.
“谢谢，caro。谢谢，”Peduzzi 用一种卡里顿俱乐部会员互递 Morning Post 时的口吻说道。这才叫生活。他不再在旅馆花园里用粪叉翻弄冻硬的粪便了。生活正在展开。
‘Until seven o’clock then, caro,’ he said, slapping the young gentleman on the back. ‘Promptly at seven.’
“那好，七点见，caro，”他说着，拍了拍那位年轻绅士的背。“七点准时。”
‘I may not be going,’ said the young gentleman putting his purse back in his pocket.
“我可能不去了，”年轻绅士说着把钱包放回口袋。
‘What,’ said Peduzzi, ‘I will have minnows, Signor. Salami, everything. You and I and the Signora. The three of us.’
“什么，”佩杜齐说，“我要小鱼，先生。萨拉米香肠，所有的东西。你我还有夫人。我们三个人。”
‘I may not be going,’ said the young gentleman, ‘very probably not. I will leave word with the padrone at the hotel office.’
“我可能不去了，”年轻绅士说，“很可能不去。我会在旅馆办公室把话留给掌柜的。”
If it happened right down close in front of you, you could see Villalta snarl at the bull and curse him, and when the bull charged he swung back firmly like an oak when the wind hits it, his legs tight together, the muleta trailing and the sword following the curve behind. Then he cursed the bull, flopped the muleta at him, and swung back from the charge, his feet firm, the muleta curving, and at each swing the crowd roaring.
如果这一幕就在你眼前，你能看见维亚尔塔对公牛咆哮并咒骂它，当公牛冲来时他像被风吹的橡树那样坚定地向后摆，双腿并拢，披帕拖在后面，剑沿着后方的弧线跟着。然后他又咒骂公牛，把披帕扑向它，从冲锋中再次后摆，双脚稳固，披帕弯曲，每一次挥动都引得人群怒吼。
When he started to kill it was all in the same rush. The bull looking at him straight in front, hating. He drew out the sword from the folds of the muleta and sighted with the same movement and called to the bull, Toro! Toro! and the bull charged and Villalta charged and just for a moment they became one. Villalta became one with the bull and then it was over. Villalta standing straight and the red hilt of the sword sticking out dully between the bull’s shoulders. Villalta, his hand up at the crowd and the bull roaring blood, looking straight at Villalta and his legs caving.
当他开始杀戮时，一切都在同一阵冲动中完成。公牛直直地盯着他，充满仇恨。他从红布（muleta）的褶子里抽出剑，随一个动作瞄准，并喊向公牛，Toro！Toro！公牛冲上来，维亚尔塔也冲上去，就在那一刻他们融为一体。维亚尔塔与公牛融为一体，然后就结束了。维亚尔塔直立着，剑的红色柄闷闷地从公牛肩间伸出。维亚尔塔举手向观众，公牛咆哮着喷血，直视着维亚尔塔，双腿塌陷。

CROSS-COUNTRY SNOW
越野滑雪

The funicular car bucked once more and then stopped. It could not go farther, the snow drifted solidly across the track. The gale scouring the exposed surface of the mountain had swept the snow surface into a wind-board crust. Nick, waxing his skis in the baggage car, pushed his boots into the toe irons and shut the clamp tight. He jumped from the car sideways on to the hard wind-board, made a jump turn and crouching and trailing his sticks slipped in a rush down the slope.
缆车又猛地一颠，然后停下。它无法再前进，雪堆牢牢地横在铁轨上。横扫山体暴露面的大风把雪面吹成了一层风板硬壳。尼克在行李车里给滑雪板打蜡，把靴子塞进鞋尖铁扣，夹紧卡子。他横向一跃离开车厢，落到坚硬的风板上，转一记跳转，蹲下并把滑雪杖拖在后面，迅速顺坡滑下。
On the white below George dipped and rose and dipped out of sight. The rush and the sudden swoop as he dropped down a steep undulation in the mountainside plucked Nick’s mind out and left him only the wonderful flying, dropping sensation in his body. He rose to a slight up-run and then the snow seemed to drop out from under him as he went down, down, faster and faster in a rush down the last, long steep slope. Crouching so he was almost sitting back on his skis, trying to keep the centre of gravity low, the snow driving like a sand-storm, he knew the pace was too much. But he held
在白雪上，George 一会儿俯冲一会儿又升起，然后俯冲出视线。他沿山坡一个陡起陡落下落时的猛冲和突然俯冲，把 Nick 的思绪拽走，只剩下身体里那种美妙的飞翔、下坠的感觉。他上升到一个小的上坡，然后雪仿佛在他脚下消失，他一下又往下、往下，以越来越快的速度冲下最后那段长而陡的斜坡。半蹲着几乎像坐在滑雪板上一样，试图把重心放低，雪像沙暴一样扑打着，他知道速度太快了。但他坚持着。
it. He would not let go and spill. Then a patch of soft snow, left in a hollow by the wind, spilled him and he went over and over in a clashing of skis, feeling like a shot rabbit, then stuck, his legs crossed, his skis sticking straight up and his nose and ears jammed full of snow.
他不肯放手让自己摔倒。然后一块被风吹在洼处的松软雪把他掀翻了，他翻来覆去，滑雪板撞击作响，感觉像只被射中的兔子，最后卡住了，双腿交叉，滑雪板笔直朝上，他的鼻子和耳朵都塞满了雪。
George stood a little farther down the slope, knocking the snow from his wind jacket with big slaps.
George 站在坡下稍远的地方，用大力拍打着风衣把雪拍掉。
‘You took a beauty, Mike,’ he called to Nick. ‘That’s lousy soft snow. It bagged me the same way.’
“你抓住了个好线路，Mike，”他冲 Nick 叫道，“那雪糟透了。它也把我给整包了。”
‘What’s it like over the khud?’ Nick kicked his skis around as he lay on his back and stood up.
“河沟那边怎么样？”尼克躺着用脚一蹬把滑雪板转过来，然后站起来。
‘You’ve got to keep to your left. It’s a good fast drop with a Christy at the bottom on account of a fence.’
“你得靠左走。那段是个又快又陡的下坡，底下有个 Christy 动作，要注意，那里有栅栏。”
‘Wait a sec and we’ll take it together.’
“等一下，我们一起下。”
‘No, you come on and go first. I like to see you take the khuds.’
“不，你先去吧。我要看你怎么下这些沟坎。”
Nick Adams came up past George, big back and blond head still faintly snowy, then his skis started slipping at the edge and he swooped down, hissing in the crystalline powder snow and seeming to float up and down as he went up and down the billowing khuds. He held to his left at the end, as he rushed toward the fence, keeping his knees locked tight together and turning his body like tightening a screw brought his skis sharply around to the right in a smother of snow and slowed into a loss of speed parallel to the hillside and the wire fence.
尼克·亚当斯从乔治身旁上来，宽阔的背和金色的头发上仍带着淡淡的雪痕，然后他的滑雪板在边缘开始打滑，他俯冲下去，在结晶般的粉雪中嘶嘶作响，似乎在起伏的 khuds（丘陵）上来回漂浮。他在尽头向左保持，当他冲向栅栏时，膝盖紧紧并拢，身体像拧螺丝一样转动，使滑雪板在一阵雪雾中骤然向右回转，速度降下来，变成与山坡和铁丝栅栏平行的滑行。
He looked up the hill. George was coming down in telemark position, kneeling; one leg forward and bent, the other trailing; his sticks hanging like some insect’s thin legs, kicking up puffs of snow as they touched the surface and finally the whole kneeling, trailing figure coming around in a beautiful right curve, crouching, the legs shot forward and back, the body leaning out against the swing, the sticks accenting the curve like points of light, all in a wild cloud of snow.
他向上看去。乔治以 telemark 姿势下滑，跪着；一条腿向前弯曲，另一条拖在后面；他的杖像某种昆虫的细腿一样垂着，触及雪面时掀起一阵阵雪雾，最终整个跪着、拖着的身影在一个优美的右弯中转过，蹲着，双腿向前后伸展，身体向外倾以抵住摆动，滑杖如光点般强调着曲线，所有这些都在一片狂野的雪云中。
‘I was afraid to Christy,’ George said, ‘the snow was too deep. You made a beauty.’
“我当时吓坏了，Christy，”乔治说，“雪太深了。你滑得真漂亮。”
‘I can’t telemark with my leg,’ Nick said.
“我的腿滑不了 telemark，”尼克说。
Nick held down the top strand of the wire fence with his ski and George slid over. Nick followed him down the road. They thrust bent-kneed along the road into a pine forest. The road became
尼克用滑雪板压住铁丝网的上端，乔治滑了过去。尼克跟着他沿着路下去。他们弯着膝沿着路向一片松林推行。路变成
polished ice, stained orange and a tobacco yellow from the teams hauling logs. The skiers kept to the stretch of snow along the side. The road dipped sharply to a stream and then ran straight up-hill. Through the woods they could see a long, low-eaved, weatherbeaten building. Through the trees it was a faded yellow. Closer the window frames were painted green. The paint was peeling. Nick knocked his clamps loose with one of his ski sticks and kicked off the skis.
抛光的冰，被运木队留下的橙色和烟草黄染色。滑雪者都走在路边的一段积雪上。路急剧下降到一条小溪，然后又直直地上坡。透过树林他们看见一栋低矮檐口、饱经风霜的建筑。透过树木它是褪色的黄色。靠近时窗框被漆成了绿色。油漆正在剥落。尼克用一根滑雪杖把固定器敲松，踢掉滑雪板。
‘We might as well carry them up there,’ he said.
“我们还是把它们扛上去吧，”他说。
He climbed the steep road with the skis on his shoulder, kicking his heel nails into the icy footing. He heard George breathing and kicking in his heels just behind him. They stacked the skis against the side of the inn and slapped the snow off each other’s trousers, stamped their boots clean, and went in.
他把滑雪板扛在肩上爬上陡峭的路，用后跟蹬进冰冷的路面。他听到乔治就在身后喘气并用后跟蹬地。他们把滑雪板靠在旅馆侧墙，拍掉彼此裤子上的雪，跺干净靴子，然后走了进去。
Inside it was quite dark. A big porcelain stove shone in the corner of the room. There was a low ceiling. Smooth benches back of dark, wine-stained tables were along each side of the rooms. Two Swiss sat over their pipes and two decies of cloudy new wine next to the stove. The boys took off their jackets and sat against the wall on the other side of the stove. A voice in the next room stopped singing and a girl in a blue apron came in through the door to see what they wanted to drink.
里面相当黑。角落里有一只大的瓷制火炉在发光。天花板很低。两侧房间里靠墙放着光滑的长凳，背靠着被酒渍弄暗的桌子。炉子旁坐着两个叼着烟斗的瑞士人，面前放着两杯浑浊的新酒。男孩们脱下外套，靠着炉子另一侧的墙坐下。隔壁房间里有人唱的歌声停了，一个围着蓝色围裙的女孩从门里进来，想看看他们想喝什么。
‘A bottle of Sion,’ Nick said. ‘Is that all right, Gidge?’
“来一瓶 Sion，”Nick 说。“可以吗，Gidge？”
‘Sure,’ said George. ‘You know more about wine than I do. I like any of it.’
“当然，”George 说。“你比我更懂酒。我什么都能喝。”
The girl went out.
女孩走了出去。
‘There’s nothing really can touch skiing, is there?’ Nick said. ‘The way it feels when you first drop off on a long run.’
“滑雪真是无可比拟，不是吗？”尼克说。“第一次从高处长坡起滑的感觉。”
‘Huh,’ said George. ‘It’s too swell to talk about.’
“哼，”乔治说。“好得无法用言语形容。”
The girl brought the wine in and they had trouble with the cork. Nick finally opened it. The girl went out and they heard her singing in German in the next room.
女孩端来酒来，他们塞子开了半天。最后是尼克把它拧开。女孩走出去，他们听见她在隔壁房间用德语唱歌。
"Those specks of cork in it don’t matter,’ said Nick.
“酒里那些小小的塞屑无所谓，”尼克说。
‘I wonder if she’s got any cake.’
“我想知道她有没有蛋糕。”
‘Let’s find out.’
“去看看吧。”
The girl came in and Nick noticed that her apron covered swellingly her pregnancy. I wonder why I didn’t see that when she first came in, he thought.
女孩走了进来，尼克注意到她的围裙把怀孕的肚子包得鼓鼓的。他心想：我不知道为什么她刚来时我没看出来。
‘What were you singing?’ he asked her.
“你刚才在唱什么？”他问她。
‘Opera, German opera.’ She did not care to discuss the subject. ‘We have some apple strudel if you want it.’
“歌剧，德语歌剧。”她不想讨论这个话题。“如果你们想要的话，我们有苹果卷。”
‘She isn’t so cordial, is she?’ said George.
“她不太热情，是吧？”乔治说。
‘Oh, well. She doesn’t know us and she thought we were going to kid her about her singing, maybe. She’s from up where they speak German probably and she’s touchy about being here, and then she’s got that baby coming without being married and she’s touchy.’
“哦，也许吧。她不认识我们，她以为我们会取笑她的唱歌。她可能来自讲德语的地方，对于待在这里很敏感，而且她还未婚就怀了孩子，这也让她敏感。”
‘How do you know she isn’t married?’
“你怎么知道她没结婚？”
‘No ring. Hell, no girls get married around here till they’re knocked up.’
“没有订婚戒指。见鬼，这里没有女孩结婚，除非她们先怀孕。”
The door came open and a gang of woodcutters from up the road came in, stamping their boots and steaming in the room. The waitress brought in three litres of new wine for the gang and they sat at the two tables, smoking and quiet, with their hats off, leaning back against the wall or forward on the table. Outside the horses on the wood sledges made an occasional sharp jangle of bells as they tossed their heads.
门开了，一帮上游来的伐木工人进来，踏着靴子把热气带进房间。女招待端来三升新酒给那群人，他们坐在两张桌子旁，抽着烟，安静着，摘着帽子，有的人靠在墙上往后仰，有的人趴在桌子上往前倾。外面，拉着木雪橇的马偶尔甩头，铃铛发出尖锐的叮当声。
George and Nick were happy. They were fond of each other. They knew they had the run back home ahead of them.
乔治和尼克很高兴。他们彼此喜爱。他们知道回家的路还在前面等着他们。
‘When have you got to go back to school?’ Nick asked.
“你什么时候得回学校？”尼克问。
‘To-night,’ George answered. ‘I’ve got to get the ten-forty from Montreux.’
“今晚，”乔治回答。“我得赶十点四十分从蒙特勒出发的车。”
‘I wish you could stick over and we could do the Dent du Lys to-morrow.’
“我真希望你能多待一晚，明天我们可以去爬莱斯峰（Dent du Lys）。”
‘I got to get educated,’ George said. ‘Gee, Mike, don’t you wish we could just bum together? Take our skis and go on the train to where there was good running and then go on and put up at pubs and go right across the Oberland and up the Valais and all through the Engadine and just take repair kit and extra sweaters and pyjamas in our rucksacks and not give a damn about school or anything.’
“我得去受教育，”乔治说。“天哪，迈克，你难道不希望我们能混日子一起流浪吗？背上滑雪板，坐火车去雪道好的地方，然后继续住客栈，一路穿过奥伯兰，翻越瓦莱，横越整个恩加丁，背包里只带修理工具、多一套毛衣和睡衣，根本不管学校什么的。”
‘Yes, and go through the Schwarzwald that way. Gee, the swell places.’
“是啊，也那样穿过黑森林（Schwarzwald）。天哪，真是太棒的地方了。”
‘That’s where you went fishing last summer, isn’t it?’
“那就是你去年夏天去钓鱼的地方，不是吗？”
‘Yes.’
“是的。”
They ate the strudel and drank the rest of the wine.
他们吃完了千层酥，喝光了余下的酒。
George leaned back against the wall and shut his eyes.
乔治靠着墙往后靠，闭上了眼睛。
‘Wine always makes me feel this way,’ he said.
“酒总是让我有这种感觉，”他说。
‘Feel bad?’ Nick asked.
“感觉糟糕？”尼克问。
‘No. I feel good, but funny.’
“不。感觉不错，只是奇怪。”
‘I know,’ Nick said.
“我知道，”尼克说。
‘Sure,’ said George.
“当然，”乔治说。
‘Should we have another bottle?’ Nick asked.
“我们再来一瓶吗？”尼克问。
‘Not for me,’ George said.
“我不来，”乔治说。
They sat there, Nick leaning his elbows on the table, George slumped back against the wall.
他们坐在那里，尼克肘子撑在桌上，乔治靠着墙瘫着。
‘Is Helen going to have a baby?’ George said, coming down to the table from the wall.
“海伦要生孩子了吗？”乔治一边从墙边走到桌旁一边说。
‘Yes.’
“是的。”
‘When ?’
“什么时候？”
‘Late next summer.’
“明年夏末。”
‘Are you glad?’
“你高兴吗？”
‘Yes. Now.’
“是的。现在高兴。”
‘Will you go back to the States?’
“你会回美国吗？”
‘I guess so.’
“我想会吧。”
‘Do you want to?’
“你想吗？”
‘No.’
“不要。”
‘Does Helen?’
“海伦想吗？”
‘No.’
“不要。”
George sat silent. He looked at the empty bottle and the empty glasses.
乔治默默坐着。他看着空瓶子和空杯子。
‘It’s hell, isn’t it?’ he said.
“这简直是地狱，不是吗？”他说。
‘No. Not exactly,’ Nick said.
“不。并不完全是，”尼克说。
‘Why not?’
“为什么不？”
‘I don’t know,’ Nick said.
“我不知道，”尼克说。
‘Will you ever go skiing together in the States?’ George said.
“你们将来会在美国一起去滑雪吗？”乔治说。
‘I don’t know,’ said Nick.
“我不知道，”尼克说。
‘The mountains aren’t much,’ George said.
“那些山不怎么样，”乔治说。
‘No,’ said Nick. ‘They’re too rocky. There’s too much timber and they’re too far away.’
“不，”Nick 说。“那儿太多岩石。树木太多，而且离得太远。”
‘Yes,’ said George, ‘that’s the way it is in California.’
“是啊，”George 说，“在加利福尼亚就是这样。”
‘Yes,’ Nick said, ‘that’s the way it is everywhere I’ve ever been.’
“是啊，”Nick 说，“我去过的任何地方都是这样。”
‘Yes,’ said George, ‘that’s the way it is.’
“是啊，”George 说，“就是这样。”
The Swiss got up and paid and went out.
瑞士人起身付了钱然后出去。
‘I wish we were Swiss,’ George said.
“但愿我们是瑞士人，”乔治说。
‘They’ve all got goitre,’ said Nick.
“他们都有甲状腺肿，”尼克说。
‘I don’t believe it,’ George said.
“我不相信，”乔治说。
‘Neither do I,’ said Nick.
“我也不想，”尼克说。
They laughed.
他们笑了。
‘Maybe we’ll never go skiing again, Nick,’ George said.
“也许我们再也不会去滑雪了，尼克，”乔治说。
‘We’ve got to,’ said Nick .‘It isn’t worth while if you can’t.’
“我们得去，”尼克说。“如果不能去就不值得去。”
‘We’ll go, all right,’ George said.
“我们会去的，”乔治说。
‘We’ve got to,’ Nick agreed.
“我们必须去，”尼克同意道。
‘I wish we could make a promise about it,’ George said.
“要是我们能就此做个承诺就好了，”乔治说。
Nick stood up. He buckled his wind jacket tight. He leaned over George and picked up the two ski poles from against the wall. He stuck one of the ski poles into the floor.
尼克站起来，把风衣扣紧。他俯身从墙边拿起两根滑雪杖，把一根插进地板里。
‘There isn’t any good in promising,’ he said.
“答应没有什么好处，”他说。
They opened the door and went out. It was very cold. The snow had crusted hard. The road ran up the hill into the pine trees.
他们开了门走了出去。天很冷。雪已经结成了硬壳。路沿着山坡延伸进松林。
They took down their skis from where they leaned against the wall of the inn. Nick put on his gloves. George was already started up the road, his skis on his shoulder. Now they would have the run home together.
他们把滑雪板从靠在客栈墙边的地方取了下来。Nick 戴上手套。George 已经扛着滑雪板朝路上走去了。现在他们将一起滑回家。
I heard the drums coming down the street and then the fifes and the pipes and then they came around the corner, all dancing. The street was full of them. Maera saw him and then I saw him. When they stopped the music for the crouch he hunched down in the street with them all and when they started it again he jumped up and went dancing down the street with them. He was drunk all right.
我听到鼓声沿着街道传来，随后是短笛和风笛，然后他们绕过拐角出现了，大家都在跳舞。街上全是他们。Maera 看见了他，随后我也看见了。当他们为了蹲下这一段停下音乐时，他和他们一起在街上弯下身子；音乐再次响起时，他跳起来跟着他们一起沿街跳舞。他确实喝醉了。
You go down after him, said Maera, he hates me.
你去把他拉下去，玛埃拉说，他恨我。
So I went down and caught up with them and grabbed him while he was crouched down waiting for the music to break loose and said, Come on, Luis. For Christ’s sake you’ve got bulls this afternoon. He didn’t listen to me, he was listening so hard for the music to start.
所以我下去追上他们，抓住他，那时他蹲着等着音乐爆开，我说，过来吧，路易斯。看在上帝的份上，你今天下午还有公牛要斗。他没听我说话，他正绷紧耳朵等音乐开始。
I said, Don’t be a damn fool, Luis. Come on back to the hotel.
我说，别傻了，路易斯。快回旅馆去。
Then the music started up again and he jumped up and twisted away from me and started dancing. I grabbed his arm and he pulled loose and said, Oh leave me alone. You’re not my father.
这时音乐又响起来，他跳起来一扭身就要甩开我开始跳舞。我抓住他的胳膊，他挣脱了说，哦，别管我。你又不是我父亲。
I went back to the hotel and Maera was on the balcony looking out to see if I’d be bringing him back. He went inside when he saw me and came downstairs disgusted.
我回到旅馆，马埃拉站在阳台上向外看，想看我是否会把他带回来。他看到我就进去了，下来时满脸厌恶。
Well, I said, after all he’s just an ignorant Mexican savage.
“唉，”我说，“毕竟他不过是个无知的墨西哥野蛮人。”
Yes, Maera said, and who will kill his bulls after he gets a cornada?
“是啊，”马埃拉说，“他被牛角刺了以后谁来杀他的公牛？”
We, I suppose, I said.
“大概是我们吧，”我说。
Yes, we, said Maera. We kills the savagu bulls, and the drunkards’ bulls, and the riau-riau dancers’ bulls. Yes. We kill them. We kill them all right. Yes. Yes. Yes.
“是的，我们，”Maera 说。“我们杀那些野牛，也杀那些醉汉的牛，还有 riau-riau 舞者的牛。是的。我们杀它们。我们都把它们杀掉。是的。是的。是的。”

MY OLD MAN
我的老头

I guess looking at it, now, my old man was cut out for a fat guy, one of those regular little roly fat guys you see around, but he sure never got that way, except a little toward the last, and then it wasn’t his fault, he was riding over the jumps only and he could afford to carry plenty of weight then. I remember the way he’d pull on a rubber shirt over a couple of jerseys and a big sweat shirt over that, and get me to run with him in the forenoon in the hot sun. He’d have, maybe, taken a trial trip with one of Razzo’s skins early in the
我想现在回想起来，我老头天生就该是个胖子，那种你到处都能见到的圆滚滚的小胖子，但他一辈子几乎没变成那样，只有在晚年才稍微发福一点，那也不是他的错，那时他只在跳台上骑马，能承受得起多带点儿重量。我记得他会把一件橡胶汗衫套在两件羊毛衫外面，再在外面套一件大号运动衫，然后让我在上午烈日下跟他一起跑步。他大概早年会跟 Razzo（音）家的某匹马皮先试驾一趟。
morning after just getting in from Torino at four o’clock in the morning and beating it out to the stables in a cab and then with the dew all over everything and the sun just starting to get going, I’d help him pull off his boots and he’d get into a pair of sneakers and all these sweaters and we’d start out.
在都灵凌晨四点刚到，匆匆打车赶到马厩，随后在露水遍布万物、太阳刚刚升起的时候，我会帮他脱下靴子，他换上运动鞋，套上这些毛衣，然后我们就出发了。
‘Come on, kid,’ he’d say, stepping up and down on his toes in front of the jocks’ dressing-room, ‘let’s get moving.’
“来吧，孩子，”他会说，踮着脚在运动员更衣室门前前后跳，“咱们动起来。”
Then we’d start off jogging around the infield once, maybe, with him ahead, running nice, and then turn out the gate and along one of those roads with all the trees along the sides of them that run out from San Siro. I’d go ahead of him when we hit the road and I could run pretty good and I’d look around and he’d be jogging easy just behind me and after a little while I’d look around again and he’d begun to sweat. Sweating heavy and he’d just be dogging it along with his eyes on my back, but when he’d catch me looking at him he’d grin and say, ‘Sweating plenty?’ When my old man grinned, nobody could help but grin too. We’d keep right on running out toward the mountains and then my old man would yell, ‘Hey, Joe!’ and I’d look back and he’d be sitting under a tree with a towel he’d had wrapped around his waist wrapped around his neck.
然后我们会开始绕内场小跑一圈，可能是这样，他在前面，跑得挺好，然后出门沿着一条从圣西罗伸出的、两旁种满树的路跑去。上了路我就会跑在他前面，当时我跑得还不错，我会回头看，他就在我后面轻松地慢跑，过了一会我又回头一看，他已经开始出汗了。汗大把大把地流，他只是慢吞吞地跟着，把眼睛盯着我的背，但当他发现我看着他时就会咧嘴笑着问：“出汗多吗？”我老爹一笑，谁也控制不住自己跟着笑。我们会一直跑向群山，然后我老爹会喊：“嘿，乔！”我一回头，他就坐在树下，腰上围着的毛巾现在搭在了脖子上。
I’d come back and sit down beside him and he’d pull a rope out of his pocket an art skipping rope out in the sun with the sweat pouring off his face and him skıpping rope out in the white dust with the rope going cloppetty, cloppetty, clop, clop, clop, and the sun hotter, and him working harder up and down a patch of the road. Say, it was a treat to see my old man skip rope, too. He could whirr it fast or lop it slow and fancy. Say, you ought to have seen wops look at us sometimes, when they’d come by, going into town walking along with big white steers hauling the cart. They sure looked as though they thought the old man was nuts. He’d start the rope whirring till they’d stop dead still and watch him, then give the steers a cluck and a poke with the goad and get going again.
我会回去坐在他旁边，他就从口袋里掏出一根绳子，在太阳下跳着花样跳绳，汗水顺着脸流，他在白色尘土里跳绳，绳子发出“咔嗒咔嗒、咔、咔、咔”的声音，太阳更烈，他更卖力地在路的一段来回跳。说实话，看我老爸跳绳也真是件赏心悦目的事。他能把绳子甩得很快，也能慢慢悠闲地花式跳。你该看看那些意大利佬有时候经过我们时看我们的样子，他们拉着装满大白牛的车往城里走。看起来他们真觉得我老头儿疯了。他会把绳子甩得嗡嗡响，直到他们停在那儿盯着看，然后咔哒一声唤牛、用刺棒一戳，车又动起来了。
When I’d sit watching him working out in the hot sun I sure felt fond of him. He sure was fun and he done his work so hard and he’d finish up with a regular whirring that’d drive the sweat out on his face like water and then sling the rope at the tree and come over and sit down with me and lean back against the tree with the towel and a sweater wrapped around his neck.
当我坐着看他在烈日下锻炼时，我真有点喜欢他。他确实很有意思，干活也非常卖力，最后总是来个真正的甩绳，把汗像水一样从脸上逼出来，然后把绳子扔到树上，过来和我坐下，靠着树，毛巾和毛衣围着脖子。
‘Sure it’s hell keeping it down, Joe,’ he’d say, and lean back and shut his eyes and breathe long 'and deep, ‘it ain’t like when you’re a kid.’ Then he’d get up and before he started to cool we’d jog along back to the stables. That’s the way it was keeping down to weight. He was worried all the time. Most jocks can just about ride off all they want to. A jock loses about a kilo every time he rides, but my old man was sort of dried out and he couldn’t keep down his kilos without all that running.
“‘当然了，保持体重真是折磨人，乔，’他会说，靠着往后闭上眼睛长长地深深地喘气，‘这可不像你小时候。’然后他会起身，在还没凉下来之前我们就慢跑回马厩。就是这样保持体重。他一直很担心。大多数骑师几乎可以随便骑到想骑为止。一个骑师每次骑完大约会减掉一公斤，但我老爸有点干瘪，没法靠那些跑步把体重保持住。
I remember once at San Siro, Regoli, a little wop, that was riding for Buzoni, came out across the paddock going to the bar for something cool; and flicking his boots with his whip, after he’d just weighed in and my old man had just weighed in too, and came out with the saddle under his arm looking red-faced and tired and too big for his silks and he stood there looking at young Regoli standing up to the outdoors bar, cool and kid-looking, and I said, ‘What’s the matter, Dad?’ 'cause I thought maybe Regoli had bumped him or something and he just looked at Regoli and said, ‘Oh, to hell with it,’ and went on to the dressing-room.
我记得有一次在圣西罗赛场，雷戈利，一个骑给布佐尼的小意大利裔骑师，穿过检录区去酒吧买点冷饮；他刚称完体重，还用马鞭轻弹着靴子，我老爸也刚称完体重，抱着马鞍走出来，脸红又累，衣服显得太大，他站在那里看着站在户外吧台边、显得冷静又有孩子气的年轻雷戈利。我就问，‘怎么了，爸？’因为我以为也许雷戈利碰了他什么的，他只是看了看雷戈利，说，‘算了吧，见鬼去吧，’然后走向更衣室。”
Well, it would have been all right, maybe, if we’d stayed in Milan and ridden at Milan and Torino, 'cause if there ever were any easy courses, it’s those two. ‘Pianola, Joe,’ my old man said when he dismounted in the winning stall after what the wops thought was a hell of a steeplechase. I asked him once. ‘This course rides itself. It’s the pace you’re going at, that makes riding the jumps dangerous, Joe. We ain’t going any pace here, and they ain’t really bad jumps either. But it’s the pace always - not the jumps - that makes the trouble.’
也许本来会没事的，要是我们待在米兰，在米兰和都灵参加赛马会跑赛，因为如果有哪两处赛道算容易的，那就是这两处。‘Pianola，Joe，’我老子在赢马厩下马时说，那场被那些意大利佬以为是了不得的障碍赛之后。我曾经问过他。‘这赛道自己会走。是你跑的速度让跨栏变危险，Joe。我们在这儿压根儿就没什么速度，那些栏也并不算真糟。但总是速度——不是栏——惹的麻烦。’
San Siro was the swellest course I’d ever seen but the old man said it was a dog’s life. Going back and forth between Mirafiore and San Siro and riding just about every day in the week with a train ride every other night.
San Siro 是我见过最豪华的赛场，但我老子说那生活简直像狗。来回奔波于 Mirafiore 和 San Siro 之间，几乎一周七天都在骑马，每隔一个晚上还坐火车一趟。
I was nuts about the horses, too. There’s something about it, when they come out and go up the track to the post. Sort of dancy and tight looking with the jock keeping a tight hold on them and maybe easing off a little and letting them run a little going up. Then once they were at the barrier it got me worse than anything. Especially at San Siro with that big green infield and the mountains way off and the fat wop starter with his big whip and the jocks fiddling them around and then the barrier snapping up and that bell going off and
我也疯狂迷恋赛马。每当马匹出场，沿跑道走向起跑柱时，总有一种特别的感觉。那样子有点像跳舞，又显得紧绷，骑师紧紧拉住缰绳，也许有时稍微放松一点，让它们上坡时稍微奔一会儿。可一旦到了起跑闸，那种感觉比任何时候都强烈。尤其是在 San Siro，那里有那片巨大的绿色内场，远处是连绵群山，还有那位胖乎乎的意大利裔发令员，拿着粗大的鞭子，骑师们忙着调整马匹，随即起跑闸啪地一响，钟声响起来，然后
them all getting off in a bunch and then commencing to string out. You know the way a bunch of skins gets off. If you’re up in the stand with a pair of glasses all you see is them plunging off and then that bell goes off and it seems like it rings for a thousand years and then they come sweeping round the turn. There wasn’t ever anything like it for me.
它们一窝蜂地冲出去，渐渐拉开。你知道一群瘦骨嶙峋的马那种起跑的样子。如果你在看台上带着一副眼镜，只能看到它们扑腾着冲下去，然后钟声响着，似乎要响上一千年，接着它们便呼啸着转过弯。对我来说，从来没有什么能比得上那一刻。
But my old man said one day, in the dressing-room, when he was getting into his street clothes, ‘None of these things are horses, Joe. They’d kill that bunch of skates for their hides and hoofs up at Paris.’ That was the day he’d won the Premio Commercio with Lantorna shooting her out of the field the last hundred metres like pulling a cork out of a bottle.
但我老爸有一天在更衣室里穿便服时说：“这些可都不是马，乔。他们会把那群滑头剥了皮，连蹄子都卖到巴黎去。” 那是他赢得 Premio Commercio 的那一天，Lantorna 在最后一百米像拔塞子似的把她们从场上射出去。
It was right after the Premio Commercio that we pulled out and left Italy. My old man and Holbrook and a fat wop in a straw hat that kept wiping his face with a handkerchief were having an argument at a table in the Galleria. They were all talking French and the two of them was after my old man about something. Finally he didn’t say anything any more but just sat there and looked at Holbrook, and the two of them kept after him, first one talking and then the other, and the fat wop always butting in on Holbrook.
正是在赢了 Premio Commercio 后我们就撤离离开了意大利。我老爸、霍尔布鲁克和一个戴草帽、总用手帕擦脸的胖意大利佬在嘉利利亚的一张桌子旁争论。他们都说法语，两个一直在追着我老爸问这问那。最后他不再说话，只是坐着看着霍尔布鲁克，两个轮流劝他，而那个胖意大利佬总是插着话对霍尔布鲁克。
‘You go out and buy me a Sportsman, will you, Joe?’ my old man said, and handed me a couple of soldi without looking away from Holbrook.
“你出去给我买辆 Sportsman，好吗，乔？”我老爸说着，把几枚索尔迪递给我，眼睛没从霍尔布鲁克身上移开。
So I went out of the Galleria and walked over to in front of the Scala and bought a paper, and came back and stood a little way away because I didn’t want to butt in and my old man was sitting back in his chair looking down at his coffee and fooling with a spoon and Holbrook and the big wop were standing and the big wop was wiping his face and shaking his head. And I came up and my old man acted just as though the two of them weren’t standing there and said, ‘Want an ice, Joe?’ Holbrook looked down at my old man and said slow and careful, ‘You son of a bitch,’ and he and the fat wop went out through the stables.
于是我走出歌剧院，走到斯卡拉剧院门前买报纸，回来后站在稍远处，因为我不想插嘴。老爸坐在椅子上低头看着咖啡，玩着勺子，Holbrook 和那个大意大利佬站着，大意大利佬在擦脸摇头。我走上前，老爸装作两个人根本没站在那儿一样，说：“要来块冰吗，Joe？”Holbrook 慢慢而小心地看着我老爸说：“你这个混蛋，”然后他和那个胖意大利佬走出了马厩。
My old man sat there and sort of smiled at me, but his face was white and he looked sick as hell and I was scared and felt sick inside because I knew something had happened and I didn’t see how anybody could call my old man a son of a bitch, and get away with it. My old man opened up the Sportsman and studied the handicaps for a while, and then he said, ‘You got to take a lot of things in this
我老爸坐在那里对我有点笑意，但脸色苍白，看起来病得要命，我也害怕，心里难受，因为我知道发生了什么事，我想不通谁会敢当面叫我老爸混蛋还能逍遥法外。老爸翻开了 Sportsman，研究赛马让分表一会儿，然后他说，“在这儿你得接受很多事——”
world, Joe.’ And three days later we left Milan for good on the Turin train for Paris, after an auction sale out in front of Turner’s stables of everything we couldn’t get into a trunk and a suitcase.
世界，乔。”三天后，我们坐都灵开往巴黎的火车永远离开了米兰，先在特纳马厩前举行了一场拍卖，把所有装不进一只行李箱和一只手提箱的东西全都卖了。
We got into Paris early in the morning in a long, dirty station the old man told me was the Gare de Lyon. Paris was an awful big town after Milan. Seems like in Milan everybody is going somewhere and all the trams run somewhere and there ain’t any sort of a mix-up, but Paris is all balled up and they never do straighten it out. I got to like it, though, part of it, anyway, and say, it’s got the best race courses in the world. Seems as though that were the thing that keeps it all going and about the only thing you can figure on is that every day the buses will be going out to whatever track they’re running at, going right out through everything to the track. I never really got to know Paris well, because I just came in about once or twice a week with the old man from Maisons and he always sat at the Café de la Paix on the Opera side with the rest of the gang from Maisons and I guess that’s one of the busiest parts of the town. But, say, it is funny that a big town like Paris wouldn’t have a Galleria, isn’t it?
我们清早到达巴黎，进了一个又长又脏的车站，老人告诉我那是里昂车站。相比米兰，巴黎真是个大得可怕的城镇。好像在米兰人人都有目的地，电车都往某个方向开，从来不会乱套；但巴黎却乱成一团，从来也理不顺。不过我还是开始喜欢上它的，至少部分地方，而且，说实话，它有世界上最好的赛马跑道。好像那就是支撑它一切运转的东西，几乎可以肯定每天都有公共汽车开向当天举行比赛的跑道，直接穿过一切直达赛场。我从来没真正熟悉过巴黎，因为我只是每周和老人从梅松来一两次，他总和梅松那群人在歌剧院那边的和平咖啡馆坐着，我想那是城里最热闹的地段之一。但说起来也有意思，像巴黎这样的大城竟然没有一个购物长廊（Galleria），是不是很奇怪？
Well, we went out to live at Maisons-Lafitte, where just about everybody lives except the gang at Chantilly, with a Mrs. Meyers that runs a boarding house. Maisons is about the swellest place to live I’ve ever seen in all my life. The town ain’t so much, but there’s a lake and a swell forest that we used to go off bumming in all day, a couple of us kids, and my old man made me a sling shot and we got a lot of things with it but the best one was a magpie. Young Dick Atkinson shot a rabbit with it one day and we put it under a tree and were all sitting around and Dick had some cigarettes and all of a sudden the rabbit jumped up and beat it into the brush and we chased it but we couldn’t find it. Gee, we had fun at Maisons. Mrs. Meyers used to give me lunch in the morning and I’d be gone all day. I learned to talk French quick. It’s an easy language.
好吧，我们搬去住在梅松-拉菲特，那儿几乎成了人人都住的地方，除了尚蒂伊那一帮，还有个开寄宿房的梅耶斯太太。梅松大概是我一生中见过最体面的居住地。小镇本身倒不怎么样，但有个湖和一片漂亮的森林，我们几个孩子常一整天去那里闲逛，我老爸给我做了一个弹弓，我们用它打到不少东西，最棒的是一只喜鹊。年轻的迪克·阿特金森有一天用弹弓打到了一只兔子，我们把它放在树下，大家都围着坐着，迪克有些香烟，突然那兔子一跃就钻进灌木丛，我们去追却找不着。天啊，我们在梅松玩得可开心了。梅耶斯太太早上常给我午餐，我整天都出去。我学法语学得很快。这语言容易学。
As soon as we got to Maisons, my old man wrote to Milan for his licence and he was pretty worried till it came. He used to sit around the Café de Paris in Maisons with the gang, there were lots of guys he’d known when he rode up at Paris, before the war, lived at Maisons, and there’s a lot of time to sit around because the work around a racing stable, for the jocks, that is, is all cleaned up by nine o’clock in the morning. They take the first bunch of skins out to gallop at 5.30 in the morning and they work the second lot at
一到梅松，我们老头就给米兰写信要他的赛马执照，在拿到之前他挺担心的。他常常和那群人在梅松的巴黎咖啡馆闲坐，那些人里有许多他在战前当骑师、住在梅松、曾在巴黎上场时认识的朋友。围绕着赛马厩的工作——就骑师而言——很早就收工了，所以有很多时间闲坐。他们早上五点半把第一拨马牵出去疾驰，第二拨在...
8 o’clock. That means getting up early all right and going to bed early, too. If a jock’s riding for somebody too, he can’t go boozing around because the trainer always has an eye on him if he’s a kid and if he ain’t a kid he’s always got an eye on himself. So mostly if a jock ain’t working he sits around the Café de Paris with the gang and they can all sit around about two or three hours in front of some drink like a vermouth and seltz and they talk and tell stories and shoot pool and it’s sort of like a club or the Galleria in Milan. Only it ain’t really like the Galleria because there everybody is going by all the time and there’s everybody around at the tables.
八点。那就意味着要早起，同样也得早睡。如果骑师也是为别人骑马，他也不能到处酗酒，因为如果他还年轻，训练师总盯着他；要是他不年轻，他自己也会有所节制。所以大多数时候，骑师不工作时就和一帮人在巴黎咖啡馆坐着，他们可以在一杯如苦艾酒兑气泡水之类的饮料面前坐上两三个小时，聊天、讲故事、打台球，有点像一个俱乐部或米兰的加莱里亚。只是又不完全像加莱里亚，因为那里人们总是在来来往往，桌子周围总是有人。
Well, my old man got his licence all right. They sent it through to him without a word and he rode a couple of times. Amiens, up country and that sort of thing, but he didn’t seem to get any engagement. Everybody liked him and whenever I’d come into the Café in the forenoon I’d find somebody drinking with him because my old man wasn’t tight like most of these jockeys that have got the first dollar they made riding at the World’s Fair in St. Louis in nineteen ought four. That’s what my old man would say when he’d kid George Burns. But it seemed like everybody steered clear of giving my old man any mounts.
我老爹确实拿到执照了。他们毫无声息地把证寄给他，他也骑了几次。亚眠、内地那些地方，诸如此类，但似乎没人给他安排任何出场。大家都喜欢他，每当我上午进咖啡馆，总能发现有人和他一起喝一杯，因为我老爹不像大多数那种在一九○四年圣路易斯世界博览会上靠第一次骑赛就赚到第一块钱的骑师那样整天醉醺醺的。那就是我老爹拿乔治·伯恩斯开玩笑时会说的话。但似乎人人都回避给我老爹任何坐骑。
We went out to wherever they were running every day with the car from Maisons and that was the most fun of all. I was glad when the horses came back from Deauville and the summer. Even though it meant no more bumming in the woods, ‘cause then we’d ride to Enghien or Tremblay or St. Cloud and watch them from the trainers’ and jockeys’ stand. I sure learned about racing from going out with that gang and the fun of it was going every day.
我们每天乘梅松那辆车去他们比赛的任何地方，那是最有意思的。我很高兴赛马从多维尔赶回并结束了夏天。尽管那意味着不能再在树林里混日子了，因为那时我们会骑到昂吉昂、特朗布莱或圣克卢，站在训练师和骑师的看台上看赛。我跟那群人一起出去时确实学到了很多赛马知识，最有趣的是每天都能去。
I remember once out at St. Cloud. It was a big two hundred thousand franc race with seven entries and War Cloud a big favourite. I went around to the paddock to see the horses with my old man and you never saw such horses. This War Cloud is a great big yellow horse that looks just like nothing but run. I never saw such a horse. He was being led around the paddocks with his head down and when he went by me I felt all hollow inside he was so beautiful. There never was such a wonderful, lean, running built horse. And he went around the paddock putting his feet just so and quiet and careful and moving easy like he knew just what he had to do and not jerking and standing up on his legs and getting wild eyed like you see these selling platers with a shot of dope in
我记得有一次在圣克劳。那是场两十万法郎的大赛，有七匹马参赛，War Cloud 是大热门。我和我老爹去围场看马，你从来没见过这样的马。这匹 War Cloud 是一匹大大的黄马，看起来就像唯一会做的就是跑。我从没见过这样的马。他在围场里被牵着，低着头，当他从我身边走过时，他美得让我内心空荡荡的。从来没有过如此优秀、瘦削、为奔跑而造的马。他在围场里踱步，落脚恰到好处，安静小心，步伐轻松，仿佛清楚自己必须做什么，不会像那些卖盘马因打了点药而猛地发作、竖起腿来、眼睛发狂那样。
them. The crowd was so thick I couldn’t see him again except just his legs going by and some yellow and my old man started out through the crowd and I followed him over to the jocks’ dressingroom back in the trees and there was a big crowd around there, too, but the man at the door in a derby nodded to my old man and we got in and everybody was sitting around and getting dressed and pulling shirts over their heads and pulling boots on and it all smelled hot and sweaty and linimenty and outside was the crowd looking in.
人太多了，我再也看不见他，只能看见他的腿走过去，还有一些黄色的东西，我父亲钻过人群，我跟着他到树丛后面的运动员更衣室，那里也围着一大群人，但门口戴礼帽的那个人向我父亲点了点头，我们就进去了，大家都坐着穿衣服，把衬衫从头上拉下来，套靴子，空气里全是闷热、汗味和活络油的气味，外面的人群在往里看。
The old man went over and sat down beside George Gardner that was getting into his pants and said, ‘What’s the dope, George?’ just in an ordinary tone of voice, 'cause there ain’t any use him feeling around because George either can tell him or he can’t tell him.
老头走过去在乔治·加德纳旁边坐下，乔治正在往裤子里套腿，说：“有什么内幕，乔治？”用的是平常的口气，因为他摸不着门路，乔治要么能告诉他，要么就不能。
‘He won’t win,’ George says very low, leaning over and buttoning the bottoms of his breeches.
“他不会赢，”乔治把身子往前倾，低声说，一边扣着马裤的下摆。
‘Who will?’ my old man says, leaning over close so nobody can hear.
“谁会赢？”我父亲凑过去，低声问，怕被人听见。
‘Foxless,’ George says, ‘and if he does, save me a couple of tickets.’
“Foxless，”乔治说，“要是他赢了，给我留两张票。”
My old man says something in a regular voice to George and George says, ‘Don’t ever bet on anything I tell you,’ kidding like, and we beat it out and through all the crowd that was looking in, over to the 100 franc mutuel machine. But I knew something big was up because George is War Cloud’s jockev. On the way he gets one of the yellow odds-sheets with the starting-prices on and War Cloud is only paying 5 for 10, Cefisidote is next at 3 to I and fifth down the list this Foxless at 8 to 1. My old man bets five thousand on Foxless to win and puts on a thousand to place and we went around back of the grandstand to go up the stairs and get a place to watch the race.
我老爹用平常的口气对乔治说了几句，乔治打趣地说：“别听我说的去赌。”我们就挤出去，穿过那些往里看的拥挤人群，走向那台 100 法郎的互助下注机。但我知道大事要发生了，因为乔治是 War Cloud 的骑师。路上他拿到一张印着开赛赔率的黄色赛果单，War Cloud 只开 5 比 10，Cefisidote 紧随其后是 3 比 1，名单第五就是这匹 Foxless，8 比 1。我老爹在 Foxless 赢上下注了五千，又下了一千让它进位（place），然后我们绕到看台后面，上楼找个地方看比赛。
We were jammed in tight and first a man in a long coat with a grey tall hat and a whip folded up in his hand came out and then one after another the horses, with the jocks up and a stable boy holding the bridle on each side and walking along, followed the old guy. That big yellow horse War Cloud came first. He didn’t look so big when you first looked at him until you saw the length of his legs and the whole way he’s built and the way he moves. Gosh, I never saw such a horse. George Gardner was riding him and they moved along slow, back of the old guy in the grey tall hat that walked along like he was a ring master in a circus. Back of War Cloud, moving
我们被挤得很紧，先是一个穿长外套、戴灰色高礼帽、手里折着一根马鞭的人走了出来，随后一匹接一匹的马出来，骑手跨在马上，每边都有一个马童牵着缰绳并走在旁边，跟在那位老人后面。那匹大黄色的马叫 War Cloud 最先出来。刚看时它并不显得特别大，直到你看到它那长长的腿、整体的体格和动作方式。天啊，我从没见过这样的马。George Gardner 骑着它，他们缓缓前行，跟在那位戴灰色高礼帽、走路像马戏团指挥者的老人后面。在 War Cloud 后面，行进着...
along smooth and yellow in the sun, was a good looking black with a nice head with Tommy Archibald riding him; and after the black was a string of five more horses all moving along slow in a procession past the grandstand and the pesage. My old man said the black was Foxless and I took a good look at him and he was a nice-looking horse, all right, but nothing like War Cloud.
那匹在阳光下毛色平滑而微黄、长得好看的黑马上坐着汤米·阿奇博尔德；在那匹黑马后面跟着五匹马，一字排开慢慢走过看台和检阅台。我老人说那匹黑马叫 Foxless，我仔细看了看，确实是一匹漂亮的马，不过比不上 War Cloud。
Everybody cheered War Cloud when he went by and he sure was one swell-looking horse. The procession of them went around on the other side past the pelouse and then back up to the near end of the course and the circus master had the stable boys turn them loose one after another so they could gallop by the stands on their way up to the post and let everybody have a good look at them. They weren’t at the post hardly any time at all when the gong started and you could see them way off across the infield all in a bunch starting on the first swing like a lot of little toy horses. I was watching them through the glasses and War Cloud was running well back, with one of the bays making the pace. They swept down and around and came pounding past and War Cloud was way back when they passed us and this Foxless horse in front and going smooth. Gee, it’s awful when they go by you and then you have to watch them go farther away and get smaller and smaller and then all bunched up on the turns and then come around towards into the stretch and you feel like swearing and god-damming worse and worse. Finally they made the last turn and came into the straightaway with this Foxless horse way out in front. Everybody was looking funny and saying ‘War Cloud’ in a sort of sick way and them pounding nearer down the stretch, and then something came out of the pack right into my glasses like a horse-headed yellow streak and everybody began to yell ‘War Cloud’ as though they were crazy. War Cloud came on faster than I’d ever seen anything in my life and pulled up on Foxless that was going fast as any black horse could go with the jock flogging hell out of him with the gad and they were right dead neck and neck for a second but War Cloud seemed going about twice as fast with those great jumps and that head out - but it was while they were neck and neck that they passed the winning post and when the numbers went up in the slots the first one was 2 and that meant that Foxless had won.
当战云跑过去时，大家都为他喝彩，他确实是一匹极漂亮的马。它们的队伍绕到另一边，经过草坪，然后又回到赛道近端，马戏团的负责人让马厩的伙计们一个接一个把马放开，好让它们在跑向起跑柱的路上从看台前疾驰而过，让大家好好看看。它们在起跑柱那里几乎没停多久，铃声一响，你就能看到它们在内场那边成群地出发，第一次转弯时像一群小玩具马。我用望远镜看着，战云落在后面很远的位置，一匹栗色马领跑。它们猛冲下来绕了一圈，轰然跑过，我们这边经过时战云还远远落在后面，而这匹无狐尾马在前面跑得平稳。哎，当它们从你身边跑过，然后你不得不看着它们越跑越远、变得越来越小、在弯道上又聚拢起来，然后朝直道方向跑过来时，那感觉真糟糕，你想咒骂，甚至越骂越厉害。 最后他们拐过最后一个弯，进入直道，Foxless 那匹马远远领先。大家都神色古怪，带着一种病态的语气在说“War Cloud”，它们一路疾驰下来，然后有匹马从马群里冲出来，像一条马头般的黄色箭线直接冲到我眼前，大家开始像疯了一样喊“War Cloud”。War Cloud 奔得比我有生以来见过的任何马都快，赶上了正在飞奔的 Foxless，那匹黑马在骑师用马鞭狠抽之下也跑得很快，两匹马短暂并驾齐驱，但 War Cloud 看上去跳得更大、头伸得更前，速度似乎快了差不多一倍——不过正当它们并驾齐驱时越过了终点线，当牌盘上的号码亮起，第一位是 2，那就意味着 Foxless 赢了。
I felt all trembly and funny inside and then we were jammed in with the people going downstairs to stand in front of the board
我感到全身发颤、奇怪，然后我们被挤在人群里下楼去站到牌盘前。
where they’d post what Foxless paid. Honest, watching the race I’d forgot how much my old man had bet on Foxless. I’d wanted War Cloud to win so damned bad. But now it was all over it was swell to know we had the winner.
他们会把 Foxless 的赔率贴出来。说真的，看赛马时我忘了我老爸在 Foxless 上压了多少钱。我真他妈盼着 War Cloud 赢。可现在一切都结束了，知道我们压中了获胜者，感觉真好。
‘Wasn’t it a swell race, Dad?’ I said to him.
“不是一场精彩的比赛吗，爸？”我对他说。
He looked at me sort of funny with his derby hat on the back of his head. ‘George Gardner’s a swell jockey all right,’ he said. ‘It sure took a great jock to keep that War Cloud horse from winning.’
他戴着礼帽，帽檐放在后脑勺，上下打量了我一下，表情有点古怪。“George Gardner 确实是个了不起的骑师，”他说。“要不是他骑得那么好，那匹 War Cloud 可就赢不了。”
Of course I knew it was funny all the time. But my old man saying that right out like that sure took the kick all out of it for me and I didn’t get the real kick back again ever, even when they posted the numbers upon the board and the bell rang to pay off and we saw that Foxless paid 67.50 for 10 . All round people were saying, ‘Poor War Cloud! Poor War Cloud!’ And I thought, I wish I were a jockey and could have rode him instead of that son of a bitch. And that was funny, thinking of George Gardner as a son of a bitch because I’d always liked him and besides he’d given us the winner, but I guess that’s what he is, all right.
其实我一直觉得这很可笑。但我老爸就那么直说出来，确实把我心里的劲全打没了，从此我再也没找回那种真正的快感，即使他们把赔率贴到牌子上，铃声响起开始兑付，我们看到 Foxless 的赔率是 10 投 67.50。四周的人都在说，‘可怜的 War Cloud！可怜的 War Cloud！’我心想，要是我能做个骑师，能骑他的该有多好，别让那个混蛋去骑。想到把 George Gardner 叫混蛋还挺好笑的，因为我一直挺喜欢他，而且他还让我们赢了，不过我猜那就是他该有的样子。
My old man had a big lot of money after that race and he took to coming into Paris oftener. If they raced at Tremblay he’d have them drop him in town on their way back to Maisons and he and I’d sit out in front of the Café de la Paix and watch the people go by. It’s funny sitting there. There’s streams of people going by and all sorts of guys come up and want to sell you things, and I loved to sit there with my old man. That was when we’d have the most fun. Guys would come by selling funny rabbits that jumped if you squeezed a bulb and they’d come up to us and my old man would kid them. He could talk French just like English and all those kind of guys knew him 'cause you can always tell a jockey - and then we always sat at the same table and they got used to seeing us there. There were guys selling matrimonial papers and girls selling rubber eggs that when you squeezed them a rooster came out of them and one old wormy-looking guy that went by with postcards of Paris, showing them to everybody, and, of course, nobody ever bought any, and then he would come back and show the under side of the pack and they would all be smutty postcards and lots of people would dig down and buy them.
我爸在那场赛马之后有了一大笔钱，就开始更常来巴黎。如果他们在特朗布莱赛马，他会让车在回梅松的路上把他放在城里，然后他和我就坐在和平咖啡馆门外看人来人往。坐在那里挺有意思的。人流像小溪一样涌过，各种各样的人上前想卖东西给你，我喜欢和我爸坐在那里。那是我们最开心的时候。有人推着会跳的滑稽小兔子来，要是你挤压一个气囊它就会跳，他们会走到我们跟前，我爸会和他们开玩笑。他法语说得跟英语一样好，所有那类人都认识他——你总能看出一个骑师——然后我们总是坐在同一张桌子上，他们也习惯看到我们坐在那里。有人卖结婚证书样本的，有姑娘卖橡皮做的鸡蛋，挤一挤会跳出一只公鸡来，还有一个看起来又老又扭曲的家伙带着巴黎明信片走来走去，给大家看，当然没人买，然后他会回来把一叠明信片翻到背面，背面全是下流的图片，很多人就翻找着去买。
Gee, I remember the funny people that used to go by. Girls around supper time looking for somebody to take them out to eat and they’d
哎，我记得那些过去常来的人都很有趣。傍晚时分一些姑娘找人带她们出去吃饭，她们会
speak to my old man and he’d make some joke at them in French and they’d pat me on the head and go on. Once there was an American woman sitting with her kid daughter at the next table to us and they were both eating ices and I kept looking at the girl and she was awfully good looking and I smiled at her and she smiled at me but that was all that ever come of it because I looked for her mother and her every day and I made up ways that I was going to speak to her and I wondered if I got to know her if her mother would let me take her out to Auteuil or Tremblay but I never saw either of them again. Anyway, I guess it wouldn’t have been any good, anyway, because looking back on it I remember the way I thought out would be best to speak to her was to say, "Pardon me, but perhaps I can give you a winner at Enghien to-day?’ and, after all, maybe she would have thought I was a tout instead of really trying to give her a winner.
跟我老爸说话，他会用法语对她们开个玩笑，她们就会摸摸我的头然后走了。有一次隔壁桌坐着一个美国女人和她的小女儿，她们都在吃冰激凌，我一直盯着那个女孩看，她漂亮得很，我朝她笑了笑，她也回以微笑，但也就仅此而已，因为我天天找她们母女俩，看她们有没有来，我想着好几种办法要跟她说话，也想知道如果我认识她的话她妈妈会不会允许我带她去 Auteuil 或 Tremblay，但我再也没见过她们。总之，估计也不会有什么结果，毕竟回想起来，我记得当时我想的最合适的搭话办法是说：“打扰了，也许我今天能在 Enghien 给您指个赢家？”可说到底，也许她会以为我是个票贩子，而不是确实想给她指路。
We’d sit at the Café de la Paix, my old man and me, and we had a big drag with the waiter because my old man drank whisky and it cost five francs, and that meant a good tip when the saucers were counted up. My old man was drinking more than I’ve ever seen him, but he wasn’t riding at all now and besides he said that whisky kept his weight down. But I noticed he was putting it on, all right, just the same. He’d busted away from his old gang out at Maisons and seemed to like just sitting around on the boulevard with me. But he was dropping money every day at the track. He’d feel sort of doleful after the last race, if he’d lost on the day, until we’d get to our table and he’d have his first whisky and then he’d be fine.
我们会坐在和平咖啡馆，我和我老爸，他和服务员大聊特聊，因为我老爸喝威士忌，一杯要五法郎，这样算下来小费也不少。我老爸那阵比我见过的任何时候都喝得多，可他现在根本不骑马，而且他说威士忌能保持体重。但我注意到他确实在发福，只是没说。他已经脱离了在梅松斯的旧伙子们，似乎更喜欢和我一起在林荫大道上闲坐。但他每天都在赛马场输钱。要是当天输了，他在最后一场赛跑后会有点闷闷不乐，直到我们坐到桌前，他喝了第一杯威士忌就又精神了。
He’d be reading the Paris-Sport and he’d look over at me and say, ‘Where’s your girl, Joe?’ to kid me on account I had told him about the girl that day at the next table. And I’d get red, but I liked being kidded about her. It gave me a good feeling. ‘Keep your eye peeled for her, Joe,’ he’d say, ‘she’ll be back.’
他会看着《Paris-Sport》，然后看着我说：“你的那个女孩在哪儿，乔？”逗我，因为我那天跟他讲了隔壁桌那女孩的事。我会脸红，但我喜欢被拿来开玩笑，感觉不错。“盯着点她，乔，”他说，“她会回来的。”
He’d asked me questions about things and some of the things I’d say he’d laugh. And then he’d get started talking about things. About riding down in Egypt, or at St. Moritz on the ice before my mother died, and about during the war when they had regular races down in the south of France without any purses, or betting or crowds or anything just to keep the breed up. Regular races with the jocks riding hell out of the horses. Gee, I could listen to my old man talk by the hour, especially when he’d had a couple or so of drinks.
他会问我一些事，我有些回答会让他笑。然后他就会开始讲起那些事情。讲在埃及骑马，或者在圣莫里茨冰面上，在我母亲去世前的那些事；还有战争期间他们在法国南部定期赛马，没有奖金，没有赌博，也没有人群什么的，就是为了保持这种血统。正规比赛，骑师们把马逼得拼命跑。天哪，尤其是他喝了两杯酒后，我可以听我老头儿一个小时地讲下去。
He’d tell me about when he was a boy in Kentucky and going coon hunting, and the old days in the States before everything went on the bum there. And he’d say, ‘Joe, when we’ve got a decent stake, you’re going back there to the States and go to school.’
他会告诉我他小时候在肯塔基去捕浣熊的事，还有在美国一切变糟之前的旧日时光。他会说：“乔，只要我们有了一笔像样的钱，你就回美国去上学。”
‘What’ve I got to go back there to go to school for when everything’s on the bum there?’ I’d ask him.
“那边都烂成那样我还回去上学干什么？”我会问他。
‘That’s different,’ he’d say and get the waiter over and pay the pile of saucers and we’d get a taxi to the Gare St. Lazare and get on the train out to Maisons.
“那又不同，”他说着招来侍者付了一堆茶碟的钱，我们就打车到圣拉扎尔车站，上了开往梅松的火车。
One day at Auteuil after a selling steeplechase, my old man bought in the winner for 30,000 francs. He had to bid a little to get him but the stable let the horse go finally and my old man had his permit and his colours in a week. Gee, I felt proud when my old man was an owner. He fixed it up for stable space with Charles Drake and cut out coming in to Paris, and started his running and sweating out again, and him and I were the whole stable gang. Our horse’s name was Gilford, he was Irish bred and a nice, sweet jumper. My old man figured that training him and riding him, himself, he was a good investment. I was proud of everything and I thought Gilford was as good a horse as War Cloud. He was a good, solid jumper, a bay, with plenty of speed on the flat, if you asked him for it, and he was a nice-looking horse, too.
有一天在奥泰伊的售卖障碍赛之后，我老爸用三万法郎买下了头马。为了把他买到，得稍微出个价，但马厩最终放人了，老爸一周内就拿到许可和马衣。天啊，我真为老爸当马主而自豪。他和查尔斯·德雷克安排好马厩位置，不再进巴黎，使马停止参赛，重新开始训练和出汗，他和我就是整个马厩的全部。我们的马名叫吉尔福德，爱尔兰血统，是个漂亮、温顺的跳跃马。我老爸估计由他亲自训练并骑乘，会是个不错的投资。我为一切感到骄傲，觉着吉尔福德和 War Cloud 一样好。他是个结实可靠的跳马，栗褐色，平地上也有很好的速度，只要你向他要，他看起来也很体面。
Gee, I was fond of him. The first time he started with my old man up, he finished third in a 2500 metre hurdle race and when my old man got off him, all sweating and happy in the place stall, and went in to weigh, I felt as proud of him as though it was the first race he’d ever placed in. You see, when a guv ain’t been riding for a long time, you can’t make yourself really believe that he has ever rode. The whole thing was different now, 'cause down in Milan, even big races never seemed to make any difference to my old man, if he won he wasn’t ever excited or anything, and now it was so I couldn’t hardly sleep the night before a race and I knew my old man was excited, too, even if he didn’t show it. Riding for yourself makes an awful difference.
天哪，我挺喜欢他的。他第一次和我老爹一起出赛，是在一场 2500 米障碍赛里拿了第三名；当我老爹从马上下来，满头大汗、在马厩区高兴得不得了，走进去称重的时候，我为他感到和第一次得名似的自豪。你看，当一个师傅好久没上场骑马，你就是不能真正相信他曾经骑过马。现在一切都不同了，因为在米兰，即便是大赛也似乎对我老爹毫无影响，他赢了也从不激动什么，而现在情况是我前一晚几乎睡不着，而且我知道我老爹也激动，尽管他不表现出来。为自己而骑差别可大了。
Second time Gilford and my old man started, was a rainy Sunday at Auteuil, in the Prix du Marat, a 4500 metre steeplechase. As soon as he’d gone out I beat it up in the stand with the new glasses my old man had bought for me to watch them. They started way over at the far end of the course and there was some trouble at the barrier.
吉尔福德和我老爹第二次一起出赛，是在一个下雨的星期天，在奥泰伊的 Prix du Marat，一场 4500 米的越野障碍赛。他一出场我就带着我老爹新买给我的望远镜冲上看台去看。他们从赛道远端那头出发，栅栏那儿出了点麻烦。
Something with goggle blinders on was making a great fuss and rearing around and busted the barrier once, but I could see my old man in our black jacket, with a white cross and a black cap, sitting up on Gilford, and patting him with his hand. Then they were off in a jump and out of sight behind the trees and the gong going for dear life and the pari-mutuel wickets rattling down. Gosh, I was so excited, I was afraid to look at them, but I fixed the glasses on the place where they would come out back of the trees and then out they came with the old black jacket going third and they all sailing over the jump like birds. Then they went out of sight again and then they came pounding out and down the hill and all going nice and sweet and easy and taking the fence smooth in a bunch, and moving away from us all solid. Looked as though you could walk across their backs they were all so bunched and going so smooth. Then they bellied over the big double Bullfinch and something came down. I couldn’t see who it was, but in a minute the horse was up and galloping free and the field, all bunched still, sweeping around the long left turn into the straightaway. They jumped the stone wall and came jammed down the stretch toward the big waterjump right in front of the stands. I saw them coming and hollered at my old man as he went by, and he was leading by about a length and riding way out, and light as a monkey, and they were racing for the water-jump. They took off over the big hedge of the waterjump in a pack and then there was a crash, and two horses pulled sideways out of it, and kept on going, and three others were piled up. I couldn’t see my old man anywhere. One horse kneed himself up and the jock had hold of the bridle and mounted and went slamming on after the place money. The other horse was up and away by himself, jerking his head and galloping with the bridle rein hanging and the jock staggered over to one side of the track against the fence. Then Gilford rolled over to one side off my old man and got up and started to run on three legs with his front off hoof dangling and there was my old man laying there on the grass flat out with his face up and blood all over the side of his head. I ran down the stand and bumped into a jam of people and got to the rail and a cop grabbed me and held me and two big stretcher-bearers were going out after my old man and around on the other side of the course I saw three horses, strung way out, coming out of the trees and taking the jump.
带着护目镜的某匹马闹得很凶，直立起来把栏杆撞坏了好一回，但我看见穿黑色马衣、戴着黑帽、背上有白十字的老头儿坐在吉尔福德背上，用手拍着它。然后它们一跃而起，消失在树后，鸣锣声响个不停，赛马盘口的票箱叮当作响。天哪，我紧张得不敢直视它们，但我把望远镜对准它们会从树后冲出来的地方，然后它们带着那件老黑马衣从第三位冲出，全都像鸟儿一样越过障碍。接着又看不见了，随后又重重地冲出来，顺着山坡跑下去，节奏都好极了，轻松平稳，一群人利落地跨过围栏，整队往前走得很结实。看上去你都可以踏着它们的背走过去——它们挤得那么紧，动作又那么顺。然后它们翻越了那道大双杆障碍，出了点状况。我一时看不清是谁，但片刻后那匹马起来自由狂奔，赛群仍然挤成一团，挥着长长的左弯进入直道。 他们跃过了石墙，撞成一团向看台前的大水跳冲下来。我看见他们过来，朝着从那儿经过的老头大声喊，老头领先大约一马身，骑得很外展，轻得像猴子，他们正为水跳冲刺。他们成群越过水跳那边的大树篱，然后一阵撞击，两匹马被撞得侧着冲了出去，继续奔去，另外三匹马则跌成一堆。我哪儿也看不见我老头。一匹马跪起身来，骑师抓住缰绳，跨上马背继续猛冲去争名次。另一匹马自己站起来奔走着，甩着头，缰绳垂着，骑师踉跄着靠在跑道一侧的栅栏上。然后吉尔福德从我老头身上一滚，起来开始一条前腿悬着跑着，我老头就平躺在草地上仰着脸，头的一侧满是血。 我冲下看台，撞进一堆人群，挤到栏杆边，一个警察抓住我按住不放，两名大号抬担架的人正朝我爸那里过去，在跑道另一侧我看见三匹马，从树丛里拉得很开地出来，跳了过去。
My old man was dead when they brought him in and while a doctor was listening to his heart with a thing plugged in his ears, I heard a shot up the track that meant they’d killed Gilford. I lay down beside my old man, when they carried the stretcher into the hospital room, and hung on to the stretcher and cried and cried, and he looked so white and gone and so awfully dead, and I couldn’t help feeling that if my old man was dead maybe they didn’t need to have shot Gilford. His hoof might have got well. I don’t know. I loved my old man so much.
他们把我爸抬进来时他已经死了，医生把听诊器塞到耳朵里听他的心脏时，我听到跑道那边响了一枪，意味着他们已经把吉尔福德打死了。当他们把担架抬进病房时，我侧躺在我爸旁边，抱住担架哭个不停，他看起来那么苍白、那么不在了、那么可怕地死了，我忍不住觉得如果我爸死了，也许就没必要去打吉尔福德。他的蹄子可能会好起来。我不知道。我是多么爱我爸。
Then a couple of guys came in and one of them patted me on the back and then went over and looked at my old man and then pulled a sheet off the cot and spread it over him; and the other was telephoning in French for them to send the ambulance to take him out to Maisons. And I couldn’t stop crying, crying and choking, sort of, and George Gardner came in and sat down beside me on the floor and put his arm around me and says, ‘Come on, Joe, old boy. Get up and we’ll go out and wait for the ambulance.’
然后有几个人进来了，其中一个拍了拍我的背，然后走过去看我父亲，把床铺上的一床单掀下来铺在他身上；另一个用法语打电话，让他们派救护车把他送到 Maisons 去。我止不住哭，哭得又哽咽似的，乔治·加德纳进来，坐在我旁边的地板上，搂着我说，‘来吧，乔，老兄。起来，我们出去等救护车。’
George and I went out to the gate and I was trying to stop bawling and George wiped off my face with his handkerchief and we were standing back a little ways while the crowd was going out of the gate and a couple of guys stopped near us while we were waiting for the crowd to get through the gate and one of them was counting a bunch of mutuel tickets and he said, ‘Well, Butler got his, all right.’
乔治和我走到大门口，我在努力止住嚎哭，乔治用手帕擦了擦我的脸。我们站在后面一点，等人群从门口出去，等人群过去的时候有几个人在我们附近停下，其中一个正数着一叠赌票，他说，‘嗯，巴特勒那笔他是赢了。’
The other guy said, ‘I don’t give a good goddam if he did, the crook. He had it coming to him on the stuff he’s pulled.’
另一个人说，‘我才不管他他妈的符不符呢，那个骗子。他活该，看看他干了些什么。’
‘I’ll say he had,’ said the other guy, and tore the bunch of tickets in two.
‘我也这么说，’另一个人说着，把那叠票撕成了两半。
And George Gardner looked at me to see if I’d heard and I had all right, and he said, ‘Don’t you listen to what those bums said, Joe. Your old man was one swell guy.’
乔治·加德纳看着我，想知道我有没有听见，我当然听见了。他说：“别听那些混混说的，乔。你父亲是个了不起的人。”
But I don’t know. Seems like when they get started they don’t leave a guy nothing.
可我也不太清楚。好像他们一旦开口就什么都不留给人了。
Maera lay still, his head on his arms, his face in the sand. He felt warm and sticky from the bleeding. Each time he felt the horn coming. Sometimes the bull only bumped him with his head. Once the horn went all the way through him and he felt it go into the sand. Someone had the bull by the tail. They were swearing at him and flopping the cape in his face. Then the bull was gone. Some men picked Maera up and started to run with him toward the barriers through the gate out the passageway around under the grandstand to the infirmary. They laid Maera down on a cot and one of the men went out for the doctor. The others stood around. The doctor came running from the corral where he had been sewing up picador horses. He had to stop and wash his hands. There was a great shouting going on in the grandstand overhead. Maera felt everything getting larger and larger and then smaller and smaller. Then it got larger and larger and larger and then smaller and smaller. Then everything commenced to run faster and faster as when they speed up on a cinematograph film. Then he was dead.
马埃拉静静地躺着，头靠在手臂上，脸贴在砂地上。他因流血感到温热而粘糊。每当他感觉到牛角靠近。有时公牛只是用头把他顶了一下。有一次牛角彻底穿过了他，他感觉到它刺进了砂地里。有人抓住了公牛的尾巴。他们对着他骂着，并把斗篷在他脸前拍动。然后公牛走了。有些人把马埃拉抬起来，开始带着他朝围栏方向跑，穿过闸门，沿着看台下面的通道到医务室。他们把马埃拉放在担架上，其中一个人出去去找医生。其他人站在周围。医生从畜栏那边跑过来，那里他一直在给旁骑手的马缝合伤口。他不得不停下来洗手。上面的看台里喧闹声震天。马埃拉感到一切逐渐变得越来越大，然后又越来越小。接着又变得越来越大越来越大，然后又越来越小越来越小。然后一切开始像放映机放电影时加速一样越来越快。然后他死了。

BIG TWO-HEARTED RIVER: PART I
大两心河：第一部分

The train went on up the track out of sight, around one of the hills of burnt timber. Nick sat down on the bundle of canvas and bedding the baggage man had pitched out of the door of the baggage car. There was no town, nothing but the rails and the burned-over country. The thirteen saloons that had lined the one street of Seney had not left a trace. The foundations of the Mansion House hotel stuck up above the ground. The stone was chipped and split by the fire. It was all that was left of the town of Seney. Even the surface had been burned off the ground.
火车沿着铁轨驶上去，绕过一座烧焦木林的小山，很快看不见了。Nick 坐在行李工从行李车门口扔出来的那捆帆布和被褥上。没有城镇，只有铁轨和被烧过的荒地。曾经沿着 Seney 那条街排列的十三家酒馆全都不见了踪影。Mansion House 旅馆的地基从地面露了出来。石头被火烧得剥落开裂。那是 Seney 镇剩下的全部。连地表也被烧掉了。
Nick looked at the burned-over stretch of hillside, where he had expected to find the scattered houses of the town and then walked down the railroad track to the bridge over the river. The river was there. It swirled against the log piles of the bridge. Nick looked down into the clear, brown water, coloured from the pebbly bottom, and watched the trout keeping themselves steady in the current with wavering fins. As he watched them they changed their posi-
Nick 看着被烧过的山坡，他本以为那里会有零星散落的房屋，然后沿着铁轨走到河上的桥边。河还在。河水在桥的木桩周围旋转。Nick 往下看，清澈的棕色水因为卵石底显出颜色，他看着鳟鱼用颤动的鱼鳍在水流中稳住身子。当他看着它们时，它们改变了位—
tions by quick angles, only to hold steady in the fast water again. Nick watched them a long time.
位，迅速转出角度，又在急流中重新稳住。Nick 看了它们很久。
He watched them holding themselves with their noses into the current, many trout in deep, fast moving water, slightly distorted as he watched far down through the glassy convex surface of the pool, its surface pushing and swelling smooth against the resistance of the log-driven piles of the bridge. At the bottom of the pool were the big trout. Nick did not see them at first. Then he saw them at the bottom of the pool, big trout looking to hold themselves on the gravel bottom in a varying mist of gravel and sand, raised in spurts by the current.
他看着它们把鼻子顶着水流站稳脚跟，许多鳟鱼在深而急的水里游动，通过水潭那光滑凸起的表面往下看时略微变形，水面在桥那由木桩撑起的一排排桩的阻力下平滑地推进和隆起。水潭底下是大的鳟鱼。Nick 起初没有看到它们。然后他在水潭底看见了它们，大条鳟鱼试图在砾石底上站住脚跟，在不断变化的砾砂雾中稳住，时而被水流一阵阵扬起。
Nick looked down into the pool from the bridge. It was a hot day. A kingfisher flew up the stream. It was a long time since Nick had looked into a stream and seen trout. They were very satisfactory. As the shadow of the kingfisher moved up the stream, a big trout shot upstream in a long angle, only his shadow marking the angle, then lost his shadow as he came through the surface of the water, caught the sun, and then, as he went back into the stream under the surface, his shadow seemed to float down the stream with the current, unresisting, to his post under the bridge where he tightened facing up into the current.
Nick 从桥上向下望进水潭。那天很热。一只翠鸟顺着溪流飞起。Nick 很久没有向溪里望去并见到鳟鱼了。它们令人非常满足。随着翠鸟的影子顺流移动，一条大鳟鱼以一个长长的角度向上游射去，只有它的影子标出那角度，接着当它穿过水面时影子消失，抓住了阳光，然后当它在水下回到溪流里时，它的影子似乎随着水流不抵抗地顺流漂向它在桥下的那个位置，那里它迎着水流收紧身体站稳。
Nick’s heart tightened as the trout moved. He felt all the old feeling.
尼克的心随着鳟鱼的挣动而紧缩。他重温了所有旧日的感觉。
He turned and looked down the stream. It stretched away, pebblybottomed with shallows and big boulders and a deep pool as it curved away around the foot of a bluff.
他转过身向下游看去。那条小溪蜿蜒延伸，河床砾石遍布，有浅滩和大卵石，河道在峭壁脚下弯曲处有一个深潭。
Nick walked back up the ties to where his pack lay in the cinders beside the railway track. He was happy. He adjusted the pack harness around the bundle, pulling straps tight, slung the pack on his back, got his arms through the shoulder straps and took some of the pull off his shoulders by leaning his forehead against the wide band of the tump-line. Still, it was too heavy. It was much too heavy. He had his leather rod-case in his hand and leaning forward to keep the weight of the pack high on his shoulders he walked along the road that paralleled the railway track, leaving the burned town behind in the heat, and then turned off around a hill with a high, fire-scarred hill on either side on to a road that went back into the country. He walked along the road feeling the ache from the pull of the heavy pack. The road climbed steadily. It was hard work walking up-hill.
尼克沿着枕木朝回走，走到他的背包放在铁路旁炉渣里的地方。他很高兴。他把背包的胸背带在包裹周围调整好，拉紧带子，把背包扛到背上，把胳膊穿过肩带，然后把额头倚在宽宽的顶带上以减轻些肩部的拉力。尽管如此，仍然太重了。实在太重了。他手里拿着皮制鱼竿盒，身体前倾以保持背包的重心高压在肩上，沿着与铁轨平行的路走去，把被烧毁的小镇留在身后炽热之中，然后在两侧各有一座高大的、受火灼伤的山丘处绕路进入一条回到乡间的道路。他沿着路走着，感觉沉重背包拉扯带来的疼痛。路持续上坡。上坡走路很费劲。
His muscles ached and the day was hot, but Nick felt happy. He felt he had left everything behind, the need for thinking, the need to write, other needs. It was all back of him.
他的肌肉酸痛，天气很热，但尼克感到高兴。他觉得自己已经把一切抛在身后，不再需要思考，不再需要写作，其他的需要也都不再重要。那一切都成了他的过去。
From the time he had gotten down off the train and the baggage man had thrown his pack out of the open car door things had been different. Seney was burned, the country was burned over and changed, but it did not matter. It could not all be burned. He knew that. He hiked along the road, sweating in the sun, climbing to cross the range of hills that separated the railway from the pine plains.
自从他从火车上跳下，行李员把他的背包从敞开的车门扔出去后，一切就变得不同了。塞尼被烧毁了，乡野被烧得焦黑改变了，但那并不重要。不可能全部都被烧尽。他知道这一点。他沿着路徒步行进，在阳光下汗流浃背，攀爬越过那一排把铁路和松林平原隔开的山丘。
The road ran on, dipping occasionally, but always climbing. Nick went on up. Finally the road after going parallel to the burnt hillside reached the top. Nick leaned back against a stump and slipped out of the pack harness. Ahead of him, as far as he could see, was the pine plain. The burned country stopped off at the left with the range of hills. On ahead islands of dark pine trees rose out of the plain. Far off to the left was the line of the river. Nick followed it with his eye and caught glints of the water in the sun.
那条路一直延伸，时而下坡，但总是在向上爬。尼克继续向上走。最后，那条路在与被烧的山坡并行一段后到达了山顶。尼克靠在一根树桩上，解开了背包的胸背带。放眼前方，尽他所见，都是松林平原。被烧毁的地区在左侧于那排山丘处结束。前方平原上耸立着几座黑色的松树林岛。很远的左侧有条河流的轮廓。尼克用目光追随着它，看见阳光下水面闪烁的光点。
There was nothing but the pine plain ahead of him, until the far blue hills that marked the Lake Superior height of land. He could hardly see them, faint and far away in the heat-light over the plain. If he looked too steadily they were gone. But if he only half-looked they were there, the far-off hills of the height of land.
前面一望无际只有松林平原，直到那标示苏必利尔湖分水岭的远处蓝色山峦。他几乎看不清它们，在平原上方热光中淡淡地远远地隐去。如果他目不转睛地看，山就消失了。但如果他只是半看着，它们又在那儿，远处的分水岭山峦。
Nick sat down against the charred stump and smoked a cigarette. His pack balanced on top of the stump, harness holding ready, a hollow moulded in it from his back. Nick sat smoking, looking out over the country. He did not need to get his map out. He knew where he was from the position of the river.
Nick 靠在烧焦的树桩上坐下，抽起了一支烟。他的背包平衡地放在树桩顶上，胸背带系着待命，从他的背部压出一个凹痕。Nick 坐着抽烟，眺望着这片土地。他不需要拿出地图。从河流的位置就能判断自己在哪里。
As he smoked, his legs stretched out in front of him, he noticed a grasshopper walk along the ground and up on to his woollen sock. The grasshopper was black. As he had walked along the road, climbing, he had started many grasshoppers from the dust. They were all black. They were not the big grasshoppers with yellow and black or red and black wings whirring out from their black wing sheathing as they fly up. These were just ordinary hoppers, but all a sooty black in colour. Nick had wondered about them as he walked, without really thinking about them. Now, as he watched the black hopper that was nibbling at the wool of his sock with its fourway lip, he realized that they had all turned black from living
他抽着烟，双腿伸在前面，注意到一只蚱蜢沿地面爬到他的羊毛袜上。那只蚱蜢是黑色的。当他沿路爬行时，已从尘土里惊起许多蚱蜢。它们全是黑色的。不是那种飞起时从黑色翅鞘中拍出黄黑或红黑翅膀的大蚱蜢。只是普通的蚱蜢，但全都是煤烟般的黑色。Nick 在走路时曾对它们感到好奇，却并未多想。现在，当他看着那只用四瓣口器啃咬着他袜子羊毛的黑色蚱蜢，他意识到它们全部因为生活在被烧过的土地上而变黑了。
in the burned-over land. He realized that the fire must have come the year before, but the grasshoppers were all black now. He wondered how long they would stay that way.
他意识到大火一定是在前年燃过，但这些蚱蜢现在都变黑了。他想知道它们会保持这样多久。
Carefully he reached his hand down and took hold of the hopper by the wings. He turned him up, all his legs walking in the air, and looked at his jointed belly. Yes, it was black too, iridescent where the back and head were dusty.
他小心地把手伸下去，抓住那只蚱蜢的翅膀。他把它翻过来，所有的腿都在空中蹬动，查看它那分节的腹部。是的，腹部也是黑色的，背和头上因覆着尘土而显出彩虹般的光泽。
‘Go on, hopper,’ Nick said, speaking out loud for the first time. ‘Fly away somewhere.’
“走吧，蚱蜢，”Nick 说，这是他第一次大声说话。“飞到别处去吧。”
He tossed the grasshopper into the air and watched him sail away to a charcoal stump across the road.
他把蚱蜢抛向空中，看着它飞到路对面的一个炭黑色树桩上。
Nick stood up. He leaned his back against the weight of his pack where it rested upright on the stump and got his arms through the shoulder straps. He stood with the pack on his back on the brow of the hill looking out across the country toward the distant river and then struck down the hillside away from the road. Underfoot the ground was good walking. Two hundred vards down the hillside the fire line stopped. Then it was sweet fern, growing ankle high, to walk through, and clumps of jack pines; a long undulating country with frequent rises and descents, sandy underfoot and the country alive again.
Nick 站了起来。他背靠着直立在树桩上的沉重背包的重量，把手穿过肩带。他背着背包站在山脊上，眺望远处通向那条河的原野，然后顺着山坡向远离公路的方向下去。脚下的地面便于行走。下山二百码处火线止住了。然后就是寸踝高的甜蕨丛，穿行其间，还有一丛丛的刺松；绵延起伏的旷野，频繁有高有低，脚下为沙质，乡野又恢复了生机。
Nick kept his direction by the sun. He knew where he wanted to strike the river and he kept on through the pine plain, mounting small rises to see other rises ahead of him and sometimes from the top of a rise a great solid island of pines off to his right or his left. He broke off some sprigs of the heathery sweet fern, and put them under his pack straps. The chafing crushed it and he smelled it as he walked.
尼克靠着太阳辨认方向。他知道自己要到哪里下到河边，便沿着松林平原继续行进，爬上小丘以便能看到前方的其它山岗，有时从山岗顶上能望见右侧或左侧一大片坚实的松树岛。他掰下几枝带有石南花香的甜蕨，塞在背带下面。背带摩擦把它压碎了，走路时他闻得到那股气味。
He was tired and very hot, walking across the uneven, shadeless pine plain. At any time he knew he would strike the river by turning off to his left. It could not be more than a mile away. But he kept on toward the north to hit the river as far upstream as he could go in one day’s walking.
他又累又热，走在这片凹凸不平、没有树荫的松林平原上。他随时知道只要向左转就能抵达那条河。河不可能离他超过一英里。但他仍向北走，想在一天的行程里尽量上游赶到河边。
For some time as he walked Nick had been in sight of one of the big islands of pine standing out above the rolling high ground he was crossing. He dipped down and then as he came slowly up to the crest of the ridge he turned and made toward the pine trees.
走着走着，尼克一直能看到一座在他所穿越的起伏高地上突出的大片松树岛。他先下坡，然后慢慢爬上山脊顶，转身朝那片松林走去。
There was no underbrush in the island pine trees. The trunks of the trees went straight up or slanted toward each other. The trunks
那片松林里没有灌木。树干笔直向上或相互倾斜。树干
were straight and brown without branches. The branches were high above. Some interlocked to make a solid shadow on the brown forest floor. Around the grove of trees was a bare space. It was brown and soft underfoot as Nick walked on it. This was the over-lapping of the pine needle floor, extending out beyond the width of the high branches. The trees had grown tall and the branches moved high, leaving in the sun this bare space they had once covered with shadow. Sharp at the edge of this extension of the forest floor commenced the sweet fern.
树干笔直呈褐色，没有分枝。分枝都长得很高。有些树枝交错在一起，在褐色的林地上投下浓密的阴影。树丛周围是一片空地。尼克走在上面，脚下松软而褐色。那是松针堆积的延伸，超出了高枝的投影宽度。树长得很高，枝叶升得很高，在阳光下留下了这片它们曾用阴影覆盖的裸地。在这片林地延伸的边缘，刺柏丛生，锋利而开始。
Nick slipped off his pack and lay down in the shade. He lay on his back and looked up into the pine trees. His neck and back and the small of his back rested as he stretched. The earth felt good against his back. He looked up at the sky, through the branches, and then shut his eyes. He opened them and looked up again. There was a wind high up in the branches. He shut his eyes again and went to sleep.
尼克卸下背包，躺在阴凉处。他仰面躺着，仰望松树。他伸展着，颈背和腰部都有了支撑，后背贴着泥土，感觉很好。他透过枝叶仰望天空，然后闭上眼睛。他又睁开眼睛，再次向上看。高高的枝头有风在吹。他又闭上眼睛，睡着了。
Nick woke stiff and cramped. The sun was nearly down. His pack was heavy and the straps painful as he lifted it on. He leaned over with the pack on and picked up the leather rod-case and started out from the pine trees across the sweet fern swale, toward the river. He knew it could not be more than a mile.
尼克醒来时身体僵痛、肌肉绷紧。太阳快要落山了。他的背包很重，肩带在举起时疼得厉害。他背着包弯下身，拎起皮制钓竿筒，穿过马尾松林，走过覆盆子丛生的洼地，朝河边走去。他知道不会超过一英里。
He came down a hillside covered with stumps into a meadow. At the edge of the meadow flowed the river. Nick was glad to get to the river. He walked upstream through the meadow. His trousers were soaked with the dew as he walked. After the hot day, the dew had come quickly and heavily. The river made no sound. It was too fast and smooth. At the edge of the meadow, before he mounted to a piece of high ground to make camp, Nick looked down the river at the trout rising. They were rising to insects come from the swamp on the other side of the stream when the sun went down. The trout jumped out of water to take them. While Nick walked through the little stretch of meadow alongside the stream, trout had jumped high out of water. Now as he looked down the river, the insects must be settling on the surface, for the trout were feeding steadily all down the stream. As far down the long stretch as he could see, the trout were rising, making circles all down the surface of the water, as though it were starting to rain.
他沿着布满树桩的山坡下到一片草地。草地的边缘就是河流。尼克很高兴走到河边。他沿着草地向上游走去。走着走着裤子被露水打湿了。经过一整天的酷热，露水来得又快又重。河水没有声音，流得太急又太平滑。在草地边缘，在他爬上一处高地扎营之前，尼克向下望去，只见鳟鱼在跃出水面。夕阳下，来自河对面沼泽的昆虫飞来，鳟鱼跳出水面去捕食它们。尼克沿着水流旁那一小段草地走时，鳟鱼曾高高跃出水面。现在当他向下望去，昆虫大概正在落到水面上，鳟鱼在整条溪流上稳定地觅食。从他能看得最远的下游那头起，鳟鱼不断跃出，在水面上圈圈荡漾，仿佛要下起雨来。
The ground rose, wooded and sandy, to overlook the meadow, the stretch of river and the swamp. Nick dropped his pack and rod-
地面上升，长着树木，夹着沙地，俯瞰着草地、那段河流和沼泽。尼克放下了行囊和钓竿——
case and looked for a level piece of ground. He was very hungry and he wanted to make his camp before he cooked. Between two jack-pines, the ground was quite level. He took the axe out of the pack and chopped out two projecting roots. That levelled a piece of ground large enough to sleep on. He smoothed out the sandy soil with his hand and pulled all the sweet fern bushes by their roots. His hands smelled good from the sweet fern. He smoothed the uprooted earth. He did not want anything making lumps under the blankets. When he had the ground smooth, he spread his three blankets. One he folded double, next to the ground. The other two he spread on top.
他检查了一下行李，找了一处平坦的地方。他非常饿，想在做饭前先搭好营。两株刺松之间，地面相当平坦。他从背包里拿出斧头，砍掉了两根突出的树根。这样就把一块足够睡觉的地面弄平了。他用手把沙土抚平，把所有甜蕨灌木连根拔起。手上带着甜蕨的清香。他把被连根拔起的泥土弄平。他不想让毯子下面有任何坎坷。把地面弄平后，他摊开三条毯子。把一条对折后放在最底下。其他两条摊在上面。
With the axe he slit off a bright slab of pine from one of the stumps and split it into pegs for the tent. He wanted them long and solid to hold in the ground. With the tent unpacked and spread on the ground, the pack, leaning against a jack-pine, looked much smaller. Nick tied the rope that served the tent for a ridge-pole to the trunk of one of the pine trees and pulled the tent up off the ground with the other end of the rope and tied it to the other pine. The tent hung on the rope like a canvas blanket on a clothes line. Nick poked a pole he had cut up under the back peak of the canvas and then made it a tent by pegging out the sides. He pegged the sides out taut and drove the pegs deep, hitting them down into the ground with the flat of the axe until the rope loops were buried and the canvas was drum tight.
他用斧头从一截树桩上削下一块亮亮的松木板，然后劈成帐篷的桩子。他要把桩做得又长又结实，以便牢牢钉在地里。把帐篷卸包铺在地上后，背包靠在一棵针叶松上看起来小了许多。尼克把用作横梁的帐篷绳子一端系在一棵松树干上，然后拉起另外一端把帐篷从地面提起来，系在另一棵松树上。帐篷像挂在晾衣绳上的帆布毯一样挂在绳子上。尼克把他砍来的竿子塞到帆布后峰下，然后通过把侧边拉平钉牢把它变成了帐篷。他把侧边拉得绷紧，把桩子钉得很深，用斧头的平面把它们敲进地里，直到绳圈被埋住，帆布绷得像鼓皮一样紧。
Across the mouth of the tent Nick fixed cheesecloth to keep out mosquitoes. He crawled inside under the mosquito bar with various things from the pack to put at the head of the bed under the slant of the canvas. Inside the tent the light came through the brown canvas. It smelled pleasantly of canvas. Already there was something mysterious and home-like. Nick was happy as he crawled inside the tent. He had not been unhappy all day. This was different though. Now things were done. There had been this to do. Now it was done. It had been a hard trip. He was very tired. That was done. He had made his camp. He was settled. Nothing could touch him. It was a good place to camp. He was there, in the good place. He was in his home where he had made it. Now he was hungry.
尼克在帐篷口上固定了纱布以防蚊子。他钻进防蚊帐，从行囊里掏出各种东西，放在床头，靠着斜搭的帆布。在帐篷里面，光线透过褐色的帆布照进来。帆布有一种令人愉快的气味。已经有了一种神秘而舒适的感觉。尼克爬进帐篷时很高兴。他整天都不觉得沮丧。但这次不同。现在事情都办妥了。原本要做的事已经做完。路途很辛苦。他很累。那也结束了。他扎好了营。他安顿下来了。没有什么能动摇他。这里是个好扎营的地方。他在这儿，在好地方。他在自己搭建的家里。现在他饿了。
He came out, crawling under the cheesecloth. It was quite dark outside. It was lighter in the tent.
他爬出帐篷，从纱布下钻出来。外面已经相当黑了。帐篷里要亮一些。
Nick went over to the pack and found, with his fingers, a long
尼克走到行囊边，用手指摸到一根长的
nail in a paper sack of nails, in the bottom of the pack. He drove it into the pine tree, holding it close and hitting it gently with the flat of the axe. He hung the pack up on the nail. All his supplies were in the pack. They were off the ground and sheltered now.
他把一颗钉子钉在装钉子的纸袋里，钉在包底。他把钉子钉进松树，手握着钉子，用斧面的侧面轻轻敲打。然后把包挂在了钉子上。他所有的补给都在那个包里。现在它们离地并且有了遮蔽。
Nick was hungry. He did not believe he had ever been hungrier. He opened and emptied a can of pork and beans and a can of spaghetti into the frying-pan.
尼克饿了。他不相信自己曾经饿得更厉害过。他把一罐猪肉豆罐头和一罐意大利面倒进煎锅里。
I’ve got a right to eat this kind of stuff, if I’m willing to carry it,’ Nick said. His voice sounded strange in the darkening woods. He did not speak again.
“我要是愿意背，就有权吃这种东西，”尼克说。他的声音在渐暗的树林里听起来很奇怪。他再也没说话。
He started a fire with some chunks of pine he got with the axe from a stump. Over the fire he stuck a wire grill, pushing the four legs down into the ground with his boot. Nick put the frying-pan on the grill over the flames. He was hungrier. The beans and spaghetti warmed. Nick stirred them and mixed them together. They began to bubble, making little bubbles that rose with difficulty to the surface. There was a good smell. Nick got out a bottle of tomato catchup and cut four slices of bread. The little bubbles were coming faster now. Nick sat down beside the fire and lifted the frying-pan off. He poured about half the contents out into a tin plate. It spread slowly on the plate. Nick knew it was too hot. He poured on some tomato catchup. He knew the beans and spaghetti were still too hot. He looked at the fire, then at the tent, he was not going to spoil it all by burning his tongue. For years he had never enjoyed fried bananas because he had never been able to wait for them to cool. His tongue was very sensitive. He was very hungry. Across the river in the swamp, in the almost dark, he saw a mist rising. He looked at the tent once more. All right. He took a full spoonful from the plate.
他用从树桩上用斧头劈下的几块松木生起了火。火上他撑起了一只铁丝烤架，用靴子把四条腿竖到地里。Nick 把煎锅放在烤架上、在火焰上面。他更饿。豆子和意大利面被热开了。Nick 搅拌着，把它们拌在一起。它们开始冒泡，冒出的小泡艰难地上升到表面。闻起来很香。Nick 拿出一瓶番茄酱，切了四片面包。小泡现在冒得更快了。Nick 在火边坐下，把煎锅拿了起来。他把大约一半的内容物倒到一个锡盘里。它在盘子上慢慢地摊开。Nick 知道那太烫了。他又倒了些番茄酱。他知道豆子和意大利面仍然太烫。他看了看火，又看了看帐篷，他可不打算因为烫了舌头就把这一切都毁了。多年来他从未喜欢煎香蕉，因为他从来等不及让它们冷却。他的舌头很敏感。他非常饿。河对岸的沼泽里，在几乎黑暗中，他看见有雾气升起。他又看了看帐篷。好吧。 他从盘子里舀了一整勺。
‘Chrise,’ Nick said. ‘Geezus Chrise,’ he said happily.
“Chrise，”Nick 说。“Geezus Chrise，”他高兴地说。
He ate the whole plateful before he remembered the bread. Nick finished the second plateful with the bread, mopping the plate shiny. He had not eaten since a cup of coffee and a ham sandwich in the station restaurant at St. Ignace. It had been a very fine experience. He had been that hungry before, but had not been able to satisfy it. He could have made camp hours before if he had wanted to. There were plenty of good places to camp on the river. But this was good.
他把整盘都吃完才想起面包。Nick 吃完第二盘时把面包连着吃了，把盘子擦得亮晶晶的。他自从在圣伊格纳斯的车站餐厅喝了一杯咖啡和吃了一个火腿三明治后就没再吃东西了。那是一次非常美好的体验。他以前也曾饿成那样，但却无法满足。要是他想的话，本可以早几个小时就扎营。河边有很多适合扎营的好地方。但现在这样就很好。
Nick tucked two big chips of pine under the grill. The fire flared up. He had forgotten to get water for the coffee. Out of the pack he
Nick 把两大块松木塞到烤架下面。火焰窜了起来。他忘了去取煮咖啡的水。他从背包里取出
got a folding canvas bucket and walked down the hill, across the edge of the meadow, to the stream. The other bank was in the white mist. The grass was wet and cold as he knelt on the bank and dipped the canvas bucket into the stream. It bellied and pulled hard in the current. The water was ice cold. Nick rinsed the bucket and carried it full up to the camp. Up away from the stream it was not so cold.
拿着一个折叠帆布桶顺着小坡走下去，穿过草地边缘，来到小溪边。对岸淹没在白雾中。草地又湿又冷，他跪在河岸上把帆布桶浸入溪水。桶在水流中鼓起身子，被水流猛拉。水冰冷刺骨。尼克把桶冲洗干净，端着满满一桶水回到营地。离开溪流上去就不那么冷了。
