Nick drove another big nail and hung up the bucket full of water. He dipped the coffee pot half full, put some more chips under the grill on to the fire and put the pot on. He could not remember which way he made coffee. He could remember an argument about it with Hopkins, but not which side he had taken. He decided to bring it to a boil. He remembered now that was Hopkins’s way. He had once argued about everything with Hopkins. While he waited for the coffee to boil, he opened a small can of apricots. He liked to open cans. He emptied the can of apricots out into a tin cup. While he watched the coffee on the fire, he drank the juice syrup of the apricots, carefully at first to keep from spilling, then meditatively, sucking the apricots down. They were better than fresh apricots.
尼克又钉了一个大钉子，把装满水的桶挂了起来。他把咖啡壶舀到半满，把更多木屑放到烤架下面的火上，然后把壶放上去。他记不得自己煮咖啡的方式了。他记得曾经与霍普金斯为此争论过，但记不得自己当时支持哪一派。他决定把咖啡煮开。他现在记起那是霍普金斯的做法。他曾经和霍普金斯为所有事情争论过。等咖啡烧开的同时，他打开了一小罐杏子。他喜欢开罐头。他把罐头里的杏子倒进一个锡杯里。看着火上的咖啡壶，他喝着杏子的糖汁，起初小心翼翼地以免洒出来，随后沉思般地吮吸着杏子。它们比新鲜杏子还好。
The coffee boiled as he watched. The lid came up and coffee and grounds ran down the side of the pot. Nick took it off the grill. It was a triumph for Hopkins. He put sugar in the empty apricot cup and poured some of the coffee out to cool. It was too hot to pour and he used his hat to hold the handle of the coffee pot. He would not let it steep in the pot at all. Not the first cup. It should be straight Hopkins all the way. Hop deserved that. He was a very serious coffee drinker. He was the most serious man Nick had ever known. Not heavy, serious. That was a long time ago. Hopkins spoke without moving his lips. He had played polo. He made millions of dollars in Texas. He had borrowed car fare to go to Chicago, when the wire came that his first big well had come in. He could have wired for money. That would have been too slow. They called Hop’s girl the Blonde Venus. Hop did not mind because she was not his real girl. Hopkins said very confidently that none of them would make fun of his real girl. He was right. Hopkins went away when the telegram came. That was on the Black River. It took eight days for the telegram to reach him. Hopkins gave away his .22 calibre Colt automatic pistol to Nick. He gave his camera to Bill. It was to remember him always by. They were all going fishing again next summer. The Hop Head was rich. He would get a yacht and they
他看着咖啡煮开。锅盖弹起，咖啡和咖啡渣沿着壶的侧面流下来。尼克把它从烤架上拿了下来。对霍普金斯来说这是一次胜利。他在空的杏子瓷杯里放了糖，倒出一些咖啡让它凉一凉。太烫了，不能直接倒，他用帽子拿住咖啡壶的把手。他一点也不让咖啡在壶里浸泡。第一杯绝不能。整杯都要是纯霍普金斯的风格。霍普应得这个。他是个非常认真的咖啡饮者。他是尼克所认识的最认真的人。不是沉重的，是真正认真的。那是很久以前的事了。霍普金斯说话时嘴唇不动。他打过马球。在得州赚了数百万。他在电报通知他的第一口大油井打出来的时候借了车费去芝加哥。他本可以电汇要钱。但那会太慢。他们叫霍普的姑娘“金发维纳斯”。霍普不介意因为她不是他的真女友。霍普金斯非常自信地说，他们没人会取笑他的真女友。他说得对。电报来了霍普金斯就走了。那是在黑河。他等电报花了八天时间才到。霍普金斯把他的.把一把 22 口径的柯尔特自动手枪给了 Nick。他把相机给了 Bill。那是为了永远记得他。他们都计划明年夏天再去钓鱼。那个 Hopkins 很有钱。他会买一艘游艇，然后他们
would all cruise along the north shore of Lake Superior. He was excited but serious. They said good-bye and all felt bad. It broke up the trip. They never saw Hopkins again. That was a long time ago on the Black River.
会沿着苏必利尔湖南岸一起游玩。他既兴奋又严肃。他们道了别，都感到难过。那件事打断了这次旅程。他们再也没见过 Hopkins。那是在黑河上的很久以前的事了。
Nick drank the coffee, the coffee according to Hopkins. The coffee was bitter. Nick laughed. It made a good ending to the story. His mind was starting to work. He knew he could choke it because he was tired enough. He spilled the coffee out of the pot and shook the grounds loose into the fire. He lit a cigarette and went inside the tent. He took off his shoes and trousers, sitting on the blankets, rolled the shoes up inside the trousers for a pillow and got in between the blankets.
Nick 喝了那杯咖啡，那是按照 Hopkins 的方式冲的咖啡。咖啡很苦。Nick 笑了。这给故事画上了一个不错的句号。他的思路开始运转。他知道自己可以把它憋回去，因为他已经够累了。他把壶里的咖啡倒掉，把渣子抖进火里。他点上一支烟，走进帐篷。他脱下鞋子和裤子，坐在毯子上，把鞋子塞进裤腿里当枕头，钻进毯子里。
Out through the front of the tent he watched the glow of the fire, when the night wind blew on it. It was a quiet night. The swamp was perfectly quiet. Nick stretched under the blanket comfortably. A mosquito hummed close to his ear. Nick sat up and lit a match. The mosquito was on the canvas, over his head. Nick moved the match quickly up to it. The mosquito made a satisfactory hiss in the flame. The match went out. Nick lay down again under the blanket. He turned on his side and shut his eyes. He was sleepy. He felt sleep coming. He curled up under the blanket and went to sleep.
他从帐篷前面往外望着火光，被夜风一吹。夜很静。沼泽一片寂静。尼克舒舒服服地在毯子下面伸了伸。一只蚊子在他耳边嗡嗡叫。尼克坐起来划亮了一根火柴。蚊子在帆布上，在他头顶。尼克把火柴迅速移到它旁边。蚊子在火焰里发出令人满足的嘶嘶声。火柴熄了。尼克又躺回毯子下面。他侧过身闭上眼睛。他困了，感到睡意袭来。他卷起身躲在毯子里睡着了。
They hanged Sam Cardinella at six o’clock in the morning in the corridor of the county jail. The corridor was high and narrow with tiers of cells on either side. All the cells were occupied. The men had been brought in for the hanging. Five men sentenced to be hanged were in the five top cells. Three of the men to be hanged were negroes. They were very frightened. One of the white men sat on his cot with his head in his hands. The other lay flat on his cot with a blanket wrapped around his head.
他们在县监狱走廊里于早上六点绞死了萨姆·卡迪内拉。走廊又高又窄，两侧是两层的牢房。所有牢房都有人。那些人是为了绞刑被押进来的。五个被判绞刑的人被关在最上面的五个牢房里。将要被绞死的三个人是黑人。他们非常害怕。一个白人坐在床铺上，双手抱着头。另一个平躺在床铺上，头上裹着毯子。
They came out on to the gallows through a door in the wall. There were seven of them including two priests. They were carrying Sam Cardinella. He had been like that since about four o’clock in the morning.
他们从墙上的一扇门走上了绞刑架。他们共有七人，包括两名神父。他们抬着萨姆·卡迪内拉。自从大约早上四点起，他就是那副样子。
While they were strapping his legs together two guards held him up and the two priests were whispering to him. ‘Be a man, my son,’ said one priest. When they came toward him with the cap to go over his head Sam Cardinella lost control of his sphincter muscle. The guards who had been holding him up both dropped him. They were both disgusted. ‘How about a chair, Will?’ asked one of the guards. ‘Better get one,’ said a man in a derby hat.
当他们把他的腿绑在一起时，两名狱卒扶着他，两位神父在他耳边低声说话。“做个男人，我的儿子，”一位神父说。当他们拿着要套在他头上的罩兜朝他走来时，萨姆·卡迪内拉失去了对括约肌的控制。一直扶着他的狱卒两人都把他放下了。他们都感到厌恶。“来把椅子怎么样，Will？”一个狱卒问。“最好找一把，”戴圆顶软礼帽的那人说。
When they all stepped back on the scaffolding back of the drop, which was very heavy, built of oak and steel and swung on ball bearings, Sam Cardinella was left sitting there strapped tight, the younger of the two priests kneeling beside the chair. The priest skipped back on to the scaffolding, just before the drop fell.
当他们都退到掉落口后方的脚手架上时，那脚手架又重又结实，由橡木和钢建成，装在滚珠轴承上摆动，萨姆·卡迪内拉被紧绑着独自坐在那里，两位神父中年轻的那个跪在椅子旁。掉落机关落下前，神父在脚手架上往后跳开了。

BIG TWO-HEARTED RIVER: PART I

In the morning the sun was up and the tent was starting to get hot. Nick crawled out under the mosquito netting stretched across the mouth of the tent, to look at the morning. The grass was wet on his hands as he came out. He held his trousers and his shoes in his hands. The sun was just up over the hill. There was the meadow, the river and the swamp. There were birch trees in the green of the swamp on the other side of the river.
清晨太阳升起，帐篷开始变热。尼克从拉在帐篷口的蚊帐下爬出来，看着清晨。他出来时手上沾着草的湿气。他手里拽着裤子和鞋子。太阳刚刚越过山岗。那儿有草地、河流和沼泽。河对岸的沼泽绿意中有白桦树。
The river was clear and smoothly fast in the early morning. Down about two hundred yards were three logs all the way across
河水清澈，清晨流速平稳而快捷。下游大约两百码处有三根横跨全河的原木
the stream. They made the water smooth and deep above them. As Nick watched, a mink crossed the river on the logs and went into the swamp. Nick was excited. He was excited by the early morning and the river. He was really too hurried to eat breakfast, but he knew he must. He built a little fire and put on the coffee pot.
溪水被它们在上游冲洗得平缓而深。尼克看着，一只水貂顺着原木过了河，钻进了沼泽。尼克很兴奋。清晨和河流使他兴奋。他其实太匆忙以至于不想吃早餐，但他知道必须吃。他生了个小火，把咖啡壶放上去煮。
While the water was heating in the pot he took an empty bottle and went down over the edge of the high ground to the meadow. The meadow was wet with dew and Nick wanted to catch grasshoppers for bait before the sun dried the grass. He found plenty of good grasshoppers. They were at the base of the grass stems. Sometimes they clung to a grass stem. They were cold and wet with the dew, and could not jump until the sun warmed them. Nick picked them up, taking only the medium-sized brown ones, and put them into the bottle. He turned over a log and just under the shelter of the edge were several hundred hoppers. It was a grasshopper lodging house. Nick put about fifty of the medium browns into the bottle. While he was picking up the hoppers the others warmed in the sun and commenced to hop away. They flew when they hopped. At first they made one flight and stayed stiff when they landed, as though they were dead.
水壶里的水在烧的时候，他拿了一个空瓶子，顺着高地的边缘下到草地去。草地上满是露水，尼克想在太阳把草晒干之前抓些蚂蚱当饵。他找到很多好的蚂蚱。它们在草茎的根部。有时它们紧贴着一根草茎。它们被露水打湿，身体冰冷，直到太阳把它们晒暖才会跳。尼克把它们捡起来，只挑中等大小的褐色的，放进瓶子里。他掀开一块倒下的树桩，在树桩边的遮蔽处正好有几百只蚂蚱。那是个蚂蚱的栖息处。尼克把大约五十只中等褐色的放进了瓶子。当他在拣蚂蚱的时候，其他的在太阳下暖和过来，开始跳走。它们跳的时候会飞。起初它们只飞一小段，落地后僵硬地停着，好像死了似的。
Nick knew that by the time he was through with breakfast they would be as lively as ever. Without dew on the grass it would take him all day to catch a bottle full of good grasshoppers and he would have to crush many of them, slamming at them with his hat. He washed his hands at the stream. He was excited to be near it. Then be walked up to the tent. The hoppers were already jumping stiffly in the grass. In the bottle, warmed by the sun, they were jumping in a mass. Nick put in a pine stick as a cork. It plugged the mouth of the bottle enough, so the hoppers could not get out and left plenty of air passage.
尼克知道等他吃完早饭时它们会像从前一样活跃起来。草上没了露水，他要抓满一瓶好蝗虫得花上一整天，他还得压死很多，拿帽子猛拍它们。他在溪边洗了手。能在附近让他很兴奋。然后他走到帐篷那儿。草蝗已经在草丛里僵硬地跳动着。放在瓶子里，被太阳晒暖了，它们成群地跳着。尼克塞进一根松木小棍当塞子。它把瓶口堵住得差不多，蝗虫出不来，同时又留有足够的空气通道。
He had rolled the log back and knew he could get grasshoppers there every morning.
他把那根木头滚回原处，知道每天早晨都可以在那里抓到蝗虫。
Nick laid the bottle full of jumping grasshoppers against a pine trunk. Rapidly he mixed some buckwheat flour with water and stirred it smooth, one cup of flour, one cup of water. He put a handful of coffee in the pot and dipped a lump of grease out of a can and slid it sputtering across the hot skillet. On the smoking skillet he poured smoothly the buckwheat batter. It spread like lava, the grease spitting sharply. Around the edges the buckwheat
尼克把装满跳动蝗虫的瓶子靠在一棵松树干上。他迅速把一些荞麦粉和水混合，搅匀成糊状，一杯面粉，一杯水。他往壶里放了一把咖啡，从罐头里舀出一块脂肪，嘶哑地滑到热煎锅上。在冒烟的煎锅上，他平稳地倒入荞麦糊。它像熔岩一样摊开，脂肪发出尖锐的噼啪声。荞麦糊在边缘处
cake began to firm, then brown, then crisp. The surface was bubbling slowly to porousness. Nick pushed under the browned under surface with a fresh pine chip. He shook the skillet sideways and the cake was loose on the surface. I won’t try and flop it, he thought. He slid the chip of clean wood all the way under the cake, and flopped it over on to its face. It sputtered in the pan.
蛋糕开始凝固，然后变褐，继而酥脆。表面慢慢起泡，变得多孔。尼克用一片新鲜的松木片把褐色的底面撬起。他把平底锅横晃了一下，蛋糕在表面上已经松动。他心想我不打算翻跟斗。他把那片干净的木片完全滑到蛋糕下面，把蛋糕翻到表面朝下。它在锅里发出噼啪声。
When it was cooked Nick regreased the skillet. He used all the batter. It made another big flapjack and one smaller one.
熟了以后尼克又给平底锅抹了油。他把所有面糊都用完了。又做了一个大薄煎饼和一个小的。
Nick ate a big flapjack and a smaller one, covered with apple butter. He put apple butter on the third cake, folded it over twice, wrapped it in oiled paper and put it in his shirt pocket. He put the apple butter jar back in the pack and cut bread for two sandwiches.
尼克吃了一个大薄煎饼和一个小的，抹满苹果酱。他把苹果酱抹在第三个饼上，把它对折两次，用油纸包好，放进衬衫口袋里。他把苹果酱罐放回背包，切了面包做两份三明治。
In the pack he found a big onion. He sliced it in two and peeled the silky outer skin. Then he cut one half into slices and made onion sandwiches. He wrapped them in oiled paper and buttoned them in the other pocket of his khaki shirt. He turned the skillet upside down on the grill, drank the coffee, sweetened and yellow brown with the condensed milk in it, and tidied up the camp. It was a good camp.
在背包里他找到一个大洋葱。他把它劈成两半，剥去丝滑的外皮。然后把一半切成片，做了洋葱三明治。他用油纸包好，扣在卡其色衬衫的另一个口袋里。他把平底锅倒扣在炉架上，喝了咖啡，咖啡因为炼乳而呈甜而黄褐色，然后收拾营地。营地很不错。
Nick took his fly rod out of the leather rod-case, jointed it, and shoved the rod-case back into the tent. He put on the reel and threaded the line through the guides. He had to hold it from hand to hand, as he threaded it, or it would slip back through its own weight. It was a heavy, double tapered fly line. Nick had paid eight dollars for it a long time ago. It was made heavy to lift back in the air and come forward flat and heavy and straight to make it possible to cast a fly which has no weight. Nick opened the aluminium leader box. The leaders were coiled between the damp flannel pads. Nick had wet the pads at the water cooler on the train up to St. Ignace. In the damp pads the gut leaders had softened and Nick unrolled one and tied it by a loop at the end of the heavy fly line. He fastened a hook on the end of the leader. It was a small hook; very thin and springy.
尼克从皮质鱼竿盒里取出他的毛钓竿，把竿节接好，又把竿盒塞回帐篷。他装上钓线轮，并把线穿过导环。穿线时他得用手一只接一只地拿着，否则线会因自身的重量往回滑。这是一根沉重的双锥形毛钓线。很久以前尼克为它付了八美元。线做得沉重是为了能在往后抬起时把线带到空中，然后向前平直沉重地伸展开，从而能抛出没有重量的假饵。尼克打开铝制前导线盒。前导线卷在潮湿的法兰绒垫之间。尼克在坐火车到圣伊格纳斯时在饮水机处把垫子打湿了。潮湿的垫子使鱼肠前导线变软，尼克把一段展开来并把它以一个环结系在那根沉重毛钓线的末端。他在前导线末端拴了一个钩子。是个小钩子；很细且有弹性。
Nick took it from his hook book, sitting with the rod across his lap. He tested the knot and the spring of the rod by pulling the line taut. It was a good feeling. He was careful not to let the hook bite into his finger.
尼克把它从他的钩子簿里取出，钓竿横放在膝上坐着。他通过拉紧鱼线试了结头和竿的弹性。感觉很好。他小心翼翼，避免鱼钩刺到手指。
He started down to the stream, holding his rod, the bottle of grasshoppers hung from his neck by a thong tied in half hitches
他抓着鱼竿朝小溪下去，脖子上挂着一瓶蚱蜢，瓶颈用半结套在绳子上
around the neck of the bottle. His landing net hung by a hook from his belt. Over his shoulder was a long flour sack tied at each corner into an ear. The cord went over his shoulder. The sack flapped against his legs.
瓶子的颈部套在绳子上。他的抄网用钩子挂在腰带上。肩上搭着一个长长的面粉口袋，四角各系成一个耳朵。绳子搭在他的肩上。口袋拍打着他的腿。
Nick felt awkward and professionally happy with all his equipment hanging from him. The grasshopper bottle swung against his chest. In his shirt the breast pockets bulged against him with the lunch and his fly book.
尼克感到有些笨拙，但对自己满身的装备感到职业性的高兴。装蚱蜢的瓶子在胸前摆动。他衬衫的胸袋因午餐和鱼饵书鼓起来顶着。
He stepped into the stream. It was a shock. His trousers clung tight to his legs. His shoes felt the gravel. The water was a rising cold shock.
他踏入溪水。那是一阵震惊。裤子紧贴在腿上。鞋子能感觉到卵石。水是一股越来越冷的冲击。
Rushing, the current sucked against his legs. Where he stepped in, the water was over his knees. He waded with the current. The gravel slid under his shoes. He looked down at the swirl of water below each leg and tipped up the bottle to get a grasshopper.
水流湍急，水流冲击着他的腿。他踩进去的地方，水没过膝盖。他顺着水流涉行。砂砾在他鞋下滑动。他低头看着每条腿下的旋涡，把瓶口倾斜去抓一只蚱蜢。
The first grasshopper gave a jump in the neck of the bottle and went out into the water. He was sucked under in the whirl by Nick’s right leg and came to the surface a little way downstream. He floated rapidly, kicking. In a quick circle, breaking the smooth surface of the water, he disappeared. A trout had taken him.
第一只蚱蜢在瓶颈处弹起，跳进了水里。它被尼克右腿形成的漩涡吸入水下，又在下游不远处浮出水面。它迅速地漂浮着、踢动着。在一个快速的回转中，打破了水面的平静，它消失了。一条鳟鱼咬住了它。
Another hopper poked his face out of the bottle. His antennæ wavered. He was getting his front legs out of the bottle to jump. Nick took him by the head and held him while he threaded the slim hook under his chin, down through his thorax and into the last segments of his abdomen. The grasshopper took hold of the hook with his front feet, spitting tobacco juice on it. Nick dropped him into the water.
另一只蚱蜢把脸探出瓶口。它的触角颤动着，正把前腿伸出瓶子准备跳。尼克抓住它的头稳住，然后把细钩从下巴下面穿过胸部，插入腹部最后一节。蚱蜢用前足抓住钩子，向上吐着烟草汁。尼克把它放进水里。
Holding the rod in his right hand he let out line against the pull of the grasshopper in the current. He stripped off line from the rcel with his left hand and let it run free. He could see the hopper in the little waves of the current. It went out of sight.
他右手握着鱼竿，让线在水流中顺着那只草 hopper 的拉力放出去。他左手从卷线轮上放出线，让它自由滑动。他在小浪里看见那只 hopper。它渐渐隐入视线之外。
There was a tug on the line. Nick pulled against the taut line. It was his first strike. Holding the now living rod across the current, he brought in the line with his left hand. The rod bent in jerks, the trout pumping against the current. Nick knew it was a small one. He lifted the rod straight up in the air. It bowed with the pull.
线有了拉力。Nick 朝紧绷的线上用力。他这是第一次下钩。把现在有生命般的鱼竿横在水流上，他用左手收线。鱼竿一阵阵颤弯，鳟鱼在逆流中抽动。Nick 知道这条不大。他把鱼竿直直举到空中。它在拉力下弯曲。
He saw the trout in the water jerking with his head and body against the shifting tangent of the line in the stream.
他看见水中的鳟鱼用头和身子跟着水流中线的变化抽动。
Nick took the line in his left hand and pulled the trout, thumping
Nick 左手拉着线，把鳟鱼往岸上拖，砰砰作响
tiredly against the current, to the surface. His back was mottled the clear, water-over-gravel colour, his side flashing in the sun. The rod under his right arm, Nick stooped, dipping his right hand into the current. He held the trout, never still, with his moist right hand, while he unhooked the barb from his mouth, then dropped him back into the stream.
他疲倦地逆着水流，用背鳍抵着水面的碎石色，侧身在阳光下闪着光。鱼竿夹在右臂下，Nick 弯下身，把右手伸进水流里。他用湿漉漉的右手抓住那条鳟鱼，它不停地动着，他从鱼嘴上取下倒刺，然后把它放回了溪流里。
He hung unsteadily in the current, then settled to the bottom beside a stone. Nick reached down his hand to touch him, his arm to the elbow under water. The trout was steady in the moving stream, resting on the gravel, beside a stone. As Nick’s fingers touched him, touched his smooth, cool, underwater feeling he was gone, gone in a shadow across the bottom of the stream.
它在水流中摇摇欲坠地悬着，随后在一块石头旁的底部稳住了。Nick 伸手去触摸它，手臂肘部浸在水下。鳟鱼在流动的水里稳稳地伏在砾石上，靠在一块石头旁。随着 Nick 的指尖触到它，触到它那光滑、凉凉、在水下的感觉时，它消失了，像一道阴影掠过溪底，消失了。
  • He’s all right, Nick thought. He was only tired.
    它没事，Nick 想。它只是累了。
He had wet his hand before he touched the trout, so he would not disturb the delicate mucus that covered him. If a trout was touched with a dry hand, a white fungus attacked the unprotected spot. Years before when he had fished crowded streanns, with fly fishermen ahead of him and behind him, Nick had again and again come on dead trout, furry with white fungus, drifted against a rock, or floating belly up in some pool. Nick did not like to fish with other men on the river. Unless they were of your party, they spoiled it.
他在碰到鳟鱼之前先把手弄湿，这样就不会扰动覆盖在鱼身上的细腻粘液。如果用干手碰鳟鱼，未受保护的部位会被白色真菌侵袭。多年前，当他在拥挤的溪流中钓鱼，前后都是飞蝇钓者时，尼克一次又一次地碰到死鳟鱼，身上长着白色毛状真菌，漂到岩石上，或在某个池子里仰浮着。尼克不喜欢和其他男人一起在河上钓鱼。除非他们是你队里的，否则会把事弄糟。
He wallowed down the stream, above his knees in the current, through the fifty yards of shallow water above the pile of logs that crossed the stream. He did not rebait his hook and held it in his hand as he waded. He was certain he could catch small trout in the shallows, but he did not want them. There would be no big trout in the shallows this time of day.
他在溪中蹚行，水没过膝盖，穿过那堆横跨溪流的木桩上方五十码的浅水。他没有重新上饵，手里握着鱼钩跋涉。他确信自己能在浅滩钓到小鳟鱼，但他不想要那些。这个时候浅水中不会有大鳟鱼。
Now the water deepened up his thighs sharply and coldly. Ahead was the smooth dammed-back flood of water above the logs. The water was smooth and dark; on the left, the lower edge of the meadow; on the right the swamp.
现在水深骤然上到大腿，带着寒意。前方是被木桩拦住而平静下来的水面。水面平滑而昏暗；左边是草地的下缘；右边是沼泽。
Nick leaned back against the current and took a hopper from the bottle. He threaded the hopper on the hook and spat on him for good luck. Then he pulled several yards of line from the reel and tossed the hopper out ahead on to the fast, dark water. It floated down toward the logs, then the weight of the line pulled the bait under the surface. Nick held the rod in his right hand, letting the line run out through his fingers.
尼克靠着逆流坐下，从瓶子里拿出一个跳虫饵。他把跳虫套在钩子上，往它身上吐了口唾沫以求好运。然后他从卷线器上拉出好几码线，把跳虫抛到前方快速、黑暗的水面上。它顺水漂向那些木头，然后线的重量把饵拉到水面下。尼克右手握着鱼竿，让渔线从指间滑出。
There was a long tug. Nick struck and the rod came alive and
猛地一阵拉扯。尼克一提竿，鱼竿活了起来并且
dangerous, bent double, the line tightening, coming out of water, tightening, all in a heavy, dangerous, steady pull. Nick felt the moment when the leader would break if the strain increased and let the line go.
危险地，双重弯曲，渔线绷紧，从水面拉出，绷紧，全是一种沉重、危险、均匀的拉力。尼克感觉到如果拉力再增大会断掉前导线的那一瞬，于是放开了渔线。
The reel racheted into a mechanical shriek as the line went out in a rush. Too fast. Nick could not check it, the line rushing out, the reel note rising as the line ran out.
随着渔线飞速甩出，卷线器发出机械般的尖厉啸声。速度太快了。尼克无法制住它，渔线呼啸着飞出，卷线器的音调随着渔线的外滑而升高。
With the core of the reel showing, his heart feeling stopped with the excitement, leaning back against the current that mounted icily his thighs. Nick thumbed the reel hard with his left hand. It was awkward getting his thumb inside the fly reel frame.
当卷轴的芯轴露出来时，他的心因激动仿佛停止了跳动，身体向后靠在那股冰冷上升到大腿的水流上。Nick 用左手用力拇指按着线轮。把拇指伸进飞钓线轮的框里很别扭。
As he put on pressure the line tightened into sudden hardness and beyond the logs a huge trout went high out of water. As he jumped, Nick lowered the tip of the rod. But he felt, as he dropped the tip to ease he strain, the moment when the strain was too great; the hardness too tight. Of course, the leader had broken. There was no mistaking the feeling when all spring left the line and it became dry and hard. Then it went slack.
当他施加压力时，钓线骤然绷得很紧，越过倒木，一条巨大的鳟鱼高高跃出水面。当它跃起时，Nick 将鱼竿尖压低。但他感觉到，当他放低竿尖以缓和拉力的瞬间，拉力已过于强烈；绷得太紧。果然，前导线已断。那种感觉无可错认——当弹性从线中消失，线变得干硬时。然后线松了。
-His mouth dry, his heart down, Nick reeled in. He had never seen so big a trout. There was a heaviness, a power not to be held, and then the bulk of him, as he jumped. He looked as broad as a salmon.
——嘴唇干燥，心情沮丧，Nick 缩线上来。他从未见过这么大的鳟鱼。那鱼沉重有力，不可遏止，然后在它跃起时显出庞大的身体。他看起来像一条宽大的鲑鱼。
Nick’s hand was shaky. He reeled in slowly. The thrill had been too much. He felt, vaguely, a little sick, as though it would be better to sit down.
Nick 的手在发抖。他慢慢收线。那种激动过于强烈。他模糊地感到，有点恶心，好像还是坐下会好些。
The leader had broken where the hook was tied to it. Nick took it in his hand. He thought of the trout somewhere on the bottom, holding himself steady over the gravel, far down below the light, under the logs, with the hook in his jaw. Nick knew the trout’s teeth would cut through the snell of the hook. The hook would imbed itself in his jaw. He’d bet the trout was angry. Anything that size would be angry. That was a trout. He had been solidly hooked. Solid as a rock. He felt like a rock, too, before he started off. By God, he was a big one. By God, he was the biggest one I ever heard of.
领导线在钩子绑着的地方断了。尼克把它拿在手里。他想起底下某处的鳟鱼，稳稳地盘在碎石上，远离光亮，藏在木头下面，嘴里还挂着钩子。尼克知道鳟鱼的牙会咬断钩子的线。钩子会钉进它的下颚。他敢打赌那条鳟鱼正气得发狠。那么大的鱼都会生气。那就是一条鳟鱼。它被牢牢地钩住了。像岩石一样牢固。自己在开始拉动之前也觉得像块石头。天哪，它真大。天哪，它是我听说过的最大的一条。
Nick climbed out on to the meadow and stood, water running down his trousers and out of his shoes, his shoes squelchy. He went over and sat on the logs. He did not want to rush his sensations any.
尼克爬到草地上站着，水顺着裤子流下来，从鞋里流出，鞋子咯吱作响。他走过去坐在木头上。他不想加速自己的感受。
He wriggled his toes in the water, in his shoes, and got out a cigarette from his breast pocket. He lit it and tossed the match into the fast water below the logs. A tiny trout rose at the match, as it
他在水里、在鞋里扭动脚趾，从胸口袋里掏出一支烟。点着后把火柴掷进木头下急流里。一条小鳟鱼朝着那根在急流中转动的火柴跃出水面。
swung around in the fast current. Nick laughed. He would finish the cigarette.
尼克笑了。他要把这支烟抽完。
He sat on the logs, smoking, drying in the sun, the sun warm on his back, the river shallow ahead entering the woods, curving into the woods, shallows, light glittering, big water-smooth rocks, cedars along the bank and white birches, the logs warm in the sun, smooth to sit on, without bark, grey to the touch; slowly the feeling of disappointment left him. It went away slowly, the feeling of disappointment that came sharply after the thrill that made his shoulders ache. It was all right now. His rod lying out on the logs, Nick tied a new hook on the leader, pulling the gut tight until it grimped into itself in a hard knot.
他坐在木桩上，抽着烟，晒着太阳，后背被阳光温暖着，前面河水变浅进入树林，弯进树林，浅滩，光在闪烁，大块光滑如水的石头，河岸边有雪松和白桦，木桩在阳光下暖洋洋的，坐着光滑，没有树皮，摸起来发灰；那种失望的感觉慢慢离开了他。那种在使他的肩膀依然酸痛的激动之后骤然到来的失望慢慢过去了。现在一切都好。他的鱼竿放在木桩上，Nick 在主线上系了一个新钩子，把内线拉紧直到它在自己身上拧成一个结。
He baited it, then picked up the rod and walked to the far end of the logs to get into the water, where it was not too deep. Under and beyond the logs was a deep pool. Nick walked around the shallow shelf near the swamp shore until he came out on the shallow bed of the stream.
他给钩上了饵，然后拿起鱼竿走到木桩的尽头下水去，那儿水不太深。木桩下及更远处有一个深水潭。Nick 沿着沼泽岸边的浅层走，直到走到小溪的浅床上。
On the left, where the meadow ended and the woods began, a great elm tree was uprooted. Gone over in a storm, it lay back into the woods, its roots clotted with dirt, grass growing in them, rising a solid bank beside the stream. The river cut to the edge of the uprooted tree. From where Nick stood he could see deep channels, like ruts, cut in the shallow bed of the stream by the flow of the current. Pebbly where he stood and pebbly and full of boulders beyond; where it curved near the tree roots, the bed of the stream was marly and between the ruts of deep water green weed fronds swung in the current.
在左边，草地的尽头与树林的开始处，有一棵大榆树被连根拔起。被风暴掀倒后，它向树林里倒去，根部裹着泥土，草在根间生长，堆成了一道紧贴小溪的土堤。河流切到那株被连根拔起的树的边缘。从尼克站立处他能看到浅浅的河床被水流冲出深沟，像轮槽一样。站立处满是卵石，向外也是卵石并且布满巨石；当河流在树根附近弯曲时，河床呈泥灰状，在那些深水沟之间，绿色的水草叶在水流中摇摆。
Nick swung the rod back over his shoulder and forward, and the line, curving forward, laid the grasshopper down on one of the deep channels in the weeds. A trout struck and Nick hooked him.
尼克把鱼竿从肩后摆回再向前甩去，鱼线向前弯曲，把蚱蜢放在水草中一条深沟上。 一条鳟鱼咬钩，尼克把它钩住。
Holding the rod far out toward the uprooted tree and sloshing backward in the curent, Nick worked the trout, plunging, the rod bending alive, out of the danger of the weeds into the open river. Holding the rod, pumping alive against the current, Nick brought the trout in. He rushed, but always came, the spring of the rod yielding to the rushes, sometimes jerking under water, but always bringing him in. Nick eased downstream with the rushes. The rod above his head he led the trout over the net, then lifted.
把鱼竿高高伸向被连根拔起的树并朝着逆流甩去，尼克在水流中来回摇曳着那条鳟鱼，鱼猛冲着，鱼竿活生生地弯着，把鱼从水草的危险处逼到开阔的河面。尼克握着竿，迎着水流不停地控着那股力，把鳟鱼带上来。他急促地拉，但鱼总被拉上来，鱼竿的弹性在猛冲面前屈服，有时在水下抽动，但总能把鱼带上来。尼克顺着急流往下松了点。把竿举在头顶，他把鳟鱼引到网上，然后一提。
The trout hung heavy in the net, mottled trout back and silver
鳟鱼沉甸甸地挂在网里，背部斑驳，银白的
sides in the meshes. Nick unhooked him; heavy sides, good to hold, big undershot jaw, and slipped him, heaving and big sliding, into the long sack that hung from his shoulders in the water.
侧身嵌在网眼中。尼克把钩取下；厚实的身躯，抓着很稳，嘴下大且外翻，然后把它滑入长布囊中，滑进时它又大又挣扎，布囊从他肩上垂在水里。
Nick spread the mouth of the sack against the current and it filled, heavy with water. He held it up, the bottom in the stream, and the water poured out through the sides. Inside at the bottom was the big trout, alive in the water.
尼克把布囊口朝着水流张开，水就灌满了，沉甸甸的。他把囊提起，底部仍在溪流里，水从侧缝流出。囊底里有条大鳟鱼，活着泡在水中。
Nick moved downstream. The sack out ahead of him sunk heavy in the water, pulling from his shoulders.
尼克向下游移动。前面的袋子在水里沉重地沉着，拉着他的肩膀。
It was getting hot, the sun hot on the back of his neck.
天气开始热了，太阳把脖颈后面晒得很烫。
Nick had one good trout. He did not care about getting many trout. Now the stream was shallow and wide. There were trees along both banks. The trees of the left bank made short shadows on the current in the forenoon sun. Nick knew there were trout in each shadow. In the afternoon, after the sun had crossed toward the hills, the trout would be in the cool shadows on the other side of the stream.
尼克有一条大好的鳟鱼。他并不在乎抓多少鳟鱼。现在溪流变得又浅又宽。两岸都有树。左岸的树在上午的阳光下在水流上投出短短的影子。尼克知道每个影子里都有鳟鱼。下午，太阳越过朝山那边，鳟鱼就会在溪流另一侧的凉影里。
The very biggest ones would lie up close to the bank. You could always pick them up there on the Black. When the sun was down they all moved out into the current. Just when the sun made the water blinding in the glare before it went down, you were liable to strike a big trout anywhere in the current. It was almost impossible to fish then, the surface of the water was blinding as a mirror in the sun. Of course, you could fish upstream, but in a stream like the Black, or this, you had to wallow against the current and in a deep place, the water piled up on you. It was no fun to fish upstream with this much current.
最大的一些鱼会靠近岸边躺着。在黑河上你总能在那里捕到它们。太阳下山的时候它们全都游到水流中去。正当太阳把水面照得刺眼耀目、快要落山的时候，你很可能在水流的任何地方钓到一条大鳟鱼。那时几乎不可能钓鱼，水面在阳光下像镜子一样刺眼。当然你可以向上游钓，但在像黑河或这样的溪里，你得顶着水流行进，在深处水会把你顶住。顶着这么大的水流向上游钓鱼一点也不好玩。
Nick moved along through the shallow stretch watching the banks for deep holes. A beech tree grew close beside the river, so that the branches hung down into the water. The stream went back in under the leaves. There were always trout in a place like that.
尼克沿着浅滩走着，盯着河岸寻找深水坑。一棵山毛榉长得靠近河边，枝条垂到水里。溪流在树叶下回流。那种地方总有鳟鱼。
Nick did not care about fishing that hole. He was sure he would get hooked in the branches.
尼克并不想钓那个坑。他确信鱼饵会挂在树枝上。
It looked deep though. He dropped the grasshopper so the current took it under water, back in under the overhanging branch. The line pulled hard and Nick struck. The trout threshed heavily, half out of water in the leaves and branches. The line was caught. Nick pulled hard and the trout was off. He reeled in and holding the hook in his hand, walked down the stream.
不过看起来很深。他把蚂蚱放下，让水流把它冲到水下，回到那垂下的树枝下面。钓线猛地一紧，尼克一顿竿。鳟鱼剧烈挣扎，半个身子跃出水面，在叶子和枝条间翻腾。钓线被挂住了。尼克用力一拉，鱼跑了。他收线，手里拿着钩子，沿着溪流走下去。
Ahead, close to the left bank, was a big log. Nick saw it was hollow; pointing up river the current entered it smoothly, only a little ripple spread each side of the log. The water was deepening. The top of the hollow log was grey and dry. It was partly in the shadow.
前方靠左岸有一根大木头。尼克看到它是空心的；顺着河流方向，水流平滑地流进木头里，木头两侧只泛起一点涟漪。水越发深了。空心木头的顶部灰而干燥。它部分处在阴影中。
Nick took the cork out of the grasshopper bottle and a hopper clung to it. He picked him off, hooked him and tossed him out. He held the rod far out so that the hopper on the water moved into the current flowing into the hollow log. Nick lowered the rod and the hopper floated in. There was a heavy strike. Nick swung the rod against the pull. It felt as though he were hooked into the log itself, except for the live feeling.
尼克把软木塞从蚱蜢瓶里拔出来，一只蚱蜢还粘在上面。他把它摘下，钩在钩上，扔了出去。他把鱼竿伸得很远，水面上的蚱蜢随水流向空心原木的流入处移动。尼克放低鱼竿，蚱蜢随水漂进去了。猛然一记猛击。尼克顺着拉力甩动鱼竿。感觉好像整个人都被钩在原木上，除了那种活生生的感觉之外。
He tried to force the fish out into the current. It came, heavily.
他试着把鱼逼到水流里来。它沉重地游来。
The line went slack, and Nick thought the trout was gone. Then he saw him, very near, in the current, shaking his head, trying to get the hook out. His mouth was clamped shut. He was fighting the hook in the clear flowing current.
鱼线变得松弛，尼克以为鳟鱼已经跑了。然后他看见了它，就在水流里，非常近，摇着头，想把钩子弄出来。它嘴巴紧闭。在那清澈的流水中，它在与鱼钩搏斗。
Looping the line with his left hand, Nick swung the rod to make the line taut and tried to lead the trout toward the net, but he was gone, out of sight, the line pumping. Nick fought him against the current, letting him thump in the water against the spring of the rod. He shifted the rod to his left hand, worked the trout upstream, holding his weight, fighting on the rod, and then let him down into the net. He lifted him clear of the water, a heavy half circle in the net, the net dripping, unhooked him and slid him into the sack.
用左手把线圈住，尼克挥动鱼竿让鱼线拉紧，试图把鳟鱼牵向鱼网，但它已经逃脱，出现在视线之外，鱼线在抽动。尼克逆流与它搏斗，让它在水中撞击，借鱼竿的弹性压住它。他把鱼竿换到左手，顺流而上操控那条鳟鱼，靠住它的力道，在竿上与之抗衡，然后把它放入鱼网。他把它从水里提起来，网内呈现一个沉甸甸的半圆，鱼网在滴水，解下鱼钩，把它滑进鱼袋里。
He spread the mouth of the sack and looked down in at the two big trout alive in the water.
他掀开鱼袋口，俯视着袋里两条在水中活着的大鳟鱼。
Through the deepening water, Nick waded over to the hollow log. He took the sack off, over his head, the trout flopping as it came out of water, and hung it so the trout were deep in the water. Then he pulled himself up on the log and sat, the water from his trousers and boots running down in the stream. He laid his rod down, moved along to the shady end of the log and took the sandwiches out of his pocket. He dipped the sandwiches in the cold water. The current carried away the crumbs. He ate the sandwiches and dipped his hat full of water to drink, the water running out through his hat just ahead of his drinking.
尼克涉过越来越深的水走到空心树干边。他把袋子从头上脱下来，鲑鳟在出水时扑腾着，他把袋子挂好，让鱼沉在水里。然后他把自己拉上树干坐下，裤子和靴子里的水沿着流回溪里。他放下鱼竿，移到树干遮阴的一端，从口袋里掏出三明治。他把三明治蘸进冰冷的水里。水流把面包屑冲走了。他吃着三明治，用帽子舀满水喝，水在他喝之前就从帽子里沿前沿流了出来。
It was cool in the shade, sitting on the log. He took a cigarette out and struck a match to light it. The match sunk into the grey wood,
坐在树干上乘凉很凉快。他掏出一根烟，划了一根火柴点燃。火柴陷进了灰色的木头里，
making a tiny furrow. Nick leaned over the side of the log, found a hard place and lit the match. He sat smoking and watching the river.
划出一道小沟。尼克俯身靠在树干边，找到一块硬处点燃了火柴。他坐着抽烟，注视着河流。
Ahead the river narrowed and went into a swamp. The river became smooth and deep and the swamp looked solid with cedar trees, their trunks close together, their branches solid. It would not be possible to walk through a swamp like that. The branches grew so low. You would have to keep almost level with the ground to move at all. You could not crash through the branches. That must be why the animals that lived in swamps were built the way they were, Nick thought.
前面河流变窄，流入一片沼泽。河面变得平滑而深，沼泽看起来被雪松树压得结实，树干挨得很近，树枝也很密。那样的沼泽不可能走过去。树枝长得很低。要移动几乎得保持贴近地面。不能把树枝撞断。尼克想，这大概就是生活在沼泽里的动物为何长成那样的原因。
He wished he had brought something to read. He felt like reading. He did not feel like going on into the swamp. He looked down the river. A big cedar slanted all the way across the stream. Beyond that the river went into the swamp.
他希望自己带了点要读的东西。他想读书。他又不想继续走进沼泽。他向下望去。一个大雪松斜横横地挡住了整条溪流。那之后河流就流入了沼泽。
Nick did not want to go in there now. He felt a reaction against deep wading with the water deepening up under his armpits, to hook big trout in places impossible to land them. In the swamp the banks were bare, the big cedars came together overhead, the sun did not come through, except in patches; in the fast deep water, in the half light, the fishing would be tragic. In the swamp fishing was a tragic adventure. Nick did not want it. He did not want to go down the stream any farther to-day.
尼克现在不想进去。他对在水越来越深、淹到腋下的地方深涉有反感，在那些无法把大鳟鱼弄上岸的地方去勾鱼。在沼泽里，河岸光秃，粗大的雪松在头顶交织，阳光透不下来，只在斑驳处透进；在流速快而又很深的水中，在那种半明半暗里，钓鱼会是悲剧性的。在沼泽里钓鱼是一种悲剧性的冒险。尼克不想要。他今天不想再往下游走了。
He took out his knife, opened it and stuck it in the log. Then he pulled up the sack, reached into it and brought out one of the trout. Holding him near the tail, hard to hold, alive, in his hand, he whacked him against the log. The trout quivered, rigid. Nick laid him on the log in the shade and broke the neck of the other fish the same way. He laid them side by side on the log. They were fine trout.
他把刀掏出来，打开，插在原木上。然后他拉起麻袋，伸手进去拿出了一条鳟鱼。把鱼尾附近抓牢，难以抓稳，还活着，他把鱼往原木上一砸。鳟鱼抽动了一下，僵住了。尼克把它放在阴凉处的原木上，用同样的办法折断另一条鱼的颈项。他把它们并排放在原木上。都是好鳟鱼。
Nick cleaned them, slitting them from the vent to the tip of the jaw. All the insides and the gills and tongue came out in one piece. They were both males; long grey-white strips of milt, smooth and clean. All the insides clean and compact, coming out all together. Nick tossed the offal ashore for the minks to find.
尼克把它们清理干净，从肛门切到上颚的尖端。所有内脏、鳃和舌头一股脑儿就掉了出来。它们都是雄鱼；长长的灰白色精液条，光滑干净。所有内脏干净而紧凑，一起被取出。尼克把下脚料扔到岸上，让水貂去找。
He washed the trout in the stream. When he held them back up in the water they looked like live fish. Their colour was not gone yet. He washed his hands and dried them on the log. Then he laid the trout on the sack spread out on the log, rolled them up in it, tied the
他在溪水里冲洗鳟鱼。把它们重新举回水中时，看上去像活鱼一样。颜色还没褪去。他洗了手，把手擦在原木上。然后把鳟鱼放在摊在原木上的麻袋上，卷进麻袋，系好
bundle and put it in the landing net. His knife was still standing, blade stuck in the log. He cleaned it on the wood and put it in his pocket.
包裹，放进登陆网里。他的刀还插着，刀刃插在原木上。他在木头上擦了擦刀，然后把刀放进了口袋。
Nick stood up on the log, holding his rod, the landing net hanging heavy, then stepped into the water and splashed ashore. He climbed the bank and cut up into the woods, toward the high ground. He was going back to camp. He looked back. The river just showed through the trees. There were plenty of days coming when he could fish the swamp.
尼克站在原木上，手里拿着鱼竿，着陆网沉重地垂着，然后跨入水中，扑通一声上了岸。他爬上河岸，沿着林地往高处走。他正要回营地。他回头看了看。河流只是从树间露出一线。还有很多日子可以去沼泽钓鱼。

L'ENVOI
告别辞

The king was working in the garden. He seemed very glad to see me. We walked through the garden. This is the queen, he said. She was clipping a rose bush. Oh how do you do, she said. We sat down at a table under a big tree and the king ordered whisky and soda. We have good whisky anyway, he said. The revolutionary committee, he told me, would not allow him to go outside the palace grounds. Plastiras is a very good man I believe, he said, but frightfully difficult. I think he did right though shooting those chaps. If Kerensky had shot a few men things might have been altogether different. Of course the great thing in this sort of an affair is not to be shot oneself!
国王正在花园里干活。他见到我似乎很高兴。我们穿过花园。“这是王后，”他说。她正在修剪一丛玫瑰。“喔，你好，”她说。我们在一棵大树下的一张桌子旁坐下，国王点了威士忌和苏打水。“我们的威士忌也不错，”他说。他告诉我，革命委员会不允许他出宫。Plastiras 是个很好的人，我想，"但非常难相处。我想他开枪打那些家伙是对的。如果柯伦斯基（Kerensky）开枪打了几个人，事情可能会完全不同。当然，在这种事里最重要的是自己别被枪毙！"
It was very jolly. We talked for a long time. Like all Greeks he wanted to go to America.
气氛非常愉快。我们谈了很久。像所有希腊人一样，他想去美国。

MEN WITHOUT WOMEN
没有女人的男人

THE UNDEFEATED
不败者
Manuel Garcia climbed the stairs to Don Miguel Retana’s office. He set down his suitcase and knocked on the door. There was no answer. Manuel, standing in the hallway, felt there was someone in the room. He felt it through the door.
曼努埃尔·加西亚爬上楼梯，来到唐·米格尔·雷塔纳的办公室。他放下手提箱，敲了敲门。没有回应。曼努埃尔站在走廊里，感觉屋里有人。他透过门感到这一点。
‘Retana,’ he said, listening.
“雷塔纳，”他一边听着一边说。
There was no answer.
没有回答。
He’s there, all right, Manuel thought.
他在那里，确实如此，曼努埃尔想。
‘Retana,’ he said and banged the door.
“雷塔纳，”他说着砰地关上门。
‘Who’s there?’ said someone in the office.
“谁在那里？”办公室里有人说道。
‘Me, Manolo,’ Manuel said.
“我，马诺洛，”曼努埃尔说。
‘What do you want?’ asked the voice.
“你要什么？”那个声音问。
‘I want to work,’ Manuel said.
“我想工作，”曼努埃尔说。
Something in the door clicked several times and it swung open. Manuel went in, carrying his suitcase.
门上的某处咔嗒了几下，门开了。曼努埃尔提着行李箱走了进去。
A little man sat behind a desk at the far side of the room. Over his head was a bull’s head, stuffed by a Madrid taxidermist; on the walls were framed photographs and bull-fight posters.
一个矮小的男子坐在房间远侧的一张办公桌后面。他头顶上方挂着一具由马德里剥制师剥制的公牛头；墙上挂着装框的照片和斗牛海报。
The little man sat looking at Manuel.
矮小的男子坐着看着曼努埃尔。
‘I thought they’d killed you,’ he said.
“我以为他们把你杀了，”他说。
Manuel knocked with his knuckles on the desk. The little man sat looking at him across the desk.
曼努埃尔用指关节敲了敲桌子。矮小的男子坐着透过桌子看着他。
‘How many corridas you had this year?’ Retana asked.
“你今年做了多少场斗牛？”雷塔纳问。
‘One,’ he answered.
“只有一场，”他回答。
‘Just that one?’ the little man asked.
“小个子又问：“就只有那一场吗？”
‘That’s all.’
“就那些。”
‘I read about it in the papers,’ Retana said. He leaned back in the chair and looked at Manuel.
“我在报纸上读到的，”雷塔纳说。他向后靠在椅子上，看着曼努埃尔。
Manuel looked up at the stuffed bull. He had seen it often before. He felt a certain family interest in it. It had killed his brother, the promising one, about nine years ago. Manuel remembered the day. There was a brass plate on the oak shield the bull’s head was mounted on. Manuel could not read it, but he imagined it was in memory of his brother. Well, he had been a good kid.
曼努埃尔抬头看那只剥制的公牛。他以前常见到它。他对它有一种家庭式的关切。大约九年前，它杀了他的兄弟——那个有前途的。曼努埃尔记得那一天。公牛头装在橡木盾牌上，盾牌上有一块铜牌。曼努埃尔看不清字，但他想那是为了纪念他兄弟写的。好吧，他是个好孩子。
The plate said: ‘The Bull “Mariposa” of the Duke of Veragua, which accepted 9 varas for 7 caballos, and caused the death of Antonio Garcia, Novillero, April 27, 1909.’
铜牌上写着：“The Bull ‘Mariposa’ of the Duke of Veragua, which accepted 9 varas for 7 caballos, and caused the death of Antonio Garcia, Novillero, April 27, 1909.”
Retana saw him looking at the stuffed bull’s head.
雷塔纳看到他在看那只剥制的公牛头。
‘The lot the Duke sent me for Sunday will make a scandal,’ he said. "They’re all bad in the legs. What do they say about them at the Café?’
“公爵给我周日安排的那一批会引起丑闻，”他说。“它们的腿都不好。他们在咖啡馆怎么说的？”
‘I don’t know,’ Manuel said. ‘I just got in.’
“我不知道，”曼努埃尔说。“我刚进来。”
‘Yes,’ Retana said. ‘You still have your bag.’
“是的，”雷塔纳说。“你还拿着你的包。”
He looked at Manuel, leaning back behind the big desk.
他看着曼努埃尔，靠在那张大课桌后面。
‘Sit down,’ he said. ‘Take off your cap.’
“坐下，”他说。“把帽子摘了。”
Manuel sat down; his cap off, his face was changed. He looked pale, and his coleta pinned forward on his head, so that it would not show under the cap, gave him a strange look.
曼努埃尔坐下了；帽子一摘，脸色变了。他看上去很苍白，头上的小辫儿被向前别着，以免从帽子下露出来，显得很奇怪。
‘You don’t look well,’ Retana said.
“你看起来不太好，”雷塔纳说。
‘I just got out of the hospital,’ Manuel said.
“我刚从医院出来，”曼努埃尔说。
‘I heard they’d cut your leg off,’ Retana said.
“我听说他们把你腿给截了，”雷塔纳说。
‘No,’ said Manuel. ‘It got all right.’
“不，”曼努埃尔说。“没事，痊愈了。”
Retana leaned forward across the desk and pushed a wooden box of cigarettes toward Manuel.
雷塔纳向前倚过桌子，把一盒木盒香烟推向曼努埃尔。
‘Have a cigarette,’ he said.
“抽根烟吧，”他说。
‘Thanks.’
“谢谢。”
Manuel lit it.
曼努埃尔点着了它。
‘Smoke?’ he said, offering the match to Retana.
“抽烟？”他说着，把火柴递给雷塔纳。
‘No,’ Retana waved his hand, ‘I never smoke.’
“不，”雷塔纳摆了摆手，“我从不抽烟。”
Retana watched him smoking.
雷塔纳看着他抽烟。
‘Why don’t you get a job and go to work?’ he said.
“你为什么不找份工作去上班？”他说。
‘I don’t want to work,’ Manuel said. ‘I am a bull-fighter.’
“我不想工作，”曼努埃尔说。“我是个斗牛士。”
‘There aren’t any bull-fighters any more,’ Retana said.
“现在已经没有斗牛士了，”雷塔纳说。
‘I’m a bull-fighter,’ Manuel said.
“我是个斗牛士，”曼努埃尔说。
‘Yes, while you’re in there,’ Retana said.
“是的——只要你还在那里面，”雷塔纳说。
Manuel laughed.
曼努埃尔笑了。
Retana sat, saying nothing and looking at Manuel.
雷塔纳坐着，沉默不语，注视着曼努埃尔。
‘I’ll put you in a nocturnal if you want,’ Retana offered.
“要是你愿意，我可以把你安排到夜班去，”Retana 提议。
‘When?’ Manuel asked.
“什么时候？”Manuel 问。
‘To-morrow night.’
“明天夜里。”
‘I don’t like to substitute for anybody,’ Manuel said. That was the way they all got killed. That was the way Salvador got killed. He tapped with his knuckles on the table.
“我不喜欢替别人顶班，”Manuel 说。那就是他们全被干掉的原因。那就是 Salvador 被干掉的原因。他用指关节敲了敲桌子。
‘It’s all I’ve got,’ Retana said.
“这就是我全部的了，”雷塔纳说。
‘Why don’t you put me on next week?’ Manuel suggested.
“你为什么不下周让我上？”曼努埃尔建议道。
‘You wouldn’t draw,’ Retana said. ‘All they want is Litri and Rubito and La Torre. Those kids are good.’
“你不会被抽中，”雷塔纳说。“他们只想看利特里和鲁比托还有拉托雷。那些小子们很厉害。”
‘They’d come to see me get it,’ Manuel said, hopefully.
“他们会来看我被打的，”曼努埃尔抱有希望地说。
‘No, they wouldn’t. They don’t know who you are any more.’
“不会的。他们不再知道你是谁了。”
‘I’ve got a lot of stuff,’ Manuel said.
“我有很多东西，”Manuel 说。
‘I’m offering to put you on to-morrow night,’ Retana said. ‘You can work with young Hernandez and kill two novillos after the Charlots.’
“我提议明天晚上把你安排上，”Retana 说。“你可以跟年轻的 Hernandez 一起出场，Charlots 之后杀两头小牛。”
‘Whose novillos?’ Manuel asked.
“谁家的小牛？”Manuel 问。
‘I don’t know. Whatever stuff they’ve got in the corrals. What the veterinaries won’t pass in the daytime.’
“我不知道。就是畜栏里他们弄的那种东西。兽医白天不会放行的那玩意儿。”
‘I don’t like to substitute,’ Manuel said.
“我不喜欢做替补，”曼努埃尔说。
‘You can take it or leave it,’ Retana said. He leaned forward over the papers. He was no longer interested. The appeal that Manuel had made to him for a moment when he thought of the old davs was gone. He would like to get him to substitute for Larita because he could get him cheaply. He could get others cheaply too. He would like to help him, though. Still he had given him the chance. It was up to him.
“要不要随你，”雷塔纳说。他向前靠在那些文件上。他已经不再感兴。曼努埃尔触及的那一瞬间、让他想起往日的请求已经消失了。他想让他替拉丽塔顶班，因为他可以便宜雇到他。他也可以便宜雇到别人。他还是愿意帮他，尽管如此，他已经给了他机会。由他自己决定了。
‘How much do I get?’ Manuel asked. He was still playing with the idea of refusing. But he knew he could not refuse.
“我拿多少？”曼努埃尔问。他仍在盘算着要不要拒绝。但他知道自己不能拒绝。
“Two hundred and fifty pesetas,” Retana said. He had thought of five hundred, but when he opened his mouth it said two hundred and fifty.
“二百五十佩塞塔，”雷塔纳说。他原本想要五百，但当他张口时却说出了二百五十。
‘You pay Villalta seven thousand,’ Manuel said.
“你付给比亚尔塔七千，”曼努埃尔说。
‘You’re not Villalta,’ Retana said.
“你不是比亚尔塔，”雷塔纳说。
‘I know it,’ Manuel said.
“我知道，”曼努埃尔说。
‘He draws it, Manolo,’ Retana said in explanation.
“他把它抽出来了，马诺洛，”雷塔纳解释道。
‘Sure,’ said Manuel. He stood up. ‘Give me three hundred, Retana.’
“当然，”曼努埃尔说。他站起来。“给我三百，雷塔纳。”
‘All right,’ Retana agreed. He reached in the drawer for a paper.
“好吧，”雷塔纳同意。他伸手到抽屉里拿出一张纸。
‘Can I have fifty now?’ Manuel asked.
“现在能先给我五十吗？”曼努埃尔问。
‘Sure,’ said Retana. He took a fifty-peseta note out of his pocketbook and laid it, spread out flat, on the table.
“当然可以，”Retana 说。他从钱夹里掏出一张五十比塞塔纸币，摊平，放在桌上。
Manuel picked it up and put it in his pocket.
Manuel 把它拾起来，放进了口袋。
‘What about a cuadrilla?’ he asked.
“那队斗牛手怎么办？”他问。
"There’s the boys that always work for me nights,’ Retana said. ‘They’re all right.’
“有我那些总在晚上帮我干活的伙计们，”Retana 说。“他们不错。”
‘How about picadors?’ Manuel asked.
“那骑手怎么样？”曼努埃尔问。
‘They’re not much,’ Retana admitted.
“他们没多大用处，”雷塔纳承认道。
‘I’ve got to have one good pic,’ Manuel said.
“我必须找个厉害的骑手，”曼努埃尔说。
‘Get him then,’ Retana said. ‘Go and get him.’
“那就去找，”雷塔纳说，“去把他找来。”
‘Not out of this,’ Manuel said. ‘I’m not paying for any cuadrilla out of sixty duros.’
“不能出自这儿，”曼努埃尔说。“我不会用六十杜罗里的任何一队去付账。”
Retana said nothing but looked at Manuel across the big desk.
雷塔纳什么也没说，只是穿过那张大课桌看着曼努埃尔。
‘You know I’ve got to have one good pic,’ Manuel said.
“你知道我得有一次好的一枪，”曼努埃尔说。
Retana said nothing but looked at Manuel from a long way off.
雷塔纳什么也没说，只是从很远的地方看着曼努埃尔。
‘It isn’t right,’ Manuel said.
“这不对，”曼努埃尔说。
Retana was still considering him, leaning back in his chair, considering him from a long way away.
雷塔纳仍在打量他，向后靠在椅子上，从很远的距离审视他。
‘There’re the regular pics,’ he offered.
“有常规的照片，”他提议道。
‘I know,’ Manuel said. ‘I know your regular pics.’
“我知道，”曼努埃尔说。“我知道你的常规照片。”
Retana did not smile. Manuel knew it was over.
雷塔纳没有笑。曼努埃尔知道一切都结束了。
‘All I want is an even break,’ Manuel said reasoningly. ‘When I go out there I want to be able to call my shots on the bull. It only takes one good picador.’
“我只要个公平的机会，”曼努埃尔理智地说。“当我上场时，我要能掌控公牛。我只需要一个好的皮卡囊手。”
He was talking to a man who was no longer listening.
他正在对一个已经不再听他讲话的人说话。
‘If you want something extra,’ Retana said, ‘go and get it. There will be a regular cuadrilla out there. Bring as many of your own pics as you want. The charlotada is over by 10.30.’
“如果你还想多拿点儿，”雷塔纳说，“就去拿。有一支正规的斗牛队在外面。带上你想带的尽可能多的皮卡囊手。闹剧在十点半结束。”
‘All right,’ Manuel said. ‘If that’s the way you feel about it.’
“好吧，”曼努埃尔说。“既然你这么想。”
‘That’s the way,’ Retana said.
“就是这么想的，”雷塔纳说。
‘I’ll see you to-morrow night,’ Manuel said.
“明晚见，”曼努埃尔说。
‘I’ll be out there,’ Retana said.
“我会在那儿的，”雷塔纳说。
Manuel picked up his suitcase and went out.
曼努埃尔提起手提箱走了出去。
‘Shut the door,’ Retana called.
“把门关上，”雷塔纳喊道。
Manuel looked back. Retana was sitting forward looking at some papers. Manuel pulled the door tight until it clicked.
曼努埃尔回头看。雷塔纳向前坐着，正在看一些文件。曼努埃尔把门用力推紧，直到“咔哒”一声关上。
He went down the stairs and out of the door into the hot brightness of the street. It was very hot in the street and the light on the white buildings was sudden and hard on his eyes. He walked down the shady side of the street toward the Puerto del Sol. The shade felt solid and cool as running water. The heat came suddenly as he crossed the intersecting streets. Manuel saw no one he knew in all the people he passed.
他下了台阶，走出门，来到街上耀眼的热光中。街上非常热，白色建筑在阳光下光亮刺眼。他沿着街的阴凉一侧朝太阳门走去。阴凉像流水一样坚实而凉爽。每当他穿过交叉的街道，热浪便骤然袭来。曼努埃尔在人群中没有看到认识的人。
Just before the Puerto del Sol he turned into a café.
就在通往太阳门的路口，他转进了一家咖啡馆。
It was quiet in the café. There were a few men sitting at tables against the wall. At one table four men played cards. Most of the men sat against the wall smoking, empty coffee-cups and liqueurglasses before them on the tables. Manuel went through the long room to a small room in back. A man sat at a table in the corner asleep. Manuel sat down at one of the tables.
咖啡馆里很安静。几个人靠着墙坐在桌旁。一张桌子上四个人在打牌。大多数人靠着墙坐着抽烟，桌上放着喝剩的咖啡杯和利口酒杯。曼努埃尔穿过长厅来到后面一个小房间。角落里的一张桌旁坐着一个睡着了的人。曼努埃尔在其中一张桌旁坐下。
A waiter came in and stood beside Manuel’s table.
一位侍者走了进来，站在曼努埃尔的桌旁。
‘Have you seen Zurito?’ Manuel asked him.
“你见过苏里托吗？”曼努埃尔问他。
‘He was in before lunch,’ the waiter answered. ‘He won’t be back before five o’clock.’
“他上午走了，”侍者回答。“五点之前不会回来。”
‘Bring me some coffee and milk and a shot of the ordinary,’ Manuel said.
“给我来点咖啡和牛奶，加一盎司普通白兰地，”曼努埃尔说。
The waiter came back into the room carrying a tray with a big coffee-glass and a liqueur-glass on it. In his left hand he held a bottle of brandy. He swung these down to the table and a boy who had followed him poured coffee and milk into the glass from two shiny, spouted pots with long handles.
侍者端着托盘回到屋里，托盘上有一大杯咖啡杯和一只利口酒杯。他左手拿着一瓶白兰地。他把这些放到桌子上，跟着他的一个小伙子用两只闪亮、有长柄嘴的壶往杯里为咖啡和牛奶加注。
Manuel took off his cap and the waiter noticed his pigtail pinned forward on his hcad. He winked at the coffee-boy as he poured out the brandy into the little glass beside Manuel’s coffee. The coffeeboy looked at Manuel’s pale face curiously.
曼努埃尔摘下帽子，侍者注意到他辫子别在前额上。他把白兰地倒进放在曼努埃尔咖啡旁边的小杯时朝倒咖啡的男孩眨了眨眼。那个咖啡男孩好奇地看着曼努埃尔那苍白的脸。
‘You fighting here?’ asked the waiter, corking up the bottle.
“你们在这儿格斗吗？”侍者一边把瓶子塞好塞子一边问。
‘Yes,’ Manuel said. ‘To-morrow.’
“是的，”曼努埃尔说。“明天。”
The waiter stood there, holding the bottle on one hip.
侍者站着，把瓶子夹在一侧胯下。
‘You in the Charlie Chaplins?’ he asked.
“你们在查理·卓别林组吗？”他问。
The coffee-boy looked away, embarrassed.
咖啡侍童不好意思地移开了目光。
‘No. In the ordinary.’
“不。在普通的（座位）。”
‘I thought they were going to have Chaves and Hernandez,’ the waiter said.
“我以为他们要请查维斯和埃尔南德斯来，”服务员说。
‘No. Me and another.’
“不。是我和另一个人。”
‘Who? Chaves or Hernandez?’
“谁？Chaves 还是 Hernandez？”
‘Hernandez, I think.’
“我想是 Hernandez。”
‘What’s the matter with Chaves?’
“Chaves 怎么了？”
‘He got hurt.’
“他受伤了。”
‘Where did you hear that?’
“你从哪儿听来的？”
‘Retana.’
“雷塔纳。”
‘Hey, Looie,’ the waiter called to the next room. ‘Chaves got cogida.’
“喂，路易，”侍者朝隔壁房间喊道。“查维斯被抓住了。”
Manuel had taken the wrapper off the lumps of sugar and dropped them into his coffee. He stirred it and drank it down, sweet, hot and warming in his empty stomach. He drank off the brandy.
曼努埃尔把糖纸剥开，把几块糖扔进咖啡里。他搅拌着喝下去，甜的、烫的，在他空荡的胃里暖洋洋的。他把白兰地也喝了下去。
‘Give me another shot of that,’ he said to the waiter.
“再给我来一杯那个，”他对侍者说。
The waiter uncorked the bottle and poured the glass full, slopping another drink into the saucer. Another waiter had come up in front of the table. The coffee-boy was gone.
侍者拔开瓶塞，把杯子倒满，又把另一杯酒溅进碟子里。另一个侍者走到桌前。端咖啡的男孩已经不见了。
‘Is Chaves hurt bad?’ the second waiter asked Manuel.
“查维斯伤得重吗？”第二个侍者问曼努埃尔。
‘I don’t know,’ Manuel said. ‘Retana didn’t say.’
“我不知道，”曼努埃尔说。“雷塔纳没说。”
‘A hell of a lot he cares,’ the tall waiter said. Manuel had not seen him before. He must have just come up.
“他才一点也不在乎，”个子高的侍者说。Manuel 之前没见过他。他肯定是刚上来的。
‘If you stand in with Retana in this town, you’re a made man,’ the tall waiter said. ‘If you aren’t in with him, you might just as well go out and shoot yourself.’
“如果你在这镇上和 Retana 混得开，你就是有靠山的人，”个子高的侍者说。“如果你和他走不开，不如干脆出去把自己了结了。”
‘You said it,’ the other waiter who had come in said. ‘You said it then.’
“你说得没错，”刚进来的另一个侍者说。“你早就这么说了。”
‘You’re right I said it,’ said the tall waiter. ‘I know what I’m talking about when I talk about that bird.’
“你说对了，我就是这么说的，”个子高的侍者说。“说到那女人，我知道自己在说什么。”
‘Look what he’s done for Villalta,’ the first waiter said.
“看看他为 Villalta 做了什么，”第一个侍者说。
‘And that ain’t all,’ the tall waiter said. ‘Look what he’s done for Marcial Lalanda. Look what he’s done for Nacional.’
“这还不算完，”高个儿侍者说。“看看他为 Marcial Lalanda 做了什么。看看他为 Nacional 做了什么。”
‘You said it, kid,’ agreed the short waiter.
“小子，你说对了，”矮个儿侍者附和道。
Manuel looked at them, standing talking in front of his table. He had drunk his second brandy. They had forgotten about him. They were not interested in him.
曼努埃尔看着他们，站在他的桌子前说话。他已经喝了第二杯白兰地。他们把他忘了。他们对他不感兴趣。
‘Look at that bunch of camels,’ the tall waiter went on. ‘Did you ever see this Nacional II?’
“看那群骆驼，”高个儿侍者接着说。“你见过这辆 Nacional II 吗？”
‘I seen him last Sunday, didn’t I?’ the original waiter said.
“我上周日不就见过他了吗？”原来的侍者说。
‘He’s a giraffe,’ the short waiter said.
“他是只长颈鹿，”矮个儿侍者说。
‘What did I tell you?’ the tall waiter said. ‘Those are Retana’s boys.’
“我跟你说了什么？”高个儿侍者说。“那些是 Retana 的人。”
‘Say, give me another shot of that,’ Manuel said. He had poured the brandy the waiter had slopped over in the saucer into his glass and drank it while they were talking.
“喂，给我再来一杯那个，”曼努埃尔说。他把服务员在碟子里溢出来的白兰地倒进自己的杯子里，一边喝一边和他们聊天。
The original waiter poured his glass full mechanically, and the three of them went out of the room talking.
原来的服务员机械地把他的杯子重新倒满，三个人一边说着话一边走出房间。
In the far corner the man was still asleep, snoring slightly on the intaking breath, his head back against the wall.
远角落里那人还在睡，吸气时轻轻打着鼾，头靠在墙上。
Manuel drank his brandy. He felt sleepy himself. It was too hot to go out into the town. Besides there was nothing to do. He wanted to see Zurito. He would go to sleep while he waited. He kicked his suitcase under the table to be sure it was there. Perhaps it would be better to put it back under the seat, against the wall. He leaned down and shoved it under. Then he leaned forward on the table and went to sleep.
曼努埃尔喝着白兰地。他自己也觉得困了。外面太热，不适合去镇上。况且也没什么可做的。他想见祖里托。他等的时候就睡一会儿。他把手提箱踢到桌子底下，确认它在那里。也许把它放回座位下面、靠墙的位置会更好。他弯下身把它推了进去。然后他向前靠在桌子上睡着了。
When he woke there was someone sitting across the table from him. It was a big man with a heavy brown face like an Indian. He had been sitting there some time. He had waved the waiter awav and sat reading the paper and occasionally looking down at Manuel, asleep, his head on the table. He read the paper laboriously, forming the words with his lips as he read. When it tired him he looked at Manuel. He sat heavily in the chair, his black Cordoba hat tipped forward.
当他醒来时，有人坐在对面的桌子旁。那是个大个子，脸色黝黑沉重，像个印度人。他在那里已经坐了一会儿了。他把服务员打发走，坐着看报，偶尔低头看一眼睡着的曼努埃尔，他把头枕在桌上。他读报很吃力，读时嘴唇动着拼出词来。疲倦时他就看向曼努埃尔。他沉重地坐在椅子上，黑色的科尔多瓦帽向前压着。
Manuel sat up and looked at him.
曼努埃尔坐起来，看着他。
‘Hello, Zurito,’ he said.
“你好，祖里托，”他说。
‘Hello, kid,’ the big man said.
“你好，孩子，”大个子说。
‘I’ve been asleep,’ Manuel rubbed his forehead with the back of his fist.
“我刚才睡着了。”曼努埃尔用拳背擦了擦额头。
‘I thought maybe you were.’
“我还以为你是呢。”
‘How’s everything?’
“一切都好吗？”
‘Good. How is everything with you?’
“很好。你那边怎么样？”
‘Not so good.’
“不太好。”
They were both silent. Zurito, the picador, looked at Manuel’s white face. Manuel looked down at the picador’s enormous hands folding the paper to put away in his pocket.
他们都沉默了。皮卡多人祖里托看着曼努埃尔白皙的脸。曼努埃尔低头看着皮卡多那双巨大的手把纸叠好准备放进口袋。
‘I got a favour to ask you, Manos,’ Manuel said.
“我有个忙要你帮，马诺斯，”曼努埃尔说。
Manosduros was Zurito’s nickname. He never heard it without thinking of his huge hands. He put them forward on the table selfconsciously.
马诺斯杜罗斯是祖里托的绰号。他每次一听到这个绰号就会想到他那双巨大的手。他不好意思地把手伸到桌子上。
‘Let’s have a drink,’ he said.
“我们喝一杯吧，”他说。
‘Sure,’ said Manuel.
“好啊，”曼努埃尔说。
The waiter came and went and came again. He went out of the room looking back at the two men at the table.
侍者走了又来，又走又来。他出门时回头看了看桌前的两个人。
‘What’s the matter, Manolo?’ Zurito set down his glass.
“怎么了，马诺洛？”祖里托放下杯子。
‘Would you pic two bulls for me to-morrow night?’ Manuel asked, looking up at Zurito across the table.
“明天晚上你能替我挑两头公牛吗？”曼努埃尔抬头看着桌对面的祖里托问道。
‘No,’ said Zurito. ‘I’m not pic-ing.’
“不，”祖里托说道。“我不替人挑。”
Manuel looked down at his glass. He had expected that answer; now he had it. Well, he had it.
曼努埃尔低头看着自己的酒杯。他早就料到这个答案；现在果真如此。好吧，他就这么接受了。
‘I’m sorry, Manolo, but I’m not pic-ing.’ Zurito looked at his hands.
“对不起，马诺洛，但我不替人挑。”祖里托看着自己的手。
‘That’s all right,’ Manuel said.
“没关系，”Manuel 说。
‘I’m too old,’ Zurito said.
“我太老了，”Zurito 说。
‘I just asked you,’ Manuel said.
“我刚问过你了，”Manuel 说。
‘Is it the nocturnal to-morrow?’
“是明晚吗？”
‘That’s it. I figured if I had just one good pic, I could get away with it.’
“就是这样。我想如果我只有一张好照片，就可以蒙混过关。”
‘How much are you getting?’
“你能挣多少钱？”
‘Three hundred pesetas.’
“三百比塞塔。”
‘I get more than that for pic-ing.’
“我拍照挣的比那多。”
‘I know,’ said Manuel. ‘I didn’t have any right to ask you.’
“我知道，”曼努埃尔说。“我没有资格问你。”
‘What do you keep on doing it for?’ Zurito asked. ‘Why don’t you cut off your coleta, Manolo?’
“你干嘛老是这样？”苏里托问。“你为什么不把你的 coleta 剪掉，马诺洛？”
‘I don’t know,’ Manuel said.
“我不知道，”曼努埃尔说。
‘You’re pretty near as old as I am,’ Zurito said.
“你差不多和我一样大了，”苏里托说。
‘I don’t know,’ Manuel said. ‘I got to do it. If I can fix it so that I get an even break, that’s all I want. I got to stick with it, Manos.’
“我不知道，”曼努埃尔说。“我得去做。如果我能把事情弄得对自己公平点，那就是我想要的。我得坚持下去，马诺斯。”
‘No, you don’t.’
“不，你不该这么做。”
‘Yes. I do. I’ve tried keeping away from it.’
“要。我得这么做。我试过不去碰它。”
‘I know how you feel. But it isn’t right. You ought to get out and stay out.’
“我知道你的感受。但这不对。你应该离开并且不要再回去。”
‘I can’t do it. Besides, I’ve been going good lately.’
“我做不到。而且，最近我状况一直很好。”
Zurito looked at his face.
祖里托看着他的脸。
‘You’ve been in the hospital.’
“你上过医院。”
‘But I was going great when I got hurt.’
“但我受伤的时候状态正好。”
Zurito said nothing. He tipped the cognac out of his saucer into his glass.
祖里托什么也没说。他把茶托里的干邑倒进了杯子里。
"The papers said they never saw a better faena,’ Manuel said.
“报纸都说他们从没见过更好的表演，”曼努埃尔说。
Zurito looked at him.
祖里托看着他。
‘You know when I get going I’m good,’ Manuel said.
“你知道一旦我开始了我就很厉害，”曼努埃尔说。
‘You’re too old,’ the picador said.
“你太老了，”骑枪手说。
‘No,’ said Manuel. ‘You’re ten years older than I am.’
“不，”曼努埃尔说。“你比我大十岁。”
‘With me it’s different.’
“我不一样。”
‘I’m not too old,’ Manuel said.
“我不老，”曼努埃尔说。
They sat silent, Manuel watching the picador’s face.
他们沉默地坐着，曼努埃尔盯着骑矛手的脸看。
‘I was going great till I got hurt,’ Manuel offered.
“我本来干得挺好的，直到我受伤了，”曼努埃尔说道。
‘You ought to have seen me, Manos,’ Manuel said, reproachfully.
“你本该看看我，马诺斯，”曼努埃尔责备地说。
‘I don’t want to see you,’ Zurito said. ‘It makes me nervous.’
“我不想看你，”祖里托说。“那会让我紧张。”
‘You haven’t seen me lately.’
“你最近没见到我了。”
‘I’ve seen you plenty.’
“我见过你很多次了。”
Zurito looked at Manuel, avoiding his eyes.
苏里托看着曼努埃尔，避开了他的目光。
‘You ought to quit it, Manolo.’
“你该收手了，马诺洛。”
‘I can’t,’ Manuel said. ‘I’m going good now, I tell you.’
“我不行，”曼努埃尔说。“我现在很好，告诉你了。”
Zurito leaned forward, his hands on the table.
苏里托向前倾，双手放在桌上。
‘Listen. I’ll pic for you and if you don’t go big to-morrow night, you’ll quit. See? Will you do that?’
“听着。我替你买单，如果你明晚不大出手，你就戒了。明白吗？你答应不？”
‘Sure.’
“好。”
Zurito leaned back, relieved.
苏里托靠了靠椅背，松了口气。
‘You got to quit,’ he said. ‘No monkey business. You got to cut the coleta.’
“你得戒了，”他说。“别搞花招。你得剪掉辫子。”
‘I won’t have to quit,’ Manuel said. ‘You watch me. I’ve got the stuff.’
“我不必戒，”曼努埃尔说。“你看着吧。我有本事的。”
Zurito stood up. He felt tired from arguing.
苏里托站起来。他觉得争论让他疲惫不堪。
‘You got to quit,’ he said. ‘I’ll cut your coleta myself.’
“你得停手，”他说。“我要亲自把你的 coleta 剪了。”
‘No, you won’t,’ Manuel said. ‘You won’t have a chance.’
“不，你不会的，”Manuel 说。“你不会有机会的。”
Zurito called the waiter.
Zurito 叫了服务员。
‘Come on,’ said Zurito. ‘Come on up to the house.’
“来吧，”Zurito 说。“上屋去吧。”
Manuel reached under the seat for his suitcase. He was happy. He knew Zurito would pic for him. He was the best picador living. It was all simple now.
曼努埃尔从座位下伸手去拿他的手提箱。他很高兴。他知道祖里托会替他挑选。他是世上最好的挑枪手。一切现在都很简单。
‘Come on up to the house and we’ll eat,’ Zurito said.
“上屋去吧，我们去吃饭，”祖里托说。
Manuel stood in the patio de caballos waiting for the Charlie Chaplins to be over. Zurito stood beside him. Where they stood it was dark. The high door that led into the bull-ring was shut. Above them they heard a shout, then another shout of laughter. Then there was silence. Manuel liked the smell of the stables about the patio de caballos. It smelt good in the dark. There was another roar from the arena and then applause, prolonged applause, going on and on.
曼努埃尔站在马厩院里等着查理·卓别林们结束。祖里托站在他旁边。他们站的地方很黑。通往斗牛场的大门关着。他们头顶上听到一声喊，然后又一阵笑声。随后寂静下来。曼努埃尔喜欢马厩围绕马厩院的气味。黑暗中闻起来很舒服。竞技场又传来一阵呼喊，随后是掌声，持续不断，连绵不绝。
‘You ever seen these fellows?’ Zurito asked, big and looming beside Manuel in the dark.
“你见过这些人吗？”祖里托在黑暗中大个儿地站在曼努埃尔旁边问道。
‘No,’ Manuel said.
“不，”曼努埃尔说。
‘They’re pretty funny,’ Zurito said. He smiled to himself in the dark.
“他们挺有意思的，”祖里托说。他在黑暗中自顾自地笑了笑。
The high, double, tight-fitting door into the bull-ring swung open
通往斗牛场的那扇高大的、双扇的、紧闭的门被推开了
and Manuel saw the ring in the hard light of the arc-lights, the plaza, dark all the way around, rising high; around the edge of the ring were running and bowing two men dressed like tramps, followed by a third in the uniform of a hotel bell-boy who stooped and picked up the hats and canes thrown down on to the sand and tossed them back up into the darkness.
曼努埃尔在弧形灯的冷硬光下看见了斗牛场，广场周围一片黑暗，高高耸起；在场地边缘有两个装扮成流浪汉的人在跑动和鞠躬，后面跟着一个穿着酒店行李员制服的第三者，他弯腰捡起扔到沙地上的帽子和手杖，又将它们掷回黑暗中。
The electric light went on in the patio.
院子里的电灯亮了。
‘I’ll climb on to one of those ponies while you collect the kids,’ Zurito said.
“你去把孩子们接上，我上去骑那匹小马，”祖里托说。
Behind them came the jingle of the mules, coming out to go into the arena and be hitched on to the dead bull.
后面随着骡子的铃铛声走来，它们出来要进场并系在那头死牛上。
The members of the cuadrilla, who had been watching the burlesque from the runway between the barrera and the seats, came walking back and stood in a group talking, under the electric light in the patio. A good-looking lad in a silver-and-orange suit came up to Manuel and smiled.
那群曾在障栏与看台之间的通道上看着滑稽表演的斗牛队员们走了回来，站成一团在院子的电灯下交谈。一个穿着银橙相间衣服的帅小伙走到曼努埃尔面前，冲他笑了。
‘I’m Hernandez,’ he said and put out his hand.
“我是埃尔南德斯，”他说着伸出手。
Manuel shook it.
曼努埃尔握住了他的手。
‘They’re regular elephants we’ve got to-night,’ the boy said cheerfully.
“今晚我们遇到的是普通大象，”那个男孩兴高采烈地说。
‘They’re big ones with horns,’ Manuel agreed.
“它们是长着象牙的大个儿，”曼努埃尔赞同道。
‘You drew the worst lot,’ the boy said.
“你抽到的是最倒霉的那头，”男孩说。
‘That’s all right,’ Manuel said. ‘The bigger they are, the more meat for the poor.’
“没关系，”曼努埃尔说，“它们越大，穷人得到的肉就越多。”
‘Where did you get that one?’ Hernandez grinned.
“你从哪儿弄来的这头？”埃尔南德斯咧嘴笑道。
‘That’s an old one,’ Manuel said. ‘You line up your cuadrilla, so I can see what I’ve got.’
“那是一头老的，”曼努埃尔说。“把你的牛群排好队，让我看看我碰到的是什么。”
‘You’ve got some good kids,’ Hernandez said. He was very cheerful. He had been on twice before in nocturnals and was beginning to get a following in Madrid. He was happy the fight would start in a few minutes.
“你们有些好孩子，”Hernandez 说。他非常高兴。他以前在夜赛中表演过两次，开始在马德里有了些追随者。他很高兴比赛几分钟后就要开始。
‘Where are the pics?’ Manuel asked.
“图片在哪儿？”Manuel 问。
‘They’re back in the corrals fighting about who gets the beautiful horses,’ Hernandez grinned.
“它们在畜栏里，为谁能得到那些漂亮的马而打起来了，”Hernandez 咧嘴笑道。
The mules came through the gate in a rush, the whips snapping, bells jangling and the young bull ploughing a furrow of sand.
骡子们一拥而入，鞭子啪嗒作响，铃铛叮当作响，年轻的公牛在沙地上犁出一道沟壑。
They formed up for the paseo as soon as the bull had gone through.
公牛一出场，他们便列队准备游行。
Manuel and Hernandez stood in front. The youths of the
曼努埃尔和埃尔南德斯站在前面。那几位斗牛帮的青年在后面，厚重的披肩卷在臂上。
cuadrillas were behind, their heavy capes furled over their arms. In back, the four picadors, mounted, holding their steep-tipped push-poles erect in the half-dark of the corral.
在后面，四名骑马长矛手就位，骑在马背上，手持尖头长矛，在马圈的昏暗中竖立着。
‘It’s a wonder Retana wouldn’t give us enough light to see the horses by,’ one picador said.
“真该死，雷塔纳就是不肯给我们足够的光，看不清马匹，”一名长矛手说道。
‘He knows we’ll be happier if we don’t get too good a look at these skins,’ another pic answered.
“他知道我们看这些兽皮看得太清会不那么高兴，”另一个骑手回答。
‘This thing I’m on barely keeps me off the ground,’ the first picador said.
“我骑的这匹马勉强把我拦在地面上，”第一个打马人说。
‘Well, they’re horses.’
“嗯，它们是马。”
‘Sure, they’re horses.’
“当然，它们是马。”
They talked, sitting their gaunt horses in the dark.
他们坐在夜色中，驾着枯瘦的马交谈。
Zurito said nothing. He had the only steady horse of the lot. He had tried him, wheeling him in the corrals and he responded to the bit and the spurs. He had taken the bandage off his right eve and cut the strings where they had tied his ears tight shut at the base. He was a good, solid horse, solid on his legs. That was all he needed. He intended to ride him all through the corrida. He had already, since he had mounted, sitting in the half-dark in the big, quilted saddle, waiting for the paseo, pic-ed through the whole corrida in his mind. The other picadors went on talking on both sides of him. He did not hear them.
祖里托什么也没说。他是这队里唯一一匹稳定的马的主人。他曾在围栏里试过它，转马，它对马嚼子和马刺都有反应。他把右眼上的绷带取下，又剪断了把耳朵在根部紧紧绑住的绳子。那是一匹好马，四蹄有力。这就是他所需要的一切。他打算在整场斗牛中骑着它。他自从跨上那只大而绗缝的马鞍、在半明半暗中坐着等候巡礼时，脑中就已经把整场斗牛想了个遍。其他的替打手在他两边继续交谈。他没有听见他们的话。
The two matadors stood together in front of their three peones, their capes furled over their left arms in the same fashion. Manuel was thinking about the three lads in back of him. They were all three Madrilenos, like Hernandez, boys about nineteen. One of them, a gipsy, serious, aloof, and dark faced, he liked the look of. He turned.
两位斗牛士并肩站在他们的三个助手面前，左臂上同样地挽着披风。曼努埃尔想着身后的那三个小伙子。他们都是马德里人，像埃尔南德斯一样，都是大约十九岁的男孩。其中一个，吉普赛人，面色黝黑，严肃，孤傲，他挺喜欢他的样子。他转过头去。
‘What’s your name, kid?’ he asked the gipsy.
“你叫什么名字，孩子？”他问那个吉普赛人。
‘Fuentes,’ the gipsy said.
“富恩特斯，”吉普赛人说。
‘That’s a good name,’ Manuel said.
“那是个好名字，”曼努埃尔说。
The gipsy smiled, showing his teeth.
吉普赛人笑着，露出牙齿。
‘You take the bull and give him a little run when he comes out,’ Manuel said.
“你拿住公牛，等它出来的时候让它跑一小段，”曼努埃尔说。
‘All right,’ the gipsy said. His face was serious. He began to think about just what he would do.
“好吧，”吉普赛人说。他的脸很严肃。他开始考虑要做什么。
‘Here she goes,’ Manuel said to Hernandez.
“她来了，”曼努埃尔对埃尔南德斯说。
‘All right. We’ll go.’
“好吧。我们走。”
Heads up, swinging with the music, their right arms swinging
抬头，随着音乐摆动，右臂随之摆动
free, they stepped out, crossing the sanded arena under the arc-lights, the cuadrillas opening out behind, the picadors riding after, behind came the bull-ring servants and the jingling mules. The crowd applauded Hernandez as they marched across the arena. Arrogant, swinging, they looked straight ahead as they marched.
自由了，他们走了出来，穿过铺着沙子的竞技场，沿着拱形灯下前行，队列在后面展开，骑手们跟在后面，随后是斗牛场的仆役和叮当作响的骡子。人群在他们穿过竞技场时为埃尔南德斯鼓掌。他们昂首阔步，自信而摆动着，行进时目光直视前方。
They bowed before the president, and the procession broke up into its component parts. The bull-fighters went over to the barrera and changed their heavy mantles for the light fighting capes. The mules went out. The picadors galloped jerkily around the ring, and two rode out the gate they had come in by. The servants swept the sand smooth.
他们在主席面前鞠躬，队列随即分成各自的组成部分。斗牛士们走到护墙旁，把沉重的披风换成轻盈的斗篷。骡子被赶出场。骑手们颠簸着围着场转，两人骑着出入时进入的那扇门。仆人们把沙子扫得平整光滑。
Manuel drank a glass of water poured for him by one of Retana’s deputies, who was acting as his manager and sword-handler. Hernandez came over from speaking with his own manager.
曼努埃尔喝了一杯由雷塔纳的一位副手为他倒的水，那位副手正担任他的经纪人兼剑手。埃尔南德斯从与自己经纪人交谈处走过来。
‘You got a good hand, kid,’ Manuel complimented him.
“你手不错，孩子，”曼努埃尔称赞道。
‘They like me,’ Hernandez said happily.
“他们喜欢我，”埃尔南德斯高兴地说。
‘How did the paseo go?’ Manuel asked Retana’s man.
“paseo 进行得怎样？”曼努埃尔问雷塔纳的人。
‘Like a wedding,’ said the handler. ‘Fine. You came out like Joselito and Belmonte.’
“像婚礼一样，”那名处理马的人说。“很好。你出来像何塞利托和贝尔蒙特那样。”
Zurito rode by, a bulky equestrian statue. He wheeled his horse and faced him toward the toril on the far side of the ring where the bull would come out. It was strange under the arc-light. He had pic-ed in the hot afternoon sun for big money. He didn’t like this arc-light business. He wished they would get started.
苏里托骑着马经过，像一座魁梧的骑马雕像。他转动马头，让马面向场地另一侧的吐牛箱，公牛将从那里出来。在弧形灯光下看起来很奇怪。他下午在烈日下为大钱做过秀。他并不喜欢这种弧形灯的事。他希望他们赶快开始。
Manuel went up to him.
曼努埃尔走到他跟前。
‘Pic him, Manos,’ he said. ‘Cut him down to size for me.’
“给我揍他，马诺斯，”他说。“把他打回原形。”
‘I’ll pic him, kid,’ Zurito spat on the sand. ‘I’ll make him jump out of the ring.’
“我会揍他的，孩子，”祖里托朝沙地吐了口唾沫。“我会让他跳出擂台。”
‘Lean on him, Manos,’ Manuel said.
“顶住他，马诺斯，”曼努埃尔说。
‘I’ll lean on him,’ Zurito said. ‘What’s holding it up?’
‘He’s coming now,’ Manuel said.
Zurito sat there, his feet in the box-stirrups, his great legs in the buckskin-covered armour gripping the horse, the reins in his left hand, the long pic held in his right hand, his broad hat well down over his eyes to shade them from the lights, watching the distant door of the toril. His horse’s ears quivered. Zurito patted him with his left hand.
The red door of the toril swung back and for a moment Zurito looked into the empty passageway far across the arena. Then the
bull came out in a rush, skidding on his four legs as he came out under the lights, then charging in a gallop, moving softly in a fast gallop, silent except as he woofed through wide nostrils as he charged, glad to be free after the dark pen.
公牛猛地冲了出来，四腿打滑着从灯光下冲出，然后奔腾起来，快速奔跑却步伐轻柔，除了冲锋时通过阔大的鼻孔发出呼哧声外寂然无声，终于脱离了黑暗的围栏，感到欣慰。
In the first row of seats, slightly bored, leaning forward to write on the cement wall in front of his knees, the substitute bull-fight critic of El Heraldo scribbled: ‘Campagnero, Negro, 42, came out at 90 miles an hour with plenty of gas -’
在第一排座位上，略显无聊，向前靠着在膝前的水泥墙上写字，El Heraldo 的替代斗牛评论员潦草地写道：“Campagnero，Negro，42，出场时速度达每小时 90 英里，动力充沛——”
Manuel, leaning against the barrera, watching the bull, waved his hand and the gipsy ran out, trailing his cape. The bull, in full gallop, picoted and charged the cape, his head down, his tail rising. The gipsy moved in a zigzag, and as he passed, the bull caught sight of him and abandoned the cape to charge the man. The gip sprinted and vaulted the red fence of the barrera as the bull struck it with his horns. He tossed into it twice with his horns, banging into the wood blindly.
曼努埃尔靠在护栏上，看着公牛，挥了挥手，吉普赛人拖着披风跑了出来。公牛全速奔来，踢着前蹄猛冲向披风，低着头，尾巴高扬。吉普赛人做出之字形移动，经过时公牛看见了他，放弃了披风去追人。吉普赛人冲刺并跃过了红色的护栏，公牛用角撞击护栏时他越了过去。公牛用角猛地撞了两下，盲目地撞在木头上。
The critic of El Heraldo lit a cigarette and tossed the match at the bull, then wrote in his note-book, ‘large and with enough horns to satisfy the cash customers, Campagnero showed a tendency to cut into the terrain of the bull-fighters.’
《埃尔·埃拉尔多》的评论家点燃了一支烟，把火柴扔向公牛，然后在笔记本上写道：“体型大、角足以满足付钱的观众，Campagnero 显示出有侵占斗牛士领域的倾向。”
Manuel stepped out on the hard sand as the bull banged into the fence. Out of the corner of his eve he saw Zurito sitting the white horse close to the barrera, about a quarter of the way around the ring to the left. Manuel held the cape close in front of him, a fold in each hand, and shouted at the bull. ‘Huh! Huh!’ The bull turned, seemed to brace against the fence as he charged in a scramble, driving into the cape as Manuel side-stepped, pivoted on his heels with the charge of the bull, and swung the cape just ahead of the horns. At the end of the swing he was facing the bull again and held the cape in the same position close in front of his body, and pivoted again as the bull recharged. Each time, as he swung, the crowd shouted.
当公牛撞上围栏时，曼努埃尔踏上坚硬的沙地。他从眼角看见祖里托骑着白马靠近围栏坐着，向左大约绕场四分之一处。曼努埃尔把披风紧握在身前，两手各握一折，大声冲公牛喊道：“哼！哼！”公牛转身，似乎在冲撞中靠在围栏上稳住，乱窜着扑向披风。曼努埃尔侧步，随着公牛的冲力在脚跟处转动，把披风甩到牛角前方刚好的位置。甩动结束时，他又面向公牛，仍把披风保持在贴近身体的同一位置，随着公牛再次冲来又转动起来。每一次他甩动时，观众都大声喊叫。
Four times he swung with the bull, lifting the cape so it billowed full, and each time bringing the bull around to charge again. Then, at the end of the fifth swing, he held the cape against his hip and pivoted, so the cape swung out like a ballet dancer’s skirt and wound the bull around himself like a belt, to step clear, leaving the bull facing Zurito on the white horse, come up and planted firm, the horse facing the bull, its ears forward, its lips nervous, Zurito,
他四次挥动斗篷，把斗篷扬起鼓满，每次都把公牛引回来再次冲锋。然后，在第五次挥动结束时，他把斗篷抵在髋部并转身，使斗篷像芭蕾舞者的裙摆般甩出，把公牛绕在自己身边像腰带一样，然后跨步后退，留下公牛面对白马上的祖里托，马靠近并站稳，马面向公牛，耳朵竖着，嘴唇紧张，祖里托，
his hat over his eyes, leaning forward, the long pole sticking out before and behind in a sharp angle under his right arm, held halfway down, the triangular iron point facing the bull.
帽檐压到眼睛上，身体前倾，长杆在右臂下呈锐角向前后伸出，握在半低的位置，三角形的铁尖朝向公牛。
El Heraldo’s second-string critic, drawing on his cigarette, his eyes on the bull, wrote: ‘the veteran Manolo designed a series of acceptable veronicas, ending in a very Belmonistic recorte that earned applause from the regulars, and we entered the tercio of the cavalry.’
《El Heraldo》的二线评论员叼着香烟，目光盯着公牛，写道：“老将马诺洛设计了一系列可接受的 veronicas，以非常贝尔蒙特式的 recorte 结束，赢得了常客的掌声，我们进入了骑兵环节（tercio of the cavalry）。”
Zurito sat his horse, measuring the distance between the bull and the end of the pic. As he looked, the bull gathered himself together and charged, his eyes on the horse’s chest. As he lowered his head to look, Zurito sunk the point of the pic in the swelling hump of muscle above the bull’s shoulder, leaned all his weight on the shaft, and with his left hand pulled the white horse into the air, front hoofs pawing, and swung him to the right as he pushed the bull under and through so the horns passed safely under the horse’s belly and the horse came down, quivering, the bull’s tail brushing his chest as he charged the cape Hernandez offered him.
祖里托跨坐马背，估量公牛与长矛末端之间的距离。正当他注视时，公牛蓄势一冲，眼睛盯着马的胸膛。祖里托低头观察时，把矛尖刺进公牛肩上那隆起的肌肉瘤里，整个身子压在矛柄上，左手把白马拉起，前蹄刨地，向右一转，同时把公牛往下和往里推，使公牛的角安全地从马腹下掠过，马颤抖着落下，公牛的尾巴在冲刺斗篷时掠过马的胸膛，赫南德斯递给他的披风被掠过。
Hernandez ran sideways, taking the bull out and away with the cape, toward the other picador. He fixed him with a swing of the cape, squarely facing the horse and rider, and stepped back. As the bull saw the horse he charged. The picador’s lance slid along his back, and as the shock of the charge lifted the horse, the picador was already half-way out of the saddle, lifting his right leg clear as he missed with the lance and falling to the left side to keep the horse between him and the bull. The horse, lifted and gored, crashed over with the bull driving into him, the picador gave a shove with his boots against the horse and lay clear, waiting to be lifted and hauled away and put on his feet.
埃尔南德斯侧身跑着，把公牛用披风引到外侧，朝另一个矛手那边。他甩动披风把公牛定住，正对着马和骑手，然后后退。当公牛看到马时就冲了上去。矛手的长矛沿着公牛的背滑过，随着冲撞的冲力把马抬起，矛手已半身腾出鞍外，右腿抬起以免被矛擦中，向左侧跌落以保持马在他与公牛之间。那匹被抬起并被角伤的马与公牛一起倒下，矛手用靴子一推马身，躲开，等着被抬起来、拉走并扶起。
Manuel let the bull drive into the fallen horse; he was in no hurry, the picador was safe; besides, it did a picador like that good to worry. He’d stay on longer next time. Lousy pics! He looked across the sand at Zurito a little way out from the barrera, his horse rigid, waiting.
曼努埃尔任由公牛顶撞倒地的马；他并不着急，矛手是安全的；再说，这样对矛手有好处，会让他下次撑得更久。可恶的表演！他望向沙地对面稍离围栏一段距离的苏里托，看到他的马僵直地等候着。
‘Huh!’ he called to the bull, ‘Tomar!’ holding the cape in both hands so it would catch his eye. The bull detached himself from the horse and charged the cape, and Manuel, running sideways and holding the cape spread wide, stopped, swung on his heels, and brought the bull sharply around facing Zurito.
“哼！”他朝公牛喊道，“托马尔！”双手举着斗篷以吸引它的注意。公牛与马分开，冲向斗篷，曼努埃尔侧身奔跑，双臂把斗篷张开，停住脚步，在脚跟上猛转，将公牛迅速逼到面向祖里托的方向。
‘Campagnero accepted a pair of varas for the death of one rosinante, with Hernandez and Manolo at the quites,’ El Heraldo’s critic wrote. 'He pressed on the iron and clearly showed he was no horselover. The veteran Zurito resurrected some of his old stuff with the pike-pole, notably the suerte - ’
《埃拉尔多》评论家写道：“坎帕涅罗为杀死一匹马罗西南特接受了两根矛，埃尔南德斯和马诺洛负责回避。他加大了铁杆的力度，明显表现出他并非爱马之人。老练的祖里托用矛杆重现了他的一些旧把戏，尤其是那套 suerte——”
‘Olé! Olé!’ the man sitting beside him shouted. The shout was lost in the roar of the crowd, and he slapped the critic on the back. The critic looked up to see Zurito, directly below him, leaning far out over his horse, the length of the pic rising in a sharp angle under his armpit, holding the pic almost by the point, bearing down with all his weight, holding the bull off, the bull pushing and driving to get at the horse, and Zurito, far out, on top of him, holding him, holding him, and slowly pivoting the horse against the pressure, so that at last he was clear. Zurito felt the moment when the horse was clear and the bull could come past, and relaxed the absolute steel lock of his resistance, and the triangular steel point of the pic ripped into the bull’s hump of shoulder muscle as he tore loose to find Hernandez’s cape before his muzzle. He charged blindly into the cape and the boy took him out into the open arena.
“Olé！Olé！”坐在他旁边的人喊道。喊声在人群的吼叫中淹没，他拍了拍那批评家的背。那批评家抬头看见 Zurito，就在他正下方，身体远远探出马背，矛竿在他腋下以一个锐角抬起，几乎用矛尖握着矛，把全部体重压在上面，用矛抵住公牛，公牛一面推挤一面想扑向马匹，而 Zurito 远远探出，趴在马背上，稳稳抓住它，紧紧抓住，然后慢慢把马顺着压力转过来，直到最后脱离出来。Zurito 感觉到马脱开、牛可以冲过去的瞬间，放松了他那绝对如钢的抵抗锁，矛那三角形的钢尖在牛挣脱时撕进了它肩上肌肉的驼峰，牛盲目地冲向赫尔南德斯在它口前挥舞的斗篷，男孩把它引出到明亮灯光下的公开场地。
Zurito sat patting his horse and looking at the bull charging the cape that Hernandez swung for him out under the bright light while the crowd shouted.
Zurito 坐着拍着他的马，盯着在明亮灯光下赫尔南德斯为他挥动的斗篷而冲过来的公牛，人群喊着。
‘You see that?’ he said to Manuel.
“你看到了吗？”他对 Manuel 说。
‘It was a wonder,’ Manuel said.
“真是奇迹，”Manuel 说。
‘I got him that time,’ Zurito said. ‘Look at him now.’
“这次是我打中的，”祖里托说。“看他现在的样子。”
At the conclusion of a closely turned pass of the cape the bull slid to his knees. He was up at once, but far out across the sand Manuel and Zurito saw the shine of the pumping flow of blood, smooth against the black of the bull’s shoulder.
在一次紧凑的冲刺过后，那头公牛跪倒在地。它立刻又站了起来，但远远地在沙地上，曼努埃尔和祖里托看见喷涌的血流在公牛肩膀的黑色上闪着光，呈现出一片光滑的亮泽。
‘I got him that time,’ Zurito said.
“这次是我打中的，”祖里托说。
‘He’s a good bull,’ Manuel said.
“这是一头好公牛，”曼努埃尔说。
‘If they gave me another shot at him, I’d kill him,’ Zurito said.
“要是再给我一次机会，我会杀了他，”Zurito 说。
“They’ll change the thirds on us,” Manuel said.
“他们会把第三轮换给我们打的，”Manuel 说。
‘Look at him now,’ Zurito said.
“现在看看他，”Zurito 说。
‘I got to go over there,’ Manuel said, and started on a run for the other side of the ring, where the monos were leading a horse out by the bridle toward the bull, whacking him on the legs with rods and all, in a procession, trying to get him toward the bull, who stood, dropping his head, pawing, unable to make up his mind to charge.
“我得过去那边，”Manuel 说着开始朝场另侧跑去，那边猴子们正牵着一匹马，拉着缰绳往公牛那边走，边走边用棍子打他的腿，像游行一样，试图把马弄向公牛。公牛站着，低着头，跺着前蹄，犹豫不决，无法下定决心去冲锋。
Zurito, sitting his horse, walking him toward the scene, not missing any detail, scowled.
苏里托坐在马上，把马牵向事发处，毫不放过任何细节，皱起了眉头。
Finally the bull charged, the horse leaders ran for the barrera, the picador hit too far back, and the bull got under the horse, lifted him, threw him on to his back.
最终公牛冲了上来，牵马的人向障栏跑去，骑马刺手刺得太靠后，公牛钻到马下，把它抬起，掀翻在背上。
Zurito watched. The monos, in their red shirts, running out to drag the picador clear. The picador, now on his feet, swearing and flopping his arms. Manuel and Hernandez standing ready with their capes. And the bull, the great, black bull, with a horse on his back, hooves dangling, the bridle caught in the horns. Black bull with a horse on his back, staggering short-legged, then arching his neck and lifting, thrusting, charging to slide the horse off, horse sliding down. Then the bull into a lunging charge at the cape Manuel spread for him.
苏里托看着。穿着红衬衫的猴子们跑出来把骑马刺手拉开。骑马刺手此刻已站起，咒骂着甩动胳膊。Manuel 和 Hernandez 持着披风站好准备。那头公牛——巨大、黑色的公牛——背上压着一匹马，马蹄无力地垂着，韁绳挂在牛角上。黑牛背负着马，短腿蹒跚，然后拱起脖子抬起、猛力顶撞，试图把马滑下，马顺势滑落。随后公牛又猛冲向 Manuel 为它展开的披风。
The bull was slower now, Manuel felt. He was bleeding badly. There was a sheen of blood all down his flank.
Manuel 感觉到公牛此刻变得较为迟缓。它在大量出血。整侧胁下闪着一道血光。
Manuel offered him the cape again. There he came, eyes open, ugly, watching the cape. Manuel stepped to the side and raised his arms, tightening the cape ahead of the bull for the veronica.
曼努埃尔又把披布递给他。他来了，眼睛睁着，狰狞，盯着披布。曼努埃尔向旁一步，举起双臂，把披布在公牛前拉紧做出真维卡（veronica）动作。
Now he was facing the bull. Yes, his head was going down a little. He was carrying it lower. That was Zurito.
现在他正面对着公牛。是的，他的头微微低了些。他把头放得更低。那是苏里托（Zurito）。
Manuel flopped the cape; there he comes; he side-stepped and swung in another veronica. He’s shooting awfully accurately, he thought. He’s had enough fight, so he’s watching now. He’s hunting now. Got his eye on me. But I always give him the cape.
曼努埃尔把披布抛出；他来了；他侧步，又换了一个真维卡。我想，他射得实在太准了。他已经打够了，所以现在开始观望了。现在是在猎捕。他盯上我了。但我总是把披布给他。
He shook the cape at the bull; there he comes; he side-stepped. Awful close that time. I don’t want to work that close to him.
他向公牛晃动披布；他来了；他侧步。那次非常靠近。我不想在离他那么近的地方做动作。
The edge of the cape was wet with blood where it had swept along the bull’s back as he went by.
斗篷的边缘因它掠过公牛的背而湿透了血。
All right, here’s the last one.
好了，这就是最后一头。
Manuel, facing the bull, having turned with him each charge, offered the cape with his two hands. The bull looked at him. Eyes watching, horns straight forward, the bull looked at him, watching.
曼努埃尔面向公牛，随着每次冲锋与它转身，用双手举着斗篷。公牛看着他。眼睛注视着，角向前伸直，公牛看着他，注视着。
‘Huh!’ Manuel said, ‘Toro!’ and leaning back, swung the cape forward. Here he comes. He side-stepped, swung the cape in back of him, and pivoted, so the bull followed a swirl of cape and then was left with nothing, fixed by the pass, dominated by the cape. Manuel swung the cape under his muzzle with one hand, to show the bull was fixed, and walked away.
“哦！”曼努埃尔说，“Toro！”他向后一仰，把斗篷向前一挥。它来了。他侧步，向身后挥舞斗篷，然后转身，公牛追随一阵斗篷的旋转，随即被孤立无物，被这道身姿定住，被斗篷主宰。曼努埃尔一手把斗篷在它口鼻下摆动，示意公牛被定住了，然后走开了。
There was no applause.
没有掌声。
Manuel walked across the sand toward the barrera, while Zurito rode out of the ring. The trumpet had blown to change the act to the planting of the banderillos while Manuel had been working with the bull. He had not consciously noticed it. The monos were spreading canvas over the two dead horses and sprinkling sawdust around them.
曼努埃尔走过沙地朝围栏走去，苏里托骑着马离开了场地。换戏目的小号声在曼努埃尔还在和公牛周旋时就吹响了，要把节目改成插花刀的环节。他并没有有意识地注意到这一点。猴子们正在把帆布铺在两匹死马身上，并在周围撒锯末。
Manuel came up to the barrera for a drink of water. Retana’s man handed him the heavy porous jug.
曼努埃尔走到围栏边去喝水。雷塔纳的人把那只沉重多孔的水壶递给了他。
Fuentes, the tall gipsy, was standing holding a pair of banderillos, holding them together, slim, red sticks, fish-hook points out. He looked at Manuel.
富恩特斯，那个高个子的吉普赛人，站着手里拿着一对花刀，把它们并在一起，细长的红木杆，鱼钩形的尖端朝外。他看着曼努埃尔。
‘Go on out there,’ Manuel said.
“上去吧，”曼努埃尔说。
The gipsy trotted out. Manuel set down the jug and watched. He wiped his face with his handkerchief.
吉普赛人小跑着走了出去。曼努埃尔放下酒壶，注视着。他用手帕擦了擦脸。
