The critic of El Heraldo reached for the bottle of warm champagne that stood between his feet, took a drink, and finished his paragraph.
《晨报》的评论家伸手去拿放在脚边那瓶温起泡香槟，喝了一口，写完了他的段落。
’ - the aged Manolo rated no applause for a vulgar series of lances with the cape and we entered the third of the palings.’
“——年长的马诺洛对一连串粗俗的斗篷刺并不买账，我们进入了第三道围栏。”
Alone in the centre of the ring the bull stood, still fixed. Fuentes, tall, flat-backed, walking toward him arrogantly, his arms spread out, the two slim, red sticks, one in each hand, held by the fingers, points straight forward. Fuentes walked forward. Back of him and to one side was a peon with a cape. The bull looked at him and was no longer fixed.
公牛独自站在斗圈中央，仍然一动不动。富恩特斯高个儿，背平，傲然向他走去，双臂张开，双手各握着一根细长的红棍，指节夹着，尖端朝前。富恩特斯向前走。 他身后偏一侧有个佩恩拿着披风。公牛看着他，不再僵住。
His eyes watched Fuentes, now standing still. Now he leaned back, calling to him. Fuentes twitched the two banderillos and the light on the steel points caught the bull’s eye.
它的目光盯着现在站定的富恩特斯。此刻它向后仰，像是在向他召唤。富恩特斯一抖那两根班德里略，钢尖闪了闪，映进了公牛的眼里。
His tail went up and he charged.
它翘起尾巴，猛然扑来。
He came straight, his eyes on the man. Fuentes stood still, leaning back, the banderillos pointing forward. As the bull lowered his head to hook, Fuentes leaned backward, his arms came together and rose, his two hands touching, the banderillos two descending red lines, and leaning forward drove the points into the bull’s shoulder, leaning far in over the bull’s horns and pivoting on the two upright sticks, his legs tight together, his body curving to one side to let the bull pass.
它直冲过来，眼睛盯着那人。富恩特斯站定，身体后仰，班德里略指向前方。公牛低头欲钩时，富恩特斯向后倾，双臂合拢上举，双手相触，那两根班德里略变成两道下落的红线，他向前倾身把尖端刺进公牛的肩膀，身体大幅前伸越过公牛的角，并以两根直立的棍为支点转身，双腿并拢，躯体向一侧弯曲让公牛从身旁冲过。
‘Olé!’ from the crowd.
“好！”人群中喊道。
The bull was hooking wildly, jumping like a trout, all four feet off the ground. The red shaft of the banderillos tossed as he jumped.
公牛猛然转向，一跃如鳟鱼，四蹄腾空。插矛的红杆在它跳动时摇摆。
Manuel, standing at the barrera, noticed that he looked always to the right.
站在围栏边的曼努埃尔注意到他总是朝右看。
‘Tell him to drop the next pair on the right,’ he said to the kid who started to run out to Fuentes with the new banderillos.
“叫他把下一对往右扔，”他对那个跑去把新插矛递给富恩特斯的孩子说。
A heavy hand fell on his shoulder. It was Zurito.
一只沉重的手落在他的肩上。是苏里托。
‘How do you feel, kid?’ he asked.
“你感觉怎么样，孩子？”他问。
Manuel was watching the bull.
曼努埃尔在看那头公牛。
Zurito leaned forward on the barrera, leaning the weight of his body on his arms. Manuel turned to him.
苏里托靠在挡墙上，身体的重量压在双臂上。曼努埃尔转向他。
‘You’re going good,’ Zurito said.
“你干得不错，”祖里托说。
Manuel shook his head. He had nothing to do now until the next third. The gipsy was very good with the banderillos. The bull would come to him in the next third in good shape. He was a good bull. It had all been easy up to now. The final stuff with the sword was all he worried over. He did not really worry. He did not even think about it. But standing there he had a heavy sense of apprehension. He looked out at the bull, planning his faena, his work with the red cloth that was to reduce the bull, to make him manageable.
曼努埃尔摇了摇头。现在直到下一场第三幕开始他也无事可做。吉普赛人在扎小旗方面非常拿手。那头公牛在下一场第三幕会以良好的状态冲向他。这是一头好牛。到目前为止一切都很顺利。最后用剑的部分才是他担心的。他并没有真正担心，甚至根本没去想它。但站在那里他感到一种沉重的忧虑。他望着那头牛，计划着他的舞步，他用来制服公牛、让它听话的红布表演。
The gipsy was walking out toward the bull again, walking heel-and-toe, insultingly, like a ballroom dancer, the red shafts of the banderillos twitching with his walk. The bull watched him, not fixed now, hunting him, but waiting to get close enough so he could be sure of getting him, getting the horns into him.
吉普赛人又朝公牛走去，脚跟着脚尖地走着，带着侮辱性的姿态，像个交际舞舞者，扎小旗的红杆随着他的步伐轻微颤动。公牛盯着他，现在不再是死死盯住，而是在猎视他，等待接近到足够的距离以确保能刺中他，把角顶进他体内。
As Fuentes walked forward the bull charged. Fuentes ran across the quarter of a circle as the bull charged and, as he passed running backward, stopped, swung forward, rose on his toes, arms straight out, and sunk the banderillos straight down into the tight of the big shoulder muscles as the bull missed him.
当富恩特斯向前走时，公牛发起了冲锋。公牛冲来时，富恩特斯横穿了四分之一圆的路程；当他边跑边倒退经过时停住，猛地向前摆动，踮起脚尖，双臂伸直，把扎小旗笔直地插进那大块肩部肌肉的紧实处，而公牛未能顶中他。
The crowd were wild about it.
人群为之狂热。
‘That kid won’t stay in this night stuff long,’ Retana’s man said to Zurito.
“那个孩子不会在晚宴这种地方呆太久，”Retana 的手下对 Zurito 说。
‘He’s good,’ Zurito said.
“他很厉害，”Zurito 说。
‘Watch him now.’
“现在看看他。”
They watched.
他们注视着。
Fuentes was standing with his back against the barrera. Two of the cuadrilla were back of him, with their capes ready to flop over the fence to distract the bull.
富恩特斯背靠着围栏站着。两名斗牛队员站在他身后，披着斗篷，准备把斗篷掀过栅栏以转移公牛的注意。
The bull, with his tongue out, his barrel heaving, was watching the gipsy. He thought he had him now. Back against the red planks. Only a short charge away. The bull watched him.
公牛伸着舌头，胸膛起伏着，正盯着吉普赛人。它以为这回抓住他了。背靠红色木板。只需短促的一冲。公牛注视着他。
The gipsy bent back, drew back his arms, the banderillos pointing at the bull. He called to the bull, stamped one foot. The bull was suspicious. He wanted the man. No more barbs in the shoulder.
吉普赛人向后弯腰，收回双臂，banderillos（banderillo 矛）指向公牛。他对公牛喊叫，一脚跺地。公牛有些疑惑。它想要那个人。不要再刺到肩膀上了。
Fuentes walked a little closer to the bull. Bent back. Called again. Somebody in the crowd shouted a warning.
富恩特斯又向公牛靠近了一点。弯下腰。又喊了一声。人群中有人大声喊出警告。
‘He’s too damn close,’ Zurito said.
“他离得太近了，”苏里托说。
‘Watch him,’ Retana’s man said.
“盯着他，”雷塔纳那边的人说。
Leaning back, inciting the bull with the banderillos, Fuentes jumped, both feet off the ground. As he jumped the bull’s tail rose and he charged. Fuentes came down on his toes, arms straight out, whole body arching forward, and drove the shafts straight down as he swung his body clear of the right horn.
富恩特斯向后倾身，用带刺的小旗挑逗公牛，然后跳起，双脚离地。当他跳起时，公牛的尾巴高扬并冲了上来。富恩特斯脚尖着地，双臂伸直，全身向前拱起，顺势将矛柄直插下去，同时把身体甩离右侧的牛角。
The bull crashed into the barrera where the flopping capes had attracted his eye as he lost the man.
公牛猛撞进了围栏，那里的垂摆披风吸引了它的注意，当时它已经把人抛在了身后。
The gipsy came running along the barrera toward Manuel, taking the applause of the crowd. His vest was ripped where he had not quite cleared the point of the horn. He was happy about it, showing it to the spectators. He made the tour of the ring. Zurito saw him go by, smiling, pointing at his vest. He smiled.
吉普赛人沿着围栏跑向曼努埃尔，接受着观众的掌声。他的背心在没能完全避开牛角尖处被撕破了。他为此感到高兴，向观众展示那处伤口。他绕着斗牛场转了一圈。祖里托看到他经过，笑着，指着他的背心。他也笑了。
Somebody else was planting the last pair of banderillos. Nobody was paying any attention.
另有几个人正插最后一对班得里洛。没有人再去注意其他事了。
Retana’s man tucked a baton inside the red cloth of a muleta, folded the cloth over it, and handed it over the barrera to Manuel. He reached in the leather sword-case, took out a sword, and holding it by its leather scabbard, reached it over the fence to Manuel. Manuel pulled the blade out by the red hilt and the scabbard fell limp.
雷塔纳的人把一根短棍塞进红色披布的褶里，把披布对折，然后把它递过围栏给曼努埃尔。他伸手进皮革佩剑鞘，抽出一把剑，握着剑的皮鞘把它递过围栏给曼努埃尔。曼努埃尔抓着红色剑柄把刀刃拔出，鞘便软塌塌地掉下。
He looked at Zurito. The big man saw he was sweating.
他看着苏里托。那位壮汉看到他在出汗。
‘Now you get him, kid,’ Zurito said.
“现在你上去，孩子，”苏里托说。
Manuel nodded.
曼努埃尔点了点头。
‘He’s in good shape,’ Zurito said.
“他状态很好，”苏里托说。
‘Just like you want him,’ Retana’s man assured him.
“就像你想要的那样，”Retana 的手下向他保证。
Manuel nodded.
Manuel 点了点头。
The trumpeter, up under the roof, blew for the final act, and Manuel walked across the arena toward where, up in the dark boxes, the president must be.
号手在屋顶下吹响了终幕号角，Manuel 越过竞技场朝着上面黑暗包厢里总统应该在的地方走去。
In the front row of seats the substitute bull-fight critic of E l E l ElE l Heraldo took a long drink of the warm champagne. He had decided it was not worth while to write a running story and would write up the corrida back in the office. What the hell was it anyway? Only a nocturnal. If he missed anything he would get it out of the morning papers. He took another drink of the champagne. He had a date at Maxim’s at twelve. Who were these bull-fighters anyway? Kids and bums. A bunch of bums. He put his pad of paper in his pocket and looked over toward Manuel, standing very much alone in the ring, gesturing with his hat in a salute toward a box he could not see high up in the dark plaza. Out in the ring the bull stood quiet, looking at nothing.
在前排座位上， E l E l ElE l Heraldo 的替补斗牛评论员大口喝着温热的香槟。他已经决定不值得写一篇现场报道，回办公室再写这场 corrida 即可。反正这算什么呢？不过是一场夜间斗牛。如果他错过了什么，到早报上补就行了。他又喝了一口香槟。他在十二点有个在 Maxim’s 的约会。那些斗牛士到底算什么？小子和无赖。一群无赖。他把记事本放进口袋，朝着站在斗牛场中央、孤零零地向着他看不见的高处黑暗看台挥帽敬礼的 Manuel 看去。场中央的公牛站着不动，望着虚无。
‘I dedicate this bull to you, Mr. President, and to the public of Madrid, the most intelligent and generous of the world,’ was what Manuel was saying. It was a formula. He said it all. It was a little long for nocturnal use.
“我把这头公牛献给你，总统先生，也献给马德里市民——世界上最聪明、最慷慨的人，”曼努埃尔正在说着。这是一句套话。他把话全部说完了。对夜间使用来说，有点长。
He bowed at the dark, straightened, tossed his hat over his shoulder, and, carrying the muleta in his left hand and the sword in his right, walked out toward the bull.
他向黑暗处鞠了一躬，挺直身子，把帽子向肩上抛去，左手拿着红帕，右手拿着剑，向公牛走去。
Manuel walked toward the bull. The bull looked at him; his eyes were quick. Manuel noticed the way the banderillos hung down on his left shoulder and the steady sheen of blood from Zurito’s pic-ing. He noticed the way the bull’s feet were. As he walked forward, holding the muleta in his left hand and the sword in his right, he watched the bull’s feet. The bull could not charge without gathering his feet together. Now he stood square on them, dully.
曼努埃尔朝公牛走去。公牛看着他；眼睛很敏捷。曼努埃尔注意到绑在它左肩上的缰带垂着，注意到祖里托刺入处那条稳定的血光。他注意到公牛的蹄子。边走边用左手持红帕、右手持剑时，他盯着公牛的蹄子看。公牛若不把蹄并拢就无法冲刺。现在它四蹄正着站着，呆滞地。
Manuel walked toward him, watching his feet. This was all right. He could do this. He must work to get the bull’s head down, so he could go in past the horns and kill him. He did not think about the sword, not about killing the bull. He thought about one thing at a time. The coming things oppressed him, though. Walking forward, watching the bull’s feet, he saw successively his eyes, his wet muzzle, and the wide, forward-pointing spread of his horns. The bull had light circles about his eyes. His eyes watched Manuel. He felt he was going to get this little one with the white face.
曼努埃尔朝他走去，盯着自己的脚看。这样可以。他能做到。他必须努力把公牛的头压低，这样才能从角下过去把它杀死。他没想着剑，也没想着杀死公牛。他一次只想着一件事。但未来的事情让他感到压抑。向前走，盯着公牛的脚，他依次看见了公牛的眼睛、湿漉漉的口吻和向前张开的宽阔牛角。公牛眼周有浅色的环。公牛的目光盯着曼努埃尔。他觉得自己会抓到这只白脸的小牛。
Standing still now and spreading the red cloth of the muleta with the sword, pricking the point into the cloth so that the sword, now held in his left hand, spread the red flannel like the jib of a boat, Manuel noticed the points of the bull’s horns. One of them was
现在站定，用剑展开红色的 muleta，将剑尖插入布中，使剑现在握在左手里，把红色法兰绒像船的前帆一样展开，曼努埃尔注意到公牛角的尖端。其中一只因撞击围栏而
splintered from banging against the barrera. The other was sharp as a porcupine quill. Manuel noticed while spreading the muleta that the white base of the horn was stained red. While he noticed these things he did not lose sight of the bull’s feet. The bull watched Manuel steadily.
碎裂了。另一只尖得像豪猪的刺。曼努埃尔在展开 muleta 时注意到牛角的白色基部被染红了。在注意这些事的同时，他没有失去对公牛脚的注视。公牛稳稳地看着曼努埃尔。
He’s on the defensive now, Manuel thought. He’s reserving himself. I’ve got to bring him out of that and get his head down. Always get his head down. Zurito had his head down once, but he’s come back. He’ll bleed when I start him going and that will bring it down.
这下他处于防守状态了，曼努埃尔想。他在保留自己。我得把他从那种状态里拉出来，让他把头低下。总要让他把头低下。祖里托曾经把头低下过一次，但他又站起来了。我一开始让他动起来他就会流血，那就能把它压下去。
Holding the muleta, with the sword in his left hand widening it in front of him, he called to the bull.
握着红色披帕，左手持剑把它在身前张开，他朝公牛喊声招呼。
The bull looked at him.
公牛看着他。
He leaned back insultingly and shook the widespread flannel.
他挑衅似地向后一仰，晃动着那件张开的法兰绒。
The bull saw the muleta. It was a bright scarlet under the arclight. The bull’s legs tightened.
公牛看见了红披帕。它在电弧灯下鲜红夺目。公牛的后腿绷紧了。
Here he comes. Whoosh! Manuel turned as the bull came and raised the muleta so that it passed over the bull’s horns and swept down his broad back from head to tail. The bull had gone clean up in the air with the charge. Manuel had not moved.
它来了。呼——！当公牛冲来时，曼努埃尔转身举起红披帕，让它从公牛的角上掠过，沿着它宽阔的背从头扫到尾。公牛随着冲锋整只腾起来。曼努埃尔纹丝未动。
At the end of the pass the bull turned like a cat coming around a corner and faced Manuel.
在这次挥动的末尾，公牛像拐角处转过来的猫一样转身面对着曼努埃尔。
He was on the offensive again. His heaviness was gone. Manuel noted the fresh blood shining down the black shoulder and dripping down the bull’s leg. He drew the sword out of the muleta and held it in the right hand. The muleta held low down in his left hand, leaning toward the left, he called to the bull. The bull’s legs tightened, his eyes on the muleta. Here he comes, Manuel thought. Yuh!
它又开始进攻了。它的沉重感消失了。曼努埃尔注意到新鲜的血从黑色的肩膀上闪着光往下流，顺着公牛的腿滴落。他从红披帕里抽出剑，右手握着。红披帕低垂在左手，身体向左倾，他朝公牛喊。公牛的后腿绷紧，目光盯着红披帕。它来了，曼努埃尔想着。哟！
He swung with the charge, sweeping the muleta ahead of the bull, his feet firm, the sword following the curve, a point of light under the arcs.
他随着冲锋挥动，挥舞着红布在公牛前方，双脚稳固，剑随弧线而动，光点在弧线下闪烁。
The bull recharged as the pase natural finished and Manuel raised the muleta for a pase de pecho. Firmly planted, the bull came by his chest under the raised muleta. Manuel leaned his head back to avoid the clattering banderillo shafts. The hot, black bull body touched his chest as it passed.
在自然传递(pase natural)结束时，公牛再次冲来，Manuel 抬起红布准备做胸部传递(pase de pecho)。公牛稳稳地踩在地上，从他胸前经过，穿过那抬起的红布。Manuel 把头往后仰以避开叮当作响的彩标矛杆。炽热的黑色公牛躯体在经过时擦过他的胸膛。
Too damn close, Manuel thought. Zurito, leaning on the barrera, spoke rapidly to the gipsy, who trotted out toward Manuel with a
太他妈近了，Manuel 心想。靠在围栏上的 Zurito 急速和吉普赛人说话，吉普赛人小跑着朝 Manuel 走来，手里拿着一件
cape. Zurito pulled his hat down low and looked out across the arena at Manuel.
斗篷。Zurito 把帽子压得很低，望着场地对面的 Manuel。
Manuel was facing the bull again, the muleta held low and to the left. The bull’s head was down as he watched the muleta.
曼努埃尔再次面对公牛，红斗篷低垂并偏向左侧。公牛低着头注视着红斗篷。
‘If it was Belmonte doing that stuff, they’d go crazy,’ Retana’s man said.
“要是贝尔蒙特在干这种把戏，他们会疯的，”雷塔纳的手下说道。
Zurito said nothing. He was watching Manuel out in the centre of the arena.
祖里托一言不发。他正注视着竞技场中央的曼努埃尔。
‘Where did the boss dig this fellow up?’ Retana’s man asked.
“老板从哪儿把这个家伙挖出来的？”雷塔纳的手下问。
‘Out of the hospital,’ Zurito said.
“送回医院去，”苏里托说。
‘That’s where he’s going damn quick,’ Retana’s man said.
“他就该快点儿去那儿，”雷塔纳的手下说。
Zurito turned on him.
苏里托转向他。
‘Knock on that,’ he said, pointing to the barrera.
“敲那个门，”他说，指着栅栏。
‘I was just kidding, man,’ Retana’s man said.
“我只是开玩笑的，伙计，”雷塔纳的人说。
‘Knock on the wood.’
“敲敲木头。”
Retana’s man leaned forward and knocked three times on the barrera.
雷塔纳的人向前倾，敲了三下栅栏。
‘Watch the arena,’ Zurito said.
“盯着竞技场，”苏里托说。
Out in the centre of the ring, under the lights, Manuel was kneeling, facing the bull, and as he raised the muleta in both hands the bull charged, tail up.
在场中央，灯光下，曼努埃尔跪着，面向公牛，他双手举起红布时，公牛尾巴竖起向前冲来。
Manuel swung his body clear and, as the bull recharged, brought around the muleta in a half-circle that pulled the bull to his knees.
曼努埃尔把身体一侧躲开，当公牛再次冲来时，他把红布画了一个半圆，把公牛牵得跪倒在地。
‘Why, that one’s a great bull-fighter,’ Retana’s man said.
“哎呀，那家伙是个了不起的斗牛士，”雷塔纳的人说。
‘No, he’s not,’ said Zurito.
“不，他不是，”苏里托说。
Manuel stood up and, the muleta in his left hand, the sword in his right, acknowledged the applause from the dark plaza.
曼努埃尔站起身，左手握着小红巾，右手握着剑，向黑暗的广场上的掌声致意。
The bull had humped himself up from his knees and stood waiting, his head hung low.
公牛从膝盖上拱起身子，低垂着头站着等待。
Zurito spoke to two of the other lads of the cuadrilla and they ran out to stand back of Manuel with their capes. There were four men back of him now. Hernandez had followed him since he first came out with the muleta. Fuentes stood watching, his cape held against his body, tall, in repose, watching, lazy-eyed. Now the two came up. Hernandez motioned them to stand one at each side. Manuel stood alone, facing the bull.
苏里托对斗阵中另外两个小伙子说了几句，他们跑上前站到曼努埃尔身后，举着他们的披帕。现在他身后有四个人。恩里克斯自从他第一次拿着小红巾出来就跟在他后面。丰特斯站着看着，披帕贴着身体，高高的，静止着，注视着，眼神慵懒。现在那两个人走过来。恩里克斯示意他们分别站在两边。曼努埃尔独自站着，面对公牛。
Manuel waved back the men with the capes. Stepping back cautiously, they saw his face was white and sweating.
曼努埃尔挥手让拿披帕的人退回去。谨慎地后退时，他们看见他的脸白得发汗。
Didn’t they know enough to keep back? Did they want to catch the bull’s eye with the capes after he was fixed and ready? He had enough to worry about without that kind of thing.
他们难道不知道应该后退一点吗？他们是不是想在公牛被固定好、准备就绪后用披帛去撞中心？他已经够烦心的了，不需要这种事。
The bull was standing, his four feet square, looking at the muleta. Manuel furled the muleta in his left hand. The bull’s eyes watched it. His body was heavy on his feet. He carried his head low, but not too low.
公牛站着，四蹄稳稳着地，盯着红布。曼努埃尔用左手把红布卷起。公牛的眼睛盯着它。它的身体重重压在蹄上。它低着头，但并不太低。
Manuel lifted the muleta at him. The bull did not move. Only his eyes watched.
曼努埃尔把红布向它抬起。公牛没有动。只有眼睛在盯着。
He’s all lead, Manuel thought. He’s all square. He’s framed right. He’ll take it.
“它全是力量，”曼努埃尔想，“它方正稳固，构架完美。它会接招的。”
He thought in bull-fight terms. Sometimes he had a thought and the particular piece of slang would not come into his mind and he could not realize the thought. His instincts and his knowledge worked automatically, and his brain worked slowly and in words. He knew all about bulls. He did not have to think about them. He just did the right thing. His eyes noted things and his body performed the necessary measures without thought. If he thought about it, he would be gone.
他用斗牛的术语思考。有时他会有一个念头，但恰当的俚语一时想不起来，便无法实现这个念头。他的本能和知识自动起作用，而他的大脑运转得缓慢且以词语形式。他对公牛无所不知。关于它们他不必去思考。他只是做对的事情。他的眼睛注意到事物，他的机身（Body[Photography]）在不经过思考的情况下执行必要的动作。如果他去想，那就完了。
Now, facing the bull, he was conscious of many things at the same time. There were the horns, the one splintered, the other smoothly sharp, the need to profile himself toward the left horn, lance himself short and straight, lower the muleta, so the bull would follow it, and, going in over the horns, put the sword all the way into a little spot about as big as a five-peseta piece straight in back of the neck, between the sharp pitch of the bull’s shoulders. He must do all this and must then come out from between the horns. He was conscious he must do all this, but his only thought was in words: ‘Corto y derecho.’
现在，面向公牛时，他同时意识到许多事。有那对角——一只是成裂片状，另一只是光滑尖锐——需要把自己的侧面朝向左角，短而直地用矛刺入，放低红布（muleta），让公牛追随，然后越过角部，把剑全部插入后颈一个大约五便士硬币大小的小点，正好在公牛肩膀的锐峰之间。他必须完成这一切，然后从两角之间出来。他意识到自己必须做这些，但他脑中唯一的念头是用词语：‘Corto y derecho.’
‘Corto y derecho,’ he thought, furling the muleta. Short and straight. Corto y y yy dercho, he drew the sword out of the muleta, profiled on the splintered left horn, dropped the muleta across his body, so his right hand with the sword on the level with his eye made the sign of the cross, and, rising on his toes, sighted along the dipping blade of the sword at the spot high up between the bull’s shoulders.
“Corto y derecho，”他想着，把小红布卷起。短而直。Corto y y yy dercho，他把剑从小红布上拔出，剑柄靠在破裂的左角上做支点，把小红布搭在身前，右手握剑与眼同高划出十字，然后踮起脚尖，沿着下沉的剑刃瞄准公牛肩膀之间高处的那个点。
Corto y derecho he launched himself on the bull.
Corto y derecho 他冲向了公牛。
There was a shock, and he felt himself go up in the air. He pushed on the sword as he went up and over, and it flew out of his
发生了一声撞击，他感到自己被掀了起来。他在被掀起并翻越的同时仍向前推剑，剑从他的
hand. He hit the ground and the bull was on him. Manuel, lying on the ground, kicked at the bull’s muzzle with his slippered feet. Kicking, kicking, the bull after him, missing him in his excitement, bumping him with his head, driving the horns into the sand. Kicking like a man keeping a ball in the air, Manuel kept the bull from getting a clean thrust at him.
手中飞出。他重重摔在地上，公牛压向了他。马努埃尔躺在地上，用穿着拖鞋的脚踢着公牛的口鼻。不断踢，公牛追着他，在激动中没能弄中他，用头顶撞他，把牛角顶进沙里。像在保持一个球在空中那样踢着，马努埃尔使得公牛无法对他发动一次干净的刺击。
Manuel felt the wind on his back from the capes flopping at the bull, and then the bull was gone, gone over him in a rush. Dark, as his belly went over. Not even stepped on.
曼努埃尔感觉到披在斗牛士斗篷上的风从他背后掠过，然后公牛消失了，猛地越过了他。黑暗，随着它越过他的腹部。连踩都没踩到。
Manuel stood up and picked up the muleta. Fuentes handed him the sword. It was bent where it had struck the shoulder-blade. Manuel straightened it on his knee and ran toward the bull, standing now beside one of the dead horses. As he ran, his jacket flopped where it had been ripped under his armpit.
曼努埃尔站起身，捡起红布。富恩特斯把剑递给他。剑在击中肩胛骨处弯了。曼努埃尔把剑放在膝盖上把它弄直，朝公牛跑去，现在站在一匹死马旁边。他跑着时，外套在腋下被撕开处晃动。
‘Get him out of there,’ Manuel shouted to the gipsy. The bull had smelled the blood of the dead horse and ripped into the canvas cover with his horns. He charged Fuentes’s cape, with the canvas hanging from his splintered horn, and the crowd laughed. Out in the ring, he tossed his head to rid himself of the canvas. Hernandez, running up from behind him, grabbed the end of the canvas and neatly lifted it off the horn.
“把它弄出去，”曼努埃尔对吉普赛人喊。公牛闻到死马的血味，用角把帆布掀破冲了进去。它带着挂在断裂角上的帆布冲向富恩特斯的斗篷，观众大笑。在场内，公牛甩头想甩掉帆布。埃尔南德斯从后面跑上去，抓住帆布的一端，干净利落地把它从角上提了下来。
The bull followed it in a half-charge and stopped still. He was on the defensive again. Manuel was walking toward him with the sword and muleta. Manuel swung the muleta before him. The bull would not charge.
公牛半冲半跟着，停了下来。它又处于防御状态。曼努埃尔手持剑和红布向它走去。曼努埃尔在他面前挥动红布。公牛不肯再冲了。
Manuel profiled toward the bull, sighting along the dipping blade of the sword. The bull was motionless, seemingly dead on his feet, incapable of another charge.
曼努埃尔沿着下垂的剑刃朝公牛突进。公牛一动不动，似乎已站立不能，无法再发起冲锋。
Manuel rose to his toes, sighting along the steel, and charged.
曼努埃尔踮起脚尖，沿着钢刃瞄准，然后冲了上去。
Again there was the shock and he felt himself being borne back in a rush, to strike hard on the sand. There was no chance of kicking this time. The bull was on top of him. Manuel lay as though dead, his head on his arms, and the bull thumped him. Bumped his back, bumped his face in the sand. He felt the horn go into the sand between his folded arms. The bull hit him in the small of the back. His face drove into the sand. The horn drove through one of his sleeves, the bull ripped it off. Manuel was tossed clear and the bull followed the capes.
又是一阵冲击，他感觉自己被猛地甩回，重重地摔在沙地上。这次没有机会踢腿。公牛压在他身上。曼努埃尔像死了一样躺着，头枕在胳膊上，公牛撞击着他。撞他的背，把他的脸撞进沙里。他感觉到牛角刺进了他双臂交叠间的沙地。公牛撞击他的腰背。他的脸被压入沙中。牛角穿破了他的一只袖子，公牛把袖子扯掉了。曼努埃尔被抛开，公牛追着斗篷冲了过去。
Manuel got up, found the sword and muleta, tried the point of
曼努埃尔爬起来，找到了剑和红帕，试探着刺向...
the sword with his thumb, and then ran toward the barrera for a new sword.
用拇指擦了擦剑，然后跑向围栏去取一把新剑。
Retana’s man handed him the sword over the edge of the barrera.
Retana 的手下把剑越过围栏递给了他。
‘Wipe off your face,’ he said.
“把脸擦干净，”他说。
Manuel, running again toward the bull, wiped his bloody face with his handkerchief. He had not seen Zurito. Where was Zurito?
曼努埃尔再次跑向公牛，用手帕擦拭着他血迹斑斑的脸。他没有看到苏里托。苏里托在哪儿？
The cuadrilla had stepped away from the bull and waited with their capes. The bull stood, heavy and dull again after the action.
斗群退到公牛一旁，拿着斗篷等候。经过那番动作，公牛又变得沉重而呆滞地站着。
Manuel walked toward him with the muleta. He stopped and shook it. The bull did not respond. He passed it right and left, left and right before the bull’s muzzle. The bull’s eyes watched it and turned with the swing, but he would not charge. He was waiting for Manuel.
曼努埃尔拿着红帕走向它。他停下并摇了摇红帕。公牛没有反应。他把红帕在公牛口鼻前左右挥动，左又右，右又左。公牛的眼睛盯着红帕，随着挥动转动，但它不肯冲刺。它在等曼努埃尔。
Manuel was worried. There was nothing to do but go in. Corto y derecho. He profiled close to the bull, crossed the muleta in front of his body and charged. As he pushed in the sword, he jerked his body to the left to clear the horn. The bull passed him and the sword shot up in the air, twinkling under the arc-lights, to fall red-hilted on the sand.
曼努埃尔焦虑起来。除了上前别无他法。Corto y derecho。他靠近公牛侧身站定，把红帕横在身前，一冲而上。当他把剑刺入时，他猛地向左一扭以避开牛角。公牛从他身旁越过，剑在空中弹起，在弧形灯下闪烁，带着红柄落在沙地上。
Manuel ran over and picked it up. It was bent and he straightened it over his knee.
曼努埃尔跑过去把剑捡起。剑弯了，他把剑放在膝上把它敲直。
As he came running toward the bull, fixed again now, he passed Hernandez standing with his cape.
当他又一次向公牛奔去，目光固定，他经过站着拿着斗篷的埃尔南德斯。
‘He’s all bone,’ the boy said encouragingly.
“他瘦得像块骨头，”男孩鼓励似地说道。
Manuel nodded, wiping his face. He put the bloody handkerchief in his pocket.
曼努埃尔点点头，擦了擦脸。他把满是鲜血的手帕放进口袋。
There was the bull. He was close to the barrera now. Damn him. Maybe he was all bone. Maybe there was not any place for the sword to go in. The hell there wasn’t! He’d show them.
那就是公牛。它现在离围栏很近了。可恶。也许它真就只有骨头。也许根本没有地方可以让剑刺进去。才不是呢！他要给他们看看。
He tried a pass with the muleta and the bull did not move. Manuel chopped the muleta back and forth in front of the bull. Nothing doing.
他用小红布试图诱刺，公牛却纹丝不动。曼努埃尔把小红布在公牛面前来回挥舞。毫无效果。
He furled the muleta, drew the sword out, profiled and drove it on the bull. He felt the sword buckle as he shoved it in, leaning his weight on it, and then it shot high in the air, end-over-ending into the crowd. Manuel had jerked clear as the sword jumped.
他把小红布卷起，拔出佩剑，侧身刺进公牛。他感觉到佩剑在推动时弯曲，自己把体重压在剑上，随后剑被抛到空中，在人群中翻转着飞出去。佩剑弹起时曼努埃尔猛地躲开了。
The first cushions thrown down out of the dark missed him. Then one hit him in the face, his bloody face looking toward the crowd. They were coming down fast. Spotting the sand. Somebody threw
从黑暗中扔下的第一个坐垫没打中他。然后一个击中了他的脸，他那张流血的脸朝向人群。他们迅速落下。看见了沙地。有人近距离扔出
an empty champagne bottle from close range. It hit Manuel on the foot. He stood there watching the dark, where the things were coming from. Then something whisked through the air and struck by him. Manuel leaned over and picked it up. It was his sword. He straightened it over his knee and gestured with it to the crowd.
一个空的香槟瓶。它打在曼努埃尔的脚上。他站在那里盯着黑暗，那些东西从那里飞出来。然后有什么东西掠过空中击中了他身边。曼努埃尔俯身把它捡起来。是他的佩剑。他把剑撑在膝上，挥动着朝人群示意。
‘Thank you,’ he said. ‘Thank you!’
“谢谢你，”他说。“谢谢你！”
Oh, the dirty bastards! Dirty bastards! Oh, the lousy, dirty bastards! He kicked into a cushion as he ran.
哦，该死的混蛋们！混蛋们！哦，该死的可恶的混蛋们！他一边跑一边踢向一个垫子。
There was the bull. The same as ever. All right, you dirty, lousy bastard!
牛在那儿。和以前一样。好吧，你这个可恶、可鄙的混蛋！
Manuel passed the muleta in front of the bull’s black muzzle.
Manuel 把 muleta 递到公牛那黑色的口鼻前。
Nothing doing.
别干了。
You won’t! All right. He stepped close and jammed the sharp peak of the muleta into the bull’s damp muzzle.
你不会的！好吧。他凑近，把 muleta 那锐利的尖端猛地插进公牛潮湿的口鼻里。
The bull was on him as he jumped back and as he tripped on a cushion he felt the horn go into him, into his side. He grabbed the horn with his two hands and rode backward, holding tight on to the place. The bull tossed him and he was clear. He lay still. It was all right. The bull was gone.
公牛在他跳开时扑了上来，他在一个垫子上绊了一下，感觉到牛角刺进了他，刺进他的侧腹。他双手抓住牛角，向后骑着，紧紧抓住那个地方。公牛把他掀了出去，他脱身了。他静静地躺着。一切都好。公牛走了。
He got up coughing and feeling broken and gone. The dirty bastards!
他咳嗽着站起来，感觉被摧残得筋疲力尽。该死的混蛋们！
‘Give me the sword,’ he shouted. ‘Give me the stuff.’
“把剑给我，”他喊道。“把东西给我。”
Fuentes came up with the muleta and the sword.
富恩特斯端着小红斗篷和剑走了过来。
Hernandez put his arm around him.
埃尔南德斯搂住了他的胳膊。
‘Go on to the infirmary, man,’ he said. ‘Don’t be a damn fool.’
“去医务室吧，伙计，”他说。“别犯蠢。”
‘Get away from me,’ Manuel said. ‘Get to hell away from me.’
“离我远点，”曼努埃尔说。“给我滚远点。”
He twisted free. Hernandez shrugged his shoulders. Manuel ran toward the bull.
他挣脱了。埃尔南德斯耸了耸肩。曼努埃尔朝公牛跑去。
There was the bull standing, heavy, firmly planted.
那头公牛站着，沉重，稳稳地立着。
All right, you bastard! Manuel drew the sword out of the muleta, sighted with the same movement, and flung himself on to the bull. He felt the sword go in all the way. Right up to the guard. Four fingers and his thumb into the bull. The blood was hot on his knuckles, and he was on top of the bull.
“好啊，你这个混蛋！”曼努埃尔把剑从红布套里抽出，瞄准时动作一致，然后扑向了公牛。他感觉剑全插进去了。一直插到护手。四根手指和拇指进了公牛。血在他的指关节上滚热，他骑在公牛身上。
The bull lurched with him as he lay on, and seemed to sink; then he was standing clear. He looked at the bull going down slowly over on his side, then suddenly four feet in the air.
公牛跟着他的身子一同摇晃着，似乎要沉下去；然后又站稳了。他看着那头公牛慢慢倒向一边，然后突然四蹄朝天。
Then he gestured at the crowd, his hand warm from the bull blood.
然后他用沾着公牛血的温热手朝人群比了比。
All right, you bastards! He wanted to say something, but he started to cough. It was hot and choking. He looked down for the muleta. He must go over and salute the president. President hell! He was sitting down looking at something. It was the bull. His four feet up. Thick tongue out. Things crawling around on his belly and under his legs. Crawling where the hair was thin. Dead bull. To hell with the bull! To hell with them all! He started to get to his feet and commenced to cough. He sat down again, coughing. Somebody came and pushed him up.
够了，你们这些混蛋！他想说点什么，但开始咳嗽起来。空气又热又呛。他低头去找小红斗布。他得过去向主席敬礼。主席个鬼！他正坐着看着什么。是那头公牛。四蹄朝天。厚厚的舌头伸出来。肚子和腿下有东西在爬。毛稀薄的地方也在爬。死掉的公牛。去他的公牛！去他的他们所有人！他开始要站起来，咳个不停。又坐回去，咳着。有人过来把他推了起来。
They carried him across the ring to the infirmary, running with him across the sand, standing blocked at the gate as the mules came in, then around under the dark passageway, men grunting as they took him up the stairway, and then laid him down.
他们把他抬过赛场到医务室，跑着把他穿过沙地，站在门口被骡子挡住了，然后绕过下面的暗通道，男人们咕哝着把他抬上楼梯，然后把他放下。
The doctor and two men in white were waiting for him. They laid him out on the table. They were cutting away his shirt. Manuel felt tired. His whole chest felt scalding inside. He started to cough and they held something to his mouth. Everybody was very busy.
医生和两个穿白衣的人在等他。他们把他安放在台子上，正在把他的衬衫割开。曼努埃尔感到疲惫，整个胸膛里面像被烫着。他开始咳嗽，他们把什么东西按在他的嘴上。每个人都很忙。
There was an electric light in his eyes. He shut his eyes.
有一盏电灯照在他的眼睛里。他闭上了眼睛。
He heard someone coming very heavily up the stairs. Then he did not hear it. Then he heard a noise far off. That was the crowd. Well, somebody would have to kill his other bull. They had cut away all his shirt. The doctor smiled at him. There was Retana.
他听见有人沉重地上楼。随后又没听见了。然后他听到远处的喧闹声，那就是人群。好吧，总得有人去杀掉他的另一头公牛。他们已经把他的衬衫全割掉了。医生朝他笑了笑。那是雷塔纳。
‘Hello, Retana!’ Manuel said. He could not hear his voice.
“你好，雷塔纳！”曼努埃尔说。他听不见自己的声音。
Retana smiled at him and said something. Manuel could not hear it.
Retana 对着他笑了笑并说了些什么。Manuel 听不见。
Zurito stood beside the table, bending over where the doctor was working. He was in his picador clothes, without his hat.
Zurito 站在桌旁，俯身看着医生在工作的地方。他穿着骑手的衣服，没戴帽子。
Zurito said something to him. Manuel could not hear it.
Zurito 对他说了些什么。Manuel 听不见。
Zurito was speaking to Retana. One of the men in white smiled and handed Retana a pair of scissors. Retana gave them to Zurito. Zurito said something to Manuel. He could not hear it.
Zurito 正在和 Retana 说话。一个穿白衣的男人笑了笑，把一把剪刀递给 Retana。Retana 又把它递给了 Zurito。Zurito 对 Manuel 说了些什么。他听不见。
To hell with this operating-table. He’d been on plenty of operat-ing-tables before. He was not going to die. There would be a priest if he was going to die.
见鬼去吧，这台手术台算什么。他之前上过不少手术台。他不会死的。如果他就要死了，会有神父的。
Zurito was saying something to him. Holding up the scissors.
祖里托在对他说话。举着剪刀。
That was it. They were going to cut off his coleta. They were going to cut off his pigtail.
就是这样。他们要把他的 coleta 剪掉。他们要把他的辫子剪掉。
Manuel sat up on the operating-table. The doctor stepped back, angry. Someone grabbed him and held him.
曼努埃尔在手术台上坐了起来。医生后退一步，愤怒。有人抓住他把他按住。
‘You couldn’t do a thing like that, Manos,’ he said.
“你不能做那样的事，马诺斯，”他说。
He heard suddenly, clearly, Zurito’s voice.
他突然清晰地听见了苏里托的声音。
‘That’s all right,’ Zurito said. ‘I won’t do it. I was joking.’
“没事的，”苏里托说，“我不会那样做。我只是开玩笑。”
‘I was going good,’ Manuel said. ‘I didn’t have any luck. That was all.’
“我那会儿状态不错，”曼努埃尔说。“只是不是走运。就这样。”
Manuel lay back. They had put something over his face. It was all familiar. He inhaled deeply. He felt very tired. He was very, very tired. They took the thing away from his face.
曼努埃尔仰躺着。他们把什么东西盖在他脸上。这一切都很熟悉。他深深吸气。他感到非常疲倦。他非常非常累。他们把东西从他脸上拿开。
‘I was going good,’ Manuel said weakly, ‘I was going great.’
“我感觉不错，”曼努埃尔虚弱地说，“我感觉非常好。”
Retana looked at Zurito and started for the door.
雷塔纳看了看苏里托，朝门口走去。
‘I’ll stay here with him,’ Zurito said.
“我会留在这里陪着他，”苏里托说。
Retana shrugged his shoulders.
雷塔纳耸了耸肩。
Manuel opened his eyes and looked at Zurito.
曼努埃尔睁开眼睛，看着祖里托。
‘Wasn’t I going good, Manos?’ he asked, for confirmation.
“Manos，我不是做得很好吗？”他问，以求确认。
‘Sure,’ said Zurito. ‘You were going great.’
“当然，”祖里托说。“你做得很棒。”
The doctor’s assistant put the cone over Manuel’s face and he inhaled deeply. Zurito stood awkwardly, watching.
医生的助手把锥形罩罩在曼努埃尔的脸上，他深深吸了一口气。祖里托尴尬地站着，看着。

IN ANOTHER COUNTRY
在别的国家

In the fall the war was always there, but we did not go to it any more. It was cold in the fall in Milan and the dark came very early. Then the electric lights came on, and it was pleasant along the streets looking in the windows. There was much game hanging outside the shops, and the snow powdered in the fur of the foxes and the wind blew their tails. The deer hung stiff and heavy and empty, and small birds blew in the wind and the wind turned their feathers. It was a cold fall and the wind came down from the mountains.
到了秋天，战争总是在那儿，但我们不再去打仗了。米兰的秋天很冷，天黑得很早。然后电灯亮起来了，沿着街道望进窗子里感觉很惬意。店外挂着许多猎物，雪花撒在狐狸的毛皮上，风吹着它们的尾巴。鹿被挂得僵硬又沉重，里面空空的，小鸟在风中被吹动，风把它们的羽毛翻动。那是一个寒冷的秋天，风从山上吹下来。
We were all at the hospital every afternoon, and there were different ways of walking across the town through the dusk to the hospital. Two of the ways were alongside canals, but they were long. Always, though, you crossed a bridge across a canal to enter the hospital. There was a choice of three bridges. On one of them a woman sold roasted chestnuts. It was warm, standing in front of her charcoal fire, and the chestnuts were warm afterward in your pocket. The hospital was very old and very beautiful, and you entered through a gate and walked across a courtyard and out a gate on the other side. There were usually funerals starting from the courtyard. Beyond the old hospital were the new brick pavilions, and there we met every afternoon and were all very polite and interested in what was the matter, and sat in the machines that were to make so much difference.
我们每天午后都去医院，傍暮时分穿过城镇去医院的路有好几条。两条路是沿着运河走的，不过路很长。无论如何，进入医院总要过一座横跨运河的桥。有三座桥可选。其中一座桥上有个妇女卖烤栗子。站在她的木炭火前很暖和，栗子随后放在你口袋里也是暖的。医院很古老也很漂亮，你从一道大门进入，穿过一个院子，从另一侧的大门出去。院子里常常有出殡的队伍。古老医院之外是新的红砖病房，我们每天午后在那里碰头，大家都很礼貌、很关心病情，坐进那些将会带来巨大改变的机器里。
The doctor came up to the machine where I was sitting and said: ‘What did you like best to do before the war? Did you practise a sport?’
医生走到我坐着的机器旁说：“战争前你最喜欢做什么？你有参加体育运动吗？”
I said: ‘Yes, football.’
我说：“有，足球。”
‘Good,’ he said. ‘You will be able to play football again better than ever.’
“很好，”他说。“你会比以前更能踢好足球的。”
My knee did not bend and the leg dropped straight from the knee to the ankle without a calf, and the machine was to bend the knee and make it move as in riding a tricycle. But it did not bend yet, and instead the machine lurched when it came to the bending part. The doctor said: "That will all pass. You are a fortunate young man. You will play football again like a champion.’
我的膝盖不能弯曲，腿从膝盖到脚踝直直地下垂，没小腿肌肉，机器是要弯曲膝盖，使它像骑三轮车时那样活动。但它还未能弯曲，机器在要弯曲的地方反而颤动了一下。医生说：“这些都会过去的。你是个幸运的年轻人。你会像冠军一样再次踢足球的。”
In the next machine was a major who had a little hand like a baby’s. He winked at me when the doctor examined his hand, which was between two leather straps that bounced up and down and flapped the stiff fingers, and said: ‘And will I too play football, captain-doctor?’ He had been a very great fencer, and before the war the greatest fencer in Italy.
下一台机器里坐着一位少校，他的手小得像婴儿。他在医生检查他的手时向我眨了眨眼，他的手被夹在两条皮带之间，上下弹动，拍打着僵硬的手指，然后他说：‘医生上尉，我也能再次踢足球吗？’ 他曾是个非常出色的击剑手，战前是意大利最出色的击剑手。
The doctor went to his office in a back room and brought a photograph which showed a hand that had been withered almost as small as the major’s, before it had taken a machine course, and after was a little larger. The major held the photograph with his good hand and looked at it very carefully. ‘A wound?’ he asked.
医生回到后屋的办公室，拿来一张照片，照片显示一只手在接受机器训练之前几乎萎缩得和少校的手一样小，而之后则稍微大一些。少校用健手握着那张照片，仔细地看着。‘是伤口吗？’他问。
‘An industrial accident,’ the doctor said.
‘一起工伤事故，’医生说。
‘Very interesting, very interesting,’ the major said, and handed it back to the doctor.
“非常有趣，非常有趣，”那位少校说着，把它递还给医生。
‘You have confidence?’
“你有信心吗？”
‘No,’ said the major.
“没有，”少校说。
There were three boys who came each day who were about the same age as I was. They were all three from Milan, and one of them was to be a lawyer, and one was to be a painter, and one had intended to be a soldier, and after we were finished with the machines, sometimes we walked back together to the Café Cova, which was next door to the Scala. We walked the short way through the communist quarter because we were four together. The people hated us because we were officers, and from a wine-shop someone called out, ‘A basso gli ufficiali!’ as we passed. Another boy who walked with us sometimes and made us five wore a black silk handkerchief across his face because he had no nose then and his face was to be rebuilt. He had gone out to the front from the military academy and been wounded within an hour after he had gone into the front line for the first time. They rebuilt his face, but he came from a very old family and they could never get the nose exactly right. He went to South America and worked in a bank. But this was a long time ago, and then we did not any of us know how it was going to be afterward. We only knew then that there was always the war, but that we were not going to it any more.
每天都有三个和我年纪差不多的男孩来。他们都是米兰人，其中一个要当律师，一个要当画家，还有一个原本打算当兵。我们在机器课上完后，有时候一同走回靠近斯卡拉剧院的 Caffè Cova。我们四个人一起，便走穿过共产党人区的近路。人们憎恨我们，因为我们是军官，路过一家酒馆时有人朝我们喊道：“A basso gli ufficiali!” 有时另一个与我们同行使人数到五人的男孩用一块黑色丝巾蒙住了半张脸，因为他当时没有鼻子，要重建面部。他曾从军校去前线，上了第一线不到一小时就受了伤。他们重建了他的面容，但他出身名门，鼻子总是做不成完美。他去了南美，在一家银行工作。但那是很久以前的事了，那时我们谁也不知道以后会怎样。 那时我们只知道战争一直存在，但我们不再去参战了。
We all had the same medals, except the boy with the black silk bandage across his face, and he had not been at the front long enough to get any medals. The tall boy with a very pale face who was to be a lawyer had been a lieutenant of Arditi and had three
我们都戴着同样的勋章，除了那个脸上戴着黑色丝绷带的男孩，他在前线的时间还不够长，拿不到任何勋章。那个面色非常苍白、将来要当律师的高个男孩曾是阿尔迪蒂的中尉，他有三枚我们每人只有一枚的那种勋章。
medals of the sort we each had only one of. He had lived a very long time with death and was a little detached. We were all a little detached, and there was nothing that held us together except that we met every afternoon at the hospital. Although, as we walked to the Cova through the tough part of town, walking in the dark, with light and singing coming out of the wine-shops, and sometimes having to walk into the street when the men and women would crowd together on the sidewalk so that we would have had to jostle them to get by, we felt held together by there being something that had happened that they, the people who disliked us, did not understand.
他与死亡相处了很长时间，有点超然。我们都多少有些超然，只有一件事把我们联系在一起——我们每天下午都在医院碰面。尽管当我们走过城里难堪的地段去 Cova 时，是在黑暗中走着，酒馆里传出灯光和歌声，有时人们在行人道上拥在一起，我们不得不走到街上才能通过，感觉那些不喜欢我们的人并不理解曾经发生过的那件事，这反而使我们觉得彼此连在了一起。
We ourselves all understood the Cova, where it was rich and warm and not too brightly lighted, and noisy and smoky at certain hours, and there were always girls at the tables and the illustrated papers on a rack on the wall. The girls at the Cova were very patriotic, and I found that the most patriotic people in Italy were the café girls - and I believe they are still patriotic.
我们自己都认识 Cova，那地方既富有又温暖，光线不太亮，在某些时段又喧闹又烟雾缭绕，桌旁总有姑娘，墙上有个架子摆着画报。Cova 的姑娘们非常爱国，我发现意大利最爱国的人是咖啡馆的姑娘——我相信她们至今仍然爱国。
The boys at first were very polite about my medals and asked me what I had done to get them. I showed them the papers, which were written in very beautiful language and full of fratellanza and abnegazione, but which really said, with the adjectives removed, that I had been given the medals because I was an American. After that their manner changed a little toward me, although I was their friend against outsiders. I was a friend, but I was never really one of them, after they had read the citations, because it had been different with them and they had done very different things to get their medals. I had been wounded, it was true; but we all knew that being wounded, after all, was really an accident. I was never ashamed of the ribbons, though, and sometimes, after the cocktail hour, I would imagine myself having done all the things they had done to get their medals; but walking home at night through the empty streets with the cold wind and all the shops closed, trying to keep near the street lights, I knew that I would never have done such things, and I was very much afraid to die, and often lay in bed at night by myself, afraid to die and wondering how I would be when I went back to the front again.
起初这些小伙子对我的勋章很礼貌，问我是如何得到它们的。我把证明拿给他们看，证明上用的是非常优美的语言，充满了 fratellanza 和 abnegazione，但把那些形容词去掉后实际上就是说：他们给我勋章是因为我是个美国人。自那以后他们对我的态度有些变化，尽管我在外人面前仍是他们的朋友。我是朋友，但在他们读过表彰词之后我从未真正成为他们中的一员，因为他们的情况不同，他们为获得勋章所做的事也完全不同。确实我受过伤；但我们都知道，受伤归根结底毕竟是个意外。 不过我从未为那些丝带感到羞愧，有时在鸡尾酒会后，我会想象自己完成了他们为赢得奖章所做的一切；但夜里走在空无一人的街道上，寒风刺骨，商店都关门了，我尽量靠近路灯行走，就知道自己永远不会做出那样的事，我非常害怕死，常常一个人躺在床上，害怕死去，想着当我再次回到前线时我会是怎样的人。
The three with the medals were like hunting-hawks; and I was not a hawk, although I might seem a hawk to those who had never hunted; they, the three, knew better and so we drifted apart. But I stayed good friends with the boy who had been wounded his first
戴着勋章的三个人像猎鹰；而我并不是猎鹰，尽管在从未打过猎的人眼里我也许像猎鹰；他们三人更清楚这一点，于是我们渐行渐远。但我和那个第一次受伤的男孩仍然保持着好朋友的关系
day at the front, because he would never know now how he would have turned out; so he could never be accepted either, and I liked him because I thought perhaps he would not have turned out to be a hawk either.
白天在前线，因为他现在永远不会知道自己会变成怎样；所以他也永远不会被接受，而我喜欢他，因为我想也许他也不会变成一只鹰。
The major, who had been the great fencer, did not believe in bravery, and spent much time while we sat in the machines correcting my grammar. He had complimented me on how I spoke Italian, and we talked together very easily. One day I had said that Italian seemed such an easy language to me that I could not take a great interest in it; everything was so easy to say. ‘Ah, yes,’ the major said. ‘Why, then, do you not take up the use of grammar?’ So we took up the use of grammar, and soon Italian was such a difficult language that I was afraid to talk to him until I had the grammar straight in my mind.
那位曾是伟大剑手的少校不相信勇气，在我们坐在机车里时常常纠正我的语法，花了很多时间。他夸奖我意大利语说得好，我们交谈得很轻松。有一天我曾说意大利语对我来说似乎很容易，所以我不能对它产生很大的兴趣；一切都如此容易说出来。 “啊，是啊，”少校说。 “那么，你为什么不开始使用语法呢？”于是我们开始学习语法，很快意大利语变得如此困难，以至于我在没把语法理清之前都不敢和他说话。
The major came very regularly to the hospital. I do not think he ever missed a day, although I am sure he did not believe in the machines. There was a time when none of us believed in the machines, and one day the major said it was all nonsense. The machines were new then and it was we who were to prove them. It was an idiotic idea, he said, ‘a theory, like another’. I had not learned my grammar, and he said I was a stupid impossible disgrace, and he was a fool to have bothered with me. He was a small man and he sat straight up in his chair with his right hand thrust into the machine and looked straight ahead at the wall while the straps thumped up and down with his fingers in them.
那位少校很定期地来医院。我想他几乎没缺过一天，尽管我确信他并不相信那些机器。曾经我们谁也不相信那些机器，有一天少校说那完全是胡扯。那时机器是新的，应由我们来检验它们。他说这是个愚蠢的想法，“又一个理论”。我还没学好语法，他说我是个愚蠢、不可救药的丢人现眼的人，他把时间花在我身上真是个傻瓜。他个子不高，坐在椅子上挺直身子，右手伸进机器，目视前方的墙，带子随着他手指的动作一上一下地拍打。
‘What will you do when the war is over, if it is over?’ he asked me. ‘Speak grammatically!’
“如果战争结束了——如果它结束了——你打算做什么？”他问我。“说话要合乎语法！”
‘I will go to the States.’
“我要去美国。”
‘Are you married?’
“你结婚了吗？”
‘No, but I hope to be.’
“没有，但我希望将来会是。”
‘The more of a fool you are,’ he said. He seemed very angry. ‘A man must not marry.’
“你越是个傻瓜，”他说。他看起来非常生气。“人就不该结婚。”
‘Why, Signor Maggiore?’
“为什么，马焦雷先生？”
‘Don’t call me “Signor Maggiore”.’
“别叫我‘马焦雷先生’。”
‘Why must not a man marry?’
“为什么人不能结婚？”
‘He cannot marry. He cannot marry,’ he said angrily. ‘If he is to lose everything, he should not place himself in a position to lose that. He should not place himself in a position to lose. He should find things he cannot lose.’
“他不能结婚。他不能结婚，”他愤怒地说。“如果他要失去一切，他就不该把自己置于会失去那些东西的境地。他不该把自己置于会失去的境地。他应该寻找那些他不能失去的东西。”
He spoke very angrily and bitterly, and looked straight ahead while he talked.
他说话时既愤怒又苦涩，说话时目光直视前方。
‘But why should he necessarily lose it?’
“但他为什么一定要失去它呢？”
‘He’ll lose it,’ the major said. He was looking at the wall. Then he looked down at the machine and jerked his little hand out from between the straps and slapped it hard against his thigh. ‘He’ll lose it,’ he almost shouted. ‘Don’t argue with me!’ Then he called to the attendant who ran the machines. ‘Come and turn this damned thing off.’
“他会失控的，”少校说。他看着墙。然后他低头看了看机器，把他那只小手从带子中抽出来，一下猛拍在大腿上。“他会失控的，”他几乎喊了出来。“别跟我争！”随后他叫来了操作机器的护工。“过来，把这该死的东西关了。”
He went back into the other room for the light treatment and the massage. Then I heard him ask the doctor if he might use his telephone and he shut the door. When he came back into the room, I was sitting in another machine. He was wearing his cape and had his hat on, and he came directly toward my machine and put his arm on my shoulder.
他回到另一间房去做光疗和按摩。然后我听见他问医生能否用一下电话，他关上了门。当他回来进屋时，我正坐在另一台机器里。他披着斗篷，戴着帽子，径直走到我的机器旁，把手搭在我肩上。
‘I am so sorry,’ he said, and patted me on the shoulder with his good hand. ‘I would not be rude. My wife has just died. You must forgive me.’
“我非常抱歉，”他说，用他那只好手拍了拍我的肩膀。“我不是有意无礼。我妻子刚刚去世。请你原谅我。”
'Oh - ’ I said, feeling sick for him. ‘I am so sorry.’
“哦——”我说，为他感到难过。“我很抱歉。”
He stood there biting his lower lip. ‘It is very difficult,’ he said. ‘I cannot resign myself.’
他站在那里咬着下唇。“这很难，”他说。“我无法让自己接受。”
He looked straight past me and out through the window. Then he began to cry. ‘I am utterly unable to resign myself,’ he said and choked. And then crying, his head up looking at nothing, carrying himself straight and soldierly, with tears on both his cheeks and biting his lips, he walked past the machines and out the door.
他目光越过我，望向窗外。然后开始哭起来。“我完全无法让自己接受，”他说着哽咽。随后哭着，抬头望着空无一物的地方，姿势挺直，像个军人，两颊挂着眼泪、咬着嘴唇，他走过机器，出了门。
The doctor told me that the major’s wife, who was very young and whom he had not married until he was definitely invalided out of the war, had died of pneumonia. She had been sick only a few days. No one expected her to die. The major did not come to the hospital for three days. Then he came at the usual hour, wearing a black band on the sleeve of his uniform. When he came back, there were large framed photographs around the wall, of all sorts of wounds before and after they had been cured by the machines. In front of the machine the major used were three photographs of hands like his that were completely restored. I do not know where the doctor got them. I always understood we were the first to use the machines. The photographs did not make much difference to the major because he only looked out of the window.
医生告诉我，那位少校的妻子死于肺炎。她很年轻，直到少校因伤被正式退伍后他才与她结婚。她只病了几天，谁也没预料到她会死。少校三天没来医院。后来他在平常的时间来了，制服袖子上戴着一条黑纱。当他回来时，墙上挂着许多大幅装框的照片，都是各种伤口在被机器治好前后的对比。在少校使用的机器前面，放着三张像他那样的手被完全修复的照片。我不知道医生从哪里弄来的。我一直以为我们是第一个使用这些机器的人。这些照片对少校没有多大影响，因为他只是望着窗外。

HILLS LIKE WHITE ELEPHANTS
白象似的山峦

The hills across the valley of the Ebro were long and white. On this side there was no shade and no trees and the station was between two lines of rails in the sun. Close against the side of the station there was the warm shadow of the building and a curtain, made of strings of bamboo beads, hung across the open door into the bar, to keep out flies. The American and the girl with him sat at a table in the shade, outside the building. It was very hot and the express from Barcelona would come in forty minutes. It stopped at this junction for two minutes and went on to Madrid.
埃布罗河谷对面的山峦绵长而苍白。这一侧没有树荫也没有树，车站在阳光下两道铁轨之间。车站侧墙紧贴着建筑，那里有一片温暖的阴影，通往酒吧的敞门上挂着一帘竹珠串，挡住苍蝇。那位美国人和同他在一起的女孩坐在建筑外的阴凉处的一张桌旁。天气非常热，开往巴塞罗那的快车四十分钟后到。它在这个交汇站停两分钟，然后继续开往马德里。
‘What should we drink?’ the girl asked. She had taken off her hat and put it on the table.
“我们喝什么？”女孩问。她摘下帽子，放在桌上。
‘It’s pretty hot,’ the man said.
“挺热的，”男人说。
‘Let’s drink beer.’
“喝啤酒吧。”
‘Dos cervezas,’ the man said into the curtain.
“来两杯啤酒，”那人对窗帘外说。
‘Big ones?’ a woman asked from the doorway.
“要大杯的吗？”门口的一个女人问。
‘Yes. Two big ones.’
“对，两大杯。”
The woman brought two glasses of beer and two felt pads. She put the felt pads and the beer glasses on the table and looked at the man and the girl. The girl was looking off at the line of hills. They were white in the sun and the country was brown and dry.
女人端来了两只啤酒杯和两块毡垫。她把毡垫和啤酒杯放在桌上，望着那男人和女孩。女孩正望着一排山岗。山岗在阳光下显得白皙，周围是棕黄干燥的土地。
‘They look like white elephants,’ she said.
“它们看起来像白象，”她说。
‘I’ve never seen one.’ The man drank his beer.
“我从没见过。”那个男人喝了他的啤酒。
‘No, you wouldn’t have.’
“是的，你不会的。”
‘I might have,’ the man said. ‘Just because you say I wouldn’t have doesn’t prove anything.’
“我可能见过，”那个男人说。“仅仅因为你说我不会见过并不能证明什么。”
The girl looked at the bead curtain. ‘They’ve painted something on it,’ she said. ‘What does it say?’
女孩看着珠帘。“他们在上面涂了什么，”她说。“上面写的是什么？”
‘Anis del Toro. It’s a drink.’
“Anis del Toro。这是一种酒。”
‘Could we try it?’
“我们能尝尝吗？”
The man called ‘Listen’ through the curtain. The woman came out from the bar.
那人透过帘子喊了声‘听着’。那个女人从酒吧里走了出来。
‘Four reales.’
“给四里亚尔。”
‘We want two Anis del Toro.’
“我们要两杯 Anis del Toro。”
‘With water?’
“加水吗？”
‘Do you want it with water?’
“你要加水吗？”
‘I don’t know,’ the girl said. ‘Is it good with water?’
“我不知道，”女孩说。“加水好喝吗？”
‘It’s all right.’
“还行。”
‘You want them with water?’ asked the woman.
“你要加水吗？”女人问。
‘Yes, with water.’
“要，加水。”
‘It tastes like liquorice,’ the girl said and put the glass down.
“尝起来像甘草，”女孩说着把杯子放下。
‘That’s the way with everything.’
“所有东西都是这样。”
‘Yes,’ said the girl. ‘Everything tastes of liquorice. Especially all the things you’ve waited so long for, like absinthe.’
“是的，”女孩说。“所有东西都带着甘草味。尤其是那些你等待了很久的东西，比如苦艾酒。”
‘Oh, cut it out.’
“哎，别闹了。”
‘You started it,’ the girl said. ‘I was being amused. I was having a fine time.’
“是你先开始的，”女孩说。“我只是觉得好玩。我玩得很开心。”
‘Well, let’s try and have a fine time.’
“好吧，那我们就尽量玩得开心些。”
‘All right. I was trying. I said the mountains looked like white elephants. Wasn’t that bright?’
“好。是我在逗。是我说那些山看起来像白象。那难道不机灵吗？”
‘That was bright.’
“那确实机灵。”
‘I wanted to try this new drink. That’s all we do, isn’t it - look at things and try new drinks?’
“我想尝尝这种新酒。我们不就是这样吗——看看东西，尝尝新酒？”
‘I guess so.’
“我想也是。”
The girl looked across at the hills.
女孩朝那边的山丘望去。
‘They’re lovely hills,’ she said. ‘Thev don’t really look like white elephants. I just meant the colouring of their skin through the trees.’
“那些山丘很漂亮，”她说。“它们看起来并不像白象。我只是指树间透出的皮色。”
‘Should we have another drink?’
“我们再喝一杯吗？”
‘All right.’
“好吧。”
The warm wind blew the bead curtain against the table.
温暖的风把珠帘吹得贴在桌上。
‘The beer’s nice and cool,’ the man said.
“啤酒挺凉快的，”那人说。
‘It’s lovely,’ the girl said.
“真漂亮，”女孩说。
‘It’s really an awfully simple operation, Jig,’ the man said. ‘It’s not really an operation at all.’
“这真的只是个非常简单的手术，吉格，”男人说。“其实根本算不上手术。”
The girl looked at the ground the table legs rested on.
女孩看着桌腿所立的地面。
‘I know you wouldn’t mind it, Jig. It’s really not anything. It’s just to let the air in.’
“我知道你不会介意的，吉格。真的没什么的。只是让空气进来而已。”
The girl did not say anything.
女孩什么也没说。
‘I’ll go with you and I’ll stay with you all the time. They just let the air in and then it’s all perfectly natural.’
“我会和你一起去，我会一直和你在一起。他们只是放了点气，然后一切就完全自然了。”
‘Then what will we do afterward?’
“那之后我们怎么办？”
‘We’ll be fine afterward. Just like we were before.’
“之后我们会没事的。就像我们以前那样。”
‘What makes you think so?’
“你凭什么这么想？”
‘That’s the only thing that bothers us. It’s the only thing that’s made us unhappy.’
“那是唯一困扰我们的事。也是唯一让我们不开心的事。”
The girl looked at the bead curtain, put her hand out and took hold of two of the strings of beads.
女孩看着珠帘，伸手抓住了两串珠子。
‘And you think then we’ll be all right and be happy?’
“那你认为我们就会没事并且幸福吗？”
‘I know we will. You don’t have to be afraid. I’ve known lots of people that have done it.’
“我知道我们会的。你不用害怕。我认识很多人都做过这事。”
‘So have I,’ said the girl. ‘And afterward they were all so happy.’
“我也认识，”女孩说，“后来他们都很快乐。”
‘Well,’ the man said, ‘if you don’t want to you don’t have to. I wouldn’t have you do it if you didn’t want to. But I know it’s perfectly simple.’
“好吧，”男人说，“如果你不想做就不用做。如果你不愿意，我也不会逼你。但我知道这事非常简单。”
‘And you really want to ?’
“你真想要吗？”
‘I think it’s the best thing to do. But I don’t want you to do it if you don’t really want to.’
“我想那是最好的办法。但如果你并不是真心愿意，我不想让你去做。”
‘And if I do it you’ll be happy and things will be like they were and you’ll love me?’
“如果我去做了，你会高兴，事情会像以前一样，你会爱我吗？”
‘I love you now. You know I love you.’
“我现在就爱你。你知道我爱你。”
‘I know. But if I do it, then it will be nice again if I say things are like white elephants, and you’ll like it?’
“我知道。但如果我去做了，那如果我说事情就像白象一样，会不会又好起来，你会喜欢那样？”
‘I’ll love it. I love it now but I just can’t think about it. You know how I get when I worry.’
“我会喜欢的。我现在就喜欢，但我就是想不起来。你知道我一担心就成什么样子。”
‘If I do it you won’t ever worry?’
“如果我这么做，你就永远不会担心了？”
‘I won’t worry about that because it’s perfectly simple.’
“那件事我不会担心，因为那完全很简单。”
‘Then I’ll do it. Because I don’t care about me.’
“那我就去做。因为我不在乎我自己。”
‘What do you mean?’
“你什么意思？”
‘I don’t care about me.’
“我不在乎我自己。”
‘Well, I care about you.’
“我在乎你。”
‘Oh, yes. But I don’t care about me. And I’ll do it and then everything will be fine.’
“哦，是的。但我不在乎我自己。我会去做的，然后一切都会好起来。”
‘I don’t want you to do it if you feel that way.’
“如果你是那种感觉，我不想让你去做。”
The girl stood up and walked to the end of the station. Across, on the other side, were fields of grain and trees along the banks of the Ebro. Far away, beyond the river, were mountains. The shadow of a cloud moved across the field of grain and she saw the river through the trees.
女孩站起身，走到工作站的尽头。对面那一侧是麦田，河岸边有一排排树，河是埃布罗河。远处，河的那边是群山。一朵云的影子掠过麦田，她透过树看见了河流。
‘And we could have all this,’ she said. ‘And we could have everything and every day we make it more impossible.’
“而且我们本可以拥有这一切，”她说。“我们本可以拥有一切，可是我们一天比一天把它变得更不可能。”
‘What did you say?’
“你刚才说什么？”
‘I said we could have everything.’
“我说过我们可以拥有一切。”
‘We can have everything.’
“我们可以拥有一切。”
‘No, we can’t.’
“不，我们不能。”
‘We can have the whole world.’
“我们可以拥有整个世界。”
‘No, we can’t.’
“不能，我们不能去。”
‘We can go anywhere.’
“我们可以去任何地方。”
‘No, we can’t. It isn’t ours any more.’
“不能，我们不能。它不再是我们的了。”
‘It’s ours.’
“它是我们的。”
‘No, it isn’t. And once they take it away, you never get it back.’
“不是的。并且一旦他们夺走了它，你就再也拿不回来了。”
‘But they haven’t taken it away.’
“但是他们并没有夺走它。”
‘We’ll wait and see.’
“我们拭目以待吧。”
‘Come back in the shade,’ he said. ‘You mustn’t feel that way.’
“回到阴凉处来，”他说。“你不该那样想。”
‘I don’t feel any way,’ the girl said. ‘I just know things.’
“我没什么感觉，”女孩说。“我就是知道一些事。”
'I don’t want you to do anything that you don’t want to do - ’
“我不想让你做任何你不愿做的事——”
‘Nor that isn’t good for me,’ she said. ‘I know. Could we have another beer?’
“也不是对我不好的事，”她说。“我知道。我们能再来一杯啤酒吗？”
'All right. But you’ve got to realize - ’
“好吧。但你得明白——”
‘I realize,’ the girl said. ‘Can’t we maybe stop talking?’
“我知道，”女孩说。“我们能不能别再谈了？”
They sat down at the table and the girl looked across at the hills on the dry side of the valley and the man looked at her and at the table.
他们坐到桌旁，女孩望向山谷干燥一侧的群山，男人看着她又看着桌子。
‘You’ve got to realize,’ he said, ‘that I don’t want you to do it if you don’t want to. I’m perfectly willing to go through with it if it means anything to you.’
“你得明白，”他说，“如果你不想做，我并不想强你。我完全愿意配合，只要这对你有意义。”
‘Doesn’t it mean anything to you? We could get along.’
“对你就一点也不重要吗？我们可以过下去的。”
‘Of course it does. But I don’t want anybody but you. I don’t want anyone else. And I know it’s perfectly simple.’
“当然是。但我只想要你。我不想要别人。而且我知道这件事非常简单。”
‘Yes, you know it’s perfectly simple.’
“是的，你知道这件事非常简单。”
‘It’s all right for you to say that, but I do know it.’
“你这样说容易，但我确实知道。”
‘Would you do something for me now?’
“你现在愿意为我做一件事吗？”
‘I’d do anything for you.’
“我会为你做任何事的。”
‘Would you please please please please please please please stop talking?’
“你能不能请请请请请请请不要再说了？”
He did not say anything but looked at the bags against the wall of the station. There were labels on them from all the hotels where they had spent nights.
他什么也没说，只是看着靠在车站墙边的行李包。包上贴着他们曾过夜的各个旅馆的标签。
‘But I don’t want you to,’ he said. ‘I don’t care anything about it.’
“但我并不想要你那样做，”他说。“我一点也不在乎。”
‘I’ll scream,’ the girl said.
“我要尖叫，”女孩说。
The woman came out through the curtains with two glasses of
那个女人从帘子后面出来，端着两杯啤酒
beer and put them down on the damp felt pads. "The train comes in five minutes,’ she said.
放在湿了的毡垫上。“火车五分钟后到，”她说。
‘What did she say?’ asked the girl.
“她刚才说什么？”女孩问。
‘That the train is coming in five minutes.’
“火车五分钟后就会到。”
The girl smiled brightly at the woman, to thank her.
女孩朝那女人灿烂一笑以示感谢。
‘I’d better take the bags over to the other side of the station,’ the man said. She smiled at him.
“我最好把行李拿到站的另一边去，”那男子说。她对他微笑。
‘All right. Then come back and we’ll finish the beer.’
“好吧。那你回来我们把啤酒喝完。”
He picked up the two heavy bags and carried them around the station to the other tracks. He looked up the tracks but could not see the train. Coming back, he walked through the bar-room, where people waiting for the train were drinking. He drank an Anis at the bar and looked at the people. They were all waiting reasonably for the train. He went out through the bead curtain. She was sitting at the table and smiled at him.
他拎起两个沉重的包，把它们搬到站台的另一侧。他顺着轨道往远处看，但看不到火车。回来的路上，他穿过酒吧间，等车的人们正在喝东西。他在吧台喝了一杯茴香酒，打量着那些人。他们都规规矩矩地等着火车。他从珠帘外走了出去。她正坐在桌旁，朝他笑。
‘Do you feel better?’ he asked.
“你感觉好点了吗？”他问。
‘I feel fine,’ she said. ‘There’s nothing wrong with me. I feel fine.’
“我感觉很好，”她说。“我没事。我感觉很好。”

THE KILLERS
杀手们

The door of Henry’s lunch-room opened and two men came in. They sat down at the counter.
亨利的午餐室门开了，两个人走了进来。他们坐在柜台旁。
‘What’s yours?’ George asked them.
“你们想吃什么？”乔治问他们。
‘I don’t know,’ one of the men said. 'What do you want to eat, Al?’
“我不知道，”其中一个人说。“你想吃什么，艾尔？”
‘I don’t know,’ said Al. ‘I don’t know what I want to eat.’
“我不知道，”艾尔说。“我不知道我想吃什么。”
Outside it was getting dark. The street-light came on outside the window. The two men at the counter read the menu. From the other end of the counter Nick Adams watched them. He had been talking to George when they came in.
外面天色渐暗。窗外的路灯亮了。柜台那两个人在看菜单。尼克·亚当斯从柜台另一头看着他们。他们进来时他还在和乔治说话。
‘I’ll have a roast pork tenderloin with apple sauce and mashed potatoes,’ the first man said.
“我要一份烤猪里脊，配苹果酱和土豆泥，”第一个人说。
‘It isn’t ready yet.’
“还没做好。”
‘What the hell do you put it on the card for ?’
“那你他妈把它写在菜单上干嘛？”
‘That’s the dinner,’ George explained. ‘You can get that at six o’clock.’
“那是晚餐，”乔治解释道。“你六点可以吃到那个。”
George looked at the clock on the wall behind the counter.
乔治看了看柜台后墙上的钟。
‘It’s five o’clock.’
“现在是五点钟。”
‘The clock says twenty minutes past five,’ the second man said.
“钟上显示是五点二十分，”第二个人说。
‘It’s twenty minutes fast.’
“它快了二十分钟。”
‘Oh, to hell with the clock,’ the first man said. ‘What have you got to eat?’
“哦，去他的钟表吧，”第一个人说。“你有什么吃的？”
‘I can give you any kind of sandwiches,’ George said. ‘You can have ham and eggs, bacon and cggs, liver and bacon, or a steak.’
“我可以给你任何种类的三明治，”乔治说。“你可以吃火腿煎蛋、培根煎蛋、肝脏配培根，或者一块牛排。”
‘Give me chicken croquettes with green peas and cream sauce and mashed potatoes.’
“给我鸡肉可乐饼配青豆和奶油酱，再来土豆泥。”
‘That’s the dinner.’
“那就是晚饭。”
‘Everything we want’s the dinner, ch? That’s the way you work it.’
“我们想要的一切都是晚饭，懂吗？你就这么操作的。”
'I can give you ham and eggs, bacon and eggs, liver - ’
“我可以给你火腿配蛋、培根配蛋、肝脏——”
‘I’ll take ham and eggs,’ the man called Al said. He wore a derby hat and a black overcoat buttoned across the chest. His face was
“我要火腿配蛋，”那个叫阿尔的男人喊道。他戴着礼帽，穿着一件黑色大衣，扣子扣到胸前。脸是
small and white and he had tight lips. He wore a silk muffler and gloves.
个子小，脸色白，嘴唇紧抿。他戴着丝围巾和手套。
‘Give me bacon and eggs,’ said the other man. He was about the same size as Al. Their faces were different, but they were dressed like twins. Both wore overcoats too tight for them. They sat leaning forward, their elbows on the counter.
“给我培根和鸡蛋，”另一个人说。他跟 Al 差不多高。面容不同，但穿着像双胞胎。他们都穿着过于紧身的外套。两人前倾着身子，胳膊肘靠在柜台上。
‘Got anything to drink?’ Al asked.
“有喝的吗？”Al 问。
‘Silver beer, bevo, ginger-ale,’ George said.
“银啤、bevo、姜汁汽水，”George 说。
‘I mean you got anything to drink?’
“我的意思是，你有啥喝的吗？”
‘Just those I said.’
“就那些我说的那些。”
‘This is a hot town,’ said the other. ‘What do they call it?’
“这是个炎热的城镇，”另一个人说。“他们叫什么名字来着？”
‘Summit.’
“Summit。”
‘Ever hear of it?’ Al asked his friend.
“你听说过吗？”艾尔问他的朋友。
‘No,’ said the friend.
“没有，”朋友说。
‘What do you do here nights?’ Al asked.
“你们晚上在这儿做什么？”艾尔问。
‘They eat the dinner,’ his friend said. ‘They all come here and eat the big dinner.’
“他们吃晚饭，”他的朋友说。“他们都来这里吃丰盛的晚饭。”
‘That’s right,’ George said.
“没错，”乔治说。
‘So you think that’s right?’ Al asked George.
“所以你觉得那是对的？”艾尔问乔治。
‘Sure.’
“当然。”
‘You’re a pretty bright boy, aren’t you?’
“你可真是个聪明的小伙子，是吧？”
‘Sure,’ said George.
“当然，”乔治说。
‘Well, you’re not,’ said the other little man. ‘Is he, Al?’
“哦，你可不是，”另一个小个子说。“他是吗，艾尔？”
‘He’s dumb,’ said Al. He turned to Nick. ‘What’s your name?’
“他哑巴，”艾尔说。他转向尼克。“你叫什么名字？”
‘Adams.’
“亚当斯。”
‘Another bright boy,’ Al said. ‘Ain’t he a bright boy, Max?’
“又是个聪明孩子，”阿尔说。“麦克斯，他不是个聪明孩子吗？”
‘The town’s full of bright boys,’ Max said.
“城里全是聪明孩子，”麦克斯说。
George put the two platters, one of ham and eggs, the other of bacon and eggs, on the counter. He set down two side-dishes of fried potatoes and closed the wicket into the kitchen.
乔治把两盘菜放在柜台上，一盘火腿和鸡蛋，另一盘培根和鸡蛋。他放下两份配菜——煎土豆，并把通往厨房的小窗关上了。
‘Which is yours?’ he asked Al.
“哪盘是你的？”他问阿尔。
‘Don’t you remember?’
“你不记得了吗？”
‘Ham and eggs.’
“火腿和鸡蛋。”
‘Just a bright boy,’ Max said. He leaned forward and took the ham and eggs. Both men ate with their gloves on. George watched them eat.
“只是个聪明的孩子，”马克斯说。他前倾身子，拿起了火腿和鸡蛋。两人戴着手套吃东西。乔治看着他们吃。
‘What are you looking at?’ Max looked at George.
“你看什么呢？”马克斯看着乔治。
‘Nothing.’
“什么也没有。”
‘The hell you were. You were looking at me.’
“你才没有。你刚才在看我。”
‘Maybe the boy meant it for a joke, Max,’ Al said.
“也许那男孩是开玩笑的，马克斯，”艾尔说。
George laughed.
乔治笑了。
‘You don’t have to laugh,’ Max said to him. ‘You don’t have to laugh at all, see?’
“你不用笑，”马克斯对他说。“你根本不用笑，明白吗？”
‘All right,’ said George.
“好吧，”乔治说。
‘So he thinks it’s all right.’ Max turned to Al. ‘He thinks it’s all right. That’s a good one.’
“所以他觉得这没问题。”马克斯转向艾尔。“他觉得没问题。真是有趣。”
‘Oh, he’s a thinker,’ Al said. They went on eating.
“哦，他是个思考者，”艾尔说。他们继续吃东西。
‘What’s the bright boy’s name down the counter?’ Al asked Max.
“柜台那边那个聪明小伙叫什么名字？”Al 问 Max。
‘Hey, bright boy,’ Max said to Nick. ‘You go around on the other side of the counter with your boy friend.’
“嘿，聪明小伙，”Max 对 Nick 说。“你和你那男朋友绕到柜台另一边去。”
‘What’s the idea?’ Nick asked.
“什么意思？”Nick 问。
‘There isn’t any idea.’
“没什么意思。”
‘You better go around, bright boy,’ Al said. Nick went around behind the counter.
“你最好绕过去，聪明小子，”阿尔说。尼克绕到柜台后面去了。
‘What’s the idea?’ George asked.
“什么意思？”乔治问。
‘None of your damn business,’ Al said. ‘Who’s out in the kitchen?’
“关你什么事，”阿尔说。“谁在厨房里？”
‘The nigger.’
“那个黑鬼。”
‘What do you mean the nigger?’
“你说的黑人是什么意思？”
‘The nigger that cooks.’
“做饭的那个黑人。”
‘Tell him to come in.’
“叫他进来。”
‘What’s the idea?’
“什么意思？”
‘Tell him to come in.’
“叫他过来。”
‘Where do you think you are?’
“你以为你在哪儿？”
‘We know damn well where we are,’ the man called Max said. ‘Do we look silly?’
“我们他妈的知道我们在哪儿，”叫马克斯的男人说。“我们看起来可笑吗？”
‘You talk silly,’ Al said to him. ‘What the hell do you argue with this kid for ? Listen,’ he said to George, ‘tell the nigger to come out here.’
“你说话傻乎乎的，”艾尔对他说。“你到底跟这孩子争什么？听着，”他说着对乔治，“叫那个黑鬼到这儿来。”
‘What are you going to do to him?’
“你要对他做什么？”
‘Nothing. Use your head, bright boy. What would we do to a nigger?’
“什么也不做。动点脑子，聪明的孩子。我们会怎么对一个黑鬼？”
George opened the slit that opened back into the kitchen. ‘Sam,’ he called. ‘Come in here a minute.’
乔治拉开那条通往厨房的门缝。“山姆，”他喊道。“进来一下。”
The door to the kitchen opened and the nigger came in. ‘What was it?’ he asked. The two men at the counter took a look at him.
厨房的门开了，那个黑鬼走了进来。“怎么了？”他问。吧台旁的两个人看了看他。
‘All right, nigger. You stand right there,’ Al said.
“好吧，黑鬼。你就站在那儿，”阿尔说。
Sam, the nigger, standing in his apron, looked at the two men sitting at the counter. ‘Yes, sir,’ he said. Al got down from his stool.
侍者萨姆站在围裙里，看着坐在柜台边的两个人。“是，先生，”他说。阿尔从凳子上站起来。
‘I’m going back to the kitchen with the nigger and bright boy,’ he said. ‘Go on back to the kitchen, nigger. You go with him, bright boy.’ The little man walked after Nick and Sam, the cook, back into the kitchen. The door shut after them. The man called Max sat at the corner opposite George. He didn’t look at George but looked in the mirror that ran along back of the counter. Henry’s had been made over from a saloon into a lunch-counter.
“我回厨房和黑鬼还有机灵小子一起去，”他说。“回厨房去，黑鬼。你跟他去，机灵小子。”那个小个子男人跟着尼克和厨师萨姆回到了厨房。门在他们身后关上了。坐在与乔治相对角落里的那个人叫马克斯。他没有看乔治，而是看着沿着柜台后面的镜子。亨利的店从酒馆改成了午餐柜台。
‘Well, bright boy,’ Max said, looking into the mirror, ‘why don’t you say something?’
“好了，机灵小子，”马克斯看着镜子说，“你怎么不说点什么？”
‘What’s it all about?’
“这是怎么回事？”
‘Hey, Al,’ Max called, ‘bright boy wants to know what it’s all about.’
“嘿，阿尔，”马克斯喊道，“聪明的家伙想知道这是怎么回事。”
‘Why don’t you tell him?’ Al’s voice came from the kitchen.
“你为什么不告诉他？”阿尔的声音从厨房传来。
‘What do you think it’s all about?’
“你觉得这是怎么回事？”
‘I don’t know.’
“我不知道。”
‘What do you think?’
“你觉得呢？”
Max looked into the mirror all the time he was talking.
马克斯在说话时一直看着镜子。
‘I wouldn’t say.’
“我不敢说。”
‘Hey, Al, bright boy says he wouldn’t say what he thinks it’s all about.’
“嘿，阿尔，聪明小子说他不肯说他认为这一切是怎么回事。”
‘I can hear you, all right,’ Al said from the kitchen. He had propped open the slit that dishes passed through into the kitchen with a catsup bottle. ‘Listen, bright boy,’ he said from the kitchen to George. ‘Stand a little farther along the bar. You move a little to the left, Max.’ He was like a photographer arranging for a group picture.
“我听得见，”阿尔从厨房里说。他用一瓶番茄酱顶着那扇能把碟子递进厨房的小窗。“听着，聪明小子，”他从厨房朝乔治说。“往吧台那边再往前站一点。马克斯，你往左挪一点。”他像个在为合影摆队的摄影师。
‘Talk to me, bright boy,’ Max said. ‘What do you think’s going to happen?’
“跟我说说，聪明小子，”马克斯说。“你认为会发生什么？”
George did not say anything.
乔治什么也没说。
‘I’ll tell you,’ Max said. ‘We’re going to kill a Swede. Do you know a big Swede named Ole Andreson?’
“我告诉你，”马克斯说。“我们要去杀一个瑞典人。你认识一个叫 Ole Andreson 的大个子瑞典人吗？”
‘Yes.’
“认识。”
‘He comes here to eat every night, don’t he ?’
“他每晚都来这里吃饭，对不对？”
‘Sometimes he comes here.’
“有时候他来。”
‘He comes here at six o’clock, don’t he?’
“他六点来这里，是吧？”
‘If he comes.’
“如果他来的话。”
‘We know all that, bright boy,’ Max said. ‘Talk about something else. Ever go to the movies?’
“这些我们都知道了，聪明孩子，”马克斯说。“聊点别的。你去看过电影吗？”
‘Once in a while.’
“偶尔去。”
‘You ought to go to the movies more. The movies are fine for a bright boy like you.’
“你应该多去看电影。像你这么聪明的孩子，电影最合适不过了。”
‘What are you going to kill Ole Andreson for? What did he ever do to you?’
“你打算为什么杀了奥勒·安德烈森？他到底对你做过什么？”
‘He never had a chance to do anything to us. He never even seen us.’
“他根本没有机会对我们做什么。他甚至都没见过我们。”
‘And he’s only going to see us once,’ Al said from the kitchen.
“他也只会见我们一次，”阿尔从厨房里说。
‘What are you going to kill him for, then?’ George asked.
“那你打算为什么杀他？”乔治问。
‘We’re killing him for a friend. Just to oblige a friend, bright boy.’
“我们是为朋友杀他的。只是帮个朋友的忙，聪明的小子。”
‘Shut up,’ said Al from the kitchen. ‘You talk too goddam much.’
“闭嘴，”阿尔从厨房里说，“你他妈的嘴太多了。”
‘Well, I got to keep bright boy amused. Don’t I, bright boy?’
“好吧，我得让聪明小子有趣。对吧，聪明小子？”
‘You talk too damn much,’ Al said. ‘The nigger and my bright boy are amused by themselves. I got them tied up like a couple of girl friends in the convent.’
“你他妈话太多了，”艾尔说。“那个黑人和我那聪明的小伙子自顾自乐呢。我把他们绑得跟修道院里的一对女友似的。”
‘I suppose you were in a convent?’
“我猜你是在修道院待过？”
‘You never know.’
“谁知道呢。”
‘You were in a kosher convent. That’s where you were.’
“你是在犹太教规修道院里待过。你就是在那儿。”
George looked up at the clock.
乔治抬头看了看钟。
‘If anybody comes in you tell them the cook is off, and if they keep after it, you tell them you’ll go back and cook yourself. Do you get that, bright boy?’
“如果有人进来，你就告诉他们厨子不在，要是他们一直追问，你就告诉他们你会回去自己做饭。明白了吗，聪明的孩子？”
‘All right,’ George said. ‘What you going to do with us afterward?’
“好吧，”乔治说。“你打算之后怎么处置我们？”
‘That’ll depend,’ Max said. ‘That’s one of those things you never know at the time.’
“那要看情况，”马克斯说。“那种事当时是无法预料的。”
George looked up at the clock. It was a quarter past six. The door from the street opened. A street-car motorman came in.
乔治抬头看了看钟。现在是六点一刻。街道那边的门开了。一个电车司机走了进来。
‘Hello, George,’ he said. ‘Can I get supper?’
“你好，乔治，”他说，“我能吃点晚饭吗？”
‘Sam’s gone out,’ George said. ‘He’ll be back in about half an hour.’
“萨姆出去了，”乔治说，“他大约半小时后会回来。”
‘I’d better go up the street,’ the motorman said. George looked at the clock. It was twenty minutes past six.
“我最好上街去一趟，”电车司机说。乔治又看了看钟。现在是六点二十分。
"That was nice, bright boy,’ Max said. ‘You’re a regular little gentleman.’
“那孩子真聪明，干得好，”马克斯说。“你真是个小绅士。”
‘He knew I’d blow his head off,’ Al said from the kitchen.
“他知道我会把他头打掉，”艾尔从厨房里说。
‘No,’ said Max. ‘It ain’t that. Bright boy is nice. He’s a nice boy. I like him.’
“不，”马克斯说。“不是那样。‘聪明孩子’是好意。他是个好孩子。我喜欢他。”
At six-fifty-five George said, ‘He’s not coming.’
六点五十五，乔治说：“他不会来了。”
Two other people had been in the lunch-room. Once George had gone out to the kitchen and made a ham-and-egg sandwich ‘to go’ that a man wanted to take with him. Inside the kitchen he saw Al, his derby hat tipped back, sitting on a stool beside the wicket with the muzzle of a sawed-off shotgun resting on the ledge. Nick and the cook were back to back in the corner, a towel tied in each of their mouths. George had cooked the sandwich, wrapped it up in oiled paper, put it in a bag, brought it in, and the man had paid for it and gone out.
午餐室里还有其他两个人。乔治曾走到厨房为一个要带走食物的男人做了一个火腿煎蛋三明治。进了厨房，他看到阿尔，软礼帽往后歪着，坐在小门旁的凳子上，锯短霰弹枪的枪口搁在窗台上。尼克和厨师背靠背坐在角落里，嘴里各塞着一条毛巾。乔治把三明治煎好，用油纸包好，放进袋子，端了进来，那个男人付了钱然后出去了。
‘Bright boy can do everything,’ Max said. ‘He can cook and everything. You’d make some girl a nice wife, bright boy.’
“聪明孩子什么都会，”马克斯说。“他会做饭什么的。你要是找个姑娘当媳妇儿，那人可走运了，聪明孩子。”
‘Yes?’ George said. ‘Your friend, Ole Andreson, isn’t going to come.’
“是吗？”乔治说。“你那个朋友，奥勒·安德烈森，是不会来了。”
‘We’ll give him ten minutes,’ Max said.
“我们再等他十分钟，”马克斯说。
Max watched the mirror and the clock. The hands of the clock marked seven o’clock, and then five minutes past seven.
马克斯盯着镜子和钟表看。钟表的指针指向七点，然后是七点零五分。
‘Come on, Al,’ said Max. ‘We better go. He’s not coming.’
“快点，阿尔，”马克斯说。“我们最好走。他不会来了。”
‘Better give him five minutes,’ Al said from the kitchen.
“还是再给他五分钟吧，”阿尔从厨房里说。
In the five minutes a man came in, and George explained that the cook was sick.
在那五分钟里，一个人走了进来，乔治解释说厨师病了。
‘Why the hell don’t you get another cook?’ the man asked. ‘Aren’t you running a lunch-counter?’ He went out.
“你为什么他妈的不换个厨子？”那人问。“你不是在经营个午餐柜台吗？”他说完就出去了。
‘Come on, Al,’ Max said.
“快点，阿尔，”马克斯说。
‘What about the two bright boys and the nigger?’
“那两个聪明的小伙子和那个黑鬼怎么样？”
‘They’re all right.’
“他们没问题。”
‘You think so?’
“你觉得呢？”
‘Sure. We’re through with it.’
“当然。我们已经结束了。”
‘I don’t like it,’ said Al. ‘It’s sloppy. You talk too much.’
“我不喜欢，”艾尔说。“太马虎了。你话太多了。”
‘Oh, what the hell,’ said Max. ‘We got to keep amused, haven’t we?’
“唉，算了，”马克斯说。“我们得找点乐子，不是吗？”
‘You talk too much, all the same,’ Al said. He came out from the kitchen. The cut-off barrels of the shotgun made a slight bulge under the waist of his too tight-fitting overcoat. He straightened his coat with his gloved hands.
“你还是太多话了，”阿尔说着。他从厨房走出来。截短的霰弹枪枪管在他那件过紧的大衣腰部下方略微隆起。他戴着手套把大衣整理了下。
‘So long, bright boy,’ he said to George. ‘You got a lot of luck.’
“再见了，聪明小子，”他对乔治说，“你真走大运。”
‘That’s the truth,’ Max said. ‘You ought to play the races, bright boy.’
“确实如此，”马克斯说，“你该去赛马场试试，聪明小子。”
The two of them went out the door. George watched them, through the window, pass under the arc-light and cross the street.
两人从门外走了出去。乔治透过窗户看着他们走过弧形灯下，再穿过街道。
In their tight overcoats and derby hats they looked like a vaudeville team. George went back through the swinging-door into the kitchen and untied Nick and the cook.
他们穿着紧身大衣、戴着碗形帽，看起来像一队滑稽戏团。乔治穿过厨房那扇会摆动的门，回去解开了绑着尼克和厨师的绳子。
‘I don’t want any more of that,’ said Sam, the cook. ‘I don’t want any more of that.’
“我再也受不了那个了，”厨师山姆说。“我再也受不了那个了。”
Nick stood up. He had never had a towel in his mouth before.
尼克站了起来。他以前从未把毛巾塞在嘴里。
‘Say,’ he said. ‘What the hell?’ He was trying to swagger it off.
“喂，”他说，“这他妈的是什么？”他努力装出一副无所谓的样子。
‘They were going to kill Ole Andreson,’ George said. ‘They were just going to shoot him when he came in to eat.’
“他们要杀奥勒·安德烈森，”乔治说。“他进来吃饭时，他们就准备枪毙他。”
‘Ole Andreson?’
“奥勒·安德烈森？”
‘Sure.’
“当然。”
The cook felt the corners of his mouth with his thumbs.
厨子用拇指摸了摸嘴角。
‘They all gone?’ he asked.
“他们都走了吗？”他问。
‘Yeah,’ said George. ‘They’re gone now.’
“是的，”乔治说。“他们现在都走了。”
‘I don’t like it,’ said the cook. ‘I don’t like any of it at all.’
“我可不喜欢，”厨子说。“我一点都不喜欢。”
‘Listen,’ George said to Nick. ‘You better go see Ole Andreson.’
“听着，”乔治对尼克说。“你最好去看看 Ole Andreson。”
‘All right.’
“好吧。”
‘You better not have anything to do with it at all,’ Sam, the cook, said. ‘You better stay way out of it.’
“你最好一点也别插手，”厨师萨姆说。“你最好远离这事。”
‘Don’t go if you don’t want to,’ George said.
“要是不想去就别去，”乔治说。
‘Mixing up in this ain’t going to get you anywhere,’ the cook said. ‘You stay out of it.’
“掺合这事没好处，”厨师说。“你别管这事。”
‘I’ll go see him,’ Nick said to George. ‘Where does he live?’
“我去见他，”尼克对乔治说。“他住在哪儿？”
The cook turned away.
厨子转过身去。
‘Little boys always know what they want to do,’ he said.
“男孩子总知道他们想做什么，”他说。
‘He lives up at Hirsch’s rooming-house,’ George said to Nick.
“他住在赫希的寄宿屋上面，”乔治对尼克说。
‘I’ll go up there.’
“我上去。”
Outside the arc-light shone through the bare branches of a tree. Nick walked up the street beside the car-tracks and turned at the next arc-light down a side-street. Three houses up the street was Hirsch’s rooming-house. Nick walked up the two steps and pushed the bell. A woman came to the door.
路灯的弧形光透过光秃秃的树枝投射出来。尼克沿着车辙走在街上，在下一个路灯处转进一条侧街。往前数三个房子就是赫希的寄宿屋。尼克上了两级台阶，按了门铃。一个女人来开门。
‘Is Ole Andreson here?’
“奥勒·安德森在吗？”
‘Do you want to see him?’
“你想见他吗？”
‘Yes, if he’s in.’
“是的，他在。”
Nick followed the woman up a flight of stairs and back to the end of the corridor. She knocked on the door.
尼克跟着那个女人上了一段楼梯，回到走廊尽头。她敲了敲门。
‘Who is it?’
“谁啊？”
‘It’s somebody to see you, Mr. Andreson,’ the woman said.
“有人来看您，安德烈森先生，”女人说。
‘It’s Nick Adams.’
“是尼克·亚当斯。”
‘Come in.’
“进来吧。”
Nick opened the door and went into the room. Ole Andreson was lying on the bed with all his clothes on. He had been a heavyweight prizefighter and he was too long for the bed. He lay with his head on two pillows. He did not look at Nick.
尼克打开门走进房间。奥勒·安德烈森穿着所有衣服躺在床上。他曾是重量级职业拳击手，床对他来说太短了。他枕着两个枕头躺着。没有看尼克。
‘What was it?’ he asked.
“怎么了？”他问。
‘I was up at Henry’s,’ Nick said, ‘and two fellows came in and tied up me and the cook, and they said they were going to kill you.’
“我在亨利家，”尼克说，“两个家伙进来把我和厨子绑了起来，还说要杀了你。”
It sounded silly when he said it. Ole Andreson said nothing.
他说出来听着傻。奥勒·安德烈松什么也没说。
‘They put us out in the kitchen,’ Nick went on. ‘They were going to shoot you when you come in to supper.’
“他们把我们关在厨房里，”尼克继续说。“他们打算在你来吃晚饭的时候枪杀你。”
Ole Andreson looked at the wall and did not say anything.
奥勒·安德烈松望着墙，一言不发。
‘George thought I better come and tell you about it.’
“乔治觉得我最好过来告诉你这件事。”
‘There isn’t anything I can do about it,’ Ole Andreson said.
“我对此也帮不上忙，”奥勒·安德烈松说。
‘I’ll tell you what they were like.’
“我跟你说说他们是什么样子的。”
‘I don’t want to know what they were like,’ Ole Andreson said.
“我不想知道他们是什么样子的，”奥勒·安德烈松说。
He looked at the wall. ‘Thanks for coming to tell me about it.’
他看着墙。“谢谢你来告诉我这件事。”
‘That’s all right.’
“没事的。”
Nick looked at the big man lying on the bed.
尼克看着躺在床上的大个子。
‘Don’t you want me to go and see the police?’
“你不想我去报警吗？”
‘No,’ Ole Andreson said. ‘That wouldn’t do any good.’
“不行，”奥勒·安德烈森说。“那没用。”
‘Isn’t there something I could do?’
“我不能做点什么吗？”
‘No. There ain’t anything to do.’
“不。没什么可做的。”
‘Maybe it was just a bluff.’
“也许那只是虚张声势。”
‘No. It ain’t just a bluff.’
“不是。这可不只是诈唬。”
Ole Andreson rolled over toward the wall.
老安德烈森翻身朝墙那边躺去。
‘The only thing is,’ he said, talking toward the wall, ‘I just can’t make up my mind to go out. I been in here all day.’
“只是，”他朝墙那边说，“我就是下不了决心出去。我一整天都呆在这里了。”
‘Couldn’t you get out of town?’
“你不能离开小镇吗？”
‘No,’ Ole Andreson said. ‘I’m through with all that running around.’
“不，”奥勒·安德烈森说。“我受够了那种四处奔波的日子。”
He looked at the wall.
他看着墙。
‘There ain’t anything to do now.’
“现在什么都做不了了。”
‘Couldn’t you fix it up some way?’
“你不能想办法补救一下吗？”
‘No. I got in wrong.’ He talked in the same flat voice. ‘There ain’t anything to do. After a while I’ll make up my mind to go out.’
“没有。我走错了。”他用同样平淡的声音说。“没什么可做的。过一会儿我会决定出去的。”
‘I better go back and see George,’ Nick said.
“我还是回去看看乔治吧，”尼克说。
‘So long,’ said Ole Andreson. He did not look toward Nick. ‘Thanks for coming around.’
“再见了，”奥勒·安德烈松说。他没有看尼克。“谢谢你来一趟。”
Nick went out. As he shut the door he saw Ole Andreson with all his clothes on, lying on the bed looking at the wall.
尼克走了出去。关上门时，他看到奥勒·安德烈松穿着全套衣服躺在床上，看着墙。
‘He’s been in his room all day,’ the landlady said downstairs. ‘I guess he don’t feel well. I said to him: “Mr. Andreson, you ought to go out and take a walk on a nice fall day like this,” but he didn’t feel like it.’
“他一整天都待在房间里，”楼下的女房东说道。“我想他可能不舒服。我跟他说：‘Andreson 先生，像这么好的秋日你应该出去走走，’但他不愿意。”
‘He doesn’t want to go out.’
“他不想出去。”
‘I’m sorry he don’t feel well,’ the woman said. ‘He’s an awfully nice man. He was in the ring, you know.’
“真抱歉他不舒服，”女人说。“他人非常好。你知道，他曾在拳台里。”
‘I know it.’
“我知道。”
‘You’d never know it except from the way his face is,’ the woman said. They stood talking just inside the street door. ‘He’s just as gentle.’
“你光看脸是看不出来的，”女人说。他们站在街门里头聊着。“他一样很温和。”
‘Well, good night, Mrs. Hirsch,’ Nick said.
“嗯，晚安，Hirsch 太太，”Nick 说。
‘I’m not Mrs. Hirsch,’ the woman said. ‘She owns the place. I just look after it for her. I’m Mrs. Bell.’
“我不是 Hirsch 太太，”女人说。“那是她的房子。我只是替她看着。我是 Bell 太太。”
‘Well, good night, Mrs. Bell,’ Nick said.
“嗯，晚安，Bell 太太，”Nick 说。
‘Good night,’ the woman said.
“晚安，”女人说。
Nick walked up the dark street to the corner under the arc-light, and then along the car-tracks to Henry’s eating-house. George was inside, back of the counter.
Nick 沿着黑暗的街道走到拐角处的圆弧路灯下，然后顺着车轨走到 Henry 的食堂。George 在里面，柜台后面。
‘Did you see Ole?’
“你见到 Ole 了吗？”
‘Yes,’ said Nick. ‘He’s in his room and he won’t go out.’
“见过，”Nick 说。“他在自己的房间里，不肯出来。”
The cook opened the door from the kitchen when he heard Nick’s voice.
厨子听见尼克的声音就从厨房把门打开了。
‘I don’t even listen to it,’ he said and shut the door.
“我根本不听那个，”他说着又把门关上了。
‘Did you tell him about it?’ George asked.
“你跟他提过这事吗？”乔治问道。
‘Sure. I told him but he knows what it’s all about.’
“当然。我跟他提过，但他知道这是怎么回事。”
‘What’s he going to do?’
“他会做什么？”
‘Nothing.’
“什么也不会做。”
‘They’ll kill him.’
“他们会杀了他。”
‘I guess they will.’
“我想他们会的。”
‘He must have got mixed up in something in Chicago.’
“他大概在芝加哥惹上了麻烦。”
‘I guess so,’ said Nick.
“我想是吧，”尼克说。
‘It’s a hell of a thing.’
“真是一件可怕的事。”
‘It’s an awful thing,’ Nick said.
“真糟糕，”尼克说。
They did not say anything. George reached down for a towel and wiped the counter.
他们什么也没说。乔治弯腰拿起毛巾擦了擦柜台。
‘I wonder what he did?’ Nick said.
“我想知道他干了什么？”尼克说。
‘Double-crossed somebody. That’s what they kill them for.’
“背叛了谁。这就是他们杀人的原因。”
‘I’m going to get out of this town,’ Nick said.
“我要离开这个城镇，”尼克说。
‘Yes,’ said George. ‘That’s a good thing to do.’
“是的，”乔治说，“那是件好事。”
‘I can’t stand to think about him waiting in the room and knowing he’s going to get it. It’s too damned awful.’
“我受不了想着他在房间里等着，知道自己会挨打。太可怕了。”
‘Well,’ said George, ‘you better not think about it.’
“好吧，”乔治说，“你最好别去想它。”

CHE TI DICE LA PATRIA?

The road of the pass was hard and smooth and not yet dusty in the early morning. Below were the hills with oak and chestnut trees, and far away below was the sea. On the other side were snowy mountains.
山口的路在清晨既坚硬又平滑，还没有尘土。下面是长着橡树和栗树的山丘，远处山下是大海。另一边是白雪覆盖的山脉。
We came down from the pass through wooded country. There were bags of charcoal piled beside the road, and through the trees we saw charcoal-burners’ huts. It was Sunday and the road, rising and falling, but always dropping away from the altitude of the pass, went through the scrub woods and through villages.
我们从山口下行，穿过林区。路旁堆着木炭袋，通过树木可以看到烧炭人的小屋。那天是星期天，路起起伏伏，但总是从山口的高处往下延伸，穿过灌木林和村庄。
Outside the villages there were fields with vines. The fields were brown and the vines coarse and thick. The houses were white, and in the streets the men, in their Sunday clothes, were playing bowls. Against the walls of some of the houses there were pear trees, their branches candelabraed against the white walls. The pear trees had been sprayed, and the walls of the houses were stained a metallic blue-green by the spray vapour. There were small clearings around the villages where the vines grew, and then the woods.
村外是种着葡萄藤的田地。田地呈褐色，葡萄藤粗壮粗糙。房屋是白色的，街上男人们穿着礼服在玩地掷球。几栋房屋的墙边有梨树，枝桠像枝形烛台一样靠在白墙上。梨树被喷过药，房屋的墙被喷雾的蒸气染成了一种金属蓝绿色。村庄周围有小片开阔地种着葡萄藤，随后就是树林。
In a village, twenty kilometres above Spezia, there was a crowd in the square, and a young man carrying a suitcase came up to the car and asked us to take him to Spezia.
在一个村子里，离斯佩齐亚二十公里上方，广场上有一群人，一个提着手提箱的年轻人走到车前，请我们带他去斯佩齐亚。
‘There are only two places, and they are occupied,’ I said. We had an old Ford coupé.
“只有两个座位，都有人了，”我说。我们开的是一辆旧福特轿跑车。
‘I will ride on the outside.’
“我就坐在外面。”
‘You will be uncomfortable.’
“你会很不舒服的。”
‘That makes nothing. I must go to Spezia.’
“那没关系。我得去斯佩齐亚。”
‘Should we take him?’ I asked Guy.
“我们要带他吗？”我问盖伊。
‘He seems to be going anyway,’ Guy said. The young man handed in a parcel through the window.
“他看上去反正要走，”盖伊说。那个年轻人把一个包裹递进窗户。
‘Look after this,’ he said. Two men tied his suitcase on the back of the car, above our suitcases. He shook hands with everyone, explained that to a Fascist and a man as used to travelling as himself there was no discomfort, and climbed up on the running-board on
“帮我照看一下这个，”他说。两个人把他的手提箱绑在车后面，放在我们的行李上面。他和每个人握手，解释说对一个法西斯分子和一个像他这样惯于旅行的人来说没有什么不便，然后爬上了踏板，坐在上面。
the left-hand side of the car, holding on inside, his right arm through the open window.
汽车的左侧，他在里面抓着，把右臂穿出敞开的车窗。
