He took a paper-covered book out of the pocket of his coat and opened it; then laid it down on the table and lit his pipe. He leaned forward on the table to read and puffed at his pipe. Then he closed the book and put it back in his pocket. He had too much paperwork to get through. He could not enjoy reading until it was done. Outside, the sun went behind a mountain and there was no more light on the wall of the hut. A soldier came in and put some pine branches, chopped into irregular lengths, into the stove. ‘Be soft, Pinin,’ the adjutant said to him. "The major is sleeping.’
“是的，少校长官，”副官回答。他向后靠在椅子上打了个哈欠。他从外套口袋里拿出一本有纸套的书，翻开；然后把书放在桌上，点上烟斗。他俯身靠在桌上阅读，一边抽着烟斗。随后他合上书，把它放回口袋里。他有太多公文要处理。直到办完，他无法享受阅读。外面，太阳落到一座山后，草屋的墙上不再有光。一名士兵进来，把一些被砍成不规则长度的松枝放进炉子里。“轻点，皮宁，”副官对他说。“少校在睡觉。”
Pinin was the major’s orderly. He was a dark-faced boy, and he fixed the stove, putting the pine wood in carefully, shut the door, and went into the back of the hut again. The adjutant went on with his papers.
皮宁是少校的勤务兵。他是个黑脸的男孩，仔细地整理炉子，把松木小心地放好，关上门，又回到草屋后部。副官继续处理他的文件。
“Tonani,” the major called.
“托纳尼，”少校叫道。
‘Signor maggiore ?’
“少校长官？”
‘Send Pinin in to me.’
“把皮宁叫来见我。”
‘Pinin!’ the adjutant called. Pinin came into the room. ‘The major wants you,’ the adjutant said.
“皮宁！”副官喊道。皮宁走进房间。“少校找你，”副官说。
Pinin walked across the main room of the hut toward the major’s door. He knocked on the half-opened door. ‘Signor maggiore?’
皮宁穿过小屋的主屋朝少校的门走去。他敲了敞着半扇的门。“西尼奥尔·马焦雷？”
‘Come in,’ the adjutant heard the major say, ‘and shut the door.’
“进来，”副官听到少校说，“把门关上。”
Inside the room the major lay on his bunk. Pinin stood beside the bunk. The major lay with his head on the rucksack that he had stuffed with spare clothing to make a pillow. His long, burned, oiled face looked at Pinin. His hands lay on the blankets.
在房间里，Major 躺在他的铺位上。Pinin 站在铺位旁。Major 把头枕在他用备用衣物塞成的背包上当枕头。他那张又长又晒黑、抹了油的脸看着 Pinin。双手放在毯子上。
‘You are nineteen?’ he asked.
“你十九岁了？”他问。
‘Yes, signor maggiore.’
“是的，signor maggiore。”
‘You have ever been in love?’
“你曾经谈过恋爱吗？”
‘How do you mean, signor maggiore?’
“你什么意思，校官先生？”
‘In love - with a girl?’
“是谈恋爱——和一个女孩？”
‘I have been with girls.’
“我和女孩在一起过。”
‘I did not ask that. I asked if you had been in love - with a girl?’
“我不是那意思。我问你是不是谈过恋爱——和一个女孩？”
‘Yes, signor maggiore.’
“是的，少校先生。”
‘You are in love with this girl now? You don’t write her. I read all your letters.’
“你现在爱上这个女孩了？你不写信给她。我看过你所有的信。”
‘I am in love with her,’ Pinin said, ‘but I do not write to her.’
“我爱她，”皮宁说，“但我不写信给她。”
‘You are sure of this?’
“你确定吗？”
‘I am sure.’
“我确定。”
‘Tonani,’ the major said in the same tone of voice, ‘can you hear me talking?’
“Tonani，”那位专业说着同样的语气，“你能听到我说话吗？”
There was no answer from the next room.
隔壁房间没有回答。
‘He cannot hear,’ the major said. ‘And you are quite sure that you love a girl?’
“他听不到，”那位专业说。“你很确定你爱一个女孩吗？”
‘I am sure.’
“我确信。”
‘And,’ the major looked at him quickly, ‘that you are not corrupt?’
“还有，”那位专业看着他，目光一转，“你没有腐败吧？”
‘I don’t know what you mean, corrupt.’
“我不知道你指的腐败是什么意思。”
‘All right,’ the major said. ‘You needn’t be superior.’
“好吧，”那位专业说，“你不必摆出高人一等的样子。”
Pinin looked at the floor. The major looked at his brown face, down and up him, and at his hands. Then he went on, not smiling, 'And you don’t really want - ’ the major paused. Pinin looked at the floor. 'That your great desire isn’t really - ’ Pinin looked at the floor. The major leaned his head back on the rucksack and smiled. He was really relieved: life in the army was too complicated. ‘You’re a good boy,’ he said. ‘You’re a good boy, Pinin. But don’t be superior and be careful someone else doesn’t come along and take you.’
皮宁低头看着地板。少校看着他那棕色的脸，对他上下打量，又看了看他的手。然后他继续说，面无笑意，“你其实并不是真的想——”少校停顿了一下。皮宁低头看着地板。“你的最大愿望并不真的是——”皮宁低头看着地板。少校把头靠在背包上笑了。他真的松了口气：当兵的日子太复杂了。“你是个好孩子，”他说。“你是个好孩子，皮宁。但别自以为高人一等，小心别被别人抢走了。”
Pinin stood still beside the bunk.
皮宁站在铺位旁一动不动。
‘Don’t be afraid,’ the major said. His hands were folded on the blankets. ‘I won’t touch you. You can go back to your platoon if you like. But you had better stay on as my servant. You’ve less chance of being killed.’
“别怕，”少校说着。他的手叠在毯子上。“我不会碰你。如果你愿意，可以回你的排去。但你最好留在我这里当仆人。你被杀的可能性会小些。”
‘Do you want anything of me, signor maggiore?’
“您要我做什么吗，signor maggiore？”
‘No,’ the major said. ‘Go on and get on with whatever you were doing. Leave the door open when you go out.’
“不，”少校说。“继续你刚才在做的事。出去的时候把门开着。”
Pinin went out, leaving the door open. The adjutant looked up at him as he walked awkwardly across the room and out the door. Pinin was flushed and moved differently than he had moved when he brought the wood for the fire. The adjutant looked after him and smiled. Pinin came in with more wood for the stove. The major, lying on his bunk, looking at his cloth-covered helmet and his snowglasses that hung from a nail on the wall, heard him walk across the floor. The little devil, he thought, I wonder if he lied to me.
皮宁出去了，把门开着。副官看着他尴尬地穿过房间走出门的样子。皮宁脸色红润，走路的样子不同于他刚给炉子搬柴时的样子。副官看着他离开，微微一笑。皮宁又拿着更多的柴进来了。少校躺在铺位上，看着挂在墙钉上的布罩头盔和雪镜，听见他走过地板的声音。那个小混蛋，他想，我想知道他有没有对我撒谎。

TEN INDIANS
十个印第安人

After one Fourth of July, Nick, driving home late from town in the big wagon with Joe Garner and his family, passed nine drunken Indians along the road. He remembered there were nine because Joe Garner, driving along in the dusk, pulled up the horses, jumped down into the road and dragged an Indian out of the wheel rut. The Indian had been asleep, face down in the sand. Joe dragged him into bushes and got back up on the wagon box.
一个七月四日之后的晚上，尼克深夜从镇上驾着大车回家，车上还有乔·加纳和他一家人，路上遇到九个醉醺醺的印第安人。他记得是九个，因为在薄暮中行驶的乔·加纳勒住马，跳下车把一个印第安人从车轮辙里拖了出来。那个印第安人面朝下睡在沙地里。乔把他拖到灌木丛里，然后又爬回车斗上。
‘That makes nine of them,’ Joe said, ‘just between here and the edge of town.’
“那就九个了，”乔说，“就从这儿到镇边。”
‘Them Indians,’ said Mrs. Garner.
“那些印第安人，”加纳太太说。
Nick was on the back seat with the two Garner boys. He was looking out from the back seat to see the Indian where Joe had dragged him alongside of the road.
尼克坐在后座，和两个加纳家的男孩在一起。他从后座向外看，想看看乔把他拖到路边的那个印第安人。
‘Was it Billy Tabeshaw?’ Carl asked.
“是比利·塔贝肖吗？”卡尔问。
‘No.’
“没有。”
‘His pants looked mighty like Billy.’
“他的裤子看起来很像比利的那条。”
‘All Indians wear the same kind of pants.’
“所有印第安人都穿那种裤子。”
‘I didn’t see him at all,’ Frank said. ‘Pa was down into the road and back up again before I seen a thing. I thought he was killing a snake.’
“我根本没看见他，”弗兰克说。“爸下到路上又回来了，我一丁点儿动静都没看见。我还以为他在打蛇呢。”
‘Plenty of Indians’ll kill snakes to-night, I guess,’ Joe Garner said.
“今晚恐怕会有不少印第安人去打蛇，”乔·加纳说。
‘Them Indians,’ said Mrs. Garner.
“那些印第安人，”加纳太太说。
They drove along. The road turned off from the main highway and went up into the hills. It was hard pulling for the horses and the boys got down and walked. The road was sandy. Nick looked back from the top of the hill by the school house. He saw the lights of Petoskey and, off across Little Traverse Bay, the lights of Harbour Springs. They climbed back in the wagon again.
他们继续行驶。路从主干道转出，往山上走。马拉得很吃力，男孩们下车步行。路是沙土的。尼克在校舍旁的山顶回望。他看见佩托斯基的灯火，穿过小特拉弗斯湾远处是哈伯斯普林斯的灯光。他们又爬上了马车。
‘They ought to put some gravel on that stretch,’ Joe Garner said. The wagon went along the road through the woods. Joe and Mrs. Garner sat close together on the front seat. Nick sat between the two boys. The road came out into a clearing.
“他们该在那段路上铺些碎石子，”乔·加纳说。马车沿着穿过树林的路前行。乔和加纳太太挨坐在前座。尼克坐在两个男孩中间。路通到了一个空地。
‘Right here was where Pa ran over the skunk.’
“就在这儿，爸把臭鼬给压死了。”
‘It was farther on.’
“是在更前面。”
‘It don’t make no difference where it was,’ Joe said without turning his head. ‘One place is just as good as another to run over a skunk.’
“在哪儿压到臭鼬无所谓，”乔没转头说。“哪儿压到臭鼬都一样。”
‘I saw two skunks last night,’ Nick said.
“我昨晚看到两只臭鼬，”尼克说。
‘Where?’
“哪里？”
‘Down by the lake. They were looking for dead fish along the beach.’
“湖边。他们在海滩上找死鱼。”
‘They were coons probably,’ Carl said.
“大概是浣熊，”卡尔说。
‘They were skunks. I guess I know skunks.’
“是臭鼬。我想我认得臭鼬。”
‘You ought to,’ Carl said. ‘You got an Indian girl.’
“你应该的，”卡尔说。“你娶了个印度女孩。”
‘Stop talking that way, Carl,’ said Mrs. Garner.
“别那样说，卡尔，”加纳太太说。
‘Well, they smell about the same.’
“嗯，她们闻起来差不多。”
Joe Garner laughed.
乔·加纳笑了。
‘You stop laughing, Joe,’ Mrs. Garner said. ‘I won’t have Carl talk that way.’
“你别笑了，乔，”加纳太太说。“我不允许卡尔那样说话。”
‘Have you got an Indian girl, Nickie?’ Joe asked.
“你有印度女孩吗，尼基？”乔问。
‘No.’
“没有。”
‘He has too, Pa,’ Frank said. ‘Prudence Mitchell’s his girl.’
“他有的，爸爸，”弗兰克说。“普鲁登斯·米切尔是他的女朋友。”
‘She’s not.’
“她不是。”
‘He goes to see her every day.’
“他每天都去看她。”
‘I don’t.’ Nick, sitting between the two boys in the dark, felt hollow and happy inside himself to be teased about Prudence Mitchell. ‘She ain’t my girl,’ he said.
“我没去。”尼克坐在黑暗中两个男孩中间，听别人拿普鲁登斯·米切尔开玩笑，他心里既空虚又快乐。“她不是我的女朋友，”他说。
‘Listen to him,’ said Carl. ‘I see them together every day.’
“听他说的，”卡尔说。“我每天都看到他们在一起。”
‘Carl can’t get a girl,’ his mother said. ‘Not even a squaw.’
“卡尔追不到女孩，”他母亲说。“连个印第安女孩都不行。”
Carl was quiet.
卡尔沉默了。
‘Carl ain’t no good with girls,’ Frank said.
“卡尔不会哄女孩，”弗兰克说。
‘You shut up.’
“你闭嘴。”
‘You’re all right, Carl,’ Joe Garner said. ‘Girls never got a man anywhere. Look at your pa.’
“你没事的，卡尔，”乔·加纳说。“女孩从来帮不了男人。看看你老爹。”
‘Yes, that’s what you would say,’ Mrs. Garner moved close to Joe as the wagon jolted. ‘Well, you had plenty of girls in your time.’
“是啊，你肯定会这么说。”加纳太太在马车颠簸时靠近乔说。“好吧，你当年也有很多女人。”
‘I’ll bet Pa wouldn’t ever have had a squaw for a girl.’
“我打赌爸是绝不会娶个印第安老婆当姑娘的。”
‘Don’t you think it,’ Joe said. ‘You better watch out to keep Prudie, Nick.’
“别这么想，”乔说。“尼克，你最好小心点，别把普鲁迪给拐走了。”
His wife whispered to him and Joe laughed.
他的妻子低声对他耳语，乔笑了。
‘What you laughing at?’ asked Frank.
“你笑什么？”弗兰克问。
‘Don’t you say it, Garner,’ his wife warned. Joe laughed again.
“别说出来，加纳，”他的妻子警告道。乔又笑了。
‘Nickie can have Prudence,’ Joe Garner said. ‘I got a good girl.’
“妮姬可以有普鲁登斯，”乔·加纳说。“我有个好姑娘。”
‘That’s the way to talk,’ Mrs. Garner said.
“就是这么说的，”加纳太太说。
The horses were pulling heavily in the sand. Joe reached out in the dark with the whip.
马在沙地上使劲拉。乔在黑暗中伸手拿着鞭子。
‘Come on, pull into it. You’ll have to pull harder than this tomorrow.’
“来吧，往里拉。明天你得比现在更用力。”
They trotted down the long hill, the wagon jolting. At the farmhouse everybody got down. Mrs. Garner unlocked the door, went inside, and came out with a lamp in her hand. Carl and Nick unloaded the things from the back of the wagon. Frank sat on the front seat to drive to the barn and put up the horses. Nick went up the steps and opened the kitchen door. Mrs. Garner was building a fire in the stove. She turned from pouring kerosene on the wood.
他们小跑着下长坡，马车颠簸。到农舍时大家都下了车。加纳太太开了门，走进去，又端着灯出来。卡尔和尼克把东西从车后卸下来。弗兰克坐在前座上要赶到谷仓去拴马。尼克上了台阶，打开了厨房门。加纳太太正在炉子里生火。她一边往木柴上浇煤油，一边转过身来。
‘Good-bye, Mrs. Garner,’ Nick said. ‘Thanks for taking me.’
“再见，Garner 太太，”Nick 说。“谢谢你带我来。”
‘Oh shucks, Nickie.’
“哎呀，Nickie。”
‘I had a wonderful time.’
“我度过了愉快的时光。”
‘We like to have you. Won’t you stay and eat some supper?’
“我们很高兴你来。要不要留下来吃点晚饭？”
‘I better go. I think Dad probably waited for me.’
“我还是走吧。我想爸爸大概在等我。”
‘Well, get along then. Send Carl up to the house, will you?’
“那你快去吧。把 Carl 叫到房子里来，好吗？”
‘All right.’
“好吧。”
‘Good night, Nickie.’
“晚安，Nickie。”
‘Good night, Mrs. Garner.’
“晚安，加纳太太。”
Nick went out the farmyard and down to the barn. Joe and Frank were milking.
尼克出了农场院子，走到谷仓去。乔和弗兰克正在挤奶。
‘Good night,’ Nick said. ‘I had a swell time.’
“晚安，”尼克说。“我过得很愉快。”
‘Good night, Nick,’ Joe Garner called. ‘Aren’t you going to stay and eat?’
“晚安，尼克，”乔·加纳喊道。“你不留下来吃点东西吗？”
‘No, I can’t. Will you tell Carl his mother wants him?’
“不了，我不能。你能告诉卡尔他妈妈要他来吗？”
‘All right. Good night, Nickie.’
“好吧。晚安，尼基。”
Nick walked barefoot along the path through the meadow below the barn. The path was smooth and the dew was cool on his bare feet. He climbed a fence at the end of the meadow, went down through a ravine, his feet wet in the swamp mud, and then climbed up through the dry beech woods until he saw the lights of the cottage. He climbed over the fence and walked around to the front porch. Through the window he saw his father sitting by the table, reading in the light of the big lamp. Nick opened the door and went in.
尼克赤脚沿着谷仓下方草地里的小路走。小路平滑，露水打在他赤裸的脚上凉凉的。他在草地尽头翻过篱笆，沿着一条峡谷下去，脚浸在沼泽泥里，然后又爬上干燥的山毛榉林，直到看见小屋的灯光。他翻过篱笆，绕到前廊。透过窗户他看见父亲坐在桌旁，在大灯的光下读书。尼克推开门走了进去。
‘Well, Nickie,’ his father said, ‘was it a good day?’
“怎么样，尼基，”他父亲说，“今天过得愉快吗？”
‘I had a swell time, Dad. It was a swell Fourth of July.’
“我过得很痛快，爸。真是个爽透了的独立日。”
‘Are you hungry?’
“你饿了吗？”
‘You bet.’
“那当然。”
‘What did you do with your shoes?’
“你把鞋子放哪儿了？”
‘I left them in the wagon at Garner’s.’
“我把他们留在加纳家的马车里了。”
‘Come on out to the kitchen.’
“到厨房来吧。”
Nick’s father went ahead with the lamp. He stopped and lifted the lid of the ice-box. Nick went on into the kitchen. His father brought in a piece of cold chicken on a plate and a pitcher of milk and put them on the table before Nick. He put down the lamp.
尼克的父亲拿着灯先走。他停下，掀开冰箱的盖子。尼克继续走进厨房。他父亲端来一盘冷鸡和一壶牛奶，放在尼克面前的桌子上。然后他放下了灯。
‘There’s some pie too,’ he said. ‘Will that hold you?’
“还有馅饼，”他说。“够你吃吗？”
‘It’s grand.’
“真漂亮。”
His father sat down in a chair beside the oilcloth-covered table. He made a big shadow on the kitchen wall.
他的父亲在铺着油布的桌子旁的椅子上坐下。他在厨房的墙上投下一个大大的影子。
‘Who won the ball game?’
“谁赢了球赛？”
‘Petoskey. Five to three.’
“佩托斯基。五比三。”
His father sat watching him eat and filled his glass from the milk-pitcher. Nick drank and wiped his mouth on his napkin. His father reached over to the shelf for the pie. He cut Nick a big piece.
他父亲坐着看他吃东西，又从奶壶里给杯子倒满。尼克喝了口水，用餐巾擦了擦嘴。他父亲伸手到架子上拿起馅饼，给尼克切了一大块。
It was huckleberry pie.
那是越橘馅饼。
‘What did you do, Dad?’
“爸爸，你做了什么？”
‘I went out fishing in the morning.’
“我早上去钓鱼了。”
‘What did you get?’
“你钓到什么了？”
‘Only perch.’
“只有鲈鱼。”
His father sat watching Nick eat the pie.
他父亲坐着看着尼克吃馅饼。
‘What did you do this afternoon?’ Nick asked.
“你今天下午做了什么？”尼克问道。
‘I went for a walk up by the Indian camp.’
“我到印第安人营地那边去散步了。”
‘Did you see anybody?’
“你看到谁了吗？”
‘The Indians were all in town getting drunk.’
“那些印第安人都到镇上去喝醉了。”
‘Didn’t you see anybody at all?’
“你一个人也没看到吗？”
‘I saw your friend, Prudie.’
“我看到你朋友，普鲁迪了。”
‘Where was she?’
“她在哪儿？”
‘She was in the woods with Frank Washburn. I ran on to them. They were having quite a time.’
“她在林子里，和弗兰克·沃什本在一起。我跑过去找到他们。他们正玩得挺疯的。”
His father was not looking at him.
他父亲没有看他。
‘What were they doing?’
“他们在做什么？”
‘I didn’t stay to find out.’
“我没留在那儿去看个究竟。”
‘Tell me what they were doing.’
“告诉我他们在做什么。”
‘I don’t know,’ his father said. ‘I just heard them threshing around.’
“我不知道，”他父亲说。“我只听见他们在那儿哗啦哗啦地忙活。”
‘How did you know it was them?’
“你怎么知道是他们的？”
‘I saw them.’
“我看见他们了。”
‘I thought you said you didn’t see them.’
“我记得你说你没看见他们。”
‘Oh, yes, I saw them.’
“哦，是的，我看见了他们。”
‘Who was it with her?’ Nick asked.
“她和谁在一起？”尼克问。
‘Frank Washburn.’
“弗兰克·沃什本。”
'Were they - were they - ’
“他们——他们是——”
‘Were they what?’
“他们是什么？”
‘Were they happy?’
“他们幸福吗？”
‘I guess so.’
“我想是吧。”
His father got up from the table and went out the kitchen screen door. When he came back Nick was looking at his plate. He had been crying.
他父亲从桌旁站起，走出厨房的纱门。回来时，Nick 正盯着他的盘子。他刚刚哭过。
‘Have some more?’ His father picked up the knife to cut the pie.
“再来点吗？”他父亲拿起刀切派。
‘No,’ said Nick.
“不，”尼克说。
‘You better have another piece.’
“你最好再吃一块。”
‘No, I don’t want any.’
“不，我不要。”
His father cleared off the table.
他父亲清理了桌子。
‘Where were they in the woods?’ Nick asked.
“他们在林子里哪儿？”尼克问。
‘Up back of the camp.’ Nick looked at his plate. His father said, ‘You better go to bed, Nick.’
“营地后面那边。”尼克看着他的盘子。他父亲说：“你最好去睡觉，尼克。”
‘All right.’
“好吧。”
Nick went into his room, undressed, and got into bed. He heard his father moving around in the living-room. Nick lay in the bed with his face in the pillow.
尼克进了房间，脱了衣服，上了床。他听见父亲在客厅里走动。尼克脸埋在枕头里躺在床上。
‘My heart’s broken,’ he thought. ‘If I feel this way my heart must be broken.’
“我的心碎了，”他想。“如果我有这种感觉，我的心一定是碎了。”
After a while he heard his father blow out the lamp and go into his own room. He heard a wind come up in the trees outside and felt it come in cool through the screen. He lay for a long time with his face in the pillow, and after a while he forgot to think about Prudence and finally he went to sleep. When he awoke in the night he heard the wind in the hemlock trees outside the cottage and the waves of the lake coming in on the shore, and he went back to sleep. In the morning there was a big wind blowing and the waves were running high up on the beach and he was awake a long time before he remembered that his heart was broken.
过了一会儿，他听见父亲把灯吹灭，回到自己的房间。他听见外面树上刮起了风，透过纱窗吹进来凉意。他把脸埋在枕头上躺了很久，过了一会儿他忘了去想普鲁登斯，终于睡着了。夜里醒来时，他又听见小屋外铁杉树上的风声和湖水拍岸的声音，然后又睡过去。早晨刮起大风，海浪高涨拍到海滩，他醒来很久才想起自己的心是碎的。

A CANARY FOR ONE
一只金丝雀为一人

The train passed very quickly a long, red stone house with a garden and four thick palm trees with tables under them in the shade. On the other side was the sea. Then there was a cutting through red stone and clay, and the sea was only occasionally and far below against rocks.
火车很快地经过一座长长的红石房子，房子有花园，四棵粗壮的棕榈树下有桌子遮着荫凉。另一边是大海。然后火车穿过一段红石与粘土的切口，海只偶尔出现在很远的下方，拍击着礁石。
‘I bought him in Palermo,’ the American lady said. ‘We only had an hour ashore and it was Sunday morning. The man wanted to be paid in dollars and I gave him a dollar and a half. He really sings very beautifully.’
“我在巴勒莫买的，”那位美国女士说。“我们只在岸上呆了一个小时，而且是星期天早晨。那人想要用美元付，我给了他一块五美元。他唱得确实很动听。”
It was very hot in the train and it was very hot in the lit salon compartment. There was no breeze came through the open window. The American lady pulled the window-blind down and there was no more sea, even occasionally. On the other side there was glass, then the corridor, then an open window, and outside the window were dusty trees and an oiled road and flat fields of grapes, with greystone hills behind them.
火车里很热，带灯的沙龙车厢里也很热。开着的窗户里没有一丝凉风吹进来。美国女士把窗帘拉了下来，连海景也看不见了，连偶尔能看到的也没了。另一侧是玻璃，然后是走廊，然后是一个开着的窗户，窗外是满是灰尘的树、有油渍的道路和平坦的葡萄地，远处是灰色石头的山丘。
There was smoke from many tall chimneys - coming into Marseilles, and the train slowed down and followed one track through many others into the station. The train stayed twenty-five minutes in the station at Marseilles and the American lady bought a copy of the Daily Mail and a half-bottle of Evian water. She walked a little way along the station platform, but she stayed near the steps of the car because at Cannes, where it stopped for twelve minutes, the train had left with no signal of departure and she had gotten on only just in time. The American lady was a little deaf and she was afraid that perhaps signals of departure were given and that she did not hear them.
有许多高烟囱冒着烟——进入马赛时，火车放慢了速度，沿着一条轨道穿过众多其他轨道进站。火车在马赛站停了二十五分钟，那位美国女士买了一份《每日邮报》和半瓶依云矿泉水。她在站台上走了一小段路，但一直待在车厢台阶附近，因为在戛纳停了十二分钟时，火车无任何发车信号就已经开了，她几乎是及时赶上车的。那位美国女士有点耳背，她担心也许发过发车信号而她没有听到。
The train left the station in Marseilles and there was not only the switch-yards and the factory smoke but, looking back, the town of Marseilles and the harbour with stone hills behind it and the last of the sun on the water. As it was getting dark the train passed a farmhouse burning in a field. Motor-cars were stopped along the road and bedding and things from inside the farmhouse were spread in the
火车驶离马赛站，视线里不仅有调车场和工厂的烟雾，回头看去还有马赛城和港口，港后是石质山丘，水面上映着最后的夕阳。天色渐暗时，火车经过一户在田地里失火的农舍。马路旁停着汽车，农舍里铺盖和物品都摊在外面。
field. Many people were watching the house burn. After it was dark the train was in Avignon. People got on and off. At the news-stand Frenchmen, returning to Paris, bought that day’s French papers. On the station platform were negro soldiers. They wore brown uniforms and were tall and their faces shone, close under the electric light. Their faces were very black and they were too tall to stare. The train left Avignon station with the negroes standing there. A short white sergeant was with them.
田地。许多人在看着房子着火。天黑后火车到了阿维尼翁。人上人下。在报摊前，回巴黎的法国人买着当天的法文报纸。站台上有黑人士兵。他们穿着棕色制服，个子高，脸在电灯下近处闪着光。他们的脸非常黑，太高而不便直视。火车带着那些黑人离开了阿维尼翁站。一个矮小的白人中士和他们在一起。
Inside the lit salon compartment the porter had pulled down the three beds from inside the wall and prepared them for sleeping. In the night the American lady lay without sleeping because the train was a rapide and went very fast and she was afraid of the speed in the night. The American lady’s bed was the one next to the window. The canary from Palermo, a cloth spread over his cage, was out of the draught in the corridor that went into the compartment washroom. There was a blue light outside the compartment, and all night the train went very fast and the American lady lay awake and waited for a wreck.
在有灯的沙龙车厢里，搬运工把墙内放下的三张床拉了出来，准备睡觉。夜里那位美国女士躺着却睡不着，因为那列车是快车，行驶得很快，她害怕夜间的速度。美国女士的床在靠窗那一张。来自巴勒莫的金丝雀，笼子上盖着布，放在通往车厢洗手间的走廊里，免受风吹。车厢外有一盏蓝色的灯，整夜火车都开得很快，那位美国女士睁着眼等着出事故。
In the morning the train was near Paris, and after the American lady had come out from the wash-room, looking very wholesome and middle-aged and American in spite of not having slept, and had taken the cloth off the birdcage and hung the cage in the sun, she went back to the restaurant-car for breakfast. When she came back to the lit salon compartment again, the beds had been pushed back into the wall and made into seats, the canary was shaking his feathers in the sunlight that came through the open window, and the train was much nearer Paris.
早晨火车已接近巴黎，那个美国女士从盥洗室出来，虽然没睡，但看起来很健康、称得上中年且典型的美国人，她把罩在鸟笼上的布拿掉，把笼子挂在阳光下，然后回到餐车去吃早饭。等她回到有铺位的沙龙车厢时，铺位已被推回墙边并改成座位，金丝雀在开着的窗户透进来的日光下抖动羽毛，火车也更接近巴黎了。
‘He loves the sun,’ the American lady said. ‘He’ll sing now in a little while.’
“他喜欢阳光，”美国女士说。“过一会儿他就会唱了。”
The canary shook his feathers and pecked into them. ‘I’ve always loved birds,’ the American lady said. ‘I’m taking him home to my little girl. There - he’s singing now.’
金丝雀抖了抖羽毛，用喙啄着羽毛。“我一直很喜欢鸟，”美国女士说。“我要把他带回去给我的小女儿。看——他现在在唱了。”
The canary chirped and the feathers on his throat stood out, then he dropped his bill and pecked into his feathers again. The train crossed a river and passed through a very carefully tended forest. The train passed through many outside of Paris towns. There were tram-cars in the towns and big advertisements for the Belle Jardinière and Dubonnet and Pernod on the walls toward the train. All that the train passed through looked as though it were before break-
金丝雀啾啾叫着，喉部的羽毛竖起，然后它垂下喙又啄回自己的羽毛。火车越过一条河，穿过一片精心打理的树林。火车经过了许多巴黎外围的城镇。城镇里有有轨电车，朝着火车方向的墙上贴着 Belle Jardinière、Dubonnet 和 Pernod 的大幅广告。火车所经过的一切看上去仿佛还是早餐时间之前——
fast. For several minutes I had not listened to the American lady, who was talking to my wife.
几分钟里我没有听美国那位女士说话，她正在和我妻子谈话。
‘Is your husband American too?’ asked the lady.
“你丈夫也是美国人吗？”那位女士问。
‘Yes,’ said my wife. ‘We’re both Americans.’
“是的，”我妻子说。“我们都是美国人。”
‘I thought you were English.’
“我还以为你是英国人。”
‘Oh, no.’
“哦，不是。”
‘Perhaps that was because I wore braces,’ I said. I had started to say suspenders and changed it to braces in the mouth, to keep my English character. The American lady did not hear. She was really quite deaf; she read lips, and I had not looked toward her. I had looked out of the window. She went on talking to my wife.
“也许是因为我穿了背带，”我说。我本来要说 suspenders（吊裤带/背带），但在嘴里改成了 braces，以保持我的英国风格。那位美国女士没听见。她实际上相当聋；靠读唇语，她是靠看唇形的，而我并没有看向她。我一直在望着窗外。她继续和我妻子说话。
‘I’m so glad you’re Americans. American men make the best husbands,’ the American lady was saying. ‘That was why we left the Continent, you know. My daughter fell in love with a man in Vevey.’ She stopped. ‘They were simply madly in love.’ She stopped again. ‘I took her away, of course.’
“我太高兴你们是美国人了。美国男人最适合做丈夫，”那位美国女士说。“这就是我们离开欧洲大陆的原因，你知道的。我的女儿在维韦爱上了一个男人。”她停了。“他们简直是疯狂地相爱。”她又停了。“当然，我把她带走了。”
‘Did she get over it?’ asked my wife.
“她克服了吗？”我妻子问。
‘I don’t think so,’ said the American lady. ‘She wouldn’t eat anything and she wouldn’t sleep at all. I’ve tried so very hard, but she doesn’t seem to take an interest in anything. She doesn’t care about things. I couldn’t have her marrying a foreigner.’ She paused. 'Someone, a very good friend, told me once, “No foreigner can make an American girl a good husband”."
“我觉得没有，”那位美国女士说。“她什么也吃不下，也睡不着。我已经尽力了，但她似乎对任何事都提不起兴趣。她对这些事毫不在意。我不能让她嫁给一个外国人。”她停顿了一下。“有人——一个非常好的朋友——曾经对我说，‘没有哪个外国人能做一个美国女孩的好丈夫。’”
‘No,’ said my wife, ‘I suppose not.’
“不，”我妻子说，“我想是的。”
The American lady admired my wife’s travelling-coat, and it turned out that the American lady had bought her own clothes for twenty years now from the same maison de couture in the Rue Saint Honoré. They had her measurements, and a vendeuse who knew her and her tastes picked the dresses out for her and they were sent to America. They came to the post-office near where she lived uptown in New York, and the duty was never exorbitant because they opened the dresses there in the post-office to appraise them and they were always very simple-looking and with no gold lace nor ornaments that would make the dresses look expensive. Before the present vendeuse, named Thérèse, there had been another vendeuse, named Amélie. Altogether there had only been these two in the twenty years. It had always been the same couturier. Prices, however, had gone up. The exchange, though, equalized that. They had
那位美国女士赞赏我妻子的旅行外衣，结果发现这位美国女士二十年来一直在 Rue Saint Honoré同一家时装屋买衣服。他们有她的尺寸，一位了解她和她品味的女售货员为她挑选礼服，然后寄到美国。衣服寄到她在纽约上城附近住处附近的邮局，关税从来不高，因为他们在邮局打开这些衣服来估价，而且这些衣服看起来总是很朴素，没有金线或装饰让礼服显得昂贵。在现任的那位女售货员 Thérèse 之前，还有一位叫 Amélie 的女售货员。二十年来总共只有这两位。裁缝师一直是同一个。不过价钱确实涨了。汇率却把这抵消了。他们
her daughter’s measurements now too. She was grown up and there was not much chance of their changing now.
现在也有她女儿的尺寸了。她已经长大了，尺寸现在大概也不会有什么变化。
The train was now coming into Paris. The fortifications were levelled but grass had not grown. There were many cars standing on tracks - brown wooden restaurant-cars and brown wooden sleepingcars that would go to Italy at five o’clock that night, if that train still left at five; the cars were marked Paris-Rome, and cars, with seats on the roofs, that went back and forth to the suburbs with, at certain hours, people in all the seats and on the roofs, if that were the way it were still done, and passing were the white walls and many windows of houses. Nothing had eaten any breakfast.
火车此刻正要进巴黎。防御工事已被夷为平地，但草还未长起来。轨道上停着许多车厢——褐色木制的餐车和褐色木制的卧车，今晚五点会开往意大利，如果那趟车还在五点发车；车厢上标着 Paris-Rome，还有那些屋顶有座位的车厢，来回往返郊区，在某些时段，所有座位和屋顶上都坐满了人，如果仍然是那样的做法，路过的是房屋的白墙和许多窗户。谁也没吃早餐。
‘Americans make the best husbands,’ the American lady said to my wife. I was getting down the bags. ‘American men are the only men in the world to marry.’
“美国人最会做丈夫，”那位美国太太对我妻子说。我正搬下行李。“美国男人是世上唯一会结婚的男人。”
‘How long ago did you leave Vevey?’ asked my wife.
“你们多久以前离开维韦的？”我妻子问。
"Two years ago this fall. It’s her, you know, that I’m taking the canary to.’
“今年秋天是两年前。是拿那只金丝雀给她的，你知道的。”
‘Was the man your daughter was in love with a Swiss?’
“你女儿爱上的那个人是瑞士人吗？”
‘Yes,’ said the American lady. ‘He was from a very good family in Vevey. He was going to be an engineer. They met there in Vevey. They used to go on long walks together.’
“是的，”那位美国女士说。“他是来自 Vevey 一个很好的家庭。他本来要当工程师。他们是在 Vevey 认识的。他们常常一起去长途散步。”
‘I know Vevey,’ said my wife. ‘We were there on our honeymoon.’
“我知道 Vevey，”我妻子说。“我们蜜月时去过那里。”
‘Were you really? That must have been lovely. I had no idea, of course, that she’d fall in love with him.’
“真的去过？那一定很美。我当然完全不知道，她会爱上他。”
‘It was a very lovely place,’ said my wife.
“那是个非常可爱的地方，”我妻子说。
‘Yes,’ said the American lady. ‘Isn’t it lovely? Where did you stop there?’
“是啊，”那位美国女士说。“是不是很可爱？你们在那里住在哪里？”
‘We stayed at the Trois Couronnes,’ said my wife.
“我们住在三王冠酒店，”我妻子说。
‘It’s such a fine old hotel,’ said the American lady.
“那是一家如此古老而出色的酒店，”那位美国女士说。
‘Yes,’ said my wife. ‘We had a very fine room and in the fall the country was lovely.’
“是的，”我妻子说。“我们住的是一间很不错的房间，秋天那里的乡村非常美。”
‘Were you there in the fall?’
“你们秋天去过那里吗？”
‘Yes,’ said my wife.
“是的，”我妻子说。
We were passing three cars that had been in a wreck. They were splintered open and the roofs sagged in.
我们路过三辆出了事故的车。它们被撞得散架，车顶塌陷。
‘Look,’ I said. ‘There’s been a wreck.’
“看，”我说，“出了事故。”
The American lady looked and saw the last car. ‘I was afraid of just that all night,’ she said. ‘I have terrific presentiments about
那位美国女士看着，看到最后一辆车。“我整晚都在害怕会是这种事，”她说。“我有强烈的不祥预感，关于
things sometimes. I’ll never travel on a rapide again at night. There must be other comfortable trains that don’t go so fast.’
有时候会这样。我再也不会在夜里乘坐快速火车了。一定还有别的舒适列车，跑得没那么快。
Then the train was in the dark of the Gare de Lyons, and then stopped and porters came up to the windows. I handed bags through the windows, and we were out on the dim longness of the platform, and the American lady put herself in charge of one of three men from Cook’s who said: ‘Just a moment, madame, and I’ll look for your name.’
然后火车驶入里昂车站的黑暗中，停下后搬运工走到窗前。我把行李递出窗外，我们来到站台那昏暗而漫长的地方，那位美国夫人把自己托付给库克旅行社的三名工作人员中的一人，他说：“请稍等，夫人，我去查一下您的姓名。”
The porter brought a truck and piled on the baggage, and my wife said good-bye and I said good-bye to the American lady, whose name had been found by the man from Cook’s on a typewritten page in a sheaf of typewritten pages which he replaced in his pocket.
搬运工开来一辆卡车，把行李堆上去，我妻子和那位美国女士道了别，我也和她道了别，那位女士的名字是库克公司那人从一叠打字页中一张打字页上找到的，他把那张页又装回口袋里。
We followed the porter with the truck down the long cement platform beside the train. At the end was a gate and a man took the tickets.
我们跟着带着卡车的搬运工沿着火车旁那条长长的水泥站台走。在尽头有扇门，有个男人检票。
We were returning to Paris to set up separate residences.
我们要回巴黎去分开住。

AN ALPINE IDYLL
阿尔卑斯山小景

It was hot coming down into the valley even in the early morning. The sun melted the snow from the skis we were carrying and dried the wood. It was spring in the valley but the sun was very hot. We came along the road into Galtur carrying our skis and rucksacks. As we passed the churchyard a burial was just over. I said, ‘Grüss Gott,’ to the priest as he walked past us coming out of the churchyard. The priest bowed.
即使在清晨，走下山谷也很热。太阳把我们背着的滑雪板上的雪融化了，把木头晒干了。山谷里已经是春天，但太阳很毒。我们背着滑雪板和背包沿着路走进加尔图尔。经过教堂墓地时，葬礼刚结束。我对从墓地走出来、从我们身边走过的牧师说了句“Grüss Gott”。牧师点了点头。
‘It’s funny a priest never speaks to you,’ John said.
“有意思，牧师从来不跟你说话，”约翰说。
‘You’d think they’d like to say “Grüss Gott”.’
“你会以为他们会喜欢说‘Grüss Gott’。”
‘They never answer,’ John said.
“他们从不回答，”约翰说。
We stopped in the road and watched the sexton shovelling in the new earth. A peasant with a black beard and high leather boots stood beside the grave. The sexton stopped shovelling and straightened his back. The peasant in the high boots took the spade from the sexton and went on filling in the grave-spreading the earth evenly as a man spreading manure in a garden. In the bright May morning the grave-filling looked unreal. I could not imagine anyone being dead.
我们停在路边，看着殡葬工把新土铲进墓坑。一个留着黑胡子、穿着高皮靴的农夫站在墓旁。殡葬工停下铲土，伸直了背。穿高靴的农夫从殡葬工手里接过铁锹，继续填土——把土摊得均匀，像人在菜园里铺粪一样。在明亮的五月早晨，填墓看起来不真实。我无法想象有人已经死了。
‘Imagine being buried on a day like this,’ I said to John.
“想想在这样的日子里被埋葬，”我对约翰说。
‘I wouldn’t like it.’
“我可不愿意。”
‘Well,’ I said, ‘we don’t have to do it.’
“嗯，”我说，“那我们就不用做。”
We went on up the road past the houses of the town to the inn. We had been skiing in the Silvretta for a month, and it was good to be down in the valley. In the Silvretta the skiing had been all right, but it was spring skiing, the snow was good only in the early morning and again in the evening. The rest of the time it was spoiled by the sun. We were both tired of the sun. You could not get away from the sun. The only shadows were made by rocks or by the hut that was built under the protection of a rock beside a glacier, and in the shade the sweat froze in your underclothing. You could not sit outside the hut without dark glasses. It was pleasant to be burned black but the sun had been very tiring. You could not rest in it. I was glad to be down away from snow. It was too late in the spring to be up in
我们沿着穿过镇上一排房屋的路上山，去了客栈。我们在 Silvretta 滑雪已经一个月了，能下到山谷里真好。在 Silvretta 滑雪还过得去，但那是春季滑雪，雪只有清晨和傍晚好。其余时间都被太阳弄坏了。我们都对太阳感到厌倦。你无法躲开太阳。唯一的阴影要么是岩石投下的，要么是那座依靠在冰川边岩石庇护下建的木屋，在阴凉处汗水会在贴身衣物上结成冰。你不能不戴太阳镜就坐在木屋外。被晒成黑褐色很惬意，但太阳实在让人疲惫。在阳光里你无法休息。我很高兴离开积雪之后能到山下。春天已太晚，不适合再去 Silvretta 山上了。
the Silvretta. I was a little tired of skiing. We had stayed too long. I could taste the snow water we had been drinking melted off the tin roof of the hut. The taste was a part of the way I felt about skiing. I was glad there were other things beside skiing, and I was glad to be down, away from the unnatural high mountain spring, into this May morning in the valley.
我对滑雪有点厌倦了。我们呆得太久了。我还能尝到我们一直喝的从木屋马口铁屋顶融下来的雪水味道。这种味道是我对滑雪感受的一部分。我很高兴除了滑雪还有别的事情可做，也很高兴能下到山谷里，离开那不自然的高山春季，来到这个山谷里的五月清晨。
The innkeeper sat on the porch of the inn, his chair tipped back against the wall. Beside him sat the cook.
旅店老板坐在旅店的门廊上，椅子往后斜靠在墙上。他身旁坐着厨师。
‘Ski-heil!’ said the innkeeper.
“滑雪万岁！”旅店老板说。
‘Heil!’ we said and leaned the skis against the wall and took off our packs.
“万岁！”我们回答着，把滑雪板靠在墙上，卸下背包。
‘How was it up above?’ asked the innkeeper.
“上面情况怎么样？”旅店老板问。
‘Schön. A little too much sun.’
“Schön。太阳有点太强了。”
‘Yes. There’s too much sun this time of year.’
“是的。这时候一年太阳太强了。”
The cook sat on in his chair. The innkeeper went in with us and unlocked his office and brought out our mail. There was a bundle of letters and some papers.
厨师坐在他的椅子上。旅店老板跟我们一起来，把他的办公室打开了，拿出了我们的信件。有一捆信和一些文件。
‘Let’s get some beer,’ John said.
“我们去喝点啤酒，”约翰说。
‘Good. We’ll drink it inside.’
“好。我们到里面去喝。”
The proprietor brought two bottles and we drank them while we read the letters.
老板拿来两瓶酒，我们一边读信一边喝。
‘We better have some more beer,’ John said. A girl brought it this time. She smiled as she opened the bottles.
“我们最好再来点啤酒，”约翰说。这次是个姑娘端来的。她在打开瓶子时微笑着。
‘Many letters,’ she said.
“好多信啊，”她说。
‘Yes. Many.’
“是的。很多。”
‘Prosit,’ she said and went out, taking the empty bottles.
“干杯，”她说着出去，拿走了空瓶子。
‘I’d forgotten what beer tasted like.’
“我都忘了啤酒是什么味道了。”
‘I hadn’t,’ John said. ‘Up in the hut I used to think about it a lot.’
“我没忘，”约翰说。“在小屋里我常常想着呢。”
‘Well,’ I said, ‘we’ve got it now.’
“好了，”我说，“我们现在明白了。”
‘You oughtn’t to ever do anything too long.’
“你绝不应该做任何事拖得太久。”
‘No. We were up there too long.’
“不。我们在那里呆得太久了。”
‘Too damn long,’ John said. ‘It’s no good doing a thing too long.’
“他妈的太久了，”约翰说。“做一件事太久没好处。”
The sun came through the open window and shone through the beer bottles on the table. The bottles were half full. There was a little froth on the beer in the bottles, not much because it was very cold. It collared up when you poured it into the tall glasses. I looked out of the open window at the white road. The trees beside the road were dusty. Beyond was a green field and a stream. There were trees along the stream and a mill with a water wheel. Through the
阳光透过开着的窗户，穿过桌上的啤酒瓶照进来。瓶子里半满着。瓶中的啤酒上有一点泡沫，不多，因为啤酒很冷。倒进高高的杯子里时会起泡。我从开着的窗望向白色的路。路旁的树有些灰尘。再远处是一片绿地和一条小溪。小溪边有树，和一座带水轮的磨坊。透过
open side of the mill I saw a long log and a saw in it rising and falling. No one seemed to be tending it. There were four crows walking in the green field. One crow sat in a tree watching. Outside on the porch the cook got off his chair and passed into the hall that led back into the kitchen. Inside, the sunlight shone through the empty glasses on the table. John was leaning forward with his head on his arms.
磨坊开着的一侧，我看到一根长木头，锯子在木头里上下起伏。好像没人看管。有四只乌鸦在绿地上走着。一只乌鸦栖在树上观看。外面门廊上，厨子从椅子上起身，穿过通往厨房的走廊走了进去。屋内，阳光透过桌上空杯照进来。约翰前倾着，头枕在胳膊上。
Through the window I saw two men come up the front steps. They came into the drinking room. One was the bearded peasant in the high boots. The other was the sexton. They sat down at the table under the window. The girl came in and stood by their table. The peasant did not seem to see her. He sat with his hands on the table. He wore his old army clothes. There were patches on the elbows.
透过窗户，我看到两个男人走上前台阶。他们走进了饮酒室。一个是穿着高靴、留着胡子的农民。另一个是教堂看守。他们在窗下的桌子旁坐下。那个女孩走进来，站在他们的桌旁。农民好像没看见她。他双手放在桌上坐着，穿着旧军装，肘部有补丁。
‘What will it be?’ asked the sexton. The peasant did not pay any attention.
“要什么？”守墓人问道。那农夫没有理会。
‘What will you drink?’
“你要喝什么？”
‘Schnapps,’ the peasant said.
“烈酒，”农夫说。
‘And a quarter litre of red wine,’ the sexton told the girl.
“还有一刻升红葡萄酒，”司丧人对姑娘说。
The girl brought the drinks and the peasant drank the schnapps. He looked out of the window. The sexton watched him. John had his head forward on the table. He was asleep.
姑娘端来酒，农夫喝了白兰地。他望着窗外。司丧人盯着他。约翰把头伏在桌上，睡着了。
The innkeeper came in and went over to the table. He spoke in dialect and the sexton answered him. The peasant looked out of the window. The innkeeper went out of the room. The peasant stood up. He took a folded ten-thousand kronen note out of a leather pocket-book and unfolded it. The girl came up.
店主进来走到桌边。他用方言说话，司丧人回答他。农夫望着窗外。店主走出房间。农夫站起来。他从皮钱包里取出一张折好的一万克朗纸币并把它展开。姑娘走上前来。
‘Alles?’ she asked.
“全部吗？”她问。
‘Alles,’ he said.
“Alles，”他说。
‘Let me buy the wine,’ the sexton said.
“让我来买酒吧，”教务员说。
‘Alles,’ the peasant repeated to the girl. She put her hand in the pocket of her apron, brought it out full of coins and counted out the change. The peasant went out the door. As soon as he was gone the innkeeper came into the room again and spoke to the sexton. He sat down at the table. They talked in dialect. The sexton was amused. The innkeeper was disgusted. The sexton stood up from the table. He was a little man with a moustache. He leaned out of the window and looked up the road.
“Alles，”农夫对那个女孩重复道。她把手伸进围裙口袋，拿出满满一手硬币，数了数找零。农夫出了门。农夫一走，店主又进了屋，跟教务员说话。他坐到桌旁。他们用方言交谈。教务员觉得有趣。店主感到厌恶。教务员从桌旁站起。他是个留着小胡子的矮小男人。他探出窗外，朝路上望去。
‘There he goes in,’ he said.
“他进去啦，”他说。
‘In the Löwen?’
“在 Löwen 吗？”
‘Ja.’
“是的。”
They talked again and then the innkeeper came over to our table. The innkeeper was a tall man and old. He looked at John asleep.
他们又谈了会儿，接着旅店老板走到我们的桌旁。旅店老板个子高，年纪大了。他看着睡着的约翰。
‘He’s pretty tired.’
“他挺累的。”
‘Yes, we were up early.’
“是的，我们很早就起床了。”
‘Will you want to eat soon?’
“你想很快吃点东西吗？”
‘Any time,’ I said. ‘What is there to eat?’
“什么时候都行，”我说。“有什么可吃的？”
‘Anything you want. The girl will bring the eating-card.’
“随你喜欢。女佣会把点餐牌拿来。”
The girl brought the menu. John woke up. The menu was written in ink on a card and the card slipped into a wooden paddle.
女孩端来了菜单。约翰醒了。菜单用墨水写在一张卡片上，卡片插进了一个木制的舀子里。
“There’s the speise-karte,’ I said to John. He looked at it. He was still sleepy.
“那就是 speise-karte，”我对约翰说道。他看了看。还带着睡意。
‘Won’t you have a drink with us?’ I asked the innkeeper. He sat down. ‘Those peasants are beasts,’ said the innkeeper.
“你愿意和我们喝一杯吗？”我问店主。他坐了下来。“那些农民是野兽，”店主说。
‘We saw that one at a funeral coming into town.’
“我们在进城时在一次葬礼上见过那个人。”
‘That was his wife.’
“那是他的妻子。”
‘Oh.’
“哦。”
‘He’s a beast. All these peasants are beasts.’
“他是个畜生。所有这些农民都是畜生。”
‘How do you mean?’
“你这话是什么意思？”
‘You wouldn’t believe it. You wouldn’t believe what just happened about that one.’
“你不会相信的。你不会相信刚才发生的那件事。”
‘Tell me.’
“告诉我。”
‘You wouldn’t believe it.’ The innkeeper spoke to the sexton. ‘Franz, come over here.’ The sexton came, bringing his little bottle of wine and his glass.
“你不会相信的。”店主对教区看守说。“Franz，过来这边。”教区看守过来，带着他的小酒瓶和杯子。
‘The gentlemen are just come down from the Wiesbadenerhütte,’ the innkeeper said. We shook hands.
“这几位先生刚从 Wiesbadenerhütte 下来的，”店主说。我们握了握手。
‘What will you drink?’ I asked.
“你要喝点什么？”我问。
‘Nothing,’ Franz shook his finger.
“什么都不要，”弗朗茨摇了摇手指。
‘Another quarter litre?’
“再来一刻升？”
‘All right.’
“好吧。”
‘Do you understand dialect?’ the innkeeper asked.
“你听得懂方言吗？”旅店老板问道。
‘No.’
“听不懂。”
‘What’s it all about?’ John asked.
“这是怎么回事？”约翰问。
‘He’s going to tell us about the peasant we saw filling the grave, coming into town.’
“他要给我们讲那个我们看到填坟的农民进城的事。”
‘I can’t understand it, anyway,’ John said. ‘It goes too fast for me.’
“我还是不明白，”约翰说，“对我来说太快了。”
‘That peasant,’ the innkeeper said, ‘to-day he brought his wife in to be buried. She died last November.’
“那个农夫，”旅店老板说，“今天他把妻子带来葬了。她是去年十一月去世的。”
‘December,’ said the sexton.
“十二月，”教会守墓人说。
‘That makes nothing. She died last December then, and he notified the commune.’
“那也无所谓。那就说她是去年十二月去世的，他通知了公社。”
‘December eighteenth,’ said the sexton.
“十二月十八日，”守墓人说。
‘Anyway, he couldn’t bring her over to be buried until the snow was gone.’
“反正，直到雪化了他也不能把她带来埋葬。”
‘He lives on the other side of the Paznaun,’ said the sexton. ‘But he belongs to this parish.’
“他住在 Paznaun 的另一边，”守墓人说。“但他属于这个教区。”
‘He couldn’t bring her out at all?’ I asked.
“他根本不能把她带出来吗？”我问。
‘No. He can only come, from where he lives, on skis until the snow melts. So to-day he brought her in to be buried and the priest, when he looked at her face, didn’t want to bury her. You go on and tell it,’ he said to the sexton. ‘Speak German, not dialect.’
“没有。他只能从住处滑雪过来，直到雪融化。所以今天他把她送来下葬，神父一看她的脸，不想把她埋。你去把话接下去，”他对教区看守说。“用德语说，不要方言。”
‘It was very funny with the priest,’ said the sexton. 'In the report to the commune she died of heart trouble. We knew she had heart trouble here. She used to faint in church sometimes. She did not come for a long time. She wasn’t strong to climb. When the priest uncovered her face he asked Olz, “Did your wife suffer much?” “No,” said Olz. “When I came in the house she was dead across the bed.”
“和神父在一起真是滑稽，”教区看守说。“在向市政当局的报告里写她死于心脏病。在这儿我们都知道她有心脏病。她有时在教堂会晕倒。她很久不来。她上不去楼梯，体力不行。神父掀开她的脸时，他问奥尔茨，‘你妻子受苦多吗？’‘没有，’奥尔茨说。‘我进屋时她已横躺在床上死了。’”
'The priest looked at her again. He didn’t like it.
神父又看了看她。他不喜欢那样。
“How did her face get that way?”
“她的脸怎么会成那样？”
" “I don’t know,” Olz said.
“我不知道，”奥尔茨说。
" “You’d better find out,” the priest said, and put the blanket back. Olz didn’t say anything. The priest looked at him. Olz looked back at the priest. “You want to know?”
“你最好查清楚，”牧师说着又把毯子盖上了。奥尔茨没有说话。牧师看着他。奥尔茨回望着牧师。“你想知道吗？”
" I must know,” the priest said.’
“我必须知道，”牧师说。
‘This is where it’s good,’ the innkeeper said. ‘Listen to this. Go on, Franz.’
“这就是它好玩的地方，”旅店老板说。“听着。继续，弗朗茨。”
" “Well,” said Olz, “when she died I made the report to the commune and I put her in the shed across the top of the big wood. When I started to use the big wood she was stiff and I put her up against the wall. Her mouth was open and when I came into the shed at night to cut up the big wood, I hung the lantern from it.”
“嗯，”奥尔茨说，“她死后我向公社报告了，就把她放在大木堆上面的棚子里。开始我准备用那堆大木头的时候她已经僵硬了，我就把她靠在墙上。她张着嘴，夜里我去棚里劈大木头时，就把灯笼挂在她上面。”
" “Why did you do that?” asked the priest.
“你为什么那样做？”神父问。
“I don’t know,” said Olz.
“我不知道，”奥尔茨说。
“Did you do that many times?”
“你那样做过很多次吗？”
" “Every time I went to work in the shed at night.”
“每次我晚上去棚里干活。”
“It was very wrong,” said the priest. “Did you love your wife?”
“那很不对，”神父说。“你爱你妻子吗？”
" “Ja, I loved her,” Olz said." I loved her fine. " ’
“是的，我爱她，”奥尔茨说。“我很爱她。”
‘Did you understand it all?’ asked the innkeeper. 'You understand it all about his wife?"
“你都明白了吗？”旅店老板问。“你都明白关于他妻子的事吗？”
‘I heard it.’
“我听见了。”
‘How about eating?’ John asked.
“吃点什么？”约翰问。
‘You order,’ I said. ‘Do you think it’s true?’ I asked the innkeeper.
“你点吧，”我说。“你觉得那是真的？”我问店主。
‘Sure it’s true,’ he said. ‘These peasants are beasts.’
“当然是真的，”他说。“这些农民就是畜生。”
‘Where did he go now?’
“他现在去哪儿了？”
‘He’s gone to drink at my colleague’s, the Löwen.’
“他去我同事那儿喝了，在 Löwen。”
‘He didn’t want to drink with me,’ said the sexton.
“他不想和我一起喝，”守墓人说。
‘He didn’t want to drink with me, after he knew about his wife,’ said the innkeeper.
“他知道他妻子的事后就不想和我一起喝了，”旅店老板说。
‘Say,’ said John. ‘How about eating?’
“说，”约翰说。“吃点什么怎么样？”
‘All right,’ I said.
“好，”我说。

A PURSUIT RACE
追逐赛

William Campbell had been in a pursuit race with a burlesque show ever since Pittsburgh. In a pursuit race, in bicycle racing, riders start at equal intervals to ride after one another. They ride very fast because the race is usually limited to a short distance and if they slow their riding another rider who maintains his pace will make up the space that separated them equally at the start. As soon as a rider is caught and passed he is out of the race and must get down from his bicycle and leave the track. If none of the riders are caught the winner of the race is the one who has gained the most distance. In most pursuit races, if there are only two riders, one of the riders is caught inside of six miles. The burlesque show caught William Campbell at Kansas City.
自从匹兹堡以后，威廉·坎贝尔就像跟着一场滑稽剧一样，参加着一场追逐赛。在自行车赛的追逐赛中，车手们以相等的时间间隔出发，互相追赶。由于比赛通常限定在较短的距离内，他们骑得很快；如果他们放慢速度，保持速度的其他车手就会弥补出发时拉开的距离。一旦有车手被追上并超过，就被淘汰，必须从自行车上下来并离开赛道。如果没有人被追上，获胜者就是获得最大领先距离的那位。在大多数追逐赛中，如果只有两名车手，其中一人通常在六英里内就会被追上。威廉·坎贝尔在堪萨斯城被那场滑稽剧追上了。
William Campbell had hoped to hold a slight lead over the burlesque show until they reached the Pacific coast. As long as he preceded the burlesque show as advance man he was being paid. When the burlesque show caught up with him he was in bed. He was in bed when the manager of the burlesque troupe came into his room and after the manager had gone out he decided that he might as well stay in bed. It was very cold in Kansas City and he was in no hurry to go out. He did not like Kansas City. He reached under the bed for a bottle and drank. It made his stomach feel better. Mr. Turner, the manager of the burlesque show, had refused a drink.
威廉·坎贝尔本想在滑稽剧团到达太平洋海岸之前，稍微领先他们一些。只要他作为前导先于滑稽剧团，他就有工资可领。等滑稽剧团追上他时，他已经上床睡了。滑稽剧团经理进了他的房间，他仍在床上；经理走后，他决定干脆继续躺着。堪萨斯城很冷，他并不急着出去。他不喜欢堪萨斯城。他伸手到床底拿起一瓶酒喝了，觉得胃舒服些。滑稽剧团的经理特纳先生拒绝喝酒。
William Campbell’s interview with Mr. Turner had bcen a little strange. Mr. Turner had knocked on the door. Campbell had said: ‘Come in!’ When Mr. Turner came into the room he saw clothing on a chair, an open suitcase, the bottle on a chair beside the bed, and someone lying in the bed completely covered by the bedclothes.
威廉·坎贝尔与特纳先生的会面有点奇怪。特纳先生敲了门。坎贝尔说：“进来！”特纳先生进了房间，看到椅子上有衣服，打开的手提箱，床边椅子上的那瓶酒，以及床上有人完全被被褥盖住躺着。
‘Mister Campbell,’ Mr. Turner said.
“坎贝尔先生，”特纳先生说。
‘You can’t fire me,’ William Campbell said from underneath the covers. It was warm and white and close under the covers. ‘You can’t fire me because I’ve got down off my bicycle.’
“你解雇不了我，”威廉·坎贝尔从被子下面说。被窝里暖和、洁白而紧贴。“你解雇不了我，因为我已经从自行车上下来。”
‘You’re drunk,’ Mr. Turner said.
“你喝醉了，”特纳先生说。
‘Oh, yes,’ William Campbell said, speaking directly against the sheet and feeling the texture with his lips.
“哦，是的，”威廉·坎贝尔说，嘴贴着床单说话，感觉着床单的质地。
‘You’re a fool,’ Mr. Turner said. He turned off the electric light. The electric light had been burning all night. It was now ten o’clock in the morning. ‘You’re a drunken fool. When did you get into this town?’
“你是个傻瓜，”特纳先生说。他关掉了电灯。电灯整夜都在亮着。现在是上午十点。“你这个酒鬼傻瓜。你什么时候进这镇的？”
‘I got into this town last night,’ William Campbell said, speaking against the sheet. He found he liked to talk through a sheet. ‘Did you ever talk through a sheet?’
“我昨晚进的这个镇，”威廉·坎贝尔说，嘴贴着床单说话。他发现自己喜欢通过床单说话。“你曾经通过床单说话吗？”
‘Don’t try to be funny. You aren’t funny.’
“别逗了。你一点也不幽默。”
‘I’m not being funny. I’m just talking through a sheet.’
“我不是在逗。我只是隔着被单说话。”
‘You’re talking through a sheet all right.’
“你确实是隔着被单说话。”
‘You can go now, Mr. Turner,’ Campbell said. ‘I don’t work for you any more.’
“你现在可以走了，特纳先生，”坎贝尔说。“我不再为你工作了。”
‘You know that anyway.’
“你本来就知道的。”
‘I know a lot,’ William Campbell said. He pulled down the sheet and looked at Mr. Turner. ‘I know enough so I don’t mind looking at you at all. Do you want to hear what I know?’
“我知道很多，”威廉·坎贝尔说。他拉开床单，看着特纳先生。“我知道得够多，所以我一点也不介意看着你。你想听我知道什么吗？”
‘No.’
“不想。”
‘Good,’ said William Campbell. ‘Because really I don’t know anything at all. I was just talking.’ He pulled the sheet up over his face again. ‘I love it under a sheet,’ he said. Mr. Turner stood beside the bed. He was a middle-aged man with a large stomach and a bald head and he had many things to do. ‘You ought to stop off here, Billy, and take a cure,’ he said. ‘I’ll fix it up if you want to do it.’
“好，”威廉·坎贝尔说。“因为实际上我什么都不知道。我只是随便说说。”他又把床单拉过脸。“我喜欢躲在床单下面，”他说。特纳先生站在床边。他是个中年人，肚子很大，头顶光秃秃的，事情很多。“比利，你应该在这儿歇一歇，治治病，”他说。“如果你想的话，我会帮你安排的。”
‘I don’t want to take a cure,’ William Campbell said. ‘I don’t want to take a cure at all. I am perfectly happy. All my life I have been perfectly happy.’
“我不想去疗养，”威廉·坎贝尔说。“我根本不想去疗养。我非常快乐。我的一生都很快乐。”
‘How long have you been this way?’
“你这样有多久了？”
‘What a question!’ William Campbell breathed in and out through the sheet.
“什么问题啊！”威廉·坎贝尔透过床单吸气又呼气。
‘How long have you been stewed, Billy?’
“比利，你发闷有多久了？”
‘Haven’t I done my work?’
“我没把活儿干好吗？”
‘Sure. I just asked you how long you’ve been stewed, Billy.’
“是的。只是我问你你被灌醉多久了，比利。”
‘I don’t know. But I’ve got my wolf back,’ he touched the sheet with his tongue. ‘I’ve had him for a week.’
“我不知道。但我的狼回来了，”他用舌头舔了舔床单。“我已经有他一个星期了。”
‘The hell you have.’
“胡扯。”
‘Oh, yes. My dear wolf. Every time I take a drink he goes outside
“哦，是的。我亲爱的小狼。每次我喝一口酒它就会跑到屋外。
the room. He can’t stand alcohol. The poor little fellow.’ He moved his tongue round and round on the sheet. ‘He’s a lovely wolf. He’s just like he always was.’ William Campbell shut his eyes and took a deep breath.
它受不了酒。可怜的小家伙。”他在床单上绕着舌头转动，“它是只可爱的狼。一直都像以前那样。”威廉·坎贝尔闭上眼睛，深吸一口气。
‘You got to take a cure, Billy,’ Mr. Turner said. ‘You won’t mind the Keeley. It isn’t bad.’
“你得去疗养，比利，”特纳先生说，“你不会介意基利治疗的。并不难受。”
‘The Keeley,’ William Campbell said. ‘It isn’t far from London.’ He shut his eyes and opened them, moving the eyelashes against the sheet. ‘I just love sheets,’ he said. He looked at Mr. Turner.
“基利，”威廉·坎贝尔说，“离伦敦不远。”他闭上又睁开眼睛，睫毛擦着床单动了动。“我就是爱床单，”他说。他看着特纳先生。
‘Listen, you think I’m drunk.’
“听着，你以为我喝醉了。”
‘You are drunk.’
“你喝醉了。”
‘No, I’m not.’
“没有，我没喝。”
‘You’re drunk and you’ve had D.Ts.’
“你喝醉了，而且出现戒断谵妄了。”
‘No.’ William Campbell held the sheet around his head. ‘Dear sheet,’ he said. He breathed against it gently. ‘Pretty sheet. You love me, don’t you, sheet? It’s all in the price of the room. Just like in Japan. No,’ he said. ‘Listen, Billy, dear Sliding Billy, I have a surprise for you. I’m not drunk. I’m hopped to the eyes.’
“没有。”威廉·坎贝尔把床单围在头上。“亲爱的床单，”他说。他轻轻地朝床单呼气。“漂亮的床单。你爱我，不是吗，床单？这一切都算在房价里。就像在日本。没有，”他说。“听着，比利，亲爱的大滑头比利，我给你一个惊喜。我没醉。我眼睛都冒光了。”
‘No,’ said Mr. Turner.
“没有，”特纳先生说。
‘Take a look.’ William Campbell pulled up the right sleeve of his pyjama jacket under the sheet, then shoved the right forearm out. ‘Look at that.’ On the forearm, from just above the wrist to the elbow, were small blue circles around tiny dark blue punctures. The circles almost touched one another. ‘That’s the new development,’ William Campbell said. ‘I drink a little now once in a while, just to drive the wolf out of the room.’
“看一看。”威廉·坎贝尔把睡衣上衣的右袖在床单下拉起来，然后把右前臂伸出来。“看看这个。”在前臂上，从腕关节上方到肘部，有一圈圈小小的蓝色圆圈，围着深蓝色的小点孔。那些圆圈几乎相互接触。“这是新情况，”威廉·坎贝尔说。“我现在偶尔喝一点，就为了把房间里的狼赶走。”
‘They got a cure for that,’ ‘Sliding Billy’ Turner said.
“那有治的，”“大滑头”特纳说。
‘No,’ William Campbell said. ‘They haven’t got a cure for anything.’
“不会的，”威廉·坎贝尔说。“他们对任何病都没治法。”
‘You can’t just quit like that, Billy,’ Turner said. He sat on the bed.
“你不能就这么退出，毕利，”特纳说。他坐在床上。
‘Be careful of my sheet,’ William Campbell said.
“小心别弄到我的床单，”威廉·坎贝尔说。
‘You can’t just quit at your age and take to pumping yourself full of that stuff just because you got in a jam.’
“你这个年纪不能就这么放弃，然后因为遇到麻烦就不停给自己打那玩意儿。”
‘There’s a law against it. If that’s what you mean.’
“有法律禁止那样做。如果你是那个意思的话。”
‘No, I mean you got to fight it out.’
“不是，我的意思是你得拼个你死我活。”
Billy Campbell caressed the sheet with his lips and his tongue. ‘Dear sheet,’ he said. ‘I can kiss this sheet and see right through it at the same time.’
比利·坎贝尔用嘴唇和舌头抚着床单。“亲爱的床单，”他说，“我可以亲这床单，同时透过它看见一切。”
‘Cut it out about the sheet. You can’t just take to that stuff, Billy.’
“别再那样对床单了。你可别就迷上那玩意儿，比利。”
William Campbell shut his eyes. He was beginning to feel a slight nausea. He knew that this nausea would increase steadily, without there ever being the relief of sickness, until something were done against it. It was at this point that he suggested that Mr. Turner have a drink. Mr. Turner declined. William Campbell took a drink from the bottle. It was a temporary measure. Mr. Turner watched him. Mr. Turner had been in this room much longer than he should have been, he had many things to do; although living in daily association with people who used drugs, he had a horror of drugs, and he was very fond of William Campbell; he did not wish to leave him. He was very sorry for him and he felt a cure might help. He knew there were good cures in Kansas City. But he had to go. He stood up.
威廉·坎贝尔闭上了眼睛。他开始感到轻微的恶心。他知道这种恶心会不断加重，而永远不会有呕吐的缓解，除非采取措施来对抗它。就在这时，他建议特纳先生喝一杯。特纳先生拒绝了。威廉·坎贝尔从瓶子里喝了一口。这只是权宜之计。特纳先生注视着他。特纳先生在这屋子里呆得比他应该的时间要长，他有许多事情要做；虽然天天与吸毒者为伍，他却对毒品怀有恐惧，而且他非常喜欢威廉·坎贝尔；他不愿离开他。他很为他感到难过，觉得戒毒可能有帮助。他知道堪萨斯城有好的戒毒所。但他得走了。他站了起来。
‘Listen, Billy,’ William Campbell said, ‘I want to tell you something. You’re called “Sliding Billy”. That’s because you can slide. I’m called just Billy. That’s because I never could slide at all. I can’t slide, Billy. I can’t slide. It just catches. Every time I try it, it catches.’ He shut his eyes. ‘I can’t slide, Billy. It’s awful when you can’t slide.’
“听着，比利，”威廉·坎贝尔说，“我想告诉你一件事。你叫‘滑溜比利’。那是因为你会滑。我就叫比利。那是因为我从来不会滑。我不会滑，比利。我不会滑。总是卡住。每次我试，都卡住。”他闭上了眼睛。“我不会滑，比利。当你不会滑的时候，真可怕。”
‘Yes,’ said ‘Sliding Billy’ Turner.
“是的，”‘滑溜比利’特纳说。
‘Yes, what?’ William Campbell looked at him.
“是的，什么事？”威廉·坎贝尔看着他。
‘You were saying.’
“你刚才在说话。”
‘No,’ said William Campbell. ‘I wasn’t saying. It must have been a mistake.’
“不，”威廉·坎贝尔说。“我没在说。一定是搞错了。”
‘You were saying about sliding.’
“你刚才在说关于滑倒的事。”
'No. It couldn’t have been about sliding. But listen, Billy, and I’ll tell you a secret. Stick to sheets, Billy. Keep away from women and horses and, and - ’ he stopped ’ - eagles, Billy. If you love horses you’ll get horse-s _, and if you love eagles you’ll get eagle-s … ’ He stopped and put his head under the sheet.
“不。不可能是关于滑倒的。不过听着，比利，我告诉你个秘密。贴着床单，别离开床单，比利。别招惹女人，也别招惹马，还有，和——”他停住了，“——鹰，比利。如果你爱马你会得马病，如果你爱鹰你会得鹰病……”他停了，把头埋到床单下面。
‘I got to go,’ said ‘Sliding Billy’ Turner.
“我得走了，”‘滑翔比利’特纳说。
‘If you love women you’ll get a dose,’ William Campbell said. ‘If you love horses -’
“如果你爱女人你会遭殃，”威廉·坎贝尔说。“如果你爱马——”
‘Yes, you said that.’
“是的，你说过了。”
‘Said what?’
“说什么？”
‘About horses and eagles.’
“关于马和鹰。”
‘Oh, yes. And if you love sheets.’ He breathed on the sheet and
“哦，是的。还有，如果你爱床单的话。”他把气息吹到床单上，
stroked his nose against it. ‘I don’t know about sheets,’ he said. ‘I just started to love this sheet.’
用鼻子擦了擦它。“我不太懂床单，”他说。“我只是刚开始爱上这床单。”
‘I have to go,’ Mr. Turner said. ‘I got a lot to do.’
“我得走了，”特纳先生说。“我有很多事要做。”
‘That’s all right,’ William Campbell said. ‘Everybody’s got to go.’
“没关系，”威廉·坎贝尔说。“大家都得走。”
‘I better go.’
“我最好走了。”
‘All right, you go.’
“好吧，你走吧。”
‘Are you all right, Billy?’
“你没事吧，比利？”
‘I was never so happy in my life.’
“我这辈子从未如此幸福过。”
‘And you’re all right?’
“那你真的没事？”
‘I’m fine. You go along. I’ll just lie here for a little while. Around noon I’ll get up.’
“我没事。你先走吧。我就躺一会儿。到中午左右我会起来。”
But when Mr. Turner came up to William Campbell’s room at noon William Campbell was sleeping and as Mr. Turner was a man who knew what things in life were very valuable he did not wake him.
但当特纳先生中午来到威廉·坎贝尔的房间时，威廉·坎贝尔正在睡觉，而特纳先生是个知道生活中哪些东西很宝贵的人，所以他没有叫醒他。

TO-DAY IS FRIDAY
今天是星期五

Three Roman soldiers are in a drinking-place at eleven o’clock at night. There are barrels around the wall. Behind the wooden counter is a Hebrew wine-seller. The three Roman soldiers are a little cockeyed.
三个罗马士兵在晚上十一点钟坐在一家酒馆里。墙边堆着酒桶。木制柜台后面是一个希伯来酒商。三个罗马士兵都有点醉。
ist soldier You tried the red?
第一士兵 你尝过那红的么？
2nd soldier No, I ain’t tried it.
第二名士兵 没，有试过。
ist soldier You better try it.
第一名士兵 你最好试试。
2nd soldier All right, George, we’ll have a round of the red.
第二名士兵 好吧，乔治，我们来一回合红的。
hebrew wine-seller Here you are, gentlemen. You’ll like that. (He sets down an earthenware pitcher that he has filled from one of the casks) That’s a nice little wine.
犹太卖酒者 给你们，先生们。你们会喜欢的。（他放下一个他从酒桶里装满的陶罐）这是个不错的小酒。
ist soldier Have a drink of it yourself. (He turns to the third Roman soldier who is leaning on a barrel) What’s the matter with you?
第一名士兵 自己喝点吧。（他转向倚在桶上的第三名罗马士兵）你怎么了？
3 rd soldier I got a gut-ache.
第三名士兵 我肚子疼。
2nd soldier You’ve been drinking water.
第二名士兵 你一直喝的是水。
ist soldier Try some of the red.
第一名士兵 试点红的吧。
3rd soldier I can’t drink the damn stuff. It makes my gut sour.
第三个士兵 我喝不了这该死的东西。它让我胃里发酸。
ist soldier You been out here too long.
第一个士兵 你在这儿呆太久了。
3rd soldier Hell, don’t I know it?
第三个士兵 天哪，我难道不知道吗？
ist soldier Say, George, can’t you give this gentleman something to fix up his stomach?
第一个士兵 说，乔治，你不能给这位先生拿点什么来治治他的胃吗？
hebrew wine-seller I got it right here.
希伯来卖酒的 我这儿就有。
(The third Roman soldier tastes the cup that the wine-seller has mixed for him)
（第三个罗马士兵尝了卖酒人为他调的杯酒）
3 rd soldier Hey, what you put in that, camel chips?
第三士兵 嘿，你往里面放了什么，骆驼屎吗？
wine-seller You drink that right down, Lootenant. That’ll fix you up all right.
卖酒的 你把它一饮而尽，少尉。那可会把你整好。
3rd soldier Well, I couldn’t feel any worse.
第三个士兵 好吧，我不会感觉更糟了。
ist soldier Take a chance on it. George fixed me up fine the other day.
第一士兵 抓住机会试试吧。乔治前几天把我照顾得很好。
wine-seller You were in bad shape, Lootenant. I know what fixes up a bad stomach.
酒贩 你当时状态很差，长官。我知道怎么治好不舒服的胃。

(The third Roman soldier drinks the cup down)
（第三个罗马士兵把杯子喝光）

3rd soldier Jesus Christ. (He makes a face)
第三个士兵 耶稣基督。（他做了个鬼脸）
2nd soldier That false alarm!
第二个士兵 假警报啊！
ist soldier Oh, I don’t know. He was pretty good in there to-day.
第一个士兵 哦，我也不清楚。今天他在那儿挺厉害的。
2nd soldier Why didn’t he come down off the cross?
第二个士兵 他怎么不从十字架上下来？
ist soldier He didn’t want to come down off the cross. That’s not his play.
第一士兵 他可不想从十字架上下来。那不是他的戏。
2ND soldier Show me a guy that doesn’t want to come down off the cross.
第二士兵 给我找一个不想从十字架上下来的人来看看。
ist soldier Aw, hell, you don’t know anything about it. Ask George there. Did he want to come down off the cross, George?
第一士兵 啊，见鬼，你哪儿懂这事。问问那边的乔治。他想从十字架上下来吗，乔治？
wine-seller I’ll tell you, gentlemen, I wasn’t out there. It’s a thing I haven’t taken any interest in.
酒贩 我告诉你们，先生们，我可不曾在场。这事我一点兴趣都没有。
2ND soldier Listen, I seen a lot of them - here and plenty of other places. Any time you show me one that doesn’t want to get down off the cross when the time comes - when the time comes, I mean - I’ll climb right up with him.
第二个士兵 听着，我见过很多——在这里和许多其他地方。只要你给我看一个到时候不想从十字架上下来的——我说的是到时候——我就跟他一起爬上去。
ist soldier I thought he was pretty good in there to-day.
第一个士兵 我以为他今天在里面表现得相当不错。
3 rd soldier He was all right.
第三个士兵 他没问题。
2nd soldier You guys don’t know what I’m talking about. I’m not saying whether he was good or not. What I mean is, when the time comes. When they first start nailing him, there isn’t none of them wouldn’t stop it if they could.
第二个士兵 你们这些人不知道我在说什么。我不是说他好不好。我的意思是，到时候。当他们刚开始钉他上去时，没有一个人会不想阻止的，如果他们能的话。
ist soldier Didn’t you follow it, George?
第一士兵 你没跟上吗，乔治？
wine-seller No, I didn’t take any interest in it, Lootenant.
卖酒人 没有，长官，我对那事一点兴趣都没有。
ist soldier I was surprised how he acted.
第一士兵 我对他那样的表现感到吃惊。
3rd soldier The part I don’t like is the nailing them on. You know, that must get to you pretty bad.
第三士兵 我不喜欢的部分是把他们钉上去。你知道的，那一定会把你折磨得很厉害。
2nd soldier It isn’t that that’s so bad, as when they first lift 'em up. (He makes a lifting gesture with his two palms together) When the weight starts to pull on 'em. That’s when it gets 'em.
第二个士兵 并不是说那样很糟，而是当他们刚被抬起来的时候。(他双掌合拢做抬举的手势) 当重力开始拉扯他们的时候。那时他们才吃不消。
3 rd 3 rd  3^("rd ")3^{\text {rd }} soldier It takes some of them pretty bad.
3 rd 3 rd  3^("rd ")3^{\text {rd }} 士兵 那会把他们折磨得很厉害。
ist soldier Ain’t I seen 'em? I seen plenty of them. I tell you, he was pretty good in there to-day.
第一士兵 难道我没见过他们吗？我见过不少。我跟你说，他今天在里面表现得相当不错。
(The second Roman soldier smiles at the Hebrew wine-seller)
（第二个罗马士兵对着希伯来卖酒的微笑）
2nd soldier You’re a regular Christer, big boy.
第二个士兵 你可真像个基督徒，大男孩。
ist soldier Sure, go on and kid him. But listen while I tell you something. He was pretty good in there to-day.
第一个士兵 当然，继续逗他去吧。但听我说件事。他今天在里面干得相当不错。
2ND soldier What about some more wine?
第二个士兵 再来点酒如何？
(The wine-seller looks up expectantly. The third Roman soldier is sitting with his head down. He does not look well)
（卖酒的人期待地抬起头。第三个罗马士兵低着头坐着。他看上去身体不太好）
3 rd soldier I don’t want any more.
第三个士兵 我不要了。
2nd soldier Just for two, George.
第二个士兵 就两杯，乔治。
(The wine-seller puts out a pitcher of wine, a size smaller than the last one. He leans forward on the wooden counter)
（酒贩端出一壶酒，比上一壶小一号。他向木柜台前倾）
ist soldier You see his girl?
第一个士兵 你看到他那女孩了吗？
2nd soldier Wasn’t I standing right by her?
第二个士兵 我不是正站在她身边吗？
ist soldier She’s a nice-looker.
第一个士兵 她看起来不错。
2ND soldier I knew her before he did. (He winks at the wineseller)
第二个士兵 我在他之前就认识她。（他向卖酒的眨眼）
ist soldier I used to see her around the town.
第一个士兵 我以前常在城里见到她。
2ND soldier She used to have a lot of stuff. He never brought her no good luck.
第二个士兵 她以前有很多东西。他从没给她带来好运。
ist soldier Oh, he ain’t lucky. But he looked pretty good to me in there to-day.
第一个士兵 哦，他不走运。但我看他今天在那儿挺精神的。
2ND soldier What became of his gang?
第二个士兵 他的那帮人怎么样了？
ist soldier Oh, they faded out. Just the women stuck by him.
第一个士兵 哦，他们都散了。只有那些女人还留着他。
2ND soldier They were a pretty yellow crowd. When they seen him go up there they didn’t want any of it.
第 2 名士兵 他们是一群黄皮肤的漂亮人。当他们看见他上去时，他们谁也不愿意上。
ist soldier The women stuck all right.
第 1 名士兵 女人们坚持下来了。
2nd soldier Sure, they stuck all right.
第 2 名士兵 当然，她们都坚持下来了。
ist soldier You see me slip the old spear into him?
第 1 名士兵 你看我把那根旧矛插进他了吗？
2nd soldier You’ll get into trouble doing that some day.

ist soldier It was the least I could do for him. I’ll tell you he looked pretty good to me in there to-day.
第一个士兵 我不过是尽了我能为他做的最少的事。我告诉你，他今天在那里面看起来对我来说相当不错。
hebrew wine-seller Gentlemen, you know I got to close.
希伯来卖酒者 先生们，你们知道我要关门了。
ist soldier We’ll have one more round.
第一个士兵 我们再来一回合。
2nd soldier What’s the use? This stuff don’t get you anywhere. Come on, let’s go.
第 2 名士兵 有什么用？这玩意儿对你没任何好处。走吧，走。
ist soldier Just another round.
第 1 名士兵 只再来一回合。

ist soldier Just one more.
第 1 名士兵 只再来一个。
2nd soldier No, come on. We’re going to go. Good night, George. Put it on the bill.
第二名士兵 不，来吧。我们要走了。晚安，乔治。记在账上。
wine-seller Good night, gentlemen. (He looks a little worried) You couldn’t let me have a little something on account, Lootenant?

第二名士兵 去你的吧，乔治！星期三发工资。
wine-seller It’s all right, Lootenant. Good night, gentlemen.

(The three Roman soldiers go out the door into the street. Outside in the street)
（三个罗马士兵出门到街上。外面在街上）
2nd soldier George is a kike just like all the rest of them.
第二个士兵：乔治是个犹太佬，就像他们所有人一样。
