‘You do,’ she said. 'That makes it worse, of course.
“你明白，”她说，“那当然更糟。”
‘Sure,’ he said, looking at her. ‘I’ll understand all the time. All day and all night. Especially all night. I’ll understand. You don’t have to worry about that.’
“当然，”他看着她说。“我会一直明白的。整天整夜。尤其是整夜。我会明白。你不用为此担心。”
‘I’m sorry,’ she said.
“对不起。”她说。
'If it was a man - ’
“要是是个男人——”
'Don’t say that. It wouldn’t be a man. You know that. Don’t you trust me?"
“别那样说。不会是个男人。你知道的。你不信任我吗？”
‘That’s funny,’ he said. ‘Trust you. That’s really funny.’
“真有意思，”他说。“信你。真是太有意思了。”
‘I’m sorry,’ she said. ‘That’s all I seem to say. But when we do understand each other there’s no use to pretend we don’t.’
“对不起，”她说。“好像我只会说这句话。但当我们彼此理解时，假装不理解也毫无意义。”
‘No,’ he said. ‘I suppose not.’
“不，”他说。“我想也是。”
‘I’ll come back if you want me.’
“如果你要我，我会回来的。”
‘No. I don’t want you.’
“不。我不想要你。”
Then they did not say anything for a while.
然后他们沉默了一会儿。
‘You don’t believe I love you, do you ?’ the girl asked.
“你不相信我爱你，是吗？”女孩问道。
‘Let’s not talk rot,’ the man said.
“别胡说，”男人说。
‘Don’t you really believe I love you?’
“你真的不相信我爱你吗？”
‘Why don’t you prove it?’
“你干嘛不证明给我看？”
‘You didn’t use to be that way. You never asked me to prove anything. That isn’t polite.’
“你以前不是这样的。你从没要求我证明什么。那样不礼貌。”
‘You’re a funny girl.’
“你真有趣。”
‘You’re not. You’re a fine man and it breaks my heart to go off and leave you -’
“你才不是。你是个好人，我要离开你真的让我心碎——”
‘You have to, of course.’
“你当然得这么做。”
‘Yes,’ she said. ‘I have to and you know it.’
“是的，”她说。“我得这么做，你知道的。”
He did not say anything and she looked at him and put her hand out again. The barman was at the far end of the bar. His face was white and so was his jacket. He knew these two and thought them a handsome young couple. He had seen many handsome young couples break up and new couples form that were never so handsome long. He was not thinking about this, but about a horse. In half an hour he could send across the street to find if the horse had won.
他什么也没说，她看着他又伸出手去。吧台远端的酒保站着，脸色发白，夹克也是白色的。他认识这两个人，觉得他们是一对英俊的年轻夫妻。他见过许多英俊的年轻夫妻分崩离析，又有新的夫妻出现，但这些新夫妻也不会长久保持那样的英俊。他并没有在想着这些，而是在想着一匹马。半小时后他可以派人去街对面看看那匹马是否赢了。
‘Couldn’t you just be good to me and let me go?’ the girl asked.
“你就不能对我好一点，放我走吗？”那个女孩问。
‘What do you think I’m going to do?’
“你以为我要做什么？”
Two people came in the door and went up to the bar.
两个人走进门，走到吧台前。
‘Yes, sir,’ the barman took the orders.
“是的，先生，”酒保接过了点单。
‘You can’t forgive me? When you know about it?’ the girl asked. ‘No.’
“你不能原谅我？你都知道这事了？”女孩问。“不能。”
‘You don’t think things we’ve had and done should make any difference in understanding?’
“你不认为我们曾经拥有和做过的事情在理解上应该有什么影响吗？”
" “Vice is a monster of such fearful mien,” " the young man said bitterly, ‘that to be something or other needs but to be seen. Then we something, something, then embrace.’ He could not remember the words. ‘I can’t quote,’ he said.
“‘恶行是如此可怕面貌的怪物，’”年轻人苦涩地说， “‘只要被看见就成了某物。然后我们成了某物，然后相拥。’ 他记不清原话了。‘我不会引用，’他说。”
‘Let’s not say vice,’ she said. ‘That’s not very polite.’
“别说‘恶行’，”她说。“那不太礼貌。”
‘Perversion,’ he said.
“变态，”他说。
‘James,’ one of the clients addressed the barman, ‘you’re looking very well.’
“詹姆斯，”其中一位客人对酒保说，“你看起来很好。”
‘You’re looking very well yourself,’ the barman said.
“你自己也看起来很好，”酒保说。
‘Old James,’ the other client said. ‘You’re fatter, James.’
“老詹姆斯，”另一位客人说，“你胖了，詹姆斯。”
‘It’s terrible,’ the barman said, ‘the way I put it on.’
“可怕得很，”酒保说，“我就是这么发胖的。”
‘Don’t neglect to insert the brandy, James,’ the first client said.
“别忘了放入白兰地，詹姆斯，”第一个顾客说。
‘No, sir,’ said the barman. ‘Trust me.’
“不会的，先生，”酒保说。“信我。”
The two at the bar looked over at the two at the table, then looked back at the barman again. Toward the barman was the comfortable direction.
吧台那两个人看了看桌子那两个人，又回头看了看酒保。朝酒保那边是舒服的方向。
‘I’d like it better if you didn’t use words like that,’ the girl said. ‘There’s no necessity to use a word like that.’
“我更希望你别用那种词，”女孩说。“没必要用那样的词。”
‘What do you want me to call it?’
“你要我怎么称呼它？”
‘You don’t have to call it. You don’t have to put any name to it.’
“你不必叫它什么。你不必给它起任何名字。”
‘That’s the name for it.’
“那就是它的名字。”
‘No,’ she said. ‘We’re made up of all sorts of things. You’ve known that. You’ve used it well enough.’
“不，”她说。“我们是由各种东西组成的。你知道这一点。你足够用得好。”
‘You don’t have to say that again.’
“你不必再说一遍了。”
‘Because that explains it to you.’
“因为那会让你明白的。”
‘All right,’ he said. ‘All right.’
“好吧，”他说，“好吧。”
‘You mean all wrong. I know. It’s all wrong. But I’ll come back. I told you I’d come back. I’ll come back right away.’
“你的意思是完全错了。我知道。都错了。但我会回来的。我告诉过你我会回来的。我会马上回来的。”
‘No, you won’t.’
“不会的，你不会的。”
‘I’ll come back.’
“我会回来的。”
‘No, you won’t. Not to me.’
“不会的，你不会的。不会回到我这里。”
‘You’ll see.’
“你会看到的。”
‘Yes,’ he said. ‘That’s the hell of it. You probably will.’
“是的，”他说。“这就是糟糕的地方。你很可能会的。”
‘Of course I will.’
“当然我会。”
‘Go on, then.’
“那就去吧。”
‘Really?’ She could not believe him, but her voice was happy.
“真的？”她不敢相信他，但声音很高兴。
‘Go on,’ his voice sounded strange to him. He was looking at her, at the way her mouth went and the curve of her cheekbones, at her eyes and at the way her hair grew on her forehead and at the edge of her ear and at her neck.
“继续，”他的声音听起来对他自己很陌生。他看着她，看着她嘴唇的样子和颧骨的曲线，眼睛，以及头发在额头边缘和耳际的生长方式，还有她的脖颈。
‘Not really. Oh, you’re too sweet,’ she said. ‘You’re too good to me.’
“并不是。哦，你真是太甜了，”她说。“你对我太好了。”
‘And when you come back tell me all about it.’ His voice sounded very strange. He did not recognize it. She looked at him quickly. He was settled into something.
“等你回来把一切都告诉我。”他的声音听起来很奇怪。他认不出这是自己的声音。她迅速看了他一眼。他沉浸在某种状态中。
‘You want me to go?’ she asked seriously.
“你要我走吗？”她严肃地问。
‘Yes,’ he said seriously. ‘Right away.’ His voice was not the same, and his mouth was very dry. ‘Now,’ he said.
“是的，”他严肃地说。“马上去。”他的声音变了，嘴很干。“现在，”他说。
She stood up and went out quickly. She did not look back at him. He watched her go. He was not the same-looking man as he had been before he had told her to go. He got up from the table, picked up the two checks and went over to the bar with them.
她站起来，快步走了出去。她没有回头看他。他看着她离开。和叫她走之前相比，他看起来已不是同一个人。他从桌旁站起，拿起两张账单，走到吧台去。
‘I’m a different man, James,’ he said to the barman. ‘You see in me quite a different man.’
“詹姆斯，我是个不同的人，”他对酒保说。“你看见的我完全不同了。”
‘Yes, sir?’ said James.
“是吗，先生？”詹姆斯说。
‘Vice,’ said the brown young man, ‘is a very strange thing, James.’ He looked out the door. He saw her going down the street. As he looked in the glass, he saw he was really quite a different-looking man. The other two at the bar moved down to make room for him.
“恶习，”褐肤的年轻人说，“是一件非常奇怪的事，詹姆斯。”他看向门外。他看见她沿着街走去。当他在镜中看自己时，发现自己真的是个长相相当不同的人。吧台上的另外两个人挪开了位置，好给他留地方。
‘You’re right there, sir,’ James said.
“您说得对，先生，”詹姆斯说。
The other two moved down a little more, so that he would be quite comfortable. The young man saw himself in the mirror behind the bar. ‘I said I was a different man, James,’ he said. Looking into the mirror he saw that this was quite true.
另外两人又往下挪了一些，好让他坐得很舒服。年轻人在吧台后面的镜子里看见了自己。“我说过我是个不同的人，詹姆斯，”他说。看着镜子，他发现这话相当真实。
‘You look very well, sir,’ James said. ‘You must have had a very good summer.’
“您看起来很好，先生，”詹姆斯说。“您这夏天一定过得很好。”

A WAY YOU'LL NEVER BE
一种你永远不会成为的方式

The attack had gone across the field, been held up by machine-gun fire from the sunken road and from the group of farm houses, encountered no resistance in the town, and reached the bank of the river. Coming along the road on a bicycle, getting off to push the machine when the surface of the road became too broken, Nicholas Adams saw what had happened by the position of the dead.
攻势越过了田地，在下陷的公路和那群农舍处被机枪火力阻止，在镇上没有遇到抵抗，直抵河岸。尼古拉斯·亚当斯沿着路骑自行车来到这里，路面太破碎时就下车推车，从尸体的分布看出了事情的经过。
They lay alone or in clumps in the high grass of the fields and along the road, their pockets out, and over them were flies and around each body or group of bodies were the scattered papers.
他们孤零零地或成簇地躺在田野的高草和路旁，口袋翻出，苍蝇在他们身上盘旋，每具尸体或每群尸体周围散落着纸张。
In the grass and the grain, beside the road, and in some places scattered over the road, there was much material: a field kitchen, it must have come over when things were going well; many of the calf-skin-covered haversacks, stick bombs, helmets, rifles, sometimes one butt-up, the bayonets stuck in the dirt, they had dug quite a little at the last; stick bombs, helmets, rifles, entrenching tools, ammunition boxes, starshell pistols, their shells scattered about, medical kits, gas masks, empty gas mask cans, a squat, tripodded machine-gun in a nest of empty shells, full belts protruding from the boxes, the watercooling can empty and on its side, the breech block gone, the crew in odd positions, and around them, in the grass, more of the typical papers.
在路边的草丛和谷物间，在路上零星散落的地方，有许多东西：一个野战炊事车，那一定是在局势顺利时搬过来的；许多犊皮覆盖的背囊、stick bombs、头盔、步枪，有时是一只枪托朝天，刺刀插在泥土里，他们最后把地翻了一阵；stick bombs、头盔、步枪、铲具、弹药箱、照明弹手枪，弹壳散落一地，医药箱、防毒面具、空的防毒面具罐，一挺蹲伏的、三脚架支起的机枪在一堆空弹壳里，满布带从箱子里露出来，水冷罐空了并侧倒，后膛块不见了，机组成员姿势杂乱，周围的草地上还有更多典型的文件。
There were mass prayer books, group postcards showing the machine-gun unit standing in ranked and ruddy cheerfulness as in a football picture for a college annual; now they were humped and swollen in the grass; propaganda postcards showing a soldier in Austrian uniform bending a woman backward over a bed; the figures were impressionistically drawn; very attractively depicted and had nothing in common with actual rape in which the woman’s skirts are pulled over her head to smother her, one comrade sometimes sitting upon the head. There were many of these inciting cards which had evidently been issued just before the offensive. Now they were scattered with the smutty postcards, photographic; the small photographs of village girls by village photographers, the occasional
有成堆的祈祷书，成组的明信片上印着机枪班排成队、面带红光的样子，像学院年鉴里的足球队合影；现在它们都被扔在草地上，隆起鼓胀；还有宣传画明信片，画上一个穿奥地利军服的士兵把一名妇女压在床上向后弯；人物是印象派式地画成的；画得很有吸引力，与真实的强奸毫无共同之处——真实的强奸里妇女的裙子会被拽过头盖住她，有时一个同伴还会坐在她的头上。还有许多这样的煽动性卡片，显然是在攻势前不久发出来的。现在它们和那些下流的明信片、摄影照片混杂在一起；乡村摄影师拍的村姑的小照片，零零散散的。
pictures of children, and the letters, letters, letters. There was always much paper about the dead and the debris of this attack was no exception.
孩子们的照片，还有那些信件、信件、信件。关于死者总是有很多纸张，这次袭击的残骸也不例外。
These were new dead and no one had bothered with anything but their pockets. Our own dead, or what he thought of, still, as our own dead, were surprisingly few, Nick noticed. Their coats had been opened too and their pockets were out, and they showed, by their positions, the manner and the skill of the attack. The hot weather had swollen them all alike regardless of nationality.
这些是新死的，没人管他们除了掏口袋。尼克注意到，我们自己的人，或者他仍旧认为是我们自己的人，出人意料地少。他们的外套也被打开，口袋被翻出来，从他们的姿势可以看出攻击的方式和技巧。炎热的天气使他们无论国籍如何都同样浮肿。
The town had evidently been defended, at the last, from the line of the sunken road and there had been few or no Austrians to fall back into it. There were only three bodies in the street and they looked to have been killed running. The houses of the town were broken by the shelling and the street had much rubble of plaster and mortar and there were broken beams, broken tiles, and many holes, some of them yellow-edged from the mustard gas. There were many pieces of shell, and shrapnel balls were scattered in the rubble. There was no one in the town at all.
显然城镇最后是在塌陷的公路一线被防守的，几乎没有奥地利人退回到那里。街上只有三具尸体，看上去是跑着被打死的。城镇的房屋被炮火破坏，街道上到处是石膏和砂浆的瓦砾，还有断梁、碎瓦，以及许多弹坑，其中一些因芥子气而呈现黄色边缘。到处是炮弹碎片，弹片球散落在瓦砾中。城里根本没有人。
Nick Adams had seen no one since he had left Fornaci, although, riding along the road through the over-foliaged country, he had seen guns hidden under screens of mulberry leaves to the left of the road, noticing them by the heat-waves in the air above the leaves where the sun hit the metal. Now he went on through the town, surprised to find it deserted, and came out on the low road beneath the bank of the river. Leaving the town there was a bare open space where the road slanted down and he could see the placid reach of the river and the low curve of the opposite bank and the whitened, sun-baked mud where the Austrians had dug. It was all very lush and overgreen since he had seen it last and becoming historical had made no change in this, the lower river.
尼克·亚当斯自离开福尔纳奇后便再未见过任何人，尽管他沿着穿过浓密植被的公路骑行时，曾在路左侧的桑叶屏蔽下看到藏着的枪支，通过阳光照在金属上方叶片上方空气中的热浪认出它们。现在他继续穿过小镇，惊讶地发现小镇空无一人，随后来到河岸下方的低路。离开小镇处有一片裸露的空地，公路倾斜下来，他可以看到那平静的河段、对岸低矮的弯曲河岸，以及奥地利人挖掘过后晒白的泥地。自他上次看到这里以来一切都变得非常茂盛、绿意盎然，而这条下游的河流即使随着历史变迁也未见改变。
The battalion was along the bank to the left. There was a series of holes in the top of the bank with a few men in them. Nick noticed where the machine-guns were posted and the signal rockets in their racks. The men in the holes in the side of the bank were sleeping. No one challenged. He went on and as he came around a turn in the mud bank a young second lieutenant with a stubble of beard and red-rimmed, very bloodshot eyes pointed a pistol at him.
营地沿着左边的堤岸排开。堤顶上有一排战壕，里头坐着几个士兵。尼克注意到机关枪的驻地和架子上的信号火箭。堤侧土坑里的士兵在睡觉。没有人盘问。他继续前进，刚绕过堤岸的一个弯，就被一个留着胡茬、眼眶发红、血丝明显的年轻少尉用手枪指着。
‘Who are you?’
“你是谁？”
Nick told him.
尼克告诉了他。
‘How do I know this?’
“我怎么知道这是真的？”
Nick showed him the tessera with photograph and identification and the seal of the third army. He took hold of it.
尼克把带照片和身份证明并盖有第三军印章的凭证给他看。他接过了它。
‘I will keep this.’
“我会收着的。”
‘You will not,’ Nick said. ‘Give me back the card and put your gun away. There. In the holster.’
“你不会的，”尼克说。“把卡还给我，把枪收起来。就那儿。放进枪套里。”
‘How am I to know who you are?’
“我怎么知道你是谁？”
‘The tessera tells you.’
“tessera 告诉你。”
‘And if the tessera is false? Give me that card.’
“如果 tessera 是假的呢？把那张卡给我。”
‘Don’t be a fool,’ Nick said cheerfully. ‘Take me to your company commander.’
“别傻了，”尼克愉快地说。“带我去找你的连长。”
‘I should send you to battalion headquarters.’
“我应该把你送到营部去。”
‘All right,’ said Nick. ‘Listen, do you know the Captain Paravicini? The tall one with the small moustache who was an architect and speaks English?’
“好吧，”尼克说。“听着，你认识帕拉维奇尼上尉吗？就是那个留着小胡子、身材高、曾是建筑师并会说英语的那位？”
‘You know him?’
“你认识他？”
‘A little.’
“有点儿。”
‘What company does he command?’
“他指挥哪支部队？”
‘The second.’
“第二个。”
‘He is commanding the battalion.’
“他在指挥大队。”
‘Good,’ said Nick. He was relieved to know that Para was all right. ‘Let us go to the battalion.’
“好，”尼克说。他知道帕拉没事，心里松了口气。“我们去大队那儿吧。”
As Nick had left the edge of the town three shrapnel had burst high and to the right over one of the wrecked houses and since then there had been no shelling. But the face of this officer looked like the face of a man during a bombardment. There was the same tightness and the voice did not sound natural. His pistol made Nick nervous.
当尼克离开城镇边缘时，有三枚杀伤弹在高处并向右方的其中一栋被毁房屋上空爆炸，从那以后就没有再遭到炮击。但这名军官的脸看起来像在轰炸中的人。表情同样紧绷，声音也不自然。他的手枪使尼克感到紧张。
‘Put it away,’ he said. ‘There’s the whole river between them and you.’
“把它放下，”他说。“他们和你之间隔着整条河。”
‘If I thought you were a spy I would shoot you now,’ the second lieutenant said.
“如果我觉得你是间谍，我现在就把你枪毙了，”少尉说。
‘Come on,’ said Nick. ‘Let us go to the battalion.’ This officer made him very nervous.
“快走吧，”尼克说。“我们去营部。”这位军官让他非常紧张。
The Captain Paravicini, acting major, thinner and more Englishlooking than ever, rose when Nick saluted from behind the table in the dugout that was battalion headquarters.
代理少校帕拉维奇尼上尉，比以往更瘦、更显英国人模样，当尼克在战壕里营部的桌后敬礼时站了起来。
‘Hello,’ he said. ‘I didn’t know you. What are you doing in that uniform?’
“你好，”他说。“我认不出你了。你穿那套制服干什么？”
‘They’ve put me in it.’
“他们让我穿的。”
‘I am very glad to see you, Nicolo.’
“我很高兴见到你，尼科洛。”
‘Right. You look well. How was the show?’
“是吗。你看起来不错。演出怎么样？”
‘We made a very fine attack. Truly. A very fine attack. I will show you. Look.’
“我们的进攻做得非常好。真的。非常好。我给你看。看。”
He showed on the map how the attack had gone.
他在地图上指示了进攻的经过。
‘I came from Fornaci,’ Nick said. ‘I could see how it had been. It was very good.’
“我来自福尔纳奇，”尼克说。“我能看出当时的情形。非常不错。”
‘It was extraordinary. Altogether extraordinary. Are you attached to the regiment?’
“这太非同寻常了。完全非同寻常。你隶属于哪个团？”
‘No. I am supposed to move around and let them see the uniform.’
“不会。我应当走来走去，让他们看到这身制服。”
‘How odd.’
“真奇怪。”
‘If they see one American uniform that is supposed to make them believe others are coming.’
“如果他们看到一件美国制服，就会让他们相信还有其他人要来。”
‘But how will they know it is an American uniform?’
“可他们怎么会知道那是美国的制服？”
‘You will tell them.’
“你会把这事告诉他们的。”
‘Oh. Yes, I see. I will send a corporal with you to show you about and you will make a tour of the lines.’
“噢。是的，我明白。我会派一个下士跟你一起去给你带路，你会巡视一圈阵地。”
‘Like a bloody politician,’ Nick said.
“像个该死的政客，”尼克说。
‘You would be much more distinguished in civilian clothes. They are what is really distinguished.’
“穿便装会显得更有气派。便装才是真正有气派的。”
‘With a homburg hat,’ said Nick.
“戴着一顶霍姆堡帽，”Nick 说。
‘Or with a very furry fedora.’
“或者戴着一顶很毛绒的软呢礼帽。”
‘I’m supposed to have my pockets full of cigarettes and postal cards and such things,’ Nick said. ‘I should have a musette full of chocolate. These I should distribute with a kind word and a pat on the back. But there weren’t any cigarettes and postcards and no chocolate. So they said to circulate around anyway.’
“我本应该把口袋塞满香烟和明信片之类的东西，”Nick 说。“我应该带一个装满巧克力的小背包。我会伴着好话和拍拍背把这些分发出去。但没有香烟也没有明信片，也没有巧克力。所以他们还是说让我到处转转。”
‘I’m sure your appearance will be very heartening to the troops.’
“我相信你的出场会极大鼓舞部队士气。”
‘I wish you wouldn’t,’ Nick said. ‘I feel badly enough about it as it is. In principle, I would have brought you a bottle of brandy.’
“我真希望你别这么做，”尼克说，“我已经够难受的了。原则上我本来会给你带一瓶白兰地。”
‘In principle,’ Para said and smiled, for the first time, showing yellowed teeth. 'Such a beautiful expression. Would you like some Grappa?’
“‘原则上’，”帕拉说并微笑，这是她第一次露出笑容，露出发黄的牙齿。“多美的一个词。你想要点格拉帕吗？”
‘No, thank you,’ Nick said.
“不，谢谢，”尼克说。
‘It hasn’t any ether in it.’
“它里头可没加醚。”
‘I can taste that still,’ Nick remembered suddenly and completely.
“我还能记得那股味道，”尼克突然且完全地想起。
‘You know I never knew you were drunk until you started talking coming back in the camions.’
“你知道吗，直到你在卡车上回来的路上开始说话，我才知道你那时喝醉了。”
‘I was stinking in every attack,’ Nick said.
“每次出击我都醉得一塌糊涂，”尼克说。
‘I can’t do it,’ Para said. ‘I took it in the first show, the very first show, and it only made me very upset and then frightfully thirsty.’
“我做不了，”帕拉说。“我在第一场演出就喝了，第一场，就那一下，它只是让我非常不安，然后口渴得要命。”
‘You don’t need it.’
“你不用它。”
‘You’re much braver in an attack than I am.’
“你在进攻时比我勇敢得多。”
‘No,’ Nick said. ‘I know how I am and I prefer to get stinking. I’m not ashamed of it.’
“不，”尼克说。“我知道我是什么样子，我宁愿把自己喝得烂醉。我不为此感到羞耻。”
‘I’ve never seen you drunk.’
“我从没见你醉过。”
‘No?’ said Nick. ‘Never? Not when we rode from Mestre to Portogrande that night and I wanted to go to sleep and used the bicycle for a blanket and pulled it up under my chin?’
“没有？”尼克说。“从来没有？那晚我们从 Mestre 骑到 Portogrande 的时候，我想睡觉，用自行车当毯子把它拉到下巴下，那时候也没有？”
‘That wasn’t in the lines.’
“那不在台词里。”
‘Let’s not talk about how I am,’ Nick said. ‘It’s a subject I know too much about to want to think about it any more.’
“别谈我是什么样子了，”尼克说。“这是个我太熟悉、再也不想去想的话题。”
‘You might as well stay here a while,’ Paravicini said. ‘You can take a nap if you like. They didn’t do much to this in the bombardment. It’s too hot to go out yet.’
“你不妨在这儿多呆会儿，”Paravicini 说。“如果你愿意可以小睡一会儿。在轰炸里他们没怎么破坏这里。现在出去还太热。”
‘I suppose there is no hurry.’
“我想应该不急。”
‘How are you really?’
“你到底怎么样？”
‘I’m fine. I’m perfectly all right.’
“我很好。我完全没事。”
‘No. I mean really.’
“不。我的意思是真的怎么样。”
‘I’m all right. I can’t sleep without a light of some sort. That’s all I have now.’
“我没事。没有点灯我睡不着。现在就只有这个了。”
‘I said it should have been trepanned. I’m no doctor but I know that.’
“我说应该开颅的。我不是医生，但我知道那是该做的事。”
‘Well, they thought it was better to have it absorb, and that’s what I got. What’s the matter? I don’t seem crazy to you, do I?’
“嗯，他们觉得让它吸收比较好，所以就那样处理了。我怎么了？我看起来像疯子吗？”
‘You seem in top-hole shape.’
“你看起来状态极好。”
‘It’s a hell of a nuisance once they’ve had you certified as nutty,’ Nick said. ‘No one ever has any confidence in you again.’
“被人证明神经有问题之后可真麻烦，”尼克说。“没有人还会再信任你了。”
‘I would take a nap, Nicolo,’ Paravicini said. ‘This isn’t battalion headquarters as we used to know it. We’re just waiting to be pulled out. You oughtn’t to go out in the heat now - it’s silly. Use that bunk.’
“我建议你打个盹，尼科洛，”帕拉维奇尼说。“这里可不是我们以前熟悉的营总部。我们只是等着被撤走。你现在不该在热天外出——太傻了。去那张铺板上躺着吧。”
‘I might just lie down,’ Nick said.
“我倒是想躺一会儿，”尼克说。
Nick lay on the bunk. He was very disappointed that he felt this way and more disappointed, even, that it was so obvious to Captain Paravicini. This was not as large a dugout as the one where that
尼克躺在铺板上。他为自己会有这种感觉感到非常失望，更失望的是，这对帕拉维奇尼上尉来说竟然如此明显。这个掩蔽所没有那个地方的那么大，那个地方是...
platoon of the class of 1899, just out at the front, got hysterics during the bombardment before the attack, and Para had had him walk them two at a time outside to show them nothing would happen, he wearing his own chin strap tight across his mouth to keep his lips quiet. Knowing they could not hold it when they took it. Knowing it was all a bloody bells - If he can’t stop crying, break his nose to give him something else to think about. I’d shoot one but it’s too late now. They’d all be worse. Break his nose. They’ve put it back to five-twenty. We’ve only got four minutes more. Break that other silly bugger’s nose and kick his silly ass out of here. Do you think they’ll go over? If they don’t, shoot two and try to scoop the others out some way. Keep behind them, sergeant. It’s no use to walk ahead and find there’s nothing coming behind you. Bail them out as you go. What a bloody bells. All right. That’s right. Then, looking at the watch, in that quiet tone, that valuable quiet tone, ‘Sovoia’. Making it cold, no time to get it, he couldn’t find his own after the cave-in, one whole end had caved in; it was that started them; making it cold up that slope the only time he hadn’t done it stinking. And after they came back the teleferica house burned, it seemed, and some of the wounded got down four days later and some did not get down, but we went up and we went back and we came down - we always came down. And there was Gaby Deslys, oddly enough, with feathers on; you called me baby doll a year ago tadada you said that I was rather nice to know tadada with feathers on, with feathers off, the great Gaby, and my name’s Harry Pilcer, too, we used to step out of the far side of the taxis when it got steep going up the hill and he could see that hill every night when he dreamed with Sacré Cœur, blown white, like a soap bubble. Sometimes his girl was there and sometimes she was with someone else and he could not understand that, but those were the nights the rivers ran so much wider and stiller than it should and outside of Fossalta there was a low house painted yellow with willows all around it and a low stable and there was a canal, and he had been there a thousand times and never seen it, but there it was every night as plain as the hill, only it frightened him. That house meant more than anything and every night he had it. That was what he needed but it frightened him especially when the boat lay there quietly in the willows on the canal, but the banks weren’t like this river. It was all lower, as it was at Portogrande, where they had seen them come wallowing
1899 届那个刚到前线的小队，在轰炸期间在进攻前就歇斯底里了，帕拉让他两个人一组把他们带到外面走走，以示不会发生什么事，他自己把下巴带紧紧勒在嘴上以压住唇声。知道他们一旦接手就坚持不住。知道这一切都是他妈的闹剧——如果他止不住哭，就打断他的鼻子让他有别的事可想。我会开枪打一个，但现在太晚了。他们都会更糟。打断他的鼻子。他们把时间又改回到五点二十。我们只剩四分钟了。把另一个傻瓜的鼻子也打断，把他那傻逼踢出去。你认为他们会冲过去吗？如果他们不冲，就枪毙两个，想办法把其他人弄出去。紧贴他们后面，中士。往前走却发现后面什么都没来是没用的。边走边给他们撑腰。真他妈的闹剧。好。对。然后，看着表，用那种平静的声调，那有价值的平静声调，说：“Sovoia”。 把它弄冷，没时间去取，塌方后他找不到自己的，整整一端塌了；就是那次把他们给惹起来的；在那坡上把它弄冷——他唯一一次没做的是那臭事。等他们回来后，缆车站房子好像烧了，有些受伤的人四天后下来了，有些没能下来，但我们上去了又回来了又下来了——我们总是下来了。还有加比·德莱斯，真奇怪，戴着羽毛；你一年前叫我宝贝娃娃 啦啦啦 你说我还挺好认识的 啦啦啦 戴着羽毛，不戴羽毛，伟大的加比，我也是哈里·皮尔塞，我们常在计程车的另一侧下车，上坡变陡时他每晚都能在梦里看到那座山和圣心堂，被吹得白茫茫的，像一个肥皂泡。 有时他的女孩在那儿，有时她和别人一起，他无法理解，但那些夜晚河水流得比应有的更宽更静，福萨尔塔外有一座低矮的黄屋，周围都是柳树，旁边有一座低矮的马厩，还有一条运河，他去过那里千百次却从未见过它，但它每晚都在那里，和那座丘一样清晰，只是让他害怕。那座房子意味着一切，他每晚都拥有它。那正是他所需要的，但它令他害怕，尤其当小船静静地停在运河的柳树间时，可是河岸又不像这条河。 一切都更低，就像在波托格兰德，他们曾看到它们在那里打滚
across the flooded ground holding the rifles high until they fell with them in the water. Who ordered that one? If it didn’t get so damned mixed up he could follow it all right. That was why he noticed everything in such detail to keep it all straight so he would know just where he was, but suddenly it confused without reason as now, he lying in a bunk at battalion headquarters, with Para commanding a battalion and he in a bloody American uniform. He sat up and looked around; they all watching him. Para was gone out. He lay down again.
他们提着步枪穿过被淹的地面，步枪高举着，直到步枪和他们一起倒在水里。是谁下的那个命令？要不是全他妈地弄得一团糟，他本来可以把一切都跟得清清楚楚。这就是为什么他注意到每一件事的细节，以便把一切理顺，好让自己知道确切的位置，可突然间一切又无缘无故地混乱起来，就像现在这样，他躺在营指挥部的一张铺位上，Para 指挥着一个营，而他穿着该死的美国军服。他坐起来环顾四周；他们都在看着他。Para 已经出去了。他又躺下。
The Paris part came earlier and he was not frightened of it except when she had gone off with someone else and the fear that they might take the same driver twice. That was what frightened about that. Never about the front. He never dreamed about the front now any more but what frightened him so that he could not get rid of it was that long yellow house and the different width of the river. Now he was back here at the river, he had gone through that same town, and there was no house. Nor was the river that way. Then where did he go each night and what was the peril, and why would he wake, soaking wet, more frightened than he had ever been in a bombardment, because of a house and a long stable and a canal?
巴黎的部分来得更早，除非她和别的男人走了，并且担心他们可能会两次用同一个司机，否则他并不害怕那段时间。那正是让他害怕的地方。从来不是正面战场。他现在再也不会梦见正面战场，但把他吓得无法摆脱的是那座长长的黄色房子和河流不同的宽度。现在他回到这条河边，他已经经过同一座城镇，但那里没有那座房子。河也不是那样。那他每晚到底去哪里，危险在哪里，为什么他会醒来时浑身湿透，比在轰炸中还要害怕，只因为一座房子、一间长厩和一条运河？
He sat up, swung his legs carefully down; they stiffened any time they were out straight for long; returned the stares of the adjutant, the signallers and the two runners by the door and put on his clothcovered trench helmet.
他坐起身，小心地把腿摆下来；一旦腿长时间伸直就会僵硬；回以门口副官、通信兵和两个跑腿的注视，戴上了那顶布包铁盔。
‘I regret the absence of the chocolate, the postal-cards and cigarettes,’ he said. ‘I am, however, wearing the uniform.’
“我很遗憾没有巧克力、明信片和香烟，”他说，“不过，我穿着制服。”
‘The Major is coming back at once,’ the adjutant said. In that army an adjutant is not a commissioned officer.
“少校马上就回来了，”副官说。在那支军队里，副官并不是一名委任军官。
‘The uniform is not very correct,’ Nick told them. ‘But it gives you the idea. There will be several millions of Americans here shortly.’
“制服不太合身，”尼克对他们说。“但这能让你们有个印象。很快这里会有好几百万美国人。”
‘Do you think they will send Americans down here?’ asked the adjutant.
“你认为他们会派美国人来这里吗？”副官问。
‘Oh, absolutely. Americans twice as large as myself, healthy, with clean hearts, sleep at night, never been wounded, never been blown up, never had their heads caved in, never been scared, don’t drink, faithful to the girls they left behind them, many of them never had crabs, wonderful chaps. You’ll see.’
“哦，当然会。比我壮两倍的美国人，健康，心脏干净，晚上睡得好，从未受过伤，从未被炸过，从未被打破头，从未害怕，不喝酒，对他们留下的姑娘忠诚，很多人从没得过阴虱，了不起的小伙子们。你们会看到的。”
‘Are you an Italian?’ asked the adjutant.
“你是意大利人吗？”副官问。
‘No, American. Look at the uniform. Spagnolini made it but it’s not quite correct.’
“不，American。看军服。Spagnolini 做的，但不太对。”
‘A North or South American?’
“是北美人还是南美人？”
‘North,’ said Nick. He felt it coming on now. He would quiet down.
“北美人，”Nick 说。他感觉怒火正上来。他会平静下来。
‘But you speak Italian.’
“但你会说意大利语。”
'Why not? Do you mind if I speak Italian? Haven’t I a right to speak Italian?’
“为什么不？你介意我说意大利语吗？我没有权利说意大利语吗？”
‘You have Italian medals.’
“你有意大利的勋章。”
‘Just the ribbons and the papers. The medals come later. Or you give them to people to keep and the people go away; or they are lost with your baggage. You can purchase others in Milan. It is the papers that are of importance. You must not feel badly about them. You will have some yourself if you stay at the front long enough.’
“只是绶带和证件。勋章以后会来的。要么你把它们给别人保管，而那些人又离开了；要么它们随着行李丢失了。你可以在米兰买到别的。重要的是那些证件。你不必为此难过。如果你在前线呆得够久，你自己也会有的。”
‘I am a veteran of the Iritrea campaign,’ said the adjutant stiffly. ‘I fought in Tripoli.’
“我是伊利特里亚战役的老兵，”副官僵硬地说。“我曾在的黎波里作战。”
‘It’s quite something to have met you,’ Nick put out his hand. ‘Those must have been trying days. I noticed the ribbons. Were you, by any chance, on the Carso?’
“能见到你真是太好了，”尼克伸出手。“那些日子一定很艰难。我注意到缎带。你是不是在卡尔索服役过？”
‘I have just been called up for this war. My class was too old.’
“我刚被征召参战。我的班级太老了。”
‘At one time I was under the age limit,’ Nick said. ‘But now I am reformed out of the war.’
“有一阵子我还没到年龄，”尼克说。“但现在我已被免去参战资格。”
‘But why are you here now?’
“那你现在为什么还在这里呢？”
‘I am demonstrating the American uniform,’ Nick said. ‘Don’t you think it is very significant? It is a little tight in the collar but you will see untold millions wearing this uniform swarming like locusts. The grasshopper, you know, what we call the grasshopper in America, is really a locust. The true grasshopper is small and green and comparatively feeble. You must not, however, make a confusion with the seven-year locust or cicada which emits a peculiar sustained sound which at the moment I cannot recall. I try to recall it but I cannot. I can almost hear it and then it is quite gone. You will pardon me if I break off our conversation?’
“我是在展示美式军装，”尼克说。“你不觉得这很有意义吗？领口有点紧，但你会看到无数人穿着这种制服像蝗虫般蜂拥而至。你知道的，我们在美国称之为 grasshopper（蚱蜢）的那种，其实真的是 locust（蝗虫）。真正的 grasshopper 是小而绿色、相对衰弱的。不过你千万别把它和七年蝉或 cicada（蝉）混淆了，后者会发出一种奇特而持久的声音，我现在一时想不起来。我努力想回忆，可就是想不起来。我几乎能听见那声音，然后它又完全消失了。如果我打断我们的谈话，希望你不要介意？”
‘See if you can find the major,’ the adjutant said to one of the two runners. ‘I can see you have been wounded,’ he said to Nick.
“去看看能不能找到少校，”副官对两个跑腿中的一个说。“我看得出你受伤了，”他对尼克说。
‘In various places,’ Nick said. ‘If you are interested in scars I can show you some very interesting ones but I would rather talk about
“在好几个地方，”尼克说。“如果你对伤疤感兴趣，我可以给你看些很有意思的，但我更愿意谈论
grasshoppers. What we call grasshoppers that is; and what are, really, locusts. These insects at one time played a very important part in my life. It might interest you and you can look at the uniform while I am talking.’
我们所说的 grasshoppers（蚱蜢）；也就是那些其实是 locusts（蝗虫）的。那些昆虫曾在我的生活中扮演过非常重要的角色。也许你会感兴趣，你可以在我说话的时候看看这套制服。”
The adjutant made a motion with his hand to the second runner who went out.
参谋用手示意第二个跑腿出去。
‘Fix your eyes on the uniform. Spagnolini made it, you know. You might as well look, too,’ Nick said to the signallers. ‘I really have no rank. We’re under the American consul. It’s perfectly all right for you to look. You can stare, if you like. I will tell you about the American locust. We always preferred one that we called the medium-brown. They last the best in water and fish prefer them. The larger ones that fly make a noise somewhat similar to that produced by a rattlesnake rattling his rattlers, a very dry sound, have vivid coloured wings, some are bright red, others yellow barred with black, but their wings go to pieces in the water and they make a very blowsy bait, while the medium-brown is a plump, compact, succulent hopper that I can recommend as far as one may well recommend something you gentlemen will probably never encounter. But I must insist that you will never gather a sufficient supply of these insects for a day’s fishing by pursuing them with your hands or trying to hit them with a bat. That is sheer nonsense and a useless waste of time. I repeat, gentlemen, that you will get nowhere at it. The correct procedure, and one which should be taught all young officers at every small-arms course if I had anything to say about it, and who knows but what I will have, is the employment of a seine or net made of common mosquito netting. Two officers holding this length of netting at alternate ends, or let us say one at each end, stoop, hold the bottom extremity of the net in one hand and the top extremity in the other and run into the wind. The hoppers, flying with the wind, fly against the length of netting and are imprisoned in its folds. It is no trick at all to catch a very great quantity indeed, and no officer, in my opinion, should be without a length of mosquito netting suitable for the improvisation of one of these grasshopper seines. I hope I have made myself clear, gentlemen. Are there any questions? If there is anything in the course you do not understand please ask questions. Speak up. None? Then I would like to close on this note. In the words of that great soldier and gentleman, Sir Henry Wilson: Gentlemen, either you
“盯着制服看。Spagnolini 做的，你们知道的。你们也不妨看看，”Nick 对信号手们说。“我其实没有军衔。我们归美国领事管。你们看也完全没关系。你们要是愿意可以直盯着看。我会跟你们讲美国蝗虫。我们总是偏爱一种我们叫做中褐色的。它们在水里保存得最好，鱼也更喜欢它们。那些能飞的大型蝗虫发出的声音有点像响尾蛇摇尾的声音，是一种非常干燥的声音，翅膀颜色鲜艳，有的鲜红，有的黄色带黑条，但它们的翅膀在水里会散开，变成很糟的饵料；而中褐色的是那种丰满、结实、多汁的跳虫，就我所能推荐的范围来说，我可以推荐它，尽管诸位先生很可能永远不会遇到它们。不过我必须强调，诸位，用手去追逐它们或试图用球棒打它们，绝不可能在一天的捕鱼中凑够足够的数量。那纯属胡闹，是对时间的无谓浪费。我再说一遍，先生们，你们根本不会有任何进展。” 正确的程序——如果由我来决定，并且我不知道将来会不会有机会决定的话，这应该在每一位年轻军官的每一次轻武器课程上教授——是使用用普通蚊帐布制成的拖网或网。两名军官各握网的一端，或者说每人一端，弯腰，一手拿住网的下端，另一手拿住上端，然后迎风奔跑。随风飞行的蝗虫迎着网飞来，被网的褶皱困住。要捕获大量蝗虫根本不是什么技巧，我认为任何军官都不应没有一段适合即兴制作这种捕蝗拖网的蚊帐布。我希望我讲得清楚，诸位。有问题吗？如果课程中有你不明白的地方，请提问。大胆说。没有？那么我想以此结束。 用那位伟大的将军兼绅士 Sir Henry Wilson 的话说：诸位，要么你们
must govern or you must be governed. Let me repeat it. Gentlemen, there is one thing I would like to have you remember. One thing I would like you to take with you as you leave this room. Gentlemen, either you must govern - or you must be governed. That is all, gentlemen. Good-day.’
必须统治，否则就得被统治。让我再重复一遍，先生们，有一件事我希望你们记住。一件事我希望你们离开这个房间时带走。先生们，要么你们统治——要么你们被统治。就这些，先生们。再见。
He removed his cloth-covered helmet, put it on again and, stooping, went out the low entrance of the dugout. Para, accompanied by the two runners, was coming down the line of the sunken road. It was very hot in the sun and Nick removed the helmet.
他摘下布罩头盔，又戴上，然后弯身从掩体低矮的入口走了出去。帕拉跟着两个信使沿着下沉的道路走下来了。太阳下很热，尼克把头盔又摘了下来。
‘There ought to be a system for wetting these things,’ he said. ‘I shall wet this one in the river.’ He started up the bank.
“这些东西应该有一个弄湿的办法，”他说。“我要把这个在河里弄湿。”他开始往河岸上爬。
‘Nicolo,’ Paravicini called. ‘Nicolo. Where are you going?’
“尼科洛，”帕拉维奇尼喊道。“尼科洛。你要去哪儿？”
‘I don’t really have to go.’ Nick came down the slope, holding the helmet in his hands. "They’re a damned nuisance wet or dry. Do you wear yours all the time?’
“我其实不必去。”尼克拿着头盔从坡上走下来。“不管湿的干的，它们都讨厌死了。你一直戴着你的头盔吗？”
‘All the time,’ said Para. ‘It’s making me bald. Come inside.’
“一直戴着，”帕拉说。“戴得我都秃了。进来吧。”
Inside Para told him to sit down.
进到屋里，帕拉让他坐下。
‘You know they’re absolutely no damned good,’ Nick said. ‘I remember when they were a comfort when we first had them, but I’ve seen them full of brains too many times.’
“你知道它们完全没用，”尼克说。“我记得刚有它们的时候还觉得挺安慰，可我见过太多次里面都是脑浆了。”
‘Nicolo,’ Para said. ‘I think you should go back. I think it would be better if you didn’t come up to the line until you had those supplies. There’s nothing here for you to do. If you move around, even with something worth giving away, the men will group and that invites shelling. I won’t have it.’
“尼科洛，”帕拉说。“我觉得你应该回去。你最好别在拿到那些补给之前上到前线来。这里没什么事需要你做。如果你四处走动，即便带着值得分发的东西，士兵们会聚拢在一起，那就会招来炮击。我不会允许的。”
‘I know it’s silly,’ Nick said. ‘It wasn’t my idea. I heard the brigade was here so I thought I would see you or someone else I knew. I could have gone to Zenzon or to San Dona. I’d like to go to San Dona to see the bridge again.’
“我知道这很傻，”尼克说。“这不是我的主意。我听说旅在这儿，所以想来看看你或其他我认识的人。我本可以去曾宗（Zenzon）或圣多纳（San Dona）。我想去圣多纳再看看那座桥。”
‘I won’t have you circulating around to no purpose,’ Captain Paravicini said.
“我不准你无目的地到处转，”帕拉维奇尼上尉说。
‘All right,’ said Nick. He felt it coming on again.
“好吧，”尼克说。他又感觉那种预感要来了。
‘You understand?’
“你明白吗？”
‘Of course,’ said Nick. He was trying to hold it in.
“当然，”尼克说。他在努力压抑住情绪。
‘Anything of that sort should be done at night.’
“这种事应该在夜里做。”
‘Naturally,’ said Nick. He knew he could not stop it now.
“自然，”尼克说。他知道现在已经无力阻止了。
‘You see, I am commanding the battalion,’ Para said.
“你看，我现在指挥营，”帕拉说。
‘And why shouldn’t you be?’ Nick said. Here it came. ‘You can read and write, can’t you?’
“那为什么不行？”尼克说。话到此处。“你会读会写，不是吗？”
‘Yes,’ said Para gently.
“是的，”帕拉温和地说。
‘The trouble is you have a damned small battalion to command. As soon as it gets to strength again they’ll give you back your company. Why don’t they bury the dead? I’ve seen them now. I don’t care about seeing them again. They can bury them any time as far as I’m concerned and it would be much better for you. You’ll all get bloody sick.’
“问题是你要指挥的营实在太少。等补到编制，他们就把连队还给你了。为什么他们不把死人埋了？我现在已经见过他们了。我不想再看第二次。对我来说他们什么时候埋都行，而且那对你更好。你们都会被传染得很严重的。”
‘Where did you leave your bicycle?’
“你把自行车放在哪儿了？”
‘Inside the last house.’
“放在最后一间房子里。”
‘Do you think it will be all right?’
“你觉得它会没事吗？”
‘Don’t worry,’ Nick said. ‘I’ll go in a little while.’
“别担心，”尼克说。“我过会儿就进去。”
‘Lie down a little while, Nicolo.’
“趴一会儿，尼科洛。”
‘All right.’
“好吧。”
He shut his eyes and in place of the man with the beard who looked at him over the sights of the rifle, quite calmly before squeezing off, the white flash and clublike impact, on his knees, hotsweet choking, coughing it on to the rock while they went past him, he saw a long, yellow house with a low stable and the river much wider than it was and stiller. ‘Christ,’ he said, ‘I might as well go.’
他闭上眼睛，取代那名留着胡子、在瞄准镜上方平静地看着他的人——就在扣动扳机前，白色的火光和棍棒般的冲击声——跪在地上，既热又甜，窒息，咳着把它吐到岩石上，当他们从他身边经过时，他看到一座长长的黄房子，带着矮小的马厩，河比现在宽很多，也更平静。“该死，”他说，“我干脆就走吧。”
He stood up.
他站了起来。
‘I’m going, Para,’ he said. ‘I’ll ride back now in the afternoon. If any supplies have come I’ll bring them down to-night. If not I’ll come at night when I have something to bring.’
“我要走了，帕拉，”他说。“下午我会骑马回去。如果有补给来我今晚会带下来。如果没有，等我有东西要带来就夜里过来。”
‘It is still hot to ride,’ Captain Paravicini said.
“现在骑马还是很热，”帕拉维奇尼上尉说。
‘You don’t need to worry,’ Nick said. ‘I’m all right now for quite a while. I had one then but it was easy. They’re getting much better. I can tell when I’m going to have one because I talk so much.’
“你不用担心，”尼克说。“我现在还好，会好一段时间。我当时也犯过一次，但挺容易的。它们越来越好了。我能预感到要犯的时候，因为我说话太多了。”
‘I’ll send a runner with you.’
“我会派个信使和你一起走。”
‘I’d rather you didn’t. I know the way.’
“我还是希望你别去。我知道路。”
‘You’ll be back soon?’
“你很快就会回来？”
‘Absolutely.’
“当然会。”
‘Let me send - ’
“让我打个招呼——”
‘No,’ said Nick. ‘As a mark of confidence.’
“不，”尼克说。“作为一种信任的表示。”
‘Well, Ciaou then.’
“好吧，那就 Ciaou。”
‘Ciaou,’ said Nick. He started back along the sunken road toward where he had left the bicycle. In the afternoon the road would be shady once he had passed the canal. Beyond that there were trees on both sides that had not been shelled at all. It was on that stretch
“Ciaou，”尼克说。他沿着陷下去的道路往回走，朝他放自行车的地方走去。下午一过运河那边路就会有阴影。再往前两边有些树根本没有被炮轰过。就是在那一段
that, marching, they had once passed the Terza Savoia cavalry regiment riding in the snow with their lances. The horses’ breath made plumes in the cold air. No, that was somewhere else. Where was that?
他们曾经行军时，看到特尔扎·萨沃亚骑兵团在雪里骑着马，手持长矛。马的呼气在冷空气中成了白雾。不，对，那是在别的地方。那是在哪儿？
‘I’d better get to that damned bicycle,’ Nick said to himself. ‘I don’t want to lose the way to Fornaci.’
“我最好去把那该死的自行车拿上，”尼克自言自语道。“我可不想迷路到福尔纳奇去。”

THE MOTHER OF A QUEEN
女王的母亲

When his father died he was only a kid and his manager buried him perpetually. That is, so he would have the plot permanently. But when his mother died his manager thought they might not always be so hot on each other. They were sweethearts; sure he’s a queen, didn’t you know that, of course he is. So he just buried her for five years.
他父亲死的时候他还只是个孩子，他的经理就把他葬成了永葬。也就是说，为了让他能永久拥有那块墓地。但他母亲死的时候，他的经理想他们之间的关系可能不会永远那么密切。他们是恋人；当然他是个女王，你不知道吗，当然是的。于是他只把她安葬了五年。
Well, when he came back to Mexico from Spain he got the first notice. It said it was the first notice that the five years were up and would he make arrangements for the continuing of his mother’s grave. It was only twenty dollars for perpetual. I had the cash box then and I said let me attend to it, Paco. But he said no, he would look after it. He’d look after it right away. It was his mother and he wanted to do it himself.
好吧，他从西班牙回到墨西哥时收到了第一通知。上面写着这是关于五年期满的第一通知，问他是否要安排延续他母亲的墓期。永久安葬费只要二十美元。那时我管着现金箱，我说让我来办吧，帕科。但他说不，他会照顾这事。他会马上去办。那是他母亲，他想亲自处理。
Then in a week he got the second notice. I read it to him and I said I thought he had looked after it.
然后一周后他又收到第二张通知。我把它念给他听，还以为他已经处理好了。
No, he said, he hadn’t.
“不，”他说，“我还没处理。”
‘Let me do it,’ I said. ‘It’s right here in the cash box.’
“让我来做，”我说。“钱就在钱箱里。”
No, he said. Nobody could tell him what to do. He’d do it himself when he got around to it. ‘What’s the sense in spending money sooner than necessary?’
“不，”他说。没人能指使他干什么。他会在他愿意的时候自己去做。‘有什么必要比必要时更早花钱吗？’
‘All right,’ I said, ‘but see you look after it.’ At this time he had a contract for six fights at four thousand pesos a fight besides his benefit fight. He made over fifteen thousand dollars there in the capital alone. He was just tight, that’s all.
“好吧，”我说，“但你得自己去处理。”那时他已有一份合同，六场比赛，每场四千比索，外加一场他的募捐赛。光在首都就挣了超过一万五千美元。他就是小气，仅此而已。
The third notice came in another week and I read it to him. It said that if he did not make the payment by the following Saturday his mother’s grave would be opened and her remains dumped on the common boneheap. He said he would go attend to it that afternoon when he went to town.
第三张通知又在一周后来了，我把内容念给他听。上面说如果他下个星期六之前不付清，她母亲的坟墓就要被打开，把遗骸扔到公用骨堆里去。他说他下午入城时会去办这事。
‘Why not have me do it?’ I asked him.
“为什么不让我去办？”我问他。
‘Keep out of my business,’ he said. ‘It’s my business and I’m going to do it.’
“别管我的事，”他说。“是我的事，我要我自己去办。”
‘All right, if that’s the way you feel about it,’ I said. ‘Do your own business.’
“好吧，既然你这么想，”我说，“那你自己办吧。”
He got the money out of the cash box, although then he always carried a hundred or more pesos with him all the time, and he said he would look after it. He went out with the money and so of course I thought he had attended to it.
他从钱箱里把钱拿出来，尽管那之后他总是随身带着一百比索或更多，他说他会处理的。他带着钱出去了，所以我当然以为他已经办妥了。
A week later the notice came that they had no response to the final warning and so his mother’s body had been dumped on the boneheap; on the public boneheap.
一周后来了通知，说他们对最后通牒没有回应，于是他母亲的遗体被丢到了骨堆上；在公众的骨堆上。
‘Jesus Christ,’ I said to him, ‘you said you’d pay that and you took money out of the cash box to do it and now what’s happened to your mother? My God, think of it! The public boneheap and your own mother. Why didn’t you let me look after it? I would have sent it when the first notice came.’
“我的天哪，”我对他说，“你说你会付的，还从钱箱里拿了钱去付，可现在你母亲怎么了？天哪，想想看！公众的骨堆，还有你自己的母亲。你为什么不让我来处理？要是第一通知来的时候我就寄走了。”
‘It’s none of your business. It’s my mother.’
“这不关你的事。她是我母亲。”
‘It’s none of m y m y mym y business, yes, but it was your business. What kind of blood is it in a man that will let that be done to his mother? You don’t deserve to have a mother.’
“这不关 m y m y mym y 的事，没错，但本来就是你的事。一个男人的血性是什么样的，居然让别人那样对他母亲？你不配有母亲。”
‘It is my mother,’ he said. ‘Now she is so much dearer to me. Now I don’t have to think of her buried in one place and be sad. Now she is all about me in the air, like the birds and the flowers. Now she will always be with me.’
“她是我母亲，”他说。“现在她对我更可贵了。现在我不用想到她被埋在一个地方而难过。现在她像鸟儿和花朵一样环绕在我周围。现在她会永远和我在一起。”
‘Jesus Christ,’ I said, ‘what kind of blood have you anyway? I don’t want you even to speak to me.’
“我的天哪，”我说，“你到底有什么血性？我甚至不想你和我说话。”
‘She is all around me,’ he said. ‘Now I will never be sad.’
“她就在我身边，”他说。“现在我永远不会悲伤了。”
At that time he was spending all kinds of money around women trying to make himself seem a man and fool people, but it didn’t have any effect on people that knew anything about him. He owed me over six hundred pesos and he wouldn’t pay me. ‘Why do you want it now?’ he’d say. 'Don’t you trust me? Aren’t we friends?"
那时他在女人面前花天酒地各种挥霍，想让自己看起来像个男子汉，愚弄别人，但对那些了解他的人毫无作用。他欠我六百多比索不还。我催他，他就说： “你为什么现在要钱？你不信任我吗？我们不是朋友吗？”
‘It isn’t friends or trusting you. It’s that I paid the accounts out of my own money while you were away and now I need the money back and you have it to pay me.’
“这不是信任不信任的问题。是你走的时候账我先垫付了，现在我需要把钱要回来，而你正好有钱可以还我。”
‘I haven’t got it.’
“我没有钱。”
‘You have it,’ I said. ‘It’s in the cash box now and you can pay me.’
“你得到了，”我说。“现在它在钱箱里，你可以付给我了。”
‘I need that money for something,’ he said. ‘You don’t know all the needs I have for money.’
“我需要那笔钱，”他说。“你不知道我还有多少需要钱的地方。”
‘I stayed here all the time you were in Spain and you authorized me to pay these things as they came up, all these things of the house, and you didn’t send any money while you were gone and I paid over
“在你去西班牙的时候我一直住在这里，你又授权我把这些家里的开销一项项付了出来，你走的时候没寄过钱来，我都付了，超过了”
six hundred pesos in my own money and now I need it and you can pay me.’
六百比索是我的钱，现在我需要用，你得把钱付给我。
‘I’ll pay you soon,’ he said. ‘Right now I need the money badly.’
“我很快会付给你的，”他说。“现在我急需用钱。”
‘For what?’
“为了什么？”
‘For my own business.’
“为了我自己的生意。”
‘Why don’t you pay me some on account?’
“你为什么不先付我一部分呢？”
‘I can’t,’ he said. ‘I need that money too badly. But I will pay you.’
“我不能，”他说，“我太需要那笔钱了。但我会付你的。”
He had only fought twice in Spain, they couldn’t stand him there, they saw through him quick enough, and he had seven new fighting suits made and this is the kind of thing he was: he had them packed so badly that four of them were ruined by sea water on the trip back and he couldn’t even wear them.
他只在西班牙打过两次架，那里的人受不了他，他们很快就看穿了他，他做了七套新的格斗服，就是这种人：他把它们收包得很糟，回来航程中有四套被海水弄坏，连穿都穿不了。
‘My God,’ I said to him, ‘you go to Spain. You stay there the whole season and only fight two times. You spend all the money you took with you on suits and then have them spoiled by salt water so you can’t wear them. That is the kind of season you have and then you talk to me about running your own business. Why don’t you pay me the money you owe me so I can leave?’
“天哪，”我对他说，“你去西班牙。你整个赛季都待在那里却只打两次。你把带去的钱全花在衣服上，然后又被海水弄坏穿不了。这就是你过的赛季，然后你还跟我谈自己做生意。你为什么不把欠我的钱付给我，让我走？”
‘I want you here,’ he said, ‘and I will pay you. But now I need the money.’
“我想要你留在这儿，”他说，“我会付你的。但现在我需要那笔钱。”
‘You need it too badly to pay for your own mother’s grave to keep your mother buried. Don’t you?’ I said.
“你太需要它了，连付你自己母亲的墓钱都不愿意，把你母亲葬着。不是吗？”我说。
‘I am happy about what has happened to my mother,’ he said. ‘You cannot understand.’
“我为我母亲发生的事感到高兴，”他说。“你无法理解。”
‘Thank Christ I can’t,’ I said. ‘You pay me what you owe me or I will take it out of the cash box.’
“谢天谢地我也不能理解，”我说。“你把欠我的钱付给我，不然我就从钱箱里拿。”
‘I will keep the cash box myself,’ he said.
“我自己会看着钱箱，”他说。
‘No, you won’t,’ I said.
“不，你不会的，”我说。
That very afternoon he came to me with a punk, some fellow from his own town who was broke, and said, ‘Here is a paesano who needs money to go home because his mother is very sick.’ This fellow was just a punk, you understand, a nobody he’d never seen before, but from his home town, and he wanted to be the big, generous matador with a fellow townsman.
就在那天午后，他带着一个小混混来找我，那人是他家乡的某个家伙，破产了，他说：“这是个同乡，得回家去，因为他母亲病得很重。” 你要明白，这家伙只是个小混混，一个他从未见过的无名之辈，但同乡嘛，他想在同乡面前装出大方慷慨的样子。
‘Give him fifty pesos from the cash box,’ he told me.
“从现金箱里给他五十比索，”他说。
‘You just told me you had no money to pay me,’ I said. ‘And now you want to give fifty pesos to this punk.’
“你刚才告诉我你没钱付我，”我说。“现在你又要把五十比索给这个小混混。”
‘He is a fellow townsman,’ he said, ‘and he is in distress.’
“他是同乡，”他说，“他遇到了困难。”
‘You bitch,’ I said. I gave him the key of the cash box. ‘Get it yourself. I’m going to town.’
“你这个婊子，”我说着把钱箱的钥匙递给了他。“自己去拿。我现在要进城。”
‘Don’t be angry,’ he said. ‘I’m going to pay you.’
“别生气，”他说。“我会付你的。”
I got the car out to go to town. It was his car but he knew I drove it better than he did. Everything he did I could do better. He knew it. He couldn’t even read and write. I was going to see somebody and see what I could do about making him pay me. He came out and said, ‘I’m coming with you and I’m going to pay you. We are good friends. There is no need to quarrel.’
我把车开出来要进城。那是他的车，可他知道我开的比他好。他做的每一件事我都能做得更好。他知道这一点。他甚至不会识字。我是要去见个人，看看能不能让他付钱。他走出来说，‘我要跟你去，我会付你的。我们是好朋友，没必要争吵。’
We drove into the city and I was driving. Just before we came into the town he pulled out twenty pesos.
我们开车进城，是我开车。就在进城前他掏出了二十比索。
‘Here’s the money,’ he said.
“钱在这儿，”他说。
‘You motherless bitch,’ I said to him and told him what he could do with the money. ‘You give fifty pesos to that punk and then offer me twenty when you owe me six hundred. I wouldn’t take a nickel from you. You know what you can do with it.’
“你这个无母的婊子，”我对他说，并告诉他可以拿这钱去做什么。“你先给那个小混混五十比索，然后在欠我六百的情况下才拿出二十来给我。我不会从你这里拿一分钱。你知道该拿它去做什么。”
I got out of the car without a peso in my pocket and I didn’t know where I was going to sleep that night. Later I went out with a friend and got my things from his place. I never spoke to him again until this year. I met him walking with three friends in the evening on the way to the Callao cinema in the Gran Via in Madrid. He put his hand out to me.
我下车时口袋里一个比索都没有，晚上要睡在哪里也不知道。后来我和一个朋友出去，把我的东西从他那儿拿回来了。从那以后我再也没和他说过话，直到今年。我在马德里 Gran Vía 通往 Callao 电影院的路上，傍晚遇见他和三个朋友一起走。他向我伸出了手。
‘Hello, Roger, old friend,’ he said to me. ‘How are you? People say you are talking against me. That you say all sorts of unjust things about me.’
“你好，罗杰，老朋友，”他对我说。“你好吗？人们说你在背后说我的坏话。说了各种不公正的事。”
‘All I say is you never had a mother,’ I said to him. That’s the worst thing you can say to insult a man in Spanish.
“我只说你从来没有母亲，”我对他说。那是在西班牙语里侮辱一个人最严重的话。
‘That’s true,’ he said. ‘My poor mother died when I was so young it seems as though I never had a mother. It’s very sad.’
“那倒是真的，”他说。“我可怜的母亲在我还很小的时候就去世了，似乎我从未有过母亲。真是可悲。”
There’s a queen for you. You can’t touch them. Nothing, nothing can touch them. They spend money on themselves or for vanity, but they never pay. Try to get one to pay. I told him what I thought of him right there on the Gran Via, in front of three friends, but he speaks to me now when I meet him as though we were friends. What kind of blood is it that makes a man like that?
你看，那就是女王。你碰不到她们。没有什么，什么都碰不着她们。她们为自己或虚荣花钱，但她们从不付账。试着让她们付账看看。我就在格兰维亚当着三个朋友的面当场把我对他的看法告诉了他，但现在每当我遇到他时，他却像朋友一样和我说话。是什么样的血统造就了那样一个人？

ONE READER WRITES
一位读者写道

She sat at the table in her bedroom with a newspaper folded open before her and only stopping to look out of the window at the snow which was falling and melting on the roofs as it fell. She wrote this letter, writing it steadily with no necessity to cross out or rewrite anything.
她坐在卧室的桌旁，面前摊着一张报纸，偶尔停下来向窗外望去，望着雪花落下又落在屋顶上融化。她写了这封信，写得很平稳，无需删改或重写任何内容。
Roanoke, Virginia
弗吉尼亚州罗阿诺克
February 6th, 1933
1933 年 2 月 6 日
Dear Doctor,
尊敬的医生：
May I write you for some very important advice - I have a decision to make and don’t know just whom to trust most, I dare not ask my parents - and so I come to you - and only because I need not see you, can I confide in you even. Now here is the situation - I married a man in U.S. service in 1929 and that same year he was sent to China, Shanghai - he stayed three years - and came home - he was discharged from the service some few months ago - and went to his mother’s home in Helena, Arkansas. He wrote for me to come home-I went, and found he is taking a course of injections and I naturally ask, and found he is being treated for I don’t know how to spell the word but it sounds like this ‘sifilus’ - Do you know what I mean - now tell me will it ever be safe for me to live with him again - I did not come in close contact with him at any time since his return from China. He assures me he will be OK after this doctor finishes with him - Do you think it right - I often heard my Father say one could well wish themselves dead if once they became a victim of that malady - I believe my Father but want to believe my Husband most-Please, please tell me what to do - I have a daughter born while her Father was in China-
我可以写信向您征求一些非常重要的建议吗——我有一个决定要做，却不知道最该相信谁；我不敢去问父母——所以我来找您——并且仅仅因为不必见您面，我才敢向您倾诉。事情是这样的——我在 1929 年与一名在美军服役的男子结婚，同年他被派赴中国，去上海——他在那里待了三年——然后回国——几个月前他从军中退伍——回到他母亲在阿肯色州赫勒纳的家。他写信叫我回去——我回去了，发现他在接受一系列注射治疗，我自然问起，才知道他正在治疗一种我不会拼写的病，不过发音像是“sifilus”——您明白我指的是什么吗——现在请告诉我，我将来还可以和他安全同住吗——自他从中国回来后，我在任何时候都没有与他有过密切接触。 他向我保证这个医生治完他就会没事——您觉得这是对的吗——我常听我父亲说，如果有人一旦成了那种病的受害者，宁愿希望自己早死——我相信我父亲的话，但更想相信我丈夫——请，请告诉我该怎么办——我有个女儿，是她父亲在中国的时候生的——
Thanking you and trusting wholly in your advice I am and signed her name.
感谢您，完全信任您的建议，我就是这样签了她的名字。
Maybe he can tell me what’s right to do, she said to herself. Maybe he can tell me. In the picture in the paper he looks like he’d know.
也许他能告诉我该怎么做，她对自己说。也许他能告诉我。报纸上的那张照片里，他看起来好像知道该怎么做。
He looks smart, all right. Every day he tells somebody what to do. He ought to know. I want to do whatever is right. It’s such a long time though. It’s a long time. And it’s been a long time. My Christ, it’s been a long time. He had to go wherever they sent him, I know, but I don’t know what he had to get it for. Oh, I wish to Christ he wouldn’t have got it. I don’t care what he did to get it. But I wish to Christ he hadn’t ever got it. It does seem like he didn’t have to have got it. I don’t know what to do. I wish to Christ he hadn’t got any kind of malady. I don’t know why he had to get a malady.
他看起来很聪明，确实。每天他都在告诉别人该做什么。他应该知道。我想做任何正确的事。不过时间太长了。太长了。已经很久了。我的天，太久了。他不得不去他们派他去的地方，我知道，但我不知道他为什么非得去那个地方。哦，我真希望他没去。我不在乎他为去那里做了什么。但我真希望他从来没去过。看起来似乎他并非非得去不可。我不知道该怎么办。我真希望他没有得任何病。我不明白他为什么要得病。

HOMAGE TO SWITZERLAND
向瑞士致敬

PART I
第一部分

PORTRAIT OF MR. WHEELER IN MONTREUX
蒙特勒惠勒先生画像

Inside the station café it was warm and light. The wood of the tables shone from wiping and there were baskets of pretzels in glazed paper sacks. The chairs were carved, but the seats were worn and comfortable. There was a carved wooden clock on the wall and a bar at the far end of the room. Outside the window it was snowing.
火车站咖啡室里既暖和又明亮。桌子的木面因擦拭而闪光，釉纸袋里装着一篮篮椒盐卷饼。椅子雕有花纹，但座位已磨旧却很舒适。墙上挂着一只雕花木钟，房间尽头有个吧台。窗外正在下雪。
Two of the station porters sat drinking new wine at the table under the clock. Another porter come in and said the SimplonOrient Express was an hour late at Saint-Maurice. He went out. The waitress came over to Mr. Wheeler’s table.
两个工作站的搬运工坐在钟下的桌旁喝着新酒。另一个搬运工走进来说 SimplonOrient Express 在 Saint-Maurice 晚了一小时。他出去了。女服务员走到 Wheeler 先生的桌旁。
‘The Express is an hour late, sir,’ she said. ‘Can I bring you some coffee?’
“特快晚了一小时，先生，”她说。“我可以给您拿点咖啡吗？”
‘If you think it won’t keep me awake.’
“如果你认为它不会让我清醒的话。”
‘Please?’ asked the waitress.
“请？”女服务员问道。
‘Bring me some,’ said Mr. Wheeler.
“给我来一些，”惠勒先生说。
‘Thank you.’
“谢谢你。”
She brought the coffee from the kitchen and Mr. Wheeler looked out the window at the snow falling in the light from the station platform.
她从厨房端来咖啡，惠勒先生看着窗外站台灯光下飘落的雪。
‘Do you speak other languages besides English?’ he asked the waitress.
“除了英语你还会说别的语言吗？”他问女服务员。
‘Oh, yes, sir. I speak German and French and the dialects.’
“哦，是的，先生。我会说德语和法语，还有方言。”
‘Would you like a drink of something?’
“您想喝点什么吗？”
‘Oh, no, sir. It is not permitted to drink in the café with the clients.’
“哦，不，先生。和客人在咖啡馆里喝酒是不允许的。”
‘You won’t take a cigar?’
“您不抽雪茄吗？”
‘Oh, no, sir. I don’t smoke, sir.’
“哦，不，先生。我不抽烟，先生。”
‘That is all right,’ said Mr. Wheeler. He looked out of the window again, drank the coffee, and lit a cigarette.
“那没关系，”惠勒先生说。他又望向窗外，喝了咖啡，点了一根烟。
‘Fräulein,’ he called. The waitress came over.
“Fräulein，”他喊道。女服务员走了过来。
‘What would you like, sir?’
“先生，您想要什么？”
‘You,’ he said.
“你，”他说。
‘You must not joke me like that.’
“你别拿我开这种玩笑。”
‘I’m not joking.’
“我不是在开玩笑。”
‘Then you must not say it.’
“那你就别说。”
‘I haven’t time to argue,’ Mr. Wheeler said. ‘The train comes in forty minutes. If you’ll go upstairs with me I’ll give you a hundred francs.’
“我没时间争论，”威勒先生说。“火车四十分钟后到。你要是跟我上楼，我给你一百法郎。”
‘You should not say such things, sir. I will ask the porter to speak with you.’
“先生，你不应当这么说。我会请行李员来和您说话。”
‘I don’t want a porter,’ Mr. Wheeler said. ‘Nor a policeman, nor one of those boys that sell cigarettes. I want you.’
“我不要行李员，”威勒先生说。“也不要警察，也不要那些卖香烟的孩子。我要的是你。”
‘If you talk like that you must go out. You cannot stay here and talk like that.’
“你这样说话就得出去。你不能留在这里这样说话。”
‘Why don’t you go away then? If you go away I can’t talk to you.’
“那你干嘛不走？你要是走了我就不能跟你说话了。”
The waitress went away. Mr. Wheeler watched to see if she spoke to the porters. She did not.
女服务员走开了。威勒先生看着，想看她是否会跟搬运工说话。她没有。
‘Mademoiselle!’ he called. The waitress came over. ‘Bring me a bottle of Sion, please.’
“小姐！”他喊道。女服务员走过来。“请给我拿一瓶 Sion。”
‘Yes, sir.’
“好的，先生。”
Mr. Wheeler watched her go out, then come in with the wine and bring it to his table. He looked toward the clock.
威勒先生看着她出去，又端着酒进来，把酒放到他的桌上。他朝钟看了看。
‘I’ll give you two hundred francs,’ he said.
“我给你两百法郎，”他说。
‘Please do not say such things.’
“请不要说那样的话。”
‘Two hundred francs is a great deal of money.’
“两百法郎是一大笔钱。”
‘You will not say such things!’ the waitress said. She was losing her English. Mr. Wheeler looked at her interestedly.
“你不能这么说！”女服务员说。她的英语越来越差了。惠勒先生带着兴趣看着她。
‘Two hundred francs.’
“二百法郎。”
‘You are hateful.’
“你真讨厌。”
‘Why don’t you go away then? I can’t talk to you if you’re not here.’
“那你干脆走开不就得了？如果你不在这儿我就无法跟你说话。”
The waitress left the table and went over to the bar. Mr. Wheeler drank the wine and smiled to himself for some time.
女服务员离开了桌子走到吧台。惠勒先生喝了酒，自己微笑了好一会儿。
‘Mademoiselle,’ he called. The waitress pretended not to hear him. ‘Mademoiselle,’ he called again. The waitress came over.
“小姐，”他喊道。女服务员装作没听见。“小姐，”他又喊道。女服务员走了过来。
‘You wish something?’
“您要什么？”
‘Very much. I’ll give you three hundred francs.’
“很想要。我给你三百法郎。”
‘You are hateful.’
“你真可恨。”
‘Three hundred francs Swiss.’
“三百法郎，瑞士的。”
She went away and Mr. Wheeler looked after her. A porter opened the door. He was the one who had Mr. Wheeler’s bags in his charge.
她走开了，惠勒先生看着她。一个行李员替他开了门。正是那个负责惠勒先生行李的人。
‘The train is coming, sir,’ he said in French. Mr. Wheeler stood up.
“火车要来了，先生，”他用法语说。惠勒先生站了起来。
‘Mademoiselle,’ he called. The waitress came toward the table. ‘How much is the wine?’
“小姐，”他喊道。女服务员向桌边走来。“这瓶酒多少钱？”
‘Seven francs.’
“七法郎。”
Mr. Wheeler counted out eight francs and left them on the table. He put on his coat and followed the porter on to the platform where the snow was falling.
惠勒先生数了八法郎，留下在桌上。他穿上外套，跟着搬运工走向站台，雪正下着。
‘Au revoir, Mademoiselle,’ he said. The waitress watched him go. He’s ugly, she thought, ugly and hateful. Three hundred francs for a thing that is nothing to do. How many times have I done that for nothing. And no place to go here. If he had sense he would know there was no place. No time and no place to go. Three hundred francs to do that. What people those Americans.
“再见，小姐，”他说。女服务员看着他离去。她心想：他长得丑，丑又可憎。三百法郎换来一件根本无关紧要的事。我为这种事白做过多少次。这里又无处可去。如果他有常识就会知道没有去处。既没有时间也没有地方可去。为那事付三百法郎。美国人真是奇怪。
Standing on the cement platform beside his bags, looking down the rails toward the headlight of the train coming through the snow, Mr. Wheeler was thinking that it was very inexpensive sport. He had only spent, actually, aside from the dinner, seven francs for a bottle of wine and a franc for the tip. Seventy-five centimes would have been better. He would have felt better now if the tip had been seventy-five centimes. One franc Swiss is five francs French. Mr. Wheeler was headed for Paris. He was very careful about money and did not care for women. He had been in that station before and he knew there was no upstairs to go to. Mr. Wheeler never took chances.
站在行李旁的水泥站台上，向下望着穿过雪地、朝着火车头灯驶来的铁轨，惠勒先生心想这真是便宜的消遣。事实上，除去晚餐，他只花了七法郎买了一瓶酒，又花了一法郎给小费。七十五生丁会更好。他现在要是给了七十五生丁会觉得更好。一法郎瑞士币等于五法郎法国币。惠勒先生正前往巴黎。他对钱很小心，也不喜欢女人。他以前来过这个车站，知道那里没有楼上可去。惠勒先生从不冒险。

PART II
第二部分

MR. JOHNSON TALKS ABOUT IT AT VEVEY
约翰逊先生在维韦谈起这件事

Inside the station café it was warm and light; the tables were shiny from wiping and on some there were red and white striped tablecloths; and there were blue and white striped tablecloths on others and on all of them baskets with pretzels in glazed paper sacks. The chairs were carved but the wood seats were worn and comfortable. There was a clock on the wall, a zinc bar at the far end of the room, and outside the window it was snowing. Two of the station porters sat drinking new wine at the table under the clock.
在工作站咖啡馆里很温暖，光线明亮；桌子被擦得发亮，有些铺着红白相间的条纹桌布；另一些铺着蓝白相间的条纹桌布，所有桌上都有装在上光纸袋里的椒盐脆饼的篮子。椅子有雕刻，但木座位已被磨得舒适。墙上有一只钟，房间远端有一根锌制吧台，窗外在下雪。两个站台搬运工坐在钟下的桌旁喝着新酒。
Another porter came in and said the Simplon-Orient Express was an hour late at Saint-Maurice. The waitress came over to Mr. Johnson’s table.
另一个搬运工走进来说简柏—东方快车在圣莫里斯晚点一小时。女服务员走到约翰逊先生的桌边。
‘The Express is an hour late, sir,’ she said. 'Can I bring you some coffee?’
“快车晚点一小时，先生，”她说。“我可以给您端点咖啡吗？”
‘If it’s not too much trouble.’
“如果不太麻烦的话。”
‘Please?’ asked the waitress.
“请？”女服务员问道。
‘I’ll take some.’
“我要一些。”
‘Thank you.’
“谢谢你。”
She brought the coffee from the kitchen and Mr. Johnson looked out the window at the snow falling in the light from the station platform.
她从厨房端来咖啡，约翰逊先生望着窗外站台灯光下飘落的雪。
‘Do you speak other languages besides English?’ he asked the waitress.
“你除了英语还会说别的语言吗？”他问女服务员。
‘Oh, yes, I speak German and French and the dialects.’
“哦，会的，我会德语和法语，还有方言。”
‘Would you like a drink of something?’
“您想喝点什么吗？”
‘Oh, no, sir, it is not permitted to drink in the café with the clients.’
“哦，不，先生，和客人在咖啡馆里喝酒是不允许的。”
‘Have a cigar?’
“要雪茄吗？”
‘Oh, no, sir,’ she laughed. ‘I don’t smoke, sir.’
“哦，不，先生，”她笑着说。“我不抽烟，先生。”
‘Neither do I,’ said Johnson. ‘It’s a dirty habit.’
“我也不抽，”约翰逊说。“这是个肮脏的习惯。”
The waitress went away and Johnson lit a cigarette and drank the coffee. The clock on the wall marked a quarter to ten. His watch was a little fast. The train was due at ten-thirty - an hour late meant eleven-thirty. Johnson called to the waitress.
女服务员走开了，约翰逊点燃了一支香烟，喝了咖啡。墙上的钟指着九点四十五。他的表快了一点。火车应该十点三十分到——晚到一小时就是十一点三十分。约翰逊叫住了女服务员。
‘Signorina!’
“Signorina！”
‘What would you like, sir?’
“先生，您想要什么？”
‘You wouldn’t like to play with me?’ Johnson asked. The waitress blushed.
“你不想和我玩玩吗？”约翰逊问。女服务员脸红了。
‘No, sir.’
“不，先生。”
‘I don’t mean anything violent. You wouldn’t like to make up a party to see the night life of Vevey? Bring a girl friend if you like.’
“我不是说要做什么出格的事。你不想凑个队伍去看看韦韦的夜生活吗？要是想的话可以带个女友来。”
‘I must work,’ the waitress said. ‘I have my duty here.’
“我得工作，”女服务员说。“我在这儿有我的职责。”
‘I know,’ said Johnson. ‘But couldn’t you get a substitute? They used to do that in the Civil War.’
“我知道，”约翰逊说。“但你不能找个人代班吗？内战的时候人们常那样做。”
‘Oh, no, sir. I must be here myself in person.’
“哦，不，先生。我必须亲自待在这里。”
‘Where did you learn your English?’
“你在哪学的英语？”
‘At the Berlitz school, sir.’
“在 Berlitz 学校，先生。”
‘Tell me about it,’ Johnson said. ‘Were the Berlitz undergraduates a wild lot? What about all this necking and petting? Were there many smoothies? Did you ever run into Scott Fitzgerald?’
“跟我说说，”约翰逊说。“那些 Berlitz 的本科生都是放荡不羁的吗？那些亲热和抚摸的事儿怎样？有很多冰沙吗？你有没有碰见过 Scott Fitzgerald？”
‘Please?’
“请？”
‘I mean were your college days the happiest days of your life? What sort of team did Berlitz have last fall?’
“我是说，你的大学时光是你一生中最幸福的日子吗？Berlitz 去年秋天的队怎么样？”
‘You are joking, sir?’
“你在开玩笑，先生？”
‘Only feebly,’ said Johnson. ‘You’re an awfully good girl. And you don’t want to play with me?’
“只是有点儿，”约翰逊说。“你真是个好姑娘。你不想和我一起玩吗？”
‘Oh, no, sir,’ said the waitress. ‘Would you like me to bring you something?’
“哦，不，先生，”女服务员说。“您要我给您拿点什么吗？”
‘Yes,’ said Johnson. ‘Would you bring me the wine list?’
“是的，”约翰逊说。“把酒单拿来给我好吗？”
‘Yes, sir.’
“好的，先生。”
Johnson walked over with the wine list to the table where the three porters sat. They looked up at him. They were old men.
约翰逊拿着酒单走到三个行李搬运工坐着的桌子旁。他们抬头看着他。他们都是老人。
‘Wollen Sie trinken?’ he asked. One of them nodded and smiled.
“Wollen Sie trinken?” 他问。其中一个点了点头，笑了。
‘Oui, monsieur.’
“Oui, monsieur。”
‘You speak French?’
“你会说法语吗？”
‘Oui, monsieur.’
“Oui, monsieur。”
‘What shall we drink? Connais vous des champagnes?’
“我们喝点什么？您认识香槟吗？”
‘Non, monsieur.’
“不是的，先生。”
‘Faut les connaître,’ said Johnson. ‘Fräulein,’ he called the waitress. ‘We will drink champagne.’
“得认识他们，”约翰逊说。“姑娘，”他喊服务员，“我们要喝香槟。”
‘Which champagne would you prefer, sir?’
“您想要哪一种香槟，先生？”
‘The best,’ said Johnson. ‘Laquelle est le best?’ he asked the porters.
“最好的，”约翰逊说。“哪一种是最好的？”他问搬运工。
‘Le meilleur?’ asked the porter who had spoken first.
“最好的？”第一个说话的搬运工问道。
‘By all means.’
“那当然。”
The porter took out a pair of gold-rimmed glasses from his coat pocket and looked over the list. He ran his finger down the four typewritten names and prices.
搬运工从外套口袋里拿出一副金边眼镜，翻看着名单。他用手指沿着四个打字的名字和价格往下滑。
‘Sportsman,’ he said. ‘Sportsman is the best.’
“运动型，”他说。“运动型是最好的。”
‘You agree, gentlemen?’ Johnson asked the other porters. The one porter nodded. The other said in French, ‘I don’t know them personally but I’ve often heard speak of Sportsman. It’s good.’
“你们同意吗，先生们？”约翰逊问其他搬运工。一个搬运工点了点头。另一个用法语说：“我不认识他们本人，但我常听人提起 Sportsman。挺好的。”
‘A bottle of Sportsman,’ Johnson said to the waitress. He looked at the price on the wine card: eleven francs Swiss. ‘Make it two Sportsmen. Do you mind if I sit here with you?’ he asked the porter who had suggested Sportsman.
“来一瓶 Sportsman，”约翰逊对女服务员说。他看了酒单上的价格：十一瑞士法郎。“来两瓶 Sportsman。你介意我坐在这儿跟你一起吗？”他问那位建议 Sportsman 的搬运工。
‘Sit down. Put yourself here, please.’ The porter smiled at him. He was folding his spectacles and putting them away in their case. ‘Is it the gentleman’s birthday?’
“坐下。请把自己放在这里。”搬运工朝他微笑。他正把眼镜叠好放进眼镜盒里。“是先生的生日吗？”
‘No,’ said Johnson. ‘It’s not a fête. My wife has decided to divorce me.’
“不是，”约翰逊说。“这不是节日。我妻子决定和我离婚。”
‘So,’ said the porter. ‘I hope not.’ The other porter shook his head. The third porter seemed a little deaf.
“那么，”门房说，“我希望不是。”另一个门房摇了摇头。第三个门房似乎有点听不清。
‘It is doubtless a common experience,’ said Johnson, ‘like the first visit to the dentist or the first time a girl is unwell, but I have been upset.’
“这无疑是一种常见的经历，”约翰逊说，“就像第一次去看牙医或一个女孩第一次生病一样，但我被弄得心烦意乱。”
‘It is understandable,’ said the oldest porter. ‘I understand it.’
“这是可以理解的，”年纪最大的门房说。“我能理解。”
‘None of you gentlemen is divorced?’ Johnson asked. He had stopped clowning with the language and was speaking good French now and had been for some time.
“你们诸位先生中没有人离婚吗？”约翰逊问。他已不再用法语开玩笑，现在说的是标准法语，而且已经有一阵子了。
‘No,’ said the porter who had ordered Sportsman. ‘They don’t divorce much here. There are gentlemen who are divorced but not many.’
“不，”那位叫人订了《Sportsman》的搬运工说，“这里离婚不多。有些绅士离过婚，但不多。”
‘With us,’ said Johnson, ‘it’s different. Practically everyone is divorced.’
“我们这儿，”Johnson 说，“就不一样了。几乎人人都离过婚。”
‘That’s true,’ the porter confirmed. ‘I’ve read it in the paper.’
“那倒是真的，”搬运工证实道。“我在纸上读过。”
‘I myself am somewhat in retard,’ Johnson went on. ‘This is the first time I have been divorced. I am thirty-five.’
“我自己有点落后，”Johnson 继续说，“这是我第一次离婚。我三十五岁。”
‘Mais vous êtes encore jeune,’ said the porter. He explained to the two others. ‘Monsieur n’a que trente-cinq ans.’ The other porters nodded. ‘He’s very young,’ said one.
“Mais vous êtes encore jeune，”门房说道。他向另外两个人解释道。“先生才三十五岁。”其他门房点点头。“他很年轻，”其中一个说。
‘And it is really the first time you’ve been divorced?’ asked the porter.
“而且这真的是您第一次离婚？”门房问。
‘Absolutely,’ said Johnson. ‘Please open the wine, mademoiselle.’
“完全是，”约翰逊说。“小姐，请开酒。”
‘And it is very expensive ?’
“那很贵吗？”
‘Ten thousand francs.’
“万元法郎。”
‘Swiss money?’
“瑞士法郎？”
‘No, French money.’
“不是，法国法郎。”
‘Oh, yes. Two thousand francs Swiss. All the same it’s not cheap.’
“哦，是啊。两千瑞士法郎。不过说实话也不便宜。”
‘No.’
“不要。”
‘And why does one do it?’
“那人为什么要这么做？”
‘One is asked to.’
“有人要求他这么做。”
‘But why do they ask that?’
“但他们为什么要这么要求？”
‘To marry someone else.’
“嫁给别人。”
‘But it’s idiotic.’
“但这太愚蠢了。”
‘I agree with you,’ said Johnson. The waitress filled the four glasses. They all raised them.
“我同意你的看法，”约翰逊说。女服务员把四只杯子倒满。他们都举起杯子。
‘Prosit,’ said Johnson.
“干杯，”约翰逊说。
‘A votre santé, monsieur,’ said the porter. The other two porters said ‘Salut’. The champagne tasted like sweet pink cider.
“为您的健康，先生，”门童说。其他两个门童说“Salut”。香槟尝起来像甜的玫瑰色苹果酒。
‘Is it a system always to respond in a different language in Switzerland?’ Johnson asked.
“在瑞士，是不是总要用不同的语言来回应？”约翰逊问。
‘No,’ said the porter. ‘French is more cultivated. Besides, this is la Suisse Romande.’
“不，”门童说。“法语更有教养。此外，这里是法语区（la Suisse Romande）。”
‘But you speak German?’
“但你会说德语吗？”
‘Yes. Where I come from they speak German.’
“是的。我来自的地方讲德语。”
‘I see,’ said Johnson, ‘and you say you have never been divorced?’
“我明白了，”约翰逊说，“你说你从未离过婚？”
‘No. It would be too expensive. Besides, I have never married.’
“没有。那太贵了。而且，我从未结过婚。”
‘Ah,’ said Johnson. ‘And these other gentlemen?’
“啊，”约翰逊说，“那这些其他先生呢？”
‘They are married.’
“他们结婚了。”
‘You like being married?’ Johnson asked one of the porters.
“你喜欢已经结婚吗？”约翰逊问其中一个搬运工。
‘What?’
“什么？”
‘You like the married state?’
“你喜欢已婚的状态吗？”
‘Oui. C’est normale.’
“Oui. C’est normale.”
‘Exactly,’ said Johnson. ‘Et vous, monsieur?’
“Exactly，”Johnson 说。“Et vous, monsieur?”
‘Ça va,’ said the other porter.
“Ça va，”另一个搬运工说。
‘Pour moi,’ said Johnson, ‘ça ne va pas.’
“Pour moi，”Johnson 说，“ça ne va pas。”
‘Monsieur is going to divorce,’ the first porter explained.
“先生要离婚了，”第一个门房解释道。
‘Oh,’ said the second porter.
“哦，”第二个门房说。
‘Ah ha,’ the third porter said.
“啊哈，”第三个门房说。
‘Well,’ said Johnson, ‘the subject seems to be exhausted. You’re not interested in my troubles,’ he addressed the first porter.
“好吧，”约翰逊说，“这个话题看来是聊不到头了。你们对我的烦恼不感兴趣，”他对第一个门房说。
‘But, yes,’ said the porter.
“不过，是的，”门房说。
‘Well, let’s talk about something else.’
“好吧，那我们聊点别的吧。”
‘As you wish.’
“随您。”
‘What can we talk about?’
“我们能聊些什么？”
‘You do the sport ?’
“你打这项运动吗？”
‘No,’ said Johnson. ‘My wife does, though.’
“没有，”Johnson 说。“不过我妻子打。”
‘What do you do for amusement?’
“你平时有什么娱乐？”
‘I am a writer.’
“我是个作家。”
‘Does that make much money?’
“那赚很多钱吗？”
‘No. But later on when you get known it does.’
“不会。不过以后你出名了就会。”
‘It is interesting?’
“有意思吗？”
‘No,’ said Johnson, ‘it is not interesting. I am sorry, gentlemen, but I have to leave you. Will you please drink the other bottle?’
“不，”约翰逊说，“没意思。抱歉，先生们，我得走了。你们能把另一瓶喝了吗？”
‘But the train does not come for three-quarters of an hour.’
“但是火车要三个小时的四分之三才来。”
‘I know,’ said Johnson. The waitress came and he paid for the wine and his dinner.
“我知道，”约翰逊说。女服务员走来，他付了酒钱和晚餐的钱。
‘You going out, sir?’ she asked.
“先生您要出去吗？”她问。
‘Yes,’ said Johnson, ‘just for a little walk. I’ll leave my bags here.’
“是的，”约翰逊说，“就出去散散步。我把行李留在这里。”
He put on his muffler, his coat, and his hat. Outside the snow was falling heavily. He looked back through the window at the three porters sitting at the table. The waitress was filling their glasses from the last wine of the opened bottle. She took the unopened bottle back to the bar. That makes them three francs something apiece, Johnson thought. He turned and walked down the platform. Inside the café he had thought that talking about it would blunt it; but it had not blunted it; it had only made him feel nasty.
他戴上围巾、外套和帽子。外面大雪正纷纷落下。他通过窗户回头看着坐在桌旁的三个搬运工。女侍在把开了的那瓶酒的最后一点倒进他们的酒杯。她把未开封的那瓶拿回吧台。约翰逊想，这样算来每人三法郎多一点儿。他转身走下站台。进到咖啡馆时，他以为谈论此事会使之钝化；但并没有钝化；只是让他感到恶心。

PART III
第三部分

THE SON OF A FELLOW MEMBER AT TERRITET
泰瑞泰特一位会员之子

In the station café at Territet it was a little too warm; the lights were bright and the tables shiny from polishing. There were baskets with pretzels in glazed paper sacks on the tables and cardboard pads for beer glasses in order that the moist glasses would not make rings on the wood. The chairs were carved but the wooden seats were worn and quite comfortable. There was a clock on the wall, a bar at the far end of the room, and outside the window it was snowing. There was an old man drinking coffee at a table under the clock and reading the evening paper. A porter came in and said the SimplonOrient Express was an hour late at Saint-Maurice. The waitress came over to Mr. Harris’s table. Mr. Harris had just finished dinner.
在特里泰站的咖啡厅里有点太暖和；灯光明亮，桌子被擦得发亮。桌上有装在釉纸袋里的椒盐卷饼篮子，还有啤酒杯用的纸垫，以免湿杯在木桌上留下圈儿。椅子雕着花纹，但木座位已经磨得很平，很舒服。墙上挂着一只钟，房间远端有个吧台，窗外正下着雪。钟下的一张桌旁有位老人喝着咖啡，看着晚报。一个搬运工走进来说 SimplonOrient Express 在圣-莫里斯晚点一小时。女服务员走到哈里斯先生的桌边。哈里斯先生刚吃完晚饭。
‘The Express is an hour late, sir. Can I bring you some coffee?’
“快车晚点一小时，先生。我给您来点咖啡吗？”
‘If you like.’
“随便。”
‘Please?’ asked the waitress.
“要来吗？”女服务员问道。
‘All right,’ said Mr. Harris.
“好吧，”哈里斯先生说。
‘Thank you, sir,’ said the waitress.
“谢谢您，先生，”女服务员说。
She brought the coffee from the kitchen and Mr. Harris put sugar in it, crunched the lumps with his spoon, and looked out of the window at the snow falling in the light from the station platform.
她从厨房端来咖啡，哈里斯先生往里加了糖，用勺子把糖块压碎，然后望着窗外在工作站灯光下飘落的雪。
‘Do you speak other languages besides English?’ he asked the waitress.
“除了英语你还会说其他语言吗？”他问女服务员。
‘Oh, yes, sir. I speak German and French and the dialects.’
“哦，是的，先生。我会说德语和法语，还有方言。”
‘Which do you like best?’
“你最喜欢哪种？”
“They are all very much the same, sir. I can’t say I like one better than another.’
“它们都差不多，先生。我不能说我更喜欢哪一种。”
‘Would you like a drink of something or a coffee?’
“您要喝点什么还是来杯咖啡？”
‘Oh, no, sir, it is not permitted to drink in the café with the clients.’
“哦，不，先生，和客人一起在咖啡馆里喝酒是不允许的。”
‘You wouldn’t take a cigar?’
“您不来一支雪茄吗？”
‘Oh, no, sir,’ she laughed. ‘I don’t smoke, sir.’
“哦，不，先生，”她笑道。“我不抽烟，先生。”
‘Neither do I,’ said Harris. ‘I don’t agree with David Belasco.’
“我也不抽，”哈里斯说。“我不同意大卫·贝拉斯科的看法。”
‘Please?’
“请问？”
‘Belasco. David Belasco. You can always tell him because he has his collar on backwards. But I don’t agree with him. Then, too, he’s dead now.’
“贝拉斯科。大卫·贝拉斯科。你总能认出他，因为他把衣领反穿着。但我不同意他的看法。而且，他现在也死了。”
‘Will you excuse me, sir?’ asked the waitress.
“先生，您要借过一下吗？”女服务员问。
‘Absolutely,’ said Harris. He sat forward in the chair and looked out of the window. Across the room the old man had folded his paper. He looked at Mr. Harris and then picked up his coffee cup and saucer and walked to Harris’s table.
“当然可以，”哈里斯说。他在椅子上向前坐了坐，望向窗外。房间对面那位老人已经叠好了报纸。他看了看哈里斯，然后端起咖啡杯和碟子，走到哈里斯的桌边。
‘I beg your pardon if I intrude,’ he said in English, ‘but it has just occurred to me that you might be a member of the National Geographic Society.’
“如果打扰了请见谅，”他用英语说，“但我刚想到您可能是国家地理学会的会员。”
‘Please sit down,’ Harris said. The gentleman sat down.
“请坐，”哈里斯说。那位绅士坐下了。
‘Won’t you have another coffee or a liqueur?’
“再来一杯咖啡或利口酒吗？”
‘Thank you,’ said the gentleman.
“谢谢，”那位绅士说。
‘Won’t you have a kirsch with me?’
“你不跟我来一杯樱桃白兰地吗？”
‘Perhaps. But you must have it with me.’
“也许吧。但你必须跟我一起喝。”
‘No, I insist.’ Harris called the waitress. The old gentleman took out from an inside pocket of his coat a leather pocket-book. He took off a wide rubber band and drew out several papers, selected one, and handed it to Harris.
“不，非要你来不可。”哈里斯叫来了女服务员。那位老先生从外套内袋拿出一个皮质票夹。他取下一条宽大的橡皮筋，抽出几张纸，挑了一张递给哈里斯。
‘That is my certificate of membership,’ he said. ‘Do you know Frederick J. Roussel in America?’
“那是我的会籍证书，”他说。“你在美国认识 Frederick J. Roussel 吗？”
‘I’m afraid I don’t.’
“恐怕我不知道。”
‘I believe he is very prominent.’
“我相信他非常出名。”
‘Where does he come from? Do you know what part of the States?’
“他来自哪里？你知道他是哪个州的吗？”
‘From Washington, of course. Isn’t that the headquarters of the Society?’
“当然是华盛顿。那不是协会的总部吗？”
‘I believe it is.’
“我相信是的。”
‘You believe it is. Aren’t you sure?’
“你相信是的。你就不肯定吗？”
'I’ve been away a long time,” Harris said.
“我离开很久了，”哈里斯说。
‘You’re not a member, then?’
“那你不是会员？”
‘No. But my father is. He’s been a member for a great many years.’
“不。他是。他当了多年的会员了。”
‘Then he would know Frederick J. Roussel. He is one of the officers of the Society. You will observe that it is by Mr. Roussel that I was nominated for membership.’
“那他会认识 Frederick J. Roussel。他是社团的某位官员。你会注意到，是 Roussel 先生提名我为会员的。”
‘I’m awfully glad.’
“我非常高兴。”
‘I am sorry you are not a member. But you could obtain nomination through your father?’
“很遗憾你不是会员。不过你可以通过你父亲获得提名吗？”
‘I think so,’ said Harris. ‘I must when I go back.’
“我想是的，”哈里斯说。“回去的时候我必须去刊登。”
‘I would advise you to,’ said the gentleman. ‘You see the magazine, of course?’
“我建议你去，”那位先生说。“你当然看过那本杂志吧？”
‘Absolutely.’
“当然看过。”
‘Have you seen the number with the coloured plates of the North American fauna?’
“你看过那期带有北美动物彩色插图的那期吗？”
‘Yes. I have it in Paris.’
“有的。我在巴黎有一本。”
'And the number containing the panorama of the volcanoes of Alaska?’
“那本关于阿拉斯加火山全景的那一期呢？”
‘That was a wonder.’
“那真是奇观。”
‘I enjoyed very much, too, the wild animal photographs of George Shiras three.’
“我也非常喜欢乔治·希拉斯三世的野生动物照片。”
‘They were damned fine.’
“它们真他妈出色。”
‘I beg your pardon?’
“请你再说一遍？”
'They were excellent. That fellow Shiras - ’
“‘它们很棒。那个家伙希拉斯——’”
‘You call him that fellow?’
“你竟然叫他‘那个家伙’？”
‘We’re old friends,’ said Harris.
“我们是老朋友，”哈里斯说。
‘I see. You know George Shiras three. He must be very interesting.’
“是吗。我明白了。你认识乔治·希拉斯三世。他一定很有趣。”
‘He is. He’s about the most interesting man I know.’
“是的。他是我所认识的人里最有趣的一个。”
‘And do you know George Shiras two? Is he interesting too?’
“那你认识乔治·希拉斯二世吗？他也有趣吗？”
‘Oh, he’s not so interesting.’
“哦，他并不那么有趣。”
‘I should imagine he would be very interesting.’
“我想他应该会很有趣。”
‘You know, a funny thing. He’s not so interesting. I’ve often wondered why.’
“你知道，很奇怪。他并不那么有趣。我常常想知道为什么。”
‘H’m,’ said the gentleman. ‘I should have thought anyone in that family would be interesting.’
“嗯，”那位绅士说，“我本以为那个家里的人都会很有趣。”
‘Do you remember the panorama of the Sahara Desert?’ Harris asked.
“你还记得撒哈拉沙漠的全景吗？”哈里斯问道。
‘The Sahara Desert? That was nearly fifteen years ago.’
“撒哈拉沙漠？那几乎是十五年前的事了。”
‘That’s right. That was one of my father’s favourites.’
“没错。那是我父亲最喜欢的曲目之一。”
‘He doesn’t prefer the newer numbers?’
“他不更喜欢新的那些曲子吗？”
‘He probably does. But he was very fond of the Sahara panorama.’
“他大概是的。但他很喜欢撒哈拉的全景。”
‘It was excellent. But to me its artistic value far exceeded its scientific interest.’
“那很出色。但对我来说，它的艺术价值远远超过了它的科学趣味。”
‘I don’t know,’ said Harris. ‘The wind blowing all that sand and that Arab with his camel kneeling toward Mecca.’
“我不知道，”哈里斯说。“风把那些沙子吹得飞舞，加上那个阿拉伯人和他跪着面朝麦加的骆驼。”
‘As I recall, the Arab was standing holding the camel.’
“我记得，那个阿拉伯人是站着扶着骆驼的。”
‘You’re quite right,’ said Harris. ‘I was thinking of Colonel Lawrence’s book.’
“你说得对，”哈里斯说。“我在想劳伦斯上校的书。”
‘Lawrence’s book deals with Arabia, I believe.’
“我相信劳伦斯的书是关于阿拉伯的。”
‘Absolutely,’ said Harris. ‘It was the Arab reminded me of it.’
“确实如此，”哈里斯说。“是那位阿拉伯人让我想起它来。”
‘He must be a very interesting young man.’
“他一定是个非常有趣的年轻人。”
‘I believe he is.’
“我相信他是。”
‘Do you know what he is doing now?’
“你知道他现在在做什么吗？”
‘He’s in the Royal Air Force.’
“他在皇家空军服役。”
‘And why does he do that?’
“那他为什么要那样做？”
‘He likes it.’
“他喜欢的。”
‘Do you know if he belongs to the National Geographic Society?’
“你知道他是不是属于 National Geographic Society 吗？”
‘I wonder if he does.’
“我想知道他是不是。”
‘He would make a very good member. He is the sort of person they want as a member. I would be very happy to nominate him if you think they would like to have him.’
“他会成为一个非常合适的会员。他是那种他们想要的会员。如果你认为他们会愿意接纳他，我会很高兴提名他。”
‘I think they would.’
“我想他们会的。”
‘I have nominated a scientist from Vevey and a colleague of mine from Lauzanne and they were both elected. I believe they would be very pleased if I nominated Colonel Lawrence.’
“我提名了来自 Vevey 的一位科学家和我在 Lauzanne 的一位同事，他们都被选上了。我相信如果我提名 Lawrence 上校，他们会很高兴。”
‘It’s a splendid idea,’ said Harris. ‘Do you come here to the café often?’
“这是个极好的主意，”Harris 说。“你常来这家咖啡馆吗？”
‘I come here for coffee after dinner.’
“我晚饭后来这里喝咖啡。”
‘Are you in the University?’
“你在大学里吗？”
‘I am not active any longer.’
“我已不再任教了。”
‘I’m just waiting for the train,’ said Harris. ‘I’m going up to Paris and sail from Havre for the States.’
“我只是等火车，”哈里斯说。“我要上去去巴黎，然后从勒阿弗尔坐船回美国。”
‘I have never been to America. But I would like to go very much. Perhaps I shall attend a meeting of the society some time. I would be very happy to meet your father.’
“我从未去过美国。但我非常想去。也许我将来会去参加该学会的某次会议。我会很高兴见到你父亲。”
'I’m sure he would have liked to meet you but he died last year. Shot himself, oddly enough."
“我相信他本来会很想见你的，可他去年死了。奇怪的是自杀了。”
‘I am very truly sorry. I am sure his loss was a blow to science as well as to his family.’
“我真的非常抱歉。我相信他的去世对科学界和他的家人都是一个打击。”
‘Science took it awfully well.’
“科学界倒是受得很坦然。”
‘This is my card,’ Harris said. ‘His initials were E. J. instead of E. D. I know he would have liked to know you.’
“这是我的名片，”哈里斯说。“他的名字缩写是 E. J.，不是 E. D. 我知道他本来会很想认识你的。”
‘It would have been a great pleasure.’ The gentleman took out a card from the pocket-book and gave it to Harris. It read:
“那会是莫大的荣幸。”那位绅士从名片夹里取出一张名片递给哈里斯。名片上写着：
DR. SIGISMUND WYER, PH.D.
Member of the National Geographic Society, Washington, D.C., U.S.A.
美国华盛顿特区国家地理学会会员
‘I will keep it very carefully,’ Harris said.
“我会把它好好保存的，”哈里斯说道。

A DAY'S WAIT
一天的等待

He came into the room to shut the windows while we were still in bed and I saw he looked ill. He was shivering, his face was white, and he walked slowly as though it ached to move.
他进了屋去关窗，那时我们还在床上，我看见他显得不舒服。浑身发抖，脸色苍白，走路缓慢，仿佛动一下都很疼。
‘What’s the matter, Schatz?’
“怎么了，亲爱的？”
‘I’ve got a headache.’
“我头疼。”
‘You better go back to bed.’
“你最好回去睡觉。”
‘No. I’m all right.’
“不要。我没事。”
‘You go to bed. I’ll see you when I’m dressed.’
“你去睡吧。我穿好衣服再见你。”
But when I came downstairs he was dressed, sitting by the fire, looking a very sick and miserable boy of nine years. When I put my hand on his forehead I knew he had a fever.
但当我下楼时，他已经穿好衣服，坐在火炉旁，看上去像个九岁病恹恹、可怜的小男孩。我把手放在他的额头时，就知道他发烧了。
‘You go up to bed,’ I said, ‘you’re sick.’
“你上楼去睡吧，”我说，“你病了。”
‘I’m all right,’ he said.
“我没事，”他说。
When the doctor came he took the boy’s temperature.
医生来的时候，他给男孩量了体温。
‘What is it?’ I asked him.
“多少？”我问他。
‘One hundred and two.’
“一百零二。”
Downstairs, the doctor left three different medicines in different coloured capsules with instructions for giving them. One was to bring down the fever, another a purgative, the third to overcome an acid condition. The germs of influenza can only exist in an acid condition, he explained. He seemed to know all about influenza and said there was nothing to worry about if the fever did not go above one hundred and four degrees. This was a light epidemic of 'flu and there was no danger if you avoided pneumonia.
楼下，医生把三种不同药物装在不同颜色的胶囊里，并交代了服用说明。一个是降温的，另一个是泻药，第三个是用来克服酸性状态的。他解释说，流感的病菌只能在酸性环境中存活。他似乎对流感了如指掌，并说如果发烧不超过一百零四度就无需担心。这是一次轻微的流感流行，只要避免肺炎就没有危险。
Back in the room I wrote the boy’s temperature down and made a note of the time to give the various capsules.
回到房间，我把男孩的体温记下来，并记下了给不同胶囊的时间。
‘Do you want me to read to you?’
“你要我给你念书吗？”
