‘All right. If you want to,’ said the boy. His face was very white and there were dark areas under his eyes. He lay still in the bed and seemed very detached from what was going on.
“好吧。如果你愿意的话。”男孩说。他的脸很白，眼睛下方有暗沉的圈。他躺在床上一动不动，似乎对正在发生的事漠不关心。
I read aloud from Howard Pyle’s Book of Pirates; but I could see he was not following what I was reading.
我朗读着 Howard Pyle 的《Book of Pirates》；但我能看出来他并没有跟上我读的内容。
‘How do you feel, Schatz ?’ I asked him.
“你感觉怎么样，Schatz？”我问他。
‘Just the same, so far,’ he said.
“到现在为止还是一样，”他说。
I sat at the foot of the bed and read to myself while I waited for it to be time to give another capsule. It would have been natural for him to go to sleep, but when I looked up he was looking at the foot of the bed, looking very strangely.
我坐在床脚，自言自语地读着，等着吃下一颗胶囊的时间到。按理说他应该睡着了，但我抬头看时，他正看着床脚，表情很奇怪。
‘Why don’t you try to go to sleep? I’ll wake you up for the medicine.’
“你为什么不试着睡一会儿？到吃药的时候我会叫你的。”
‘I’d rather stay awake.’
“我宁愿醒着。”
After a while he said to me, ‘You don’t have to stay in here with me, Papa, if it bothers you.’
过了一会儿，他对我说：“爸爸，如果这让你不舒服，你不用一直待在这儿陪我。”
‘It doesn’t bother me.’
“这倒不困扰我。”
‘No, I mean you don’t have to stay if it’s going to bother you.’
“不是，我的意思是如果这会让你不舒服，你不用留下来。”
I thought perhaps he was a little lightheaded and after giving him the prescribed capsules at eleven o’clock I went out for a while.
我想他也许有点头晕，于是十一点给了他规定的胶囊后，我出去了一会儿。
It was a bright, cold day, the ground covered with a sleet that had frozen so that it seemed as if all the bare trees, the bushes, the cut brush and all the grass and the bare ground had been varnished with ice. I took the young Irish setter for a little walk up the road and along a frozen creek, but it was difficult to stand or walk on the glassy surface and the red dog slipped and slithered and I fell twice, hard, once dropping my gun and having it slide away over the ice.
那是个阳光明媚、寒冷的日子，地面被一层冻雹覆盖，冻得仿佛所有的裸树、灌木、被砍过的灌丛以及所有的草地和裸露的土地都被冰漆了一层。我带着那只年轻的爱尔兰雪达犬沿着路上和一条结冰的小溪散步，但在光滑的冰面上站立或行走都很困难，那只红毛犬滑来滑去，我两次重重地摔倒，有一次把猎枪掉了，枪顺着冰面滑走了。
We flushed a covey of quail under a high bank with overhanging brush and I killed two as they went out of sight over the top of the bank. Some of the covey lit in trees, but most of them scattered into brush piles and it was necessary to jump on the ice-coated mounds of brush several times before they would flush. Coming out while you were poised unsteadily on the icy, springy brush they made difficult shooting and I killed two, missed five, and started back pleased to have found a covey close to the house and happy there were so many left to find on another day.
我们在一个河岸高坡下带着垂悬灌木的地方惊起了一群鹌鹑，我在它们越过坡顶消失视野时打死了两只。群里有些落在树上，但大多数散入灌木堆，必须几次踩在结着冰的刷状灌木墩上，把它们震出来。它们在你不稳地站在冰冷、有弹性的灌木上时飞出，使得射击变得困难，我打死了两只，射偏了五发，然后满意地折回，因为发现离屋子这么近就有一群，而且高兴地想着另一天还能找到这么多。
At the house they said the boy had refused to let anyone come into the room.
在屋里他们说那个男孩拒绝让任何人进屋。
‘You can’t come in,’ he said. ‘You mustn’t get what I have.’
“你们不能进来，”他说。“你们不能得到我有的东西。”
I went up to him and found him in exactly the position I had left him, white-faced, but with the tops of his cheeks flushed by the fever, staring still, as he had stared, at the foot of the bed.
我走到他跟前，发现他正以我离开时的完全相同的姿势，面色苍白，但两颊上端因发烧而泛红，仍然像刚才那样盯着床脚发呆。
I took his temperature.
我给他量了体温。
‘What is it?’
“多少？”
‘Something like a hundred,’ I said. It was one hundred and two and four-tenths.
“差不多一百度，”我说。实际上是 100.4 度。
‘It was a hundred and two,’ he said.
“原来是 100.2，”他说。
‘Who said so?’
“谁那么说的？”
‘The doctor.’
“医生。”
‘Your temperature is all right,’ I said. ‘It’s nothing to worry about.’
“你的体温没问题，”我说。“不用担心。”
‘I don’t worry,’ he said, ‘but I can’t keep from thinking.’
“我不担心，”他说，“但我无法停止思考。”
‘Don’t think,’ I said. ‘Just take it easy.’
“别想了，”我说，“就放轻松。”
‘I’m taking it easy,’ he said, and looked straight ahead. He was evidently holding tight on to himself about something.
“我都放轻松了，”他说，目光直直向前。他显然在某事上紧紧压抑着自己。
‘Take this with water.’
“把这个和水一起服下。”
‘Do you think it will do any good?’
“你觉得会有用吗？”
‘Of course it will.’
“当然会的。”
I sat down and opened the Pirate book and commenced to read, but I could see he was not following, so I stopped.
我坐下，翻开那本《海盗》书开始读，但我看见他并没有在听，于是停了下来。
‘About what time do you think I’m going to die?’ he asked.
“你觉得我大概什么时候会死？”他问。
‘What?’
“什么？”
‘About how long will it be before I die?’
“我大概还要多久才会死？”
‘You aren’t going to die. What’s the matter with you?’
“你不会死的。你怎么了？”
‘Oh, yes, I am. I heard him say a hundred and two.’
“哦，会的。我听见他说一百二。”
‘People don’t die with a fever of one hundred and two. That’s a silly way to talk.’
“发一百二的烧是不会死的。那样说话太傻了。”
‘I know they do. At school in France the boys told me you can’t live with forty-four degrees. I’ve got a hundred and two.’
“我知道他们是这么说的。 在法国上学时男孩们跟我说人不能活在四十四度。 我发烧一百零二。”
He had been waiting to die all day, ever since nine o’clock in the morning.
他从早上九点起就一直在等死。
‘You poor Schatz,’ I said. ‘Poor old Schatz. It’s like miles and kilometres. You aren’t going to die. That’s a different thermometer. On that thermometer thirty-seven is normal. On this kind it’s ninetyeight.’
“你这可怜的 Schatz，”我说。“可怜的老 Schatz。那就像英里和公里的区别。你不会死的。那是另一种温度计。在那种温度计上三十七度是正常。在这种上就是九十八。”
‘Absolutely,’ I said. ‘It’s like miles and kilometres. You know, like how many kilometres we make when we do seventy miles in the car?’
“确实，”我说。“就像英里和公里的区别。你知道的，就像我们开车时七十英里能走多少公里？”
‘Oh,’ he said.
“哦，”他说。
But his gaze at the foot of the bed relaxed slowly. The hold over himself relaxed too, finally, and the next day it was very slack and he cried very easily at little things that were of no importance.
但他看着床脚的目光慢慢放松了。他对自己的控制也终于放松了，第二天他非常松弛，常为一些无关紧要的小事轻易哭出声来。

A NATURAL HISTORY OF THE DEAD
死者的自然史

It has always seemed to me that the war has been omitted as a field for the observations of the naturalist. We have charming and sound accounts of the flora and fauna of Patagonia by the late W. H. Hudson, the Reverend Gilbert White has written most interestingly of the Hoopoe on its occasional and not at all common visits to Selborne, and Bishop Stanley has given us a valuable, although popular, Familiar History of Birds. Can we not hope to furnish the reader with a few rational and interesting facts about the dead? I hope so.
战争作为博物学家观察对象的领域，一直似乎被忽略了。已故 W. H. Hudson 对巴塔哥尼亚的动植物有有趣而可靠的记述，Gilbert White 牧师曾非常有趣地写过戴胜偶尔到访且绝非常见的塞尔本，而 Stanley 主教则为我们提供了一部虽然通俗但有价值的《鸟类通史》。我们难道不能希望为读者提供一些关于死者的理性且有趣的事实吗？我希望可以。
When that persevering traveller, Mungo Park, was at one period of his course fainting in the vast wilderness of an African desert, naked and alone, considering his days as numbered and nothing appearing to remain for him to do but to lie down and die, a small moss-flower of extraordinary beauty caught his eye. "Though the whole plant,’ says he, ‘was no larger than one of my fingers, I could not contemplate the delicate formation of its roots, leaves and capsules without admiration. Can that Being who planted, watered and brought to perfection, in this obscure part of the world, a thing which appears of so small importance, look with unconcern upon the situation and suffering of creatures formed after his own image? Surely not. Reflections like these would not allow me to despair; I started up and, disregarding both hunger and fatigue, travelled forward, assured that relief was at hand; and I was not disappointed.’
当那位坚韧不拔的旅行者芒戈·帕克在他旅途的某一阶段，赤身独处、虚弱不堪地昏倒在非洲荒漠的广袤荒野中，认为自己的日子已屈指可数，眼前似乎除了躺下去死别无他法时，一朵极为美丽的小苔花映入他的眼帘。“尽管整个植物，”他说，“不比我的一根手指大多少，我却无法不对其根、叶和胶囊的精致构造怀有敬意。那位在这世界偏僻角落栽种、灌溉并使之完美的存在，会对于按其形象造就的生灵的处境和苦难漠不关心吗？绝不会。这样的反思不允许我绝望；我猛地站起，不顾饥饿与疲惫，向前行走，确信援助就在眼前；结果我并未失望。”
With a disposition to wonder and adore in like manner, as Bishop Stanley says, can any branch of Natural History be studied without increasing that faith, love and hope which we also, every one of us, need in our journey through the wilderness of life? Let us therefore see what inspiration we may derive from the dead.
正如 Stanley 主教所说，以同样的惊奇与崇敬的心情，难道有哪一门自然史的分支不会在研究中增强那种信仰、爱与希望吗？我们每个人在生命荒野的旅程中也都需要这些。那就让我们看看从死者那里可以获得怎样的启发。
In war the dead are usually the male of the human species, although this does not hold true with animals, and I have frequently seen dead mares among the horses. An interesting aspect of war, too, is that it is only there that the naturalist has an opportunity to observe the dead of mules. In twenty years of observation in civil
在战争中，死者通常是人类这个物种的雄性，尽管这在动物界并不成立；我常常在马群中见到死去的母马。战争还有一个有趣之处：只有在那里，自然学家才有机会观察骡子的死状。在二十年的平民生活观察中，
life I had never seen a dead mule and had begun to entertain doubts as to whether these animals were really mortal. On rare occasions I had seen what I took to be dead mules, but on close approach these always proved to be living creatures who seemed to be dead through their quality of complete repose. But in war these animals succumb in much the same manner as the more common and less hardy horse.
我从未见过死骡子，并开始怀疑这些动物是否真的会死亡。极少数情况下我曾见过我以为是死骡子的个体，但靠近一看这些总被证明是活着的生物，只是因完全安静而显得像死了一样。但在战争中，这些动物的死亡方式与那些更常见且不那么耐劳的马大体相同。
Most of the mules that I saw dead were along mountain roads or lying at the foot of steep declivities whence they had been pushed to rid the road of their encumbrance. They seemed a fitting enough sight in the mountains where one was accustomed to their presence, and looked less incongruous there than they did later, at Smyrna, where the Greeks broke the legs of all their baggage animals and pushed them off the quay into the shallow water to drown. The numbers of broken-legged mules and horses drowning in the shallow water called for a Goya to depict them. Although, speaking literally, one can hardly say that they called for a Goya since there has only been one Goya, long dead, and it is extremely doubtful if these animals, were they able to call, would call for pictorial representation of their plight but, more likely, would, if they were articulate, call for someone to alleviate their condition.
我见过的大多数死骡子都散落在山路旁，或躺在陡坡脚下，被推下去以清除路障。在那些人们习以为常有骡子的山里，它们看上去也算合适，比起后来在士麦那看到的情景要不那么不协调：在那里，希腊人把所有负重牲畜折断腿后推到码头浅水里淹死。浅水中那些断腿骡马的数量，本应由一位戈雅来描绘。尽管从字面上说，这些动物并不能“呼唤”戈雅——毕竟只曾有一位戈雅，早已逝去——而且这些动物即便能呼叫，也极可能不会要求以画作来表现它们的困境；更有可能的是，如果它们能表达，会呼求有人来减轻它们的痛苦。
Regarding the sex of the dead it is a fact that one becomes so accustomed to the sight of all the dead being men that the sight of a dead woman is quite shocking. I first saw inversion of the usual sex of the dead after the explosion of a munition factory which had been situated in the countryside near Milan, Italy. We drove to the scene of the disaster in trucks along poplar-shaded roads, bordered with ditches containing much minute animal life, which I could not clearly observe because of the great clouds of dust raised by the trucks. Arriving where the munition plant had been, some of us were put to patrolling about those large stocks of munitions which for some reason had not exploded, while others were put at extinguishing a fire which had gotten into the grass of an adjacent field; which task being concluded, we were ordered to search the immediate vicinity and surrounding fields for bodies. We found and carried to an improvised mortuary a good number of these and, I must admit, frankly, the shock it was to find that these dead were women rather than men. In those days women had not yet commenced to wear their hair cut short, as they did later for several
关于尸体性别这一点，事实是人们习惯于看到的死者大多为男性，以至于看到女性尸体会令人大为震惊。我第一次见到死者性别反常，是在意大利米兰附近一处军火工厂爆炸之后。我们沿着两旁栽着杨树的道路乘卡车赶到灾区，道路两侧的沟渠里有许多细小的动物生命，但由于卡车扬起的大量尘土，我看不清楚它们。到达军火厂原址时，我们中有些人被派去巡逻那些出于某种原因没有爆炸的大量弹药堆，有些人被派去扑灭已经蔓延到邻近田地草丛中的火；这项任务完成后，我们被命令搜寻灾区附近及周围田地的尸体。我们发现并抬到临时停尸房的尸体相当多，我必须坦白承认，令我震惊的是这些死者竟然是女性而不是男性。那时的妇女还没有像后来那样把头发剪短，像这样发生变化之前...
years in Europe and America, and the most disturbing thing, perhaps because it was the most unaccustomed, was the presence, and, even more disturbing, the occasional absence of this long hair. I remember that after we had searched quite thoroughly for the complete dead we collected fragments. Many of these were detached from a heavy, barbed-wire fence which had surrounded the position of the factory and from the still existent portions of which we picked many of these detached bits which illustrated only too well the tremendous energy of high explosive. Many fragments we found a considerable distance away in the fields, they being carried farther by their own weight.
在欧洲和美国的那些年里，最令人不安的事情，也许正因为它最不习以为常，是这些长发的存在，更令人不安的是，偶尔这些长发也会消失。我记得在我们相当彻底地寻找完整的尸体之后，收集了碎片。许多碎片是从围绕厂房阵地的粗重带刺铁丝网脱落下来的，我们从仍然存在的部分上摘下了许多这些脱落的碎片，这些碎片恰到好处地说明了高爆炸药的巨大能量。许多碎片我们在田地里发现了相当远的距离，是它们自身的重量把它们带得更远。
On our return to Milan I recall one or two of us discussing the occurrence and agreeing that the quality of unreality and the fact that there were no wounded did much to rob the disaster of a horror which might have been much greater. Also the fact that it had been so immediate and that the dead were in consequence still as little unpleasant as possible to carry and deal with made it quite removed from the usual battlefield experience. The pleasant, though dusty, ride through the beautiful Lombard countryside also was a compensation for the unpleasantness of the duty and on our return, while we exchanged impressions, we all agreed that it was indeed fortunate that the fire which broke out just before we arrived had been brought under control as rapidly as it had and before it had attained any of the seemingly huge stocks of unexploded munitions. We agreed too that the picking up of the fragments had been an extraordinary business; it being amazing that the human body should be blown into pieces which exploded along no anatomical lines, but rather divided as capriciously as the fragmentation in the burst of a high explosive shell.
回到米兰时，我记得我们中有一两个人讨论过那次事件，并一致认为那种不真实的感觉以及没有受伤者这一事实，大大减弱了这场本可能更加可怕的灾难的恐怖性。还有它发生得如此突然，因而死者在搬运和处理时仍尽可能地不令人不快，这一点也使它与通常的战场经历大为不同。穿过美丽的伦巴第乡间那段虽有些尘土飞扬但愉快的骑行，也补偿了执行这一任务的令人不快之处。我们返回时交换了各自的感受，都同意确实很幸运，在我们到达前不久突然燃起的火焰已被迅速控制住，而且在达到任何看似巨大的未爆弹药堆之前就被扑灭了。我们还一致认为收拾那些碎片是一件非同寻常的事；令人惊讶的是人身竟能被炸成碎片，而这些碎片并非沿着任何解剖学的线爆裂，而是像高爆弹壳爆炸时的碎片那样任性地分裂。
A naturalist, to obtain accuracy of observation, may confine himself in his observations to one limited period and I will take first that following the Austrian offensive of June, 1918, in Italy as one in which the dead were present in their greatest numbers, a withdrawal having been forced and an advance later made to recover the ground lost so that the positions after the battle were the same as before except for the presence of the dead. Until the dead are buried they change somewhat in appearance each day. The colour change in Caucasian races is from white to yellow, to yellow-green, to black. If left long enough in the heat the flesh comes to resemble coal-tar,
为了获得观察的准确性，博物学家可以将自己的观察限定在某一有限时期内。我先选取 1918 年 6 月奥地利人在意大利发动攻势之后的那段时期，把它作为死者数量最多的一段——当时被迫撤退，随后又发起反攻以收复失地，因此战后各处阵地与战前相同，只是多了许多尸体。在尸体下葬之前，它们每天的外貌都会有些变化。高加索人种的肤色变化是从白色到黄色，接着到黄绿色，再到黑色。如果在高温下放置得足够久，尸肉的颜色会变得像煤焦油。
especially where it has been broken or torn, and it has quite a visible tar-like iridescence. The dead grow larger each day until sometimes they become quite too big for their uniforms, filling these until they seem blown tight enough to burst. The individual members may increase in girth to an unbelievable extent and faces fill as taut and globular as balloons. The surprising thing, next to their progressive corpulence, is the amount of paper that is scattered about the dead. Their ultimate position, before there is any question of burial, depends on the location of the pockets in the uniform. In the Austrian army these pockets were in the back of the breeches and the dead, after a short time, all consequently lay on their faces, the two hip pockets pulled out and, scattered around them in the grass, all those papers their pockets contained. The heat, the flies, the indicative positions of the bodies in the grass, and the amount of paper scattered are the impressions one retains. The smell of a battlefield in hot weather one cannot recall. You can remember that there was such a smell, but nothing ever happens to you to bring it back. It is unlike the smell of a regiment, which may come to you suddenly while riding in the street car and you will look across and see the man who has brought it to you. But the other thing is gone as completely as when you have been in love; you remember things that happened, but the sensation cannot be recalled.
尤其是在已经破裂或撕开处能看到，有一种明显的沥青状虹彩。尸体每天都在胀大，直到有时变得完全不适合他们的军服，把这些军服撑得仿佛要爆裂。个别的尸体胀大的程度令人难以置信，脸部变得像气球一样绷紧而圆鼓。令人惊讶的事，除了他们日益肥胀之外，就是散落在尸体周围的纸张之多。在埋葬问题尚未出现之前，他们最终的体位取决于军服口袋的位置。在奥地利军队，这些口袋在裤子的后面，尸体不久之后全都面朝下躺着，两个臀部口袋被拉出，口袋里所有的纸张散落在草地上。炎热、苍蝇、草地上尸体所呈现的位置以及散落的纸张数量，是人们记忆中的印象。热天战场的气味是无法回忆起的。你可以记得曾有那样一种气味，但没有什么能让它重现在你面前。 它不像一支团的气味，那种气味可能在你乘电车时突然扑来，你会朝对面看去，看到把它带给你的人。但另一种感觉已经完全消失了，就像你曾经坠入爱河；你记得发生过的事情，但那种感觉无法被召回。
One wonders what that persevering traveller, Mungo Park, would have seen on a battlefield in hot weather to restore his confidence. There were always poppies in the wheat in the end of June and in July, and the mulberry trees were in full leaf and one could see the heat waves rise from the barrels of the guns where the sun struck them through the screens of leaves; the earth was turned a bright yellow at the edge of holes where mustard gas shells had been and the average broken house is finer to see than one that has been shelled, but few travellers would take a good full breath of that early summer air and have any such thoughts as Mungo Park about those formed in His own image.
人们不禁要想，那位坚持不懈的旅行者蒙戈·帕克在炎热的战场上会看到什么以恢复他的信心。六月末和七月里，麦田里总有罂粟，桑树叶子已长得茂密，从叶帘间照到枪管上，热浪可以看见从枪管上升起；地面在芥子气弹曾落处的洞边呈现出明亮的黄色，平均破损的房屋比被炮轰过的房子看起来更漂亮，但很少有旅行者会深深吸一口初夏的空气，并像蒙戈·帕克那样对那些按自我形象造就者形成的东西产生任何类似的想法。
The first thing that you found about the dead was that, hit badly enough, they died like animals. Some quickly from a little wound you would not think would kill a rabbit. They died from little wounds as rabbits die sometimes from three or four small grains of shot that hardly seem to break the skin. Others would die like cats; a skull broken in and iron in the brain, they lie alive two days like
关于死人你首先会发现的一点是：受重击的话，他们像动物一样死去。有些人会因为看起来不足以致命的小伤而迅速死亡，就像有时兔子会因三四颗小散弹而死，那些弹片几乎看不见破皮一样。另一些则像猫一样死去；颅骨被砸碎，铁器嵌入大脑，他们还活着躺着两天。
cats that crawl into the coal bin with a bullet in the brain and will not die until you cut their heads off. Maybe cats do not die then, they say they have nine lives. I do not know, but most men die like animals, not men. I’d never seen a natural death, so called, and so I blamed it on the war and like the persevering traveller, Mungo Park, knew that here was something clse, that always absent something else, and then I saw one.
那些钻进煤箱脑袋中插着子弹却死不掉的猫，除非你把它们的头砍下来才能死。也许猫真有九条命，他们说是这样。我不知道，但大多数人死得像畜生，不像男人。我从未见过所谓的自然死亡，所以我把它归咎于战争，就像那位坚持不懈的旅行者芒戈·帕克一样，知道这里有某种接近但总缺少的东西，然后我看见了一次。
The only natural death I’ve ever seen, outside of loss of blood, which isn’t bad, was death from Spanish influenza. In this you drown in mucus, choking, and how you know the patient’s dead is: at the end he turns to be a little child again, though with his manly force, and fills the sheets as full as any diaper with one vast, final, yellow cataract that flows and dribbles on after he’s gone. So now I want to see the death of any self-called Humanist 1 1 ^(1){ }^{1} because a persevering traveller like Mungo Park or me lives on and maybe yet will live to see the actual death of members of this literary sect and watch the noble exits that they make. In my musings as a naturalist it has occurred to me that while decorum is an excellent thing some must be indecorous if the race is to be carried on since the position prescribed for procreation is indecorous, highly indecorous, and it occurred to me that perhaps that is what these people are, or were: the children of decorous cohabitation. But regardless of how they started I hope to see the finish of a few, and speculate how worms will try that long preserved sterility; with their quaint pamphlets gone to bust and into footnotes all their lust.
我见过的唯一一种自然死亡，除去失血那类并不糟糕的情况，就是西班牙流感致死。那种死法是被粘液淹死、窒息，你知道病人死了的标志是：到最后他又变成了一个小孩，尽管还保有男子的力气，能把床单像尿布一样装满，一股巨大的、最后的黄色分泌物流着、滴着，直到他走了。所以现在我想看看任何自称为 Humanist 的人怎么死，因为像芒戈·帕克或我这样坚持不懈的旅行者会活下去，也许将来还会活着看到这个文学教派成员的真正死亡，看看他们那种高贵的谢幕。作为一个博物学者，我思索时想到了，虽然端庄是好东西，但如果要延续种族，总得有人不端庄，因为为繁衍所规定的体位是不端庄的，非常不端庄，我想到或许这些人就是那样的，或者曾是：端庄同居所生的孩子。但不管他们如何起始，我希望看到其中几个人的终结，并猜想蛆虫将如何应对那长期保存的无菌；那些古怪的小册子破产入注释后，他们所有的欲望也随之而去。
While it is, perhaps, legitimate to deal with these self-designated citizens in a natural history of the dead, even though the designation may mean nothing by the time this work is published, yet it is unfair to the other dead, who were not dead in their youth of choice, who owned no magazines, many of whom had doubtless never even read a review, that one has seen in the hot weather with a half-pint of maggots working where their mouths have been. It was not always hot weather for the dead, much of the time it was the rain that washed them clean when they lay in it and made the earth soft when they were buried in it and sometimes then kept on until the earth was mud and washed them out and you had to bury them
也许，把这些自封为公民的人列入一本关于死者的自然史中是正当的，尽管到这本书出版时这种称谓可能已毫无意义，然而这样做对其他死者不公平——那些并非在青年时期自愿去死的人，那些没有杂志的拥有者，其中许多人大概甚至从未读过一篇书评——在炎热的天气里，人们看到他们嘴部曾在之处有半品脱的蛆在爬动。这些死者并非总是遇到炎热的天气，大多数时候是雨水把他们躺着时冲洗干净，把他们下葬时使土地变得松软，有时雨还会一直下，直到土地变成泥浆把他们冲出来，你不得不重新埋葬他们
again. Or in the winter in the mountains you had to put them in the snow and when the snow melted in the spring someone else had to bury them. They had beautiful burying grounds in the mountains, war in the mountains is the most beautiful of all war, and in one of them, at a place called Pocol, they buried a general who was shot through the head by a sniper. This is where those writers are mistaken who write books called Generals Die in Bed, because this general died in a trench dug in snow, high in the mountains, wearing an Alpini hat with an eagle feather in it and a hole in front you couldn’t put your little finger in and a hole in back you could put your fist in, if it were a small fist and you wanted to put it there, and much blood in the snow. He was a damned fine general, and so was General von Behr who commanded the Bavarian Alpenkorps troops at the battle of Caporetto and was killed in his staff car by the Italian rearguard as he drove into Udine ahead of his troops, and the titles of all such books should be Generals Usually Die in Bed, if we are to have any sort of accuracy in such things.
又或者在山区的冬天你得把他们放在雪里，等到春天雪化了就得由别人去埋他们。山区有美丽的墓地，山地战争是所有战争中最美的，在其中一个叫波科尔（Pocol）的地方，他们埋葬了一位被狙击手打穿头部的将军。那些写《将军们在床上死去》（Generals Die in Bed）之类书的作家在这里就错了，因为这位将军死在一条在雪中挖的战壕里，高处的山上，戴着一顶带有鹰羽的阿尔皮尼帽，帽前有个连你小手指都伸不进去的洞，帽后有个你若是有只小拳头并愿意的话可以把拳头塞进去的洞，雪里有很多血。他是个他妈的好将军，贝尔将军（General von Behr）也一样，后者在卡波雷托战役指挥巴伐利亚阿尔卑斯军团（Bavarian Alpenkorps）时，被意大利后卫在他驾车领先部队驶入乌迪内（Udine）时用随从车击毙，所有那类书的标题如果要准确些，应当叫《将军们通常在床上死》（Generals Usually Die in Bed）。
In the mountains, too, sometimes, the snow fell on the dead outside the dressing station on the side that was protected by the mountain from any shelling. They carried them into a cave that had been dug into the mountainside before the earth froze. It was in this cave that a man whose head was broken as a flower-pot may be broken, although it was all held together by membranes and a skilfully applied bandage now soaked and hardened, with the structure of his brain disturbed by a piece of broken steel in it, lay a day, a night, and a day. The stretcher-bearers asked the doctor to go in and have a look at him. They saw him each time they made a trip and even when they did not look at him they heard him breathing. The doctor’s eyes were red and the lids swollen, almost shut from tear gas. He looked at the man twice; once in daylight, once with a flashlight. That too would have made a good etching for Goya, the visit with the flashlight, I mean. After looking at him the second time the doctor believed the stretcher-bearers when they said the soldier was still alive.
在山里，有时也会下雪，雪落在受山体保护、免遭炮火轰击的敷伤站外的死者身上。他们把人抬进在土冻结之前在山坡上挖好的一个山洞。就是在这个山洞里，一个人的头被打得像花盆那样碎，尽管头颅仍由薄膜和一块现在已经被浸湿并变硬的熟练包扎维系着，脑结构被一块断钢片扰乱，他躺着一日、一夜又一日。担架兵们请医生进去看看他。他们每次出行都会看到他，即便不看也能听见他的呼吸声。医生的眼睛发红，眼睑肿得几乎闭合，几乎被催泪瓦斯熏得成这样。他看了那人两次：一次在白昼，一次用手电筒。我是说，用手电筒去看那次，也可以成为戈雅的好版画。第二次看过后，医生相信担架兵的话，说那个士兵还活着。
‘What do you want me to do about it?’ he asked.
“你要我怎么做？”他问。
There was nothing they wanted done. But after a while they asked permission to carry him out and lay him with the badly wounded.
他们不需要做任何事。但过了一会儿，他们请求许可把他抬出去，和重伤者们放在一起。
‘No. No. No!’ said the doctor, who was busy. ‘What’s the matter? Are you afraid of him?’
“不。不。不！”忙碌的医生说，“怎么了？你们怕他吗？”
‘We don’t like to hear him in there with the dead.’
“我们不愿意听见他和死人在那儿的声音。”
‘Don’t listen to him. If you take him out of there you will have to carry him right back in.’
“别听他的。如果你们把他从那里抬出去，就得把他再抬回去。”
‘We wouldn’t mind that, Captain Doctor.’
“我们不会介意的，船长医生。”
‘No,’ said the doctor. ‘No. Didn’t you hear me say no?’
“不，”医生说。“不。你没听到我说不吗？”
‘Why don’t you give him an overdose of morphine?’ asked an artillery officer who was waiting to have a wound in his arm dressed.
“你为什么不给他注射过量吗啡？”一名正等着包扎手臂伤口的炮兵军官问道。
‘Do you think that is the only use I have for morphine? Would you like me to have to operate without morphine? You have a pistol, go out and shoot him yourself.’
“你以为吗啡只有这个用处吗？你想让我在没有吗啡的情况下开刀吗？你有手枪，自己出去把他打了去吧。”
‘He’s been shot already,’ said the officer. ‘If some of you doctors were shot you’d be different.’
“他已经被枪打过了，”军官说。“要是你们这些医生被打了就另当别论了。”
‘Thank you very much,’ said the doctor waving a forceps in the air. ‘Thank you a thousand times. What about these eyes?’ He pointed the forceps at them. ‘How would you like these?’
“非常感谢，”医生一边挥着一把镊子说。“多谢你一千遍。这些眼睛怎么办？”他把镊子指向他们。“你们想要这些吗？”
‘Tear gas. We call it lucky if it’s tear gas.’
“催泪瓦斯。要是催泪瓦斯我们就算走运了。”
‘Because you leave the line,’ said the doctor. ‘Because you come running here with your tear gas to be evacuated. You rub onions in your eyes.’
“因为你离开防线，”医生说。“因为你带着催泪瓦斯跑到这儿来要求撤离。你把洋葱揉进自己的眼睛。”
‘You are beside yourself. I do not notice your insults. You are crazy.’
“你失了常。我没把你的侮辱放在心上。你疯了。”
The stretcher-bearers came in.
担架员进来了。
‘Captain Doctor,’ one of them said.
“队长医生，”其中一个人说。
‘Get out of here!’ said the doctor.
“滚出去！”医生说。
They went out.
他们出去了。
‘I will shoot the poor fellow,’ the artillery officer said. ‘I am a humane man. I will not let him suffer.’
“我会把可怜的家伙枪决的，”炮兵军官说。“我是个有人道的人。我不会让他受苦的。”
‘Shoot him then,’ said the doctor. ‘Shoot him. Assume the responsibility. I will make a report. Wounded shot by lieutenant of artillery in first curing post. Shoot him. Go ahead, shoot him.’
“那就枪毙他吧，”医生说。“枪毙他。承担责任。我会写报告的。受伤者在第一救护站被炮兵中尉射伤。枪毙他。去吧，枪毙他。”
‘You are not a human being.’
“你不是个人。”
‘My business is to care for the wounded, not to kill them. That is for gentlemen of the artillery.’
“我的职责是照顾受伤的人，不是要杀他们。那是炮兵绅士的事。”
‘Why don’t you care for him then?’
“那你为什么不照顾他呢？”
‘I have done so. I have done all that can be done.’
“我已经照顾过了。我已经尽了所有能做的。”
‘Why don’t you send him down on the cable railway?’
“那你为什么不把他用缆索铁路送下去？”
'Who are you to ask me questions? Are you my superior officer?
“你有什么资格问我问题？你是我的上级军官吗？
Are you in command of this dressing-post? Do me the courtesy to answer.’
你是这个输液处的主管吗？请给我个答复。”
The lieutenant of artillery said nothing. The others in the room were all soldiers and there were no other officers present.
炮兵中尉什么也没说。房间里其他人全是士兵，没别的军官在场。
‘Answer me,’ said the doctor holding a needle up in his forceps. ‘Give me a response.’
“回答我，”医生一边用镊子举着针头一边说。“给我一个响应。”
‘F- yourself,’ said the artillery officer.
“去你妈的，”炮兵军官说。
‘So,’ said the doctor. ‘So, you said that. All right. All right. We shall see.’
“是吗，”医生说。“是吗，你说了。好吧。好吧。我们走着瞧。”
The lieutenant of artillery stood up and walked toward him.
炮兵中尉站起来，朝他走去。
‘F- yourself,’ he said. ‘F- yourself. F- your mother. F- your sister…’
“去你妈的，”他说。“去你妈的。去你妈的你妈。去你妈的你妹妹……”
The doctor tossed the saucer full of iodine in his face. As he came toward him, blinded, the lieutenant fumbled for his pistol. The doctor skipped quickly behind him, tripped him and, as he fell to the floor, kicked him several times and picked up the pistol in his rubber gloves. The lieutenant sat on the floor holding his good hand to his eyes.
医生把盛着碘酒的碟子泼在他脸上。当他被弄得失明朝他扑过来时，中尉慌忙摸枪。医生迅速绕到他身后，绊倒了他，趁他跌在地上又踢了他好几脚，并戴着橡胶手套拾起了手枪。中尉坐在地上，把好着的手捂在眼睛上。
‘I’ll kill you!’ he said. ‘I’ll kill you as soon as I can see.’
“我要杀了你！”他说。“我一看见就要杀了你。”
‘I am the boss,’ said the doctor. ‘All is forgiven since you know I am the boss. You cannot kill me because I have your pistol. Sergeant! Adjutant! Adjutant!’
“我是老板，”医生说。“既然你知道我是老板，一切都被原谅了。你杀不了我，因为我拿着你的手枪。中士！副官！副官！”
‘The adjutant is at the cable railway,’ said the sergeant.
“副官在缆车那儿，”中士说。
‘Wipe out this officer’s eyes with alcohol and water. He has got iodine in them. Bring me the basin to wash my hands. I will take this officer next.’
“用酒精和水把这个军官的眼睛擦干净。他眼里进了碘酒。把洗手盆拿来让我洗手。我接下去处理这位军官。”
‘You won’t touch me.’
“你别碰我。”
‘Hold him tight. He is a little delirious.’
“把他按住。他有点神志不清。”
One of the stretcher-bearers came in.
其中一名担架兵走了进来。
‘Captain Doctor.’
“队长医生。”
‘What do you want?’
“你要什么？”
'The man in the dead-house - ’
“太平间里的那个人——”
‘Get out of here.’
“滚出去。”
‘Is dead, Captain Doctor. I thought you would be glad to know.’
“他死了，上尉医生。我以为你会高兴知道这个消息。”
‘See, my poor licutenant? We dispute about nothing. In time of war we dispute about nothing.’
“看吧，我可怜的中尉？我们争论的毫无意义。战时我们争论的都是无关紧要的事。”
‘F- you,’ said the lieutenant of artillery. He still could not see. ‘You’ve blinded me.’
“操你，”炮兵中尉说。他仍然看不见。“你把我弄瞎了。”
‘It is nothing,’ said the doctor. ‘Your eyes will be all right. It is nothing. A dispute about nothing.’
“没事的，”医生说。“你的眼睛会没事的。没事的。都是为了无关紧要的争执。”
‘Ayee! Ayee! Ayee!’ suddenly screamed the lieutenant. ‘You have blinded me! You have blinded me!’
“哎哟！哎哟！哎哟！”中尉突然尖叫道。“你把我弄瞎了！你把我弄瞎了！”
‘Hold him tight,’ said the doctor. ‘He is in much pain. Hold him very tight.’
“把他按紧，”医生说。“他很痛。把他按得很紧。”

WINE OF WYOMING
怀俄明的酒

It was a hot afternoon in Wyoming; the mountains were a long way away and you could see snow on their tops, but they made no shadow, and in the valley the grain-fields were yellow, the road was dusty with cars passing, and all the small wooden houses at the edge of town were baking in the sun. There was a tree made shade over Fontan’s back porch and I sat there at a table and Madame Fontan brought up cold beer from the cellar. A motor car turned off the main road and came up the side road, and stopped beside the house. Two men got out and came in through the gate. I put the bottles under the table. Madame Fontan stood up.
那是怀俄明州的一个炎热的下午；群山很远，你能看到山顶的积雪，但山并不投下阴影，山谷里的谷地已成黄色，路上因汽车来往而尘土飞扬，镇边所有的小木屋都在太阳下烘晒。Fontan 家的后廊有一棵树投下荫凉，我坐在那张桌旁，Fontan 夫人从地窖里端来冰啤酒。一辆汽车从主路拐入小路，开到屋边停下。两个人下车，从大门走了进来。我把瓶子放到桌子下面。Fontan 夫人站了起来。
‘Where’s Sam?’ one of the men asked at the screen door.
“山姆在哪儿？”其中一个人在纱门口问。
‘He ain’t here. He’s at the mines.’
“他不在。他在矿上。”
‘You got some beer?’
“你有啤酒吗？”
‘No. Ain’t got any beer. That’s a last bottle. All gone.’
“没有。没有啤酒了。那是最后一瓶。全没了。”
‘What’s he drinking?’
“他喝的是什么？”
‘That’s a last bottle. All gone.’
“那是最后一瓶了。全没了。”
‘Go on, give us some beer. You know me.’
“来嘛，给我们些啤酒。你认识我。”
‘Ain’t got any beer. That’s a last bottle. All gone.’
“没有啤酒了。那是最后一瓶。全没了。”
‘Come on, let’s go some place where we can get some real beer,’ one of them said, and they went out to the car. One of them walked unsteadily. The motor car jerked in starting, whirled on the road, and went on and away.
“来吧，咱们去能喝到真啤酒的地方，”其中一个人说着，他们走向汽车。一个人走得摇摇晃晃。汽车发动车时一阵颠簸，在路上急转，然后开走了。
‘Put the beer on the table,’ Madame Fontan said. ‘What’s the matter, yes, all right. What’s the matter? Don’t drink off the floor.’
“把啤酒放桌上，”芳塔纳夫人说。“怎么了，好啦。怎么了？别把酒洒到地上喝。”
‘I don’t know who they were,’ I said.
“我不知道他们是谁，”我说。
‘They’re drunk,’ she said. ‘That’s what makes the trouble. Then they go somewhere else and say they got it here. Maybe they don’t even remember.’ She spoke French, but it was only French occasionally, and there were many English words and some English constructions.
“他们喝醉了，”她说。“这就是麻烦的根源。然后他们去别的地方说是在这里弄到的。也许他们甚至都不记得。”她说法语，但只是偶尔用法语，话里夹了许多英语单词和一些英语句法。
‘Where’s Fontan?’
“Fontan 在哪里？”
‘Il fait de la vendange. Oh, my God, il est crazy pour le vin.’
“Il fait de la vendange。哦，我的天，他对酒痴迷。”
‘But you like the beer?’
“但你喜欢啤酒吗？”
‘Oui, j’aime la bière, mais Fontain, il est crazy pour le vin.’
“Oui，j’aime la bière，但 Fontain，他对酒痴迷。”
She was a plump old woman with a lovely ruddy complexion and white hair. She was very clean and the house was very clean and neat. She came from Lens.
她是个丰满的老太太，皮肤红润漂亮，白发。她很干净，房子也很干净整洁。她来自朗斯。
‘Where did you eat?’
“你在哪里吃的？”
‘At the hotel.’
“在酒店。”
‘Mangez ici. Il ne faut pas manger à l’hôtel ou au restaurant. Mangez ici!’
“Mangez ici. Il ne faut pas manger à l’hôtel ou au restaurant. Mangez ici!”
‘I don’t want to make you trouble. And besides they eat all right at the hotel.’
“我不想给你添麻烦。而且他们在酒店吃得还行。”
‘I never eat at the hotel. Maybe they eat all right there. Only once in my life I ate at a restaurant in America. You know what they gave me? They gave me pork that was raw!’
“我从不在酒店吃饭。也许他们在那里吃得还行。我一生中只有一次在美国的餐馆里吃过饭。你知道他们给了我什么吗？他们给了我没熟的猪肉！”
‘Really?’
“真的？”
‘I don’t lie to you. It was pork that wasn’t cooked! Et mon fils il est marié avec une américaine, et tout le temps il a mangé les beans en can.’
“我没骗你。那是没煮熟的猪肉！Et mon fils il est marié avec une américaine, et tout le temps il a mangé les beans en can.”
‘How long has he been married?’
“他结婚多久了？”
‘Oh, my God, I don’t know. His wife weighs two hundred twenty-five pounds. She don’t work. She don’t cook. She gives him beans en can.’
“哦，我的天，我不知道。她太太体重二百二十五磅。她不工作。她不做饭。她给他罐装豆子吃。”
‘What does she do?’
“她做什么？”
‘All the time she reads. Rien que des books. Tout le temps elle stay in bed and read books. Already she can’t have another baby. She’s too fat. There ain’t any room.’
“她老是看书。只看书。整天她躺在床上看书。她已经不能再生孩子了。她太胖了。没有空间了。”
‘What the matter with her?’
“她怎么了？”
‘She reads books all the time. He’s a good boy. He works hard. He worked in the mines; now he works on a ranch. He never worked on a ranch before, and the man that owns the ranch said to Fontan that he never saw anybody work better on that ranch than that boy. Then he comes home and she feeds him nothing.’
“她整天看书。那孩子很好。他很勤快。他在矿山工作过；现在在牧场工作。他以前从没在牧场干过，牧场主人对 Fontan 说，他从没见过有人在那牧场干得比那孩子更好。然后他回家，她不给他好好吃饭。”
‘Why doesn’t he get a divorce?’
“他为什么不离婚？”
‘He ain’t got no money to get a divorce. Besides, il est crazy pour elle.’
“他没钱离婚。再说了，il est crazy pour elle。”
‘Is she beautiful?’
“她漂亮吗？”
‘He thinks so. When he brought her home I thought I would die. He’s such a good boy and works hard all the time and never run around or make any trouble. Then he goes away to work in the oil-
“他是这么认为的。把她带回家时我以为自己会死。他是个好孩子，一直很努力工作，从不乱跑也不惹事。然后他到油田去工作——
fields and brings home this Indienne that weighs right then one hundred eighty-five pounds.’
回家时带回了这个印第安女人，当时她刚好有一百八十五磅重。”
‘Elle est Indienne?’
“她是印第安人吗？”
‘She’s Indian all right. My God, yes. All the time she says sonofa bitsh goddam. She don’t work.’
“她完全是印度人。天哪，确实。她一直都在说 sonofa bitsh goddam。她不干活。”
‘Where is she now?’
“她现在在哪儿？”
‘Au show.’
“Au 秀。”
‘Where’s that?’
“那在哪儿？”
‘Au show. Moving pictures. All she does is read and go to the show.’
“啊，电影院。会看电影。她除了看书就是去看电影。”
‘Have you got any more beer?’
“你还有啤酒吗？”
‘My God, yes. Sure. You come and eat with us to-night.’
“我的天，当然有。一定有。你今晚来和我们一起吃饭吧。”
‘All right. What should I bring?’
“好。我要带什么吗？”
‘Don’t bring anything. Nothing at all. Maybe Fontan will have some of the wine.’
“什么也别带。什么都不要。也许 Fontan 会有些酒。”
That night I had dinner at Fontan’s. We ate in the dining-room and there was a clean tablecloth. We tried the new wine. It was very light and clear and good, and still tasted of the grapes. At the table there were Fontan and Madame and the little boy, André.
那天晚上我在 Fontan 家吃晚饭。我们在餐厅用餐，桌布是干净的。我们尝了新酒。酒很淡、清澈、好喝，仍带着葡萄的味道。桌上有 Fontan 和夫人，还有小男孩安德烈。
‘What did you do to-day?’ Fontan asked. He was an old man with small mine-tired body, a drooping grey moustache, and bright eyes, and was from the Centre near Saint-Etienne.
“你今天干了什么？”Fontan 问。他是个瘦小的老人，身子略显疲惫，灰色胡须下垂，眼睛明亮，来自靠近圣艾蒂安的中部地区。
‘I worked on my book.’
“我在写我的书。”
‘Were your books all right?’ asked Madame.
“你的账本都没问题吗？”夫人问道。
‘He means he writes a book like a writer. Un roman,’ Fontan explained.
“他的意思是他像一个作家那样写书。Un roman，”丰塔恩解释道。
‘Pa, can I go to the show?’ André asked.
“爸爸，我可以去看表演吗？”安德烈问。
‘Sure,’ said Fontan. André turned to me.
“当然可以，”丰塔恩说。安德烈转向我。
‘How old do you think I am? Do you think I look fourteen years old?’ He was a thin little boy, but his face looked sixteen.
“你觉得我多大了？你觉得我看起来像十四岁吗？” 他是个瘦小的男孩，但脸看上去有十六岁。
‘Yes. You look fourteen.’
“是的。你看起来十四岁。”
‘When I go to the show I crouch down like this and try to look small.’ His voice was very high and breaking. ‘If I give them a quarter they keep it all, but if I give them only fifteen cents they let me in all right.’
“我去看演出时就这么蹲着，尽量让自己显得小。” 他的声音很高，带着破裂感。“如果我给他们二十五美分，他们就都要走，但如果我只给十五美分，他们就会让我进来。”
‘I only give you fifteen cents, then,’ said Fontan.
“那我就只给你十五美分，” 方塔恩说。
‘No. Give me the whole quarter. I’ll get it changed on the way.’
“不。把整整一季给我。我回去路上会去换的。”
‘Il faut revenir tout de suite après le show,’ Madame Fontan said.
“Il faut revenir tout de suite après le show，”Madame Fontan 说。
‘I come right back.’ André went out the door. The night was cooling outside. He left the door open and a cool breeze came in.
“我马上回来。”André出了门。外面夜色在变凉。他把门开着，一股凉风吹了进来。
‘Mangez!’ said Madame Fontan. ‘You haven’t eaten anything.’ I had eaten two helpings of chicken and French fried potatoes, three ears of sweet corn, some sliced cucumbers, and two helpings of salad.
“Mangez！”Madame Fontan 说，“你什么都没吃。”我已经吃了两份鸡肉和炸薯条，三穗甜玉米，一些黄瓜片，和两份沙拉。
‘Perhaps he wants some kek,’ Fontan said.
“也许他想要些 kek，”Fontan 说。
‘I should have gotten some kek for him,’ Madame Fontan said. ‘Mangez du fromage. Mangez du crimcheez. Vous n’avez rien mangé. I ought have gotten kek. Americans always eat kek.’
“我本该给他带些 kek 的，”Madame Fontan 说。“Mangez du fromage. Mangez du crimcheez. Vous n’avez rien mangé. 我本应该带 kek。美国人总是吃 kek。”
‘Mais j’ai rudement bien mangé.’
“Mais j’ai rudement bien mangé.”
‘Mangez! Vous n’avez rien mangé. Eat it all. We don’t save anything. Eat it all up.’
“Mangez! Vous n’avez rien mangé. 吃光它。我们什么都不留。全都吃完。”
‘Eat some more salad,’ Fontan said.
“再多吃点沙拉吧，”方坦说。
‘I’ll get some more beer,’ Madame Fontan said. ‘If you work all day in a book-factory you get hungry.’
“我去再拿点啤酒，”方坦夫人说。“如果你整天在书厂里干活，你会饿的。”
‘Elle ne comprend pas que vou êtes écrivain,’ Fontan said. He was a delicate old man who used the slang and knew the popular songs of his period of military service in the end of the 1890’s. ‘He writes the books himself,’ he explained to Madame.
“Elle ne comprend pas que vous êtes écrivain，”方坦说。他是一个体弱的老人，常用他在 19 世纪 90 年代末服役期间学到的俚语和流行歌曲。“他自己写书，”他向夫人解释。
‘You write the books yourself?’ Madame asked.
“你自己写书？”夫人问。
‘Sometimes.’
“有时吧。”
‘Oh!’ she said. ‘Oh ! You write them yourself. Oh! Well, you get hungry if you do that too. Mangez! Je vais chercher de la bière.’
“哦！”她说。“哦！你自己写的。哦！那样的话你也会饿的。Mangez！Je vais chercher de la bière。”
We heard her walking on the stairs to the cellar. Fontan smiled at me. He was very tolerant of people who had not his experience and worldly knowledge.
我们听见她走下通往地窖的楼梯声。Fontan 朝我微笑。他对那些没有他经验和世故的人很宽容。
When André came home from the show we were still sitting in the kitchen and were talking about hunting.
当 André从演出回家时，我们还坐在厨房里，正在谈论狩猎。
‘Labour day we all went to Clear Creek,’ Madame said. ‘Oh, my God, you ought to have been there all right. We all went in the truck. Tout le monde est allé dans le truck. Nous sommes partis le dimanche. C’est le truck de Charley.’
“劳动节那天我们都去了清溪，”夫人说。“哦，我的天，你们本该去的。我们都坐卡车去的。Tout le monde est allé dans le truck. Nous sommes partis le dimanche. C’est le truck de Charley.”
‘On a mangé, on a bu du vin, de la bière, et il y avait aussi un français qui a apporté de l’absinthe,’ Fontan said. ‘Un français de la Californie!’
“我们吃了，喝了葡萄酒，啤酒，还有一个法国人带来了苦艾酒，”Fontan 说。“一个来自加州的法国人！”
‘My God, nous avons chanté. There’s a farmer comes to see what’s the matter, and we give him something to drink, and he stayed with us awhile. There was some Italians come too, and they want to stay with us too. We sung a song about the Italians and they don’t
“我的天，我们唱歌。There's a farmer comes to see what’s the matter, and we give him something to drink, and he stayed with us awhile. 有个农夫来看看发生了什么，我们给了他点东西喝，他在我们这里待了一会儿。还有一些意大利人也来了，他们也想和我们待在一起。我们唱了一首关于意大利人的歌，他们不理解。”
understand it. They didn’t know we didn’t want them, but we didn’t have nothing to do with them, and after a while they went away.’
“他们不知道我们不想要他们，但我们和他们没什么来往，过了一会儿他们就走了。”
‘How many fish did you catch?’
“你抓了多少鱼？”
"Très peu. We went to fish a little while, but then we came back to sing again. Nous avons chanté, vous savez.’
“Très peu。我们去钓了一会儿鱼，但后来又回去继续唱歌。Nous avons chanté，vous savez。”
‘In the night,’ said Madame, ‘toutes les femmes dort dans le truck. Les hommes à côté du feu. In the night I hear Fontan come to get some more wine, and I tell him, Fontan, my God, leave some for to-morrow. To-morrow they won’t have anything to drink, and then they’ll be sorry.’
“夜里，”夫人说，“toutes les femmes dort dans le truck。Les hommes à côté du feu。夜里我听到 Fontan 来再取些酒，我就对他说，Fontan，my God，留一点给明天。明天他们就没得喝了，到时他们会后悔的。”
‘Mais nous avons tout bu,’ Fontan said. ‘Et le lendemain il ne reste rien.’
“Mais nous avons tout bu，”Fontan 说。“Et le lendemain il ne reste rien。”
‘What did you do?’
“你干了什么？”
‘Nous avons pêché sérieusement.’
“Nous avons pêché sérieusement。”
‘Good trout, all right, too. My God, yes. All the same; half-pound one ounce.’
“好鳟鱼，确实不错。天哪，没错。不过；半磅一盎司。”
‘How big?’
“多大？”
‘Half-pound one ounce. Just right to eat. All the same size; halfpound one ounce.’
“半磅一盎司。正好吃。大小都一样；半磅一盎司。”
‘How do you like America?’ Fontan asked me.
“你觉得美国怎么样？”方唐问我。
‘It’s my country, you see. So I like it, because it’s my country. Mais on ne mange pas très bien. D’antan, oui. Mais maintenant, no.’
“这是我的国家，你看。所以我喜欢它，因为它是我的国家。Mais on ne mange pas très bien。过去可以。但现在，不行。”
‘No,’ said Madame. ‘On ne mange pas bien.’ She shook her head. ‘Et aussi, il y a trop de Polack. Quand j’étais petite ma mère m’a dit, “vous mangez comme les Polacks.” Je n’ai jamais compris ce que c’est qu’un Polack. Mais maintenant en Amérique je comprends. Il y a trop de Polack. Et, my God, ils sont sales, les Polacks.’
“不，”太太说。“On ne mange pas bien。”她摇头。“而且，Polack 太多了。小时候我母亲对我说，‘你们吃得像 Polacks。’我从没明白 Polack 是什么。但现在在美国我明白了。Polack 太多了。天哪，他们很脏，Polacks。”
‘It is fine for hunting and fishing,’ I said.
“打猎和钓鱼都很好，”我说。
‘Oui. Ca, c’est le meilleur. La chasse et la pêche,’ Fontan said. ‘Qu’est-ce que vous avez comme fusil?’
“Oui。Ça, c’est le meilleur。La chasse et la pêche，”Fontan 说。“Qu’est-ce que vous avez comme fusil？”
‘A twelve-gauge pump.’
“一支 12 号泵动霰弹枪。”
‘Il cst bon, le pump,’ Fontan nodded his head.
“Il c’est bon, le pump，”Fontan 点点头。
‘Je veux aller à la chasse moi-même,’ André said in his high little boy’s voice.
“Je veux aller à la chasse moi-même，”André用他那尖细的小男孩声音说。
‘Tu ne peux pas,’ Fontan said. He turned to me.
“Tu ne peux pas，”Fontan 说。他转向我。
‘Ils sont des sauvages, les boys, vous savez. Ils sont des sauvages. Ils veulent shooter les uns les autres.’
“Ils sont des sauvages, les boys, vous savez. Ils sont des sauvages. Ils veulent shooter les uns les autres.”
‘Je veux aller tout seul,’ André said, very shrill and excited.
“Je veux aller tout seul，”André说得很刺耳、很激动。
‘You can’t go,’ Madame Fontan said. ‘You are too young.’
“你不能去，”方当夫人说。“你太年轻了。”
‘Je veux aller tout seul,’ André said shrilly. ‘Je veux shooter les rats d’eau.’
“Je veux aller tout seul，”安德烈尖声说。“Je veux shooter les rats d’eau。”
‘What are rats d’eau ?’ I asked.
“什么是 rats d’eau？”我问。
‘You don’t know them? Sure you know them. What they call the muskrats.’
“你不知道它们？你当然知道。就是他们所说的 muskrats（麝鼠）。 ”
André had brought the twenty-two-calibre rifle out from the cupboard and was holding it in his hands under the light.
安德烈把那支.22 口径步枪从橱柜里拿出来，在灯光下把玩着。
‘Ils sont des sauvages,’ Fontan explained. ‘Ils veulent shooter les uns les autres.’
“他们是野蛮人，”丰坦解释道。“他们想互相射杀。”
‘Je veux aller tout seul,’ André shrilled. He looked desperately along the barrel of the gun. ‘Je vous shooter les rats d’eau. Je connais beaucoup de rats d’eau.’
“我想一个人去，”安德烈尖声说。他绝望地沿着枪管看去。“我要射那些水鼠。我认识很多水鼠。”
‘Give me the gun,’ Fontan said. He explained again to me. ‘They’re savages. They would shoot one another.’
“把枪给我，”丰坦说。他又向我解释了一遍。“他们是野蛮人。他们会互相射杀。”
André held tight on to the gun.
安德烈紧紧抓着枪。
‘On peut looker. On ne fait pas de mal. On peut looker.’
“On peut looker. On ne fait pas de mal. On peut looker.”
‘Il est crazy pour le shooting,’ Madame Fontan said. ‘Mais il est trop jeune.’
“Il est crazy pour le shooting，”Fontan 夫人说。“Mais il est trop jeune。”
André put the twenty-two-calibre rifle back in the cupboard.
安德烈把那支二二口径的步枪放回了橱柜。
‘When I’m bigger I’ll shoot the muskrats and the jack-rabbits too,’ he said in English. ‘One time I went out with papa and he shot a jack-rabbit just a little bit and I shot it and hit it.’
“等我长大了我也要打麝鼠和草原兔，”他用英语说。“有一次我跟爸爸出去，他只差一点就打中一只草原兔，我打中了它。”
‘C’est vrai,’ Fontan nodded. ‘Il a tué un jack.’
“C’est vrai，”方塔恩点头说。“他打死了一只 jack。”
‘But he hit it first,’ André said. ‘I want to go all by myself and shoot all by myself. Next year I can do it.’ He went over in a corner and sat down to read a book. I had picked it up when we came into the kitchen to sit after supper. It was a library book - Frank on a Gunboat.
“但他先打中的，”安德烈说。“我想自己一个人去，全自己打。明年我就能做到。”他走到角落坐下看书。我是在我们晚饭后到厨房坐下时拿起这本书的。那是一本图书馆的书——Frank on a Gunboat。
‘Il aime les books,’ Madame Fontan said. ‘But it’s better than to run around at night with the older boys and steal things.’
“Il aime les books，”方塔恩夫人说。“但这总比晚上跟大男孩们一起到处跑去偷东西要好。”
‘Books are all right,’ Fontan said. ‘Monsieur il fait les books.’
“书本倒是没错，”方唐说。“Monsieur il fait les books.”
‘Yes, that’s so, all right. But too many books are bad,’ Madame Fontan said. ‘Ici, c’est une maladie, les books. C’est comme les churches. Ici il y a trop de churches. En France il y a seulement les catholiques et les protestants – et très peu de protestants. Mais ici rien que de churches. Quand j’étais venu ici je disais, oh, my God, what are all the churches?’
“是啊，没错。但书太多就不好了，”方唐夫人说。“Ici, c’est une maladie, les books. C’est comme les churches. Ici il y a trop de churches. En France il y a seulement les catholiques et les protestants – et très peu de protestants. Mais ici rien que de churches. Quand j’étais venu ici je disais, oh, my God, what are all the churches?”
‘C’est vrai,’ Fontan said. ‘Il y a trop de churches.’
“C’est vrai，”方唐说。“Il y a trop de churches.”
‘The other day,’ Madame Fontan said, ‘there was a little French girl here with her mother, the cousin of Fontan, and she said to me, “En Amérique il ne faut pas être catholique. It’s not good to be catholique. The Americans don’t like you to be catholique. It’s like the dry law.” I said to her, “What you going to be? Heh? It’s better to be catholique if you’re catholique.” But she said, “No, it isn’t any good to be catholique in America.” But I think it’s better to be catholique if you are. Ce n’est pas bon de changer sa religion. My God, no.’
“前几天，”方唐夫人说，“有个法国小女孩跟她妈妈一起来，是方唐的表亲，她跟我说，‘En Amérique il ne faut pas être catholique. It’s not good to be catholique. The Americans don’t like you to be catholique. It’s like the dry law.’ 我就跟她说，‘你打算成为什么？Heh? 如果你是天主教，做天主教比较好。’ 可她说，‘不，在美国做天主教不好。’ 但我认为如果你是天主教就最好做天主教。Ce n’est pas bon de changer sa religion. 我的天，不。’
‘You go to the mass here?’
“你在这里去弥撒吗？”
‘No, I don’t go in America, only sometimes in a long while. Mais je reste catholique. It’s no good to change the religion.’
“没有，我在美国不去，只是很久才去一次。Mais je reste catholique。我仍然是天主教徒。信仰换不了。”
‘On dit que Schmidt est catholique,’ Fontan said.
“On dit que Schmidt est catholique，”Fontan 说。
‘On dit, mais on ne sait jamais,’ Madame Fontan said. ‘I don’t think Schmidt is catholique. There’s not many catholique in America.’
“On dit，但谁也说不准，”Madame Fontan 说。“我不认为 Schmidt 是天主教徒。美国天主教的人不多。”
‘We are catholique,’ I said.
“我们是天主教徒，”我说。
‘Sure, but you live in France,’ Madame Fontan said. ‘Je ne crois pas que Schmidt est catholique. Did he ever live in France?’
“当然，可你住在法国，”方丹夫人说。“我不认为 Schmidt 是天主教徒。他曾经住过法国吗？”
‘Les Polacks sont catholiques,’ Fontan said.
“波兰人是天主教徒，”方丹说。
‘That’s true,’ Madame Fontan said. ‘They go to church, then they fight with knives all the way home and kill each other all day Sunday. But they’re not real catholiques. They’re Polack catholiques.’
“那倒是，”方丹夫人说。“他们去教堂，然后一路打刀回家，整天星期天互相残杀。但他们不是真正的天主教徒。他们是波兰式的天主教徒。”
‘All catholiques are the same,’ Fontan said. ‘One catholique is like another.’
“所有天主教徒都一样，”方坦说。“一个天主教徒就像另一个天主教徒。”
‘I don’t believe Schmidt is catholique,’ Madame Fontan said. ‘That’s awful funny if he’s catholique. Moi, je ne crois pas.’
“我不相信施密特是天主教徒，”方坦太太说。“如果他是天主教徒那可真奇怪。我可不信。”
‘Il est catholique,’ I said.
“他是天主教徒，”我说。
‘Schmidt is catholique,’ Madame Fontan mused. ‘I wouldn’t have believed it. My God, il est catholique.’
“施密特是天主教徒，”方坦太太若有所思地说。“我真不敢相信。天哪，他是天主教徒。”
‘Marie va chercher de la bière,’ Fontan said. ‘Monsieur a soif - moi aussi.’
“Marie 去拿啤酒，”Fontan 说。“先生渴了——我也渴。”
‘Yes, all right,’ Madame Fontan said from the next room. She went downstairs and we heard the stairs creaking. André sat reading in the corner. Fontan and I sat at the table, and he poured the beer from the last bottle into our two glasses, leaving a little in the bottom.
“好，好吧，”Fontan 太太从隔壁房间说道。她下了楼，我们听见楼梯在吱吱作响。André坐在角落里看书。Fontan 和我坐在桌旁，他把最后一瓶啤酒倒进我们的两个杯子里，杯底留了点。
‘C’est un bon pays pour la chasse,’ Fontan said. ‘J’aime beaucoup shooter les canards.’
“这里是个打猎的好地方，”Fontan 说。“我很喜欢射击鸭子。”
‘Mais il y a très bonne chasse aussi en France,’ I said.
“但在法国也有很好的猎场，”我说。
‘C’est vrai,’ Fontan said. ‘Nous avons beaucoup de gibier là-bas.’
“C’est vrai，”Fontan 说。“Nous avons beaucoup de gibier là-bas。”
Madame Fontan came up the stairs with the beer bottles in her hands. ‘Il est catholique,’ she said. ‘My God, Schmidt est catholique.’
Fontan 夫人手里拿着啤酒瓶上了楼。“Il est catholique，”她说。“My God，Schmidt est catholique。”
‘You think he’ll be the President?’ Fontan asked.
“你认为他会成为总统吗？”Fontan 问。
‘No,’ I said.
“不，”我说。
The next afternoon I drove out to Fontan’s, through the shade of the town, then along the dusty road, turning up the side road and leaving the car beside the fence. It was another hot day. Madame Fontan came to the back door. She looked like Mrs. Santa Claus, clean and rosy-faced and white-haired, and waddling when she walked.
第二天下午我开车去方唐家，穿过镇上的树荫，然后沿着尘土飞扬的路，拐进旁边的小路，把车停在篱笆边。又是一个炎热的日子。方唐夫人从后门出来。她看起来像圣诞老人的太太，干净、两颊泛红、白发苍苍，走起路来一摇一摆的。
‘My God, hello,’ she said. ‘It’s hot, my God.’ She went back into the house to get some beer. I sat on the back porch and looked through the screen and the leaves of the tree at the heat and, away off, the mountains. There were furrowed brown mountains, and above them three peaks and a glacier with snow that you could see through the trees. The snow looked very white and pure and unreal. Madame Fontan came out and put down the bottles on the table.
“我的天哪，你好，”她说。“热死了，我的天哪。”她回屋去拿啤酒。我坐在后廊，通过纱窗和树叶望着外面的热气，远处是群山。那些是沟壑纵横的褐色山峦，山上有三座峰和一片冰川，你可以透过树木看到雪。雪看上去非常洁白、纯净，像不真实的东西。方唐夫人走出来，把瓶子放在桌上。
‘What you see out there?’
“你在那儿看见什么？”
‘The snow.’
“雪。”
‘C’est jolie, la neige.’
“雪真美。”
‘Have a glass, too.’
“你也喝一杯吧。”
‘All right.’
“好吧。”
She sat down on a chair beside me. ‘Schmidt,’ she said. ‘If he’s the President, you think we get the wine and beer all right?’
她在我旁边的一把椅子上坐下。“施密特，”她说，“如果他是总统，你觉得我们能拿到酒和啤酒吗？”
‘Sure,’ I said. ‘Trust Schmidt.’
“当然，”我说。“信得过施密特。”
‘Already we paid seven hundred fifty-five dollars in fines when they arrested Fontan. Twice the police arrested us and once the governments. All the money we made all the time Fontan worked in the mines and I did washing. We paid it all. They put Fontan in jail. Il n’a jamais fait de mal à personne.’
“当他们抓住冯坦时，我们已经付了七百五十五美元的罚款。警察两次抓我们，政府一次。冯坦在矿里工作的时候我们所有挣的钱我都拿去洗衣服了。我们把钱都交了。他们把冯坦关进监狱。Il n’a jamais fait de mal à personne.”
‘He’s a good man,’ I said. ‘It’s a crime.’
“他是个好人，”我说。“这是罪行。”
'We don’t charge too much money. The wine one dollar a litre. The beer ten cents a bottle. We never sell the beer before it’s good. Lots of places they sell the beer right away when they make it, and then it gives everybody a headache. What’s the matter with that?
“我们不收太多钱。酒一升一美元。啤酒一瓶十美分。我们从不在啤酒还没好之前就卖。很多地方他们刚做出来就卖啤酒，那样会让每个人头疼。这有什么问题吗？”
They put Fontan in jail and they take seven hundred fifty-five dollars.’
“他们把冯坦关进监狱，还要没收七百五十五美元。”
‘It’s wicked,’ I said. ‘Where is Fontan?’
“太残忍了，”我说。“冯坦在哪儿？”
‘He stays with the wine. He has to watch it now to catch it just right,’ she smiled. She did not think about the money any more. ‘Vous savez, il est crazy pour le vin. Last night he brought a little bit home with him, what you drank, and a little bit of the new. The last new. It ain’t ready yet, but he drank a little bit, and this morning he put a little bit in his coffee. Dans son café, vous savez? Il est crazy pour le vin! Il est comme ça. Son pays est comme ça. Where I live in the north they don’t drink any wine. Everybody drinks beer. By where we lived there was a big brewery right near us. When I was a little girl I didn’t like the smell of the hops in the carts. Nor in the fields. Je n’aime pas les houblons. No, my God, not a bit. The man that owns the brewery said to me and my sister to go to the brewery and drink the beer, and then we’d like the hops. That’s true. Then we liked them all right. He had them give us the beer. We liked them all right then. But Fontan, il est crazy pour le vin. One time he killed a jack-rabbit and he wanted me to cook it with a sauce with wine, make a black sauce with wine and butter and mushrooms and onion and everything in it, for the jack. My God, I make the sauce all right, and he eat it all and said, “La sauce est meilleure que le jack.” Dans son pays c’est comme ça. Il y a beaucoup de gibier et de vin. Moi, j’aime les pommes de terre, le saucisson, et la bière. C’est bon, la bière. C’est très bon pour la santé.’
“他守着酒。他现在得盯着它，好在酿得正好时就拿出来，”她笑着说。她不再去想钱的事了。“Vous savez, il est crazy pour le vin。昨晚他带了一点回家，就是你喝的那点，还有一点新的。最后那批新的。还没完全好，但他喝了一点，今早他还往咖啡里放了一点。Dans son café, vous savez? 他对酒着了迷！他就是这样。他的国家就是这样。我在北边住的地方人们不喝葡萄酒。大家都喝啤酒。我们住的地方附近有一家很大的啤酒厂，就在我们旁边。小时候我不喜欢车上啤酒花的气味。田里也不喜欢。Je n’aime pas les houblons。不，天哪，一点也不喜欢。拥有那家啤酒厂的男人对我和我姐姐说去酒厂喝啤酒，然后我们就会喜欢啤酒花。那是真的。后来我们确实喜欢上了。是他们给我们啤酒喝。我们那时候就喜欢了。但 Fontan，il est crazy pour le vin。有一次他杀了一只长耳野兔，他想让我用酒来做酱，为那兔子做一个黑色的酱，用酒、黄油、蘑菇和洋葱什么的，全都放进去，为那只兔子做菜。” 我的天，我把酱汁做好了，他全吃了，还说：“La sauce est meilleure que le jack。”在他那个国家就是这样。那里有很多野味和葡萄酒。我喜欢土豆、香肠和啤酒。啤酒很好。对健康很有好处。’
‘It’s good,’ I said. ‘It and wine too.’
“‘很好，’我说。‘啤酒和葡萄酒也都好。’”
‘You’re like Fontan. But there was a thing here that I never saw. I don’t think you’ve ever seen it either. There were Americans came here and they put whisky in the beer.’
“‘你像 Fontan。但这里有件事我从来没见过。我想你也没见过。以前有美国人来，把威士忌兑在啤酒里。’”
‘No,’ I said.
“不，”我说。
‘Oui. My God, yes, that’s true. Et aussi une femme qui a vomis sur la table!’
“Oui。我的天，是的，那是真的。Et aussi une femme qui a vomis sur la table！”
‘Comment?’
“Comment？”
‘C’est vrai. Elle a vomis sur la table. Et après elle a vomis dans ses shoes. And afterward they come back and say they want to come again and have another party the next Saturday, and I say no, my God, no! When they came I locked the door.’
“C’est vrai。她在桌子上吐了。Et après elle a vomis dans ses shoes。然后他们回来又说下个星期六想再来参加另一个 party，我说不，天哪，不行！他们来的时候我把门锁上了。”
‘They’re bad when they’re drunk.’
“他们喝醉了就很可怕。”
‘In the winter-time when the boys go to the dance they come in
“冬天男孩子们去跳舞的时候，他们回来时……”
the cars and wait outside and say to Fontan, “Hey, Sam, sell us a bottle wine,” or they buy the beer, and then they take the moonshine out of their pockets in a bottle and pour it in the beer and drink it. My God, that’s the first time I ever saw that in my life. They put whisky in the beer. My God, I don’t understand that!’
汽车停在外面等着，对 Fontan 说：“嘿，Sam，卖给我们一瓶酒吧，”或者他们买啤酒，然后从口袋里掏出装在瓶子里的私酿酒，倒进啤酒里喝。我的天，那是我这辈子第一次见到这样的事。他们把威士忌倒进啤酒里。我的天，我不明白！
‘They want to get sick, so they’ll know they’re drunk.’
“他们就是想弄得生病，好让自己知道自己喝醉了。”
‘One time a fellow comes here came to me and said he wanted me to cook them a big supper and they drink one two bottles of wine, and their girls come too, and then they go to the dance. All right, I said. So I made a big supper, and when they come already they drank a lot. Then they put whisky in the wine. My God, yes. I said to Fontan, “On va être malade!” “Oui,” il dit. Then these girls were sick, nice girls, too, all-right girls. They were sick right at the table. Fontan tried to take them by the arm and show them where they could be sick all right in the cabinet, but the fellows said no, they were all right right there at the table.’
“有一次一个人来找我，说要我给他们做一顿丰盛的晚饭，他们喝上一两瓶酒，女孩也一起来，然后他们去跳舞。好啊，我就答应了。所以我做了丰盛的晚饭，他们来的时候已经喝了很多。后来他们在酒里掺了威士忌。天哪，是的。我对 Fontan 说，‘On va être malade!’ 他回答说，‘Oui。’然后那些女孩都吐了，都是好女孩，也都不错。在桌子上就吐了。Fontan 想拉着她们的胳膊，给她们找个地方好好去吐，在橱柜里，但那些男人说不，他们就要在桌子上吐。”
Fontan had come in. ‘When they come again I locked the door. “No,” I said. “Not for hundred fifty dollars.” My God, no.’
Fontan 进来了。“他们再来我就把门锁上。‘不行，’我说。‘哪怕一百五十美元也不行。’天哪，绝不行。”
"There is a word for such people when they do like that, in French,’ Fontan said. He stood looking very old and tired from the heat.
“用法语有个词专门形容这种人，像他们那样做的，”Fontan 说。他站着，看上去因为热又很老又很累。
‘What?’
“什么？”
‘Cochon,’ he said delicately, hesitating to use such a strong word. ‘They were like the cochon. C’est un mot très fort,’ he apologized, 'mais vomir sur la table - ’ he shook his head sadly.
“Cochon，”他小心地说，犹豫着要不要用这么重的词。“他们像 cochon。C’est un mot très fort，”他道歉道，“mais vomir sur la table——”他悲伤地摇摇头。
‘Cochons,’ I said. ‘That’s what they are - cochons. Salauds.’
“Cochons，”我说。“他们就是——cochons。Salauds。”
The grossness of the words was distasteful to Fontan. He was glad to speak of something else.
这些粗俗的话让方当感到厌恶。他很高兴换个话题。
‘Il y a des gens très gentils, très sensibles, qui viennent aussi,’ he said. ‘There are officers from the fort. Very nice men. Good fellas. Everybody that was ever in France they want to come and drink wine. They like wine all right.’
“Il y a des gens très gentils, très sensibles, qui viennent aussi，”他说。“There are officers from the fort。Very nice men。Good fellas。Everybody that was ever in France they want to come and drink wine。They like wine all right。”
‘There was one man,’ Madame Fontan said, ‘and his wife never lets him get out. So he tells her he’s tired, and goes to bed, and when she goes to the show he comes straight down here, sometimes in his pyjamas with just a coat over them. “Maria, some beer,” he says, “for God’s sake.” He sits in his pyjamas and drinks the beer, and then he goes up to the fort and gets back in bed before his wife comes home from the show.’
“有一个人，”方丹夫人说，“他老婆从不让他出门。于是他告诉她自己累了，上床睡觉；等她去看演出时，他就直接跑到这儿来，有时还穿着睡衣外面只套件外衣。‘玛丽亚，来点啤酒，求你了。’他说。他穿着睡衣坐着喝啤酒，然后上到堡垒那儿，再在他老婆从演出回来之前回去上床。”
‘C’est un original,’ Fontan said, ‘mais vraiment gentil. He’s a nice fella.’
“C’est un original，”方丹说，“mais vraiment gentil。他是个古怪的人，但真好。He’s a nice fella.”
‘My God, yes, nice fella all right,’ Madame Fontan said. ‘He’s always in bed when his wife gets back from the show.’
“天哪，是的，确实是个好人，”方丹夫人说。“他老婆从演出回来时他总是在床上。”
‘I have to go away to-morrow,’ I said. ‘To the Crow Reservation. We go there for the opening of the prairie-chicken season.’
“我明天得走，”我说。“去克劳保护区。我们去那里参加草原鸡季的开幕。”
‘Yes? You come back here before you go away. You come back here all right?’
“是吗？你在走之前得回来。你一定要回来，好吗？”
‘Absolutely.’
“当然。”
‘Then the wine will be done,’ Fontan said. ‘We’ll drink a bottle together.’
“那酒就能喝完了，”Fontan 说。“我们一起喝一瓶。”
‘Three bottles,’ Madame Fontan said.
“三瓶，”Madame Fontan 说。
‘I’ll be back,’ I said.
“我会回来的，”我说。
‘We count on you,’ Fontan said.
“我们指望你，”Fontan 说。
‘Good night,’ I said.
“晚安，”我说。
We got in early in the afternoon from the shooting-trip. We had been up that morning since five o’clock. The day before we had had good shooting, but that morning we had not seen a prairie-chicken. Riding in the open car, we were very hot and we stopped to eat our lunch out of the sun, under a tree beside the road. The sun was high and the patch of shade was very small. We ate sandwiches and crackers with sandwich filling on them, and were thirsty and tired, and glad when we finally were out and on the main road back to town. We came up behind a prairie-dog town and stopped the car to shoot at the prairie-dogs with the pistol. We shot two, but then stopped because the bullets that missed glanced off the rocks and the dirt, and sung off across the fields, and beyond the fields there were some trees along a watercourse, with a house, and we did not want to get in trouble from stray bullets going toward the house. So we drove on, and finally were on the road coming down-hill toward the outlying houses of the town. Across the plain we could see the mountains. They were blue that day, and the snow on the high mountains shone like glass. The summer was ending, but the new snow had not yet come to stay on the high mountains; there was only the old sun-melted snow and the ice, and from a long way away it shone very brightly.
我们下午早些时候从打猎回来。那天早上我们从五点就起了。前一天我们打得很好，但那天早上没有看到一只草原鸡。坐在敞篷车里，我们很热，于是停在路旁的一棵树下，躲在树荫里吃午饭。太阳很高，阴影很小。我们吃了三明治和抹了馅料的薄脆饼，口渴又疲倦，终于离开去镇上的主路时感到很高兴。我们从一处土拨鼠镇后面赶来，停下车用手枪向土拨鼠射击。我们射中了两只，但随后停了，因为未命中子弹在岩石和土里擦出声，越飞越远，飞过田地，田地那边沿着水道有几棵树和一所房子，我们可不想因走火把子弹射向房子惹麻烦。于是我们继续开车，终于走在下坡路上向城镇外围的房屋驶去。远处平原对面能看到群山。那天它们是蓝色的，高山上的雪像玻璃一样闪着光。 夏天快要结束，但新雪还未降下并停留在高山上；只有被太阳融化了的旧雪和冰，从很远处看闪着明亮的光。
We wanted something cool and some shade. We were sunburned and our lips blistered from the sun and alkali dust. We turned up
我们想找点凉快和阴影。我们都被晒伤了，嘴唇被太阳和碱尘晒起了水泡。我们转进
the side road to Fontan’s, stopped the car outside the house, and went in. It was cool inside the dining-room. Madame Fontan was alone.
通往 Fontan 家的小路，在屋外把车停下，走了进去。饭厅里很凉快。Fontan 夫人一个人在那里。
‘Only two bottles beer,’ she said. ‘It’s all gone. The new is no good yet.’
“只有两瓶啤酒，”她说。“都卖完了。新货还不行。”
I gave her some birds. ‘That’s good,’ she said. ‘All right. Thanks. That’s good.’ She went out to put the birds away where it was cooler. When we finished the beer I stood up. ‘We have to go,’ I said.
我给了她几只鸟。“那很好，”她说。“好吧。谢谢。那很好。”她出去把鸟放到凉快的地方。我们喝完啤酒我站起来。“我们得走了，”我说。
‘You come back to-night all right? Fontan he’s going to have the wine.’
“你今晚回来，好吗？Fontan 他会准备酒的。”
‘We’ll come back before we go away.’
“我们走之前会回来。”
‘You go away?’
“你们要走？”
‘Yes. We have to leave in the morning.’
“是的。我们明天早上得走。”
‘That’s too bad you go away. You come to-night. Fontan will have the wine. We’ll make a fête before you go.’
“可惜你要走了。你今晚过来吧。Fontan 会有酒。我们在你走之前办个宴会。”
‘We’ll come before we go.’
“我们走之前会来。”
But that afternoon there were telegrams to send, the car to be gone over - a tyre had been cut by a stone and needed vulcanizing - and, without the car, I walked into the town, doing things that had to be done before we could go. When it was supper-time I was too tired to go out. We did not want a foreign language. All we wanted was to go early to bed.
但那天下午有电报要发，汽车要检查——一个轮胎被石子割破，需要硫化修补——没有车的话，我便步行进城，去做一些出发前必须办的事情。到了吃晚饭的时候我累得不想出门。我们不想要外语。我们只想早点上床睡觉。
As I lay in bed before I went to sleep, with all the things of the summer piled around ready to be packed, the windows open and the air coming in cool from the mountains, I thought it was a shame not to have gone to Fontan’s - but in a little while I was asleep. The next day we were busy all morning packing and ending the summer. We had lunch and were ready to start by two o’clock.
当我躺在床上准备睡觉时，夏日的东西堆在四周等着打包，窗户开着，山间吹来的空气凉爽，我觉得没去看望方塔那家真是可惜——但不久我就睡着了。第二天我们一早忙着打包，结束这个夏天。我们吃了午饭，准备两点钟出发。
‘We must go and say good-bye to the Fontans,’ I said.
“我们得去跟方塔那家道别，”我说。
‘Yes, we must.’
“是的，我们得去。”
‘I’m afraid they expected us last night.’
“我怕他们昨晚就等着我们了。”
‘I suppose we could have gone.’
“我想我们本可以去了。”
‘I wish we’d gone.’
“我真希望我们去了。”
We said good-bye to the man at the desk at the hotel, and to Larry and our other friends in the town, and then drove out to Fontan’s. Both Monsieur and Madame were there. They were glad to see us. Fontan looked old and tired.
我们在酒店的接待处向那位男士道别，又向镇上的拉里和其他朋友道别，然后开车去芳丹家。夫人和法兰先生都在。他们很高兴见到我们。法兰看上去又老又累。
‘We thought you would come last night,’ Madame Fontan said.
“我们还以为你们昨晚会来呢，”芳丹太太说。
‘Fontan had three bottles of wine. When you did not come he drank it all up.’
“Fontan 有三瓶酒。你不来时他把都喝了。”
‘We can only stay a minute,’ I said. ‘We just came to say goodbye. We wanted to come last night. We intended to come, but we were too tired after the trip.’
“我们只能待一会儿，”我说。“我们只是来道别。我们本想昨晚来。我们打算来，但旅途太累了。”
‘Go get some wine,’ Fontan said.
“去拿点酒来，”Fontan 说。
‘There is no wine. You drank it all up.’
“没有酒了。你把都喝光了。”
Fontan looked very upset.
丰塔看起来很不高兴。
‘I’ll go get some,’ he said. ‘I’ll just be gone a few minutes. I drank it up last night. We had it for you.’
“我去拿一些，”他说。“我就去一会儿。昨晚我把它喝光了。我们是为你留的。”
‘I knew you were tired. “My God,” I said, “they’re too tired all right to come”,’ Madame Fontan said. ‘Go get some wine, Fontan.’
“我就知道你们累了。‘天哪，’我说，‘他们确实太累了，来不了，’”丰塔夫人说。“去拿点酒来，丰塔。”
‘I’ll take you in the car,’ I said.
“我开车送你去，”我说。
‘All right,’ Fontan said. ‘That way we’ll go faster.’
“好吧，”Fontan 说。“这样我们走得快些。”
We drove down the road in the motor car and turned up a side road about a mile away.
我们坐汽车沿着路开去，大约一英里后转上一条小路。
‘You’ll like that wine,’ Fontan said. ‘It’s come out well. You can drink it for supper to-night.’
“你会喜欢那葡萄酒的，”Fontan 说。“这次酿得不错。今晚可以拿来当晚饭的酒喝。”
We stopped in front of a frame house. Fontan knocked on the door. There was no answer. We went around to the back. The back door was locked too. There were empty tin cans around the back door. We looked in the window. There was nobody inside. The kitchen was dirty and sloppy, but all the doors and windows were tight shut.
我们在一栋木架房子前停下。Fontan 敲了门。没有回应。我们绕到后面去。后门也上了锁。后门周围有空的铁罐。我们从窗户往里看。屋里没人。厨房既脏又凌乱，但所有的门窗都关得严严实实。
‘That son of a bitch. Where is she gone out?’ Fontan said. He was desperate.
“那个婊子养的。她去哪里了？”Fontan 说。他绝望了。
‘I know where I can get a key,’ he said. ‘You stay here.’ I watched him go down to the next house down the road, knock on the door, talk to the woman who came out, and finally come back. He had a key. We tried it on the front door and the back, but it wouldn’t work.
“我知道哪里能拿到钥匙，”他说，“你留在这儿。”我看着他走到路旁的下一户人家，敲门，与出来的女人说话，最后回来了。他拿到了一把钥匙。我们试了前门和后门，但都打不开。
‘That son of a bitch,’ Fontan said. ‘She’s gone away somewhere.’
“那个婊子养的，”Fontan 说。“她不知道跑哪儿去了。”
Looking through the window I could see where the winc was stored. Close to the window you could smell the inside of the house. It smelled sweet and sickish like an Indian house. Suddenly Fontan took a loose board and commenced digging at the earth beside the back door.
透过窗户我能看到那只小酒柜放在哪里。靠近窗户处能闻到屋内的气味。闻起来甜而带点腥，就像印度人的屋子。突然 Fontan 取下一块松动的木板，开始在后门旁的土里挖掘。
‘I can get in,’ he said. ‘Son of a bitch, I can get in.’
“我能进去，”他说。“他妈的，我能进去。”
There was a man in the back yard of the next house doing something to one of the front wheels of an old Ford.
隔壁那所房子后院有一个人在把玩一辆老福特的前轮什么东西。
‘You better not,’ I said. ‘That man will see you. He’s watching.’
“你最好别干，”我说。“那个人会看见你的。他在看着呢。”
Fontan straightened up. ‘We’ll try the key once more,’ he said. We tried the key and it did not work. It turned half-way in either direction.
Fontan 站直了。“我们再试一次钥匙，”他说。我们试了钥匙，但不管用。它在任一方向上都只转到一半。
‘We can’t get in,’ I said. ‘We better go back.’
“我们进不去，”我说。“我们还是回去吧。”
‘I’ll dig up the back,’ Fontan offered.
“我来把后门挖开，”方塔恩提议。
‘No, I wouldn’t let you take the chance.’
“不，我不会让你冒这个险。”
‘I’ll do it.’
“我来做。”
‘No,’ I said. ‘That man would see. Then they would seize it.’
“不，”我说。“那个人会看到。然后他们就会夺走它。”
We went out to the car and drove back to Fontan’s, stopping on the way to leave the key. Fontan did not say anything but swear in English. He was incoherent and crushed. We went in the house.
我们出了车，开回方谭家，路上停车把钥匙放下。方谭一句话也没说，只用英语咒骂。他语无伦次，一副被压垮的样子。我们进了屋。
‘That son of a bitch!’ he said. ‘We couldn’t get the wine. My own wine that I made.’
“那个混蛋！”他说。“我们拿不到葡萄酒。是我自己酿的酒。”
All the happiness went from Madame Fontan’s face. Fontan sat down in a corner with his head in his hands.
方谭太太脸上的所有喜色都消失了。方谭坐在角落里，双手抱着头。
‘We must go,’ I said. ‘It doesn’t make any difference about the wine. You drink to us when we’re gone.’
“我们得走，”我说。“酒的事无所谓。我们走了你就为我们干一杯。”
‘Where did that crazy go?’ Madame Fontan asked.
“那疯子去哪儿了？”方丹夫人问。
‘I don’t know,’ Fontan said. ‘I don’t know where she go. Now you go away without any wine.’
“我不知道，”方丹说。“我不知道她去哪儿了。现在你走了，连酒也没了。”
‘That’s all right,’ I said.
“没关系，”我说。
‘That’s no good,’ Madame Fontan said. She shook her head.
“那可不行，”方坦夫人说。她摇了摇头。
‘We have to go,’ I said. ‘Good-bye and good luck. Thank you for the fine times.’
“我们得走了，”我说。“再见，祝你们好运。谢谢你们的美好时光。”
Fontan shook his head. He was disgraced. Madame Fontan looked sad.
方坦摇了摇头。他蒙受了耻辱。方坦夫人看起来很伤心。
‘Don’t feel bad about the wine,’ I said.
“别为那瓶酒难过，”我说。
‘He wanted you to drink his wine,’ Madame Fontan said. ‘You can come back next year?’
“他是想让你喝他的酒，”丰塔夫人说。“你明年还能回来吗？”
‘No. Maybe the year after.’
“不。也许是后年。”
‘You see?’ Fontan said to her.
“你看见了吗？”丰唐对她说。
‘Good-bye,’ I said. ‘Don’t think about the wine. Drink some for us when we’re gone.’ Fontan shook his head. He did not smile. He knew when he was ruined.
“再见，”我说。“别想着那酒了。我们走后替我们喝点儿。”丰唐摇了摇头。他没有笑。他知道自己已经毁了。
‘That son of a bitch,’ Fontan said to himself.
“那个混蛋，”丰塔纳心里想着。
‘Last night he had three bottles,’ Madame Fontan said to comfort him. He shook his head.
“他昨晚喝了三瓶，”丰塔纳夫人安慰他说。 他摇了摇头。
‘Good-bye,’ he said.
“再见，”他说。
Madame Fontan had tears in her eyes.
丰塔纳夫人眼里含着泪。
‘Good-bye,’ she said. She felt badly for Fontan.
“再见，”她说。她为方坦感到难过。
‘Good-bye,’ we said. We all felt very badly. They stood in the doorway and we got in, and I started the motor. We waved. They stood together sadly on the porch. Fontan looked very old, and Madame Fontan looked sad. She waved to us and Fontan went in the house. We turned up the road.
“再见，”我们说。我们都非常难过。他们站在门口，我们上了车，我发动了引擎。我们挥手告别。他们伤感地站在门廊上。方坦看起来非常苍老，方坦夫人显得很忧伤。她向我们挥手，方坦走进了屋子。我们沿着路转回去。
‘They felt so badly. Fontan felt terribly.’
“他们都很难过。方坦痛苦极了。”
‘We ought to have gone last night.’
“我们昨晚应该走的。”
‘Yes, we ought to have.’
“是的，我们应该去的。”
We were through the town and out on the smooth road beyond, with the stubble of grain-fields on each side and the mountains off to the right. It looked like Spain, but it was Wyoming.
我们已经通过了小镇，驶上了外面的平整公路，两旁是割过的谷田残茬，右侧远处是山峦。看上去像西班牙，其实是怀俄明。
‘I hope they have a lot of good luck.’
“希望他们走运。”
‘They won’t,’ I said, ‘and Schmidt won’t be President either.’
“他们不会的，”我说，“施密特也不会当总统的。”
The cement road stopped. The road was gravelled now and we left the plain and started up between two foot-hills; the road in a curve and commencing to climb. The soil of the hills was red, the sage grew in grey clumps, and as the road rose we could see across the hills and away across the plain of the valley to the mountains. They were farther away now and they looked more like Spain than ever. The road curved and climbed again, and ahead there were some grouse dusting in the road. They flew as we came toward them, their wings beating fast, then sailing in long slants, and lit on the hillside below.
水泥路停止了。路面变成了碎石路，我们离开了平原，开始在两座小山之间上行；道路弯曲着，开始攀升。山地的土壤是红色的，鼠尾草成灰色簇状生长，随着路升高，我们能越过山峦，看见山谷平原一直延伸到远处的群山。山峰现在更远了，看起来比任何时候都更像西班牙。路又弯又爬，前方有几只松鸡在路上扑腾它们的灰尘。我们向它们走来时它们惊飞，翅膀快速扇动，随后长斜线滑翔，停在下面的山坡上。
"They are so big and lovely. They’re bigger than European partridges.’
“它们又大又漂亮。比欧洲的鹧鸪还大。”
‘It’s a fine country for la chasse, Fontan says.’
“Fontan 说这是个适合打猎的好地方。”
‘And when the chasse is gone?’
“那猎趣一去不返怎么办？”
‘They’ll be dead then.’
“到那时他们就死了。”
‘The boy won’t.’
“男孩不会。”
‘There’s nothing to prove he won’t,’ I said.
“没有什么能证明他不会，”我说。
‘We ought to have gone last night.’
“我们本该昨晚就走的。”
‘Oh, yes,’ I said. ‘We ought to have gone.’
“哦，是的，”我说。“我们本该去的。”

THE GAMBLER, THE NUN, AND THE RADIO
赌徒、修女与收音机

They brought them in around midnight and then, all night long, everyone along the corridor heard the Russian.
他们大约在午夜被抬了进来，然后整夜，走廊上的每个人都听见了那个俄罗斯人。
‘Where is he shot?’ Mr. Frazer asked the night nurse.
“他是哪里中枪的？”弗雷泽先生问夜班护士。
‘In the thigh, I think.’
“我想是大腿。”
‘What about the other one?’
“另一个怎么样？”
‘Oh, he’s going to die, I’m afraid.’
“哦，恐怕他要死了。”
‘Where is he shot?’
“他哪里中弹？”
‘Twice in the abdomen. They only found one of the bullets.’
“腹部中两枪。他们只找到了一颗子弹。”
They were both beet workers, a Mexican and a Russian, and they were sitting drinking coffee in an all-night restaurant when someone came in the door and started shooting at the Mexican. The Russian crawled under a table and was hit, finally, by a stray shot fired at the Mexican as he lay on the floor with two bullets in his abdomen. That was what the paper said.
他们俩都是甜菜工人，一个墨西哥人，一个俄国人，正坐在通宵营业的餐馆里喝咖啡，这时有人走进门来朝那个墨西哥人开枪。俄国人爬到桌子底下，最终被朝倒在地上、腹部中两枪的墨西哥人开的一发流弹击中。报纸就是这么写的。
The Mexican told the police he had no idea who shot him. He believed it to be an accident.
墨西哥人告诉警察他完全不知道谁射的。他相信这是个意外。
‘An accident that he fired eight shots at you and hit you twice, there?’
“一个意外是他朝你连开八枪却只中你两枪，对吧？”
‘Si, señor,’ said the Mexican, who was named Cavetano Ruiz.
“是的，先生，”那名墨西哥人说，他叫卡瓦塔诺·鲁伊斯。
‘An accident that he hit me at all, the cabron,’ he said to the interpreter.
“他居然打到我了，那个该死的，”他对翻译说。
‘What does he say?’ asked the detective sergeant, looking across the bed at the interpreter.
“他说什么？”侦探班长望着床对面的翻译问。
‘He says it was an accident.’
“他说是意外。”
‘Tell him to tell the truth, that he is going to die,’ the detective said.
“告诉他实话——他说他要死了，”侦探说道。
‘Na,’ said Cayetano. ‘But tell him that I feel very sick and would prefer not to talk so much.’
“不要，”卡耶塔诺说。“但告诉他我觉得很难受，不想多说。”
‘He says that he is telling the truth,’ the interpreter said. Then, speaking confidently, to the detective, ‘He don’t know who shot him. They shot him in the back.’
“他说他在说真话，”翻译说。然后自信地对侦探说，“他不知道是谁打的。他是从背后被打的。”
‘Yes,’ said the detective. ‘I understand that, but why did the bullets all go in the front?’
“是的，”侦探说。“我明白，但为什么子弹全是打在正面？”
‘Maybe he is spinning around,’ said the interpreter.
“也许他在打转，”翻译说。
‘Listen,’ said the detective, shaking his finger almost at Cayetano’s nose, which projected, waxen yellow, from his dead-man’s face in which his eyes were alive as a hawk’s, ‘I don’t give a damn who shot you, but I’ve got to clear this thing up. Don’t you want the man who shot you to be punished? Tell him that,’ he said to the interpreter.
“听着，”侦探说着几乎把手指戳到卡耶塔诺那突出的、蜡黄色的鼻子上，那鼻子从他那死人般的脸上伸出来，而他的眼睛却像苍鹰一样有生气，“我才不在乎谁打的你，但我得把这事查清楚。你难道不想把打你的人绳之以法吗？把这话告诉他，”他对翻译说。
‘He says to tell who shot you.’
“他说要你告诉是谁打的你。”
‘Mandarlo al carajo,’ said Cayetano, who was very tired.
“Mandarlo al carajo，”卡耶塔诺说，他很累。
‘He says he never saw the fellow at all,’ the interpreter said. ‘I tell you straight they shot him in the back.’
“他说他根本没见过那家伙，”翻译说。“我跟你直说，他们是从背后把他打死的。”
‘Ask him who shot the Russian.’
“问问他谁打死了那个俄罗斯人。”
‘Poor Russian,’ said Cavetano. ‘He was on the floor with his head enveloped in his arms. He started to give cries when they shoot him and he is giving cries ever since. Poor Russian.’
“可怜的俄罗斯人，”卡韦塔诺说。“他倒在地上，头抱在臂弯里。他被打的时候开始喊叫，从那以后一直在喊。可怜的俄罗斯人。”
‘He says some fellow that he doesn’t know. Maybe the same fellow that shot him.’
“他说是个他不认识的人。也许就是那个打他的同一个人。”
‘Listen,’ the detective said. ‘This isn’t Chicago. You’re not a gangster. You don’t have to act like a moving picture. It’s all right to tell who shot you. Anybody would tell who shot them. That’s all right to do. Suppose you don’t tell who he is and he shoots somebody else. Suppose he shoots a woman or a child. You can’t let him get away with that. You tell him,’ he said to Mr. Frazer. ‘I don’t trust that damn interpreter.’
“听着，”侦探说。“这儿不是芝加哥。你又不是匪徒。你不必像电影里那样演。把谁打的告诉出来没关系。任何人都会告诉是谁打的。那样做完全可以。假如你不告诉他是谁，他又去打伤别人怎么办。假如他打伤了一个妇女或孩子。你不能让他逍遥法外。你要告诉他，”他对弗雷泽先生说。“我不信那个该死的翻译。”
‘I am very reliable,’ the interpreter said. Cayetano looked at Mr. Frazer.
“我很可靠，”翻译说。卡耶塔诺看着弗雷泽先生。
‘Listen, amigo,’ said Mr. Frazer. ‘The policeman says that we are not in Chicago but in Hailey, Montana. You are not a bandit and this has nothing to do with the cinema.’
“听着，朋友，”弗雷泽先生说。“警察说我们不是在芝加哥而是在蒙大拿的海利。你不是土匪，这事跟电影一点关系都没有。”
‘I believe him,’ said Cayetano softly. ‘Ya lo creo.’
“我相信他，”卡耶塔诺轻声说。“Ya lo creo.”
‘One can, with honour, denounce one’s assailant. Every one does it here, he says. He says what happens if after shooting you, this man shoots a woman or a child?’
“有人可以光明正大地揭发袭击者。这里人人都这么做，”他说。“他说如果在射伤你之后，这个人去射杀一个女人或小孩，会怎样？”
‘I am not married,’ Cayetano said.
“我没结婚，”卡亚塔诺说。
‘He says any woman, any child.’
“他说任何女人，任何小孩。”
‘The man is not crazy,’ Cayetano said.
“那人不是疯子，”卡亚塔诺说。
‘He says you should denounce him,’ Mr. Frazer finished.
“他说你应该谴责他，”弗雷泽先生说完。
‘Thank you,’ Cayctano said. 'You are of the great translators. I speak English, but badly. I understand it all right. How did you break your leg?’
“谢谢你，”卡雅塔诺说。“你是伟大的翻译者。我会说英语，但说得很差。我都能明白。你是怎么摔断腿的？”
‘A fall off a horse.’
“从马上摔下来的。”
‘What bad luck. I am very sorry. Does it hurt much?’
“真倒霉。非常抱歉。很疼吗？”
‘Not now. At first, yes.’
“不，现在不行。起初，可以。”
‘Listen, amigo,’ Cayetano began, ‘I am very weak. You will pardon me. Also I have much pain; enough pain. It is very possible that I die. Please get this policeman out of here because I am very tired.’ He made as though to roll to one side; then held himself still.
“听着，amigo，”Cayetano 开始说，“我很虚弱。请你原谅我。我也很疼；疼得够呛。很可能我会死。请把这个警察带走吧，因为我太累了。”他说着像要向一边翻过去；然后又停住了。
'I told him everything exactly as you said and he said to tell you, truly, that he doesn’t know who shot him and that he is very weak and wishes you would question him later on, 'Mr. Frazer said.
“我把一切都按你说的原样告诉他了，他让我一定要转告你，他不知道谁开枪打他的，他很虚弱，希望你能稍后再审问他，”Frazer 先生说。
‘He’ll probably be dead later on.’
“他可能过一会儿就死了。”
‘That’s quite possible.’
“那很有可能。”
‘That’s why I want to question him now.’
“这就是我现在要审问他的原因。”
‘Somebody shot him in the back, I tell you,’ the interpreter said.
“我告诉你，一定是有人从背后把他打的，”翻译员说。
‘Oh, for Chrisake,’ the detective sergeant said, and put his notebook in his pocket.
“哦，天哪，”侦探警长说着，把他的笔记本放进口袋。
Outside in the corridor the detective sergeant stood with the interpreter beside Mr. Frazer’s wheeled chair.
走廊外，侦探警司和翻译一同站在弗雷泽先生的轮椅旁。
‘I suppose you think somebody shot him in the back too?’
“我猜你也觉得有人从背后打了他一枪？”
‘Yes,’ Frazer said. ‘Somebody shot him in the back. What’s it to you?’
“是的，”弗雷泽说。“有人从背后打了他。关你什么事？”
‘Don’t get sore,’ the sergeant said. ‘I wish I could talk spick.’
“别生气，”警司说。“我真希望我能说一口流利的英语。”
‘Why don’t you learn?’
“你为什么不学学？”
‘You don’t have to get sore. I don’t get any fun out of asking that spick question. If I could talk spick it would be different.’
“你不用生气。我问那个尖锐的问题并没有什么乐趣。如果我会讲流利的话就不一样了。”
‘You don’t need to talk Spanish,’ the interpreter said. ‘I’m a very reliable interpreter.’
“你不需要讲西班牙语，”翻译说。“我是个非常可靠的翻译。”
‘Oh, for Chrisake,’ the sergeant said. ‘Well, so long. I’ll come up and see you.’
“哦，看在上帝的份上，”中士说。“好吧，回头见。我会过来看看你的。”
‘Thanks. I’m always in.’
“谢谢。我总是在。”
‘I guess you are all right. That was bad luck all right. Plenty bad luck.’
“我想你说得对。那确实是不幸。非常不幸。”
‘It’s coming along good now since he spliced the bone.’
“自从他接好骨头之后，现在进展得不错。”
‘Yes, but it’s a long time. A long, long time.’
“是的，但还需要很久。很、很久。”
‘Don’t let anybody shoot you in the back.’
“别让任何人从背后射你。”
"That’s right,’ he said. ‘That’s right. Well, I’m glad you’re not sore.’
“没错，”他说。“没错。嗯，我很高兴你不生气。”
‘So long,’ said Mr. Frazer.
“再见，”弗雷泽先生说。
Mr. Frazer did not see Cayetano again for a long time, but each morning Sister Cecilia brought news of him. He was so uncomplaining she said and he was very bad now. He had peritonitis and they thought he could not live. Poor Cayetano, she said. He had such beautiful hands and such a fine face and he never complains. The odour, now, was really terrific. He would point toward his nose with one finger and smile and shake his head, she said. He felt badly about the odour. It embarrassed him, Sister Cecilia said. Oh, he was such a fine patient. He always smiled. He wouldn’t go to confession to Father but he promised to say his prayers, and not a Mexican had been to see him since he had been brought in. The Russian was going out at the end of the week. I could never feel anything about the Russian, Sister Cecilia said. Poor fellow, he suffered too. It was a greased bullet and dirty and the wound infected, but he made so much noise and then I always like the bad ones. That Cayetano, he’s a bad one. Oh, he must really be a bad one, a thoroughly bad one, he’s so fine and delicately made and he’s never done any work with his hands. He’s not a beet worker. I know he’s not a beet worker. His hands are as smooth and not a callous on them. I know he’s a bad one of some sort. I’m going down and pray for him now. Poor Cayetano, he’s having a dreadful time and he doesn’t make a sound. What did they have to shoot him for? Oh, that poor Cayetano! I’m going right down and pray for him.
