弗雷泽先生很久没有再见到卡耶塔诺，但每天早晨塞西莉亚修女都会带来他的消息。她说他一点也不抱怨，现在病得很重。他得了腹膜炎，大家认为他活不成了。可怜的卡耶塔诺，她说。他的手多么漂亮，脸多么俊秀，他从不抱怨。现在的气味，真是可怕。他总是用一根手指指向自己的鼻子，笑着摇头，她说。他为那股气味很难受。塞西莉亚修女说，这让他很尴尬。哦，他是个多么好的病人。他总是微笑。他不肯去向神父忏悔，但答应会祷告，自从被送进来后，就没有墨西哥人来探望他。那个俄罗斯人将在本周末出院。我从来对那个俄罗斯人没有什么感觉，塞西莉亚修女说。可怜的家伙，他也受了苦。是被油污弹打伤又脏，伤口感染，但他叫得很厉害，而我总是喜欢那些坏的病人。那个卡耶塔诺，他是个坏人。哦，他一定真是个坏人，彻头彻尾的坏人，他长得那么秀气那么娇嫩，从来没用手干过活。他不是甜菜工人。我知道他不是甜菜工人。 他的手又光滑，手上没有一处茧。我知道他有某种毛病。我现在要下去为他祈祷。可怜的卡耶塔诺，他正遭受折磨却一句也不出声。他们为什么非得把他打死不可？哦，可怜的卡耶塔诺！我现在就下去为他祈祷。
She went right down and prayed for him.
她走下去为他祈祷。
In that hospital a radio did not work very well until it was dusk. They said it was because there was so much ore in the ground or something about the mountains, but anyway it did not work well at all until it began to get dark outside; but all night it worked beautifully and when one station stopped you could go farther west and pick up another. The last one that you could get was Seattle, Washington, and due to the difference in time, when they signed off at four o’clock in the morning it was five o’clock in the morning in the hospital; and at six o’clock you could get the morning revellers in Minneapolis. That was on account of the difference in time, too, and Mr. Frazer used to like to think of the morning revellers arriving at the studio and picture how they would look getting off a street car before daylight in the morning carrying their instruments. Maybe that was wrong and they kept their instruments at the place
在那家医院里收音机一直直到黄昏才工作得比较好。他们说是因为地下有太多矿石，或者是山脉的缘故，总之在外面开始天暗之前收音机根本不好使；但整晚它都工作得很漂亮，一个台停了就可以往西再找另一个。最后能接到的一个台是华盛顿州的西雅图，因时差关系，他们凌晨四点签播下线时医院里已是凌晨五点；而到了六点你又能接到明尼阿波利斯的早晨狂欢者。这也是因为时差，弗雷泽先生常常喜欢想象那些早晨的狂欢者来到广播站，并想象他们清晨天未亮从电车上下来携带着乐器的样子。也许他想错了，他们把乐器存放在那地方不拿出来。
they revelled, but he always pictured them with their instruments. He had never been in Minneapolis and believed he probably would never go there, but he knew what it looked like that early in the morning.
他们沉浸其中，但他总是想象着他们抱着乐器的样子。他从未去过明尼阿波利斯，并且认为自己大概也永远不会去那里，但他知道那座城市清晨的模样。
Out of the window of the hospital you could see a field with tumbleweed coming out of the snow, and a bare clay butte. One morning the doctor wanted to show Mr. Frazer two pheasants that were out there in the snow, and pulling the bed toward the window, the reading light fell off the iron bedstead and hit Mr. Frazer on the head. This does not sound so funny now but it was very funny then. Everyone was looking out the window, and the doctor, who was a most excellent doctor, was pointing at the pheasants and pulling the bed toward the window, and then, just as in a comic section, Mr. Frazer was knocked out by the leaded base of the lamp hitting the top of his head. It seemed the antithesis of healing or whatever people were in the hospital for, and everyone thought it was very funny, as a joke on Mr. Frazer and on the doctor. Everything is much simpler in a hospital, including the jokes.
从医院的窗外可以看到一片长着风滚草、雪已露出的田野，还有一个光秃的粘土小丘。一天早晨，医生想给弗雷泽先生看窗外雪地里的两只雉，便把病床往窗边拉，结果床上的阅读灯从铁床架上掉下来，砸在了弗雷泽先生的头上。现在听起来也许不太好笑，但当时确实非常滑稽。每个人都在朝窗外看，那个医生——是个极好的医生——一边指着雉，一边把床往窗边拉，结果就像漫画里一样，灯的铅质底座砸中了他的头顶，把弗雷泽先生敲晕了。这似乎与疗愈或人们住院的目的完全相反，大家都觉得很好笑，把这事当作对弗雷泽先生和对医生的一个玩笑。在医院里一切都简单得多，包括笑话。
From the other window, if the bed was turned, you could see the town, with a little smoke above it, and the Dawson mountains looking like real mountains with the winter snow on them. Those were the two views since the wheeled chair had proved to be premature. It is really best to be in bed if you are in a hospital: since two views, with time to observe them, from a room the temperature of which you control, are much better than any number of views seen for a few minutes from hot, empty rooms that are waiting for someone else, or just abandoned, which you are wheeled in and out of. If you stay long enough in a room the view, whatever it is, acquires a great value and becomes very important and you would not change it, not even by a different angle. Just as, with the radio, there are certain things that you become fond of, and you welcome them and resent the new things. The best tunes they had that winter were ‘Sing Something Simple’, ‘Singsong Girl’ and ‘Little White Lies’. No other tunes were as satisfactory, Mr. Frazer felt. ‘Betty Co-ed’ was a good tune too, but the parody of the words which came unavoidably into Mr. Frazer’s mind, grew so steadily and increasingly obscene that there being no one to appreciate it, he finally abandoned it and let the song go back to football.
从另一扇窗户看去，如果把床转过来，就能看到镇子，镇子上方飘着一点烟，Dawson 山脉像真山一样，披着冬雪。自从那辆有轮子的椅子被证明是为时过早后，这就是两处景致。住院时最好还是躺在床上：因为在你能控制室温的房间里，有时间去观察的两处景致，要比从闷热、空荡、等待别人的或已被弃置的房间里被推进推出、只看几分钟的任何数量的景致好得多。如果你在一个房间里呆得够久，不论景致是什么，它都会获得巨大的价值，变得非常重要，你不会想换掉它，甚至不会想换一个不同的角度。就像收音机一样，有些东西你会喜欢上，你会欢迎它们并对新事物产生反感。那年冬天他们听到的最好的曲子是《Sing Something Simple》、《Singsong Girl》和《Little White Lies》。没有别的曲子能让 Frazer 先生感到满意。《Betty Co-ed》也是一首好曲子，但伴随而来的对歌词的戏仿不可避免地出现在 Frazer 先生脑中。 弗雷泽的思想变得如此持续且越来越下流，以至于没有人能够欣赏，他最终放弃了，让那首歌又回到足球上去了。
About nine o’clock in the morning they would start using the X-ray machine, and then the radio, which, by then, was only getting Hailey, became useless. Many people in Hailey who owned radios protested about the hospital’s X-ray machine which ruined their morning reception, but there was never any action taken, although many felt it was a shame the hospital could not use their machine at a time when people were not using their radios.
大约在早上九点，他们会开始使用 X-ray 机，然后收音机——到那时只能收到海利的信号——就变得没用了。许多在海利拥有收音机的人抱怨医院的 X-ray 机破坏了他们的晨间接收，但从未有任何行动采取，尽管许多人觉得很可惜医院不能在大家不使用收音机的时候使用他们的机器。
About the time when it became necessary to turn off the radio Sister Cecilia came in.
差不多到了不得不关掉收音机的时候，修女塞西莉亚走了进来。
‘How’s Cayetano, Sister Cecilia?’ Mr. Frazer asked.
“塞雅塔诺怎么样，塞西莉亚修女？”弗雷泽先生问道。
‘Oh, he’s very bad.’
“哦，他很糟。”
‘Is he out of his head?’
“他神志不清吗？”
‘No, but I’m afraid he’s going to die.’
“不，只是我怕他快要死了。”
‘How are you?’
“你怎么样？”
‘I’m very worried about him, and do you know that absolutely no one has come to see him? He could die just like a dog for all those Mexicans care. They’re really dreadful.’
“我很担心他，你知道吗，竟然一个人都没来探望他？对那些墨西哥人来说，他就像条狗似的随时可以死去。他们真可怕。”
‘Do you want to come up and hear the game this afternoon?’
“你想上来听今天下午的比赛吗？”
‘Oh, no,’ she said. ‘I’d be too excited. I’ll be in the chapel praying.’
“哦，不，”她说。“我会太激动的。我会在小礼拜堂里祈祷。”
‘We ought to be able to hear it pretty well,’ Mr. Frazer said. ‘They’re playing out on the coast and the difference in time will bring it late enough so we can get it all right.’
“我们应该能听得很清楚，”弗雷泽先生说。“他们在海岸那边比赛，时差会让比赛晚一些开始，这样我们就能完整地听完。”
‘Oh, no. I couldn’t do it. The world series nearly finished me. When the Athletics were at bat I was praying right out loud: “Oh, Lord, direct their batting eyes! Oh, Lord, may he hit one! Oh, Lord, may he hit safely!” Then when they filled the bases in the third game, you remember, it was too much for me. “Oh, Lord, may he hit it out of the lot! Oh, Lord, may he drive it clean over the fence!” Then you know when the Cardinals would come to bat it was simply dreadful. “Oh, Lord, may they not see it! Oh, Lord, don’t let them even catch a glimpse of it. Oh, Lord, may they fan!” And this game is even worse. It’s Notre Dame. Our Lady. No, I’ll be in the chapel. For Our Lady. They’re playing for Our Lady. I wish you’d write something sometime for Our Lady. You could do it. You know you could do it, Mr. Frazer.’
“哦，不。我可做不到。世界大赛差点把我折腾死。运动家队打击的时候我都要当着声儿祈祷：‘哦，主啊，引导他们的击球目光！哦，主啊，愿他击中一个！哦，主啊，愿他安打！’然后你还记得第三场他们把垒都占满的时候，这对我来说太过分了。‘哦，主啊，愿他把球打出场外！哦，主啊，愿他把球直接打过围栏！’然后你知道红雀队一轮到他们上场时简直可怕。‘哦，主啊，愿他们看不见球！哦，主啊，别让他们连一眼都瞧见。哦，主啊，愿他们被三振！’而这场比赛更糟。是圣母大学。我们的圣母。不，我要去小礼拜堂。为圣母。他们是在为圣母而战。我希望你有时能为圣母写点什么。你能做到的。你知道你能做到，弗雷泽先生。”
‘I don’t know anything about her that I could write. It’s mostly been written already,’ Mr. Frazer said. ‘You wouldn’t like the way I write. She wouldn’t care for it either.’
“我对她不了解，没什么可写的。关于她的东西大多已经有人写过了，”弗雷泽先生说。“你不会喜欢我写的方式。她也不会喜欢。”
‘You’ll write about her sometime,’ Sister said. ‘I know you will. You must write about Our Lady.’
“你迟早会写她的，”修女说。“我知道你会的。你必须写我们的圣母。”
‘You’d better come up and hear the game.’
“你最好上去听比赛。”
‘It would be too much for me. No, I’ll be in the chapel doing what I can.’
“那对我来说太过分了。不，我会在礼拜堂里尽我所能。”
That afternoon they had been playing about five minutes when a probationer came into the room and said, ‘Sister Cecilia wants to know how the game is going?’
那天下午他们才打了大约五分钟，一个见习修女走进房间，说： “塞西莉亚修女想知道比赛进行得怎么样？”
“Tell her they have a touchdown already.”
“告诉她他们已经达阵了。”
In a little while the probationer came into the room again.
过了一会儿，见习护士又进了房间。
‘Tell her they’re playing them off their feet,’ Mr. Frazer said.
“告诉她他们把对手打得落花流水，”弗雷泽先生说。
A little later he rang the bell for the nurse who was on floor duty. ‘Would you mind going down to the chapel or sending word to Sister Cecilia that Notre Dame has them fourteen to nothing at the end of the first quarter and that it’s all right. She can stop praying.’
不久他按铃叫了值楼层的护士。“你是否介意下去礼拜堂，或是告诉塞西莉亚修女，圣母大学在第一节结束时以十四比零领先，没事了。她可以停止祈祷了。”
In a few minutes Sister Cecilia came into the room. She was very excited. ‘What does fourteen to nothing mean? I don’t know anything about this game. That’s a nice safe lead in baseball. But I don’t know anything about football. It may not mean a thing. I’m going right back down to the chapel and pray until it’s finished.’
几分钟后，修女塞西莉亚走进房间。她非常激动。“十四比零是什么意思？我对这场比赛一点也不懂。那在棒球里是个稳妥的领先分。但我对橄榄球一窍不通。也许这根本没什么用。我现在就要回礼拜堂祈祷，直到结束。”
‘They have them beaten,’ Frazer said. ‘I promise you. Stay and listen with me.’
“他们已经稳赢了，”弗雷泽说。“我向你保证。留下来和我一起听吧。”
‘No. No. No. No. No. No. No,’ she said. ‘I’m going right down to the chapel to pray.’
“不。不。不。不。不。不。不会的，”她说。“我现在就要回礼拜堂祈祷。”
Mr. Frazer sent down word whenever Notre Dame scored, and finally, when it had been dark a long time, the final result.
每当 Notre Dame 得分，弗雷泽先生就有人下来通报，最后，当天色已深很久，才报出最终结果。
‘How’s Sister Cecilia?’
“西西里亚修女怎么样了？”
‘They’re all at chapel,’ she said.
“他们都在礼拜堂，”她说。
The next morning Sister Cecilia came in. She was very pleased and confident.
第二天早晨西西里亚修女进来了。她非常高兴且自信。
‘I knew they couldn’t beat Our Lady,’ she said. ‘They couldn’t. Cayetano’s better too. He’s much better. He’s going to have visitors. He can’t see them yet, but they are going to come and that will make him feel better and know he’s not forgotten by his own people. I went down and saw that O’Brien boy at Police Headquarters and told him that he’s got to send some Mexicans up to see poor Cayctano. He’s going to send some this afternoon. Then that poor man will fcel better. It’s wicked the way no one has come to see him.’
“我就知道他们斗不过圣母，”她说，“他们斗不过的。卡耶塔诺也好了。好得多了。他要有人来看他。他还不能见人，但他们会来，这会让他感觉好些，也知道他自己的同胞没有忘记他。我下去在警察局见了那个奥布赖恩小伙子，告诉他必须派些墨西哥人上来看看可怜的卡耶塔诺。他今天下午会派一些来的。那可怜的人就会感觉好些。没有人来看他真是太邪恶了。”
That afternoon about five o’clock three Mexicans came into the room.
那天下午大约五点，三个墨西哥人走进房间。
‘Can one?’ asked the biggest one, who had very thick lips and was quite fat.
“可以吗？”最大个的那人问，他嘴唇很厚，身材相当肥胖。
‘Why not?’ Mr. Frazer answered. ‘Sit down, gentlemen. Will you take something?’
“为什么不可以？”弗雷泽先生回答道。“请坐，诸位。要点什么吗？”
‘Many thanks,’ said the big one.
“非常感谢，”那个大个儿说。
‘Thanks,’ said the darkest and smallest one.
“谢谢，”最黑、最瘦小的那个说。
‘Thanks, no,’ said the thin one. ‘It mounts to my head.’ He tapped his head.
“不用了，谢谢，”瘦高的那个说。“这会冲上我的头。”他敲了敲自己的头。
The nurse brought some glasses. ‘Please give them the bottle,’ Frazer said. ‘It is from Red Lodge,’ he explained.
护士端来一些眼镜。“请把瓶子给他们，”弗雷泽说。“这是来自 Red Lodge 的，”他解释道。
‘That of Red Lodge is the best,’ said the big one. ‘Much better than that of Big Timber.’
“Red Lodge 的那个最好，”高大的那个说。“比 Big Timber 的好得多。”
‘Clearly,’ said the smallest one, ‘and costs more too.’
“显然，”个子最小的说，“而且更贵。”
‘In Red Lodge it is of all prices,’ said the big one.
“在红屋镇什么价都有，”个子大的说。
‘How many tubes has the radio?’ asked the one who did not drink.
“不喝酒的那位问：‘这台收音机有多少只电子管？’”
‘Seven.’
“七只。”
‘Very beautiful,’ he said. ‘What does it cost?’
“非常漂亮，”他说。“多少钱？”
‘I don’t know,’ Mr. Frazer said. ‘It is rented.’
“我不知道，”弗雷泽先生说。“这是租来的。”
‘You gentlemen are friends of Cayetano?’
“你们是卡亚塔诺的朋友吗？”
‘No,’ said the big one. ‘We are friends of he who wounded him.’
“不，”个子高的说。“我们是伤了他那个人的朋友。”
‘We were sent here by the police,’ the smallest one said.
“我们是被警察派来的，”最小的那个说道。
‘We have a little place,’ the big one said. ‘He and I,’ indicating the one who did not drink. ‘He has a little place too,’ indicating the small, dark one. ‘The police tell us we have to come-so we come.’
“我们有一个小地方，”高个儿说。“他和我，”指着那个不喝酒的。“他也有一个小地方，”指着那个又矮又黑的。“警察叫我们来——所以我们就来了。”
‘I am very happy you have come.’
“你们来了我很高兴。”
‘Equally,’ said the big one.
“彼此彼此，”高个儿说。
‘Will you have another little cup?’
“你再来一小杯吗？”
‘Why not?’ said the big one.
“为什么不？”高个的说。
‘With your permission,’ said the smallest one.
“征得你的许可，”最小的说。
‘Not me,’ said the thin one. ‘It mounts to my head.’
“我不要，”瘦的说。“这会冲上我的头。”
‘It is very good,’ said the smallest one.
“很好，”最小的那个说。
‘Why not try some?’ Mr. Frazer asked the thin one. ‘Let a little mount to your head.’
“为什么不试一试？”弗雷泽先生问瘦高的那个。“让点酒上头。”
‘Afterwards comes the headache,’ said the thin one.
“之后就是头痛，”瘦高的那个说。
‘Could you not send friends of Cayetano to see him?’ Frazer asked.
“你不能派卡耶塔诺的朋友去看看他吗？”弗雷泽问。
‘He has no friends.’
“他没有朋友。”
‘Every man has friends.’
“每个人都有朋友。”
‘This one, no.’
“这个没有。”
‘What does he do?’
“他是做什么的？”
‘He is a card-player.’
“他是个赌徒。”
‘Is he good?’
“他会玩吗？”
‘I believe it.’
“我相信。”
‘From me,’ said the smallest one, ‘he won one hundred and eighty dollars. Now there is no longer one hundred and eighty dollars in the world.’
“跟我，”最矮的那个说，“他赢了一百八十美元。现在世界上再也没有一百八十美元了。”
‘From me,’ said the thin one, ‘he won two hundred and eleven dollars. Fix yourself on that figure.’
“从我这儿，”瘦子说，“他赢了两百一十一美元。就定这个数字吧。”
‘I never played with him,’ said the fat one.
“我从没和他一起玩过，”胖子说。
‘He must be very rich,’ Mr. Frazer suggested.
“他一定很有钱，”弗雷泽先生建议道。
‘He is poorer than we,’ said the little Mexican. ‘He has no more than the shirt on his back.’
“小个墨西哥人说，‘他比我们还穷。他身上只有一件衬衫。’”
‘And that shirt is of little value now,’ Mr. Frazer said. ‘Perforated as it is.’
“那件衬衫现在也没什么价值了，”弗雷泽先生说。“都被穿孔了。”
‘Clearly.’
“显然如此。”
‘The one who wounded him was a card-player?’
“伤他的人是个打牌的？”
‘No, a beet worker. He has had to leave town.’
“不，是个甜菜工人。他不得不离开城里。”
‘Fix yourself on this,’ said the smallest one. ‘He was the best guitar player ever in this town. The finest.’
“记住这一点，”最小的那个说。“他曾是这城里最好的吉他手。最出色的。”
‘What a shame.’
“真可惜。”
‘I believe it,’ said the biggest one. ‘How he could touch the guitar.’
“我信得过，”最大的那个说。“他弹吉他的手法真是了得。”
‘There are no good guitar players left?’
“难道就没有好吉他手了吗？”
‘Not the shadow of a guitar player.’
“连个吉他手的影子都没有。”
‘There is an accordion player who is worth something,’ the thin man said.
“有个手风琴手还行，”瘦子说。
‘There are a few who touch various instruments,’ the big one said. ‘You like music?’
“大个儿的说：‘有几个会碰几种乐器，你喜欢音乐吗？’”
‘How would I not?’
“我怎么会不喜欢？”
‘We will come one night with music? You think the sister would allow it? She seems very amiable.’
“我们会在某个有音乐的夜晚来吗？你认为修女会允许吗？她看起来很和蔼。”
‘I am sure she would permit it when Cayetano is able to hear it.’
“我确定当 Cayetano 能听到的时候她会允许的。”
‘Is she a little crazy?’ asked the thin one.
“她有点疯了吗？”瘦的人问道。
‘Who?’
“谁？”
‘That sister.’
“那个修女。”
‘No,’ Mr. Frazer said. ‘She is a fine woman of great intelligence and sympathy.’
“不是，”弗雷泽先生说。“她是位聪明又富有同情心的好女人。”
‘I distrust all priests, monks and sisters,’ said the thin one.
“我不信任所有的神父、修士和修女，”瘦高的那个说。
‘He had bad experiences when a boy,’ the smallest one said.
“他小时候有不好的经历，”个子最小的那个说。
‘I was an acolyte,’ the thin one said proudly. ‘Now I believe in nothing. Neither do I go to mass.’
“我曾是个侍从，”瘦子自豪地说。“现在我什么都不信了。我也不去弥撒。”
‘Why? Does it mount to your head?’
“为什么？酒上头了吗？”
‘No,’ said the thin one. ‘It is alcohol that mounts to my head. Religion is the opium of the poor.’
“不，”瘦子说。“上我的头的是酒。宗教是穷人的鸦片。”
‘I thought marijuana was the opium of the poor,’ Frazer said.
“我还以为大麻才是穷人的鸦片，”Frazer 说。
‘Did you ever smoke opium?’ the big one asked.
“你抽过鸦片吗？”高个子问。
‘No.’
“没有。”
‘Nor I,’ he said. ‘It seems it is very bad. One commences and cannot stop. It is a vice.’
“我也没有，”他说。“好像很糟。一旦开始就停不下来。是一种恶习。”
‘Like religion,’ said the thin one.
“像宗教，”瘦子说。
‘This one,’ said the smallest Mexican, ‘is very strong against religion.’
“这个人，”最小的墨西哥人说，“对宗教非常反感。”
‘It is necessary to be very strong against something,’ Mr. Frazer said politely.
“人总需要对什么事有强烈的反对，”弗雷泽先生礼貌地说。
‘I respect those who have faith even though they are ignorant,’ the thin one said.
“我尊重那些有信仰即便无知的人，”瘦高的那位说。
‘Good,’ said Mr. Frazer.
“好，”弗雷泽先生说。
‘What can we bring you?’ asked the big Mexican. 'Do you lack for anything?’
“我们给你拿点什么？”那个魁梧的墨西哥人问道。“你还有什么需要吗？”
‘I would be glad to buy some beer if there is good beer.’
“如果有好啤酒的话，我很愿意买些啤酒。”
‘We will bring beer.’
“我们会拿来啤酒的。”
‘Another copita before you go?’
“在你走之前再来一杯小酒吗？”
‘It is very good.’
“这非常好。”
‘We are robbing you.’
“我们在抢劫你。”
‘I can’t take it. It goes to my head. Then I have a bad headache and sick at the stomach.’
“我受不了。它上头。接着我就头疼，胃也难受。”
‘Good-bye, gentlemen.’
“再见，先生们。”
‘Good-bye and thanks.’
“再见，谢谢你。”
They went out and there was supper and then the radio, turned to be as quiet as possible and still be heard, and the stations finally signing off in this order: Denver, Salt Lake City, Los Angeles and Seattle. Mr. Frazer received no picture of Denver from the radio. He could see Denver from the Denver Post, and correct the picture from the Rocky Mountain News. Nor did he ever have any feel of
他们出去了，吃了晚饭，然后收音机响起，调到能尽量安静又还能听见的音量，电台最终按这个顺序停播：丹佛、盐湖城、洛杉矶和西雅图。弗雷泽先生没有从收音机上收到丹佛的影像。他可以从《丹佛邮报》上看到丹佛，并从《落基山新闻》上校正那幅影像。他也从未对...
Salt Lake City or Los Angeles from what he heard from those places. All he felt about Salt Lake City was that it was clean, but dull, and there were too many ballrooms mentioned in too many big hotels for him to see Los Angeles. He could not feel it for the ballrooms. But Seattle he came to know very well, the taxicab company with the big white cabs (each cab equipped with radio itself) he rode in every night out to the roadhouse on the Canadian side where he followed the course of parties by the musical selections they phoned for. He lived in Seattle from two o’clock on, each night, hearing the pieces that all the different people asked for, and it was as real as Minneapolis, where the revellers left their beds each morning to make that trip down to the studio. Mr. Frazer grew very fond of Seattle, Washington.
从那些地方听到的消息看，不是盐湖城就是洛杉矶。他对盐湖城的感觉只是干净，但沉闷，而且有太多大酒店里提到的舞厅，以至于他无法体会洛杉矶。他对舞厅没有感觉。但西雅图他却非常熟悉，那家有着大白色出租车的德士公司（每辆车都装有无线电），他每晚都坐那家的车到加拿大一侧的路边酒馆，按人们打电话点播的乐曲来追踪队伍的动向。他从每晚两点开始住在西雅图，听着各种不同的人点的曲目，那种感觉就像明尼阿波利斯一样真实，狂欢者们每天早晨起床去录音室的路程。弗雷泽先生非常喜欢华盛顿州的西雅图。
The Mexicans came and brought beer but it was not good beer. Mr. Frazer saw them but he did not feel like talking and when they went he knew they would not come again. His nerves had become tricky and he disliked seeing people while he was in this condition. His nerves went bad at the end of five weeks, and while he was pleased they lasted that long yet he resented being forced to make the same experiment when he already knew the answer. Mr. Frazer had been through this all before. The only thing which was new to him was the radio. He played it all night long, turned so low he could barely hear it, and he was learning to listen to it without thinking.
墨西哥人来了，带来了啤酒，但那并不是好啤酒。弗雷泽先生看见他们，但他并不想说话，等他们走了他就知道他们不会再来。他的神经变得敏感，在这种状态下他不喜欢见人。他的神经在五周结束时出了问题，虽然他很高兴它们能坚持那么久，但他对被迫在已知答案的情况下再做同样的试验心存怨恨。弗雷泽先生以前经历过这一切。对他来说唯一新鲜的是收音机。他整夜开着，调得极低，几乎听不见，他正在学着不去思考地听它。
Sister Cecilia came into the room about ten o’clock in the morning on that day and brought the mail. She was very handsome, and Mr. Frazer liked to see her and to hear her talk, but the mail, supposedly coming from a different world, was important. However, there was nothing in the mail of any interest.
那天上午十点左右，塞西莉亚修女走进房间，带来了邮件。她很漂亮，弗雷泽先生喜欢看见她、听她讲话，但那些据说来自另一个世界的邮件很重要。然而，邮件里没有任何有趣的东西。
‘You look so much better,’ she said. ‘You’ll be leaving us soon.’
“你看起来好多了，”她说。“你很快就要离开我们了。”
‘Yes,’ Mr. Frazer said. ‘You look very happy this morning.’
“是的，”弗雷泽先生说。“你今天早上看起来很高兴。”
‘Oh, I am. This morning I feel as though I might be a saint.’
“哦，是的。今天早晨我感觉自己好像可能会成为圣人。”
Mr. Frazer was a little taken aback at this.
弗雷泽先生对此有些吃惊。
‘Yes,’ Sister Cecilia went on. "That’s what I want to be. A saint. Ever since I was a little girl I’ve wanted to be a saint. When I was a girl I thought if I renounced the world and went into the convent I would be a saint. That was what I wanted to be and that was what
“是的，”塞西莉亚修女继续说。“那就是我想成为的。一个圣人。自从我还是个小女孩起我就想成为圣人。小时候我以为只要我舍弃尘世，进修道院我就会成为圣人。那是我想成为的，也是我
I thought I had to do to be one. I expected I would be a saint. I was absolutely sure I would be one. For just a moment I thought I was one. I was so happy and it seemed so simple and easy. When I awoke in the morning I expected I would be a saint, but I wasn’t. I’ve never become one. I want so to be one. All I want is to be a saint. That is all I’ve ever wanted. And this morning I feel as though I might be one. Oh, I hope I will get to be one.’
认为必须做的，才能成为圣人。我本以为我会成为圣人。我完全肯定我会成为。有那么一刻我以为自己就是圣人。我是那么高兴，觉得一切是那么简单和容易。早晨醒来时我还以为自己会是圣人，可我并不是。我从未成为过。我多么想成为一个。我的全部愿望就是成为圣人。这是我一直以来的唯一愿望。今天早晨我感觉我可能会成为一个。哦，我希望我能成为一个。”
‘You’ll be one. Everybody gets what they want. That’s what they always tell me.’
“你会成为的。每个人都会得到他们想要的。他们总是这样跟我说。”
‘I don’t know now. When I was a girl it seemed so simple. I knew I would be a saint. Only I believed it took time when I found it did not happen suddenly. Now it seems almost impossible.’
“我现在不知道了。小时候感觉很简单。我知道我会成圣。只是后来发现并非瞬间发生，才相信需要时间。现在看起来几乎不可能。”
‘I’d say you had a good chance.’
“我觉得你很有希望。”
‘Do you really think so? No, I don’t want just to be encouraged. Don’t just encourage me. I want to be a saint. I want to be a saint.’
“你真的这么认为？不，我不想只是被鼓励。别只是鼓励我。我想成为圣人。我想成为圣人。”
‘Of course you’ll be a saint,’ Mr. Frazer said.
“当然你会成圣的，”弗雷泽先生说。
‘No, probably I won’t be. But, oh, if I could only be a saint! I’d be perfectly happy.’
“不，可能不会。但，哦，要是我能成为圣人就好了！我会完全幸福的。”
‘You’re three to one to be a saint.’
“你成圣的几率是三比一。”
‘No, don’t encourage me. But, oh, if I could only be a saint! If I could only be a saint!’
“不，别鼓励我。但，哦，要是我能成为圣人就好了！要是我能成为圣人就好了！”
‘How’s your friend Cayetano?’
“你朋友凯亚塔诺怎么样了？”
‘He’s going to get well, but he’s paralysed. One of the bullets hit the big nerve that goes down through his thigh and that leg is paralysed. They only found it out when he got well enough so that he could move.’
“他会好起来的，可是瘫痪了。有一颗子弹打到了那条经过大腿的粗神经，腿就瘫痪了。只有等他好到可以动的时候才发现的。”
‘Maybe the nerve will regenerate.’
“也许那条神经会再生。”
‘I’m praying that it will,’ Sister Cecilia said. ‘You ought to see him.’
“我在祈祷会的，”塞西莉亚修女说。“你应该去看看他。”
‘I don’t feel like seeing anybody.’
“我不想见任何人。”
‘You know you’d like to see him. They could wheel him in here.’
“你知道你会想见他的。他们可以把他推到这里来。”
‘All right.’
“好吧。”
They wheeled him in, thin, his skin transparent, his hair black and needing to be cut, his eyes very laughing, his teeth bad when he smiled.
他们把他推进来，瘦削，皮肤透明，头发黑且该剪了，眼睛笑眯眯的，笑起来牙齿有点坏。
‘Hola, amigo ! Que tal?’
“Hola, amigo！Que tal？”
‘As you see,’ said Mr. Frazer. ‘And thou?’
“正如你所见，”弗雷泽先生说。“你呢？”
‘Alive and with the leg paralysed.’
“还活着，但那条腿瘫痪了。”
‘Bad,’ Mr. Frazer said. ‘But the nerve can regenerate and be as good as new.’
“糟糕，”弗雷泽先生说。“但神经可以再生，恢复如新。”
‘So they tell me.’
“他们是这么跟我说的。”
‘What about the pain?’
“那疼痛呢？”
'Not now. For a while I was crazy with it in the belly. I thought the pain alone would kill me."
“不现在。那会儿肚子疼得我快要发疯。我以为只有疼痛会把我杀了。”
Sister Cecilia was observing them happily.
塞西莉亚修女正愉快地看着他们。
‘She tells me you never made a sound,’ Mr. Frazer said.
“她告诉我你一点声音也没出过，”弗雷泽先生说。
‘So many people in the ward,’ the Mexican said deprecatingly. ‘What class of pain do you have?’
“病房里这么多人，”墨西哥人带着轻蔑地说。“你是什么级别的疼痛？”
‘Big enough. Clearly not as bad as yours. When the nurse goes out I cry an hour, two hours. It rests me. My nerves are bad now.’
“够大的。显然不如你的严重。护士出去的时候我会哭一小时，两小时。那能让我休息。我的神经现在不好。”
‘You have the radio. If I had a private room and a radio I would be crying and yelling all night long.’
“你有收音机。如果我有单人病房和收音机，我会整夜又哭又喊。”
‘I doubt it.’
“我怀疑。”
‘Hombre, si. It’s very healthy. But you cannot do it with so many people.’
“人，当然。那很健康。但你不能在这么多人面前做。”
‘At least,’ Mr. Frazer said, ‘the hands are still good. They tell me you make your living with the hands.’
“至少，”弗雷泽先生说，“手艺仍然好。他们告诉我你靠手艺谋生。”
‘And the head,’ he said, tapping his forehead. ‘But the head isn’t worth as much.’
“还有脑袋，”他敲了敲额头说。“但脑袋没那么值钱。”
‘Three of your countrymen were here.’
“你们国家的三个人来过这里。”
‘Sent by the police to see me.’
“是警察派来见我的。”
‘They brought some beer.’
“他们带来了一些啤酒。”
‘It probably was bad.’
“大概不太好喝。”
‘It was bad.’
“糟糕。”
‘To-night, sent by the police, they come to serenade me.’ He laughed, then tapped his stomach. ‘I cannot laugh yet. As musicians they are fatal.’
“今晚，他们被警察派来为我奏乐。”他笑了，然后拍了拍自己的胃。“我还不能笑。作为音乐家，他们可是致命的。”
‘And the one who shot you?’
“还有那个枪击你的人？”
‘Another fool. I won thirty-eight dollars from him at cards. That is not to kill about.’
“另一个傻瓜。我在牌局上赢了他三十八美元。为了这点不会去杀人的。”
‘The three told me you win much money.’
“他们三个告诉我你赢了很多钱。”
‘And am poorer than the birds.’
“而我比鸟儿还穷。”
‘How?’
“怎么会？”
‘I am a poor idealist. I am the victim of illusions.’ He laughed, then grinned and tapped his stomach. ‘I am a professional gambler but I like to gamble. To really gamble. Little gambling is all crooked. For real gambling you need luck. I have no luck.’
“我是个可怜的理想主义者。我是幻想的牺牲品。”他笑了，然后露出笑容，拍了拍他的胃。“我是个职业赌徒，但我喜欢赌博。真正地赌博。小赌全是作假。要真正赌博你需要运气。我没有运气。”

‘Never?’ ‘Never. I am completely without luck. Look, this cabron who shoots me just now. Can he shoot? No. The first shot he fires into nothing. The second is intercepted by a poor Russian. That would seem to be luck. What happens? He shoots me twice in the belly. He is a lucky man. I have no luck. He could not hit a horse if he were holding the stirrup. All luck.’ ‘I thought he shot you first and the Russian after.’ ‘No, the Russian first, me after. The paper was mistaken.’ ‘Why didn’t you shoot him?’ ‘I never carry a gun. With my luck, if I carried a gun I would be hanged ten times a year. I am a cheap card player, only that.’ He stopped, then continued. ‘When I make a sum of money I gamble and when I gamble I lose. I have passed at dice for three thousand dollars and crapped out for the six. With good dice. More than once.’ ‘Why continue?’ ‘If I live long enough the luck will change. I have bad luck now for fifteen years. If I ever get any good luck I will be rich.’ He grinned. ‘I am a good gambler, really I would enjoy being rich.’ ‘Do you have bad luck with all games?’ ‘With everything and with women.’ He smiled again, showing his bad teeth. ‘Truly?’ ‘Truly.’ ‘And what is there to do?’ ‘Continue, slowly, and wait for luck to change.’ ‘But with women?’ ‘No gambler has luck with women. He is too concentrated. He works nights. When he should be with the woman. No man who works nights can hold a woman if the woman is worth anything.’ ‘You are a philosopher.’ ‘No, hombre. A gambler of the small towns. One small town, then another, another, then a big town, then start over again.’ “Then shot in the belly.” ‘The first time,’ he said. ‘That has only happened once.’ ‘I tire you talking?’ Mr. Frazer suggested. ‘No,’ he said. ‘I must tire you.’ ‘And the leg?’
“从不？” “从不。我完全没有运气。你看，刚才这个杀了我的 cabron。他会射击吗？不会。他的第一枪对着空气打。第二枪被一个可怜的俄国人拦截了。那似乎应该算是运气。结果怎么样？他朝我肚子上连开两枪。他是个幸运的人。我没有运气。他就算抓着马镫也打不中马。都是运气。” “我以为他先打你，后来打了俄国人。” “不，先是俄国人，然后是我。报纸弄错了。” “你为什么不射他？” “我从不带枪。以我的运气，要是带了枪，我一年得被绞十次。我只是个糟糕的赌徒，仅此而已。” 他停了一下，又接着说：“我有了钱就去赌博，赌博就输钱。我在色子上赢过三千美元，也在六点上滚了个空。用的是好骰子。不止一次。” “为什么还要继续？” “如果我活得够久，运气会变的。我现在已经厄运缠身十五年了。如果哪天我有了好运，我会变得富有。” 他咧嘴笑了笑，“我其实是个不错的赌徒，真的会喜欢成为有钱人。” “你在所有游戏上都倒霉吗？” “所有事，连女人也一样。” 他又笑了，露出那副坏牙。 “真的吗？” “真的。”“‘那有什么可做的？’ ‘继续，慢慢来，等运气好转。’ ‘但和女人呢？’ ‘没有赌徒会在女人那儿走运。他太专注。晚上工作。该陪女人的时候不在。任何夜间工作的人，如果那个女人有价值，是留不住她的。’ ‘你是哲学家。’ ‘不，hombre（朋友）。小镇的赌徒。一个小镇，然后另一个，再一个，然后是大城，再从头开始。’ “然后中腹部一枪。” ‘第一次，’他说。‘那只发生过一次。’ ‘我说话把你说烦了吗？’弗雷泽先生提议道。 ‘不，’他说。‘应该是我把你说烦了。’ ‘那条腿呢？’

‘I have no great use for the leg. I am all right with the leg or not. I will be able to circulate.’
‘那条腿我用处不大。有了腿或没腿我都行。我还能活动。’
‘I wish you luck, truly, and with all my heart,’ Mr. Frazer said.
‘我真心祝你好运，衷心的，’弗雷泽先生说。
‘Equally,’ he said. ‘And that the pain stops.’
“同样，”他说。“而且痛苦会停止。”
‘It will not last, certainly. It is passing. It is of no importance.’
“这不会持续，很快就会过去。无关紧要。”
‘That it passes quickly.’
“希望它快点过去。”
‘Equally.’
“同样。”
That night the Mexicans played the accordion and other instruments in the ward and it was cheerful and the noise of the inhalations and exhalations of the accordion, and of the bells, the traps and the drum came down the corridor. In that ward there was a rodeo rider who had come out of the chutes on Midnight on a hot dusty afternoon with the big crowd watching, and now, with a broken back, was going to learn to work in leather and to cane chairs when he got well enough to leave the hospital. There was a carpenter who had fallen with a scaffolding and broken both ankles and both wrists. He had lit like a cat but without a cat’s resiliency. They could fix him up so that he could work again but it would take a long time. There was a boy from a farm, about sixteen years old, with a broken leg that had been badly set and was to be rebroken. There was Cayetano Ruiz, a small-town gambler with a paralysed leg. Down the corridor Mr. Frazer could hear them all laughing and merry with the music made by the Mexicans who had been sent by the police. The Mexicans were having a good time. They came in, very excited, to see Mr. Frazer and wanted to know if there was anything he wanted them to play, and they came twice more to play at night of their own accord.
那天晚上墨西哥人在病房里拉起了手风琴和其他乐器，显得很欢快，手风琴的吸气与呼气声、铃铛声、小鼓声和陷阱声沿着走廊传来。在那个病房里有一个牛仔表演骑手，他在一个炎热多尘的下午从闸口骑着名叫 Midnight 的马摔了下来，当时有一大群人在观看，而现在他背部断了，康复后要学做皮具和编藤椅，以便出院后能工作。还有一个木匠，从脚手架上摔下来，双脚踝和双手腕都断了。他落地像猫一样，但没有猫的弹性。可以把他修理好，让他还能工作，但要花很长时间。还有一个来自农场的少年，约十六岁，腿摔断且骨折对位不良，要重新敲断再复位。还有 Cayetano Ruiz，一个小镇赌徒，腿瘫痪了。弗雷泽先生在走廊尽头能听到他们在墨西哥人伴奏下的笑声与欢闹，那些墨西哥人是警察派来的。他们玩得很高兴，兴奋地进来看弗雷泽先生。 弗雷泽想知道他们是否想让他点什么曲子，他们又两次自发地在夜里来演奏。
The last time they played Mr. Frazer lay in his room with the door open and listened to the noisy, bad music and could not keep from thinking. When they wanted to know what he wished played, he asked for the ‘Cucaracha’, which has the sinister lightness and deftness of so many of the tunes men have gone to die to. They played noisily and with emotion. The tune was better than most of such tunes, to Mr. Frazer’s mind, but the effect was all the same.
最后一次他们演奏时，弗雷泽先生躺在打开门的房间里，听着喧闹粗糙的音乐，忍不住思绪万千。当他们问他想听什么曲子时，他要了《Cucaracha》，那曲子带有一种险恶的轻快和机敏，像许多曾经让人赴死的曲调。 他们又喧闹又激动地演奏着。 在弗雷泽先生看来，这旋律比大多数类似的曲子都要好，但效果却完全一样。
In spite of this introduction of emotion, Mr. Frazer went on thinking. Usually he avoided thinking all he could, except when he was writing, but now he was thinking about those who were playing and what the little one had said.
尽管这种情感被引入，弗雷泽先生仍继续沉思。 通常他尽可能避免思考，除非在写作时，但现在他在想那些演奏的人以及小个子说的话。
Religion is the opium of the people. He believed that, that dyspeptic little joint-keeper. Yes, and music is the opium of the people. Old mount-to-the-head hadn’t thought of that. And now economics is the opium of the people; along with patriotism the opium of the people in Italy and Germany. What about sexual intercourse; was that an opium of the people? Of some of the people. Of some of the best of the people. But drink was a sovereign opium of the people, oh, an excellent opium. Although some prefer the radio, another opium of the people, a cheap one he had just been using. Along with these went gambling, an opium of the people if there ever was one, one of the oldest. Ambition was another, an opium of the people, along with a belief in any new form of government. What you wanted was the minimum of government, always less government. Liberty, what we believed in, now the name of a MacFadden publication. We believed in that although they had not found a new name for it yet. But what was the real one? What was the real, the actual, opium of the people? He knew it very well. It was gone just a little way around the corner in that well-lighted part of his mind that was there after two or more drinks in the evening; that he knew was there (it was not really there of course). What was it? He knew very well. What was it? Of course; bread was the opium of the people. Would he remember that and would it make sense in the daylight? Bread is the opium of the people.
宗教是人民的鸦片。他相信这一点，那位消化不良的小关节保管员。是的，音乐也是人民的鸦片。把山扛到头顶的老家伙以前没想到这一点。现在经济学是人民的鸦片；在意大利和德国，连同爱国主义也是人民的鸦片。性交怎么样；那也是人民的鸦片吗？对某些人来说是。对某些最优秀的人来说是。但酒是人民的至尊鸦片，哦，一种极好的鸦片。虽然有人更喜欢收音机，另一种人民的鸦片，一种便宜的，他刚才一直在用。和这些一起的还有赌博，如果说有哪样是人民的鸦片的话，赌博就是其中之一，是最古老的之一。野心也是一种，人民的鸦片，连同对任何新型政府的信仰。你想要的是最少的政府，永远是更少的政府。自由，我们所信仰的东西，现在成了 MacFadden 某刊物的名称。我们信仰它，尽管他们还没为它找到一个新名字。但真正的是什么？真正的、实际的人民的鸦片是什么？他非常清楚。 它就消失在他心里那个在晚上喝两杯或更多酒后会出现的、光线很好的一角，那个他知道会存在的地方（当然它并不真正存在）。那是什么？他非常清楚。那是什么？当然；面包是人民的鸦片。他会记得这句话吗，白天看它是否有意义？面包是人民的鸦片。
‘Listen,’ Mr. Frazer said to the nurse when she came. ‘Get that little thin Mexican in here, will you, please?’
“听着，”弗雷泽先生在护士来时对她说。“把那个瘦小的墨西哥人叫进来，好吗，拜托？”
‘How do you like it?’ the Mexican said at the door.
“你觉得如何？”门口的墨西哥人说。
‘Very much.’
“非常喜欢。”
‘It is a historic tune,’ the Mexican said. ‘It is the tune of the real revolution.’
“这是首有纪念意义的曲子，”那位墨西哥人说。“这是一次真正革命的曲调。”
‘Listen,’ said Mr. Frazer. ‘Why should the people be operated on without an anaesthetic?’
“听着，”弗雷泽先生说。“为什么要在不打麻药的情况下给人民做手术呢？”
‘I do not understand.’
“我不明白。”
‘Why are not all the opiums of the people good? What do you want to do with the people?’
“为什么人民的所有鸦片都不好？你想对人民做什么？”
‘They should be rescued from ignorance.’
“他们应该从无知中被拯救出来。”
‘Don’t talk nonsense. Education is an opium of the people. You ought to know that. You’ve had a little.’
“别胡说。教育是人民的鸦片。你应该知道的。你也受过一点教育。”
‘You do not believe in education?’
“你不相信教育？”
‘No,’ said Mr. Frazer. ‘In knowledge, yes.’
“不，”弗雷泽先生说，“相信知识。”
‘I do not follow you.’
“我不明白你的意思。”
‘Many times I do not follow myself with pleasure.’
“很多时候我自己也不太愿意跟随我自己。”
‘You want to hear the “Cucaracha” another time?’ asked the Mexican worriedly.
“您想再听一次《Cucaracha》吗？”墨西哥人担心地问。
‘Yes,’ said Mr. Frazer. ‘Play the “Cucaracha” another time. It’s better than the radio.’
“想，”弗雷泽先生说。“再放一次《Cucaracha》。比收音机好。”
Revolution, Mr. Frazer thought, is no opium. Revolution is a catharsis; an ecstasy which can only be prolonged by tyranny. The opiums are for before and for after. He was thinking well, a little too well.
弗雷泽先生想，革命不是鸦片。革命是一种宣泄；一种只能通过暴政来延长的狂喜。鸦片是用在之前和之后的。他想得好，甚至有些想得过头了。
They would go now in a little while, he thought, and they would take the ‘Cucaracha’ with them. Then he would have a little spot of the giant killer and play the radio, you could play the radio so that you could hardly hear it.
他想，他们一会儿就会走，而且会带上“Cucaracha”。然后他会喝一点那种杀手酒，播放收音机，你可以把收音机开得几乎听不见。

FATHERS AND SONS
父与子

There had been a sign to detour in the centre of the main street of this town, but cars had obviously gone through, so, believing it was some repair which had been completed, Nicholas Adams drove on through the town along the empty, brick-paved street, stopped by traffic lights that flashed on and off on this traffic-less Sunday, and would be gone next year when the payments on the system were not met; on under the heavy trees of the small town that are a part of your heart if it is your town and you have walked under them, but that are only too heavy, that shut out the sun and that dampen the houses for a stranger; out past the last house and on to the highway that rose and fell straight away ahead with banks of red dirt sliced cleanly away and the second-growth timber on both sides. It was not his country but it was the middle of fall and all of this country was good to drive through and to see. The cotton was picked and in the clearings there were patches of corn, some cut with streaks of red sorghum, and, driving easily, his son asleep on the seat by his side, the day’s run made, knowing the town he would reach for the night, Nick noticed which cornfields had soy beans or peas in them, how the thickets and the cut-over land lay, where the cabins and houses were in relation to the fields and the thickets; hunting the country in his mind as he went by; sizing up each clearing as to feed and cover and figuring where you would find a covey and which way they would fly.
镇上主街中央本来竖着一块绕行标志，但显然有车辆从那儿开过去了，所以尼古拉斯·亚当斯以为那只是已修完的工事，便沿着空荡的砖铺街继续开过小镇。红绿灯在这个没有车流的星期日闪着又灭着；当系统的付款不到位时这些灯明年就会被撤掉；车子穿过小镇那沉重的树荫——如果那是你的故乡而你曾在树下行走，那么这些树就是你心的一部分；但对外乡人来说，它们只是过于阴沉，遮蔽了阳光，使房屋潮湿；出了最后一座房子，便驶上了公路，公路在前方坡起又降下，两旁是被整齐剖去的红土坡和二次生林。这不是他的故乡，但正值深秋，开车穿行其间，所见皆令人心旷神怡。 棉花已摘完，空地上有玉米田，有的夹着一条条红高粱的痕迹，开车轻松，他儿子靠在旁边的座位上睡着了，当天的行程已完成，心里知道夜里会到哪个城镇。Nick 注意到哪些玉米地里种了大豆或豌豆，疏林和砍伐过的地块怎样分布，木屋和房子相对于田地和疏林的位置；一边走一边在脑海里勘察着这片乡间；估量每块空地的饲料和掩蔽情况，算出哪里会有一群雉，雉会向哪个方向飞去。
In shooting quail you must not get between them and their habitual cover, once the dogs have found them, or when they flush they will come pouring at you, some rising steep, some skimming by your ears, whirring into a size you have never seen them in the air as they pass, the only way being to turn and take them over your shoulder as they go, before they set their wings and angle down into the thicket. Hunting this country for quail as his father taught him, Nicholas Adams started thinking about his father. When he first thought about him it was always the eyes. The big frame, the quick movements, the wide shoulders, the hooked, hawk nose, the beard
打鹌鹑时，一旦猎犬把它们找到了，就不要站在它们和它们常去的掩蔽处之间；一旦它们起飞就会向你扑来，有的直上高飞，有的掠过你的耳旁，掠过时在空中发出你从未见过的振翅声，它们只有一种应对办法：在它们振翅并斜俯进灌丛之前，转身在肩头上迎下它们。像他父亲教他的那样在这片地里打鹌鹑时，尼古拉斯·亚当斯开始想着他父亲。刚开始想起他父亲时，首先总是想到那双眼睛。那副大体格、敏捷的动作、宽阔的肩膀、弯钩般的鹰钩鼻、胡子
that covered the weak chin, you never thought about - it was always the eyes. They were protected in his head by the formation of the brows; set deep as though a special protection had been devised for some very valuable instrument. They saw much farther and much quicker than the human eye sees and they were the great gift his father had. His father saw as a big-horn ram or as an eagle sees, literally.
遮住软下颌的东西你从不去想——你总是想着那双眼睛。它们在他头部被眉骨的结构所保护；深深地陷着，仿佛为某件非常珍贵的器官设计了特别的防护。它们看得远且快，远比人眼看得远、看得快，这是他从父亲那里继承来的伟大天赋。他的父亲看东西就像大角羊或雄鹰那样，确实如此。
He would be standing with his father on one shore of the lake, his own eyes were very good then, and his father would say, ‘They’ve run up the flag.’ Nick could not see the flag or the flag pole. ‘There,’ his father would say, ‘it’s your sister Dorothy. She’s got the flag up and she’s walking out on to the dock.’
他会和父亲站在湖的一岸，那时他的视力很好，父亲会说：“他们把旗子升上去了。”Nick 看不见旗子或旗杆。“在那里，”父亲会说，“是你妹妹 Dorothy。她把旗子升起来了，正走到码头上去。”
Nick would look across the lake and he could see the long wooded shore-line, the higher timber behind, the point that guarded the bay, the clear hills of the farm and the white of their cottage in the trees, but he could not see any flag pole, or any dock, only the white of the beach and the curve of the shore.
Nick 会望向湖对岸，能看见那长长的林木海岸线、后面的高地林木、守护海湾的岬角、农场的清晰山丘以及树林中他们小屋的白色，但他看不见任何旗杆或任何码头，只看见海滩的白色和海岸的弧线。
‘Can you see the sheep on the hillside toward the point?’
“你能看到朝岬角那边山坡上的羊吗？”
‘Yes.’
“能。”
They were a whitish patch on the grey-green of the hill.
它们在灰绿色的山上是一片发白的斑块。
‘I can count them,’ his father said.
“我能数清它们，”他父亲说。
Like all men with a faculty that surpasses human requirements, his father was very nervous. Then, too, he was sentimental, and, like most sentimental people, he was both cruel and abused. Also, he had much bad luck, and it was not all of it his own. He had died in a trap that he had helped only a little to set, and they had all betrayed him in their various ways before he died. All sentimental people are betrayed so many times. Nick could not write about him yet, although he would, later, but the quail country made him remember him as he was when Nick was a boy and he was very grateful to him for two things: fishing and shooting. His father was as sound on those two things as he was unsound on sex, for instance, and Nick was glad that it had been that way; for someone has to give you your first gun or the opportunity to get it and use it, and you have to live where there is game or fish if you are to learn about them, and now, at thirty-eight, he loved to fish and to shoot exactly as much as when he first had gone with his father. It was a passion that had never slackened and he was very grateful to his father for bringing him to know it.
像所有拥有超出人类所需才能的男人一样，他的父亲非常紧张。再者，他多愁善感，而像大多数多愁善感的人一样，他既残酷又遭受虐待。另外，他很不走运，而且这并非全是他的错。他死在了一个他只帮了点忙设置的陷阱里，而且在他死之前，他们都以各自的方式背叛了他。所有多愁善感的人都被背叛过那么多次。尼克还不能写他的事，尽管他后来会写，但鹌鹑猎场让他记起了小时候的父亲，他非常感激父亲给了他两样东西：钓鱼和射击。他父亲在这两样事上与在性方面的不健全形成鲜明对比，尼克很高兴事情是这样；因为总得有人把你的第一把枪交给你，或给你得到并使用它的机会，你还得住在有猎物或鱼的地方，才能学会这些东西，而现在，到了三十八岁，他对钓鱼和射击的热爱和刚跟父亲去时一模一样。这是一种从未减弱的激情，他非常感激父亲让他认识到这一点。
While for the other, that his father was not sound about, all the equipment you will ever have is provided and each man learns all there is for him to know about it without advice; and it makes no difference where you live. He remembered very clearly the only two pieces of information his father had given him about that. Once when they were out shooting together Nick shot a red squirrel out of a hemlock tree. The squirrel fell, wounded, and when Nick picked him up bit the boy clean through the ball of the thumb.
而对于另一个，也就是他父亲对其不放心的那种人，所有你将拥有的装备都已备齐，每个人都在没有建议的情况下学会了该知道的一切；住在哪里并不重要。他清楚地记得父亲给他的仅有的两条关于那件事的信息。一次他们一起去打猎，Nick 把一只红松鼠从一棵铁杉树上打了下来。松鼠掉下来了，受了伤，当 Nick 把它捡起时，咬破了男孩的大拇指掌垫。
‘The dirty little bugger,’ Nick said and smacked the squirrel’s head against the tree. ‘Look how he bit me.’
“这该死的小家伙，”Nick 说着把松鼠的头朝树砸去。“看它咬的多深。”
His father looked and said, ‘Suck it out clean and put some iodine on when you get home.’
他父亲看了看说：“把脏东西吸干净，回家后擦点碘酒。”
‘The little bugger,’ Nick said.
“这小家伙，”Nick 说。
‘Do you know what a bugger is?’ his father asked him.
“你知道什么是兽交者吗？”他父亲问他。
‘We call anything a bugger,’ Nick said.
“我们什么都可以叫兽交者，”尼克说。
‘A bugger is a man who has intercourse with animals.’
“兽交者就是与动物发生性关系的人。”
‘Why?’ Nick said.
“为什么？”尼克说。
‘I don’t know,’ his father said. ‘But it is a heinous crime.’
“我不知道，”他父亲说。“但那是可憎的罪行。”
Nick’s imagination was both stirred and horrified by this and he thought of various animals but none seemed attractive or practical and that was the sum total of direct sexual knowledge bequeathed him by his father except on one other subject. One morning he read in the paper that Enrico Caruso had been arrested for mashing.
尼克的想象力因此既被激发又感到震惊，他想到了各种动物，但没有哪一种显得有吸引力或实际可行，而这就是他父亲留给他的全部直接性知识的总和，除了另一个话题。有一天早晨，他从报纸上读到恩里科·卡鲁索因“mashing”被捕。
‘What is mashing?’
“什么是 mashing？”
‘It is one of the most heinous of crimes,’ his father answered. Nick’s imagination pictured the great tenor doing something strange, bizarre and heinous with a potato masher to a beautiful lady who looked like the pictures of Anna Held on the inside of cigar boxes. He resolved, with considerable horror, that when he was old enough he would try mashing at least once.
“那是最可憎的罪行之一，”他父亲回答。尼克的想象把这位伟大的男高音描绘成用土豆捣碎器对一位像雪茄盒内侧印的安娜·赫尔德照片那样美丽的女士做出奇怪、古怪且可憎的事情。他震惊地决定，等自己够大了，至少要尝试一次 mashing。
His father had summed up the whole matter by stating that masturbation produced blindness, insanity and death, while a man who went with prostitutes would contract hideous venereal diseases and that the thing to do was to keep your hands off of people. On the other hand his father had the finest pair of eyes he had ever seen and Nick had loved him very much and for a long time. Now, knowing how it had all been, even remembering the earliest times before things had gone badly was not good remembering. If he
他父亲把这事归结为：手淫会导致失明、发疯和死亡；而与妓女发生关系则会染上可怕的性病；因此应当别碰别人。另一方面，他父亲有一双他见过的最好的眼睛，尼克曾经非常、很长时间地爱着他。现在，知道了一切之后，甚至连在事情变坏之前的早期记忆也不能算是美好的回忆。如果他
wrote it he could get rid of it. He had gotten rid of many things by writing them. But it was still too early for that. There were still too many people. So he decided to think of something else. There was nothing to do about his father and he had thought it all through many times. The handsome job the undertaker had done on his father’s face had not blurred in his mind and all the rest of it was quite clear, including the responsibilities. He had complimented the undertaker. The undertaker had been both proud and smugly pleased. But it was not the undertaker that had given him that last face. The undertaker had only made certain dashingly executed repairs of doubtful artistic merit. The face had been making itself and being made for a long time. It had modelled fast in the last three years. It was a good story but there were still too many people alive for him to write it.
他写出来就能摆脱它。他通过写作摆脱过许多东西。但现在写还为时过早。活着的人太多了。所以他决定去想别的事。他对父亲无能为力，这事他已经想透了许多遍。殡葬承办人在他父亲脸上做的那番精致处理并没有在他脑海中模糊，其余的也都很清楚，包括那些责任。他称赞了殡葬承办人。殡葬承办人既自豪又得意洋洋。但把父亲最后那张面容赋予他的人并不是殡葬承办人。殡葬承办人只做了若干看似潇洒但艺术价值可疑的修补。那张脸早已在形成并被塑造。过去三年里它迅速成形。那是个好故事，但活着的人仍然太多，他写不下去。
Nick’s own education in those earlier matters had been acquired in the hemlock woods behind the Indian camp. This was reached by a trail which ran from the cottage through the woods to the farm and then by a road which wound through the slashings to the camp. Now if he could feel all of that trail with bare feet. First there was the pine-needle loam through the hemlock woods behind the cottage where the fallen logs crumbled into wood dust and long splintered pieces of wood hung like javelins in the trees that had been struck by lightning. You crossed the creek on a log and if you stepped off there was the black muck of the swamp. You climbed a fence out of the woods and the trail was hard in the sun across the field with cropped grass and sheep sorrel and mullen growing and to the left the quaky bog of the creek bottom where the killdeer plover fed. The spring house was in that creek. Below the barn there was fresh warm manure and the other old manure was caked dry on top. Then there was another fence and the hard, hot trail from the barn to the house and the hot sandy road that ran down to the woods, crossing the creek, on a bridge this time, where the cat-tails grew that you soaked in kerosene to make jacklights with for spearing fish at night.
尼克早年在这些事情上的学习，是在印第安人营地后面的铁杉林里获得的。那儿有一条小路，从小屋穿过树林到农场，然后沿着一条穿过伐木地蜿蜒的路到营地。现在如果他能用赤脚感受整条小路。先是小屋后面铁杉林中的松针腐土，倒下的原木化为木屑，长长的碎木片像标枪一样挂在被闪电击中的树上。你要走过小溪要踩在一根原木上，一旦你踏下去就是沼泽的黑泥。你从树林里翻过一段栅栏，阳光下小路在田地里坚硬，草被剪短，生着酸模和毛茛，左侧是小溪底的颤抖沼泽，杀鸻在那儿觅食。泉水房就在那条小溪里。谷仓下面有新鲜温热的粪堆，旧粪堆则干硬地结在上面。 然后又有一道篱笆，从谷仓到房子的那条又硬又热的小径，还有那条通向树林的炎热沙土路，过溪时这次有座桥，桥边长着用来浸煤油做夜间刺鱼用的照明火把的蒲草。
Then the main road went off to the left, skirting the woods and climbing the hill, while you went into the woods on the wide clay and shale road, cool under the trees, and broadened for them to skid out the hemlock bark the Indians cut. Now, as he rode along the highway in the car and it was getting dark, Nick was all through thinking about his father. The end of the day never made him think of him. The end of the day had always belonged to Nick alone and he never felt right unless he was alone at it. His father came back to him in the fall of the year, or in
现在，当他坐在车里沿着公路行驶，天色渐暗，尼克已经完全不去想他的父亲了。一天的结束从来不会让他想起父亲。一天的结束一直只属于尼克自己，除非独自度过，否则他总感觉不对。父亲在秋天或在...
the early spring when there had been jacksnipe on the prairie, or when he saw shocks of corn, or when he saw a lake, or if he ever saw a horse and buggy, or when he saw, or heard, wild geese, or in a duck blind; remembering the time an eagle dropped through the whirling snow to strike a canvas-covered decoy, rising, his wings beating, the talons caught in the canvas. His father was with him, suddenly, in deserted orchards and in new-ploughed fields, in thickets, on small hills, or when going through dead grass, whenever splitting wood or hauling water, by grist mills, cider milis and dams and always with open fires. The towns he lived in were not towns his father knew. After he was fifteen he had shared nothing with him.
早春时分草原上有斑尾画眉鸟的时候，或他看到玉米秆的时候，或看到湖泊的时候，或看到马车的时候，或听到或看到野雁的时候，或在鸭盲时；记得有一次一只鹰在旋转的雪中俯冲，击中一个覆盖着帆布的诱饵，起飞时翅膀拍动，爪子被帆布钩住。他的父亲在那些时刻突然出现在他身边：在荒废的果园里和新犁过的田地上，在灌木丛中、在小山岗上，或穿过枯草时，在劈柴或打水的时候，在磨坊、苹果酒厂和水坝旁，而且总是有露天篝火。他生活过的城镇不是他父亲所熟悉的城镇。十五岁以后，他与父亲再无共享。
His father had frost in his beard in cold weather and in hot weather he sweated very much. He liked to work in the sun on the farm because he did not have to and he loved manual work, which Nick did not. Nick loved his father but hated the smell of him and once when he had to wear a suit of his father’s underwear that had gotten too small for his father it made him feel sick and he took it off and put it under two stones in the creek and said that he had lost it. He had told his father how it was when his father had made him put it on but his father had said it was freshly washed. It had been, too. When Nick had asked him to smell of it his Father sniffect at it indignantly and said that it was clean and fresh. When Nick came home from fishing without it and said he lost it he was whipped for lying.
他父亲在冷天胡子上有霜，在热天汗流浃背。他喜欢在农场的太阳下干活，因为他不必（做别的事），而且他喜欢体力活，Nick 不喜欢。Nick 爱他的父亲，但讨厌他的气味。有一次当他不得不穿上一件已经对他父亲来说太小的父亲的内衣时，他感到恶心，就脱下来放在溪里的两块石头下面，并说自己丢了。他曾把实情告诉父亲，当时父亲让他穿上，但父亲说那是刚洗过的。确实是刚洗过的。当 Nick 让父亲闻闻时，父亲愤然嗤了一声，说那是干净新鲜的。Nick 从钓鱼回家不见那件内衣并说丢了，就因为撒谎挨了打。
Afterwards he had sat inside the woodshed with the door open, his shotgun loaded and cocked, looking across at his father sitting on the screen porch reading the paper, and thought, ‘I can blow him to hell. I can kill him.’ Finally he felt his anger go out of him and he felt a little sick about it being the gun that his father had given him. Then he had gone to the Indian camp, walking there in the dark, to get rid of the smell. There was only one person in his family that he liked the smell of; one sister. All the others he avoided all contact with. That sense blunted when he started to smoke. It was a good thing. It was good for a bird dog but it did not help a man.
之后他坐在柴棚里，门开着，猎枪上膛并扳着枪机，望着坐在带纱窗的门廊上看报的父亲，心想：“我可以把他炸成碎片。我可以杀了他。”最后他感觉怒气从身上散去了，对那把是父亲给他的枪感到有点恶心。然后他走到印第安人营地，天黑着走去，为了摆脱那股气味。他家里只有一个人他喜欢她的气味；一个妹妹。其他所有人他都避而不接触。开始抽烟后那种感觉变得迟钝了。这是件好事。对猎鸟犬有好处，但对人没什么帮助。

男孩醒着。他看着坐在他旁边的男孩。他本以为自己很孤单，但这个男孩一直陪着他。他想知道有多久了。“我们过去整天出门打黑松鼠，”他说。“我父亲每天只给我三发子弹，因为他说那样能教会我打猎，而且男孩子到处乱敲打枪不是什么好事。我跟一个叫比利·吉尔比的男孩和他妹妹特鲁迪一起去。我们差不多整个夏天几乎每天都去。”

‘It’s hard to say,’ Nick Adams said. Could you say she did first what no one has ever done better and mention plump brown legs, flat belly, hard little breasts, well holding arms, quick searching tongue, the flat eyes, the good taste of mouth, then uncomfortably, tightly, sweetly, moistly, lovely, tightly, achingly, fully, finally, unendingly, never-endingly, never-to-endingly, suddenly ended, the great bird flown like an owl in the twilight, only in daylight in the woods and hemlock needles stuck against your belly. So that when you go in a place where Indians have lived you smell them gone and all the empty pain killer bottles and the flies that buzz do not kill the sweetgrass smell, the smoke smell and that other like a fresh cased marten skin. Nor any jokes about them nor old squaws take that away. Nor the sick sweet smell they get to have. Nor what they did finally. It wasn’t how they ended. They all ended the same. Long time ago good. Now no good.
“很难说，”尼克·亚当斯说。能不能说她先做了没有人做得更好的事，然后提到丰满的褐色腿、平坦的腹部、坚实的小胸、支撑有力的手臂、敏捷探寻的舌头、平静的眼睛、口中的好味道；接着不自在地、紧贴地、甜美地、湿润地、可爱地、紧密地、痛楚般地、完全地、终于地、无尽地、永无止境地、永不结束地、突然结束了，那只大鸟像暮色中的猫头鹰一样飞走了，只在白昼的树林里，铁杉针刺在你的腹上。所以当你走进印第安人曾经居住的地方，你会闻到他们离去的气息，所有空的止痛药瓶和嗡嗡作响的苍蝇也带不走甜草的气味、烟熏的味道和那另一种像新剥的貂皮的味道。也没有任何关于他们的笑话，也没有年老的老婆子能把这些带走。也没有他们那种病态的甜味能被带走。也没有他们最终所做之事。并不是他们如何结束。他们都以同样的方式结束。很久以前是好的。现在不行了。
And about the other. When you have shot one bird flying you have shot all birds flying. They are all different and they fly in different ways but the sensation is the same and the last one is as good as the first. He could thank his father for that.
至于另一种。当你打下一只飞鸟时，你就打下了所有的飞鸟。它们各不相同，飞行方式也不同，但那种感觉是相同的，最后一只和第一只是一样好的。他可以为此感谢他的父亲。

“如果我看你小心谨慎的话，十二岁。”
‘I wish I was twelve now.’
‘我要是现在十二岁该多好。’
‘You will be, soon enough.’
‘你很快就会了。’
‘What was my grandfather like? I can’t remember him except that he gave me an air rifle and an American flag when I came over from France that time. What was he like?’
‘我祖父是个什么样的人？我记不得他了，只记得那次我从法国回来的时候他送了我一把气步枪和一面美国国旗。他是个什么样的人？’
‘He’s hard to describe. He was a great hunter and fisherman and he had wonderful eyes.’
‘他很难形容。他是个出色的猎人和渔夫，而且他有一双很棒的眼睛。’
‘Was he greater than you?’
“他比你更厉害吗？”
‘He was a much better shot and his father was a great wing shot too.’
“他射击准很多，他父亲也是个了不起的飞鸟射手。”
‘I’ll bet he wasn’t better than you.’
“我敢打赌，他不比你强。”
‘Oh, yes he was. He shot very quickly and beautifully. I’d rather see him shoot than any man I ever knew. He was alwavs very disappointed in the way I shot.’
“哦，是的，他比我强。他射得又快又漂亮。我宁愿看他射击，也不愿看我认识的任何人射。他总是对我射击的方式很失望。”
‘Why do we never go to pray at the tomb of my grandfather?’
“我们为什么从不去我祖父的墓前祈祷？”
‘We live in a different part of the country. It’s a long way from here.’
“我们住在国家的另一边。离这儿很远。”
‘In France that wouldn’t make any difference. In France we’d go. I think I ought to go to pray at the tomb of my grandfather.’
“在法国那就不一样了。在法国我们会去。我想我应该去祖父的墓前祈祷。”
‘Some time we’ll go.’
“改天我们会去的。”
‘I hope we won’t live somewhere so that I can never go to pray at your tomb when you are dead.’
“我希望我们别住到那种地方去，否则你死后我就没法去你的坟前祈祷了。”
‘We’ll have to arrange it.’
“我们得把这事安排好。”
‘Don’t you think we might all be buried at a convenient place? We could all be buried in France. That would be fine.’
“你不觉得我们可以都埋在一个方便的地方吗？我们都可以埋在法国。那样挺好。”
‘I don’t want to be buried in France,’ Nick said.
“我不想埋在法国，”Nick 说。
‘Well, then, we’ll have to get some convenient place in America. Couldn’t we all be buried out at the ranch?’
“那好吧，我们得在美国找个方便的地方葬，到农场里不能都埋了吗？”
‘That’s an idea.’
“这是个主意。”
‘Then I could stop and pray at the tomb of my grandfather on the way to the ranch.’
“那我去农场的路上就可以顺便在我祖父的墓前祈祷了。”
‘You’re awfully practical.’
“你真实用。”
‘Well, I don’t feel good never to have even visited the tomb of my grandfather.’
“嗯，我总感觉不好，居然连我祖父的坟墓也没去过。”
‘We’ll have to go,’ Nick said. ‘I can see we’ll have to go.’
“我们得去，”尼克说。“我看我们得去。”

海明威，欧内斯特，1899–1961。
The first forty-nine storie 51
《前四十九篇故事》51
  1. His father looked down at him.
    他的父亲低头看着他。
    ‘All right. Come on, then,’ his father said. ‘Give me the book, I’ll put it in my pocket.’
    “好吧，那就来吧，”他的父亲说。“把书给我，我把它放进口袋里。”
    ‘I know where there’s black squirrels, Daddy,’ Nick said.
    “爸爸，我知道哪里有黑色的松鼠，”尼克说。
    ‘All right,’ said his father. ‘Let’s go there.’
    “好吧，”他的父亲说。“我们去那里。”
  2. ‘Maybe not to you,’ said Doctor Wilcox.
    “也许你去不了，”威尔科克斯医生说。
    ‘You hear him, Horace?’ Doc Fischer said. ‘You hear him? Having discovered my vulnerable, point, my achilles tendon, so to speak, the doctor pursues his advantage.’
    “你听见他说什么了吗，霍勒斯？”费舍尔医生说。“听见了吗？他发现了我的弱点，可以说是我的阿喀琉斯腱，医生就乘机追赶。”
    ‘You’re too damned smart,’ Doctor Wilcox said.
    “你聪明过头了，”威尔考克斯医生说。
